reviewed_competitors.title: Concept Component Analysis: A Principled Approach for Concept Extraction in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior unsupervised linear-unmixing method for LLM activations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sparse ConCA derives a linear-mixture view of LLM representations from a latent-variable model of concept log-posteriors and evaluates twelve sparse unmixing variants. ICA Lens instead applies classical non-Gaussian FastICA without ConCA's concept-posterior derivation, but contributes a more complete layer-wise fitting, browsing, human-audit, probing, and intervention workflow.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering Universal Geometry in Embeddings with ICA
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yamagiwa et al. already use ICA to expose interpretable semantic axes in pretrained word and image embeddings and compare their alignment across languages, algorithms, and modalities. ICA Lens extends ICA from static embeddings to contextual residual streams, adds LLM-specific convergence engineering, and evaluates supervised feature utility, so its novelty is the practical LLM-activation workflow rather than interpretable ICA axes per se.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploring Interpretability of Independent Components of Word Embeddings with Automated Word Intruder Test
reviewed_competitors.relationship: prior human and automated audit of ICA components
reviewed_competitors.difference: Musil and Marecek quantify ICA word-embedding interpretability with both human and LLM word-intruder tests and show component combinations support lexical retrieval. ICA Lens evaluates contextual LLM states and richer prompt/ERF/SAEBench evidence, but is not the first systematic human-facing evaluation of ICA-derived language representations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Higher-Order Correlations Among Semantic Components in Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct negative evidence on the independence interpretation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Oyama et al. explicitly show that semantically meaningful higher-order dependencies remain among ICA embedding components and visualize their dependency structure. ICA Lens measures one-dimensional kurtosis and semantic usefulness but never tests residual mutual or higher-order dependence, so 'independent components' should not be read as empirically verified independent sources.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. train an overcomplete sparse reconstruction dictionary and test causal responsibility on IOI; ICA Lens avoids dictionary training and returns at most hidden-width signed axes, but does not reproduce the native behavioral causal test.

reviewed_competitors.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: evaluation framework and partial benchmark source
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAEBench evaluates more than 200 SAEs across eight metrics and finds proxy gains do not reliably transfer to practical tasks; ICA Lens imports sparse probing and TPP subsets but does not run the suite's full disentanglement, unlearning, or application battery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kantamneni et al. stress-test sparse probing under scarcity, imbalance, noise, and shift and find strong non-SAE ensembles usually match SAEs; ICA Lens reports standard probing curves but does not test those harder regimes or whether ICA adds value beyond an ensemble of raw-activation baselines.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inference-Time Decomposition of Activations (ITDA): A Scalable Approach to Interpreting Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: ITDA greedily builds activation dictionaries with matching pursuit using about 1% of SAE time/data and demonstrates 70B/405B and cross-model comparisons; ICA Lens is simpler and stronger on its selected probes but is fit independently per model and evaluated only through 2B scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Qwen-Scope: Turning Sparse Features into Development Tools for Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qwen-Scope releases SAEs for seven dense and MoE Qwen variants and evaluates steering, evaluation analysis, data workflows, SFT, and RL uses; ICA Lens analyzes one 2B Qwen model and stops at probe-defined intervention rather than native development workflows.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: Matryoshka SAEs jointly preserve general features in small nested dictionaries and specific features at larger widths, with probing and targeted erasure evidence; ICA Lens has one square-or-reduced resolution per layer and cannot represent a comparable hierarchy.

reviewed_competitors.title: BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: BatchTopK allocates a variable number of active latents per example while directly controlling average sparsity and improves reconstruction over TopK; ICA Lens uses dense signed square coordinates and maximizes non-Gaussianity rather than reconstruction or adaptive per-example sparsity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gated SAEs separate feature selection from magnitude estimation to reduce L1 shrinkage and report reconstruction/interpretability tradeoffs through 7B models; ICA Lens has no learned gate, explicit sparse code, or matched reconstruction-fidelity evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Jumping Ahead: Improving Reconstruction Fidelity with JumpReLU Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: JumpReLU directly optimizes L0 sparsity with a discontinuous activation and achieves high reconstruction fidelity at fixed sparsity; ICA Lens trades overcomplete reconstruction for a cheap non-Gaussian basis and therefore needs a distortion-matched native-behavior comparison before superiority claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Model Circuits Are Sparse in the Neuron Basis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arora et al. show that pre-down-projection MLP neurons can be as sparse as SAE features for circuit tracing and give native causal and steering evidence on subject-verb agreement and city-state-capital relations without additional feature training. ICA Lens instead rotates residual streams for layer-wide semantic browsing and probe utility, but does not supply comparable native-behaviour circuit evidence; the current neuron-basis result further narrows any implication that a learned or fitted rotation is required for training-free interpretability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Foundations of Interpretable Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barbiero et al. already claim a general actionable definition based on user-relative inference equivariance, derive concept structures and architectural consequences, propose a general blueprint, and introduce the PyTorch Concepts library. SIM replaces that central definition with a premise-symmetry-constraint template and adds Lagrangian dynamics, PDE-bounded reasoning, and new case studies; its novelty is therefore an extension and reformulation, not the team's first general actionable interpretability framework or software blueprint.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Compositional Interpretability for XAI
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tull et al. formalise models and interpretations with category-theoretic string diagrams, cover deterministic, probabilistic, quantum, causal, and concept models, and derive diagrammatic explanation operations. SIM is more directly tied to differentiable constraints and training/architecture recipes, but covers a narrower smooth concept-based instantiation and does not displace the earlier general compositional formalism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics of Learning: A Lagrangian perspective to different learning paradigms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo and Schoelkopf already postulate stationary learning paths and derive classic algorithms, Bellman optimality, and Adam from a learning Lagrangian. SIM cites and specialises that mechanics analogy to a potential containing interpretability penalties; the Lagrangian machinery itself is inherited, while the proposed interpretability constraints are the new content.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bronstein et al. already organise broad neural architecture families around invariances and provide constructive geometric recipes for incorporating structure. SIM transfers that symmetry-first design principle to user-relative interpretability and adds concept and reasoning constraints, but its general deductive pattern is an application of an established architecture-design methodology.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards A Rigorous Science of Interpretable Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Doshi-Velez and Kim distinguish application-grounded, human-grounded, and functionally grounded evaluation and insist that interpretability claims be tied to tasks and users. SIM supplies candidate mathematical constraints and construction recipes, but its experiments largely stay at the functionally grounded level and do not perform the human-grounded validation the earlier framework calls for.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretable Machine Learning: Fundamental Principles and 10 Grand Challenges
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rudin et al. already frame interpretable modelling through problem-specific structures and constraints across sparse logic, scoring systems, additive models, case-based reasoning, disentanglement, physics constraints, and Rashomon sets. SIM offers a single three-premise mathematical vocabulary, but its claim of generality is less empirically developed and its premises intentionally omit many domain-specific notions catalogued by this prior work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking Explainable Machine Learning as Applied Statistics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordt et al. treat explanations as statistics of high-dimensional functions whose interpretation depends on a concrete question and expert practice. SIM instead defines selected interpretability properties directly on model/concept geometry and seeks architecture-level enforcement; the applied-statistics view highlights that a formally invariant object can still fail to answer the user's actual question.

reviewed_competitors.title: HardNet: Hard-Constrained Neural Networks with Universal Approximation Guarantees
reviewed_competitors.difference: HardNet appends differentiable closed-form layers that satisfy multiple input-dependent inequality constraints and proves universal approximation while training end to end. SIM's hard-compilation branch is broader as a conceptual template for interpretability, but its ordered-prototype and PDE constructions lack comparable correctness and capacity guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Robust Interpretability with Self-Explaining Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: SENN specifies explicitness, faithfulness, and stability, builds concept-based self-explaining architectures, and adds tailored regularisation with benchmark experiments. SIM subsumes a version of SENN in its taxonomy and adds user semantics plus a general constraint language, but does not empirically compare its derived models against SENN or validate equivalent faithfulness/stability outcomes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Concept Bottleneck Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: canonical architecture implementing prediction through concepts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Koh et al. make labels depend on supervised intermediate concepts by construction and test human concept corrections on x-rays and birds. SIM generalises this pattern as Architecture II, relaxes exact concept scores toward order preservation, and proposes broader reasoning classes, but its claimed iff characterisation is false without global assumptions and its experiments do not match CBM's task-level concept-intervention evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning with Explanation Constraints
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pukdee et al. formalise a priori explanation constraints, provide expectation, generalisation, and Rademacher-complexity analysis, and develop a variational algorithm compared with augmented-Lagrangian baselines on synthetic and real datasets. SIM distinctly derives selected penalties from target-user premises and symmetries and proposes hard architectural compilation, but lacks the earlier work's learning-theoretic guarantees and broader quantitative evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Categorical Foundations of Explainable AI: A Unifying Theory
reviewed_competitors.difference: This same-team predecessor already claims rigorous definitions of explanation, categorical models of existing learning schemes and architectures, and foundations for XAI taxonomies. SIM changes the formalism to target-user premises, symmetries, differentiable constraints, and Lagrangian or architectural recipes; it is therefore a new synthesis and operationalisation, not the team's first unifying mathematical theory of explainability.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This work develops information and description-length tools for adaptively reused holdouts; the present paper operationalizes a severe natural-language channel for autonomous ML research and adds empirical reproduction.

reviewed_competitors.difference: The Ladder releases rounded score improvements with reusable-holdout guarantees; this paper uses an even coarser one-bit improvement transcript and a stratified bound tailored to research-agent search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rip van Winkle's Razor: A Simple Estimate of Overfit to Test Data

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Prompt Engineering May Not Require Rethinking Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work uses a language-model prior to obtain PAC-Bayes-style prompt generalization bounds; it is static and classification-focused but sharper than raw vocabulary-token counting, the refinement explicitly suggested here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Natural Analysts in Adaptive Data Analysis

reviewed_competitors.difference: Natural Analysts restricts adaptive behavior through recency, anchoring, and contractive dynamics and includes gradient-descent-like analysts; the reviewed paper instead measures low-information natural-language and feedback channels in resettable ML agents.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do ImageNet Classifiers Generalize to ImageNet?
reviewed_competitors.difference: New ImageNet test sets reveal sizeable absolute accuracy drops even while model ordering and progress mostly transfer; this demonstrates why same-distribution holdout reuse is not equivalent to out-of-distribution generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Meta-Analysis of Overfitting in Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: The meta-analysis finds little leaderboard overfitting across more than 100 Kaggle competitions; the present paper asks whether compressible agent strategies explain the same empirical puzzle in autonomous ML research.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2019 proceedings, volume 32, paper hash ee39e503b6bedf0c98c388b7e8589aca

reviewed_competitors.title: Overtuning in Hyperparameter Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work finds overtuning common and reports tuned configurations can be roughly 10% worse than defaults or first trials on fresh data; it cautions against generalizing this paper's limited-overfit result beyond its agent and task regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Skill Reuse as Compression in Agentic RL

reviewed_competitors.difference: ReuseRL regularizes RL trajectories toward a reusable skill dictionary and measures in- and out-of-distribution task success; the reviewed paper audits post-search ML strategies and holdout feedback without training the agent policy for compressibility.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1 (2026-05-29), marked work in progress

reviewed_competitors.title: MLE-bench: Evaluating Machine Learning Agents on Machine Learning Engineering
reviewed_competitors.difference: MLE-bench evaluates agents on 75 Kaggle competitions and studies resource scaling and contamination; this paper uses eight controlled task environments to isolate information bottlenecks rather than overall competition success.

reviewed_competitors.title: MLAgentBench: Evaluating Language Agents on Machine Learning Experimentation

reviewed_competitors.title: AIDE: AI-Driven Exploration in the Space of Code
reviewed_competitors.difference: AIDE uses tree-structured code search for data-science agents and evaluates resulting solutions; this paper abstracts from search policy to ask whether whatever is discovered survives compressed, fresh-agent reproduction.

reviewed_competitors.title: AIRA_2: Overcoming Bottlenecks in AI Research Agents

reviewed_competitors.difference: AIRA_2 uses a Hidden Consistent Evaluation protocol and reports that an apparent MLE-bench generalization gap was evaluation noise rather than memorization, while scaling asynchronous search on MLE-bench-30 and AIRS-Bench. The reviewed paper instead audits information flow with prompt and one-bit bottlenecks, but does not compare against hidden-consistent evaluation or disentangle measurement noise in its three-run search comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Trainable hardware for dynamical computing using error backpropagation through physical media
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct physical-dynamical backpropagation antecedent that predates the paper's framing that physical reservoirs are effectively frozen.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hermans et al. physically backpropagate through a reciprocal nonlinear dynamical medium, train input and output masks on a task requiring memory and nonlinearity, and conceptually allow trainable mixing; they do not learn masses, stiffnesses, and damping or derive a horizon-dependent damping band.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep physical neural networks trained with backpropagation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct end-to-end physical-training antecedent with mechanical, electronic, and optical substrates.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Physics-Aware Training demonstrates backpropagation-guided control of real physical transformations, including an oscillating mechanical plate, but trains hierarchical input transformations rather than the oscillator network's internal mass-damping-stiffness dynamics and does not study delayed-memory closure.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Nature version of record, volume 601 pages 549-555 (2022-01-26), DOI 10.1038/s41586-021-04223-6

reviewed_competitors.title: Random Oscillators Network for Time Series Processing
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest oscillator-reservoir comparator: a heterogeneous oscillator network with fixed internal connections, explicit stability theory, long-memory tasks, and edge-of-stability analysis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: RON deliberately keeps oscillator connections random and untrained and reports broad sequence and chaotic-forecasting benchmarks; the reviewed paper instead learns physical parameters and directly sweeps learned-versus-frozen recall, but on a much smaller empirical task suite.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: PMLR volume 238 proceedings version, AISTATS 2024, pages 4807-4815 (2024-05-02)

reviewed_competitors.title: On the difficulty of learning chaotic dynamics with RNNs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Provides a direct theoretical link between Lyapunov spectra, chaotic recurrent dynamics, and exploding or vanishing training gradients.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes RNN trajectory learning broadly and proves gradient behavior for dynamical regimes; the reviewed paper specializes the tension to damping in a mechanical oscillator network and adds a learned-versus-frozen recall sweep.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do Reservoir Computers Work Best at the Edge of Chaos?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct contrary evidence for the paper's interpretation that settling near a Lyapunov transition is intrinsically desirable.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Carroll gives two reservoir examples where capacity decreases near the edge of stability and argues edge optimality is not universal; the reviewed paper observes settled dampings near one measured crossing on one recall substrate but does not compare that operating point against task-optimal fixed damping.

reviewed_competitors.title: Asymptotic Stability in Reservoir Computing
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Theoretical reservoir-stability antecedent that quantitatively characterizes the stable-to-chaotic frontier under input drive.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies the recurrent-kernel large-reservoir limit and stability tuning, not trainable mechanical parameters or gradient memory; it shows the stability frontier itself was already an explicit quantitative object before the reviewed damping-band synthesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Recurrent neural networks: vanishing and exploding gradients are not the end of the story
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest modern trainability-memory theory showing long memory creates parameter sensitivity even without classical exploding gradients and explaining structural advantages of state-space models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zucchet and Orvieto analyze recurrent parameter sensitivity and element-wise recurrence generally; the reviewed paper proposes damping as a single mechanical control variable but does not measure the optimizer-sensitive quantities highlighted there.

reviewed_competitors.title: Recent Advances in Physical Reservoir Computing: A Review
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Field-defining physical-reservoir account documenting the standard fixed-reservoir, trained-readout convention invoked by the paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The review supports the conventional baseline but surveys many physical substrates and motivations; it does not imply that physical transformations cannot be trained, a stronger premise already qualified by direct physical-backpropagation work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Coupled Oscillatory Recurrent Neural Network (coRNN): An Accurate and (Gradient) Stable Architecture for Learning Long Time Dependencies
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct controlled-oscillator and stable-gradient antecedent omitted from the original competitive panel.
reviewed_competitors.difference: coRNN discretizes a controlled nonlinear second-order oscillator system, proves hidden-state gradient bounds, and evaluates long-dependency benchmarks. It does not learn literal masses, spring potentials, and damping or formulate a learned-versus-frozen damping band, but it directly narrows claims that oscillator training must fail beyond a damping-defined horizon and is a much stronger architecture baseline than the paper's basic linear recurrence.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, revised 2021-03-14 (v1 submitted 2020-10-02); ICLR 2021 conference version

reviewed_competitors.title: UnICORNN: A Recurrent Model for Learning Very Long Time Dependencies
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Structure-preserving oscillator alternative designed specifically to avoid exploding and vanishing gradients over very long horizons.
reviewed_competitors.difference: UnICORNN uses a structure-preserving discretization of an undamped Hamiltonian oscillator system and supplies rigorous hidden-gradient bounds plus broad long-memory experiments. It lies outside the reviewed dissipative family, so it is not a counterexample to a correctly restricted dissipative theorem, but it shows that alternate oscillator parameterization and conservation structure evade the paper's general rhetorical claim that long-horizon trainable oscillators face unavoidable damping-band closure.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: PMLR volume 139 proceedings version, ICML 2021, pages 9168-9178, conference dates 2021-07-18 through 2021-07-24

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Flossing: Improving Gradient Descent through Dynamic Control of Jacobians
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct Lyapunov-spectrum intervention and evaluation baseline for the paper's proposed edge-of-chaos regularization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gradient Flossing differentiably regularizes forward Lyapunov exponents toward zero, measures both long-term Jacobian norm and condition number, and tests training across several RNN architectures and temporal tasks. The reviewed paper mentions an optional largest-exponent penalty but does not evaluate it, measures only one exponent, and provides no gradient-conditioning or intervention ablation.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2023 poster primary OpenReview record, published 2023-09-21 and last modified 2024-01-16

reviewed_competitors.difference: It is a statistical estimator for canonical directions rather than an alignment-versus-prediction phase diagram, but it is a direct operator-level predecessor for the paper's CCA/RRR unification and highlights the finite-sample regularization problem omitted by the population thresholds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Skip a Layer or Loop it? Test-Time Depth Adaptation of Pretrained LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct same-author precursor that introduces answer-aware MCTS over skipped, repeated, and reordered pretrained layers on a per-sample basis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The precursor establishes oracle chain-of-layers existence and reports shorter/correcting paths but still searches each test example; POLAR's substantive addition is a learned up-front segment-program predictor intended to amortize that search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dr.LLM: Dynamic Layer Routing in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior learned-router competitor, also trained from MCTS supervision to skip, execute, or repeat frozen pretrained blocks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dr.LLM makes sequential local decisions from intermediate hidden states and repeats individual layers; POLAR predicts the whole route before execution and operates on bounded contiguous segments. This narrows POLAR novelty to coordination and representation rather than learned skip/repeat routing itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: MACRO: Markov Chain Routing of Transformer Layers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct post-publication competitor current at the review date that learns distributions over layer skips, repeats, and residual-add moves without changing base weights.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MACRO uses a context-dependent Markov policy and top-k Viterbi decoding and reports a 9.4x route-search reduction plus gains over Dr.LLM; POLAR instead uses semantic input cross-attention and a bounded packed-segment program. A matched comparison is absent because MACRO appeared after POLAR.

reviewed_competitors.title: Router-Tuning: A Simple and Effective Approach for Enabling Dynamic-Depth in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior lightweight dynamic-depth method and the source of the MindSkip baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Router-Tuning learns attention-based per-token layer skipping for efficiency and does not repeat blocks; POLAR jointly skips and repeats input-level contiguous segments and targets accuracy as well as cost, but depends on expensive offline oracle traces.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Layer-skipping in Pre-trained LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior plug-in routing method for token-dependent layer skipping in a frozen pretrained LLM and the source of the FlexiDepth baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: FlexiDepth adds routers and adapters to vary layers by generated token and reports that irregular routes do not yet yield wall-clock speedup; POLAR predicts one input-level route before generation, permits repetition, and reports latency on one model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest trained recurrent-depth architecture combining shared parameters with token-level adaptive recursion.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mixture-of-Recursions trains a recursive transformer and token routers jointly and changes active-token attention and KV caching; POLAR retrofits fully frozen standard layer stacks and repeats pretrained contiguous segments, avoiding base training but offering weaker token-level adaptation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inner Thinking Transformer: Leveraging Dynamic Depth Scaling to Foster Adaptive Internal Thinking
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior recurrent-depth model that routes difficult tokens through extra internal thinking steps.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Inner Thinking Transformer requires architecture-aware training, residual thinking connections, token routing, and step encodings; POLAR uses existing frozen layers and an external controller, trading native recurrent training for retrofit convenience.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational adaptive recurrent-depth transformer with shared computation and a halting mechanism.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Universal Transformers are designed and trained around recurrent transition blocks with per-position adaptive computation; POLAR instead composes heterogeneous layers from a pretrained conventional stack and does not retrain those layers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior evidence that repeated transformer computation and inference-time loop counts can improve algorithmic length generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Looped Transformers train a shared block for controlled recurrence and study length extrapolation; POLAR repeats selected segments of an ordinarily trained pretrained LLM and studies math-answer accuracy and execution cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prompt-based Depth Pruning of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior prompt-conditioned up-front routing method, published as PuDDing at ICML 2025.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PuDDing trains a lightweight prompt router to choose the best layer-omission set from a data-derived option library before the LLM executes. It cannot repeat segments or synthesize POLAR's bounded operation programs, but it means that prompt-based one-shot depth selection predates POLAR; the remaining novelty is coordinated joint skip/repeat segment composition and its MCTS-derived representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Intuitive physics understanding emerges from self-supervised pretraining on natural videos
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior study comparing predictive video representation objectives on violation-of-expectation physics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It establishes that latent masked prediction outperforms pixel prediction and language-mediated models under a surprise protocol; this paper extends the question across more backbone generations, probe capacities, layers, and MVP but lacks equally controlled objective matching.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct earlier layerwise and mechanistic probing competitor on V-JEPA and VideoMAE encoders.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It scans every layer and analyzes elementary motion subspaces, attention, unit tuning, and steering; this paper covers more model families and a shortcut-aware natural-video benchmark but samples only four depths and does not intervene on representations.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Invisible Hand of Physics: When Video Diffusion Models Know More Than They Show
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct contemporary diffusion-representation competitor using the same plausibility paradigm.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It reverses complete diffusion trajectories in WAN, CogVideoX, and LTX and probes every block and time, whereas this paper includes only LTX among diffusion models and trades trajectory resolution for cross-family and probe-capacity comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Shortcut-aware Video-QA Benchmark for Physical Understanding via Minimal Video Pairs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct benchmark antecedent whose data are adapted into the paper's strongest evaluation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MVP keeps identical questions and opposing answers and requires paired VideoQA correctness, finding the best open VLM at 40.2 percent versus 25 percent chance; this paper drops the questions and converts a filtered subset into video-only binary labels, creating a materially different task that needs separate validity checks.

reviewed_competitors.title: IntPhys 2: Benchmarking Intuitive Physics Understanding In Complex Synthetic Environments
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct benchmark antecedent and contrary baseline evidence.
reviewed_competitors.difference: IntPhys 2 introduces the four-clip scene protocol and reports most evaluated models near 50 percent individual classification against near-perfect humans; this paper trains supervised probes over frozen features and reaches higher scene-ordering scores for selected models.

reviewed_competitors.title: IntPhys: A Framework and Benchmark for Visual Intuitive Physics Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: The original work defines carefully matched possible-impossible scenes and future-mask prediction baselines; this paper uses its successor for frozen probing but does not add a generator-shift or human-surprise validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: LikePhys: Evaluating Intuitive Physics Understanding in Video Diffusion Models via Likelihood Preference
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing training-free internal evaluation of intuitive physics in diffusion models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: LikePhys uses the denoising objective itself as a valid-invalid likelihood preference and validates it against human preference over twelve scenarios; this paper uses learned probes, reaches deeper layer comparisons, and includes encoders but lacks a model-native or human-aligned score.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pixels to Principles: Probing Intuitive Physics Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct probing competitor that separates visual feature availability from downstream use.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It probes stages of multimodal models on GRASP and IntPhys 2 and reports that vision encoders can preserve plausibility cues that language components fail to use; this paper similarly measures frozen accessibility but does not test whether the native model consumes the recovered signal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Latent Video Prediction Learns Better World Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing matched-capacity comparison of predictive and masked-reconstruction video encoders.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It compares V-JEPA 2.1, V-JEPA 2, VideoPrism, and VideoMAEv2 across five robustness axes at matched capacity and finds a consistent latent-prediction profile; this paper targets physics labels directly but uses unmatched models, so the competitor offers stronger objective attribution and weaker physics specificity.

reviewed_competitors.title: RigidBench: Evaluating Rigid-Body Physics in Video Generation Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest post-publication benchmark and mechanistic competitor, current at the review date, that measures physical trajectories and probes whether a diffusion model uses represented object position.
reviewed_competitors.difference: RigidBench separates ten simulator-grounded motion, geometry, identity, background, and visual metrics and adds teacher-forced probes plus interventions showing represented position is used during denoising. This paper spans more frozen encoder families and layers, but its binary plausibility readouts do not measure trajectory error or causal use.

reviewed_competitors.title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication behavior-level competitor that evaluates explicit physical laws and calibrated parameters in video world-model outputs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: GAUGE uses real trajectories and task-specific observables over 22 controlled families and finds that plausible equation form can hide wrong acceleration, momentum transfer, or oscillation timing. This paper probes internal label accessibility at broader model depth but cannot reveal those quantitative physical errors.

reviewed_competitors.title: CaliBench: Are the Stochastic Dynamics of Video World Models Physically Calibrated?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication native-generation competitor testing whether stochastic physical outcomes follow known reference distributions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CaliBench separates scorability from distributional calibration and reports widespread mode concentration across six generators; this paper instead trains discriminative probes on frozen features, so even a high probe score offers no evidence that a model's generated outcome distribution is calibrated.

reviewed_competitors.title: PhyGround: Benchmarking Physical Reasoning in Generative World Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current behavior-level benchmark that operationalizes physical laws and validates judgments with a large controlled human study.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PhyGround evaluates eight generators on 250 prompts and 13 laws using 459 annotators, 5,796 complete annotations, more than 37.4K fine-grained labels, and a specialized open judge. The target offers internal layer/probe comparisons across encoder families, but its binary supervised readouts neither test generated physical behavior nor provide PhyGround's per-law human validation; this further narrows any inference from representation accessibility to physical understanding.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantizable Transformers: Removing Outliers by Helping Attention Heads Do Nothing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bondarenko et al. argue that softmax attention heads create outliers because they lack a direct no-op and add gated attention to make doing nothing easy. The present paper formalizes near-zero sink values as one of two sink computations, contrasts it with broadcast, and evaluates the combination with registers in ViTs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo et al. identify active-dormant heads whose extreme tokens absorb attention while value-output norms collapse, directly anticipating the no-op/value-drain interpretation in LLMs. This paper adds an explicit broadcast alternative, controlled two-task signatures, and a ViT intervention study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Vision Transformers Need Registers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Darcet et al. introduce learned register tokens to absorb high-norm artifacts and improve dense visual features, motivating the workspace/broadcast side of the current framing. The present paper interprets registers as hosts for both contentful broadcast and no-op sinks and combines them with explicit gating.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. benchmark attention gates at LLM scale and attribute broad gains to nonlinearity, sparsity, and removal of sinks. The present work transports a gating variant to LeJEPA ViTs and gives it a no-op interpretation, but does not isolate that mechanism from the more general effects emphasized by Qiu et al.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unified View of Attention and Residual Sinks: Outlier-Driven Rescaling is Essential for Transformer Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. connect attention and residual sinks through outlier-driven rescaling and argue that the phenomenon can be essential to training. That mechanism is not equivalent to a no-op/broadcast functional split and supplies a competing explanation that the current diagnostic plots do not directly rule out.

reviewed_competitors.title: Vision Transformers Don't Need Trained Registers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jiang et al. identify register neurons and construct training-free register tokens that can match trained-register benefits without retraining. This weakens any implication that a learned register architecture is uniquely required for broadcast and suggests a closer capacity-controlled intervention for the current hypothesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do All Vision Transformers Need Registers? A Cross-Architectural Reassessment
reviewed_competitors.difference: This reassessment tests register claims across vision-transformer architectures and sizes and reports that the need and effect are not universal. It sets the missing generalization test for the current single-family LeJEPA mitigation result and cautions against making register complementarity architecture-independent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Optimal Data Mixtures
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shukor et al. fit additive and joint empirical laws across model size, token count, and mixture in language, vision, and multimodal settings. This paper derives a lower-parameter capacity-plus-noise form and matches or exceeds that law from a single smaller scale, but covers fewer modalities and rests on stronger theory assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ye et al. use an empirical exponential mixture surface nested with model- and step-scaling laws and also study continual training. The present work replaces that functional fit with an interpretable capacity allocation and finite-data term, reporting substantially lower Pile-mixture MRE.

reviewed_competitors.title: RegMix: Data Mixture as Regression for Language Model Pre-Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: RegMix trains hundreds of very small proxy models and uses a flexible regressor to rank mixtures at much larger scale. The present law uses fewer parameters and an explicit N,D mechanism, but RegMix makes fewer shared-head/disjoint-tail assumptions and has demonstrated transfer up to 7B/100B-token runs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Mixture Optimization: A Multi-fidelity Multi-scale Bayesian Framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Bayesian framework treats mixture, scale, and training horizon as sequential experimental choices and models extrapolation uncertainty, reporting 2.6x to 3.3x search speedups. The present work supplies a stronger mechanistic parametric prior and direct large-scale mixtures but no posterior uncertainty or adaptive run allocation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Domain-Aware Scaling Laws Uncover Data Synergy
reviewed_competitors.difference: Domain-Aware Scaling Laws estimates direct transfer plus pairwise synergy and interference from observational open-model variation. That explicitly targets the interactions suppressed by a disjoint-tail approximation, while this paper offers a much more parameter-efficient mechanistic law and prospective mixture-training tests.

reviewed_competitors.difference: PPO clips relative likelihood ratios to enable minibatch reuse; DRPO instead applies smooth reweighting based on sampled-token absolute probability displacement and targets LLM vocabulary tails.

reviewed_competitors.title: Truly Proximal Policy Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Truly PPO adds rollback and a KL-based trigger to enforce proximity with monotonic-improvement theory; it does not use the sampled-token Binary-TV proxy or analyze long-tailed LLM ratios.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simple Policy Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: SPO replaces hard ratio clipping with a smooth ratio-space quadratic; DRPO borrows smooth enforcement but adds a behavior-probability factor to obtain absolute-displacement rather than Pearson-chi-square geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking the Trust Region in LLM Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: DPPO introduces Binary-TV and top-k divergence masks to fix ratio geometry; DRPO's nominal contribution is replacing its hard mask with smooth correction, but the reported methods use unequal thresholds and therefore do not experimentally share a boundary.

reviewed_competitors.title: Ratio-Variance Regularized Policy Optimization for Efficient LLM Fine-tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: R2VPO constrains the second central moment of importance ratios and supports stale-data reuse through a primal-dual scheme; DRPO remains pointwise and on sampled-token absolute displacement, without a global ratio-variance budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: TROLL: Trust Regions improve Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: TROLL projects a sparse set of important token logits into differentiable token-level KL regions; it constrains more of the output distribution at higher per-token optimization cost, whereas DRPO uses one sampled probability and a closed-form weight.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prosperity before Collapse: How Far Can Off-Policy RL Reach with Stale Data on LLMs?
reviewed_competitors.difference: M2PO masks extreme importance-weight outliers through a second-moment trust criterion and targets rollouts stale by many updates; DRPO smooths every sampled token using absolute displacement and does not demonstrate comparable staleness tolerance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work attributes mismatch largely to BF16 rounding and stabilizes RL by using FP16 without changing the objective; it is a direct negative control for whether DRPO gains arise from divergence geometry or merely numerical policy alignment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Uniform Token-Level Trust Region in LLM Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: CPPO replaces position-independent token control with a finite-horizon-motivated position schedule and cumulative prefix-divergence budget. It directly exposes DRPO's remaining pointwise limitation: DRPO smooths sampled-token displacement but neither tightens early-token updates nor tracks accumulated autoregressive drift.

reviewed_competitors.difference: TQCompressor already improves neural-network Kronecker tensor decomposition through permutations and demonstrates compressed GPT-2. EinSort's narrower advance is content-derived, axis-dependent sorting with shared-permutation tradeoffs, explicit order-statistic analyses, and KV/VLM/VLA evaluations.

reviewed_competitors.title: TensorGPT: Efficient Compression of Large Language Models based on Tensor-Train Decomposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: TensorGPT applies training-free tensor-train decomposition to GPT embedding layers and reports device latency; EinSort changes the entry ordering before arbitrary tensor-network decomposition and targets weights and KV caches beyond embeddings.

reviewed_competitors.title: ASVD: Activation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for Compressing Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: ASVD rescales weights with activation statistics and covers both weight and KV-cache low-rank compression without permutation metadata; EinSort uses index ordering and can optionally wrap the same activation-aware preconditioning.

reviewed_competitors.title: SVD-LLM: Truncation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for Large Language Model Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: SVD-LLM uses truncation-aware whitening and sequential low-rank updates with no learned index transform; EinSort tries to expose a more compressible spectrum before factorization and reports larger gains on its VLM/VLA tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Palu: Compressing KV-Cache with Low-Rank Projection
reviewed_competitors.difference: Palu compresses hidden dimensions through medium-grained low-rank projections and supplies fused GPU kernels with measured speedups; EinSort reports better reconstruction through sorting but currently slows decoding and lacks fused reordering kernels.

reviewed_competitors.title: ReCalKV: Low-Rank KV Cache Compression via Head Reordering and Offline Calibration
reviewed_competitors.difference: ReCalKV reorders structurally similar key heads and calibrates values before grouped SVD, avoiding per-cache content permutations; EinSort uses finer axis-coupled element ordering and pays explicit permutation storage for each compressed tensor.

reviewed_competitors.title: AA-SVD : Anchored and Adaptive SVD for Large Language Model Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: AA-SVD explicitly models upstream distribution shift and refines transformer blocks to compensate accumulated error; EinSort does not model cross-layer error in its core method and instead searches for a permutation that reduces local factorization rank.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Brain Decomposition for Accurate LLM Low-Rank Approximation
reviewed_competitors.difference: OBD-LLM derives bidirectional whitening from a Kronecker-factored Hessian and gives a closed-form weight approximation; EinSort is largely objective-agnostic but introduces a discrete ordering search and separate permutation/sign costs.

reviewed_competitors.title: KV-CoRE: Benchmarking Data-Dependent Low-Rank Compressibility of KV-Caches in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: KV-CoRE measures optimal SVD compressibility layer by layer across domains and languages and relates normalized effective rank to downstream degradation. It does not reorder entries or provide a deployed codec, but it supplies the data-dependent rank audit missing from EinSort's short-context, model-specific sorting studies.

reviewed_competitors.title: VarRate: Training-Free Variable-Rate KV Cache Compression for Long-Context LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: VarRate allocates a nonzero token-specific low-rank budget from query salience and reports matched-memory LongBench results without content-permutation codes. EinSort instead rearranges tensor entries before factorization, evaluates 64-token prefill plus 64-token decode in its main KV setup, and has not shown the same long-context rate-quality comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Regularization in Matrix Factorization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work studies near-origin gradient dynamics and minimum-nuclear-norm behavior in matrix factorization; the Muon paper argues that a projected polar flow selects flatter finite interpolants instead, but only in a different constrained flow.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Loss Does Not See the Basis, but Adam Does
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work analyzes optimizer gauge equivariance in underdetermined matrix sensing, includes Muon among equivariant rules, and finds spectrum-tail-dependent recovery; it directly narrows a universal flat-spectrum or non-low-rank interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon Optimizes Under Spectral Norm Constraints
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper places Muon inside spectral-norm-constrained optimization; the reviewed work asks which finite interpolant a projected polar flow selects and shows that fixed-radius geometry favors a flat spectrum rather than nuclear concentration.

reviewed_competitors.title: PolarGrad: A Class of Matrix-Gradient Optimizers from a Unifying Preconditioning Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: PolarGrad unifies matrix-gradient optimizers through polar preconditioning and analyzes practical updates; the reviewed paper focuses on one projected self-polar interpolation flow and one-step noise sensitivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convergence Bound and Critical Batch Size of Muon Optimizer
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work already derives Muon convergence and critical batch size from nonconvex rate analysis; the reviewed theorem offers a distinct local polar-Frechet signal-noise formula but cannot claim the first Muon critical-batch account.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral Flattening Is All Muon Needs: How Orthogonalization Controls Learning Rate and Convergence
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work attributes stable learning rates and convergence to flattened updates under a Kronecker curvature model; the reviewed paper instead gives a conditional weight-spectrum shape criterion on an interpolation manifold.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uniform Spectral Growth and Convergence of Muon in LoRA-Style Matrix Factorization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper proves uniform spectral growth and convergence in a regularized LoRA-style factorization; the reviewed work studies projected contraction and finite-interpolant selection in underdetermined regression.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon is Not That Special: Random or Inverted Spectra Work Just as Well
reviewed_competitors.difference: Random- and inverted-spectrum updates reportedly match Muon in tested regimes, suggesting local alignment or descent potential rather than flat spectra can drive performance; this is a decisive alternative to a unique flat-spectrum mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon Does Not Converge on Convex Lipschitz Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper constructs convex Lipschitz failures without error feedback; it reinforces that local smooth projected-flow results cannot support generic Muon convergence or implicit-bias claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking Muon Beyond Pretraining: Spectral Failures and High-Pass Remedies for VLA and RLVR
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work finds uniform spectral whitening can fail in VLA and RLVR and proposes high-pass polar filters; it directly supports regime dependence while offering a practical alternative not evaluated here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Muon Outperforms Adam: A Curvature Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: The curvature paper attributes a small-LM advantage to lower directional sharpness, whereas this paper emphasizes flat update and weight spectra; neither performs the cross-update intervention needed to distinguish the mechanisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Understanding the Power and Limits of the Muon Optimizer: A River-Valley Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: The river-valley paper predicts early spectral exploration but late residual-scale overshoot and proposes an AdamW handoff; that trajectory-level failure is not explained by a fixed-radius flat-spectrum variational state.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon$^p$: Muon with Fractional Spectral Powers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work interpolates between exact polar flattening and gradient descent with fractional spectral powers and reports benefits from retaining singular-value information. It is a direct alternative to treating a perfectly flat polar update as the uniquely useful geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: On MUON optimization: From non-convergence to an error analysis with Polar Express and the Newton-Schulz polynomial from implementations
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work analyzes actual finite Newton-Schulz and Polar Express implementations, proves non-convergence on a stochastic problem class for almost every mini-batch size, and gives explicit batch/error rates. It addresses the approximate implementation and batch-size regime that the reviewed exact-polar, one-step crossover leaves outside scope.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct large-rate matrix-factorization analysis proving convergence and magnitude balancing even from unbalanced initialization; it bears on both the scheduler's norm-gap story and discrete finite-step effects.

reviewed_competitors.difference: It addresses time-varying stochastic heterogeneity in LLaMA/GPT-scale training and proves a convergence rate. The present paper isolates noiseless, full-batch one-/two-step signal coupling and offers only a toy norm-based schedule, so the works are complementary but the newer method is the stronger practical comparator.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This primary study independently characterizes normalized spike tokens as sparse near-constant implicit parameters and supplies training-from-scratch architectural and optimization ablations. It causally decouples spikes from sinks through normalization, gating, and context-length changes, challenging any reading that the target's fixed-vector no-op pathway is necessary rather than one architecture-dependent route.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention Sinks Induce Gradient Sinks: Massive Activations as Gradient Regulators in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This primary work argues that massive activations regulate sink-localized gradients through the RMSNorm Jacobian and uses V-scale to preserve attention sinks while suppressing spikes. That causal separation supplies a backward-pass explanation absent from the target and shows the forward bias-template mechanism is not a complete account of why spikes emerge.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This primary work separates adaptive no-op sinks with near-zero values from broadcast sinks with nonzero values and rank-one outputs, then finds both in pretrained ViTs. Its diagnostics show why a method premised on every sink being a null-value structural bias needs head-level mechanism classification, especially for the target's cross-modal claim.

It broadens the function beyond the target's fixed no-op template and warns that excision is safe only when the rescaling role is faithfully restored.

It freezes the language model, trains L-by-H continuous gates with an auxiliary L1 sparsity penalty, and discretizes them after training; NGC instead jointly updates the LM and samples per-round block survival as native actions using outcome advantage alone.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: v3, revised 2026-05-27; priority established by v1

reviewed_competitors.title: Hold Onto That Thought: Assessing KV Cache Compression On Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: pre-existing reasoning-cache benchmark and metric warning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This multi-model, eight-benchmark study evaluates decoding-time cache compression and shows that low cache budgets can lengthen or derail reasoning traces, so cache bytes alone can trade against extra generation compute. NGC's method-dependent completion-length peak-cache ratio does not neutralize that already documented confound.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Much Cache Does Reasoning Need? Depth-Cache Tradeoffs in KV-Compressed Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper was submitted 71 minutes before NGC and studies adaptive versus oblivious cache control through pointer-chasing bounds, explicitly labeling its strongest product lower bound conjectural. It does not learn an eviction policy, but it supplies theoretical resource-capability constraints that NGC's empirical fixed-budget analysis does not test.

reviewed_competitors.title: KARA: Efficient Reasoning LLM Serving via Sliding-Window KV Cache Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: KARA uses bidirectional scoring over a recent window, expands selected tokens into flexible chunks, and integrates the policy with PagedAttention in a vLLM-based serving system. It is heuristic rather than outcome-trained, but its explicit throughput implementation is a current systems comparison missing from NGC's cache-proxy-only evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering KV Cache Eviction Policies via LLM-Guided Program Evolution
reviewed_competitors.difference: CacheCraft evolves executable eviction scorers and reports that its learned scoring family, rather than chunk structure, drives large RULER gains. Its resulting policy is a fixed prefill scorer rather than an online reasoning action, but it is a current counterexample to the dichotomy between hand-written heuristics and end-to-end weight training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral Bias and Task-Model Alignment Explain Generalization in Kernel Regression and Infinitely Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Canatar et al. derive an analytic kernel-regression generalization error from kernel eigenfunctions, task coefficients, noise, and sample count and validate it on real and synthetic data. Their theory also permits non-monotonic curves, directly contradicting the zeta paper's implicit monotone mode-accumulation picture.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectrum Dependent Learning Curves in Kernel Regression and Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon et al. derive mode-specific learning curves and staged acquisition of higher spectral components, then test them in simulations and MNIST. The zeta perspective substitutes a hard Davis-Kahan cutoff and AUC transform, but provides no empirical comparison to this established continuous spectral theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explaining Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bahri et al. distinguish variance-limited and resolution-limited regimes and connect data and width scaling to kernel spectra with experiments across architectures and datasets. This paper offers a biomedical AUC specialization but collapses potentially distinct regimes into one cutoff law and does not test it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hestness et al. measure power-law generalization curves across translation, language, vision, and speech and separate exponent from error offsets. The zeta paper proposes a spectral origin for biomedical slopes but has no measured curves and conflates concentration changes with total-signal changes.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Shape of Learning Curves: a Review
reviewed_competitors.difference: Viering and Loog document power-law, exponential, multi-stage, and ill-behaved curves, including cases where more data worsens performance, and conclude that no universal shape exists. That survey is a direct warning against promoting the unvalidated zeta form as a law rather than one falsifiable candidate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimizing Sample Size for Supervised Machine Learning with Bulk Transcriptomic Sequencing: A Learning Curve Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: This transcriptomics work estimates power-versus-sample-size by data augmentation and fitted empirical learning curves. It addresses the same planning decision in an application-specific, testable pipeline, whereas the zeta paper supplies a spectral formula but no observed omics curve or calibration study.

reviewed_competitors.title: How measurement noise limits the accuracy of brain-behaviour predictions
reviewed_competitors.difference: This study shows that measurement reliability can trade off against participant count, with smaller high-reliability samples matching or exceeding larger noisy samples. That finding exposes a missing axis in the zeta law, which treats N and representation spectra as decisive without an explicit measurement-error model.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the stability of canonical correlation analysis and partial least squares with application to brain-behavior associations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Helmer et al. use generative simulations plus cohorts near 1,000 and 20,000 to measure CCA/PLS association and loading stability and provide a power calculator; typical smaller studies are unstable. The zeta paper cites this theme but asserts CCA concentration benefits without testing whether those benefits outweigh estimation instability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reproducible brain-wide association studies require thousands of individuals
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marek et al. run billions of analyses over sample sizes 25-32,572 in three major cohorts and find small effects, sampling variability, inflation, and replication failures until samples reach the thousands. The zeta paper offers a compact spectral explanation but does not reproduce or predict these empirical thresholds or cross-cohort failures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Different scaling of linear models and deep learning in UKBiobank brain images versus machine-learning datasets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schulz et al. systematically vary training size and compare linear, kernel, and deep models on UK Biobank brain images plus reference image datasets. They observe model crossovers on MNIST/Fashion but no deep-model advantage through roughly 9,300 brain scans, making this a direct measured predecessor to the zeta paper's unsupported Figure 4 ordering.

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimation of minimal data sets sizes for machine learning predictions in digital mental health interventions
reviewed_competitors.difference: This study constructs train/test learning and convergence curves across feature sets and six classifier families in a 3,654-participant digital-mental-health dataset to estimate minimum useful sample sizes. It addresses the same planning question empirically, including model-dependent overfitting, whereas the zeta law supplies no fitted biomedical curve.

reviewed_competitors.title: How many samples to label for an application given a foundation model? Chest X-ray classification study
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nechaev et al. fit power-law learning curves across pathologies and chest-X-ray foundation models to forecast training sizes for target ROC-AUC values, testing early-slope forecasts against observed plateaus. The method is application-specific rather than spectral, but it performs the empirical prediction and validation the zeta perspective postpones.

reviewed_competitors.title: Longer scans boost prediction and cut costs in brain-wide association studies
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work derives and tests a closed-form relationship between prediction accuracy, participants, and scan duration under fixed acquisition budgets. It demonstrates that data quantity cannot be reduced to participant count or representation slope alone, directly exposing the zeta law's missing measurement-fidelity axis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Curves and Benign Overfitting of Spectral Algorithms in Large Dimensions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lu et al. derive sharp excess-risk asymptotics over the full regularization path and identify over-regularized, under-regularized, and interpolation regimes. Although posted six days after the zeta paper and not a priority challenge, it is a current example of the additional regularization regimes and non-simple curve shapes omitted by hard mode accumulation.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Parallelism Tradeoff: Limitations of Log-Precision Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational formal predecessor for the serial-capacity limitation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Merrill and Sabharwal prove circuit-complexity limits for log-precision transformers and formulate the parallelism tradeoff. The reviewed article translates that formal theme into a dynamic-state computation-graph argument, cognitive framing, and recurrence taxonomy, but supplies no stronger theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct theory and empirical predecessor for explicit-thought serial computation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. prove that T chain-of-thought steps expand constant-depth transformer expressivity to size-T circuit computation and test serial tasks. The reviewed article accepts this escape hatch but argues that emitting thought for routine state updates is inefficient and advocates implicit recurrent activation instead.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Illusion of State in State-Space Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct theoretical and empirical caveat to recurrence as a sufficient solution.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Merrill et al. prove TC0-like limitations for standard SSMs and show Mamba-style failures on state tracking. The reviewed article uses this result to distinguish mere recurrent formulation from expressive nonlinear/negative-eigenvalue step recurrence and broadens the architecture map.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unlocking State-Tracking in Linear RNNs Through Negative Eigenvalues
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct constructive predecessor for expressive linear recurrent state updates.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Grazzi et al. prove positive-eigenvalue limitations, give negative/non-triangular transition constructions for parity, modular counting, and arbitrary regular languages, and report stable 1.3B-parameter pretraining. The reviewed article cites this route as evidence that recurrence details matter but adds no matched architecture or state-tracking experiment of its own.

reviewed_competitors.title: (How) Do Language Models Track State?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical counterpoint showing successful feedforward state-tracking shortcuts.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. find that transformers learn associative-scan and parity-pruning algorithms for permutation composition and show these mechanisms can be steered. This supports the reviewed article's shortcut concession and limits its impossibility claim to arbitrary or non-composable indefinite updates rather than practical state tracking in general.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Recurrent Transformer: Greater Effective Depth and Efficient Decoding
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-concurrent direct architecture implementing layerwise recurrent state.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Oncescu et al. make each layer attend to keys and values from its own activations, give an exact tiling algorithm, and report improved C4 pretraining loss at 150M/300M parameters. The reviewed article's v4 cites this concrete system but contributes the broader taxonomy and state-tracking motivation rather than comparable implementation evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking State Tracking in Recurrent Models Through Error Control Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Subsequent direct theory and evaluation of recurrent state robustness.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chung et al. show that affine recurrent models can preserve symbolic states yet fail to correct state-separating errors, and empirically tie a distinguishability ratio to the horizon where group-state tracking collapses. This sharpens the reviewed article's recurrence-is-not-sufficient caveat from expressivity to error-control dynamics and supplies controlled evidence absent from the perspective.

reviewed_competitors.title: State Propagation Also Satisfies: A Complex-Valued State-Space Model for Deterministic State Tracking
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Subsequent direct recurrent-state method available before the review cutoff.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li and Lu propose a complex-valued recurrent state propagator and report perfect accuracy/F1 on canonical deterministic tracking tasks such as parity, modular counting, and parentheses. It operationalizes the reviewed article's implicit-state direction but is narrow and does not settle naturalistic belief tracking or the training-parallelism tradeoff.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Learning of Evolving Data Streams with Tabular Foundational Models

reviewed_competitors.title: What and How does In-Context Learning Learn? Bayesian Model Averaging, Parameterization, and Generalization

reviewed_competitors.title: Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Classical algorithmic target for online Bayesian change detection
reviewed_competitors.difference: BOCD performs exact recursive inference over run length and supports repeated online changes with explicit probabilistic models; the reviewed construction enumerates a finite single-boundary candidate set inside a transformer and does not compare to BOCD empirically.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers as Algorithms: Generalization and Stability in In-context Learning

reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes generalization and stability for ICL on iid regression examples and dynamical-system trajectories and empirically studies near-optimal algorithms; the reviewed paper adds an abrupt regime boundary and side-information hierarchy but lacks comparable stability or generalization bounds.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems with Transformers: Approximation Bounds and Depth-Separation
reviewed_competitors.difference: It provides approximation bounds and a depth separation for noisy linear dynamical systems; the reviewed paper only evaluates a two-regime LDS empirically while its theorem remains a regression construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: NOMADD: Numerical Optimization of Models Adapting to Data Drift

It requires periodwise fitted models rather than event-time metadata, but provides a current non-oracle adaptation alternative absent from the reviewed paper's two real-world ablations.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior direct grokking early-warning and causal-mechanism competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu's v3 predates the reviewed paper and reports a commutator-defect precursor across modular arithmetic, SCAN, and Dyck-1, including interventions that accelerate grokking by roughly 32% on SCAN and 50% on Dyck or delay/prevent it by suppressing orthogonal flow. The reviewed D statistic is a retrospective cross-width synthetic-graph fit with no prospective held-out prediction or D intervention, so broad priority for an architecture-agnostic early warning is not supported.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Density Matrices to Phase Transitions in Deep Learning: Spectral Early Warnings and Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: prior direct spectral early-warning and dimensionality competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hennick and Corlouer derive spectral heat capacity as an early warning under critical slowing down and participation ratio as reorganization dimensionality, then evaluate four settings including grokking. The reviewed work instead uses a random parameter graph and event-aligned finite-size exponent, without a comparable past-only forecasting test or theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nanda et al. recover the modular-addition Fourier circuit, validate it with ablations, and expose gradual circuit formation and cleanup on individual trajectories. D is task-agnostic in construction but requires a population of widths and does not reveal the computation that generalizes or yield a validated single-run decision rule.

reviewed_competitors.title: Information-Theoretic Progress Measures reveal Grokking is an Emergent Phase Transition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Clauw et al. track higher-order neuronal synergy and redundancy, identify phases before grokking, and state that these measures anticipate the event. The reviewed paper introduces a different gradient-cascade observable but does not compare forecasting performance against that representation-based signal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Toward a Physics of Deep Learning and Brains
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct avalanche, susceptibility, and finite-size-scaling predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghavasieh et al. already apply neuronal-avalanche equations, susceptibility, crackling relations, and finite-size scaling to deep networks, identify universality classes, and explicitly characterize the driven regime as quasi-critical. The reviewed paper adds grokking-aligned gradient cascades but lacks comparable tail-model and exponent-relation validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tuning Universality in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghavasieh derives stochastic information-propagation couplings, a Landau description, and distinct avalanche universality classes with activation-controlled simulations. The reviewed paper fits one exponent on a random parameter graph and explicitly leaves its universality class open.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking as a First Order Phase Transition in Two Layer Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rubin et al. analytically map feature-learning grokking in tractable two-layer teacher-student models to a first-order mixed phase and test the associated representations. The reviewed work labels a fitted D = 1 crossover an order parameter but supplies no free-energy competition, nonanalytic limit, or theorem connecting D to generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Is Grokking a Computational Glass Relaxation?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct landscape mechanism and thermodynamic-claim competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. sample an entropy landscape, report no entropy barrier in their grokking transition, and construct optimizer counterexamples to simple norm-based accounts. D is correlational and is not tested for discriminating a glass relaxation, first-order transition, gradual circuit formation, or probe-induced scaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noise-Driven Escape from Metastable Phases explains Grokking in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ersoy and Wiesner deliberately trap deep linear networks, vary SGD noise, and report Arrhenius escape behavior over two orders of magnitude in time. This later work supplies an intervention-based metastability account; the reviewed paper's D crossing remains a non-causal diagnostic and is not compared against basin/noise variables.

reviewed_competitors.title: Theorem-of-Thought: A Multi-Agent Framework for Abductive, Deductive, and Inductive Reasoning in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest direct predecessor for explicit abductive-deductive-inductive LLM orchestration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abdaljalil et al. already assign abductive, deductive, and inductive reasoning to collaborating agents, structure traces as reasoning graphs, score coherence with NLI-guided Bayesian belief propagation, release an implementation, and report gains over CoT, self-consistency, and CoT-Decoding on WebOfLies and MultiArith. reviewed_competitors.title: Typed Chain-of-Thought: A Curry-Howard Framework for Verifying LLM Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest formal-certificate alternative for auditable LLM reasoning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Perrier maps informal reasoning steps into typed proof structures so successful type checking provides a formal certificate.
