reviewed_competitors.title: Let's Verify Step by Step
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest process-supervision predecessor for externally evaluating individual reasoning steps.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lightman et al. train process reward models using 800,000 human step-level labels and report 78% on a representative MATH subset, supplying measured end-to-end gains. reviewed_competitors.title: General Purpose Verification for Chain of Thought Prompting

The reviewed framework offers persistent epistemic states, temporal validity, and hard score ceilings, but reports no quantitative reasoning outcome and assumes rather than measures its semantic checker; constraint-guided step verification with end-to-end evidence therefore predates it.

reviewed_competitors.title: LAP: Language-Action Pre-Training Enables Zero-shot Cross-Embodiment Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: LAP already demonstrates zero-shot transfer to held-out embodiments by pretraining natural-language action representations. π0.7 instead retains continuous flow-matched robot actions and uses diverse demonstrations, metadata, history, and image goals; its cross-embodiment results therefore are not the first zero-shot VLA evidence, but a different transfer route.

reviewed_competitors.title: ForeAct: Steering Your VLA with Efficient Visual Foresight Planning
reviewed_competitors.difference: ForeAct already steers an existing VLA with generated future observations and textual subtasks, reporting 0.33-second 640×480 generation on one H100 and 87.4% success over 11 real tasks. π0.7 folds multi-view goals into training as one optional context channel alongside metadata and memory, but its 1.25-second four-H100 goal path is not the first or most compute-efficient visual-foresight interface.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Analogies Enable Efficient Cross-Embodiment Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Data Analogies controls viewpoint, morphology, scene, and trajectory alignment and reports that paired cross-embodiment demonstrations improve real-world transfer by 22.5 percentage points over larger unpaired mixtures. π0.7 instead relies on broad heterogeneous pretraining and optional visual goals; its results therefore do not isolate whether raw diversity or aligned analogies cause the transfer.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Atil et al. test five LLMs, eight tasks, and ten nominally deterministic runs, reporting up to 15% accuracy variation and a 70% best-worst gap plus explicit agreement metrics. reviewed_competitors.title: How Numerical Precision Affects Arithmetical Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feng et al. provide theory and experiments showing low numeric precision limits transformer arithmetic unless model size grows sharply. Their target is representational capacity for arithmetic, whereas the present paper studies runtime finite-difference discontinuities and decision margins; it therefore cannot claim to be the first precision analysis of LLM behavior broadly.

reviewed_competitors.title: LLM-42: Enabling Determinism in LLM Inference with Verified Speculation
reviewed_competitors.difference: LLM-42 uses a fixed-shape verify-and-rollback schedule to guarantee consistency while keeping a fast dynamic-batching path. It directly addresses repeated serving outputs and measures systems overhead; the present paper instead smooths deliberately perturbed embeddings and does not guarantee deterministic tokens.

reviewed_competitors.title: CoRun: Padding is Simple and Efficient for Deterministic LLM Inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: CoRun, submitted after the reviewed paper, exploits position-invariant kernels with isolated prefill and fixed-shape decode, reports deterministic inference and 15-324% higher throughput than batch-invariant approaches. It demonstrates that the paper's broad statement that distributed systems cannot guarantee reproducibility is too strong: determinism can be engineered even if unconstrained execution remains sensitive.

reviewed_competitors.difference: WSO directly compares no-decay and decay pretraining at 1B and 8B and attributes better post-SFT adaptability to flatter minima; it overlaps the central prescription more directly, while the reviewed paper adds MPA and local step-geometry analysis but has a negative direct decay intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Model Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This study links fine-tuning loss-landscape flatness directly to forgetting and applies SAM as mitigation; the reviewed work shifts the focus upstream to pretraining checkpoints and learning-rate schedules.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This work already finds that smaller SFT learning rates improve the target-versus-general trade-off and proposes token-adaptive loss reweighting; the reviewed work contributes feature-drift diagnostics but does not evaluate test SFT performance or establish the trade-off at matched validation quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting via Loss-Adaptive Learning Rates

reviewed_competitors.difference: This earlier paper already rewrites OLS predictions as a restricted query-key-value attention module in a transformed regressor space. The present paper adds a particular tied whitening-factor/identity-FFN/data-dependent-head factorization, a scalar reachability plot, and slow-fast/Hopfield commentary, but its headline OLS-attention equivalence substantially overlaps this prior result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers as Statisticians: Provable In-Context Learning with In-Context Algorithm Selection
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bai et al. construct transformers that implement least squares, ridge, Lasso, and other procedures from labeled context with near-optimal predictive guarantees and algorithm selection. This paper uses one linear layer but obtains exactness by making its projections and head specific to the same X and Y being fitted.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Von Oswald et al. show one linear self-attention layer can realize a regression gradient step and study task-shared weights learned across regression instances. The present work contrasts this with a nominal closed-form pass, but it externally supplies the instance's inverse covariance and label statistic rather than computing them in context.

reviewed_competitors.title: Trained Transformers Learn Linear Models In-Context
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. analyze gradient-flow training of a single linear self-attention layer over random regression tasks, prove convergence to a global minimum, and characterize covariate-shift brittleness. The present experiment learns one scalar for one fixed dataset and derives a related covariance mismatch without task-distribution training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linear Transformers are Versatile In-Context Learners
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vladymyrov et al. interpret each layer as maintaining an implicit regression weight and learn preconditioned, momentum-like algorithms under heterogeneous noise. This paper instead gives a static per-instance exact factorization and does not show a reusable learned optimizer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers learn to implement preconditioned gradient descent for in-context learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ahn et al. prove that global minima or critical points of linear-transformer pretraining implement one or more preconditioned gradient steps and that the preconditioner adapts to a task distribution. Here the desired preconditioner is analytically inserted from the one dataset before the forward pass.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schlag et al. already establish formal equivalence between linearized self-attention and slow-controller/fast-weight memory updated by outer products, including capacity limitations and corrective updates. The present paper specializes a fixed/fast split to an OLS covariance factorization but does not establish a new general memory mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hopfield Networks is All You Need
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramsauer et al. prove that the modern continuous Hopfield update is equivalent to transformer attention and has exponential storage under stated conditions. The present paper offers a qualitative path from its linear OLS block to that result rather than a new capacity theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context learning of closed form solution to simple linear regression task using transformer with linear self-attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hagiwara's July 2026 follow-up constructs a linear-self-attention Transformer that approximately obtains a simple least-squares closed form in context using layer normalization and tests whether training acquires the construction under L1 regularization. It is narrower in regression dimension and only approximate, but unlike the reviewed paper it explicitly targets reusable in-context computation rather than putting the current dataset's inverse covariance and labels into fixed weights. As post-target work it does not affect April priority, but it narrows the current claim that the reviewed factorization uniquely supplies a one-pass closed-form route.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
reviewed_competitors.difference: This controlled empirical study varies optimization, data, objective, and attention operations up to 1B parameters and interprets sinks as key biases; the survey summarizes its conclusions but still identifies training dynamics as unresolved and supplies no longitudinal experiment of its own.

reviewed_competitors.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper derives mutual reinforcement on a one-to-three-layer Bigram-Backcopy task and checks predicted extreme-token properties in Llama and OLMo; the survey places it among additional theories but does not distinguish toy-task proof from large-model correlation in its top-level synthesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Vision Transformers Need Registers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This study identifies high-norm background artifacts and tests learned register tokens in supervised and self-supervised ViTs; the survey treats those artifacts as visual attention sinks and register insertion as learnable-prefix utilization, a broader label not established by the original abstract alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Softpick: No Attention Sink, No Massive Activations with Rectified Softmax
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct mitigation and closest metric antecedent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Softpick directly tests a non-sum-to-one rectified attention rule and reports 0% sink rate, sparse maps, lower kurtosis, and quantization gains on 340M and 1.8B models in current v4; the survey cites selected results but provides no head-to-head normalization against other mitigation families.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper compares more than 30 gate variants on 15B MoE and 1.7B dense models trained on 3.5T tokens and isolates post-SDPA head gating as effective; the survey uses it as central mitigation evidence but cannot generalize its cost or benefits to ViTs and MLLMs without cross-architecture trials.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention Sinks Are Provably Necessary in Softmax Transformers: Evidence from Trigger-Conditional Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct necessity-theory antecedent and boundary case
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work proves sink necessity for a specific trigger-conditional task under normalized Softmax and shows ReLU attention avoids it; it supports the survey's normalization story only under explicit conditions, whereas the survey's language about inevitable emergence across transformers is broader than the theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unified View of Attention and Residual Sinks: Outlier-Driven Rescaling is Essential for Transformer Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper argues attention and residual outliers jointly rescale non-outlier components and that clipping them can hurt stability, while explicit gated rescaling preserves function; the survey includes the theory but its generic mitigation framing can still imply that sink removal itself is the goal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Identifying and Evaluating Inactive Heads in Pretrained LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Current v4 evaluates 12 head-inactivity scores across three model families and finds attention-sink scores alone miss more than 7% of inactive heads on average, while output-norm scores identify over 12% inactive heads; the survey does not cite this direct warning against treating sink attention as a sufficient importance measure.

reviewed_competitors.title: FOCUS: Fused Observation of Channels for Unveiling Spectra
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct learned-sink application antecedent and source-audit record
reviewed_competitors.difference: FOCUS v2 trains a [SINK] token with a negative mean-attention attraction term over selected heads and reports less than 1% parameters on hyperspectral ViT interpretation; the survey's Equation 31 replaces that objective with a positive squared norm whose minimization has the opposite direction.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Mechanistic Account of Attention Sinks in GPT-2: One Circuit, Broader Implications for Mitigation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ran-Milo et al. combine structural analysis with causal interventions to identify a GPT-2 sink circuit involving learned query bias, the first-layer MLP's transformation of position, and key projection structure. Crucially, each component is individually dispensable in architectures that still form sinks, directly supporting the survey's plural-mechanism caution while limiting any inference that its proposed levels constitute one architecture-invariant circuit.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Spike, the Sparse and the Sink: Anatomy of Massive Activations and Attention Sinks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sun et al. experimentally distinguish massive activations as global implicit-parameter-like signals from attention sinks as local, head-specific short-range biases, and report that changing pre-norm causes the phenomena to decouple. This is stronger primary evidence than a simple causal chain from activation outlier to sink and reinforces the need to phenotype the two quantities separately.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Do Attention Circuits Form? Developmental Trajectories of Capability and Attention-Sink Emergence Across Three 1B-Class Architectures
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu tracks 10 checkpoints in each of Pythia 1B, OLMo 1B, and OLMoE 1B-7B and reports gradual versus abrupt BOS-attractor trajectories, plus a 10-20x token separation between induction-circuit and sink formation in the DCLM models. As a single current study it is not a general resolution, but it supplies exactly the checkpoint-level, cross-architecture evidence the survey identifies as missing and argues against one universal emergence schedule.

reviewed_competitors.title: AuditBench: Evaluating Alignment Auditing Techniques on Models with Hidden Behaviors
reviewed_competitors.difference: AuditBench evaluates 56 models with 14 hidden behaviors in agentic and tool-use settings and finds strong black-box techniques, offering more natural behavior diversity. Pando contributes 720 tightly controlled planted-rule models and an explicit faithful/none/unfaithful explanation axis, but its fixed queries and synthetic tabular behavior are less realistic.

reviewed_competitors.title: Auditing language models for hidden objectives
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marks et al. run a blind multi-team audit of one model trained to exploit reward-model errors and follow with method-specific studies, maximizing realism and investigator freedom. Pando sacrifices open-endedness for exact repeated ground truth, budget matching, and controlled rationale access, but cannot reproduce the social and adaptive dynamics of a blind audit.

reviewed_competitors.title: RelP: Faithful and Efficient Circuit Discovery in Language Models via Relevance Patching
reviewed_competitors.relationship: method source and strongest evaluated competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jafari et al. validate RelP as a computational approximation to activation patching on IOI and sparse circuits, directly comparing relevance with intervention effects. Pando tests whether RelP output improves rule prediction across hundreds of model organisms, but does not patch its RelP-ranked components, so it supplies external predictive validity rather than an internal causal-localization replication.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision
reviewed_competitors.difference: Burns et al. infer binary truth directions from unlabeled activations via logical consistency and evaluate hidden knowledge when outputs are unreliable. Pando targets a model-specific decision rule from ten labeled behaviors and compares many tool channels; it recovers behavioral policy structure rather than truth and uses supervised query labels plus an external rule extractor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mallen et al. train quirky models to answer incorrectly under a trigger and evaluate probes and anomaly detection for truth independent of output. Pando instead plants diverse decision trees and manipulates rationale faithfulness while the binary label remains correct, enabling exact field-level rule recovery but not testing knowledge-output disagreement in the same way.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eliciting Secret Knowledge from Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: The secret-knowledge benchmark evaluates whether prompts, prefills, and other elicitation techniques recover information a model has been trained to conceal, emphasizing black-box access. Pando explicitly controls whether prefills carry true, absent, or distractor information and asks whether white-box channels improve held-out policy prediction beyond the same transcript.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Turpin et al. induce natural prompt biases and show models rationalize biased answers without mentioning the true influence across 13 tasks. Pando trains disjoint distractor rationales with exact known true fields, offering cleaner causal ground truth and method comparison but a more artificial, nonadaptive form of unfaithfulness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sleeper Agents: Training Deceptive LLMs that Persist Through Safety Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hubinger et al. construct conditional backdoors whose deceptive behavior persists through safety and adversarial training, including models trained to reason about deception. Pando's model always emits the correct planted label plus a fixed wrong rationale and never reacts to the auditor, so it is a controlled faithfulness test rather than a strategic deception benchmark.

reviewed_competitors.title: Monitoring Reasoning Models for Misbehavior and the Risks of Promoting Obfuscation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baker et al. evaluate chain-of-thought monitoring and show that optimizing against monitors can promote obfuscated reasoning, directly studying adversarial pressure. Pando fixes an unfaithful rationale distribution before the audit and does not optimize the target against any method, so its robustness results cannot establish performance under monitor-aware evasion.

reviewed_competitors.title: RAVEL: Evaluating Interpretability Methods on Disentangling Language Model Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. evaluate whether representation methods disentangle entity attributes under explicit causal interchange criteria and introduce distributed alignment search. Pando evaluates whether tool summaries improve held-out behavioral rule prediction with explanation controls; it has broader audit-channel comparison but does not require an internal intervention to localize the learned rule.

reviewed_competitors.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.difference: MIB evaluates circuit localization and causal-variable localization using faithfulness, completeness, and concision criteria across four tasks and five models; attribution and mask optimization lead circuit localization while supervised DAS leads causal variables and SAEs do not beat neurons. Pando measures whether tool summaries improve prospective rule prediction under controlled rationale access, but never intervenes on its ranked internals, so it evaluates a different and weaker causal criterion.

reviewed_competitors.title: CausalGym: Benchmarking causal interpretability methods on linguistic tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: CausalGym asks whether learned representations can be intervened on to causally change targeted linguistic behavior and uses arbitrary-mapping controls; DAS performs best across Pythia scales. Pando supplies many more planted behavioral rules and explanation controls, but its field relevance evidence is input sensitivity plus score association rather than an internal causal intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: MechELK: A Mechanistic Interpretability Framework for Eliciting Latent Knowledge in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: MechELK combines SAE feature analysis, activation patching, causal probing, and representation steering on TruthfulQA, a deceptive-alignment set, and Quirky LMs, reporting direct elicitation of information hidden by incorrect or evasive outputs. Pando offers cleaner repeated ground truth and transcript-matched comparisons, whereas MechELK pursues intervention and elicitation on more natural knowledge tasks but lacks Pando's factorial rationale control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inference Time Causal Probing in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: HDMI uses the model's native output gradient to steer hidden states and evaluates intervention completeness and selectivity on CausalGym and agreement tasks. It is a direct post-Pando example of gradient information being tested through internal intervention; Pando instead finds gradient summaries predict output-relevant fields but does not establish that the scored representation mediates the planted decision.

reviewed_competitors.title: Make Continual Learning Stronger via C-Flat
reviewed_competitors.difference: C-Flat combines zeroth-order sharpness and first-order flatness at every update; Turbo retains its objective components but caches their orthogonal directions and conditionally skips extra passes.

reviewed_competitors.title: C-Flat++: Towards a More Efficient and Powerful Framework for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: C-Flat++ v2, from overlapping authors and released before Turbo, already switches selectively between SGD and C-Flat using a squared-gradient-norm sharpness proxy, emphasizes later iterations, and reports roughly 25-30% C-Flat usage. Turbo's narrower distinction is caching and rescaling both orthogonal sharpness and first-order-flatness corrections plus task-stage reuse; the target paper does not cite or compare C-Flat++.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Sharpness: A Flatness Decomposition Framework for Efficient Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: FLAD v1 decomposes sharpness perturbations into gradient-aligned and stochastic-noise components, applies the optimizer in only selected epochs, and directly compares with C-Flat across CL methods. Turbo instead reuses temporally cached orthogonal update components and norm triggers; it does not cite or compare FLAD.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAM introduces the two-pass zeroth-order min-max update in ordinary training; Turbo targets continual learning and additionally approximates a first-order flatness branch.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Efficient and Scalable Sharpness-Aware Minimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: LookSAM periodically computes and reuses an orthogonal SAM correction; Turbo extends the cache idea to both SAM-like and GAM-like components and adds task-stage scheduling and triggers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Norm Aware Minimization Seeks First-Order Flatness and Improves Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: GAM defines and optimizes first-order flatness with extra perturbed gradients; Turbo's main novelty is approximating that branch through a cached orthogonal component in CL.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Sharpness-aware Minimization for Improved Training of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: ESAM reduces cost through stochastic weight perturbation and sharpness-sensitive data selection, not temporal caching of curvature directions or continual-task scheduling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Randomized Sharpness-Aware Training for Boosting Computational Efficiency in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: RST selects SAM versus SGD using a predefined Bernoulli schedule; Turbo uses gradient-norm triggers, task-stage intervals, and cached first- as well as zeroth-order corrections.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Adaptive Policy to Employ Sharpness-Aware Minimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: AE-SAM adaptively switches SAM and ERM from landscape statistics and proves a SAM-rate result; Turbo adds first-order flatness caching and a CL-stage schedule, but its cache-bias rate remains conditional.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization Efficiently Selects Flatter Minima Late in Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shows that applying SAM only late in conventional training can match full SAM; Turbo instead lengthens reuse across continual stages and approximates two flatness terms throughout selected updates.

reviewed_competitors.title: SoftJAX & SoftTorch: Empowering Automatic Differentiation Libraries with Informative Gradients
reviewed_competitors.difference: SoftJAX/SoftTorch packages soft thresholds, Boolean/fuzzy operators, sorting/ranking, and straight-through gradients as general drop-in AD primitives with benchmarks. Minkowski Image Loss hand-builds a domain-specific sigmoid/Gödel/morphology/topology chain and additionally learns a neural emulator with geometric heads; it does not compare gradient quality against the broader library alternatives.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Surrogates via Deep Embedding
reviewed_competitors.difference: Patel et al. learn an embedding whose distance approximates edit distance or rotated-box IoU and use it to post-tune recognition/detection models, directly establishing learned surrogate losses before this paper. The present work predicts explicit physical descriptors and hard-codes monotonicity/isoperimetry, but its learned loss does not improve its downstream M score.

reviewed_competitors.title: Topology-Preserving Deep Image Segmentation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu et al. derive a differentiable loss that enforces ground-truth Betti-number topology in segmentation and evaluate topology errors across natural and biomedical data. Minkowski Image Loss instead combines multilevel area/perimeter/component summaries for continuous precipitation and supplies analytical and learned routes, but never compares to a persistent-homology loss on its own topology target.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Topological Loss Function for Deep-Learning based Image Segmentation using Persistent Homology
reviewed_competitors.difference: Clough et al. backpropagate persistent-homology topology priors expressed by Betti numbers in 2D and 3D segmentation, including weakly supervised settings. The present paper uses GUDHI only to generate filtered regression targets, then approximates or emulates them; its connected-component substitution and absence of β1 in Equation 1 narrow its topological coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiable Programming for Earth System Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gelbrecht et al. frame differentiable Earth-system models, hybrid process/ML components, calibration, and extremes at system scale. Minkowski Image Loss contributes a concrete image-morphology surrogate within this agenda, but evaluates radar super-resolution rather than differentiation through an Earth-system simulator or parameter calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Surrogate-Based Differentiable Pipeline for Shape Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rehmann et al. replace nondifferentiable meshing and simulation with a full-field 3D U-Net surrogate and optimize aerodynamic shape end to end. This paper emulates compact geometry metrics rather than a physical field and adds hard output constraints; both face optimizer-induced distribution shift, but the present paper's Figure 7 directly shows a severe version of it.

reviewed_competitors.title: DiffTune: Optimizing CPU Simulator Parameters with Learned Differentiable Surrogates
reviewed_competitors.difference: DiffTune learns a differentiable approximation to a nondifferentiable CPU simulator, optimizes simulator parameters through it, and evaluates the resulting parameters back in the original simulator. Minkowski Image Loss similarly exposes surrogate gradients, but does not close the analogous loop by validating every optimized field with the exact descriptor during downstream training or guarding against surrogate exploitation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Residual Corrective Diffusion Modeling for Km-scale Atmospheric Downscaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: CorrDiff pairs a deterministic mean predictor with residual diffusion for 25-km-to-2-km atmospheric downscaling and evaluates distributions, spectra, CRPS, and coherent weather cases. Minkowski Image Loss instead regularizes a deterministic precipitation U-Net by global geometry and uses a conditional diffusion baseline; its perfect-model OPERA setup and single-sample metrics are narrower than CorrDiff's generative uncertainty evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Geiping et al. train Huginn-0125 at 3.5B parameters on 800B tokens and evaluate reasoning gains with recurrence; the target reuses that checkpoint to resolve phase-specific cyclic states and stage metrics but does not re-evaluate its reasoning performance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Teaching Pretrained Language Models to Think Deeper with Retrofitted Recurrence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary source for the retrofitted Llama, OLMo-2, and TinyLlama checkpoints analyzed by the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: McLeish et al. propose a recurrence curriculum that converts feedforward checkpoints and show math performance per compute; the target studies their internal fixed-state and mixing-stage dynamics rather than proposing or benchmarking the retrofit method.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary source for Ouro and a direct large-scale looped-language-model competitor with entropy-regularized depth allocation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhu et al. pretrain Ouro on as many as 7.7T tokens and center performance and latent-trace alignment; the target finds Ouro's stage curves repeat but drift at extreme recurrence and distinguishes low successive change from strict endpoint convergence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Two-Scale Latent Dynamics for Recurrent-Depth Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest antecedent explicitly analyzing recurrent latent-state geometry and using it for early exit.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pappone et al. distinguish small within-block refinement from larger drift across multiple recurrent blocks and validate a second-order exit rule; the target focuses on one cyclic block's layer phases, attention stabilization, and feedforward stage repetition, without an adaptive-exit evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Latent Chain-of-Thought? Decoding the Depth-Recurrent Transformer
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct mechanistic probe of Huginn's latent reasoning and the behavioral value of more recurrences.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lu et al. use Logit Lens and Coda Lens on arithmetic, finding limited interpretable latent CoT, layer-dependent probe inconsistency, and marginal recurrence gains; the target measures dynamical and attention-stage structure across several architectures but does not decode semantic steps or test answer gains.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational feedforward stages-of-inference antecedent cited as the conceptual baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lad et al. infer four stages from layer deletion/swapping and behavioral robustness across feedforward LLMs; the target transfers the stage lens to cyclic depth recurrence using mixing diagnostics, but offers weaker behavioral validation of the claimed stage functions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention Sinks and Compression Valleys in LLMs are Two Sides of the Same Coin
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct source of the Mix-Compress-Refine interpretation, ColSum/mixing diagnostics, and massive-activation mechanism applied in the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Queipo-de-Llano et al. provide theory and targeted evidence connecting massive activations, attention sinks, and residual compression across 410M-120B feedforward models; the target applies these metrics to recurrent phases and adds one coarse MLP lesion, so the metrics themselves are antecedent rather than novel.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Theoretical and empirical antecedent for looped Transformers as depth-efficient latent-reasoning systems.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Saunshi et al. prove expressivity for iterative reasoning and compare looped with shallow and deep feedforward models on synthetic and downstream tasks; the target asks what states and attention phases recur inside trained language models, without advancing expressivity or task results.

reviewed_competitors.title: Path Independent Equilibrium Models Can Better Exploit Test-Time Computation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strong equilibrium-model antecedent linking convergent dynamics to upward generalization through interventions and per-example analysis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Anil et al. measure path independence across initializations and causally improve or degrade it to test harder-example generalization; the target resolves cyclic per-layer endpoints and attention continuity but neither tests path independence nor causally links stability to performance.

reviewed_competitors.title: End-to-end Algorithm Synthesis with Recurrent Networks: Logical Extrapolation Without Overthinking
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Key antecedent for excessive-recurrence failure and for reinjecting the problem state to stabilize recurrent computation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bansal et al. demonstrate overthinking behaviorally and use recall plus progressive training to prevent it on algorithmic extrapolation; the target studies the architectural association of input injection with endpoint dynamics but does not test a matched accuracy intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers are Better at Learning Learning Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Early looped-Transformer training and iterative-algorithm antecedent with explicit parameter-efficiency evaluation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. train looped Transformers to emulate in-context data-fitting algorithms and achieve comparable performance with under 10% of standard-Transformer parameters; the target analyzes natural-language checkpoints and stage structure rather than learning-algorithm accuracy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thinking Deeper, Not Longer: Depth-Recurrent Transformers for Compositional Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous direct recurrence-stability and compositional-generalization competitor preceding the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen combines final-output-only training, LayerScale, and identity-biased recurrence and measures a task-complexity computational frontier on graph, logic, and relational text tasks; the target gives broader pretrained-language-model internal diagnostics but no compositional task frontier or controlled stability mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stabilizing Recurrent Dynamics for Test-Time Scalable Latent Reasoning in Looped Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target direct competitor that turns stable fixed points into an explicit trainable objective and tests their relation to recurrence scaling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: STARS regularizes the Jacobian spectral radius with random loop sampling to target asymptotically stable fixed points and evaluates arithmetic and math performance across recurrence depth; the target predates it and offers descriptive cyclic-phase and stage analysis without spectral stability enforcement.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bridging the Gap Between Latent and Explicit Reasoning with Looped Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target looped latent-reasoning competitor with direct supervision and interpretability checks on intermediate thought positions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: LOTUS parallelizes latent blocks and supervises each with gold CoT-step tokens, reporting 3B-scale accuracy, 2.5x-6.9x thought-phase latency reductions, and LM-head recovery of intermediate steps; the target analyzes unsupervised recurrent states and attention stages but cannot identify semantic reasoning content.

reviewed_competitors.title: Solve the Loop: Attractor Models for Language and Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target fixed-point language-model competitor that makes convergence an explicit solver and training primitive.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Attractor Models refine backbone embeddings by solving a fixed point and train through implicit differentiation, then report language-model and reasoning quality against stable looped baselines. The target instead observes recurrence-128 phase dynamics in existing LoopLMs and does not train an equilibrium solver or compare task quality at matched convergence tolerances.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepLoop: Depth Scaling for Looped Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target architecture competitor for stabilizing tied recurrent depth through visit-aware residual scaling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepLoop derives residual-scaling rules that depend on repeated parameter visits and tests validation loss and downstream accuracy at GPT-2 scale. The target diagnoses normalization and input-injection associations but supplies neither a tied-depth scaling rule nor a controlled performance improvement.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target direct input-conditioning and fixed-point-design competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Source-Centered State Evolution constructs an input-dependent anchor that is exactly invariant at zero deviation and evaluates the resulting recurrent quality frontier. This directly narrows the target's observational input-injection result: the target finds injection associated with a recurrence-128 endpoint but neither guarantees anchor invariance nor shows that the stable architecture improves quality.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct physics RLVR competitor and negative evidence about interpreting exact answer reward as law learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: BeamPERL uses exact symbolic solvers on beam statics and finds that continued reward optimization preserves reward while robustness under moved supports deteriorates; Sim2Reason spans more mechanics phenomena and real benchmarks but omits comparable topological-shift and checkpoint-robustness tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: P1: Mastering Physics Olympiads with Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct physics-specialized reinforcement-learning competitor evaluated on olympiad problems.
reviewed_competitors.difference: P1 trains much larger and mixture-of-experts physics reasoners on curated real physics tasks and reports medal-level results across competitions; Sim2Reason's distinctive contribution is simulator-only synthetic post-training, while its one same-size checkpoint comparison is not compute- or data-matched.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Physical Reasoning with the PHYSICS Dataset
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct alternative to simulator synthesis for supplying broad, quality-controlled physics training and evaluation data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PHYSICS curates 16,568 textbook problems across mechanics, electromagnetism, thermodynamics, optics, and modern physics and introduces a rule-plus-model evaluator; Sim2Reason offers procedural quantity and controlled interventions but is centered on manually encoded mechanics and a simple numeric tolerance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Enhancing LLMs for Physics Problem-Solving using Reinforcement Learning with Human-AI Feedback
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier direct application of reinforcement learning to language-model physics problem solving.
reviewed_competitors.difference: RLHAIF compares PPO, DPO, and ReMax on the human-authored PhyQA corpus using human and AI feedback metrics; Sim2Reason removes per-answer feedback from generation by using executable simulator outcomes, but validates only final numeric proximity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Solving olympiad geometry without human demonstrations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strong antecedent for producing olympiad-level training signal from an executable synthetic world without human proof demonstrations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AlphaGeometry generates and symbolically traces back millions of exact Euclidean theorems and proofs for a neuro-symbolic solver; Sim2Reason generates approximate continuous mechanics outcomes for general language-model RL, with broader transfer but weaker verification and no proof trace.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepSeek-Prover: Advancing Theorem Proving in LLMs through Large-Scale Synthetic Data
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Large-scale executable-verifier antecedent for synthetic reasoning data and filtering.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepSeek-Prover creates roughly eight million Lean statements and proof data under an exact formal checker; Sim2Reason targets informal physical reasoning and real-benchmark transfer, but its simulator and relative-tolerance verifier cannot provide theorem-prover-level soundness.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational outcome-reward reasoning and group-policy-optimization antecedent motivating the target's RL stage.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepSeek-R1 establishes large-scale reasoning RL and distillation across general verifiable domains; Sim2Reason's novelty lies in constructing a new executable physics question source and applying GSPO rather than proposing the reasoning-RL paradigm itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: PhysGym: Benchmarking LLMs in Interactive Physics Discovery with Controlled Priors
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct counterpoint for validating whether a model discovers physical mechanisms rather than answering static simulator-derived questions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PhysGym makes agents actively design experiments under budgets and scores both hypothesis accuracy and model fidelity while systematically hiding physical priors; Sim2Reason trains on static QA and evaluates final answers, so it cannot separate mechanism discovery from learned templates as directly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spurious Local Minima are Common in Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Safran and Shamir establish spurious minima in the same Gaussian population teacher-student model through rigorous computer-assisted constructions and basin experiments; the present paper adds overlap fixed-point families and trajectory-level reachability, but its family classification is not certified exhaustive.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Effects of Mild Over-parameterization on the Optimization Landscape of Shallow ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Safran, Yehudai, and Shamir prove that duplicating neurons introduces negative Hessian directions at embedded spurious minima; the present paper numerically argues that newly coupled higher-order families can survive beyond that local construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Principle of Least Symmetry Breaking in Shallow ReLU Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arjevani and Field derive group-theoretic isotropy patterns and document limits of least symmetry breaking; the present paper maps a selected two-block pattern into Q/R dynamics and estimated attraction frequencies.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analytic Study of Families of Spurious Minima in Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks: A Tale of Symmetry II
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arjevani and Field analytically construct symmetry-indexed spurious-minimum families and study objectives and Hessian spectra at finite dimension; the present paper's incremental contribution is embedding related families in mean-field overlap trajectories and basin-frequency experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Annihilation of Spurious Minima in Two-Layer ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arjevani and Field rigorously characterize negative directions that annihilate specified spurious minima under extra units; the present paper emphasizes that this does not certify absence of distinct coupled traps born in the wider space.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hidden Minima in Two-Layer ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arjevani shows that Hessian and symmetry labels can miss whether minima are connected or hidden and uses tangency arcs for finer geometry; this narrows the present paper's claim that combining block symmetries with ODE endpoints supplies a global landscape characterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamics of stochastic gradient descent for two-layer neural networks in the teacher-student setup
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goldt and coauthors derive exact high-dimensional ODEs for online SGD and compare first- versus both-layer training under overparameterization; the present paper applies the overlap formalism to numerically map stationary families and their reachability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spurious Valleys in Two-layer Neural Network Optimization Landscapes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Venturi, Bandeira, and Bruna give width- and intrinsic-dimension conditions for absence or presence of spurious valleys across activations; the present paper is narrower in distribution and architecture but resolves selected finite-width ReLU fixed-point bands.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Gradient Flow on Population Loss to Learning with Stochastic Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kale and coauthors give conditions under which convergence of population gradient flow transfers to finite-step GD/SGD through Lyapunov potentials. The present paper instead matches online-SGD overlap ODEs to gradient flow only after the eta-squared term vanishes under eta=o_d(1), so its SGD statement is narrower and trajectory-specific.

reviewed_competitors.title: Saddle-to-Saddle Dynamics Explains A Simplicity Bias Across Neural Network Architectures
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang, Saxe, and Latham analyze invariant manifolds and saddle-to-saddle plateaus across linear, ReLU, convolutional, and attention models. This paper instead studies population-risk attractor bands and anti-aligned-unit families in a Gaussian soft-committee model; its admitted mixed-state slowdowns are adjacent but not a general saddle-to-saddle derivation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Matrix3D: Large Photogrammetry Model All-in-One
reviewed_competitors.difference: Matrix3D already uses one multimodal diffusion transformer and mask learning for pose estimation, depth prediction, and novel-view synthesis from incomplete modality pairs, then can produce 3D Gaussian splats. Rays as Pixels narrows to video and cameras, removes explicit depth/3DGS, and contributes an RGB-compatible ray latent plus two-way video flow; therefore the broad 'unified pose and generation' novelty is preceded, while direct video-trajectory joint modeling remains distinctive.

reviewed_competitors.title: Cameras as Rays: Pose Estimation via Ray Diffusion
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cameras as Rays represents cameras as distributed ray bundles and diffuses them for uncertainty-aware sparse-view pose estimation. Rays as Pixels adopts the same camera-as-rays premise but compresses origin and direction into three-channel d+o images, routes them through a pretrained video VAE, and adds camera-conditioned video synthesis; it is broader in task but less directly geometry-specialized.

reviewed_competitors.title: DiffusionSfM: Predicting Structure and Motion via Ray Origin and Endpoint Diffusion
reviewed_competitors.difference: DiffusionSfM denoises pixelwise ray origins and endpoints in a global frame to infer both scene structure and camera poses, explicitly modeling missing data and unbounded coordinates. Rays as Pixels discards explicit endpoints/depth and instead models d+o jointly with appearance video, enabling synthesis but relying on VAE decoding and Procrustes for geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: MotionCtrl: A Unified and Flexible Motion Controller for Video Generation
reviewed_competitors.difference: MotionCtrl injects known camera trajectories and separately controls camera and object motion in a video generator. Rays as Pixels makes cameras a denoised output as well as a condition and can infer poses, but its training/evaluation is static-scene dominated and does not demonstrate MotionCtrl's explicit object/camera-motion separation.

reviewed_competitors.title: VD3D: Taming Large Video Diffusion Transformers for 3D Camera Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: VD3D adapts a large video diffusion transformer with ControlNet-like spatiotemporal Plücker conditioning for known-camera generation. Rays as Pixels replaces fixed six-channel conditioning with a generated three-channel VAE modality and supports reverse pose inference, but Table 4 shows better FID/FVD at generally weaker trajectory adherence and its Plücker ablation is encoder-confounded.

reviewed_competitors.title: Wonderland: Navigating 3D Scenes from a Single Image
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wonderland uses a camera-controlled video diffusion latent to feed forward-predict 3D Gaussian scenes from one image, targeting navigable 3D reconstruction with known paths. Rays as Pixels has no explicit 3D representation and can also generate cameras; it wins reported FID/FVD but Wonderland follows Re10K trajectories more accurately in Table 4.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Sequence-to-Sequence Generative Neural Rendering
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kaleido unifies 3D and video in a decoder-only rectified-flow transformer and renders arbitrary known 6-DoF target views from arbitrary reference views without explicit 3D. Rays as Pixels additionally samples/infer cameras and uses VAE-compatible raxels; Kaleido provides much tighter DL3DV/T&T trajectory adherence in Table 4, while Rays reports better FID/FVD.

reviewed_competitors.title: VGGT: Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: VGGT directly predicts camera parameters, depth, point maps, and tracks from one to hundreds of views in under a second and is specialized for visual geometry. Rays as Pixels generates appearance and cameras without explicit 3D, but VGGT beats its mRRA on all three pose sets and is also used as the external validator for its generated trajectories.

reviewed_competitors.title: RealCam: Real-Time Novel-View Video Generation with Interactive Camera Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: RealCam distills a camera-controlled video-to-video teacher into a few-step causal streaming model and explicitly treats latency, variable length, and loop closure. It postdates Rays as Pixels and assumes a requested camera trajectory rather than generating or inferring cameras, but raises a stronger efficiency and interactive-control bar absent from the 20B joint model's evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: ActCam: Zero-Shot Joint Camera and 3D Motion Control for Video Generation
reviewed_competitors.difference: ActCam provides training-free per-frame intrinsic/extrinsic camera control together with transferred character motion and evaluates camera adherence and human preference. It does not infer camera trajectories or learn a video-camera joint distribution, but directly addresses dynamic content and control fidelity where Rays as Pixels is static-scene dominated and trails dedicated baselines.

reviewed_competitors.title: Track2Act: Predicting Point Tracks from Internet Videos enables Generalizable Robot Manipulation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Sparse point-track prediction and planning competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Track2Act predicts goal-conditioned tracks from web video and converts them to robot actions with a residual control policy; Myriad predicts open-ended stochastic scene motion and uses model-based rollout search, but only demonstrates action choice in simulated billiards.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generative Image Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: It predicts dense Fourier-domain motion textures for natural oscillatory dynamics and can render looping video; Myriad predicts arbitrary sparse 2D trajectories as causal increments and targets interactions, open-set videos, and rapid branching rather than periodic motion.

reviewed_competitors.title: DINO-Foresight: Looking into the Future with DINO
reviewed_competitors.difference: DINO-Foresight autoregressively predicts dense pretrained-VFM feature maps and attaches task heads for future scene understanding, avoiding pixels but retaining dense semantic state; Myriad predicts only selected point coordinates, making massive stochastic branching cheaper but omitting general future-feature tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: DINO-WM: World Models on Pre-trained Visual Features enable Zero-shot Planning
reviewed_competitors.difference: DINO-WM predicts dense DINO patch features under action sequences and optimizes actions in six closed environments; Myriad emits interpretable sparse point motion in open-set imagery and samples counterfactual actions cheaply, but lacks comparable multi-environment control evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Diffusion Forcing: Next-token Prediction Meets Full-Sequence Diffusion
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Causal diffusion rollout and planning competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Diffusion Forcing trains sequence tokens at independent noise levels and supports variable-horizon video/state rollout plus guidance; Myriad uses ordinary teacher-forced causal point increments with a separate flow head and gains speed by avoiding dense sequence tokens.

reviewed_competitors.title: iPOKE: Poking a Still Image for Controlled Stochastic Video Synthesis
reviewed_competitors.difference: iPOKE maps an initial frame and local poke to diverse dense videos through an invertible kinematics representation; Myriad retains only sparse trajectory dynamics, supports many query points and autoregressive branching, and therefore avoids video rendering cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: ProbDiffFlow: An Efficient Learning-Free Framework for Probabilistic Single-Image Optical Flow Estimation
reviewed_competitors.difference: ProbDiffFlow synthesizes future frames with a pretrained diffusion model and aggregates optical flow, remaining dense and paying the visual tax; Myriad is trained end to end to directly sample sparse long-horizon tracks and is designed for iterative interactions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers as Programmable Computers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Giannou et al. program a frozen looped transformer as a punchcard computer and provide the SUBLEQ-style baseline; Loom adds 21 extended opcodes, a C-subset compiler, direct one-layer subtraction, browser artifacts, and FPGA synthesis, while inheriting the same need to control finite-precision routing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simulation of Graph Algorithms with Looped Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: It augments looped transformers with graph-interaction heads and proves constructions for Dijkstra, BFS, DFS, and strongly connected components, including an explicit finite-precision limitation; Loom targets a general finite ISA and concrete C/browser/hardware deployment but provides less complete-system proof.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped ReLU MLPs May Be All You Need as Practical Programmable Computers
reviewed_competitors.difference: It constructs a 23-layer looped ReLU MLP for programmable computation without attention; Loom uses attention for random-access routing and reduces depth to eight through a wide opcode decoder and shared subtract core, but does not compare matched nonzero work or latency.

reviewed_competitors.title: ALTA: Compiler-Based Analysis of Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: ALTA compiles each high-level symbolic program, including loops, into Universal Transformer weights and studies length-invariant algorithms and learnability; Loom fixes weights to an ISA, compiles restricted C into state columns, and emphasizes reusable binaries and deployment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tracr compiles individual RASP programs such as sorting and parenthesis checking into standard decoder-only transformer weights for mechanistic ground truth; Loom instead hard-codes an interpreter-like ISA once and places each program in mutable state.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Length Generalization with Turing Programs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Universal algorithm execution and length-generalization competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Turing Programs expose text-like step traces and prove a RASP simulation of arbitrary Turing machines while empirically training transformers to generalize in length; Loom executes a concrete fixed-width binary state recurrently and does not establish unbounded length generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Softmax Transformers are Turing-Complete
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves Turing completeness for length-generalizable softmax chain-of-thought transformers under specified language and positional-encoding conditions; Loom uses a finite fixed tensor and approximate content addressing, so that theorem does not supply Loom's missing recurrent numerical guarantee.

reviewed_competitors.title: Constant Bit-size Transformers Are Turing Complete
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li and Wang prove a constant-bit-size transformer can simulate arbitrary Turing machines when context length grows sufficiently and characterize its space complexity; Loom changes ell and d with n and fixes context/state per deployed machine, prioritizing an executable finite computer over an unbounded theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Add, Multiply, and Execute Algorithmic Instructions Exactly with Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves high-probability learnability of binary permutation, addition, multiplication, and SBN using ensembles of trained two-layer networks in the infinite-width NTK regime; Loom analytically constructs one finite recurrent machine with a broader ISA and systems artifacts, but exactness beyond its local subtractor is empirical.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prystawski et al. prove a reasoning gap for chain-structured probabilistic models when training observations are local and show that intermediate-variable inference reduces bias. Nadgir et al. instead derive a branch-count/sample-dimension error surrogate and an optimal balanced degree; they do not model the training-data dependency graph as explicitly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feng et al. use circuit complexity to separate direct bounded-depth Transformer computation from constant-size autoregressive CoT constructions for arithmetic, equations, and dynamic programming. The reviewed paper is architecture-agnostic and focuses on statistical error and optimal branching, but its guarantees are conditional bounds rather than expressivity separations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. show that T CoT steps let low-depth, constant-precision Transformers realize computations described by size-T Boolean circuits, with controlled serial tasks. Nadgir et al. explain when more steps should help or hurt through branch-count error, a different question that does not characterize Transformer computational expressivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Theory of Learning with Autoregressive Chain of Thought
reviewed_competitors.difference: Joshi et al. formalize observed and latent CoT learning for iterated time-invariant next-token classes and derive sample/computational complexity, including horizon-independent sample complexity in key settings. Nadgir et al. assume the step predictor is already well trained and instead optimize a geometric error surrogate over degree and depth.

reviewed_competitors.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. already establish inverted-U accuracy versus CoT length, derive optimal-length scaling from a trade-off between subtask difficulty and accumulated errors, and test task difficulty, model capability, SFT, RL, and length-aware filtering. Nadgir et al.'s narrower new element is a class-count/intrinsic-dimension derivation that predicts a balanced degree exp(d/2), not the existence of an optimal length itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. identify concrete task properties where verbal deliberation hurts and report drops up to 36.3 percentage points across implicit learning, visual recognition, and exception-heavy classification. Nadgir et al. predict harm from small effective branching degree, but do not map that latent degree to these natural negative-task categories.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shojaee et al. evaluate reasoning and non-reasoning models in controllable puzzles, finding low-, medium-, and high-complexity regimes and eventual accuracy collapse with reduced reasoning effort. Nadgir et al. supplies a branching/depth surrogate for one possible regime transition but uses much simpler Boolean trees and does not explain the high-complexity collapse.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wei et al. establish that few-shot intermediate demonstrations can unlock large-model arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic performance. Nadgir et al. attempts to explain this phenomenon through decomposition geometry and also predicts harmful regimes, but does not reproduce the original scale-emergence comparison or establish that its degree proxy mediates those gains.

reviewed_competitors.title: Same Pre-training Loss, Better Downstream: Implicit Bias Matters for Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. establish the same-loss/different-transfer phenomenon and identify flatness as a useful implicit-bias proxy, including SAM interventions. Nexus directly inherits that evaluation frame but proposes task-minimum closeness and gradient agreement as a distinct geometry, tested at larger autoregressive scales.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAM explicitly minimizes worst-neighborhood loss to favor flat solutions and has broad supervised evidence. Nexus instead aligns gradients across microbatches to favor clustered task minima, while its appendix also claims a third-order directional-flatness effect, creating overlap that requires a matched SAM baseline at LLM scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness-Aware Pretraining Mitigates Catastrophic Forgetting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Watts et al. show that SAM, large learning rates, and short annealing can improve post-training retention at similar base-model quality, including a 1B checkpoint intervention. Nexus targets zero-shot downstream loss through closeness and reports broader pretraining scales, but lacks this direct forgetting and quantization validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: On First-Order Meta-Learning Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reptile repeatedly trains on sampled tasks and moves an initialization toward adapted weights; its analysis already connects sequential first-order updates to within-task gradient agreement. Nexus repurposes a closely related displacement mechanism across pretraining microbatches to optimize cross-source agreement without an explicit adaptation objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: PCGrad detects negative task-gradient cosine and projects away only conflicting components, improving supervised and RL multi-task learning. Nexus continuously rewards cosine agreement between random microbatches and targets OOD generalization, but does not compare whether selective conflict removal preserves specialization better.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent for Multi-task Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: CAGrad regularizes average-loss optimization by the worst local task improvement and provides convergence to an average-loss minimum. Nexus seeks average pairwise agreement through an implicit approximation; it scales to LLM pretraining but lacks CAGrad's explicit worst-task guarantee and direct task-level sampling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharp-MAML: Sharpness-Aware Model-Agnostic Meta Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sharp-MAML combines bilevel task adaptation with explicit flatness regularization and gives convergence and generalization analysis. Nexus avoids validation-task adaptation and second-order differentiation, but its claim of a combined closeness and third-order flatness bias overlaps conceptually and warrants direct ablation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wen et al. show optimizer gains often shrink with model size, can reverse late in training, and depend on optimizer-specific tuning across scales and token ratios. Nexus follows their baseline setup but uses point estimates and matched hyperparameters, so their methodology directly cautions against interpreting its monotone five-size sweep as established scaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimizers Qualitatively Alter Solutions And We Should Leverage This
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pascanu et al. broadly argue that optimizers encode qualitative inductive biases rather than only convergence speed. Nexus supplies one concrete LLM mechanism and experiment suite for that agenda, but does not establish that task-minimum closeness is the unique or best qualitative property.

reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves, under deep-linear singular-vector assumptions, that the symmetry-induced balancing gap breaks at EoS and decays monotonically, and analyzes two-period oscillations and period doubling. That prior result substantially narrows the reviewed paper's EoS novelty to its eta-drift observable, ReLU measurements, and proposed spectral exponent closure; the latter is not a comparable rigorous EoS theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Abide by the Law and Follow the Flow: Conservation Laws for Gradient Flows
reviewed_competitors.difference: It defines and computes maximal independent gradient-flow conservation laws via Lie-algebraic methods; the reviewed paper assumes a particular L-1 family and studies discrete breaking without establishing its exact rank or maximality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Regularization Implies balancedness in the deep linear network
reviewed_competitors.difference: It uses geometric invariant theory to decompose a regularizing flow on fibers from learning flow on the balanced manifold and proves exponential convergence of a balancing flow. The reviewed work instead measures plain finite-GD departure from balance and fits a spectral exponent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: It establishes progressive sharpening, short-timescale oscillation, and Hessian sharpness near 2/eta on standard architectures and datasets. The reviewed paper proposes a balance-drift regime change but tests mostly two-layer Gaussian-mixture models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Edge of Stochastic Stability: Revisiting the Edge of Stability for SGD
reviewed_competitors.difference: It identifies batch sharpness, rather than full-batch maximum Hessian eigenvalue, as the SGD stability quantity and relates batch/step size to flatter solutions. The reviewed theory is deterministic GD and does not integrate batch noise into its conservation-drift spectrum.

reviewed_competitors.title: Momentum Further Constrains Sharpness at the Edge of Stochastic Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives momentum- and batch-dependent sharpness plateaus. The reviewed exact cancellation is for plain GD, and its Adam ablation produces alpha about 0.56 outside the advertised crossover, so the claimed mechanism does not transfer to optimizer state.

reviewed_competitors.title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: It formulates EoS in the optimizer's geometry. The reviewed conservation observable uses Euclidean Frobenius norms and is not invariant under adaptive preconditioning, limiting any optimizer-universal interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Preconditioners Trigger Loss Spikes in Adam
reviewed_competitors.difference: It explains Adam spikes through second-moment decoupling and preconditioned sharpness, including large Transformers. The reviewed paper has no corresponding Adam symmetry analysis and reports an incompatible drift exponent around 0.56.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Sharpness Dynamics in NN Training with a Minimalist Example: The Effects of Dataset Difficulty, Depth, Stochasticity, and More
reviewed_competitors.difference: It gives a theoretical analysis of a one-neuron deep-linear testbed and evaluates how data difficulty, depth, stochasticity, and step size affect progressive sharpening. The reviewed work fits conservation drift on small two-layer systems and labels several finite-range regressions as theorems.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does Weight Decay Enhance Training Stability?
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies how weight decay changes progressive sharpening and architecture-dependent stability thresholds. The reviewed conservation analysis omits decay even though it directly changes layer norms and hence the advertised conserved quantities.

reviewed_competitors.difference: LARP learns holistic discrete tokens jointly with a lightweight AR prior so the latent space is reconstruction-efficient and generation-friendly. reviewed_competitors.difference: Universal Transformers introduced shared depth recurrence and dynamic per-position halting, with algorithmic and language results plus a Turing-completeness argument. reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers are Better at Learning Learning Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. show that looped transformers emulate iterative in-context learning algorithms for regression, neural networks, and trees with under 10% of standard-transformer parameters. The target paper studies composition of stored KG facts rather than in-context parameter estimation and adds systematic OOD splits, curriculum hop extrapolation, recurrence-at-inference, and causal audits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fan et al. train looped transformers on copy, parity, addition, and other tasks with a known iterative RASP-L solution and task-complexity-dependent loop counts, then adapt loops at inference. Loop, Think, & Generalize removes oracle complexity during training by using fixed or randomly sampled batch recurrence and targets parametric KG composition, at the cost of a narrower synthetic domain and threshold curriculum.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Saunshi et al. show that k layers looped L times approach kL-layer performance on addition, p-hop induction, math, and language modeling, theoretically connect loops to latent simulation of chain-of-thought, and identify a reasoning/memorization trade-off. The target paper adds an atom-level systematicity split, three-stage grokking, inference-depth curriculum extrapolation, overthinking margins, and shortcut-aware causal analysis, but offers less task and scale breadth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geiping et al. train the 3.5B-parameter Huginn on 800B tokens, iterate a recurrent block to arbitrary test depth, use input injection and adaptive halting, and report reasoning gains up to compute equivalent to a 50B model. The target paper sacrifices realism for exact KG ground truth, systematic recombination, matched-hop controls, and mechanistic/shortcut audits; its entropy-augmented halt explicitly addresses premature KL-only stopping observed on this controlled task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking of Implicit Reasoning in Transformers: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization

Loop, Think, & Generalize directly implements that suggestion through recurrent weight sharing, reports a third OOD grokking stage, and extends to curriculum depth extrapolation; much of its task formulation and diagnostic logic builds on this predecessor.

Loop, Think, & Generalize relies on zero c_proj initialization and empirically documents default-init instability/overthinking, but does not derive or enforce a stable recurrent attractor; Parcae is therefore a direct mechanism-level alternative for the paper's main failure mode.

It therefore defeats any priority claim over depth-recurrent compositional OOD or a compute-depth frontier. Loop, Think, & Generalize remains distinct in atom-level systematic recombination, its three-stage grokking account, permutation-KG hop curriculum, and substantially deeper matched-data, initialization, seed, overthinking, halting, causal, and shortcut audits.

It does not test the target's KG systematicity, but shows that looping the entire transformer block is an unablated compute choice rather than a necessary unit of recurrent reasoning.

reviewed_competitors.title: MLDemon: Deployment Monitoring for Machine Learning Systems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct deployment-monitoring competitor focused on estimating live accuracy and deciding when labels are worth querying.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MLDemon combines unlabeled shift signals with adaptive expert-label requests in a streaming, decision-theoretic framework and analyzes minimax monitoring costs. CSS attempts label-free target monitoring after offline labeled-corruption calibration and reports domain-level correlation/alarm F1, but does not model detection delay, query cost, or streaming decisions. The two offer complementary choices between no target labels and statistically grounded occasional audits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimating Model Performance Under Covariate Shift Without Labels
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Recent direct competitor for label-free target performance estimation under covariate shift, omitted from Inside-Out's comparisons.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PAPE uses a model's predictions/probabilities to estimate arbitrary confusion-matrix-derived metrics and evaluates more than 900 source-target-model combinations in tabular binary classification. Inside-Out targets image classifiers and uses internal circuits for model ranking and shift monitoring. PAPE has broader metric-estimation scope under an explicit covariate-shift setting; Inside-Out contributes a mechanistic signal but does not estimate a calibrated confusion matrix.
