reviewed_competitors.title: Does Data Scaling Lead to Visual Compositional Generalization?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Uselis et al. measure whether scaling datasets and models yields systematic recombination and report persistent gaps. The present paper seeks a representation-level necessary condition rather than another scaling curve, but its frozen-encoder experiments inherit the same exposure and split concerns.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compositional Generalization from First Principles
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wiedemer et al. derive data-support and model conditions for extrapolating a compositional data-generating process. Their guarantee does not impose exact posterior invariance across all retrained heads or orthogonal factors, so it is a competing formalization of what composition requires.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compositional Risk Minimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: CRM studies minimal diverse supports and an objective for full Cartesian generalization. It supplies the cross-like support motivation used here, while the current result adds a claimed necessary embedding geometry under a particular downstream learning rule.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linear Spaces of Meanings: Compositional Structures in Vision-Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Trager et al. model VLM embeddings as combinations of a smaller basis of ideal-word vectors and evaluate linear operations in CLIP. The present paper adds a conditional necessity result, but additive VLM factor structure itself is prior art.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deciphering the Role of Representation Disentanglement: Investigating Compositional Generalization in CLIP Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abbasi et al. empirically study how disentanglement and sparsity relate to unusual visual compositions. That work tests representation properties without claiming exact orthogonality is universally necessary; it is closer to the present empirical question than the theorem's idealized setup.

reviewed_competitors.title: When does compositional structure yield compositional generalization? A kernel theory
reviewed_competitors.difference: This kernel analysis links compositional transfer to architectural inductive biases and training dynamics without making additive orthogonal embeddings the primitive cause. It is an alternative mechanism class the checkpoint correlations do not distinguish.

reviewed_competitors.title: When and How Does CLIP Enable Domain and Compositional Generalization?
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work probes atomic visual knowledge and systematic recombination in CLIP-like models, providing task-level evidence complementary to the present factor-geometry metrics. It underscores that linear decodability alone need not imply robust compositional behavior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Visual Representation Learning Does Not Generalize Strongly Within the Same Domain
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schott et al. train more than 2,000 models on recombination, interpolation, and extrapolation splits of factorized visual datasets and find weak within-domain generalization. It is direct priority for the datasets and the distinction between factor decodability and learning the underlying mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This linear-representation analysis develops geometric criteria and empirical tests for concept directions. It predates the present use of additive factors and highlights that a task-correlated linear geometry is weaker than a necessity or causal result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Enhancing Compositional Generalization via Compositional Feature Alignment
reviewed_competitors.difference: CFA uses compositional feature alignment and orthogonalized linear heads to improve vision-language composition. It is direct priority for making factor separation an intervention; the present paper differs by claiming conditional necessity and primarily observing frozen encoders.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Object-Centric Representations Better At Compositional Generalization?
reviewed_competitors.difference: This concurrent work compares object-centric and dense representations under controlled data diversity, downstream capacity, and compute, finding conditional object-centric advantages rather than a universal necessity. It is a key discriminator for whether orthogonal additive directions are cause, correlate, or one realization among several.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thinking with Video: Video Generation as a Promising Multimodal Reasoning Paradigm
reviewed_competitors.difference: Thinking with Video argues for generation as multimodal reasoning and evaluates externally visible video solutions. reviewed_competitors.difference: Ganea et al. raise forward distribution rank with learnable monotone output nonlinearities. A nonlinear scalar output still has a Jacobian whose signal to hidden state is dimension-limited, so it does not directly address the paper's backward reachable-subspace claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Softmax Bottleneck Makes Language Models Unable to Represent Multi-mode Word Distributions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chang and McCallum show geometric failure to represent multimodal word distributions and propose a multi-facet softmax. This paper deliberately separates such forward multimode expressivity from gradient compression and tests the latter with controlled head rank.

reviewed_competitors.title: Low-Rank Softmax Can Have Unargmaxable Classes in Theory but Rarely in Practice
reviewed_competitors.difference: Grivas et al. study whether low-rank embeddings make classes impossible to predict as argmax and find the pathology rare in practice. The present paper similarly argues top-class expressivity is not the main issue, then locates a distinct optimization bottleneck in the backward projection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why do small language models underperform? Studying LM Saturation via Softmax Bottleneck
reviewed_competitors.difference: Godey et al. connect narrow hidden dimensions to late-pretraining saturation and degenerate representations in small LMs. The new work gives explicit logit-gradient rank/projection analysis and isolates head rank within a wide approximately 2B backbone rather than scaling the whole hidden state.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Kernel Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wilson et al. combine learned deep representations with spectral-mixture Gaussian-process kernels and scalable exact/approximate inference on datasets up to millions of examples. NMN uses a kernel in primal prototype form inside a finite network and avoids Gram matrices, but gives up DKL's probabilistic inference and extensive controlled evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Jayakumar et al. systematize multiplicative interactions as a unifying primitive for gating, attention, hypernetworks, and conditional computation and show strictly richer function classes. The rational unit is another multiplicative/algebraic interaction with an added inverse-distance bias; its novelty is the particular kernel geometry, not activation-free multiplicative computation.

Aether swaps in an exact rational query-key score but retains quadratic sequence complexity and provides no attention-specific ablation or approximation/scaling advantage.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Mialon et al. already apply joint-embedding SSL to heterogeneous PDE data, inject known Lie-point symmetries as augmentations, and evaluate PDE-coefficient regression as well as neural-solver improvement. The present paper removes the symmetry-specific augmentation, introduces a consecutive-window VICReg/JEPA implementation on three The Well systems, and focuses on a four-way latent-versus-pixel representation benchmark; it is not the first JEPA-style physical representation or governing-parameter probe.

reviewed_competitors.title: DISCO: learning to DISCover an evolution Operator for multi-physics-agnostic prediction
reviewed_competitors.difference: DISCO uses a large hypernetwork to infer a trajectory-specific evolution operator from a short context and explicitly integrates that operator for future-state prediction. The current study reuses the hypernetwork output as a frozen embedding for parameter regression; DISCO wins all three tables, making it both a strong baseline and evidence that physics-oriented latent operator inference can exceed the custom JEPA.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multiple Physics Pretraining for Physical Surrogate Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: MPP autoregressively pretrains one transformer across heterogeneous physical systems and demonstrates transfer for multi-step surrogate prediction. The current paper tests whether its published AViT-tiny features transfer to governing-parameter regression; MPP is worse than JEPA on two systems but better on Rayleigh-Bénard, under a different end-to-end adaptation protocol and without target-system pretraining.

reviewed_competitors.difference: V-JEPA establishes latent feature prediction as a stand-alone video SSL objective and evaluates large frozen representations on motion- and appearance-based natural-video tasks. This paper adapts the general principle to small scientific trajectory models, changes the encoder and loss to a 3D CNN with VICReg, and evaluates governing-parameter regression rather than video recognition.

reviewed_competitors.difference: VideoMAE uses extreme tube masking and pixel reconstruction to learn video-transformer features, with extensive recognition, transfer, and masking-ratio evaluation. Here a small VideoMAE is trained for six epochs per physical system and used as the pixel-space comparator; the result narrows to parameter regression and does not control architecture or convergence against JEPA.

reviewed_competitors.difference: The Well supplies the 15-TB, 16-dataset simulation collection and baseline infrastructure from which the three evaluated systems come. The current paper contributes a representation-learning evaluation slice and parameter-regression protocol, not new physical simulations or a broad benchmark over the entire collection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why do LLMs attend to the first token?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barbero et al. argue theoretically and empirically that first-token sinks let LLMs avoid over-mixing and provide controlled information flow, studying effects of context length, depth, packing, and model training. The present paper formalizes a sharper but narrower claim: every sufficiently accurate pure-softmax solution to one trigger/no-op task must sink, independent of optimization; it does not test real LLMs or the broader over-mixing mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo et al. derive an active-dormant mechanism and mutual-reinforcement training dynamics in a Bigram-Backcopy toy task, then connect them to Llama and OLMo; replacing softmax with ReLU or Adam with SGD can mitigate extreme-token phenomena. The current work removes training dynamics and proves task-level necessity under worst-case approximation, but for a more idealized pure-attention task and architecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gu et al. trace sink emergence through pretraining, data, objectives, and architecture up to 1B parameters, interpret sinks as key biases, and show unnormalized sigmoid attention avoids them. This paper supplies an expressivity theorem explaining why a normalized mechanism can need an off-state anchor on one task, but offers much less empirical breadth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Normalized Attention Without Probability Cage
reviewed_competitors.difference: Richter and Wattenhofer analyze the geometric limitations of confining attention weights and outputs to probability-simplex/convex-hull structure and evaluate alternative normalization across more than 25,000 models. The current paper narrows that general 'probability cage' concern to a formal BOS-sink necessity result for conditional no-op computation and contrasts it constructively with ReLU.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. add a head-specific sigmoid gate after softmax attention and show sink mitigation, improved stability, scaling, and long-context behavior in 1.7B dense and 15B MoE models trained on trillions of tokens. Such a gate supplies the explicit off state absent from the theorem's model and is therefore an empirical realization of the present paper's suggested remedy, not covered by its impossibility result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Softpick: No Attention Sink, No Massive Activations with Rectified Softmax
reviewed_competitors.difference: Softpick is a rectified, non-sum-to-one drop-in attention rule reported to achieve 0% sink rate, performance parity at 340M parameters, 46.97% sparsity, and better quantization. The present ReLU construction provides a toy expressivity reason non-normalization can avoid sinks, while Softpick supplies a more realistic architecture and evaluation absent here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
reviewed_competitors.difference: StreamingLLM shows that retaining initial sink-token keys and values restores sliding-window generation for up to millions of tokens and that a learned placeholder sink can improve streaming, with up to 22.2x speedup. It establishes practical usefulness but not why sinks are necessary; the present paper supplies one functional necessity mechanism without a streaming experiment.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This concurrent VLA study also finds that large pretrained policies forget much less than small policies, but it studies behavior-cloning task sequences and shows that simple Experience Replay can reach near-zero forgetting with small buffers and rapidly recover apparently lost skills. Hu et al. instead use interaction-only on-policy RL with one shared LoRA adapter, compare more CRL paradigms, and add held-out ZS and mechanism ablations; they are therefore not the only March 2026 evidence that pretraining changes robot continual learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less
reviewed_competitors.difference: RL's Razor already compares RL and SFT at matched new-task performance, links forgetting to KL shift from the base policy, argues that on-policy RL selects KL-minimal solutions, and validates the effect in language and robotic foundation models. The present paper extends the question to multi-stage VLA continual RL, LoRA, several robot suites, and CRL baselines, but its on-policy explanation and claim that RL forgets less are not new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning Naturally Mitigates Forgetting in Continual Post-Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work shows across multimodal Qwen2.5-VL tasks that reinforcement fine-tuning preserves prior and general knowledge far better than SFT, approaches multitask training, attributes the effect to selective updates rather than an explicit KL penalty, and proposes rollout-based filtering. Hu et al. move from multimodal QA to action-generating robot VLAs and continuous interaction, add LoRA/scale analysis, and focus on CRL algorithms rather than sample filtering.

reviewed_competitors.title: Wide Neural Networks Forget Less Catastrophically
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mirzadeh et al. already establish that width reduces catastrophic forgetting and analyze gradient orthogonality, sparsity, and lazy dynamics across controlled continual-learning networks. Hu et al. invoke the same high-dimensional orthogonality intuition for a 7B pretrained VLA and add a Fisher proxy, but their one small-policy ablation simultaneously changes scale, architecture, and pretraining.

reviewed_competitors.title: TAIL: Task-specific Adapters for Imitation Learning with Large Pretrained Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: TAIL benchmarks adapters, P-Tuning, and LoRA for data-efficient continual language-conditioned manipulation and reports that task-specific LoRA avoids forgetting with about one percent trainable parameters while preserving plasticity. Hu et al. use one evolving shared adapter rather than one adapter per task, learn from sparse reward instead of demonstrations, and retain constant parameter count, but are not first to connect LoRA, pretrained robot models, and continual retention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Robust Finetuning of Vision-Language-Action Robot Policies via Parameter Merging
reviewed_competitors.difference: This method interpolates fine-tuned and pretrained VLA weights, validates retention and OOD generalization in simulation and on real robots, studies scaling with pretraining data, and continually adds skills without sacrificing generalist behavior. Hu et al. include a RETAIN-style discounted merge baseline and find unconstrained sequential LoRA-GRPO stronger in their short simulator sequences, but do not provide the competitor's real-world or broad OOD evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: LIBERO: Benchmarking Knowledge Transfer for Lifelong Robot Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: LIBERO introduces 130 language-conditioned manipulation tasks, lifelong transfer metrics, task-order and pretraining studies, and already reports the unexpected result that sequential fine-tuning can outperform lifelong-learning methods in forward transfer. Hu et al. use selected four/five-task subsets and a 30-task concatenation with pretrained VLAs and online RL, adding low forgetting and held-out ZS evidence rather than originating the benchmark or the observation that plain sequential training can be competitive.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Professor Forcing adversarially aligns hidden dynamics between teacher-forced and free-running modes; EBFT uses a fixed frozen feature map and reference moment rather than a learned discriminator between rollout regimes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Calibration, Entropy Rates, and Memory in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work measures and corrects long-horizon entropy-rate drift with calibration constraints; EBFT generalizes the moment idea to high-dimensional frozen activations but does not independently validate full-distribution calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Reinforcement Learning and Distribution Matching for Fine-Tuning Language Models with no Catastrophic Forgetting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Korbak et al. explicitly formulate a target language-model distribution, relate distribution matching to KL-control and reward maximization, and import policy-gradient baselines for stable fine-tuning. EBFT instead estimates a reference-conditioned high-dimensional feature moment from paired completions and supplies an alignment-diversity reward; its particular empirical whitening reward is not an exact target-distribution gradient.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quiet-STaR: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Think Before Speaking
reviewed_competitors.difference: Quiet-STaR introduces parallel thought sampling over many token positions and rewards rationales by future-token prediction; EBFT adapts the custom-mask systems pattern to nested continuations but changes the learning signal to reference feature moments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Features as Rewards: Scalable Supervision for Open-Ended Tasks via Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: RLFR learns interpretable probes for hallucinated claims and uses their scalar output as an RL reward; EBFT avoids a task-specific probe by matching a fixed vector feature moment, but it offers no comparable independent reward-hacking audit.

reviewed_competitors.title: RLPR: Extrapolating RLVR to General Domains without Verifiers
reviewed_competitors.difference: RLPR uses the policy's token probabilities for paired reference answers as a scalar reward and adds variance-stabilization methods across general-domain and mathematical reasoning. EBFT instead matches high-dimensional frozen features and adds inter-rollout diversity, with code and translation experiments. RLPR substantially narrows any broad claim that reference-conditioned on-policy rewards are new or uniquely extend RL beyond executable verifiers.

reviewed_competitors.title: P2S: Probabilistic Process Supervision for General-Domain Reasoning Question Answering
reviewed_competitors.difference: P2S synthesizes and filters a gold reasoning chain, then scores each reasoning step by the conditional probability of its remaining suffix, providing dense process rewards without a separate reward model. EBFT uses short completion-level vector features from the paired answer and does not require a synthesized gold chain. P2S narrows the claim that dense, verifier-free, reference-conditioned on-policy supervision is new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reinforcement Learning with Conditional Expectation Reward
reviewed_competitors.difference: CER, submitted one day before EBFT v1, rewards the expected likelihood of a reference answer conditioned on the generated answer, yielding a soft model-internal verifier across mathematical and general reasoning. EBFT's defensible distinction is its vector moment objective, inter-rollout diversity, frozen feature geometry, and code/translation scope—not the broad idea of verifier-free graded rewards computed from reference answers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Embedding Distance as a Reward Signal can replace Verifiers for LLM Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Benechehab et al. also derive a dense verifier-free RL signal directly from supervised target answers, using a learned Mahalanobis-style distance between target and generated-answer embeddings and testing GRPO on Countdown. EBFT matches a vector mean across four on-policy rollouts with an explicit diversity term and tests code plus translation; the concurrent paper is much smaller and task-limited, but it defeats any broad novelty claim for using embedding proximity to replace a verifier.

reviewed_competitors.title: Escaping the Verifier: Learning to Reason via Demonstrations
reviewed_competitors.difference: RARO learns a relativistic critic from expert-policy completion pairs through inverse RL; EBFT uses the expert completion directly in a fixed feature reward and avoids critic co-training, trading adaptability for a more stationary signal.

reviewed_competitors.title: FlowRL: Matching Reward Distributions for LLM Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: FlowRL converts scalar rewards into a target distribution and balances flows to preserve diverse reasoning trajectories; EBFT matches vector representation moments without a task reward, but does not target the full reward distribution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generative Adversarial Post-Training Mitigates Reward Hacking in Live Human-AI Music Interaction
reviewed_competitors.difference: GAPT co-evolves a discriminator to prevent scalar-reward diversity collapse and validates live behavior with expert users; EBFT has a fixed representation and diversity term, but does not test adversarial feature exploitation or human interaction quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: GeneralThinker: Domain-General Reasoning through Likelihood-Guided Answer-Conditioned Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: GeneralThinker uses ground-truth-answer likelihood for response evaluation and token-wise compatibility, with clipping and direction-preserving modulation for dense credit assignment across 11 reasoning benchmarks. EBFT uses sequence-level feature moments and rollout diversity rather than likelihood-derived token credit. This later work does not alter EBFT's submission priority, but it is a current systems competitor for general verifier-free reference-conditioned optimization.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest empirical competitor for full-parameter, Gaussian-perturbation, gradient-free LLM post-training at billion-parameter scale.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. use many sequential ES generations to turn fitness-weighted perturbations into an updated single model and report advantages over RL. RandOpt spends a comparable evaluation budget on one independent population, selects top K without updating a center, and depends on inference ensembling; its contribution is parallel depth and specialist aggregation rather than a better learned parameter vector.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Blessing of Dimensionality in LLM Fine-tuning: A Variance-Curvature Perspective
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct contemporary landscape explanation for why random weight perturbations and small-population ES can improve LLM rewards.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liang et al. attribute accessible improving directions to low-dimensional curvature embedded in a high-dimensional, degenerate reward landscape and analyze non-monotonic ES/GRPO dynamics. Neural Thickets instead measures task-conditioned hit rates and cross-task diversity, proposes one-round top-K ensembling, and offers a mixed-signal pretraining toy mechanism; it does not estimate curvature or identify the effective subspace.

reviewed_competitors.title: PEP: Parameter Ensembling by Perturbation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier direct method that treats pretrained weights as the center of a Gaussian parameter ensemble and requires no extra model training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PEP tunes one perturbation variance by validation ensemble likelihood and averages all perturbed classifiers to improve likelihood/calibration; it has no task-wise top-K candidate selection, model-scale density law, or multi-task specialization analysis. Its existence means Gaussian perturbation ensembling around trained weights is not new; RandOpt's narrower novelty is selective large-population use on LLM post-training and the thicket characterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analyzing Reinforcement Learning Benchmarks with Random Weight Guessing
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor using distributions of independently guessed neural-network weights as a benchmark-complexity probe.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Oller et al. sample small policy networks from scratch and analyze score distributions to expose easy RL benchmarks; they explicitly frame random guessing as analysis rather than a learning algorithm. Neural Thickets centers perturbations on pretrained billion-parameter models, studies scaling and cross-task specialization, and selects/ensembles top candidates as a practical post-training method.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1, submitted 16 April 2020; AAMAS 2020 paper

reviewed_competitors.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct large-language-model competitor showing that full-parameter, forward-pass-only zeroth-order adaptation is practical after pretraining.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MeZO performs many paired perturbation evaluations and applies an in-place zeroth-order SGD update to one model, emphasizing inference-level memory and learned task adaptation up to 66B parameters. RandOpt performs one independent population draw, never estimates or follows a gradient, and obtains its strongest results by selecting and ensembling K perturbed checkpoints. MeZO therefore predates the broad claim that forward-only post-training of large LMs is new, while RandOpt's narrower contribution is one-round specialist selection and the density/diversity probe.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v3, revised 11 January 2024; NeurIPS 2023 oral version

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary evidence that strong reasoning adaptations can lie in an extremely low-dimensional parameterization around a pretrained LLM.
reviewed_competitors.difference: TinyLoRA trains as few as 13 shared adapter parameters with RL and reports 91% GSM8K for Qwen2.5-8B, directly supporting the idea that pretraining makes task-relevant weight changes highly accessible. It learns a single compact update rather than sampling isotropic full-parameter noise or ensembling experts, and its result concerns low trainable dimension rather than the probability mass or multi-task diversity of arbitrary nearby perturbations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spurious Rewards: Rethinking Training Signals in RLVR
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical alternative explanation for why weak or uninformative post-training signals can improve selected pretrained models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shao et al. show that GRPO with random or otherwise spurious rewards can amplify high-prior pretrained behaviors through clipping bias, with strong Qwen gains but failures on Llama3 and OLMo2. Neural Thickets instead samples raw weights without sequential policy updates and attributes success to local density and specialist diversity. The model-family dependence and concrete clipping mechanism caution against treating Qwen-local hit rates as a universal geometric phase transition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization for Efficiently Improving Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAM takes a first-order ascent perturbation and applies the gradient at that perturbed point to the current parameters; XSAM retains the ascent computation but searches a boundary direction in a two-vector plane before the descent update.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness-Aware Minimization Revisited: Weighted Sharpness as a Regularization Term
reviewed_competitors.difference: WSAM derives a fixed weighted combination of local and perturbed gradients from a sharpness regularizer; XSAM interprets the combination geometrically, uses spherical rather than linear mixing, chooses the scalar from explicit boundary losses during training, and extends it to multi-step ascent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Penalizing Gradient Norm for Efficiently Improving Generalization in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gradient-norm penalization derives a tunable first-order combination and treats SAM as one special case; XSAM does not add that regularizer and instead selects a loss-maximizing spherical direction with a dynamic scalar.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploring the Effect of Multi-step Ascent in Sharpness-Aware Minimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct multi-step SAM diagnosis and method competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: This predecessor documents that extra ascent steps need not improve generalization and proposes aggregating perturbed gradients; XSAM gives a transplanted-gradient geometric account and searches between total displacement and the final gradient instead of summing gradients.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lookbehind-SAM: k steps back, 1 step forward
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct multi-step ascent and interpolation competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lookbehind-SAM uses multiple ascent steps and linear interpolation to refine the gathered-gradient descent update, with robustness and continual-learning tests; XSAM uses spherical interpolation in a displacement-final-gradient plane and explicitly scores candidate boundary losses.

reviewed_competitors.title: Surrogate Gap Minimization Improves Sharpness-Aware Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: GSAM adds an orthogonal ascent component that reduces a Hessian-linked surrogate gap without changing perturbed loss to first order; XSAM instead changes the descent direction to oppose an explicitly probed high-loss boundary ray.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Universal Class of Sharpness-Aware Minimization Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: The universal class designs objectives for chosen Hessian functionals and parameter invariances, including Frob-SAM and Det-SAM; XSAM keeps the maximum-loss neighborhood target and focuses on a more explicit direction estimate rather than changing the sharpness functional.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stabilizing Sharpness-Aware Minimization Through A Simple Renormalization Strategy
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stable SAM renormalizes the descent gradient to match the ascent-gradient norm and analyzes a learning-rate stability regime; XSAM mainly changes direction, defaults to ||gk||, and reports no consistent stability advantage for the alternative ||g0|| scale.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: JMLR Volume 26, Paper 68, version of record published April 2025

reviewed_competitors.title: AutoLRS: Automatic Learning-Rate Schedule by Bayesian Optimization on the Fly
reviewed_competitors.difference: AutoLRS uses short candidate branches, a loss-forecast model, and Bayesian optimization to set stagewise rates during one run and reports ResNet-50, Transformer, and BERT speedups; this paper performs vastly larger offline random searches for static reusable finite-horizon shapes on much smaller workloads.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient-based Hyperparameter Optimization through Reversible Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reversible learning computes exact cross-validation hypergradients through SGD with momentum and optimizes thousands of step-size and momentum values; the reviewed deep experiments instead search low-dimensional shapes by random trials, reserving full per-step differentiation for approximate linear dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Online Learning Rate Adaptation with Hypergradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hypergradient Descent updates the global rate online with little extra computation and applies to SGD, Nesterov, and Adam; this paper discovers one seed-robust open-loop shape offline, requires a known horizon, and does not compare total tuning cost or trajectory adaptation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Population Based Training of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Population Based Training jointly trains weights and evolves hyperparameters through exploit-and-explore, producing trajectory-specific schedules with reused training compute; this paper independently retrains millions of candidates to identify a static shape that performs well across seeds.

reviewed_competitors.title: REX: Revisiting Budgeted Training with an Improved Schedule
reviewed_competitors.difference: REX proposes a specific budget-aware decay family and benchmarks it against common schedules; the reviewed paper subsumes a generalized REX family within a matched base-rate search and finds that spline and generalized-cosine families can perform as well or better on its selected workloads.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws and Compute-Optimal Training Beyond Fixed Training Durations
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work studies warmup-stable-decay schedules whose checkpoints can be extended beyond an initially fixed duration and derives compute-optimal scaling behavior; the reviewed paper explicitly excludes horizon-free schedules and evaluates shapes normalized to one prespecified short horizon.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Road Less Scheduled
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schedule-Free optimization removes the need for a prespecified decay schedule and horizon while targeting strong practical neural-network training; the reviewed method prespecifies T, spends a large offline budget on shape selection, and does not include a schedule-free baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Cyclical Learning Rates for Training Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cyclical learning rates deliberately oscillate between bounds and use range tests to reduce manual tuning; the reviewed Smooth Non-Monotonic family can express non-monotonicity, but its selected short-horizon schedules become one-shot warmup-and-decay curves and periodic policies are not directly tested.

reviewed_competitors.title: SGDR: Stochastic Gradient Descent with Warm Restarts
reviewed_competitors.difference: SGDR repeatedly restarts cosine annealing and supports anytime snapshot behavior; the reviewed study searches a single normalized finite-horizon curve, uses standard cosine only as one family, and provides no interruption or extension test.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Edge-of-Stability directly measures progressive sharpening and oscillatory full-batch neural-network dynamics near the curvature threshold; the reviewed paper observes useful transient instability in synthetic linear SGD but does not measure a corresponding causal curvature mechanism for its AdamW schedule shapes.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Balogh's earlier March 2026 paper already establishes contextual selective linearization with a d+1-parameter gate across six GPT-2/Pythia models, two architectures, and three corpora, routing 25-56% of GPT-2 computations to a linear surrogate at under 1% PPL cost and measuring fine-tuned improvements. The present paper adds a neuron-level 7+1 readout and causal consensus stratification, but is narrower in model/corpus coverage and does not implement an efficient gate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hedonic Neurons: A Mechanistic Mapping of Latent Coalitions in Transformer MLPs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chowdhury et al. explicitly search for stable neuron coalitions with non-additive joint-ablation synergy and track persistence, split, merge, and disappearance across layers in fine-tuned LLaMA, Mistral, and Pythia rerankers. The present work uses firing-rate selection, mutual exclusivity, and full-MLP ablation in GPT-2 Small; its selected N2123 intervention is null, so Hedonic Neurons supplies a stronger coalition-level causal unit while the present paper offers a simpler natural-language consensus readout.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformer Feed-Forward Layers Are Key-Value Memories
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geva et al. interpret each FFN row as a key detecting textual patterns and each output row as a value inducing vocabulary distributions, with shallow-to-semantic depth trends and composition of hundreds of active memories. The present paper shifts from individual key/value meaning to relational thresholded co-activation and conditional MLP importance, but its 'exception handler' has no individual causal effect and its semantic labels are less systematically validated.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ACL Anthology EMNLP 2021 version of record; publication_date/source_date=2021-11

reviewed_competitors.title: A Spline Theory of Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Balestriero and Baraniuk prove exact max-affine spline-operator representations for a large class of piecewise-linear networks and derive input-conditioned affine templates/partitions. The present work proposes a semantic routing interpretation of activation regions on natural data, but studies smooth GELU and therefore cannot present its empirical binary thresholds as a direct alternative characterization of the exact piecewise-affine theorem without an approximation bridge.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2018 PMLR volume 80 version of record; conference/source_date=2018-07-10 to 2018-07-15

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. address polysemanticity by learning sparse overcomplete feature directions, benchmark interpretability against neuron/PCA/ICA bases, and causally patch compact feature sets on IOI. The present paper deliberately studies relational grammar in the raw neuron basis and needs no auxiliary autoencoder, but does not test basis stability or superposition and assigns semantic roles by inspection; SAE features provide the natural control for whether the 7+1 coalition is basis-dependent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Knowledge Neurons in Pretrained Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dai et al. use integrated-gradient attribution to identify FFN neurons expressing relational facts and validate them through activation amplification/suppression and targeted knowledge editing/erasure. The present paper targets task-agnostic routing coalitions rather than factual content, but its named N2123 handler fails the targeted causal test that is central to knowledge-neuron claims, leaving the full distributed MLP—not the neuron—as the causal unit.

reviewed_competitors.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct layer-similarity and whole-block pruning predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: ShortGPT defines Block Influence as one minus input-output cosine, calibrates it on unlabeled PG19, permanently removes low-BI blocks from Llama2 and Baichuan2, and reports broad pruning benchmarks; it even finds most redundancy in middle/later AR layers. The reviewed paper uses essentially the complementary cosine score but adds token/denoising analysis, a non-adjacency constraint, native-diffusion versus AR/AR-initialized comparison, and inference-only identity bypass. Its distinct contribution is the objective-family comparison, not discovering cosine-ranked layer removal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Accelerating Inference in Large Language Models with a Unified Layer Skipping Strategy
reviewed_competitors.difference: Unified Layer Skipping already fixes one balanced non-contiguous subnetwork from a target speed ratio, supports batch decoding and KV caching, and measures actual throughput on translation and summarization. The reviewed method chooses non-adjacent blocks by hidden-state similarity and studies diffusion models and math/code, but omits a head-to-head balanced-static baseline and underspecifies its fixed calibration. Thus 'static, task-agnostic layer skipping' itself is not novel here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tracing Representation Progression: Analyzing and Enhancing Layer-Wise Similarity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jiang et al. formally compare sample-wise cosine with CKA, analyze residual-connection rotation effects, relate shallow-layer similarity to classifier accuracy, and train aligned multi-exit models across vision and NLP. The reviewed paper adopts adjacent cosine for pretrained AR/diffusion comparison and skip selection, adds token and denoising axes, but does not reproduce the stronger metric validation or control for residual-induced similarity.

reviewed_competitors.title: DiffuCoder: Understanding and Improving Masked Diffusion Models for Code Generation
reviewed_competitors.difference: DiffuCoder defines local AR-ness from consecutive generation order and global AR-ness from earliest-mask selection, showing that AR-adapted dLLMs are more autoregressive than from-scratch LLaDA and that training stages change this behavior. The reviewed paper explicitly builds on that output-level result and contributes hidden-state layer/token cosine plus a depth-removal intervention; its 'global' label remains less behaviorally direct than DiffuCoder's formal decoding-order metrics.

reviewed_competitors.title: dLLM-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Large Language Models with Adaptive Caching
reviewed_competitors.difference: The ICML 2026 dLLM-Cache reuses prompt and stable response computation across adjacent denoising steps using feature similarity and reports up to 9.1x FLOPs reduction on LongBench-HotpotQA for LLaDA/Dream. The reviewed paper removes whole depth blocks at every step for a smaller 6-25% nominal reduction and argues the axes are orthogonal; its only combined dual-cache table lacks latency and shows retention falling to 68% at six skips.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v3, revised 2026-06-06 (first submitted 2025-05-17); accepted ICML 2026

reviewed_competitors.title: dKV-Cache: The Cache for Diffusion Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: dKV-Cache uses delayed, token-conditioned key/value reuse across denoising steps and reports roughly 2-10x inference speedups with near-lossless and aggressive modes over language, math, and code. The reviewed method instead exploits depth-wise block similarity, does not require cache reuse, and gives modest wall-time savings; the two address different redundancy axes but need a controlled joint quality-latency evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Selective Attention Improves Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Selective Attention applies a constrained selection head to accumulate signals from intermediate tokens and subtract them from future attention logits, suppressing obsolete context and enabling aggressive context-buffer pruning. It reports language-modeling equivalence to roughly twice as many attention heads and substantial attention-memory reductions across context lengths. XSA instead preserves the entire softmax map and projects each output away from its current-position value direction; it targets branch specialization, not key pruning, and does not reduce quadratic attention or KV storage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differential Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Differential Transformer subtracts two separately normalized softmax attention maps with a learned coefficient, permitting negative attention to cancel irrelevant-context noise; its primary study covers language scaling and long-context retrieval, hallucination, in-context learning, and activation outliers through 13.1B parameters and much larger token budgets. XSA instead subtracts a rank-one value-space projection after one ordinary softmax, adds no learned coefficient, and is tested only through 2.7B/100B with within-training-window loss.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, revised 2025-04-07 (first submitted 2024-10-07); ICLR 2025 oral

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct post-SDPA output-modification and attention-sink competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. compare 30 gating variants and find a head-specific sigmoid gate after SDPA effective in 1.7B dense and 15B MoE models trained on up to 3.5T tokens. Its learned query-dependent sparse gate adds nonlinearity, reports under-2% latency overhead, eliminates observed attention sinks, and improves long-context extrapolation. XSA uses a fixed analytic orthogonal projection with no parameters; it has a stronger geometric guarantee but no head-selective bypass, broader-scale controls, exact overhead ratio, or extrapolation task.

reviewed_competitors.title: TLM: Token-Level Masking for Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: TLM's self-masking regularizer randomly forces a selected token to form its training representation from other tokens by masking self-attention connections, alongside sibling masking; inference returns to standard attention. It evaluates 18 datasets across four NLP task families. XSA deterministically constrains every token/head during both training and inference in value space rather than masking the self link in attention weights, so it does not literally prevent attending to the self position and incurs persistent inference arithmetic.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1, submitted 2023-10-28; EMNLP 2023 main conference

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: canonical attention-sink mechanism and direct terminology comparator
reviewed_competitors.difference: StreamingLLM identifies semantically unimportant initial tokens that absorb attention, then retains their KVs beside a rolling recent window to stabilize language modeling for up to four million tokens and 22.2x streaming speedup; it also tests a dedicated placeholder sink. XSA calls each same-position diagonal score an implicit sink but leaves scores unchanged and subtracts a value direction. It neither retains a persistent KV nor evaluates windowed streaming, so its sink relationship is analogy/compatibility rather than the same operational mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Toy Models of Superposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Elhage et al. emphasize sparse independent features, harmful interference, ReLU filtering, and regular-polytope phases; BOWS introduces realistic covariance and shows that cross terms can reconstruct correlated features constructively.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Causes Polysemanticity? An Alternative Origin Story of Mixed Selectivity from Incidental Causes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lecomte et al. attribute some polysemanticity to chance initialization, regularization, and neural noise even with spare capacity; Prieto et al. attribute organized overlap to exploitable data covariance and norm-efficient reconstruction, but do not fully separate the two mechanisms under weight decay.

reviewed_competitors.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scherlis et al. explain allocation and block-semi-orthogonal structure using importance, sparsity, and architecture in toy data; BOWS adds realistic cross-feature covariance and isolates constructive contextual reconstruction.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. ground linearity in counterfactual semantics and a causal inner product on LLaMA-2; BOWS adopts Euclidean tied-AE directions and explains their geometry from covariance, without testing the causal metric or counterfactual meaning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
reviewed_competitors.difference: Engels et al. use LLM interventions to argue that some circles are irreducible multi-dimensional computational features; Prieto et al. show visually similar circles can instead arise among one-dimensional presence coordinates from covariance, while reserving task-driven circles for value codes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hindupur et al. show SAE architecture filters concepts according to dimensionality and nonlinear separability and propose a broader extractor; BOWS studies tied-AE learned geometry with known coordinates but does not evaluate whether SAEs recover that geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Origins of Representation Manifolds in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Modell et al. theorize continuous/multidimensional feature manifolds whose on-manifold distance encodes intrinsic concept geometry in LLM activations; BOWS explains some apparent manifolds as covariance-preserving arrangements of separate binary coordinates and others as low-dimensional value codes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral Superposition: A Theory of Feature Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ivanov et al. classify saturated toy geometry through frame eigenspaces, tight frames, and association schemes; Prieto et al. trace geometry to covariance and optimization with controlled text statistics but offer less global algebraic classification.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Many Features Can a Language Model Store Under the Linear Representation Hypothesis?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Garg et al. derive worst-case capacity bounds over all k-sparse vectors and show only encoder-decoder cross-geometry is constrained; BOWS is distribution-aware, exploits forbidden/likely co-occurrences, and ties encoder to decoder, so its constructive codes occupy a narrower but more empirical regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Superposition as Lossy Compression: Measure with Sparse Autoencoders and Connect to Adversarial Vulnerability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bereska et al. estimate entropy-based effective feature counts from SAE activations and relate them observationally to adversarial training; BOWS measures known-coordinate reconstruction and geometry, directly exposes correlations, and does not test adversarial robustness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Distributional Properties Drive Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct data-distribution cause of emergent in-context learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chan et al. manipulate burstiness, rare-class frequency, dynamic meanings, and Zipf structure and show that these properties elicit ICL selectively in Transformers. The present paper instead nominates latent hierarchy and extends the target from behavior to induction heads, function vectors, and self-repair, but it does not factorially compare hierarchy against those established distributional properties.

reviewed_competitors.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest controlled study of induction-head emergence and redundancy
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh et al. use optogenetics-style activation clamping during synthetic training to identify three interacting subcircuits and the additive diversity of induction heads. The present paper offers a broader latent-hierarchy account but does not causally clamp the proposed evidence branches or distinguish subcircuits that form an induction head.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct theoretical competitor on induction-head training dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. prove gradient-flow convergence of a two-attention-layer Transformer to a generalized copier-selector-classifier induction mechanism on n-gram Markov data. That theorem is narrower but mathematically tied to an explicit architecture and optimization flow; its induction result on a flat n-gram setting is counterevidence to the present paper's unqualified claim that hierarchy is absolutely necessary.

reviewed_competitors.title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: defining primary work for the function-vector phenomenon
reviewed_competitors.difference: Todd et al. use causal mediation across diverse tasks, models, zero-shot contexts, and natural text to isolate a small set of middle-layer attention heads carrying compact task representations and test vector composition. The present paper uses a simpler source-segment attention-output patch in one PCSG model; it supplies a generative hypothesis but does not reproduce the task abstraction or cross-context controls that define the competitor's construct.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explorations of Self-Repair in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rushing and Nanda measure attention-head self-repair over full data distributions and show it is imperfect, prompt-variable, and sometimes overcorrecting, with final-LayerNorm scaling and sparse anti-erasure neurons as concrete mechanisms. The present paper proposes a data-level origin for redundancy but its concavity theorem can describe logit overcompensation without demonstrating recovery of the removed head's direct effect or separating those known mechanisms.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: v2, revised 2024-05-26; first submitted 2024-02-23; ICML 2024 / PMLR 235

reviewed_competitors.title: Unraveling Syntax: Language Modeling and the Substructure of Grammars
reviewed_competitors.relationship: current direct competitor on learning dynamics in context-free grammars
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schulz et al. formally decompose CFG language-model loss over subgrammars and find largely parallel subgrammar learning, recursion difficulty, and representation alignment, with subgrammar pretraining benefits mainly for tiny models relative to the grammar. The present paper instead uses PCSGs to correlate staged structural probes with three mechanistic metrics, but lacks the competitor's subgrammar decomposition and depth-limit analysis.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: v3, revised 2026-06-10; first submitted 2025-10-02; accepted ICML 2026

reviewed_competitors.title: Between Circuits and Chomsky: Pre-pretraining on Formal Languages Imparts Linguistic Biases
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct hierarchical-formal-language evidence at natural-language scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu et al. factorially compare formal-language classes, show hierarchical dependencies improve later natural-language loss and linguistic generalization, report a 33% token-budget saving for a 1B model, and causally implicate retained attention heads. The present paper focuses on mechanistic metrics learned directly from synthetic PCSG data and a descriptive OLMo reference rather than transfer into matched natural-language training.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational induction-head evidence and metric source
reviewed_competitors.difference: Olsson et al. present six lines of evidence connecting match-and-copy heads to a phase change in ICL, with strong causal evidence in small attention-only models and correlational evidence in larger models. The present paper adds a hierarchy hypothesis and paired DGP experiments, but its attention-score operationalization alone is weaker than the foundational causal output tests and does not prove the universal source of induction.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct reservoir-design competitor evaluated on MNIST and other temporal or event-based tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tian et al. search a spiking liquid-state machine's multi-liquid architecture, neuron allocation, connectivity, and excitatory ratio with simulated annealing, obtaining 93.2% MNIST, 92.5% NMNIST, and 84% FSDD accuracy with 1,000 neurons and reporting 61.4% fewer connections than a single LSM. reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct random-reservoir MNIST competitor emphasizing scalable physical implementation and a conventional trained readout
reviewed_competitors.difference: Antonik et al. implement a 16,384-node photonic reservoir with randomly weighted input and hidden layers, engineered image features, linear-regression training, and winner-take-all decisions; their feedforward configuration reaches 1% MNIST error and recurrent dynamics are studied numerically. RECAP uses a smaller 1,024-unit software ESN and replaces regression with quadratic pair prototypes, yielding much worse 11.7% clean error but adding a clean-only-to-MNIST-C corruption test; it does not establish hardware scalability or isolate the value of its reservoir from its readout.

reviewed_competitors.title: SoftHebb: Bayesian Inference in Unsupervised Hebbian Soft Winner-Take-All Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct Hebbian image-learning and robustness competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: SoftHebb derives an unsupervised local online WTA rule as Bayesian inference/cross-entropy minimization and reports robustness to random noise and adversarial attacks as well as convergence behavior. RECAP instead applies a heuristic supervised potentiation-decay rule only at a reservoir readout and evaluates standardized common corruptions; it is simpler but provides no optimization theory, adversarial test, or direct SoftHebb comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hebbian Deep Learning Without Feedback
reviewed_competitors.difference: Multilayer SoftHebb trains up to five feature layers without feedback, targets, or error signals and reports 99.4% MNIST, 80.3% CIFAR-10, 76.2% STL-10, and 27.3% ImageNet accuracy with an added linear classifier. RECAP leaves features random and learns only supervised class prototypes, giving lower clean accuracy but a specific MNIST-C common-corruption result and a directly incremental readout.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Forward-Forward Algorithm: Some Preliminary Investigations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Forward-Forward trains each layer with separate positive and negative forward passes and a layer-local goodness objective, eliminating the conventional backward pass while still learning representations. RECAP performs no representation learning and needs only positive labeled samples for class-prototype updates; it is more directly online at the readout but offers much less clean accuracy and no comparison with other non-backpropagation algorithms.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. already construct polynomial-size O(log T)-depth Transformer simulators for arbitrary finite automata of length T via hierarchical/Krohn-Rhodes ideas and test brittleness. Heo et al.'s Proposition 3.7 obtains a similar logarithmic layer upper bound for abelian SSMs via truncated free Lie algebras and makes its exponential worst-case width explicit, while adding continuous-state and local-error results.

reviewed_competitors.title: Structured Linear CDEs: Maximally Expressive and Parallel-in-Time Sequence Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Walker et al. design block-diagonal, sparse, and Walsh-Hadamard input-dependent transitions that retain dense-matrix expressivity, solve A5 with one layer, and report strong regular-language length generalization plus about 20-fold faster training than log-NCDEs. Heo et al. analyze how restricted layers can approximate missing order structure through depth rather than proposing a one-layer maximally expressive efficient transition.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeltaProduct: Improving State-Tracking in Linear RNNs via Householder Products
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeltaProduct uses products of n_h generalized Householder transformations, giving diagonal-plus-rank-n_h transitions with a finite-precision expressivity/efficiency knob and gains on state tracking, length extrapolation, and language modeling. It is the one-layer perfect reference in Heo et al.'s solvable table and near-zero A5 rotation baseline; the new paper explains restricted-depth compensation but does not beat this general-transition control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unlocking State-Tracking in Linear RNNs Through Negative Eigenvalues
reviewed_competitors.relationship: architecture-specific state-tracking precursor and baseline source
reviewed_competitors.difference: Grazzi et al. prove positive-eigenvalue finite-precision LRNNs cannot solve parity, characterize additional structure needed for modular counting, and show negative-eigenvalue Mamba/DeltaNet improvements at model scale. Heo et al. use Signed Mamba to show that removing the simplest spectral obstruction solves C2 but still leaves major non-abelian learnability failures; their Lie brackets cover a broader kind of order sensitivity.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Karuvally et al. introduce input-dependent skew-symmetric/unitary recurrence, prove logarithmic-precision simulation of solvable group automata, implement a parallel kernel, and report gains on modular arithmetic and time series. Heo et al. place complex diagonal behavior in their restricted hierarchy and find AUSSM fails every tested non-abelian word problem and is unstable on A5 rotation, emphasizing learnability rather than disputing formal capacity.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Effect of Depth on the Expressivity of Deep Linear State-Space Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bao et al. analyze deep linear time-invariant SSMs, showing unconstrained depth/width equivalences and advantages of depth under parameter-norm constraints, with constructive minimal-depth upper bounds and numerical tests. Heo et al. target input-dependent noncommutative order structure and local Magnus error instead, so the mechanisms differ, but the broad novelty phrase about depth and SSM expressivity should acknowledge this direct prior depth analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Theoretical Foundations of Deep Selective State-Space Models

Heo et al. connect the closely related log-signature/Magnus view to explicit Lie-extension depth classes and an approximation order, but works under stronger regularity and does not study random-feature dimension or learning guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: MInference 1.0: Accelerating Pre-filling for Long-Context LLMs via Dynamic Sparse Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: MInference identifies A-shape, vertical-slash and block-sparse head patterns offline, constructs input-dependent indices online and supplies optimized kernels, reporting up to 10x A100 prefill speedups across models/tasks. Stem uses a uniform block machinery with position-decayed budgets and value-aware scores; its tables report better aggregate accuracy at lower retained budget, but do not provide a common kernel/budget Pareto comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: FlexPrefill: A Context-Aware Sparse Attention Mechanism for Efficient Long-Sequence Inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: FlexPrefill chooses attention patterns and budgets by input/head context using Jensen-Shannon divergence and cumulative attention thresholds. Stem replaces such adaptive budget estimation with fixed absolute-position decay and adds value norms, making it simpler but potentially less robust to late evidence or head heterogeneity.

reviewed_competitors.title: XAttention: Block Sparse Attention with Antidiagonal Scoring
reviewed_competitors.difference: XAttention introduces the antidiagonal block scoring/pooling that Stem explicitly adopts and evaluates on RULER, LongBench and video with reported speedups up to 13.5x. Stem's incremental method novelty is the position-decayed per-row budget and pooled value-norm term, not the underlying block representation/kernel idea.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
reviewed_competitors.difference: StreamingLLM retains initial sink tokens plus a recent window in the KV cache to support decode/streaming for millions of tokens. Stem likewise protects early blocks but allocates prefill computation per query and is explicitly not a decoding method; StreamingLLM is therefore a conceptual predecessor for early-token preservation rather than a like-for-like prefill competitor.

reviewed_competitors.title: SeerAttention: Learning Intrinsic Sparse Attention in Your LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: SeerAttention self-distills a trainable gate to predict block sparsity and reports long-context accuracy/acceleration. It incurs calibration/training but can learn layer/head/content variation; Stem is training-free and cheaper to deploy, at the cost of fixed mu/beta and a heuristic output proxy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: NSA trains a hierarchical compression/selection design natively and targets efficient attention across pretraining, prefill and decoding. Stem is a plug-in for existing dense or sparse models and only prefill, making deployment easier but leaving decode and co-adapted sparse representations unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention Score is not All You Need for Token Importance Indicator in KV Cache Reduction: Value Also Matters
reviewed_competitors.difference: It combines attention scores with value-vector L1 norms for cumulative KV-cache/token pruning and reports improvements over score-only pruning on Llama/Vicuna LongBench. Stem's OAM uses log L2 value norms in prefill block selection and offers an output-error surrogate, but the underlying insight that attention weights alone ignore value magnitude is prior and should be credited as a close conceptual predecessor.

reviewed_competitors.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: LoRA freezes a pretrained model and learns a linear low-rank update that can be merged, reducing trainable parameters and adding no deployment latency. NOBLE borrows the parallel low-rank factorization but inserts nonlinearity, trains all paths from scratch and keeps the branch permanently; it solves architecture/pretraining efficiency rather than PEFT.

reviewed_competitors.title: LoRA+: Efficient Low Rank Adaptation of Large Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: LoRA+ proves/argues that the two low-rank factors need different learning-rate scaling at large width and reports 1-2% fine-tuning gains/up to ~2x speed. NOBLE explicitly adopts asymmetric rank-dependent parameter-group rates but extends them to full pretraining and CosNet; this also makes its architectural ablation inseparable from an existing optimizer insight.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixture-of-Subspaces in Low-Rank Adaptation
reviewed_competitors.difference: MoSLoRA inserts a learned r-by-r mixer between LoRA factors and evaluates PEFT across language, multimodal and diffusion tasks; its A-M-B skeleton matches a key part of CosNet without nonlinear activations. NOBLE's novel structural increment is periodic nonlinear processing and from-scratch permanent training, not the middle mixer itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: PEANuT: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation with Weight-aware Neural Tweakers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: nonlinear low-rank/PEFT predecessor cited under an older title
reviewed_competitors.difference: The cited v1 was titled NEAT and used compact nonlinear networks conditioned on frozen pretrained weights to approximate cumulative fine-tuning updates; the current v3 is retitled PEANuT. It establishes prior nonlinear PEFT expressivity across text/vision, while NOBLE moves nonlinearity into the activation path and evaluates training from scratch rather than weight-conditioned adaptation.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: v3 (current PEANuT); cited v1 title NEAT

reviewed_competitors.title: AuroRA: Breaking Low-Rank Bottleneck of LoRA with Nonlinear Mapping
reviewed_competitors.difference: AuroRA puts fixed and learnable nonlinear mapping, including tanh and spline components, between low-rank factors to increase LoRA fine-tuning expressivity and gives an approximation argument. NOBLE's architecture is extremely close at the branch level but uses two learned-frequency cosines and, critically, trains a permanent branch with the dense backbone from scratch.

reviewed_competitors.title: ReLoRA: High-Rank Training Through Low-Rank Updates
reviewed_competitors.difference: ReLoRA repeatedly merges and reinitializes linear low-rank updates to approximate high-rank pretraining, reporting models through 1.3B, up to 5.5 GB/GPU savings and 9-40% speed gains. NOBLE keeps a nonlinear branch and trains dense weights throughout; it may improve loss faster but does not target optimizer-state/memory savings and adds inference cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: Investigating ReLoRA: Effects on the Learning Dynamics of Small Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This controlled 11M-66M study finds ReLoRA underperforms full-rank training and can amplify rank deficiency/ill conditioning, showing that low-rank pretraining efficiency does not transfer automatically across scale. NOBLE reports positive 250M-1.5B results but lacks the matched dynamics/rank diagnostics that would show whether nonlinearity avoids the identified bottleneck.

reviewed_competitors.title: Primer: Searching for Efficient Transformers for Language Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Primer changes Transformer primitives (squared ReLU and depthwise convolution after Q/K/V) and reports compute-optimal scaling, a 4x training-cost reduction at 500M and one-third compute to matched one-shot quality at 1.9B. NOBLE is simpler to add and reports measured time-to-loss, but does not compare against this class of wider/deeper/architecture or downstream-quality-matched baselines.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: SIREN develops periodic activations and principled initialization for implicit signal representations, demonstrating high-frequency detail and derivatives across images, audio, video and PDEs. NOBLE cites this intuition to motivate cosine residuals in Transformer bottlenecks but does not transfer SIREN's spectral/derivative measurements or directly validate the claimed frequency division of labor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
reviewed_competitors.difference: StreamingLLM introduced the attention-sink phenomenon as strong, often nonsemantic attention to initial tokens and exploited preserved sink KVs for stable streaming to millions of tokens. The target does not introduce sinks or their deployment utility; it studies their training/architectural relation to massive activations and proposes a local-routing account.

reviewed_competitors.title: Massive Activations in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sun et al. established massive activations, near input-invariance, implicit-bias behavior, and their concentration of attention on corresponding tokens. The target extends this line with step-up/step-down FFN factorization and decoupling ablations, but its global implicit-parameter and spike-to-sink framing substantially builds on this predecessor.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gu et al. already traced sink emergence during pretraining across optimization, data, loss, and architecture, interpreted sinks as largely noninformative key biases, and suppressed them with unnormalized sigmoid attention up to 1B. The target adds 7B ablations, massive-activation coupling, head-dimension and loss-position results, and a dynamic-routing interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo et al. jointly analyze attention sinks, value drains, and residual peaks through an active-dormant head mechanism, prove mutual-reinforcement dynamics in a toy task, and test ReLU attention/SGD mitigations in pretrained LLMs. The target instead emphasizes pre-norm residual/FFN geometry, independent suppression, explicit gate substitution, and short-position supervision in a larger scratch recipe.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Refined Analysis of Massive Activations in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Owen et al. already show across GLU and non-GLU architectures that suppressing massive activations need not collapse perplexity or downstream performance, and combine TVR with KV bias or DynamicTanh. The target's spike-not-necessary result is therefore confirmatory; its distinctive extension is retained sink measurement and a proposed architectural bridge/local-routing split.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention Sinks and Compression Valleys in LLMs are Two Sides of the Same Coin
reviewed_competitors.difference: Queipo-de-Llano et al. already connect massive residual activations to attention sinks and representational compression, provide entropy bounds, validate models from 410M to 120B, and propose a Mix-Compress-Refine depth theory. The target focuses on why co-occurrence is contingent rather than necessary and contributes controlled normalization, gate, head-dimension, and context-position ablations, but it does not establish the first unified view.

reviewed_competitors.title: SkillLearnBench: Benchmarking Continual Learning Methods for Agent Skill Generation on Real-World Tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: SkillLearnBench compares continual skill-generation methods on real tasks and finds external feedback helpful but self-feedback vulnerable to recursive drift, whereas SkillNet focuses repository construction and does not isolate continual self-improvement dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Organizing, Orchestrating, and Benchmarking Agent Skills at Ecosystem Scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: AgentSkillOS uses hierarchical retrieval and dependency-aware composition over pools up to 200,000 skills and introduces a 30-task benchmark; SkillNet scales the repository further and adds Fabric but relies partly on AgentSkillOS's model-judged evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: SkillGenBench: Benchmarking Skill Generation Pipelines for LLM Agents
reviewed_competitors.difference: SkillGenBench pins environments, fixes execution harnesses, uses deterministic checks, and separates task-conditioned from task-agnostic generation across repository and documentation sources; it isolates generation effects more cleanly than SkillNet's end-to-end stack.

reviewed_competitors.title: OpenSkillEval: Automatically Auditing the Open Skill Ecosystem for LLM Agents

reviewed_competitors.title: SkillWeaver: Web Agents can Self-Improve by Discovering and Honing Skills
reviewed_competitors.difference: SkillWeaver discovers, practices, and refines skills within web environments for self-improvement; SkillNet targets a much larger cross-source ecosystem and graph, but its strongest task gains still use environment-specific expert traces.
