reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization or Hallucination? Understanding Out-of-Context Reasoning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. analyze out-of-context factual association in one-layer linear/bilinear attention models and attribute generalization or hallucination to gradient descent's nuclear-norm implicit bias. The target adds explicit analogy premises, trainable token mixing/value dynamics, finite-time feature-cosine guarantees, curriculum order, and an identity-bridge reduction, but the broad representation-sharing explanation for OOC transfer is prior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling the Mechanisms of Multi-Hop Reasoning in Transformers via Identity Bridge
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lin et al.'s original v1 already proposed zero-hop identity supervision, demonstrated OOD two-hop gains, and theoretically linked latent alignment to nuclear-norm implicit regularization in an Emb-MLP; v2 further frames a direct subject-to-answer association in one-layer uniform-attention and GPT-2/LLM experiments. The target's identity idea is not novel; its distinct angle is an analogy reduction and finite-time staged-gradient analysis with trainable attention/value parameters, though its positive proof is omitted.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokked Transformers are Implicit Reasoners: A Mechanistic Journey to the Edge of Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. study implicit composition and comparison after grokking, reverse-engineer learned circuits, and find OOD composition fails because facts are not shared across the needed layer regions, motivating cross-layer memory sharing. The target instead uses explicit identity examples to align entity features in a one-block OOC classifier; it does not study grokking, layer-local fact storage, or systematic OOD composition at depth.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Do LLMs Perform Two-Hop Reasoning in Context?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo et al. reverse-engineer a three-layer Transformer that learns sequential retrieval of bridge concepts under distractors and captures its phase transition in a minimal attention-only model. The target concerns out-of-context parametric composition without premise context, using feature alignment rather than a multi-layer retrieval circuit; the two mechanisms address different two-hop regimes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Emergent Analogical Reasoning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Minegishi et al. formalize analogy as correspondence between categories, study sensitivity to data, optimization, and scale, and decompose learned behavior into geometric relational alignment plus a Transformer functor, with pretrained-LLM checks. The target studies a narrower shared-property projection but adds finite-time gradient guarantees and curriculum/identity results; it cannot claim the first mechanistic feature-geometry account of Transformer analogy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformer See, Transformer Do: Copying as an Intermediate Step in Learning Analogical Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hellwig et al. train encoder-decoder Transformers on letter-string analogies, show copying-task data and heterogeneity improve new-alphabet/compositional generalization, identify an approximate algorithm, and causally steer outputs through head attention. The target offers stronger stylized optimization theory for attribute transfer, but weaker causal evidence and no generalization to novel transformations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Knowing Both Hops Is Not Enough: Understanding Two-Hop Generalization in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. find two-hop OOD success depends on consistent intermediate representations across contexts, locate failure in a lower/upper-layer mismatch, and improve it with recurrent-style circuit reuse. This supports representation consistency as a broad theme but offers a different remedy and shows two-hop generalization can be analyzed without explicit identity records, narrowing the target's necessity language.

MOUE predates that record and offers more elaborate partial connectivity and checkpoint conversion, but its claim that such reuse defines a new scaling dimension is narrowed by this simpler near-neighbor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Path-Constrained Mixture-of-Experts
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest concurrent expert-path work, explicitly treating cross-layer route explosion and coherent routing at 0.9B and 16B scale.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Loop Neural Networks study configurable recurrence/parameter sharing as an architectural continuum. MOUE specializes that idea to sparse FFN experts and learned routes, then adds reachability-aware balance and warm-start conversion; a direct Loop-style sharing baseline would help isolate the expert machinery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bigger Isn't Always Memorizing: Early Stopping Overparameterized Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: This is the closest primary predecessor: it studies the transition from diffusion generalization to memorization over training, reports memorization time scaling with dataset size, and uses a probabilistic hierarchical grammar to interpret coarse-to-fine learning—the same core ingredients used by the target paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Favero et al. frame generalization and later memorization as competing timescales and advocate dataset-size-scaled early stopping; the target paper narrows attention to an intermediate period in which held-out loss is still decreasing while weaker split-conditioned bias has already increased, adding paired-split score/sample diagnostics and a U-turn probe. The overlap substantially narrows novelty of the general dynamics and hierarchy story.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Diffusion Models Don't Memorize: The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regularization in Training
reviewed_competitors.relationship: This primary competitor likewise measures a generalization timescale and a later memorization timescale in U-Nets on realistic and synthetic data, with theory and dataset-size dependence directly relevant to the target paper's checkpoint ordering.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bonnaire et al. emphasize a widening non-memorizing training window and a model-dependent sample-size threshold beyond which infinite-time overfitting disappears; the target paper claims a subtler split bias can arise inside an apparently generalizing window and localizes it with exact hierarchical scores. The predecessor offers broader dynamics/theory, while the target offers a different bias definition rather than the first discovery of staged diffusion generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Memorization in Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Gu et al. analyze why the empirical DSM optimum can reproduce training data, introduce effective model memorization, and study how dataset size, architecture, and training procedure control whether a diffusion model approaches that optimum.
reviewed_competitors.difference: EMM targets the dataset-size threshold for recognizable memorization and includes interventions such as uninformative random labels; the target paper instead detects weak split-conditioned bias before standard memorization and connects its onset to hierarchy resolution. EMM is a stronger established baseline for claims about data scale and training procedure, while the target's distinctive contribution is earlier, non-replication bias diagnostics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Extracting Training Data from Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Carlini et al. provide the primary operational privacy comparator: a generate-and-filter pipeline extracts more than one thousand training examples from large image diffusion models and experiments across many training configurations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The extraction work demonstrates exploitable literal leakage in deployed-scale models, whereas the target reports a proxy split-affinity signal with an average exact-replication indicator below 10^-3 and performs no attack. The target may offer an earlier warning statistic, but its privacy claim requires validation against this attack-style endpoint.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Parameter merging preserves the pretrained checkpoint explicitly and requires no growing transition buffer for its core intervention; the target uses ER and studies task-to-task forgetting/recovery inside four LIBERO suites. reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu et al. attribute stability to the interaction of pretraining, parameter-efficient adaptation, and on-policy RL and often do not require replay; the target studies offline imitation learning with ER and claims pretraining plus replay. reviewed_competitors.difference: The real-world study reports severe forgetting under naive sequential finetuning and finds that well-configured ER can stabilize the full heterogeneous stream and beat joint training at equal compute. It supports the target's practical emphasis on ER but constrains the title-level implication that pretrained VLAs are inherently resistant: resistance depends on replay configuration and setting, and must survive physical distribution shift.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Arnaboldi et al. derive closed high-dimensional SGD dynamics for semantic and positional alignments in sequence single-index models. The present work extends the flavor to multiple latent features and heads and focuses on head symmetry breaking.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fundamental limits of learning in sequence multi-index models and deep attention networks: High-dimensional asymptotics and sharp thresholds
reviewed_competitors.difference: Troiani et al. derive Bayes and algorithmic thresholds for sequence multi-index models and tied low-rank deep attention, including sequential layer learning. This paper studies online optimization of a shallower multi-head predictor rather than information/computation thresholds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Dynamics of Multi-Head Softmax Attention for In-Context Learning: Emergence, Convergence, and Optimality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. prove warm-up, task allocation, convergence, and near-optimality for multi-task in-context linear regression. Their heads allocate to tasks; here heads learn mixtures of planted feature directions and global convergence is not established.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Dynamics of In-Context Learning in Linear Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. derive principal-component acquisition and saddle-to-saddle dynamics for multi-head linear self-attention, with outcomes depending on merged versus separate Q/K parameterization. This paper finds covariance-ordered specialization in nonlinear softmax attention on a different planted retrieval task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiation and Specialization of Attention Heads via the Refined Local Learning Coefficient
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. track functional differentiation and multigram circuits in a trained two-layer attention-only transformer using refined learning coefficients. The present paper supplies a planted-model mechanism but does not test whether its covariance ordering explains those empirical circuits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Loss Landscape Degeneracy and Stagewise Development in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hoogland et al. empirically associate developmental stages with loss-landscape degeneracy in language and ICL transformers. This paper derives a specific Hessian-driven symmetry-breaking story in a solvable regression model, without an LLC comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Attention to Activation: Unravelling the Enigmas of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kaul et al. introduce softmax-1 empirically to mitigate attention sinks and activation outliers in language models. The present paper repurposes its sink as a head-deactivation mechanism and proves a large-signal existence result only in the planted task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. show query-dependent per-head sigmoid gates improve large language models and suppress sinks. Their learned gate is a practical deactivation route absent from the paper's parameter-free Bayes-softmax comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-Head Attention as Ensemble Nadaraya-Watson Estimation: Variance Reduction, Decorrelation, and Optimal Head Diversity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fokoue analyzes head diversity through kernel-estimator covariance and principal angles under a fixed dimension budget. It offers a variance-reduction account of specialization distinct from this paper's SGD symmetry-breaking and redundant-output variance mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Flow Structure and Quantitative Dynamics of Multi-Head Self-Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pendharkar studies token clustering under fixed multi-head self-attention flows and identifies geometric interference between heads. The target paper instead learns the head parameters by SGD and studies feature alignment rather than token-state clustering.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Mean-Field Analysis of Multi-Head Self-Attention under Cross-Entropy Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huan and Yuan take an infinite-head measure-valued limit for causal self-attention under cross-entropy and state explicit extra conditions for convergence/stability. This paper instead takes embedding dimension large at fixed H under squared loss and derives finite order parameters.

reviewed_competitors.difference: NAG contrasts positive and negative conditioning and normalizes/refines the attention residual across image/video and few-step settings. GAG is single-conditioning and cheaper per step, but cannot claim its common-attractor theory for NAG's distinct values.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eliminating Oversaturation and Artifacts of High Guidance Scales in Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: APG decomposes the CFG score residual and suppresses its parallel component because that component drives oversaturation. GAG borrows the geometry but keeps the parallel attention component, highlighting that the useful direction is space/operator dependent and not established by analogy alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Angle Domain Guidance: Latent Diffusion Requires Rotation Rather Than Extrapolation
reviewed_competitors.difference: ADG argues high-scale latent guidance should control angular rather than norm change. GAG instead projects an attention residual and clamps its norm; both target guidance geometry, but in different internal spaces and with different theoretical objects.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Rectifying Diffusion Sampling with Perturbed-Attention Guidance
reviewed_competitors.difference: PAG creates a weakened prediction by replacing selected self-attention maps and guides away from it, usually requiring an extra prediction. GAG uses two cross-attention probability maps inside one pass and targets text alignment rather than structural self-attention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Smoothed Energy Guidance: Guiding Diffusion Models with Reduced Energy Curvature of Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: SEG uses an attention-energy view to blur queries and reduce self-attention curvature, creating a condition-free guidance branch. GAG uses a Modern Hopfield view of cross-attention and sparse/dense extrapolation, with lower NFE but narrower shared-conditioning theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Toward the Frontiers of Reliable Diffusion Sampling via Adversarial Sinkhorn Attention Guidance
reviewed_competitors.difference: ASAG perturbs self-attention transport costs with Sinkhorn iterations and guides away from the degraded prediction. GAG instead modifies shared-conditioning cross-attention directly through sparse/dense residual geometry and avoids another backbone branch.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving Sample Quality of Diffusion Models Using Self-Attention Guidance
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAG adversarially blurs attended image regions and guides away from the degraded denoising output across conditional/unconditional models. It established attention as a training-free guidance handle but incurs a second network evaluation unlike GAG.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Sparse Modern Hopfield Model
reviewed_competitors.relationship: theoretical foundation and closest retrieval theory
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu et al. derive sparse Hopfield energy, retrieval dynamics, and conditional error bounds. GAG imports those bounds as its sparse-versus-dense direction, but extends them to arbitrary cross-attention values and coordinatewise probability signs more strongly than the foundation directly warrants.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hopfield Networks is All You Need
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramsauer et al. establish continuous Hopfield retrieval and its attention equivalence, including multiple fixed-point regimes. GAG treats one attention layer as a Picard step and adds extrapolation, but its diffusion-value geometry and AA proxy are new assumptions beyond that equivalence.

reviewed_competitors.difference: GradMax adds neurons without changing the learned function and chooses their initialization by SVD to maximize gradients. reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural Teleportation moves conventional networks along parameter symmetries to change loss geometry and gradients while retaining function. TaT changes the operational target to supervised correctness selection over broad benchmark candidates and learns from all token-layer displacements rather than fitting explicit logical flow fields or relying on scalar kinematics.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Geometries of Truth Are Orthogonal Across Tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Azizian et al. show that static correctness probes are task-dependent, nearly orthogonal, and often supported on disjoint activation coordinates; mixtures and multi-task probes do not remove the problem. TaT directly targets this failure with a learned displacement sequence and reports cross-task candidate selection, but does not match their sparsity/subspace analysis or prove that its transferred score is the same feature across tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bao et al. find that static truth directions can generalize from atomic statements to logical transformations, QA, in-context learning, and external knowledge in sufficiently capable models, and evaluate selective QA. TaT instead reads ordered updates for multi-candidate reasoning and toxicity; it offers broader donor-target grids but no selective-risk, calibration, or direct comparison with their stronger truth-probe recipes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. probe reasoning-model hidden states for current and future intermediate-answer correctness, report calibrated scores, and use them for early exit with 24% fewer tokens. TaT focuses on frozen base-model candidate ranking and cross-benchmark transfer using the whole layer trajectory; it neither verifies online intermediate steps nor demonstrates calibrated early stopping.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Geometry of Truth: Emergent Linear Structure in Large Language Model Representations of True/False Datasets

reviewed_competitors.difference: Hanneke, Mehalel, and Moran analyze PAC learning of an autoregressive next-token generator after this paper and give a taxonomy in which endpoint supervision can have essentially any constant-to-linear dependence on T while full CoT supervision is T-independent. reviewed_competitors.title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Learning Autoregressive Chain-of-Thought
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li proves a rollout-length-independent, worst-case-optimal PAC rate for exact-trace learning governed by the local class's Daniely-Shalev-Shwartz dimension, introducing a rollout-stable parity dimension. This is a broader learning-theory result for full trace loss published after the Markovian paper; the Markovian work remains distinct in its inference-time endpoint/path counter, alignment/noise factors, and prompted LLM sanity checks.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Theory of Learning with Autoregressive Chain of Thought
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior on time-invariant local rules
reviewed_competitors.difference: Joshi et al. already show that iterating a fixed time-invariant next-token generator can make CoT learning sample complexity independent of chain length and analyze observed versus latent chains for general and concrete hypothesis classes. The Markovian paper's homogeneous kernel is a closely related repeated-local-rule condition, but it moves the comparison to inference-time demonstrations, introduces stochastic state coverage/margins, and empirically contrasts same versus different step semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling the Statistical Foundations of Chain-of-Thought Prompting Methods
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu et al. model multi-step prompting with a latent task variable, identify a Bayesian estimator when pretraining is sufficient, decompose prompting and model error, and obtain exponentially decaying prompting error; they also cover self-consistency, tree of thought, and selection-inference. The Markovian paper uses a much simpler finite-state count-and-argmax lens to expose alignment, coverage, and local-versus-global margins, but covers fewer prompting algorithms and does not model pretrained-LLM approximation error.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dissecting Chain-of-Thought: Compositionality through In-Context Filtering and Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct prior on CoT in-context sample efficiency
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. theoretically and empirically attribute CoT's in-context sample-efficiency gains on compositional MLPs to stepwise filtering followed by learning each component, and show how transformer layers implement that operation. The Markovian work replaces compositional functions and attention mechanisms with row-counting in stochastic kernels and isolates whether the same transition can pool evidence across steps.

reviewed_competitors.title: CoT Information: Improved Sample Complexity under Chain-of-Thought Supervision
reviewed_competitors.difference: Altabaa, Montasser, and Lafferty define a CoT information measure that quantifies how intermediate supervision separates hypotheses and derive upper and lower learning rates linking CoT risk to endpoint risk. Their framework is more information-theoretic and training-oriented; the Markovian paper gives a concrete inference-time mechanism in which repeated transitions create extra row counts, but lacks a comparable lower-bound characterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Metastable Dynamics of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Provable Benefits of Search, RL and Distillation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kim et al. model generated thoughts as a metastable Markov process with dense easy-step basins and sparse hard-step transitions, proving benefits for search that rewards sparse edges and transferring that information through RL or distillation. The present paper instead models a task's latent state transformations and compares endpoint versus full-path context samples; it does not analyze search, escape times, RL, or learned reasoning policies.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Empirical Complexity of Reasoning and Planning in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kang et al. study six natural and planning tasks and argue that CoT/ToT help by decomposing a hard problem into lower-sample-complexity steps, with tree structure preferred for computationally hard search. The Markovian paper offers sharper finite-state rates and an alignment manipulation, but its evidence is more synthetic and it never compares trees or realistic planning structure.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Curse of CoT: On the Limitations of Chain-of-Thought in In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zheng et al. test 16 LLMs on nine pattern-based ICL datasets and find CoT and reasoning variants consistently underperform direct answers, attributing failures to weak explicit pattern induction plus greater contextual distance despite compensating implicit inference. The Markovian theory offers transition misalignment and margins as different candidate failure factors, but does not evaluate those datasets, contextual-distance effects, or flawed generated rationales.

reviewed_competitors.difference: LoFiT selects a task-specific 3%-10% subset of attention heads and learns additive offset vectors, reporting LoRA-comparable results with 20x-200x fewer modified parameters. The target rejects localization in favor of all-layer post-block bottlenecks, gaining capacity and attention-path coverage but adding persistent work at every layer; LoFiT narrowly wins the target's Qwen3-4B tiny-budget average.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Gradient Descent and Sign Descent for Linear Bigram Models under Zipf's Law
reviewed_competitors.relationship: It directly compares gradient and sign descent scaling under a power-law/Zipf distribution and motivates sign descent as an Adam proxy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: That analysis is deterministic, infinite-vocabulary linear bigram optimization; the target handles stochastic one-pass finite-M random-feature regression, separates feature and target decay, and optimizes model/data/rate allocation under compute.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dimension-adapted Momentum Outscales SGD
reviewed_competitors.relationship: It studies the same PLRF compute-optimal problem with stochastic momentum and supplies a stronger optimizer baseline than vanilla SGD.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DANA obtains improved exponents by scaling momentum with model dimension and beats signSGD in part of the phase plane shown by the target paper; signSGD's distinct contribution is coordinate normalization/noise reshaping and schedule behavior, so its superiority is optimizer- and regime-specific.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws in Linear Regression: Compute, Parameters, and Data
reviewed_competitors.relationship: It provides one-pass SGD scaling laws for sketched infinite-dimensional linear regression, including the interaction of approximation, data, and model size.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its principal law averages the target under a Gaussian prior and focuses SGD; the target resolves a two-exponent deterministic target family, sign-specific drift/noise terms, and compute-optimal learning-rate and schedule phases, but only partially extends label noise.

reviewed_competitors.title: Function Vectors in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Todd et al. introduce AIE-selected attention-head Function Vectors and show strong causal transfer across contexts. The present paper reuses that construction, challenges its full format invariance, and adds RSA-selected CVs; the causal FV mechanism itself is prior work.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning Creates Task Vectors
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hendel et al. show that an ICL demonstration set can be compressed into a single task vector that modulates query processing. The present work splits this unitary picture into format-conditioned causal FVs and weaker format-invariant CVs localized at attention-head level.

reviewed_competitors.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yin and Steinhardt compare induction and FV heads across 12 models and use ablations to show FV heads drive few-shot ICL. The present paper accepts that causal role but asks whether a distinct set of heads better preserves relation geometry across format; it uses fewer model families and no necessity ablation of CV heads.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do Different Prompting Methods Yield a Common Task Representation in Language Models?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Davidson et al. already find that demonstrations and instructions elicit different, partly overlapping causal task representations and heads. The present paper studies open-ended, multilingual, and multiple-choice demonstrations and contributes an explicit RSA-selected invariant alternative rather than only documenting presentation-specific FVs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Emergent Symbolic Mechanisms Support Abstract Reasoning in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. identify symbol-abstraction, symbolic-induction, and retrieval heads that causally support abstract rule induction in Llama-3-70B. Their multi-stage circuit is stronger evidence for symbolic mechanism than CV steering alone; the present work instead isolates format-invariant relational geometry across four models and contrasts it with FV heads.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linearity of Relation Decoding in Transformer Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hernandez et al. show that many relations can be decoded by a linear transformation while documenting important failures of linear encoding. The present work localizes invariant relation information to selected head outputs and tests steering, but its cosine/RSA criterion inherits the limitation that not all relational knowledge is linearly accessible.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. formalize linear representation and argue that meaningful geometry depends on a causal, non-Euclidean inner product. The present paper uses ordinary cosine similarity to infer orthogonality and abstraction, so this prior supplies a direct caveat to its geometric interpretation and a stronger metric control not evaluated here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Provable In-Context Vector Arithmetic via Retrieving Task Concepts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bu et al. give a theoretical task-concept retrieval account for vector arithmetic and distributional generalization. The present empirical dissociation argues that one global task vector is incomplete and should be format-conditioned, but it does not test the theorem's training assumptions or supply an alternative formal model.

reviewed_competitors.difference: DAGMA introduces the exact log-det DAG characterization and central-path optimization reused by DyCausal. DyCausal's norm scaling aims to avoid DAGMA's finite spectral domain, but its published gradient drops the normalization derivative and therefore does not inherit DAGMA's gradient theorem as claimed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stable Differentiable Causal Discovery
reviewed_competitors.difference: SDCD defines explicit stability criteria and combines a spectral-radius constraint with sparse training to scale to thousands of variables. DyCausal borrows those criteria and reports faster cycle-graph behavior, but its normalized penalty is undefined at zero and its theoretical gradient is incorrect, so the stability comparison is incomplete.

reviewed_competitors.title: DYNOTEARS: Structure Learning from Time-Series Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: DYNOTEARS jointly estimates instantaneous and lagged structure with a smooth DAG constraint but assumes one stationary graph. DyCausal amortizes a graph trajectory and dominates it on the tailored dynamic benchmark, while retaining stronger smoothness, repeated-series, and local-stationarity assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: NTS-NOTEARS: Learning Nonparametric DBNs With Prior Knowledge
reviewed_competitors.difference: NTS-NOTEARS uses 1-D CNNs and NOTEARS optimization for nonlinear instantaneous and lagged DBNs, including structural priors, but keeps the graph stationary. DyCausal adds time-indexed decoding/interpolation; its advantage is dynamic adaptation rather than a new nonlinear causal function class.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causal Discovery in Semi-Stationary Time Series
reviewed_competitors.difference: PCMCI-Omega gives a sound constraint-based method for recurring semi-stationary mechanisms and explicit graph switches. DyCausal targets smoothly varying coefficients and both instantaneous/lagged weights, but does not compare against this method on periodic or abrupt regimes where interpolation may be the wrong inductive bias.

reviewed_competitors.title: Systems with Switching Causal Relations: A Meta-Causal Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Willig et al. model qualitative changes as meta-causal states in which relations emerge, disappear, or switch. That is a closer test of topological dynamics than DyCausal's synchronized smooth coefficient benchmark; DyCausal offers a scalable estimator but no discrete-state or change-point semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causal Discovery for Non-stationary Non-linear Time Series Data Using Just-In-Time Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: JIT-LiNGAM explicitly fits local linear causal models from neighboring samples under nonlinear nonstationarity and states LiNGAM conditions. DyCausal similarly relies on local invariance but amortizes graph states with a neural encoder and interpolates globally; it does not benchmark against this transparent local alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Time-Varying Dynamic Bayesian Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Song et al. already learn smoothly time-varying directed dependency structure with kernel-reweighted sparse autoregression and asymptotic consistency. DyCausal adds nonlinear amortization, instantaneous DAG constraints, and coarse interpolation, but its claim that earlier work is merely static understates this direct time-varying antecedent.

LITE reuses SOAP's rotated second moments to split sharp and flat coordinates and tune their update/damping scales, so its SOAP gains are an augmentation rather than a new preconditioner family.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct universal-subspace competitor that proposes a two-dimensional truth subspace and robust lie detector across models and scenarios.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Buerger et al. argue for a compact universal subspace and report 94% accuracy; the reviewed paper argues that universal and domain-specific directions coexist and explicitly documents sycophancy and expectation-inversion failures.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Universal Truthfulness Hyperplane Inside LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct multi-dataset competitor showing that diversity across more than 40 datasets improves a universal linear truthfulness classifier.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. scale dataset diversity and emphasize a universal hyperplane; the reviewed paper analyzes pairwise failures, partial sharing, erasure, and post-training geometry but its pooled evaluation is not leave-one-domain-out.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Geometries of Truth Are Orthogonal Across Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct negative competitor reporting task-dependent, poorly transferring probes with nearly disjoint sparse supports.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Azizian et al. emphasize orthogonality and failure of mixtures; the reviewed paper argues ordinary cosine is distorted by low-variance dimensions and uses Mahalanobis geometry plus erasure to infer partially shared directions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Detecting Strategic Deception with Linear Probes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct deployment-oriented competitor for linear probes trained on honest/deceptive instructions and roleplay, tested on insider trading and sandbagging.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goldowsky-Dill et al. report AUROC 0.96-0.999 and operating points at 1% false positives on strategic scenarios; the reviewed paper reuses these scenarios inside a broader geometry study but does not report calibrated deployment thresholds.

reviewed_competitors.title: One Probe Won't Catch Them All: Towards Targeted Deception Detection
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current direct competitor arguing that deception types are heterogeneous and that threat-model-matched probes outperform one universal probe.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Natarajan et al. quantify prompt choice as 70.6% of probe-performance variance and find only +0.032 AUC from a universal probe versus +0.108 oracle potential; this independently favors targeted detectors, while the reviewed paper frames heterogeneity as a continuous representational spectrum.

reviewed_competitors.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct truth-direction generalization study spanning logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bao et al. report that consistency depends on model capability and evaluate selective QA; the reviewed paper covers more deception domains and erasure geometry but gives less deployment-oriented calibration evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Truthful Representations Flip Under Deceptive Instructions?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct competitor on instruction-conditioned flips in truth representations, using probes and sparse autoencoders.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Long et al. study truthful, neutral, and deceptive instructions at layer and SAE-feature resolution; the reviewed paper adds expectation inversion and sycophancy, then emphasizes cross-domain linear geometry rather than sparse feature localization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Still No Lie Detector for Language Models: Probing Empirical and Conceptual Roadblocks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Early direct negative result showing basic generalization failures and questioning whether probes measure model beliefs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Levinstein and Herrmann foreground conceptual and negation failures; the reviewed paper supplies broader empirical reconciliation but retains unresolved operational assumptions about belief, honesty, and instructed output.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational direct recurrent-depth Transformer architecture for algorithmic reasoning and length generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Universal Transformers recurrently apply a shared transition block to all positions within a token-level depth loop and optionally halt per position, increasing per-token computation while retaining parallelism across positions at each recurrent step. TurboConn does not reuse the whole block within a token; it sends high-layer states across causal groups into lower layers, sacrificing prompt/training parallelism but aiming to avoid repeated full-block work during autoregressive generation and to retrofit distinct pretrained layers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Addressing Some Limitations of Transformers with Feedback Memory
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest architectural predecessor: future low-level representations directly access high-level representations of past tokens.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feedback Transformer exposes representations from previous timesteps through one feedback memory/key-value set so the current token's lowest representation can use past high-level abstractions, and evaluates language modeling, translation, and reinforcement learning. TurboConn acknowledges this direction but uses many source-specific, destination-specific additive projections between selected high and low layers, zero-initializes them for pretrained-LLM fine-tuning, and evaluates reasoning tasks. The prior work substantially narrows any claim that cross-token top-down Transformer feedback itself is new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Staircase Attention for Recurrent Processing of Sequences
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct recurrence-across-sequence competitor that trades parallel processing for tracking and language-modeling capacity.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Staircase Attention recurrently processes overlapping backward and forward token sets, with a Ladder extreme that repeats a shared Transformer, and explicitly sweeps recurrence in time versus depth. TurboConn retains the pretrained stack once per group and communicates through selected high-to-low residual bridges. Staircase supplies broader language/dialogue perplexity evidence; TurboConn supplies a lightweight pretrained-LLM retrofit and reasoning-focused results but no matched comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct continuous-reasoning competitor and source of the Coconut last-hidden-state feedback mechanism discussed by TurboConn.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Coconut feeds the final hidden state back as the next input embedding at dedicated continuous-thought steps and uses curriculum supervision to transition from language CoT, allowing multiple latent planning alternatives. TurboConn passes many intermediate hidden states to many lower layers between ordinary token groups, needs no thought tokens or changed loss, and finds its dense version better than one expected-embedding control; it does not compare with Coconut's trained continuous-thought procedure itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct algorithmic length-generalization competitor using adaptive recurrent depth.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Looped Transformers learn iterative RASP-L-style algorithms and adapt the number of shared-block loops to input length, directly targeting unseen-length arithmetic/algorithmic tasks. TurboConn instead makes path depth scale with causal sequence groups in fixed pretrained decoders and shows one parity extrapolation curve. The looped work has a more explicit iterative-algorithm training design; TurboConn avoids multiple full-block passes per generated token.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: The recurrent-depth model is pretrained at 3.5B parameters on 800B tokens and can choose many extra shared-block iterations at test time, scaling compute up to a reported 50B-parameter-equivalent load. TurboConn is only fine-tuned, uses fixed group recurrence along existing sequence length, and does not offer within-token adjustable test-time compute; in exchange it claims low incremental decode latency and preserves distinct pretrained layers rather than training a recurrent block architecture from scratch.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical and theoretical account of reasoning gains from effective depth without proportional parameter growth.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Saunshi et al. compare k-layer models looped L times with kL-layer non-looped models, analyze synthetic and language reasoning, and prove links between loops and latent simulation of CoT steps. TurboConn's central depth interpretation is aligned, but it creates distinct cross-token high-to-low paths rather than shared depth loops and provides no matched-depth theory or looped baseline. The competitor already supplies stronger evidence for 'depth, not parameters' as a general principle.

reviewed_competitors.title: PonderLM: Pretraining Language Models to Ponder in Continuous Space
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current direct latent-pondering pretraining competitor; TurboConn cites its earlier title/version.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PonderLM repeatedly converts a within-token predictive distribution to an expected embedding and re-invokes the model, learning pondering self-supervised during pretraining across GPT-2, Pythia, and LLaMA. TurboConn's soft-token control resembles one feedback step but its main method uses dense hidden-state bridges between groups and only downstream LoRA fine-tuning. PonderLM pays repeated forward-pass cost at generation; TurboConn pays sequential prefill/training cost and fixed bridge work instead.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning a world model and planning with a self-organizing, dynamic neural system
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Uncited, exceptionally direct historical predecessor to the claimed neural-field world-model/planning concept.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Toussaint learns perception-action relations in a growing self-organizing layer, encodes transitions in lateral connectivity, modulates that connectivity with motor signals, and uses a dynamic field for planning with local Hebbian mechanisms. Neural Fields as World Models instead learns a fixed-grid Amari-style convolutional predictor by backpropagation from raw visual frames, freezes it for gradient policy optimization, and analyzes motor-channel body selectivity. The newer bundle and experiments differ, but the 2003 record directly contradicts the claim that neural fields had not been explored as world models for planning/control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convolutional LSTM Network: A Machine Learning Approach for Precipitation Nowcasting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Canonical spatial recurrent predictor and the most important missing locality-matched architecture baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ConvLSTM replaces fully connected input/state transitions with learned convolutions so recurrent memory preserves spatial structure, and it outperforms FC-LSTM on spatiotemporal forecasting. The target uses a simpler continuous-time-inspired field update with one local lateral kernel and explicit motor multiplication. A ConvLSTM arm/ball control comparison would test whether Amari dynamics and motor gating add value beyond the well-established spatial-recurrence principle.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Visual Foresight for Planning Robot Motion
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct action-conditioned visual prediction and planning competitor from unlabeled interaction data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Finn and Levine combine an action-conditioned video predictor with model-predictive control and validate on a physical robot pushing novel objects, without calibrated sensing. The target instead optimizes a policy by analytic gradients through a frozen local neural field and evaluates in a simulated planar arm. It contributes stronger internal spatial interpretability and a body-channel analysis, but has a much narrower control domain and no hardware evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: World Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct latent-vector world-model predecessor and source of the target's VAE-LSTM baseline format and dream-policy motivation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ha and Schmidhuber compress images with a VAE, model latent dynamics with an MDN-RNN, and train compact controllers, including entirely inside hallucinated environments before transfer. The target deliberately rejects unstructured latent geometry for a local 2D field and trains policies through differentiable trajectories instead of controller evolution. Its one VAE-LSTM implementation is not a full reproduction of the stochastic World Models system.

reviewed_competitors.title: S2RMs: Spatially Structured Recurrent Modules
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct spatially structured recurrent world-model alternative omitted from the baseline panel.
reviewed_competitors.difference: S2RMs model a dynamical system as sparsely interacting recurrent subsystems with learned topology informed by spatial locations, evaluating cropped-video prediction and partially observed StarCraft II world modeling with OOD task generalization. The target fixes topology to a regular 2D local kernel and adds motor gain channels, yielding easier spatial readout but less flexibility for nonlocal or modular interactions. S2RMs demonstrates that spatial world-model structure predates the target outside the Amari-field framing.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Hardness of Training Deep Neural Networks Discretely
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest same-author predecessor studies deep-network training when every trainable parameter must be selected from a finite set explicitly included in the input and already obtains hardness beyond ordinary NP for engineered activations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Why ReLU? allows arbitrary polynomial-length rational witnesses rather than a listed finite parameter alphabet and proves a family-wide result for every nonlinear rational polynomial, plus exact gradient sign/bit hardness and a piecewise-linear bit-complexity contrast. The predecessor means that 'bit-model deep training can exceed NP-hardness' is not itself new; the new part is the rational-witness/activation-algebra boundary and backpropagation analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Fully Connected Neural Networks is $\exists\mathbb{R}$-Complete
reviewed_competitors.relationship: This is a primary real-valued-ERM competitor showing that training a fully connected network can be complete for the existential theory of the reals and can require irrational/algebraic solutions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It quantifies over unrestricted real weights and focuses on shallow fully connected training, while Why ReLU? changes the witness quantifier to polynomially encoded rationals and uses polynomial depth to expose exact-bit growth. The current paper's novelty is therefore not a stronger unconditional class separation than existential-real completeness, but a different digital witness model with an activation-dependent dichotomy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Complexity of Neural Network Training and ETR: Extensions with Effectively Continuous Functions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: This primary extension of existential-real training complexity treats effectively continuous activations, including sigmoid-related constructions, and establishes undecidability phenomena for sine.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It directly addresses real-valued smooth/transcendental activation semantics that Why ReLU? leaves open. The current paper instead classifies exact rational polynomial versus rational piecewise-linear computation and treats practical rounded smooth functions only through an assumed finite-output routine plus supplied backward rule; it must not be read as superseding the broader activation results in the real model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Quantized Neural Networks to Global Optimality via Semidefinite Programming
reviewed_competitors.relationship: This primary algorithmic counterpoint studies globally optimizing structured quantized polynomial-activation networks rather than only proving lower bounds.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its exact convex reformulations rely on shallow architecture and quantization/structural restrictions, whereas Why ReLU? permits polynomially deep rational networks and arbitrary rational witnesses. Together they show that quantization alone is not the boundary: depth, architecture, and whether the finite parameter set is structured determine whether polynomial activations admit algorithms or encode hard SLPs.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2021 PMLR volume 139 official version (18-24 July 2021)

reviewed_competitors.title: The Fine-Grained Complexity of Gradient Computation for Training Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: This primary gradient-complexity competitor proves conditional near-quadratic time barriers for computing attention gradients in large-language-model training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its granularity is arithmetic running time as sequence length grows and its architecture is one-layer attention under SETH-style assumptions; Why ReLU? asks whether an exact gradient sign or selected rational bit is computable at all in randomized polynomial bit time for deep polynomial circuits. The two results concern different bottlenecks, so the current paper's claim to a complexity perspective on gradients should be narrowed to exact representation complexity rather than first gradient lower bound broadly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Neural Networks is ER-complete
reviewed_competitors.relationship: This foundational primary result establishes existential-real completeness for neural-network training, motivating the present paper's contrast between real and bit-bounded witnesses.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ER-completeness captures feasibility over arbitrary reals and algebraic constraints; Why ReLU? restricts witnesses to exact rationals of polynomial encoding length and finds #P/NP behavior driven by deep activation arithmetic. The earlier result already owns the central real-ERM hardness claim, while the current contribution is the finite-encoding reformulation and its deep polynomial/ReLU split.

Its novelty is therefore coordination among heads on a simpler copying task, not stage-wise Transformer learning or Markov testbeds.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. already prove multi-head softmax gradient-flow phases and task allocation for in-context multi-task linear regression. reviewed_competitors.difference: DIVER already uses sequence-level semantic diversity as an intrinsic RLVR reward, reports Pass@1/Pass@k and out-of-domain gains, and uses potential-based shaping to preserve optimal-policy invariance. DSDR's narrower addition is a positive-only token-entropy term whose allocation depends on global distinctiveness. The current paper does not empirically compare against DIVER, and its strict-gap correctness theorem is not obviously stronger than DIVER's policy-invariance framing.

The set-dependent nature of DQO also highlights the gap in DSDR's single-rollout policy-gradient derivation; DSDR's distinct contribution is the global-to-local allocation rule.

DSDR optimizes heuristic semantic/formula diversity and reports Pass@k only as evaluation. DSDR uniquely targets within-mode entropy, while PKPO has the cleaner direct connection to the set-level success metric.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The canonical empirical demonstration that long-context language models often perform best when relevant information appears near the beginning or end and worse when it is in the middle, using multi-document question answering and key-value retrieval.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lost in the Middle measures downstream recovery accuracy and documents the U-shaped behavior; the reviewed paper proposes a structural explanation and fits normalized next-token gradient influence, but does not evaluate the retrieval tasks. It therefore addresses mechanism at a weaker observational target rather than replacing the behavioral evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A mechanistic account of extreme-token phenomena, including attention sinks, value drains, and residual-stream peaks, using toy training dynamics and analyses of Llama and OLMo heads.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Active-Dormant Attention Heads explains how specialized head states emerge through training and interact with values and residuals; the reviewed paper instead analyzes a position-distribution stochastic rollout with a scalar residual schedule and does not model head-state learning. The competitor is more feature/head-mechanistic, while the reviewed theory is more global and analytically explicit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lost in the Middle: An Emergent Property from Information Retrieval Demands in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct competing causal account that trains GPT-2- and Llama-style models under different memory demands and attributes recency to short-term retrieval and primacy to autoregressive uniform long-term retrieval plus attention sinks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This competitor locates the U-shape in learned information-retrieval demands and training dynamics; the reviewed paper locates broad pressures in masks, residual mixing, positional bias, and simplified content. Because the reviewed rollout uses learned lambda schedules, the two accounts are potentially complementary, but its 'architectural prior' framing does not experimentally separate structure from learned demand as directly.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior head-level factuality and hallucination study

The present study describes earlier repeat-sensitive heads and only proposes, without evaluating, a hallucination diagnostic.

reviewed_competitors.difference: McDougall et al. use weights-based evidence to explain 76.9% of L10H7's impact and connect repeat-conditioned suppression to self-repair. The present paper offers broader behavioral sweeps for early heads but does not recover their QK/OV algorithm or explained causal effect.

reviewed_competitors.title: Successor Heads: Recurring, Interpretable Attention Heads In The Wild
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gould et al. trace successor behavior from 31M to 12B parameters, identify shared mod-10 features, and edit behavior by vector arithmetic. The present cross-model scan stops at 708M and does not intervene on a proposed membership representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Meta-Learning Neural Bloom Filters
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rae et al. train a one-shot neural memory architecture explicitly for approximate set membership and measure compression against classical filters. The present behavior emerges under language modeling, but it neither has a fixed-memory comparison nor demonstrates that attention implements the same data structure.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Case for Learned Index Structures
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kraska et al. explicitly formulate learned indexes, including learned Bloom-filter replacements, and evaluate lookup resources and errors. The present study is novel in probing an unprompted language-model component, not in proposing that neural models can emulate membership data structures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Distance Sensitive Bloom Filters Without False Negatives
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goswami et al. define distance-sensitive membership over Hamming vectors and prove space bounds while retaining no false negatives. The present cosine-response sweep resembles approximate similarity search, but it does not establish a fixed-space representation, formal query guarantees, or a no-false-negative property.

Boule or Baguette adds a 23M-instance formal corpus, a direct depth/breadth reversal, and a width-scaling toy analysis, but its best RT format is similarly structured to expose reusable state and its topology claim is less causally isolated.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploring Length Generalization in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Early direct empirical predecessor for short-to-long generalization with scratchpads.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Anil et al. systematically test arithmetic, parity, and algorithmic tasks and show that scratchpad decomposition and positional choices affect extrapolation. The reviewed paper moves to formal propositional proofs and proposes breadth/depth as an explanatory axis, while retaining the predecessor's central warning that serialization and architecture matter.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest expressivity account of why intermediate tokens can overcome fixed-depth serial-computation limits.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feng et al. establish theoretical separations for chain-of-thought computation on serial problems. Boule or Baguette instead finds that traces can hurt narrow/deep learning under a fixed-width toy representation and contribute no universal advantage; its result is an optimization/capacity tradeoff under specialized assumptions rather than a contradiction of CoT expressivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Theory for Length Generalization in Learning to Reason
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct theoretical predecessor relating reasoning representations and computation graphs to length extrapolation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The paper analyzes when learned reasoning rules generalize over larger directed acyclic computation graphs and emphasizes representation. Boule or Baguette introduces an operational breadth/depth taxonomy and empirical formal-logic resource, but its PITA comparison does not independently manipulate graph topology and its toy proof relies on an unusually permutation-friendly target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Achieve Length Generalization But Not Robustly
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest robustness warning for apparent transformer length extrapolation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. show that successful algorithmic length generalization can be fragile to seeds and setup. The reviewed work reports multiple seeds and model families, which strengthens its qualitative reversal, yet its small per-run tests, label-prior changes, format ablations, and exact permutation construction reproduce the broader message that extrapolation is not an architecture-invariant property.

reviewed_competitors.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest later empirical work on when longer reasoning traces degrade performance.

Boule or Baguette supplies a topology-based hypothesis and formal synthetic controls, but its RT disadvantage is entangled with much longer targets, equal-step training, and non-termination, so it does not by itself establish topology rather than trace burden as the cause.

reviewed_competitors.title: The structure of the token space for large language models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest omitted priority predecessor for measuring curvature in LLM token space.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This primary study estimates intrinsic dimension and Ricci scalar curvature on token subspaces for GPT-2, LLEMMA-7B, and Mistral-7B, reports predominantly negative curvature, and relates geometry to fluency. Text Has Curvature instead constructs a contextual belief-simplex statistic at masked word slots and deploys it for controllers. That mechanism is distinct, but claims to be first to define or measure text curvature should acknowledge this earlier direct token-space record.

reviewed_competitors.title: Curved Inference: Concern-Sensitive Geometry in LLM Residual Streams
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prepublication contextual-curvature framework in LLM internal representations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Curved Inference defines pullback semantic metrics and concern-sensitive curvature in residual-stream trajectories. The reviewed paper works externally with masked-token distributions and entropic transport, making it more model-agnostic at inference time but less connected to a learned representation metric and no more intrinsically a property of raw text.

reviewed_competitors.title: Representational Curvature Modulates Behavioral Uncertainty in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest later, current-through-cutoff empirical competitor linking curvature to behavior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later work measures representational curvature, correlates it with predictive entropy/uncertainty, and includes perturbation or regularization analyses. Text Has Curvature predates it and proposes a distinct two-sided belief/Schrödinger construction plus retrieval utilities, but lacks comparable semantic validation and simpler-uncertainty controls. The later record sharpens what evidence would be needed for a causal or behavioral interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: HELM: Hyperbolic Large Language Models via Mixture-of-Curvature Experts
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest architecture-level competitor using variable curvature for language modeling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: HELM builds hyperbolic geometry and a mixture of curvature experts into the model architecture and evaluates resulting language-model behavior. Text Has Curvature leaves the generator frozen and computes a post hoc discrete transport statistic for slots and controllers. Its lower integration cost is novel, while its curvature has weaker metric grounding and no learned-geometry ablation.

reviewed_competitors.title: LLMLingua: Compressing Prompts for Accelerated Inference of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest established prompt-compression baseline family for CurvPrune's utility claim.
reviewed_competitors.difference: LLMLingua uses a compact language model, budget control, iterative token-level compression, and distribution alignment to reduce prompt length with extensive downstream evaluation. CurvPrune uses two-sided Texture scores and preserves spans, but the reviewed paper does not directly compare with LLMLingua or other strong learned compression systems, and it loses to simple baselines on two of five displayed tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct routing baseline and predecessor underlying Self-Route.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Self-Route chooses between long-context and retrieval-augmented processing using model self-reflection and evaluates the quality-cost tradeoff across datasets. Text Has Curvature adds a geometry-inspired signal and reports large token savings/gains over the cited controller, but does not isolate that signal from query anchors, guard bands, chunks, or threshold/fallback logic and supplies no confidence intervals.

reviewed_competitors.title: GLU Variants Improve Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shazeer directly evaluates GLU, Bilinear, ReGLU, GEGLU, and SwiGLU feedforwards in Transformers and motivates the variants prevalent in LLMs. The reviewed paper supplies a ReLU-gated 1D approximation construction but does not test or prove its rate for the smooth variants, so its LLM interpretation remains unverified.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mad Max: Affine Spline Insights into Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Balestriero and Baraniuk rigorously connect broad deep-network classes to affine spline operators. The reviewed work applies the spline lens specifically to multiplicative gates and derives a one-dimensional quadratic-versus-linear constructive rate rather than originating neural spline analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Error bounds for approximations with deep ReLU networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yarotsky gives rigorous upper and lower complexity bounds for ReLU approximation in Sobolev classes and shows depth advantages. The reviewed paper's result is GLU-specific and constructive but much narrower: one shallow scalar setting, no matching lower bound, and no comparison with depth-efficient ReLU networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Polynomial-Spline Neural Networks with Exact Integrals
reviewed_competitors.difference: Actor, Huang, and Trask already design a trainable piecewise-polynomial spline architecture from approximation theory and demonstrate h- and p-refinement at expected rates. The reviewed paper's novelty is that an ordinary ReLU GLU implicitly supplies a quadratic piece and yields a simple P^-3 construction, not the general idea of theory-designed polynomial neural approximants.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discontinuous Piecewise Polynomial Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Loverich uses compactly supported polynomial connections of orders one through five and reports gains from linear to quadratic and higher orders. Its discontinuous sparse architecture differs from a GLU, but it predates the GQU intuition that adding polynomial degree can improve approximation.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Multiplicative Neural Network Architecture: Locality and Regularity of Approximation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Choi and Han submitted before the reviewed paper and establish universal approximation plus locality and Bessel-regularity properties for a multiplicative architecture. They do not derive the reviewed GLU-versus-MLP P^-3/P^-2 comparison, but their prior submission narrows any broad claim that multiplicative neural approximation theory itself is new.

reviewed_competitors.difference: G-SGD constructs basis-path coordinates sufficient modulo positive scaling and optimizes in that invariant space. The target instead retains raw Euclidean weights and adds a soft norm-ratio penalty; it neither quotients the symmetry nor proves its penalty gradient stays on an orbit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Path-SGD: Path-Normalized Optimization in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Path-SGD approximates steepest descent in a path-wise geometry invariant to node rescaling and reports deep-network benchmarks. The target uses an additive gauge-dependent penalty to prefer equal adjacent norms and tests only shallow regression.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data-Dependent Path Normalization in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: This framework interpolates between path normalization and batch normalization and studies data dependence and natural-gradient connections. The target's penalty is data-independent and addresses only an incoming/outgoing norm ratio in a one-hidden-layer model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equi-normalization of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Equi-normalization iteratively performs exact function-preserving rescalings, proves convergence to a unique norm-minimizing representative, transforms momentum, and evaluates CIFAR-10/ImageNet. The target relaxes balance into a loss penalty whose Euclidean gradient is not function preserving and supplies a much narrower experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Symmetries in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Badrinarayanan et al. constrain filters to unit-norm manifolds and use manifold SGD to remove scale ambiguity. The target softly attracts paired norms to equality without changing parameterization or using a symmetry-compatible gradient geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dinh et al. use ReLU rescalings to show that parameter-space sharpness can change arbitrarily without changing a function. The target proposes an optimizer regularizer intended to select a numerically benign representative rather than using the symmetry to invalidate a generalization metric.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Teleportation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural Teleportation explicitly moves along function-preserving symmetry level sets to alter local geometry and gradients. The target tries to induce a preferred scale through a continuous penalty, but does not implement an exact teleportation or establish state transport.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Empirical Impact of Neural Parameter Symmetries, or Lack Thereof
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lim et al. modify architectures to reduce parameter symmetries and empirically study merging, connectivity, and Bayesian training. The target keeps the symmetry and selects a representative with a scalar penalty, without comparable architecture/task breadth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Weight-Balancing Fixes and Flows for Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: The TMLR work derives multiplicative weight-balancing fixes and continuous flows that minimize mixed norms within positive-homogeneous equivalence classes. It directly covers gauge selection with exact rescaling structure; the target's additive Euclidean penalty is simpler but neither clearly novel against this work nor function preserving during its own gradient flow.

reviewed_competitors.title: Outcome-Based RL Provably Leads Transformers to Reason, but Only With the Right Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ran-Milo et al. submitted first and already prove that outcome-based policy gradient trains a single-layer Transformer to learn iterative graph reasoning when the data distribution has enough simple examples, while learning becomes infeasible without that mass. The reviewed paper's narrower addition is a geometric difficulty-spectrum analysis with relay-versus-grokking time scales and finite-group Fourier gradient estimates, not the first broad proof that easy data enables outcome-RL reasoning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Provable Benefit of Curriculum in Transformer Tree-Reasoning Post-Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bu et al. prove polynomial-versus-exponential benefits for explicit depth-increasing and hint-decreasing curricula in Transformer tree reasoning. The reviewed work differs by keeping the horizon mixture fixed and deriving an implicit ordering from gradient dominance, plus comparing moderate and large gaps; it does not supersede explicit-curriculum guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Interplay of Pre-Training, Mid-Training, and RL on Reasoning Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang, Neubig, and Yue use controlled atomic/compositional tasks to show that RL gains require pretraining headroom and data at the edge of competence, and that process rewards and mid-training matter. The reviewed paper formalizes one shared-attention mechanism by which a fixed mixture can move that frontier, but assumes rather than learns the atomic base and omits process-reward comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: Curriculum Reinforcement Learning from Easy to Hard Tasks Improves LLM Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Parashar et al. explicitly schedule easy-to-hard reasoning tasks and find that fading easy tasks is essential to prevent overfitting, with policy-iteration sample-complexity analysis. The reviewed paper shows how a stationary mixture can self-order under shared alignment; its observed Qwen collapse makes the predecessor's fade-out result a material unresolved alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Reason at the Frontier of Learnability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Foster et al. adapt sampling for learnability to prioritize questions with high success variance because all-correct and all-wrong questions give weak RL signal. The reviewed theory explains a related edge-of-competence effect under a fixed spectrum, but does not compare against adaptive learnability sampling or show that retaining uniformly sampled solved tasks is preferable.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Does RL Post-training Induce Skill Composition? A Case Study on Countdown
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park, Kaur, and Arora empirically track reusable subtree skills and a structure-dependent learnability hierarchy under RL, including persistent failures for right-heavy forms. The reviewed paper supplies a formal length-based shared-attention mechanism, but it omits structural heterogeneity at equal depth that this predecessor shows can dominate difficulty.

reviewed_competitors.title: From f(x) and g(x) to f(g(x)): LLMs Learn New Skills in RL by Composing Old Ones
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yuan et al. experimentally show RL composing pretrained atomic string transformations into unseen multi-function skills and transferring composition across tasks. The reviewed work idealizes the same prerequisite-to-composition pathway and contributes phase dynamics, but its real experiments do not directly parse or verify composed atomic skills.

reviewed_competitors.title: POPE: Learning to Reason on Hard Problems via Privileged On-Policy Exploration
reviewed_competitors.difference: POPE agrees that hard on-policy tasks yield zero reward but reports that simply mixing easy and hard problems can be counterproductive through ray interference; it uses oracle prefixes to make hard rollouts solvable and transfer back. This directly bounds the reviewed claim: fixed-mixture relay needs aligned shared structure and is not a general remedy for hard-task exploration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reuse your FLOPs: Scaling RL on Hard Problems by Conditioning on Very Off-Policy Prefixes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Setlur et al.'s PrefixRL controls effective difficulty with prefixes of successful off-policy traces, proves consistency and sample-efficiency advantages, and reports back-generalization to unprefixed problems. The reviewed paper instead needs no privileged trace but only works when easy full problems raise the same alignment; no empirical comparison determines which bootstrap is more efficient beyond the frontier.
