reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Turing Machines
reviewed_competitors.difference: Graves et al. introduce discrete exact-match/exact-copy associative recall and demonstrate learned copying and retrieval with an external-memory architecture before transformers. GMC is a continuous same-marginal analogue whose match is a second-order correlation, and it explicitly studies learned PTH-to-IH circuits, modern architecture comparisons, and MSE attention dynamics; associative recall itself is not new.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
reviewed_competitors.difference: Olsson et al. establish the A-B ... A-to-B induction algorithm, its PTH/IH composition, and coincidence with an in-context-learning phase change across attention-only and large language models. GMC deliberately reproduces these signatures in a cheap controlled regression task and adds architecture and optimization analyses; circuit discovery and loss-transition coincidence are prior results.

reviewed_competitors.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh et al. use synthetic in-context classification and optogenetics-inspired activation clamping to causally identify interacting subcircuits behind induction-head phase changes. GMC uses a cleaner second-order retrieval signal and broader architecture diagnostic, but its head evidence is less causal and its deep-transformer loss transition remains theoretically unexplained.

reviewed_competitors.title: Zoology: Measuring and Improving Recall in Efficient Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zoology introduces multi-query associative recall, links 82% of a Pile perplexity gap to recall, shows attention's width advantage over gated convolutions, and designs sparse hybrids that close 97.4% of the gap. GMC instead isolates one same-marginal Gaussian correlation match, robustly exposes PTH-to-IH heads, and supports MSE theory; its architecture panel is smaller and tested at T=8.

reviewed_competitors.title: Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jelassi et al. prove a fixed-state limitation and exponential-length two-layer-transformer advantage for string copying, then test synthetic and pretrained-model retrieval. GMC targets hidden correlation-based successor retrieval rather than literal string copying and probes PTH/IH emergence, but the broad attention-versus-state-space copying gap predates it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention layers provably solve single-location regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest Gaussian sparse-location regression theory predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marion et al. analyze a latent single informative location with a fixed deterministic query/mean shift, proving asymptotic Bayes optimality and projected-gradient dynamics for a simplified attention predictor. That first-order marker permits direct location detection and does not favor a PTH-to-IH circuit; GMC enforces equal marginals and second-order query correlation, then studies empirical circuit formation and conditional empirical-MSE max-margin bias.

reviewed_competitors.title: One-layer transformers fail to solve the induction heads task
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sanford et al. prove through communication complexity that one layer requires exponentially larger size than two layers on an induction-head task. GMC empirically reproduces one-layer failure and builds its minimal model around a frozen first-stage PTH; it contributes an optimization benchmark rather than the foundational depth separation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. prove staged gradient-flow convergence under cross-entropy for a richer two-attention-layer n-gram Markov transformer with relative positions, multiple heads, FFN, and normalization. GMC's theory is simpler and conditional but addresses the natural regression MSE objective and hard-match max-margin bias; it does not yet prove full PTH/IH formation or the loss transition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Max-Margin Token Selection in Attention Mechanism
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tarzanagh et al. prove local/global max-margin token selection for softmax attention under monotone classification losses and explicitly narrow their v4 global-GD result to n=1 in one theorem. GMC adapts the margin machinery to residual-coupled MSE on exact match/copy, requiring identifiability and strong trajectory assumptions and obtaining a one-half-log norm rate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers as Support Vector Machines
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work formalizes self-attention as SVM separation of token-pair outer products and distinguishes nuclear-norm limits for factored K,Q from Frobenius-norm limits for a merged matrix, including local versus global directions. GMC uses precisely the merged Frobenius setting, fixes the value/PTH stages, and contributes a conditional MSE-specific proof rather than the general SVM equivalence.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Dong and Li already combine fixed-random local neural networks, domain decomposition, continuity coupling, and linear or nonlinear least-squares training without backpropagation. ELM-INR applies the pattern to coordinate-signal interpolation with explicit PoU blending, random Fourier coordinates, and BEAM; its broad combination of local ELM plus domain decomposition is therefore prior art, while the target task and spectral partition heuristic are narrower additions.

ELM-INR targets direct signal reconstruction rather than PDE residual solving and adds a local Fourier-energy mesh, but does not compare with this closest cited predecessor experimentally.

reviewed_competitors.title: Partition of unity networks: deep hp-approximation

ELM-INR uses that same input mechanism before frozen random ReLU features and replaces gradient training with local least squares; the paper does not isolate how much of its quality comes from Fourier coordinates versus closed-form fitting beyond one cameraman curve family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Fourier Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: same-author direct predecessor and novelty-critical overlap
reviewed_competitors.difference: KAF v1, posted a year before SGN by Zhang, Fan, Cai, and Wang, already replaces spline bases with trainable RFF, combines them with GELU through progressive channel scales, derives the same sigma=1.64 initialization, evaluates the same vision/NLP/audio/function/PDE suite, and reports the exact complex-vision numbers relabeled in SGN. SGN's identifiable increment is an input-dependent sigmoid gate that leaves the base coefficient fixed, plus a homotopy proof and GPT retrofit experiment; the target neither cites KAF nor measures that incremental change directly.

reviewed_competitors.title: FAN: Fourier Analysis Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: FAN is an accepted NeurIPS 2025 general-purpose MLP substitute that mixes learned periodic and nonperiodic components and evaluates symbolic functions, forecasting, language modeling, and image recognition with fewer parameters/FLOPs. SGN keeps the exact GELU base and uses an explicit bounded residual gate and trainable RFF projection, which offers a clearer warm-start path, but the target's own standard table does not uniformly beat FAN or other alternatives under a complete repeated-run protocol.

reviewed_competitors.title: Plastic Learning with Deep Fourier Features
reviewed_competitors.difference: Deep Fourier Features already concatenate sine and cosine in every hidden layer as a drop-in activation replacement and demonstrate sustained trainability across continual CIFAR and tiny-ImageNet settings. SGN instead preserves a GELU path, learns frequency vectors, and gates a projected spectral residual, targeting static cross-domain accuracy and pretrained retrofits; it does not compare against this prior on trainability, regularization, or continual learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Kolmogorov-Arnold Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: KAT addresses spline GPU cost and initialization by replacing B-splines with rational functions, sharing activation parameters in groups, using variance-preserving initialization, and supplying CUDA kernels. SGN uses global sine-cosine features and a residual gate rather than rational grouped activations. The target compares mainly with a large pykan spline model, not the more deployment-relevant KAT design, so its claim to be the only viable scalable basis-augmented alternative is too broad.

reviewed_competitors.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: KAN learns a univariate spline on every edge and emphasizes accuracy, scaling, and interpretability for compact scientific models. SGN gives up that explicit edge-function representation for dense global Fourier features, MLP-like accelerator operations, and warm-start compatibility. Its large-backbone efficiency advantage is plausible, but the reported KAN failures use an unmatched 478M-parameter language model and do not test optimized grouped/rational KAN implementations.

reviewed_competitors.difference: NLAFormer gives a matrix-structured Transformer construction for pointwise operations, shifts, transposition, inner products, matrix products, matrix-vector products, and assembled conjugate gradient, whereas this paper uses generic token sequence modeling for end-to-end matrix functions. It supplies precisely the scaling and OOD controls missing here, although it targets solves/eigendecompositions/log determinants rather than all five matrix functions.

reviewed_competitors.difference: AICC already applies DNNs to approximate several non-polynomial matrix functions inside coded distributed computation, whereas the target studies uncoded tiny dense matrices and adds Transformer number encodings plus one ReLU existence theorem. Its omission narrows the claim that learned matrix-function computation itself is new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.difference: McLeish et al. isolate positional digit embeddings, input injection, and recurrence as causes of length extrapolation in arithmetic, reaching 100-digit addition after training on 20 digits. The target establishes encoding sensitivity for floating-point matrix outputs but does not isolate mechanisms or test length/dimension extrapolation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Near-optimal learning of Banach-valued, high-dimensional functions via deep neural networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: theoretical predecessor and cited mechanism source
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adcock et al. provide practical existence theorems and learning procedures for Banach-valued holomorphic maps, including sample, approximation, optimization, noise, and discretization errors. The target borrows its approximate-multiplication lemma for a matrix-exponential representation bound but supplies no learning/sample-complexity theorem and has exponential width in nM.

reviewed_competitors.difference: E and Wang prove exponential DNN approximation convergence for low-dimensional analytic functions. Matrix exponential on a fixed bounded finite-dimensional cube is analytic, so this is relevant general theory; the target's distinctive part is an explicit matrix-path/Taylor architecture dependence on n and M, not neural approximability of analytic maps per se.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning advanced mathematical computations from examples

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers as Intrinsic Optimizers: Forward Inference through the Energy Principle
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior free-energy derivation of attention and residual inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: This predecessor formulates Transformer forward inference as intrinsic optimization, derives Softmax attention from a Helmholtz free-energy principle, interprets residual updates as gradient-descent steps, and develops multihead, linear-attention, and optimizer-derived variants with conditions and experiments. Kim instead adds a Fisher kinetic action, macro-thermodynamic dictionary, Goldstone/RoPE analogy, and modular-grokking fluctuation probe, but does not establish a stronger operational energy-descent law. Its omission materially narrows the claimed first-principles novelty.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hopfield Networks is All You Need
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramsauer et al. derive continuous modern Hopfield energy and update rules equivalent to Transformer attention, prove fixed-point, convergence, and storage properties, and evaluate associative retrieval and deep-learning tasks. Kim's canonical-ensemble language and Fisher action are different packaging, but the central fact that exponential attention is an energy-based associative update is not new and Kim supplies fewer convergence guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Energy Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Energy Transformer constructs a recurrent attention architecture whose update is engineered to lower a global energy and studies its fixed-point dynamics on image and graph tasks. Kim instead reverse-engineers a stationary free energy for ordinary Softmax and postulates dynamics on probabilities; it does not prove that standard Transformer layers descend the proposed energy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking as a First Order Phase Transition in Two Layer Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work analytically models competition between memorizing and generalizing solutions in tractable two-layer networks and identifies a mixed first-order transition, with phase diagrams and controlled teachers. Kim tracks a logit-variance peak in a small Transformer but does not derive competing phases, an order parameter, or the transition order, and its scaling test rejects asymptotic divergence in the observed range.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Understanding Grokking: An Effective Theory of Representation Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: prior effective-theory and phase-diagram account of grokking
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. connect grokking to learned structured representations, develop an effective theory and phase diagrams, and evaluate modular arithmetic and toy settings. Kim offers a generic attention fluctuation observable and thermodynamic terminology, but does not measure the representations or distinguish memorizing and algorithmic circuits that the earlier account makes explicit.

reviewed_competitors.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
reviewed_competitors.difference: RoFormer derives position-dependent rotations whose query-key inner product depends on relative position and evaluates them across NLP tasks. Kim relabels two-dimensional rotations as motion along a global U(1)-symmetric potential, but neither derives the relative-position interaction from spontaneous symmetry breaking nor evaluates a RoPE consequence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking as a Falsifiable Finite-Size Transition
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later study explicitly varies modular system size extensively, uses a spectral order parameter, Binder-like crossings, and model comparison, reporting Delta AIC=16.8 against a smooth crossover while leaving transition order unresolved. Kim's six-visible-point peak-height fit has R^2 about 0.2, no competing scaling models, and therefore provides much weaker evidence for criticality, although its fluctuation observable is distinct.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thermodynamic Weight Decay: Exploring Grokking Acceleration via Attention Specific Heat
reviewed_competitors.relationship: subsequent direct operationalization of the proposed observable
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later paper turns attention specific heat into a weight-decay controller, tests ten paired seeds on modular addition, and reports a mean 257-epoch or roughly 6% latency reduction with Wilcoxon p=0.049, while also documenting slingshot failures. It gives the C_v idea a causal intervention that Kim lacks, but remains one small task and does not validate Kim's macro-thermodynamic or Goldstone claims.

Haris et al. replace one-coordinate perturbation with simultaneous correlated noise and add a spectral tail lemma, but do not benchmark whether stability predicts grokking or robustness better on the same tasks.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Bhattamishra et al. compare random and trained sensitivity of Transformers and LSTMs and evaluate sparse Boolean functions including noisy sparse parity, establishing the task and low-sensitivity bias used here. Haris et al. add OU stability and an agreement regularizer, but their parity setup is less completely reported and does not revisit the earlier warning that low sensitivity alone does not directly explain all parity performance.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Hahn and Rofin isolate high sensitivity in Transformer loss landscapes, provide theory for why sensitive functions are hard, and evaluate parity and length generalization. reviewed_competitors.difference: Li and Mossel prove noise stability can decay exponentially with nonlinear hierarchy depth and derive statistical-query or gradient-learning lower bounds in Boolean and Gaussian product spaces. Haris et al. explicitly borrow the layerwise strategy, specialize to ReLU and attention cross-moments, and add a practical regularizer; their deep recurrences are less rigorous and empirically fail for gamma below one.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Noci et al. analyze covariance propagation at initialization in Transformers, connect rank collapse to vanishing query/key gradients, and study residual scaling with theory and experiments. Haris et al. reinterpret cross-input covariance as simplicity/noise stability but omit core architecture components and do not match this predecessor's initialization parameterization or gradient analysis.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Nait Saada et al. use random-matrix spectral analysis to characterize the softmax spectral gap, rank collapse across width/depth, and exploding or vanishing gradients, then evaluate an outlier-removal intervention. Haris et al. give simpler identity/hardmax cross-moment limits linked to Hermite simplicity, but omit practical scaling and provide no architecture intervention or tight deep theory.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Nanda et al. identify mechanistic circuit progress before behavioral generalization in modular addition and validate task-specific Fourier/circuit metrics. Haris et al. use the same grokking family and claim stability is a leading indicator, but provide one parity trajectory, no seed timing statistics, and no incremental comparison with mechanistic or loss-based progress measures.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Grokfast filters and amplifies slow gradient components and reports greater-than-50-fold grokking acceleration across image, language, and graph tasks with broad baselines. Haris et al.'s agreement regularizer is simpler conceptually and motivated by stability, but reports only roughly 1.35-fold changes on two algorithmic trajectories and omits this strong acceleration baseline and equal-compute comparison.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Prieto et al. attribute delayed generalization in common setups to softmax cross-entropy numerical instability, introduce StableMax and PerpGrad, and obtain grokking without explicit regularization across tasks. Haris et al. neither control numerical stability nor compare with StableMax, so earlier transitions under output agreement cannot be uniquely attributed to function noise stability.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This later study uses controlled modular-addition experiments with three to five seeds to separate depth, architecture, activation, and regularization effects and finds weight decay dominant within a narrow Goldilocks regime. It illustrates the replication and confound controls absent from Haris et al.; Haris et al.'s distinct stability objective would need to beat tuned weight decay under that protocol.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Bhattamishra et al. already compare Transformers and LSTMs on sparse Boolean functions, establish the stronger Transformer bias toward low sensitivity, and study label-noise generalization. Trapped by Simplicity changes the corruption to input features, evaluates clean-target recovery, and shows that the same bias can become harmful when the noisy Bayes rule differs from the target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why are Sensitive Functions Hard for Transformers?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hahn and Rofin explain low-sensitivity bias through sharp, isolated parameter-space solutions for sensitive functions and analyze parity and length generalization. The present paper takes that bias as a premise and studies its interaction with a noisy-feature Bayes objective rather than deriving the architecture's loss-landscape bias.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Learn Low Sensitivity Functions: Investigations and Implications
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vasudeva et al. demonstrate lower Transformer sensitivity across Boolean, vision, language, and pretrained-model settings and use low sensitivity to improve ordinary corruption robustness and track grokking. Trapped by Simplicity exposes the opposite side: under noisy-feature training, preferring low sensitivity can block recovery of a more sensitive clean target and may require rewarding, not suppressing, sensitivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noise Stability of Transformer Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Haris, Zhang, and Yoshida argue that average sensitivity misses correlated multicoordinate perturbations, derive noise-stability propagation, and regularize for greater stability on algorithmic and next-token tasks. Trapped by Simplicity instead uses average one-bit sensitivity and shows that the direction favored by robustness regularization may be wrong for latent clean-target recovery under feature-noisy training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Predicting Boolean Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Weinberger and Shayevitz define when a Boolean function equals its optimal predictor after independent bit flips and analyze majority and parity. The present paper imports that theory into neural training experiments and adds an average-sensitivity calculation and architecture-dependent failure analysis; the Bayes-rule and self-predicting concepts themselves are not new here.

reviewed_competitors.title: RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational positional-mechanism prior and the matched internal baseline generalized by StretchTime.
reviewed_competitors.difference: RoFormer uses fixed orthogonal rotations to encode absolute positions while exposing relative offsets in attention. StretchTime replaces index offsets with a learned monotone clock and uses anisotropic Hamiltonian flows; its theorem excludes exact fixed-phase matching for a prescribed non-affine warp but does not show a full RoFormer network cannot approximate the task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Time2Vec: Learning a Vector Representation of Time
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Early learnable temporal-representation prior omitted from the target's related work.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Time2Vec adds model-agnostic learned linear and periodic coordinates for synchronous or asynchronous time. StretchTime instead infers a sample-dependent cumulative pace from hidden content and injects it into relative attention; it should be compared to Time2Vec to determine whether Hamiltonian scoring adds value beyond learned periodic features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shape and Time Distortion Loss for Training Deep Time Series Forecasting Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct forecasting prior for differentiable temporal distortion under non-stationarity.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DILATE incorporates shape and differentiable time-distortion penalties into the training loss and evaluates non-stationary multi-step forecasts across backbone classes. StretchTime keeps MSE and changes attention coordinates; it neither compares with a temporal-distortion objective nor reports the phase-sensitive metrics DILATE motivates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Time Warping For Multiple Sequence Alignment
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Learnable monotone-warp mechanism prior in time-series alignment.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural Time Warping continuously relaxes discrete multiple-sequence alignment and guarantees a feasible alignment under mild conditions. StretchTime learns an implicit per-sample clock only through forecasting loss and does not align sequences or supervise tau; its novelty lies in coupling a warp to attention rather than introducing neural time warping itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Continuous-Time Linear Positional Embedding for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest positional-encoding prior for non-uniform physical time in forecasting.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CTLPE encodes observed irregular timestamps through a learned continuous linear function and compares against neural-CDE positional embeddings. StretchTime operates on regular benchmark indices and infers latent pace from content, addressing endogenous warping rather than measured gaps; the target does not test CTLPE or irregular sampling.

reviewed_competitors.title: STAEformer: Spatio-Temporal Adaptive Embedding Makes Vanilla Transformer SOTA for Traffic Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct adaptive-embedding competitor on the PEMS traffic regime where StretchTime reports its clearest wins.
reviewed_competitors.difference: STAEformer learns adaptive spatial-temporal embeddings and chronological information on five traffic datasets. StretchTime uses a general multivariate tokenization and latent monotone clock, but omits STAEformer from PEMS comparisons, so its traffic superiority is not established against the most task-specific adaptive-embedding prior.

reviewed_competitors.title: BSAT: B-Spline Adaptive Tokenizer for Long-Term Time Series Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Immediate pre-target adaptive-time and learnable-RoPE competitor omitted from the paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: BSAT places variable-length tokens at high-curvature regions with B-splines and combines learnable absolute embeddings with layer-wise learnable-base RoPE. It adapts sampling resolution rather than learning a cumulative clock and emphasizes compression, but it predates StretchTime by five weeks and directly weakens any broad claim that adaptive temporal coordinates or learnable rotary frequency are new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Non-stationary Transformers: Exploring the Stationarity in Time Series Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Non-stationary Transformers combines series stationarization with content-conditioned de-stationary attention and reports large gains for several Transformer backbones. StretchTime targets varying temporal pace through positional geometry, but does not compare against this alternative explanation and intervention for the same broad non-stationarity claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: TimesNet: Temporal 2D-Variation Modeling for General Time Series Analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Adaptive multi-periodicity baseline included in the target's main tables.
reviewed_competitors.difference: TimesNet discovers multiple periods with Fourier analysis and models intra- and inter-period variation as two-dimensional tensors across five tasks. StretchTime instead learns local pace continuously inside attention and is much smaller in the reported ETTm1 comparison, but only evaluates forecasting and does not directly verify recovered periods.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-resolution Time-Series Transformer for Long-term Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct positional and multi-period forecasting prior omitted from the comparison.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MTST uses multiple patch resolutions and relative positional encoding to capture localized high-frequency behavior and long seasonal structure simultaneously. StretchTime keeps point-level tokens and adjusts a learned clock; no matched test separates adaptive phase from the established multi-resolution route to varying periodicity.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Established channel-independent Transformer baseline used for accuracy and parameter claims.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PatchTST tokenizes fixed-length subseries and shares a Transformer across channels, reducing attention cost and extending context. StretchTime uses channel-value mixed point tokens and a learned clock; its reported 0.494M versus roughly 11.5M parameter advantage on ETTm1 is not accompanied by matched latency or tuning-budget analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: iTransformer: Inverted Transformers Are Effective for Time Series Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Established variate-token Transformer baseline used for accuracy and efficiency claims.
reviewed_competitors.difference: iTransformer inverts tokenization so attention models cross-variate correlations and MLPs model each series' temporal trace. StretchTime retains temporal tokens with explicit channel context and learned warped positions; its lower parameter count comes with a different tokenization and no equal-capacity comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: TimeMixer++: A General Time Series Pattern Machine for Universal Predictive Analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strongest broad baseline by dataset wins and the closest reported accuracy-efficiency comparator.
reviewed_competitors.difference: TimeMixer++ mixes multi-scale time and multi-resolution frequency images across eight analysis tasks. It beats StretchTime on four dataset averages and has 17 versus 13 horizon-level wins, while StretchTime reports about 55% fewer ETTm1 FLOPs. Because the authors could not reproduce its official code and copied its results, neither accuracy nor efficiency is a fully matched comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: OLinear: A Linear Model for Time Series Forecasting in Orthogonally Transformed Domain
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct linear competitor and alternate winner under the appendix's horizon-level aggregation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: OLinear decorrelates temporal features with a data-adaptive orthogonal transform and uses normalized linear multivariate mixing across 24 benchmarks. It obtains horizon-level average rank 2.08 versus StretchTime's 2.27 and is better on several less-periodic datasets, challenging a blanket need for attention or symplectic geometry; its numbers were not rerun in the target harness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linear Transformers as VAR Models: Aligning Autoregressive Attention Mechanisms with Autoregressive Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Architecture-alignment competitor represented only by an appendix linear-attention ablation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAMoVAR rearranges linear attention, MLPs, and information flow so multilayer attention retains an interpretable dynamic VAR structure. StretchTime's appendix shows its full softmax SyPE model beating a generic Linear Attention plus RoPE variant, but it does not compare against SAMoVAR's structurally aligned implementation or isolate positional warping from autoregressive alignment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational residual-connection prior and the fixed cascaded baseline ANCRe replaces.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ResNet adds identity shortcuts around adjacent residual blocks and demonstrates trainability up to 1,000 layers on vision tasks. ANCRe makes the source of each block's identity input a learned convex mixture of all earlier blocks; its modern cross-domain experiments are broader, but its depth tests are much shallower than the foundational stress cases.

reviewed_competitors.title: Highway Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Early learned gating of information flow through depth.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Highway Networks use input-dependent transform and carry gates to regulate adjacent-layer flow and train hundreds of layers. ANCRe uses input-independent scalar weights over non-adjacent source layers and a simplex constraint, so learned residual routing predates it while its all-predecessor normalized topology remains different.

reviewed_competitors.title: Densely Connected Convolutional Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: DenseNet connects each convolutional layer to every later layer by concatenating feature maps through L(L+1)/2 fixed paths, improving propagation and reuse. ANCRe adds rather than concatenates compatible representations and learns normalized scalar strengths, trading DenseNet's feature preservation for constant width and soft source selection.

reviewed_competitors.title: DARTS: Differentiable Architecture Search
reviewed_competitors.relationship: General differentiable softmax topology-search prior omitted from ANCRe's framing.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DARTS continuously relaxes candidate architecture operations and edges so architecture parameters can be optimized by gradients, then derives a discrete cell. ANCRe specializes that general idea to scalar residual paths, trains weights and topology jointly, uses ingoing normalization, and retains the soft dense mixture rather than reporting a searched discrete architecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Deep Transformer Models for Machine Translation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest early Transformer predecessor, omitted from the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dynamic Linear Combination of Layers feeds a learned linear combination of all previous layer outputs into the next Transformer layer and trains 25-30-layer encoders efficiently. ANCRe's ingoing all-predecessor mixture is structurally very close, distinguished mainly by simplex normalization, low-temperature softmax, placement at block inputs, the linear-topology case study, and broader modality tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: SkipNet: Learning Dynamic Routing in Convolutional Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: SkipNet learns per-input gates that hard-skip convolutional blocks and reduces compute by 30-90%. ANCRe's global scalar mixture never removes a block or edge per example and is aimed at training quality rather than inference savings; this contrast clarifies that ANCRe is data-trained but not dynamically routed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Deep Linear Residual Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct deep-linear optimization theory prior cited by ANCRe.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. prove discrete gradient-descent convergence for arbitrary target matrices under zero-asymmetric initialization in O(L^3 log(1/epsilon)) iterations and contrast exponential slowdown from standard initialization. ANCRe instead fixes initialization assumptions and compares two shortcut locations under gradient flow on an existential rank-deficient target; it adds topology as the variable but offers a narrower theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: ReZero is All You Need: Fast Convergence at Large Depth
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Learned residual-strength and fast-convergence competitor cited by the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ReZero gates each residual branch with one zero-initialized scalar, enabling very deep fully connected networks and 120-layer Transformers while reporting 56% faster convergence on a 12-layer language model. ANCRe learns which earlier layer feeds each destination rather than only branch strength, but does not compare against ReZero's much deeper and simpler intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Going deeper with Image Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Learned residual scaling and deep-Transformer optimization prior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CaiT introduces LayerScale, learned per-channel residual multipliers initialized near zero, with architectural changes that prevent accuracy saturation in deep image Transformers. ANCRe uses scalar inter-layer source weights and tests DiT generation, but offers no matched comparison showing topology mixing is preferable to per-channel residual scaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepNet: Scaling Transformers to 1,000 Layers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strong fixed-design depth-scaling baseline cited by ANCRe.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepNorm combines analytically chosen residual scaling and initialization to train 1,000-layer Transformers and evaluates a 200-layer 3.2B model. ANCRe learns depth mixtures and reports better C4 convergence, but only at 8-24 layers and without a DeepNorm baseline, so its 'efficient depth scaling' claim is not established at extreme depth.

reviewed_competitors.title: BranchNorm: Robustly Scaling Extremely Deep Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Training-adaptive residual scaling competitor omitted from the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: BranchNorm rescales the non-residual branch according to training stage to combine early stability with later convergence in very deep Transformers. ANCRe's coefficients are learned and source-selective but not explicitly scheduled; no comparison tests whether its gain comes from topology rather than a better residual-scale trajectory.

reviewed_competitors.title: DenseFormer: Enhancing Information Flow in Transformers via Depth Weighted Averaging
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest direct learned depth-mixture predecessor, omitted from the paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DenseFormer adds a learned depth-weighted average of current and past representations after every Transformer block, reports coherent distant-layer reuse, and reaches target perplexity with better data, memory, and inference efficiency. ANCRe normalizes source weights onto a simplex and frames them as residual topology before each block, but the core all-prior learned scalar mixing overlaps substantially and demands a head-to-head comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hyper-Connections
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct modern learned residual-routing competitor cited by ANCRe.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hyper-Connections expands residual-stream width and learns mappings that adjust feature strength across depths and dynamically rearrange layers, with LLM and vision pretraining gains. ANCRe retains one residual stream and mixes earlier block outputs using far fewer scalars; calling HC merely intra-layer understates their shared objective of learned depth connectivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: mHC: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Immediate pre-target normalized residual-routing competitor cited by ANCRe.
reviewed_competitors.difference: mHC constrains learned residual mixing matrices to a manifold that restores identity mapping and adds systems optimization for stable large-scale pretraining. ANCRe uses a simpler simplex of inter-layer scalar paths and reports under-one-percent overhead, but does not compare stability, scale, or quality with mHC despite both using normalized learned residual mixing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections for Parameter-Efficient Finetuning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target negative evidence about residual routing as a general adaptation axis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This OLMo-2 study finds mHC can adapt frozen models but identity-fixed mixing often performs better and standalone mHC does not consistently beat LoRA, while combinations are task-dependent. It addresses finetuning rather than pretraining, yet it is current evidence against assuming learned residual routing is universally beneficial and motivates regime-specific ANCRe tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent for Multi-task Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: CAGrad chooses an update near the average gradient that maximizes worst-task local improvement and proves convergence to an average-loss minimum. PCR instead posits a Gaussian zero prior on one KL-defined axis and gives a scalar MMSE result, not a multi-step convergence result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Task Weighting through Gradient Projection for Multitask Learning

reviewed_competitors.title: GTPO: Stabilizing Group Relative Policy Optimization via Gradient and Entropy Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: GTPO diagnoses contradictory token updates and entropy-driven collapse, suppresses negative updates, and removes KL regularization. PCR leaves the token-level GRPO objective in place and operates on reward/KL gradient geometry; GSPO is discussed but not benchmarked in v1.

reviewed_competitors.title: Group Causal Policy Optimization for Post-Training Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Group Causal Policy Optimization models dependencies among group responses, adjusts rewards, and regularizes toward a causally projected reference distribution. reviewed_competitors.title: Equivariance with Learned Canonicalization Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kaba et al. learn equivariant canonicalization functions that plug into ordinary backbones and establish universality across image, dynamics, and point-cloud tasks. DiffeoNN instead optimizes a per-input energy and specializes the transformation search to SVF image registration, targeting a much larger deformation family but losing exactness through regularization and finite descent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equivariant Adaptation of Large Pretrained Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mondal et al. already adapt large frozen pretrained models with a canonicalization network and dataset-dependent priors so canonical orientations match the training distribution, evaluated for deterministic groups such as rotations. DiffeoNN's generic 'any pretrained network' framing is therefore prior art; its distinct contribution is the SVF/registration energy for approximate diffeomorphisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improved Canonicalization for Model Agnostic Equivariance
reviewed_competitors.difference: Panigrahi and Mondal use contrastive learning plus optimization with a non-equivariant canonicalization network, reporting model-agnostic adaptation of large pretrained models and up to 2x speedup. DiffeoNN instead learns a VAE/adversarial image energy and optimizes an SVF, enabling nonrigid spatial deformation but with no latency comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lie Algebra Canonicalization: Equivariant Neural Operators under arbitrary Lie Groups
reviewed_competitors.difference: LieLAC performs energy canonicalization by descent in finite-dimensional Lie algebras and retrofits pretrained image classifiers and PDE operators. DiffeoNN explicitly extends this recipe to stationary velocity fields, adds image-registration regularizers, and reverses the warp for segmentation; that infinite-dimensional image-deformation specialization is the clearest incremental novelty.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equivariant Frames and the Impossibility of Continuous Canonicalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dym et al. show that continuous deterministic canonicalization or unweighted frames can be impossible for common group actions and construct weighted frames that preserve continuity. DiffeoNN uses a nonunique deterministic argmin and empirically tolerates discontinuity/local minima, but supplies no continuity or stability analysis for its diffeomorphism action.

reviewed_competitors.title: DiffKillR: Killing and Recreating Diffeomorphisms for Cell Annotation in Dense Microscopy Images
reviewed_competitors.difference: DiffKillR learns diffeomorphism-invariant cell matching and a separate registration field to propagate pixel annotations from a small archetype library in microscopy. DiffeoNN is a more generic frozen-model wrapper based on energy minimization and tests lung/synthetic segmentation plus topology classification, but DiffKillR predates the broad claim that registration plus invariance can reduce annotation needs under diffeomorphisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Canonicalization Perspective on Invariant and Equivariant Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ma et al. characterize connections and complexity relations between canonical forms and frame averaging and design optimal frames for selected actions. DiffeoNN contributes an applied registration construction for image diffeomorphisms, but its claim of a broader theoretical gap should be narrowed because substantial canonicalization theory already exists even if full infinite-dimensional SVF guarantees remain open.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This anonymous ICLR 2026 submission also decomposes ViTs, defines an averaged Lipschitz-style shift sensitivity, and fine-tunes components in isolation. It reports attention and feed-forward normalization as most sensitive, says higher sensitivity does not steadily predict performance across all blocks, and finds feed-forward normalization can match or surpass full fine-tuning at roughly 5,000x fewer parameters. That overlap and conflicting normalization result materially narrow the reviewed paper's novelty and demand a protocol-level reconciliation.

The reviewed paper adds an input-sensitivity explanation and module-level rank, but does not compare its selector head-to-head with the angle criterion under a matched budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: Three things everyone should know about Vision Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: It establishes that attention-only fine-tuning can adapt ViTs to new resolution and classification tasks while saving memory and compute. reviewed_competitors.title: Surgical Fine-Tuning Improves Adaptation to Distribution Shifts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Surgical fine-tuning shows that the best contiguous layer subset depends on whether shift is at the input, feature, or output level and provides gradient-based selectors. reviewed_competitors.title: Tuning LayerNorm in Attention: Towards Efficient Multi-Modal LLM Finetuning

The task and architecture differ, but it is a direct counterexample to treating low measured norm plasticity as generally undesirable for adaptation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploiting Layer Normalization Fine-tuning in Visual Transformer Foundation Models for Classification

reviewed_competitors.title: Sensitivity-Aware Visual Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: SPT also uses parameter sensitivity to decide where and how to adapt a ViT, then applies unstructured or structured updates. Its sensitivity is parameter/task-loss based rather than input-output expansion, making it an essential predictive-selector baseline missing from the reviewed experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling & Shifting Your Features: A New Baseline for Efficient Model Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: SSF learns small feature-wise scales and shifts, can be merged at inference, and reports gains over full fine-tuning across 26 classification datasets plus robustness/OOD tests. It makes the reviewed native LayerNorm result an incomplete proxy for what parameter-matched affine feature adaptation can achieve.

reviewed_competitors.title: Visual Prompt Tuning

reviewed_competitors.title: ExPLoRA: Parameter-Efficient Extended Pre-Training to Adapt Vision Transformers under Domain Shifts
reviewed_competitors.difference: ExPLoRA unfreezes one or two ViT blocks while applying LoRA elsewhere during self-supervised domain continuation, then fine-tunes with LoRA. It targets severe domain shift and combines block choice with low-rank updates rather than claiming one native component type is universally preferable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Canonical Rank Adaptation: An Efficient Fine-Tuning Strategy for Vision Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: CaRA tensorizes MHA projection and feed-forward weights and applies CP-decomposition low-rank adaptation, directly exploiting the component structures highlighted by the reviewed paper while controlling trainable rank. It is a stronger resource-matched adaptation comparator than full native 28M-component updates.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Smooth Is Attention?
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies tight local Lipschitz scaling for bounded unmasked and masked self-attention, including a mean-field regime. The reviewed paper builds on those tools but evaluates much looser weight-dependent bounds and turns them into an adaptation rank that Castin et al. do not claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Lipschitz Constant of Self-Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves standard dot-product self-attention is not globally Lipschitz on an unbounded domain and proposes Lipschitz L2 attention. This result forces the reviewed paper's bounded-input assumptions and shows why its finite sample average cannot be read as a global smoothness certificate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Transformers with Enforced Lipschitz Constants
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work directly intervenes on Transformer Lipschitz bounds and finds a severe smoothness-performance trade-off: matching a 145M NanoGPT baseline requires an enormous reported bound. It supports the possibility that excessive smoothness hurts capacity, but does not validate the reviewed paper's component-level proxy or causal rank.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Layer Selection for Efficient Vision Transformer Fine-Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: ALaST reallocates compute by estimating layer importance at each minibatch, freezing low-budget layers and reducing their tokens, with reported training, FLOP, and memory reductions. It is target- and time-adaptive, whereas the reviewed paper recommends a fixed across-depth component group from a precomputed sensitivity rank.

LET replaces logits and data selection with final-teacher-to-early-target hidden alignment and tests a larger 10x size gap, but its in-paper SALT comparison removes data selection and receives no dedicated tuning.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Study on Knowledge Distillation from Weak Teacher for Scaling Up Pre-trained Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This Findings of ACL 2023 study explicitly transfers from smaller/weaker teachers to larger PLMs during pretraining and analyzes teacher quality, loss weighting, and parameter remapping. LET adds billion-scale hidden late-to-early alignment, but the weak-teacher scaling question and its negative-transfer boundary are prior art.

reviewed_competitors.title: Knowledge Inheritance for Pre-trained Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Knowledge Inheritance asks how existing PLMs can benefit training larger future PLMs and uses distillation as auxiliary pretraining supervision, including analyses of teacher architecture and data. LET's distinctive part is transient late-hidden-to-early-hidden alignment at 1.4B/7B scale, not the general reuse premise.

reviewed_competitors.title: Strong Teacher Not Needed? On Distillation in LLM Pretraining
reviewed_competitors.difference: This post-LET study systematically varies model size and token budget and finds small or undertrained teachers can improve larger students when LM and KD losses are mixed, while stronger teachers can saturate or reverse gains. It provides the teacher-strength factorial analysis LET lacks and challenges LET's post-hoc attribution of GPT-2 failure simply to weak/old representations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pre-training Distillation for Large Language Models: A Design Space Exploration
reviewed_competitors.difference: It maps the LLM pretraining-distillation design space across logit processing, loss choice, scaling, and offline/online teachers, and reports that larger teachers are not always better. It primarily distills a 9B teacher to smaller students, whereas LET reverses the size direction and transfers intermediate representations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Grow Pretrained Models for Efficient Transformer Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: LiGO learns factorized width/depth operators that map small pretrained parameters into a larger model initialization and reports up to 50% compute savings across language and vision Transformers. LET avoids function/parameter mapping and permits heterogeneous architectures, but requires a live teacher during early steps and supplies far smaller training-scale evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Smart: Accelerating Large Language Model Pre-training with Small Model Initialization
reviewed_competitors.difference: HyperCloning expands a small pretrained LM's hidden dimensions while preserving its function, so the large model begins with the small model's predictive ability and needs no teacher forward pass. LET is architecture-flexible hidden guidance rather than initialization, trading broader teacher-target heterogeneity for ongoing early-phase overhead.

reviewed_competitors.title: LEMON: Lossless model expansion
reviewed_competitors.difference: LEMON initializes scaled models from smaller pretrained weights with lossless expansion and a tailored learning-rate schedule, reporting 33.2% BERT compute reduction. LET handles non-nested architectures and tokenizers in principle, but its tokenizer mapping is under-specified and it lacks a compute-matched LEMON comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stacking Your Transformers: A Closer Look at Model Growth for Efficient LLM Pre-Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: This standardized study finds depthwise stacking scalable to 7B and 750B-token training; a 7B model reaches the conventional 300B-token loss at 194B tokens, reported as 54.6% speedup. LET is architecturally less restrictive but is evaluated only to 20B tokens, so Stacking is a much stronger long-budget scalability baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: bert2BERT: Towards Reusable Pretrained Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: bert2BERT extends function-preserving initialization and two-stage pretraining to reuse smaller BERT/GPT checkpoints, reporting about 45-47% compute savings. This directly predates LET's broad 'reuse community investment' motivation, while LET differs by using representations and accepting non-nested architectures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Where to Begin: Efficient Pretraining via Subnetwork Selection and Distillation
reviewed_competitors.difference: It discovers structurally sparse subnetworks of larger checkpoints, initializes smaller models from them, and adds distillation, reporting 5.16x fewer FLOPs at a 10B-token budget for matched perplexity. Its direction is large-to-small and focuses on SLM creation, but it is a current, compute-accounted alternative for converting prior checkpoint investment into faster pretraining.

reviewed_competitors.title: FitNets: Hints for Thin Deep Nets
reviewed_competitors.difference: FitNets introduced hidden-representation hints and a mapping layer so a student's intermediate layer learns from a teacher representation, explicitly to ease optimization. LET reverses the normal capacity direction, uses the teacher's final state, targets pretraining, and anneals the loss, but hidden-layer hinting itself is longstanding.

reviewed_competitors.title: Patient Knowledge Distillation for BERT Model Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Patient KD transfers multiple intermediate BERT layers into a shallower student using explicit layer-matching strategies. The direction is strong-to-weak compression and task adaptation, whereas LET transfers one late weak-teacher state into an early strong-target layer during pretraining; it still constrains claims that cross-layer Transformer alignment is new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization: Eliciting Strong Capabilities With Weak Supervision
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies whether a strong pretrained model can exceed a weak supervisor on downstream tasks, establishing the weak-to-strong framing and performance-gap metrics. LET concerns from-scratch autoregressive pretraining and hidden representations rather than weak task labels, so this is conceptual context rather than a direct systems baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Weak-to-Strong On-Policy Distillation
reviewed_competitors.difference: W2S-OPD constructs a proxy teacher from logit differences between weak contrast models and distills it on the strong student's own rollouts, improving math/code post-training even when every source is weaker. It is not a pretraining competitor, but shows a current alternative to direct weak-teacher imitation that explicitly isolates a capability direction and avoids forcing the student toward the weak model's full representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Remarkable Robustness of LLMs: Stages of Inference?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lad et al. already infer depth-dependent stages from layer deletion/swapping, logit-lens alignment, attention, and neuron analyses across eight models. The present work compresses this into a two-phase context/prediction account and adds angular-versus-norm geometry, but does not match the antecedent's model breadth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Angular Steering: Behavior Control via Rotation in Activation Space
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vu and Nguyen formulate activation rotations and adaptive angular steering for refusal, compliance, and emotion with capability-preservation evaluations. reviewed_competitors.title: From Directions to Cones: Exploring Multidimensional Representations of Propositional Facts in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yu et al. identify multidimensional cones that causally mediate truth behavior, test cross-model transfer, and measure preservation of unrelated behavior. The present paper studies a direction/norm decomposition of generic prediction-associated states over depth, with less behavioral-selectivity evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Directions to Regions: Decomposing Activations in Language Models via Local Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shafran et al. use mixture-of-factor-analyzers regions and local covariance to model nonlinear activation geometry and benchmark localization and steering against sparse autoencoders. The present paper instead uses global centroids and pairwise angular distances, gaining a depth narrative but not testing whether local regions explain its effects better.

reviewed_competitors.title: Large language models implicitly learn to straighten neural sentence trajectories to construct a predictive representation of natural language
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hosseini and Fedorenko relate depth-wise trajectory curvature to next-word surprisal and model quality, establishing a predictive-geometry hypothesis. The present paper adds intervention-based causal leverage and an angular/norm split, although its natural-text geometry remains correlational too.

reviewed_competitors.title: Local Linearity of LLMs Enables Activation Steering via Model-Based Linear Optimal Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: Skifstad et al. explicitly model cross-layer propagation with layerwise Jacobians and closed-loop linear-quadratic control, including tracking bounds and broad behavior tasks. This later work supplies the dynamical and perturbation-gain controls absent from the present open-loop centroid phase analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Parameter Symmetry and Noise Equilibrium of Stochastic Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ziyin et al. already prove noise-driven motion along exponential symmetries to initialization-independent equilibria and explicitly use it to explain progressive sharpening/flattening. The present paper specializes that mechanism to multi-output deep linear regression and derives an exact covariance-conditioned trace and spectrum.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Thermodynamics: Entropic Forces in Deep and Universal Representation Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ziyin, Xu, and Chuang develop the entropic-force framework and balanced-factor characterization reused as Lemma 5, and already claim to reconcile flatness- and sharpness-seeking behavior. The new contribution is the explicit label-noise-spectrum solution and sharpness bounds for one solvable model, not the minimum-fluctuation principle itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Label Noise SGD Provably Prefers Flat Global Minimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damian, Ma, and Lee derive a label-noise-induced regularizer that penalizes sharp minima, with convergence, large-learning-rate, momentum, classification, and general-covariance extensions. The present result identifies a multi-output anisotropic regime where minimizing a different fluctuation functional can instead select a sharper factorization; reconciling the noise models and asymptotic regimes is essential to the claimed reversal.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Happens after SGD Reaches Zero Loss? --A Mathematical Framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Wang, and Arora derive a long-timescale SDE on a minimizer manifold with arbitrary noise covariance, directly addressing post-convergence dynamics. The present paper offers a closed-form endpoint for a richer multi-output factorization but assumes the effective-objective minimizer rather than proving the SGD path reaches it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness of Minima in Deep Matrix Factorization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kamber and Parhi give an exact top-Hessian-eigenvalue expression at arbitrary deep-matrix-factorization minimizers and characterize spectral-norm balancing for flatness. The present paper cites the concurrent formula, focuses mainly on trace, and adds which minimizer a covariance-weighted SGD effective objective selects.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep linear networks for regression are implicitly regularized towards flat minima
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marion and Chizat prove that gradient flow selects near-minimal top-eigenvalue sharpness in univariate deep-linear regression under specific initializations. The present model is multi-output and stochastic, exposing label-noise anisotropy that is impossible in a scalar output, but its trajectory guarantee is weaker.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent Converges Linearly to Flatter Minima than Gradient Flow in Shallow Linear Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Beneventano and Woodworth solve finite-step GD dynamics in a scalar depth-2 network and find large-step discretization selects flatter solutions than gradient flow. The present mechanism is minibatch-noise conditioned and can select sharper solutions, emphasizing that deterministic step-size and stochastic covariance biases need not agree.

reviewed_competitors.title: Edge of Stochastic Stability: Revisiting the Edge of Stability for SGD
reviewed_competitors.difference: Andreyev and Beneventano show that minibatch SGD stabilizes batch sharpness rather than the full-batch top Hessian eigenvalue and that smaller batches can suppress lambda_max. This is a different, large-step stability regime that the present small-eta effective theory explicitly cannot cover and that pushes sharpness in the opposite direction.

reviewed_competitors.title: SGD at the Edge of Stability: The Stochastic Sharpness Gap
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liao et al. derive a stochastic self-stabilization coupling and a closed-form noise-dependent reduction in equilibrium top-eigenvalue sharpness at the edge of stability. This later result reinforces that gradient noise can flatten in a finite-step regime, bounding any broad reading that anisotropic noise generally makes SGD seek sharpness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dinh et al. establish that function-preserving symmetries can make parameter-space minima arbitrarily sharp without changing generalization. The present paper productively uses the same issue as a selection manifold, but its trace outcome remains parameterization-specific and cannot support a generalization claim without an invariant metric.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramachandran et al. use exhaustive and reinforcement-learning search over manually composed scalar expressions and identify Swish, then validate on large vision models. The reviewed paper broadens proposals to LLM-written Python and selects on synthetic OOD error, but automated discovery and cross-architecture transfer are not new by themselves.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evolutionary Optimization of Deep Learning Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bingham et al. evolve tree-structured scalar functions, test specialization and cross-task generalization on CIFAR, and report statistical comparisons. The reviewed paper uses an LLM mutation operator, a looser program space, and synthetic-to-domain transfer, but supplies much less search and seed accounting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering Parametric Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: PANGAEA represents activations as arbitrary computation graphs, evolves their structure, and learns parameters per layer/channel over training, producing both specialized and general functions. The reviewed work removes the fixed primitive grammar through code LLMs and uses OOD proxy fitness, but its claim that earlier search required narrowly hand-built spaces should be read against PANGAEA's already flexible graphs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Activation Function Optimization through Surrogate Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work builds Act-Bench from 2,913 trained functions and uses initialization statistics plus a surrogate to reduce search cost across CNNs, ResNets, and ViTs. The reviewed paper instead pays for short child-model training and explores free-form code; it does not compare proposal efficiency or downstream rank correlation to this mature search baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evolving RL: Discovering New Activation Functions using LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: EvolveAct already combines code LLM proposals with evolutionary activation search and jointly optimizes across MinAtar and Brax environments. The reviewed paper's defensible distinction is its small synthetic regression lab, explicit OOD fitness, and transfer into vision, graph, and algorithmic tasks—not the use of LLMs and evolution to discover activations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neuro-Symbolic Activation Discovery: Transferring Mathematical Structures from Physics to Ecology for Parameter-Efficient Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper uses genetic programming to extract interpretable scientific formulas as activations and explicitly reports both successful physics-to-ecology transfer and failed physics-to-text transfer. The reviewed paper searches broader code with an LLM and evaluates larger standard architectures, but omits this direct cross-domain discovery precedent and provides less explicit boundary-condition analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evolving Multi-Channel Confidence-Aware Activation Functions for Missing Data with Channel Propagation
reviewed_competitors.difference: 3C-EA deliberately evolves multivariate activations over a value, missingness bit, and imputation confidence, and defines how the auxiliary channels propagate through the network. It postdates the reviewed paper and does not affect priority, but it shows how nonpointwise activation search can specify semantics explicitly rather than admitting arbitrary tensor coupling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks Fail to Learn Periodic Functions and How to Fix It
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ziyin et al. introduce the fixed periodic Snake activation specifically to overcome extrapolation failure on periodic functions and analyze its inductive bias. GELUSine and GELU-Sinc add bounded periodic structure to GELU and are discovered rather than hand-designed, but the central periodic-extrapolation mechanism is established prior art.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization Properties of NAS under Activation and Skip Connection Search
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhu et al. derive NTK-based generalization bounds and a train-free selection criterion for mixed activations and skip connections. The reviewed work empirically optimizes OOD error in a much broader program space, but offers no guarantee or theory connecting its proxy fitness to downstream transfer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Activation Functions for Sparse Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAFS jointly searches activation choices and hyperparameters for pruned networks across several architectures and datasets, demonstrating that activation quality is conditional on the training regime. The reviewed paper targets dense-model cross-domain transfer and free-form functional discovery, but does not jointly retune the regimes with which each activation interacts.

reviewed_competitors.title: AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
reviewed_competitors.relationship: enabling system rather than activation-specific novelty
reviewed_competitors.difference: AlphaEvolve defines the LLM-guided evolutionary code-search loop used here and demonstrates it across algorithms and infrastructure. The reviewed paper's contribution is therefore an application-specific evaluator, proxy lab, and activation findings; the search system itself is inherited.

reviewed_competitors.title: AutoML-Zero: Evolving Machine Learning Algorithms From Scratch
reviewed_competitors.difference: AutoML-Zero evolves complete learning algorithms from basic operations and demonstrates that broad program search can rediscover useful mechanisms. The reviewed paper narrows the object to activation code and adds an LLM proposal prior plus OOD fitness, so its reduced-manual-bias framing has this earlier program-evolution precedent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct functional parent and strongest baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: GELU is the exact base of GELUSine and GELU-Sinc and remains equal or better on both image tasks. The new scalar forms are small fixed periodic perturbations; their novelty lies in the search route, coefficients, and OOD-task gains rather than a wholly new activation family.

reviewed_competitors.difference: PHYRE lets agents make repeated interventions in 2D mechanics puzzles and measures sample-efficient generalization across task templates. reviewed_competitors.difference: Physion covers collisions, rolling, sliding, projectiles, and stable configurations and compares object-centric and state-aware models with human predictions. reviewed_competitors.title: Visual cognition in multimodal large language models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This prior paper measures pretrained MLLMs against human intuitive physics, causal reasoning, and psychology under controlled visual tasks. The reviewed work moves from diagnosis to an explicit GRPO/SFT training intervention and representation probes, while retaining a similarly narrow cognitive-task framing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Testing the Limits of Fine-Tuning for Improving Visual Cognition in Vision Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: The earlier study shows that ground-truth SFT improves in-domain visual cognition but not robust transfer across visual characteristics or cognitive tasks. The reviewed paper adds reward-based interaction and finds it does not consistently outperform that SFT baseline; thus its main advance is the controlled negative RL comparison and extended ablations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics Context Builders: A Modular Framework for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Physics Context Builders use simulated physical QA and specialized scene descriptions, evaluate Falling Tower and CLEVRER, and report sim-to-real gains. The reviewed paper offers a cleaner on-policy-versus-supervised comparison and cross-task matrix, but its negative results do not benchmark against PCB's modular physical context or broader scenes.

reviewed_competitors.title: PhysBench: Benchmarking and Enhancing Vision-Language Models for Physical World Understanding
reviewed_competitors.relationship: broad VLM physical-understanding benchmark and enhancement competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: PhysBench spans 10,002 interleaved examples, 19 subclasses, eight capabilities, and 75 VLMs, then improves performance by composing VLMs with specialized vision tools. The reviewed study sacrifices breadth for a causal post-training comparison and exposes transfer brittleness, but cannot generalize its negative result to PhysBench's physical domains.

reviewed_competitors.title: A little less conversation, a little more action, please: Investigating the physical common-sense of LLMs in a 3D embodied environment
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mecattaf et al. evaluate language models acting in a 3D environment and diagnose failures of physical common sense through behavior. The reviewed work adds trainable VLM policies and an SFT control, but its main loop lacks the observed multi-step environmental consequences central to embodied action.

reviewed_competitors.title: SFT Memorizes, RL Generalizes: A Comparative Study of Foundation Model Post-training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chu et al. report that online RL generalizes better than SFT on arithmetic and simple navigation under their protocols. The reviewed paper is a valuable counterexample in visual tower tasks: GRPO has one narrow advantage but no reliable overall benefit, suggesting the result depends on task, feedback loop, and interface rather than being universal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pixels to Principles: Probing Intuitive Physics Understanding in Multimodal Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pixels to Principles systematically probes where physical plausibility cues appear in multimodal models. The reviewed paper adds before/after post-training probes tied to behavioral transfer, but its same-renderer offset probe is simpler and does not causally establish that decoded variables drive output.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Diagnosis to Improvement: Probing Spatio-Physical Reasoning in Vision Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Han et al. probe stacked-object stability and improve Qwen2.5-VL with SFT and RL, but do not exhaustively cross every trained task with every related target. The reviewed paper's distinctive strength is that complete generalization matrix and its legal-output, model-size, and algorithm ablations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do Vision-Language Models Have Internal World Models? Towards an Atomic Evaluation
reviewed_competitors.difference: WM-ABench separates perception and prediction into 23 atomic dimensions across six counterfactual simulated environments and finds basic failures in 15 VLMs. The reviewed work tests whether post-training changes one controlled slice and adds behavior-versus-decoding evidence, but its results should not be extrapolated to the broader world-model taxonomy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpreting Physics in Video World Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper maps physical-plausibility and motion-variable probes across video encoders, analyzes subspace geometry, attention sensitivity, and steering, and finds intermediate-depth emergence. The reviewed work instead studies VLM post-training and shows offset/stability are already accessible but not robustly recruited; together they distinguish representation from behavior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do generative video models understand physical principles?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Physics-IQ tests whether video generators acquire mechanics, fluids, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism from passive prediction and finds realism does not imply understanding. It motivates the reviewed paper's interaction hypothesis, but the latter's one-step reward loop is too limited to adjudicate passive observation versus embodied causal experimentation broadly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Vision Language Models Cannot Reason About Physical Transformation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: subsequent broad negative VLM physics result
reviewed_competitors.difference: ConservationBench evaluates four conserved properties, paired controls, 23,040 questions, and 112 VLMs and finds systematic failures under transformation. It postdates the reviewed work and does not test interaction, but its broader controlled negative evidence reinforces the need to narrow conclusions drawn from simple tower centering.
