reviewed_competitors.title: Generalized Inversion of Nonlinear Operators
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gofer and Gilboa define generalized inverses for general sets and a normed-space pseudo-inverse through best-approximate and minimum-norm properties, with existence, uniqueness, continuity, composition, and analytic nonlinear examples. SPNN replaces the native-norm selection with a completion-induced coordinate metric and supplies a neural right-inverse plus diffusion application, but does not establish that its unspecified completion is canonical.

reviewed_competitors.title: SurVAE Flows: Surjections to Bridge the Gap between VAEs and Flows
reviewed_competitors.difference: SurVAE Flows already composes dimension-changing surjections with deterministic forward and stochastic reverse transformations for likelihood modeling. SPNN instead learns a deterministic selected right-inverse and targets reflexive algebra and back-projection, trading probabilistic coverage of a fiber for one completion-dependent representative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Diffusion Posterior Sampling for General Noisy Inverse Problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: DPS handles general noisy nonlinear measurements by posterior-score approximation and gradients through the forward model, including phase retrieval and nonlinear deblurring. NLBP offers exact consistency for a learned surjective surrogate and avoids per-step measurement gradients, but requires training a special invertible completion and reports only noiseless semantic self-consistency without a DPS comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Zero-Shot Image Restoration Using Denoising Diffusion Null-Space Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: DDNM performs closed-form range/null-space correction for many linear degradations and evaluates restoration quality extensively, including noisy DDNM+. SPNN generalizes the coordinate-replacement pattern to a learned nonlinear surjection, but its empirical evidence lacks matched restoration baselines and guarantees only consistency with g rather than the approximated operator D.

reviewed_competitors.title: Who Said Neural Networks Aren't Linear?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: coordinate-linearization predecessor from the same research line
reviewed_competitors.difference: Berman, Hallak, and Shocher transport vector-space structure through invertible neural networks so a sandwiched linear map inherits SVD, pseudo-inverse, and projection operations. SPNN permits dimension reduction through surjective coupling and a selected right-inverse, but its coordinate-completion idea overlaps this transported-structure route and leaves the operative completion less explicit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Orthogonal Subspace Learning for Language Model Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: O-LoRA trains each language task in a new low-rank subspace constrained orthogonal to previous ones, avoiding replay and preserving unseen-task generalization at the cost of taskwise parameter growth. Share seeks transfer and compression through a shared basis, but retains growing task coefficients and does not compare against O-LoRA on continual language benchmarks.

reviewed_competitors.title: InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: InfLoRA explicitly designs low-rank adaptation subspaces to eliminate new-task interference and reports state-of-the-art continual image results. Share instead recompresses task factors into shared directions to encourage transfer and reduce storage, but gives no head-to-head InfLoRA comparison or guarantee that SVD truncation protects old functional outputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compress then Serve: Serving Thousands of LoRA Adapters with Little Overhead
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct shared-basis compression and serving competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Compress Then Serve jointly compresses up to 1000 LoRAs into shared bases with adapter-specific scaling matrices, learns clusters for heterogeneous collections, and measures serving throughput. Share updates a basis continually and accepts task data, but tests only 50 incoming adapters, retains per-task coefficients, and reports no throughput or update-latency comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Merging Models on the Fly Without Retraining: A Sequential Approach to Scalable Continual Model Merging
reviewed_competitors.difference: OPCM processes task models sequentially with orthogonal projection and adaptive scaling, claims constant memory in task count, and evaluates task-order robustness on CLIP-ViT. Share is LoRA-specific and supports gradient adaptation from data, but its coefficient memory grows with tasks and it omits OPCM from the large-adapter continual-merging comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Null-Space Filtering for Data-Free Continual Model Merging: Preserving Stability, Promoting Plasticity
reviewed_competitors.difference: NUFILT filters incoming task updates through prior-response null spaces, adds a low-rank recovery adapter, and fuses updates back with no inference-time parameter growth, reporting 4-7 point gains over prior continual merging. Share preserves multiple task behaviors through shared factors and switched coefficients, offering compact personalization but not a single fused task-agnostic model or a direct stability guarantee.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lost in Latent Space: An Empirical Study of Latent Diffusion Models for Physics Emulation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lost in Latent Space studies continuous compression up to 1000x inside probabilistic physics emulators and evaluates downstream accuracy and diversity. Phaedra studies discrete fidelity across broader static transfer domains but does not show emulation value.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Value of Tokeniser Pretraining in Physics Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This controlled study shows that tokenizer pretraining helps physics emulation most when source and target domains align and introduces runtime-adjustable causal compression. reviewed_competitors.title: The Geometric Alignment Tax: Tokenization vs. Continuous Geometry in Scientific Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: The paper reports that finer discrete quantization can improve reconstruction while worsening continuous geometry. Phaedra does not measure latent geometry, mutual information, or task relevance, so its reconstruction gains cannot rule out this failure mode.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Galaxy's Guide to the Tokenizer: A Benchmark for Scientific Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Across four astronomical tokenizers in one backbone, reconstruction, localized morphology, and physical-property probes select different winners. This directly challenges using Phaedra's reconstruction suite as sufficient evidence of representation utility.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics Transformer: Tailoring Transformer for General PDE Prediction
reviewed_competitors.difference: Physics Transformer projects arbitrary discretizations onto adaptive local basis functions, decodes at arbitrary query points, and evaluates 2D and industrial 3D CFD prediction. Phaedra's discrete raster tokens are simpler and amplitude-aware but limited to independently processed fixed-grid scalar fields and reconstruction.

reviewed_competitors.difference: FSQ supplies the fixed scalar levels and implicit Cartesian-product codebook used by both Phaedra branches. Phaedra's novelty lies in allocating two specialized branches, learned recombination, and scientific evaluation, not in the quantizer itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Using the Output Embedding to Improve Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Press and Wolf establish the output matrix as a useful embedding, recommend exact parameter sharing, and analyze the tied update rule and parameter/perplexity benefits. Under that exact sharing the input matrix and transposed output matrix already coincide; PIT adds an inverse/whitening constraint, not synchronization of previously separate tied parameters.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tying Word Vectors and Word Classifiers: A Loss Framework for Language Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Inan et al. derive transpose tying from a loss framework and show reduced variables and perplexity. PIT imposes the stronger E-pseudoinverse relation through orthonormal memory and SPD metric, trading the predecessor's arbitrary shared embedding geometry for exact hidden-space recovery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Weight Tying: Learning Joint Input-Output Embeddings for Neural Machine Translation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pappas et al. explicitly study structures between no sharing and hard equality, learning a joint input-output embedding with controllable output capacity. PIT instead uses a fixed inverse constraint and a global hidden transform; it should be compared against this flexible coupling family rather than only classic tying.

reviewed_competitors.title: How to represent a word and predict it, too: Improving tied architectures for language modelling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gulordava et al. decouple hidden-state prediction from the word embedding while retaining much of tying's parameter efficiency and report comparable or better language modeling. PIT chooses inverse consistency instead; the paper does not compare whether a learned hidden-to-word transform provides the same optimization flexibility without frozen token memory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Representation Degeneration Problem in Training Natural Language Generation Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gao et al. show that likelihood training with weight tying can collapse embeddings into a narrow cone and propose a regularizer. PIT's orthonormal columns change global geometry but do not guarantee well-separated rows; it omits this direct failure diagnosis and baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analysing Word Representation from the Input and Output Embeddings in Neural Network Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Derby et al. empirically compare what input and output embeddings represent and build locally optimal intermediate embeddings from output embeddings. PIT asserts a synchronized semantic basis but does not run comparable lexical or intermediate-representation evaluations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Tuned Lens learns an affine translator for every frozen block and validates prediction fidelity, bias, feature overlap, and causal behavior in models up to 20B. PIT offers an architectural input/output identity but no layerwise probe evaluation; it does not address the intermediate-to-final distribution shift that tuned translators target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Weight Tying Biases Token Embeddings Towards the Output Space
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lopardo et al. attribute tying's input/output compromise to output-gradient dominance and causally improve early-layer computation by scaling input gradients. PIT freezes shared token directions and couples paths inversely, but does not measure gradient imbalance; this work offers a competing mechanism for both benefits and harms of tying.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Linear Decay Learning Rate Schedules and Further Refinements
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct theory-and-experiment competitor deriving horizon-aware decay schedules
reviewed_competitors.difference: Defazio et al. obtain worst-case linear decay for a wide class of optimizers and a gradient-norm-adaptive refinement that can produce warmup and rapid final annealing, then test ten deep-learning problems and LLMs against defaults including cosine. Bordelon and Mori exploit distributional power-law structure to derive task-dependent powers and a hard active constraint; their solution is more specific and asymptotically sharper inside the random-feature model but much less broadly validated and not adaptive from observed gradients.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Optimal LR Across Token Horizons
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct empirical study of horizon-dependent optimal learning rates in LLM training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bjorck et al. empirically fit how optimal LR falls with token horizon and demonstrate extrapolation from shorter LLM runs, including a retrospective Llama-1 analysis. Bordelon and Mori explain when that fall should persist after annealing and predict a contrasting hard phase, but their transformer evidence is a single 125M Adam setup and they do not deliver the empirical zero-overhead transfer rule or comparable large-scale sweep.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Warmup-Stable-Decay Learning Rates: A River Valley Loss Landscape Perspective
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct alternative mechanism and practical protocol for plateau-then-decay schedules
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wen et al. explain WSD using a conjectured river-valley nonconvex landscape and introduce WSD-S for reusable checkpoints at multiple budgets, testing 0.1B-1.2B models. Bordelon and Mori derive a superficially similar no-warmup plateau-decay path from linear spectral bias-variance control and explicitly require a fixed horizon; this provides a cleaner solvable mechanism but does not solve WSD's multi-checkpoint/anytime objective or match Wen et al.'s LLM scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Seesaw: Accelerating Training by Balancing Learning Rate and Batch Size Scheduling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct current competitor on LR-decay/batch-ramp equivalence and real training speed
reviewed_competitors.difference: Meterez et al. prove finite-sample LR-decay/batch-growth equivalence for noisy linear regression, extend it to normalized SGD as an Adam proxy, and report about 36% measured wall-clock reduction at equal FLOPs for 150M-600M models. Bordelon and Mori derive an asymptotic degenerate control family and a theoretically minimum-step ramp in power-law random features, reporting 33x fewer simulated updates but no hardware timing or adaptive-optimizer experiment. Seesaw's current v2 therefore supplies more direct systems evidence while the present paper supplies phase-dependent asymptotic exponents.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dimension-adapted Momentum Outscales SGD
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest momentum scaling-law competitor in the same power-law random-feature family
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ferbach et al. derive how dimension-adapted Nesterov acceleration improves exponents, characterize four curve shapes, and test synthetic quadratics plus LSTMs. Bordelon and Mori numerically optimize arbitrary time-varying beta and eta at fixed model structure and observe a hard-phase gain, but leave its exponent analytic form open and do not test momentum in a deep model. The former is a derived anytime/dimension-adapted algorithm; the latter is a finite-horizon control upper benchmark.

TinyLoRA reports the opposite-looking viability at much smaller counts on Qwen using a custom tied projection, so the two results make model family, basis design, benchmark, and tuning protocol essential boundary conditions rather than supporting a universal low-rank rule.

TinyLoRA explores orders-of-magnitude smaller task coordinates and RLVR, but does not measure whether its impressive in-domain gains trade off against acquisition breadth, forgetting, diversity, or out-of-domain capability.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Inductive Moment Matching offers one- or few-step single-stage training and claims distribution-level convergence, reaching 1.99 ImageNet FID at eight steps and strong two-step CIFAR results. Drifting is natively one step and empirically stronger on ImageNet, but its own appendix concedes the missing converse V=0=>p=q; IMM therefore supplies the kind of consistency guarantee that Drifting currently replaces with a generic-independence heuristic.

This paper's narrower addition is the exact bounded-support-kernel account of sparsemax/entmax/ReLUmax plus compact-kernel experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Long-Context Generalization with Sparse Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: It directly tests alpha-entmax and learnable-temperature ASEntmax in Transformers, including up to 1000x synthetic and 8x language-model length extrapolation. It overlaps the adaptive-sparsity claim and provides stronger long-context evidence; the present paper contributes the classical compact-kernel derivation and ReLUmax within Memory Mosaics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dense Associative Memory with Epanechnikov Energy
reviewed_competitors.difference: It already connects an Epanechnikov-inspired log-sum-ReLU energy to exact sparse associative retrieval and exponential memory capacity. The present paper generalizes the regression correspondence across multiple polynomial kernels and attention maps, but does not provide that storage-capacity analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaSplash: Adaptive Sparse Flash Attention
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct systems complement and efficiency benchmark
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaSplash implements alpha-entmax with custom Triton kernels and measures runtime/memory against optimized softmax. The present paper uses AdaSplash and invokes its results, but contributes no new fused kernel or efficiency measurement of its own.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Sequence-to-Sequence Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: It defines the alpha-entmax family, algorithms, gradients, and sparse sequence-to-sequence applications. The current paper reinterprets discrete alpha values as classical compact kernels and studies them in associative memories rather than introducing entmax itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Softmax to Sparsemax: A Sparse Model of Attention and Multi-Label Classification
reviewed_competitors.difference: It introduces sparsemax as Euclidean projection and derives its Jacobian/loss. The present paper's incremental contribution is the auto-normalized Epanechnikov-regression interpretation and comparison to other support mechanisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory Mosaics
reviewed_competitors.difference: It introduces the contextual/persistent associative-memory architecture used by every compact-kernel experiment here. The present work changes its contextual retrieval kernel; it is not an independent validation in a conventional Transformer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory Mosaics at scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: It scales Memory Mosaics v2 to 10B parameters and one trillion tokens, showing that the architecture itself can scale. It does not test the compact kernels here, so it narrows any inference that this sub-1B kernel study already establishes large-scale behavior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scalable-Softmax Is Superior for Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: It addresses attention dispersion by scaling softmax with input length while retaining dense support and reports language-model/retrieval long-context gains. It challenges the implication that exact zeros are necessary; the present paper instead changes kernel support and offers a kernel-estimation interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepSeekMath introduces practical critic-free GRPO as a PPO variant with group-relative standardized rewards and reports 7B math performance. The present paper does not introduce GRPO; it isolates standard-deviation scaling in an exact-gradient log-linear model and supplies a conditional curvature interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: GPG: A Simple and Strong Reinforcement Learning Baseline for Model Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: GPG removes GRPO's surrogate machinery and directly optimizes the original policy-gradient objective, reporting lower cost and consistent gains over GRPO across unimodal and multimodal tasks. It directly weakens any universal claim that GRPO needs standard-deviation normalization; the reviewed paper never compares against GPG.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uncalibrated Reasoning: GRPO Induces Overconfidence for Stochastic Outcomes
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows group standard normalization causes overconfidence for stochastic binary outcomes and that removing it restores calibration, whereas PPO/RLOO remain calibrated. The reviewed theory assumes deterministic correctness and evaluates only training accuracy, so its 'needs normalization' conclusion cannot extend to stochastic outcomes.

reviewed_competitors.title: What is the Alignment Objective of GRPO?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct theory of GRPO scale normalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: It characterizes GRPO stationary policies and how shift-and-scale reward normalization changes preference aggregation, including variants without scale normalization and with KL penalties. The reviewed paper instead studies local smoothness and stationarity-rate bounds under no KL and unique binary outputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Group Relative Policy Optimization: Insights into On-Policy and Off-Policy Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves reward improvement for on- and off-policy GRPO objectives and tests clipped off-policy training, addressing stale sampling that this paper assumes away. The reviewed novelty is specifically variance-curvature scaling, not practical on/off-policy validity.

reviewed_competitors.title: TIC-GRPO: Provable and Efficient Optimization for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
reviewed_competitors.difference: TIC-GRPO analyzes the old-policy bias of token-level importance ratios, proposes a trajectory-level correction, and claims faster convergence with math/coding tests. The reviewed paper's exact on-policy ratio-one setting avoids that central practical issue and thus covers a narrower algorithm.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: It identifies GRPO optimization bias toward longer responses and proposes Dr. GRPO, an unbiased alternative with strong 7B reasoning results. The reviewed analysis abstracts each output as one action and cannot represent token-length bias.

reviewed_competitors.title: GDPO: Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization for Multi-reward RL Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: GDPO shows joint group normalization can collapse distinct multi-reward combinations into identical advantages and decouples normalization by reward. That failure regime is excluded by this paper's single deterministic binary reward, narrowing the title-level claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning as Reasoning Unfolds: Progressive Rollout Allocation for Efficient Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: VIGOR also proves that reward variance controls RLVR gradient magnitude, but uses it to allocate rollouts rather than divide updates by standard deviation, reporting up to 2.3x fewer rollouts. It overlaps the variance-mechanism story while providing an efficiency intervention absent here.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Dark Room in the Reward Channel: Dense Prediction Rewards Collapse GRPO-Trained LLM Agents -- and The Channel, Not the Content, Decides What Works
reviewed_competitors.difference: Across 74 controlled arms it reports collapse whenever dense difference-form rewards are delivered through untouched GRPO standard-deviation normalization, and restoration when only std normalization is removed. This is a direct empirical boundary on the reviewed paper's single sparse binary reward claim and shows the normalization channel can be harmful.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational direct antecedent for intervening on chain-of-thought text and measuring whether answers condition on it.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lanham et al. manipulate mistakes, paraphrases, filler, and early answers to study faithfulness across tasks; this paper instead sweeps prefixes of a model's own long trace, adds matched-length corruptions, and studies cross-model rescue. The antecedent already cautions that answer changes under CoT intervention do not reveal the model's original latent process.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest causal-attribution antecedent for locating influential portions of long reasoning traces.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Thought Anchors replaces individual sentence-level thoughts, samples 100 continuations, and combines black-box, attention, and causal-suppression analyses; the present paper uses one fixed trace's cumulative token prefixes and one forced next-token distribution, trading local causal resolution for broad model/dataset and transfer coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Answer Convergence as a Signal for Early Stopping in Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct antecedent for measuring when an answer stabilizes during reasoning and using stability to stop inference.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu and Wang operationalize convergence into answer-consistency, end-signal boosting, and activation-based stopping policies across five tasks/models; this paper is primarily diagnostic, uses token-decile re-prompts and eventual-answer commitment, and does not evaluate a deployed stopping policy or token-accuracy Pareto frontier.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Think with Confidence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct confidence-based test-time reasoning-selection and early-filtering competitor using the same Qwen3 and gpt-oss families.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepConf uses internal confidence signals to prune low-quality parallel traces during or after generation and reports accuracy/token savings on math; this paper measures raw forced-choice confidence along one trace and diagnoses discrimination but neither selects parallel traces nor demonstrates efficiency gains.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stop When Enough: Adaptive Early-Stopping for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Training-free early-stopping competitor motivated by overthinking and redundant reflection.
reviewed_competitors.difference: REFRAIN uses a two-stage redundancy discriminator and a difficulty-adaptive SW-UCB threshold and reports 20-55% token reduction; the present work provides decile diagnostics and notes lost answers but does not implement or compare an adaptive stop controller.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thought Manipulation: External Thought Can Be Efficient for Large Reasoning Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct antecedent for inserting one model's reasoning into another and analyzing following versus rethinking.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Thought Manipulation deliberately inserts smaller-model CoTs to reduce a larger model's output tokens and reports blind-following and unnecessary-rethinking failures; this paper slices prefixes, conditions on induced wrong answers, and quantifies rescue/anchoring rather than optimizing end-to-end efficiency.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning Relay: Evaluating Stability and Interchangeability of Large Language Models in Mathematical Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest pre-submission cross-model partial-trace continuation antecedent.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reasoning Relay truncates at process-reward/log-probability thresholds and evaluates hybrid mathematical chains with a PRM across Gemma/Llama providers and receivers; this paper uses fixed source-token deciles, forced answer probabilities, GPQA/MMLU-Pro correctness, and explicit wrong-prefix rescue and anchoring.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Well Can Reasoning Models Identify and Recover from Unhelpful Thoughts?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct recovery-from-injected-thought antecedent and empirical counterpoint.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. inject four controlled classes of unhelpful thought and find weak or inverse-scaling recovery, including jailbreak implications; this paper conditions on naturally sampled prefixes whose forced answer is wrong and often finds stronger receivers can repair them, but does not know whether the underlying prefix reasoning itself is erroneous.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Reasoning LLMs Robust to Interventions on Their Chain-of-Thought?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current post-submission direct competitor testing recovery from fixed-timestep CoT interventions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Von Recum et al. apply seven benign, neutral, and adversarial perturbations across math, science, and logic and jointly measure accuracy and continuation-length cost; this paper focuses on naturally occurring cumulative prefixes, matched corruptions, forced-choice trajectories, and cross-model transfer. The later study more directly manipulates error type and quantifies recovery cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning that Travels: Dissecting How Chain-of-Thought Transfers Across Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current post-submission near-replication of provider-receiver prefix trajectories, including forced answer versus free continuation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cheng et al. explicitly distinguish answer extraction, reasoning scaffolding, and receiver competence across AIME, MMLU-Pro, and ZebraLogic and show force-answer AIME transfer can be answer leakage; the present paper predates it and uniquely emphasizes wrong-prefix rescue/anchoring and matched within-model controls, but its semantic-causation claim lacks the later paper's answer-availability diagnosis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interchangeable Token Embeddings for Extendable Vocabulary and Alpha-Equivalence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Immediate predecessor by one of the same authors; defines interchangeable tokens and alpha-covariance and supplies the random dual-part embedding baseline and core logic/copy evaluations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Işık et al. combine a shared learned semantic component with a fresh random identity component, producing favorable but not exact covariance. The present paper replaces stochastic identity embeddings with dynamic actual/placeholder streams and symmetric attention/projection, proves equivariance, achieves empirical 100% covariance, and adds conversion and propositional evaluations. The task framing, metric, datasets, and major baseline are therefore inherited rather than new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Renamer: A Transformer Architecture Invariant to Variable Renaming
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior architecture explicitly guaranteeing invariance to semantics-preserving variable renaming.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Renamer represents tokens through a view mapping and referent relation and proves renaming invariance for code/system tasks, reporting 24.79-52.8% lower CPU-simulation error than a vanilla Transformer. The present method instead creates one dynamic stream per symbol, supports equivariant symbol-valued sequence generation and post-training vocabulary expansion, and evaluates propositional/LTL witnesses. Its broad claim that current architectures lack a principled renaming mechanism must be narrowed in light of Renamer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Property Invariant Embedding for Automated Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Early direct antecedent for label-invariant formula representations and unseen-symbol generalization in automated reasoning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Olšák et al. remove original labels from graph-neural formula encodings and recover structural meaning through graph links, evaluating theorem proving, premise selection, and symbol guessing. The present paper is a sequence Transformer with explicit interchangeable-token metadata, dynamic generation streams, and a formal stream-permutation argument; it does not tackle theorem-prover scale or infer symbol structure from formula graphs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploiting Code Symmetries for Learning Program Semantics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct architectural antecedent using group-theoretic, provably equivariant self-attention for semantics-preserving code transformations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SymC derives a permutation group from program-dependence-graph code symmetries and builds equivariant attention for five program-analysis tasks. The present paper handles a simpler supplied global permutation of interchangeable tokens, supports dynamic output names and logic witnesses, and uses parallel streams; it does not encode real program dependence or scoped code symmetries.

reviewed_competitors.title: Permutation Equivariance of Transformers and Its Applications
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Theoretical Transformer-equivariance antecedent covering token and feature-coordinate permutations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu et al. show broad inter-/intra-token permutation equivariance already present in many vanilla Transformers and apply it to split-learning privacy and authorization. Their group action permutes sequence/representation coordinates, not arbitrary semantic symbol identities embedded as names. The present architecture constructs a different group action over dynamic symbol streams and symbol-valued outputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Larger They Are, the Harder They Fail: Language Models do not Recognize Identifier Swaps in Python
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Evaluation antecedent demonstrating failure under semantics-preserving identifier changes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Miceli-Barone et al. swap familiar Python identifiers in pretrained LLM prompts and document inverse-scaling failures; they propose no invariant architecture and focus on code names whose lexical meaning may matter. The present paper enforces symmetry by construction for synthetic tokens declared fully interchangeable and cannot yet establish robustness on real identifiers.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Do Transformers Learn Variable Binding in Symbolic Programs?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Task-and-mechanism antecedent for systematic variable identity tracking in ordinary Transformers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. show that a standard Transformer can learn residual-stream addressable memory and specialized heads for dereferencing assignment chains, using causal interventions. The present paper supplies an architectural identity prior and formal renaming equivariance for generation rather than explaining a learned mechanism; it has not compared against a standard model trained until systematic binding emerges.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Large Language Models Robust in Understanding Code Against Semantics-Preserving Mutations?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current evaluation competitor for prediction and reasoning stability under variable renaming and four other semantics-preserving code mutations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Orvalho and Kwiatkowska test nine pretrained LLMs on LiveCodeBench/CruxEval, include expert reasoning audits, and report drops up to 70%; they do not modify the architecture. The present paper guarantees one exact symmetry on synthetic logic but neither assesses natural-code reasoning nor other transformations, so the works address complementary robustness scope.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Names Disappear: Revealing What LLMs Actually Understand About Code
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current naming-ablation benchmark antecedent separating structural semantics from human naming cues.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Le et al. introduce semantics-preserving obfuscations and ClassEval-Obf and show both intent and execution tasks exploit naming shortcuts. The present paper assumes names are semantically empty and enforces that prior architecturally; it therefore does not cover domains where names legitimately carry intent, underscoring that identifying V_i is application dependent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks

The present method must preserve distinct symbol identity and produce equivariant symbol sequences, so it uses per-symbol streams and asymmetric projection rather than reducing all entities to one invariant set representation.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Source of the identity-target cross-correlation objective used by GAME-LoRA.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barlow Twins drives correlation between two augmentations of the same sample toward identity, where diagonal agreement is intended invariance and off-diagonal reduction acts across features. GAME-LoRA applies the same target between distinct heads and calls it cross-head decorrelation, where diagonal agreement instead forces matched head features to be highly correlated.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Mechanics of n-Player Differentiable Games
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary differentiable-games antecedent for potential/Hamiltonian structure and local game dynamics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Balduzzi et al. analyze genuinely distinct player losses, decompose game Jacobians, and propose symplectic gradient adjustment. GAME-LoRA's base players share scaled copies of one CE loss, making its potential identity immediate; it neither analyzes Hamiltonian dynamics nor uses SGA.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical antecedent for attention-head redundancy and underutilization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Michel et al. causally remove heads across translation/BERT-style models and show many are dispensable. GAME-LoRA infers redundancy from G/correlation and benchmark aggregates but does not prune or intervene on its identified coalitions to verify functional redundancy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analyzing Multi-Head Self-Attention: Specialized Heads Do the Heavy Lifting, the Rest Can Be Pruned
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Attention specialization/pruning antecedent for the claim that only a minority of heads matter.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Voita et al. use stochastic gates and L0-style pruning to connect interpretable head roles with causal performance effects. GAME-LoRA reports post-hoc clusters in one layer but supplies no causal head removal or role validation.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ACL 2019 ACL Anthology proceedings version P19-1580

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Robust Representations via Multi-View Information Bottleneck
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary multi-view information-bottleneck antecedent used to motivate the social objective.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Federici et al. define a probabilistic multi-view representation setting and optimize estimable variational objectives for paired views. GAME-LoRA treats deterministic attention heads as conditional stochastic views but never supplies an encoder noise model or estimator for its compression and conditional-TC terms.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2020 conference version, OpenReview forum B1xwcyHFDr

reviewed_competitors.title: Retrieval Head Mechanistically Explains Long-Context Factuality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. identify sparse retrieval heads across four model families, six scales, and post-training variants and causally prune them to show factuality/retrieval effects. GAME-LoRA studies one layer of one family, clusters a heuristic interaction matrix, and correlates it with benchmark scores without an equivalent causal head intervention.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2025 conference version, OpenReview forum EytBpUGB1Z

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantizable Transformers: Removing Outliers by Helping Attention Heads Do Nothing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bondarenko et al. identify softmax heads' need for zero or partial residual updates and introduce clipped softmax and gated attention to provide a no-op while reducing quantization outliers. The target paper reinterprets sink complement as the same kind of gate and adds cross-head CV balancing, but does not evaluate quantization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks
reviewed_competitors.difference: StreamingLLM demonstrates that preserving initial sink KVs stabilizes streaming through millions of tokens and proposes a dedicated sink token. It exploits sinks for KV-cache continuity rather than interpreting their complement as head routing or balancing head use.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Attention Sink Emerges in Language Models: An Empirical View
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gu et al. track sink emergence through pretraining, characterize the sink as a noninformative key bias, and remove it with unnormalized sigmoid attention up to 1B parameters. The target paper adds a complement-gate/MoE interpretation and head-balancing loss across three attention variants.

reviewed_competitors.title: Active-Dormant Attention Heads: Mechanistically Demystifying Extreme-Token Phenomena in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo et al. jointly explain sink, value-drain, and residual-peak dynamics with an input-dependent active-dormant mechanism, theory on a Bigram-Backcopy task, and pretrained-model observations. The target paper supplies the algebraic complement gate and a balancing intervention, but its single mean gate loses that work's domain dependence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why do LLMs attend to the first token?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barbero et al. argue sinks prevent over-mixing and study effects of depth, context length, and packing. That functional account warns that sinks need not be waste; the target instead treats complement mass as routing and emphasizes balanced head activation without testing over-mixing preservation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Identifying and Evaluating Inactive Heads in Pretrained LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct inactive-head metric and intervention competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sandoval-Segura et al. compare 12 scores with output-ablation tests across three model families and find output-norm scores detect inactive heads missed by first-token attention; the latter underestimates inactivity by more than 7 percent on average. This is direct negative evidence against the target's gate-only importance proxy, although the target uniquely trains with a balancing loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: Softpick: No Attention Sink, No Massive Activations with Rectified Softmax
reviewed_competitors.difference: Softpick replaces sum-to-one softmax with rectified non-normalized attention, reports zero sink rate at 340M and 1.8B, sparse maps, and better low-bit quantization. The target retains softmax or explicit gating and balances head amplitudes; it does not compare against Softpick under the same pretraining recipe.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models: Non-linearity, Sparsity, and Attention-Sink-Free
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. evaluate 30 gate variants on 15B MoE and 1.7B dense models trained on 3.5T tokens and attribute gains to post-SDPA nonlinear, query-dependent sparse gating. The target uses that gate as one arm, proposes equivalence with sink complements, and adds balancing, but trains its controlled models on far smaller budgets.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unified View of Attention and Residual Sinks: Outlier-Driven Rescaling is Essential for Transformer Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Submitted two days before the target, Qiu et al. already frame attention and residual sinks as normalization-coupled rescaling factors and show that explicit gated rescaling can absorb them. The target's remaining distinction is the per-head MoE analogy and CV load-balancing treatment of collapse, not the basic claim that a sink implements rescaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention Sinks Are Provably Necessary in Softmax Transformers: Evidence from Trigger-Conditional Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later theoretical boundary and negative evidence
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ran-Milo proves that a softmax Transformer must form a sink for a trigger-conditional default-state task and shows ReLU attention avoids it. This later result limits any general reading of sink elimination or balance as universally desirable; the target has broader LLM experiments but no task-level necessity test.

reviewed_competitors.title: N-gram Prediction and Word Difference Representations for Language Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: WDR, from the same lead and senior authors, uses contextual word-difference targets and n-gram prediction as auxiliary multi-task objectives. SCLM replaces the primary token target through an invertible B-spline interface and evaluates DLM generation, but the broader target-reformulation motivation predates it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Empowering Diffusion Models on the Embedding Space for Text Generation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct Gaussian DLM backbone and matched baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: Difformer stabilizes embedding-space text diffusion with anchor loss and noise rescaling and is the translation backbone SCLM wraps. SCLM's controlled gains therefore isolate the added B/B+ target interface more directly than comparisons with copied baselines.

reviewed_competitors.title: DINOISER: Diffused Conditional Sequence Learning by Manipulating Noises
reviewed_competitors.difference: DINOISER addresses degeneration and discreteness through noise-scale manipulation and source conditioning in Gaussian sequence diffusion. SCLM instead changes the target geometry while retaining a Difformer-style backbone and reports higher copied BLEU values, without a matched DINOISER rerun.

reviewed_competitors.title: AR-Diffusion: Auto-Regressive Diffusion Model for Text Generation
reviewed_competitors.difference: AR-Diffusion introduces position-dependent denoising schedules to recover left-to-right dependency while retaining parallel refinement. SCLM couples targets symmetrically through spline control points; Table 1 compares reported BLEU rather than matching the two mechanisms under one implementation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct discrete LM baseline and training framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: MDLM derives a Rao-Blackwellized masked-diffusion objective with strong likelihoods and arbitrary-length generation in token space. SCLM wraps MDLM's small DiT and SoftMask-style input process with curve targets, but tests only length 128 and uses a reduced training budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: Soft-Masked Diffusion Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest LM1B mechanism and quality baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: SoftMask retains top-k predicted word embeddings at nominally masked input positions to carry iterative context, an input-side solution to information loss. SCLM reimplements that mechanism and adds an output-target curve; the official current v2 postdates the target's experiment, so exact-version equivalence is not established.

reviewed_competitors.title: Block Diffusion: Interpolating Between Autoregressive and Diffusion Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Block Diffusion generates autoregressive blocks with within-block diffusion, supports KV caching and flexible lengths, and confines parallel diffusion to shorter contexts. SCLM processes an overcomplete whole-sentence curve and merely proposes future blockwise integration; it is currently cached only through length 250.

reviewed_competitors.title: Non-Autoregressive Neural Machine Translation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gu et al. establish non-autoregressive translation with fertility latent variables and sequence-level knowledge distillation, framing the multimodality problem SCLM targets. SCLM replaces fertility modeling with spline-coupled targets and shows larger matched gains when KD is absent, but still assumes a target length.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inline Vector Compression for Computational Physics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Trojak and Witherden convert three-component single-precision vectors to spherical polar form, quantize the two angles, and use a bespoke magnitude float to obtain a fixed 1.5x ratio and 1.5x GPU vector-add speedup. The target extends spherical coordinates to high-dimensional unit embeddings, omits radius, keeps angles as float32, and obtains variable entropy compression with much smaller reported error rather than fixed-bit lossy quantization.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 (2020-06-24), corresponding to Computer Physics Communications 258 (2021), article 107562

reviewed_competitors.title: ZipNN: Lossless Compression for AI Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: ZipNN is bit-exact and exploits the field-level statistics of neural-network tensors with byte grouping and entropy coding, reporting large savings for model weights. The target uses the same broad shuffle-and-code idea after a geometric transform of unit-normalized embedding outputs, reaches a higher ratio on its selected float32 embedding cases, but gives up exact reconstruction.

reviewed_competitors.title: EFloat: Entropy-coded Floating Point Format for Compressing Vector Embedding Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: EFloat already targets vector embedding models by entropy-coding signs and clustered exponents and reallocating saved bits to the significand; its EF12/EF16 formats are lossy reduced-bit representations evaluated with RMS error and NDCG. The target instead creates exponent concentration geometrically, stores full float32 angles, and applies a conventional archive codec for approximately 1.5x payload compression.

reviewed_competitors.title: TurboQuant: Online Vector Quantization with Near-optimal Distortion Rate
reviewed_competitors.difference: TurboQuant uses random rotation to induce concentrated coordinate distributions, Lloyd-Max scalar quantizers, and a residual QJL stage for near-optimal MSE or unbiased inner-product estimates, reaching 2.5-3.5 bits per KV channel and nearest-neighbor gains. The target performs no rotation or low-bit quantization and instead entropy-codes float32 spherical angles for a far lower ratio but much smaller perturbation.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1 (2025-04-28); current official arXiv record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: PolarQuant: Vector Quantization with Polar Transformation
reviewed_competitors.difference: PolarQuant applies random preconditioning, a recursive polar transform, and data-independent angle codebooks, reporting more than 4.2x KV-cache compression with strong long-context quality. The target uses the conventional d-1-angle chart on already unit-normalized embeddings, preserves each angle in float32, and depends on zstd context rather than quantization codebooks.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: AISTATS 2026 proceedings version, PMLR volume 300, OpenReview record Igzjw1Pkds

reviewed_competitors.title: PCDVQ: Enhancing Vector Quantization for Large Language Models via Polar Coordinate Decoupling
reviewed_competitors.difference: PCDVQ separates direction and magnitude, then constructs distribution-aligned codebooks for 2-bit LLM weight vectors, motivated by direction being much more sensitive than magnitude. The target handles unit embedding outputs, drops magnitude entirely, and avoids learned codebooks and low-bit quantization in favor of float32 angle entropy.

reviewed_competitors.title: 70% Size, 100% Accuracy: Lossless LLM Compression for Efficient GPU Inference via Dynamic-Length Float (DFloat11)
reviewed_competitors.difference: DFloat11 entropy-codes low-entropy BF16 model weights into dynamic-length codes and decodes them with custom GPU kernels while preserving outputs bit-for-bit, reporting about 30% model-size reduction. The target focuses on float32 unit embeddings, manufactures redundancy through spherical geometry, and is not bit-exact; its own BF16 ablation favors direct baseline coding.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lossless Tensor Compression as Program Synthesis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Brevis synthesizes reversible programs from a typed tensor-compression DSL and reports bit-exact archives smaller than ZipNN and DFloat11 on model checkpoints. It is a later current competitor for tensor archival rather than a unit-embedding codec; unlike the target it searches tensor-specific transformations and guarantees exact recovery, but does not report BEIR embedding retrieval or spherical angle coding.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh, Bachmann, and Hofmann derive exact formulas and tight rank bounds for deep-linear Hessians and validate numerical rank on ReLU and tanh networks; the target directly uses their outer-product factorization. The target's additional objective is eigenvalue magnitude, specifically a two-level spectrum and depth-L gap under whitened aligned balanced dynamics, rather than rank deficiency alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Theoretical Characterisation of the Gauss Newton Conditioning in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhao, Singh, and Lucchi give tight Gauss-Newton condition-number bounds for deep linear networks of arbitrary depth and width and extend analysis to two-layer ReLU, residual, and convolutional architectures. The target narrows to an aligned isotropic deep-linear trajectory and claims exact cluster multiplicities and an L gap for the full Hessian after the functional term decays.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Convergence Analysis of Gradient Descent for Deep Linear Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arora, Cohen, Golowich, and Hu prove linear convergence for deep-linear squared loss over whitened data under sufficient width, approximately balanced initialization, and an initial-loss condition. The target adopts that balanced/whitened framework and singular-factor dynamics, then studies Hessian clusters; its additional Hessian theorem therefore depends on a highly inherited optimization setup rather than introducing the setup itself.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2019 published OpenReview version, forum SkMQg3C5K7

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Linear Network Training Dynamics from Random Initialization: Data, Width, Depth, and Hyperparameter Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon and Pehlevan analyze large-width deep-linear training from random initialization with random data, width/depth effects, parameterization, stochastic versus repeated data, and residual networks with an infinite-depth scaling. The target gives a finite-width exact Hessian spectrum in a much more aligned deterministic setting, but does not address the random, residual, or hyperparameter-transfer regimes that can alter depth scaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Investigation into Neural Net Optimization via Hessian Eigenvalue Density
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghorbani, Krishnan, and Xiao measure full Hessian densities through training at ImageNet scale, observe rapid isolated eigenvalues and gradient concentration, and show those effects are nearly absent with batch normalization. The target provides a synthetic analytic depth mechanism under whitened data, but does not test normalization or establish that its L-gap mechanism explains the empirical outliers in modern networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Traces of Class/Cross-Class Structure Pervade Deep Learning Spectra
reviewed_competitors.difference: Papyan formally attributes outliers, spikes, bumps, and other spectral structure in classifiers to class and cross-class components. The target supplies a complementary existence example in which an active data covariance is isotropic and depth alone creates two Gauss-Newton levels; it does not refute class structure as an explanation in real classification or study how the two mechanisms combine.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometry of Neural Network Loss Surfaces via Random Matrix Theory
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pennington and Bahri approximate Hessian spectral densities at critical points with random matrix theory and show dependence on loss energy and the parameter-to-data ratio. The target instead obtains discrete exact levels for a deterministic aligned deep-linear model near convergence and emphasizes depth rather than random spectral density; its result covers a narrower but more algebraically explicit regime.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Defilippis et al. design a spectral algorithm attaining the optimal reconstruction threshold; the target's outlier equation belongs to the training Hessian after finite GD and is used to quantify why a fixed neural architecture can need more samples.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Generative Leap: Sharp Sample Complexity for Efficiently Learning Gaussian Multi-Index Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior sharp sample-complexity characterization for generic Gaussian multi-index recovery using the generative-leap exponent and an agnostic sequential spectral U-statistic.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damian et al. match a low-degree lower bound with a designed sequential estimator across generative exponents, whereas the target holds n=Θ(d), focuses on generative-exponent-two hard directions, and studies a standard two-layer GD Hessian rather than an optimal estimator.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks Learn Generic Multi-Index Models Near Information-Theoretic Limit
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary ICLR 2026 neural-network result proving near-information-theoretic learning of generic multi-index targets with more than O(1) first-layer steps.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. give an end-to-end layer-wise GD guarantee with Õ(d) samples, Õ(d²) time, whole-span power iteration, and o_d(1) test error. The target studies ordinary simultaneous first-layer GD more precisely in proportional asymptotics and supplies an exact Hessian outlier equation, but only hypothesizes end-to-end logarithmic-time recovery.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2026 published proceedings version; arXiv 2511.15120v2 cross-checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Complex Dynamics in Simple Neural Networks: Understanding Gradient Flow in Phase Retrieval
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior mechanism paper: it tracks threshold states, an informative negative Hessian direction associated with a BBP transition, and gradient-flow escape in a phase-retrieval neural network.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mannelli et al. give a statistical-physics account of phase-retrieval gradient flow and its threshold-state escape, rather than a rigorous reused-sample finite-time spectrum theorem. The target generalizes the hard direction to a multi-index subspace and derives a fixed-time outlier equation, but its claim that the outlier subsequently drives escape remains heuristic.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2020 published proceedings version; arXiv 2006.06997 cross-checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Overparametrization bends the landscape: BBP transitions at initialization in simple Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior Hessian-BBP competitor for overparameterized phase-retrieval-like teacher–student networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Annesi et al. analyze informative/uninformative Hessian transitions at initialization using field theory and show width can move the boundary toward information theory; the target rigorously follows the Hessian after reused-data GD at any fixed time and separates hard from residual outliers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Limitations of SGD for Multi-Index Models Beyond Statistical Queries
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target 2026 algorithm-specific lower-bound work for vanilla SGD on single- and multi-index targets, including potentially deep networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barzilai–Shamir prove long-horizon sample/iteration lower bounds directly for stochastic gradients without SQ noise assumptions. They do not derive the target's full-batch Hessian outlier threshold, but their broader failure framework underscores that the target's fixed-eigenvector statement is not an SGD lower bound.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: COLT 2026 PMLR volume 336 published proceedings version; arXiv 2602.05704v1 cross-checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal scaling laws in learning hierarchical multi-index models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-target contemporary work deriving rigorous cascades of spectral phase transitions and optimal rates for hierarchical multi-index targets.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Defilippis et al. analyze a restricted hierarchical class and a target-agnostic spectral estimator interpretable as small-learning-rate first-layer GD, with subspace recovery and prediction guarantees. The target covers a broader hard-subspace definition and finite-time reused-data Hessian, but does not rigorously link its cascade/plateau interpretation to prediction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Cellular automata as convolutional neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gilpin proves that any cellular automaton can be represented by a network-in-network CNN and trains convolutional models to recover arbitrary CA rules from videos. This predates SEAD's central CNN-to-CA mechanism; SEAD adds hard argmax execution, fixed-point task framing, and extreme-length parity/addition probes rather than a new CA/CNN equivalence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural GPUs Learn Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kaiser and Sutskever use a shared convolutional gated recurrence, report long addition and multiplication extrapolation from short training examples, and argue computational universality. SEAD is much smaller and hard-discrete at inference, but its one-step oracle supervision is easier than Neural GPU's end-to-end sequence learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dehghani et al. introduce a temporally shared Transformer with dynamic per-position halting, algorithmic-task gains, and conditional Turing completeness. It directly refutes the suggestion that recurrence, temporal symmetry, or adaptive computation uniquely point to cellular automata, though it retains global attention and continuous states.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. formulate a RASP-based account of when Transformers length-generalize and improve parity and addition without requiring a CA or hard symbolic projection. SEAD reaches far longer reported lengths, but uses direct local-transition labels and supplies no matched Transformer comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Interpolation to Extrapolation: Complete Length Generalization for Arithmetic Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Duan et al. use targeted attention bias and Attention Bias Calibration to obtain near-perfect arithmetic length extrapolation, including parity. Their approach remains Transformer-based and empirically finite; SEAD enforces a local recurrent rule but overstates the earlier method's partial success without a head-to-head evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fan et al. train a weight-shared Transformer loop with an adaptive number of RASP-L iterations and demonstrate length-generalizable algorithmic solutions. Both methods internalize iterative computation; SEAD restricts interaction to a CA neighborhood and hard states, while Looped Transformers preserve content-addressed global operations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Arithmetic Transformers Can Length-Generalize in Both Operand Length and Count
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cho et al. combine task-specific scratchpads and multi-level position coupling, report simultaneous operand-length/count extrapolation, and prove a one-layer Transformer construction for exponentially large addition instances. SEAD reports a much larger raw length factor for two-operand binary addition, but not operand-count generalization and not a comparable theorem about its learned weights.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Role of Sparsity for Length Generalization in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Golowich et al. formalize length generalization through fixed-size sparse token dependencies and support it with synthetic and natural-language experiments. That result motivates locality without claiming a finite-speed CA is necessary; SEAD imposes a stronger nearest-neighbor topology and tests exact symbolic execution.

reviewed_competitors.title: To Infinity and Beyond: Tool-Use Unlocks Length Generalization in State Space Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Malach et al. prove a limitation for a defined class of truly long-form SSM generation and then recover arbitrary tractable length generalization with interactive tools. SEAD cites this as evidence against continuous systems broadly, but the theorem's scope is model/task-specific and its positive result shows that internal CA discretization is not the only route.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stability and Generalization in Looped Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Labovich analyzes reachability, input dependence, geometry, recall, and normalization for looped-model fixed points and reports chess, sudoku, and prefix-sum experiments. It makes explicit that fixed-point existence alone is insufficient—precisely a condition omitted by SEAD's claim that discrete attractors automatically provide meaningful termination.

reviewed_competitors.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scherlis et al. optimize importance-weighted feature capacity and report block-semi-orthogonal geometry across toy architectures; Spectral Superposition instead derives localization from exact aggregate saturation and classifies equal-eigenvalue clusters spectrally.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Causes Polysemanticity? An Alternative Origin Story of Mixed Selectivity from Incidental Causes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lecomte et al. show polysemanticity can arise from initialization, regularization, and noise even with ample capacity; the spectral paper's main theorem instead assumes capacity saturation and therefore cannot distinguish incidental from capacity-forced overlap.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Complexity of Neural Computation in Superposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adler and Shavit bound neurons and parameters needed to compute logical operations on superposed features; Spectral Superposition characterizes static representational geometry and fixed points, without proving that a localized tight frame supports downstream computation.

reviewed_competitors.title: From superposition to sparse codes: interpretable representations in neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Klindt et al. center identifiability plus sparse coding as a route from mixed representations to concept-aligned features; Spectral Superposition assumes a feature matrix W and studies its geometry, leaving that identification step unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hindupur et al. show SAE architecture determines which intrinsic-dimensional and nonlinear concepts can be recovered; this directly limits the spectral paper's interpretation of W columns as a stable feature set, an uncertainty its theorems do not model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear

reviewed_competitors.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. derive probing and steering notions from counterfactuals and identify a causal non-Euclidean inner product; Spectral Superposition uses the ordinary Euclidean frame operator, so its eigenspaces need not preserve the language-relevant geometry Park et al. formalize.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Data Statistics to Feature Geometry: How Correlations Shape Superposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prieto et al. manipulate realistic feature correlations and show constructive interference plus semantic/cyclic geometry in tied autoencoders; Spectral Superposition gives a more abstract global classifier but does not connect its eigenstructure to data covariance or test realistic co-activation statistics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Superposition as Lossy Compression: Measure with Sparse Autoencoders and Connect to Adversarial Vulnerability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bereska et al. estimate an activation-entropy feature-count proxy from SAEs across real networks and adversarial training; Spectral Superposition measures eigenspace allocation of an assumed W, preserving geometry but offering no comparable real-network scale or robustness evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equilibrium Propagation: Bridging the Gap Between Energy-Based Models and Backpropagation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Equilibrium Propagation estimates gradients from free and weakly nudged equilibria of a scalar energy model and naturally assumes symmetric interactions. The present paper instead doubles a non-conservative feedforward state and recovers the exact reverse-mode gradient at one equilibrium/discrete trace, but it still explicitly requires W^T coupling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dual Propagation: Accelerating Contrastive Hebbian Learning with Dyadic Neurons
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dual Propagation already uses paired neuronal quantities to combine inference and teaching and reports large-scale empirical acceleration. The target's narrower addition is a Bateman-Galley-style action plus an exact 2L feedforward trace; it does not establish a better compute or hardware result than the dyadic approach.

reviewed_competitors.title: Predictive Coding Can Do Exact Backpropagation on Convolutional and Recurrent Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Song et al. show that a predictive-coding inference procedure can reproduce exact backpropagation on convolutional and recurrent networks under suitable initialization and scheduling. The present result is therefore not the first exact relaxation-to-BP equivalence; its distinctive claim is the doubled variational mechanics and nilpotent 2L synchronous trace for feedforward graphs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equilibrium Propagation for Non-Conservative Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: This concurrent work, including the target author, augments arbitrary non-conservative systems so equilibrium propagation can obtain exact gradients without a scalar conservative energy. The target specializes to acyclic feedforward W and adds a least-action interpretation and finite discrete trace, so its novelty must be separated from the broader augmented-state exact-gradient construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equilibrium Propagation with Continual Weight Updates
reviewed_competitors.difference: Continual Equilibrium Propagation interleaves neural relaxation and local weight updates, reducing phase separation but using a small-learning-rate approximation to the equilibrium gradient. The target holds parameters fixed during state relaxation and proves exact feedforward gradients, while offering no continual synaptic-update experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural ODEs train continuous-depth dynamics with an adjoint integrated backward in time and trade activation storage for recomputation. The target instead relaxes an acyclic finite network toward a fixed point and carries stress in the same forward time coordinate, but its equation still implements the transposed Jacobian action central to an adjoint.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Hindupur et al. formalize how SAE architecture assumes concept geometry, demonstrate failures under heterogeneous intrinsic dimension and nonlinear separability, and design a geometry-aware SAE. MFA adopts one explicit local-Gaussian/subspace bias instead; it does not show that its own geometry class recovers all concept types.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Engels et al. define irreducible multidimensional features, automatically find circular calendar manifolds, and causally show those exact circles support modular arithmetic. MFA additionally partitions absolute activation regions and supports density likelihood/centroid steering, but its circuit-variable evidence relies on supervised MIB masking.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Turner et al. introduce optimization-free contrastive activation addition and empirically tune signed coefficients for sentiment and detoxification. reviewed_competitors.difference: Panickssery et al. average paired positive-minus-negative residual activations and evaluate coefficient-controlled behavior on Llama 2 multiple-choice and open generation, including capability side effects. This paper generalizes qualitative alpha analysis across more models, but uses largely visual curve validation and no direct CAA performance comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Linear Representation Hypothesis and the Geometry of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. formalize linear representations through counterfactuals, derive steering connections under a causal inner product, and give a partial concept-probability result. The present paper adds token-peak, off-target, local-loss, and extreme-transformer laws, while relying on a narrower pure-concept probability model and explicitly noting disagreement over off-target constancy.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct empirical strength and side-effect predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: von Rütte et al. jointly evaluate concept elicitation and fluency, show some concepts require extensive strength tuning or confuse guidance, and empirically report tanh-like concept and quadratic loss trends. The present work provides idealized derivations for related shapes, but its tanh is under nonlinear reparameterization and its empirical quality audit is less task-balanced.

reviewed_competitors.title: LiSeCo: Linear Semantic Control for Language Generation
reviewed_competitors.difference: The current LiSeCo version uses a closed-form online controller to move activations into a prescribed allowed semantic region with probabilistic/performative guarantees and reports toxicity, sentiment, and language control. The present paper describes global-alpha laws and a search heuristic; it neither enforces a region online nor compares quality-preserving control performance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Steering Without Side Effects: Improving Post-Deployment Control of Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stickland et al.'s KL-then-steer trains the model to keep steered and unsteered benign behavior close, preventing 44 percent of jailbreak attacks while nearly preserving MT-Bench helpfulness and transferring to TruthfulQA. The present paper explains why large fixed strength causes loss, but offers no learned side-effect mitigation or comparable safety-quality numbers.

reviewed_competitors.title: To Steer or Not to Steer? Mechanistic Error Reduction with Abstention for Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hedström et al.'s MERA jointly optimizes a correction direction and calibrates when and how strongly to intervene, with a provable improve-or-abstain rule and non-degrading empirical correction across datasets and model families. The present paper motivates prompt adaptation from context-dependent peak locations but leaves the rule as future work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamically Scaled Activation Steering
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ferrando et al.'s DSAS v2 computes input- and layer-dependent scaling factors, decouples when from how to steer, and improves the toxicity-utility Pareto front with minimal overhead. The present paper supplies qualitative reasons fixed alpha should be adaptive, but does not implement, tune, or benchmark an adaptive scaler.

reviewed_competitors.title: Persona Vectors: Monitoring and Controlling Character Traits in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. automate natural-language trait-vector extraction, monitor training-induced personality shifts, and use intervention or preventative steering across evil, sycophancy, and hallucination. The present paper reuses similar concepts and generated corpora to study alpha curves, but does not evaluate monitoring, training prediction, or preventative control.

reviewed_competitors.difference: AxBench directly compares prompting, finetuning, difference-in-means, probes, SAEs, and ReFT-r1, finding prompting best for steering and DiffMean strong for concept detection. The present paper analyzes DiffMean's coefficient but does not place its proposed strength-search heuristic inside AxBench or compare against prompting and finetuning.
