reviewed_competitors.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct diagnostic and modular-addition predecessor: reverse-engineers the Fourier multiplication algorithm and defines mechanistic progress measures for memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nanda et al. validate a specific grokked Transformer's Fourier circuit with weight/activation analysis and ablations and test variants across runs; their measures explain the rise of generalization, not a late collapse. The target uses architecture-agnostic spectral summaries, extends training, and does not perform causal circuit ablations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explaining grokking through circuit efficiency
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest named phenomenon predecessor: reports ungrokking, in which a previously generalizing network regresses to low test accuracy, and explains it through competition between memorizing and generalizing circuits.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Varma et al.'s ungrokking is elicited by retraining a grokked model on a smaller dataset under a circuit-efficiency/weight-decay account; the target's anti-grokking occurs during uninterrupted prolonged optimization on the original dataset, most strongly at WD=0. Both demonstrate perfect-train/poor-test regression, so novelty is the spontaneous protocol and diagnostic, not the broad phenomenon of post-grok test loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: Progress Measures for Grokking on Real-world Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct metric baseline: introduces activation sparsity, absolute weight entropy, and approximate local circuit complexity on real-world classification grokking, including without the expected l2-norm behavior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Golechha evaluates correlations with the grokking transition in a short workshop study; the target reimplements those three measures on its MNIST MLP and argues they do not uniquely identify the later anti phase. The target does not match the predecessor's task sweep or provide a quantitative detector comparison.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, revised 2024-06-20; ICML 2024 HiLD workshop

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Networks Always Grok and Here is Why
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct real-data grokking/mechanism competitor: proposes local input-output partition complexity as a progress measure and reports delayed generalization/robustness on MLP-MNIST, CNN-CIFAR10, ResNet-Imagenette, and other settings.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Humayun et al. examine migration of linear-region complexity and broad task/architecture coverage, including a 1k-MNIST MLP, but stop at improved generalization rather than a post-peak collapse. The target's spectral detector is weight-only and cheaper to compute but is evaluated on much narrower settings and without the causal/geometric analyses used there.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking and Generalization Collapse: Insights from HTSR theory
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct same-author predecessor explicitly acknowledged by the target: already reports MNIST anti-grokking at 10^7 steps, alpha<2, Correlation Traps, MP/KS inspection, and comparison with the same four alternative measures.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The 15-page predecessor already makes the central discovery and data-free-detection claim. The 27-page target is a substantial extension adding the modular-addition Transformer, deeper prototype/Fourier analyses, the shuffled-outlier theorem, expanded controls and perturbation tables; its novelty is therefore an extended evidence package rather than first disclosure of anti-grokking.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1, submitted 2025-06-04; ICML 2025 workshop version as described by target

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking modular arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational constructive and empirical predecessor for the cyclic binary case: gives analytic DFT-weight solutions for two-layer quadratic networks and shows gradient descent/AdamW discover the corresponding modular-arithmetic features.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gromov treats k=2 cyclic modular operations and analytic sinusoidal weights. The target generalizes to arbitrary finite (including non-Abelian) groups and k inputs, derives an AGF acquisition order, and adds depth constructions; its width construction reduces to this DFT mechanism in the cyclic binary special case.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Toy Model of Universality: Reverse Engineering how Networks Learn Group Operations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct arbitrary-group binary predecessor: proposes Group Composition via Representations, reverse-engineers shallow networks across groups/architectures, and tests learned irrep circuits with ablations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chughtai et al. focus on k=2 trained-model mechanisms and find weak but not strong universality in which irreps/order appear. The target supplies a small-init dynamical score predicting irrep order, extends to k>2, and constructs depth-efficient sequence solutions, but has less causal empirical validation and engineers separated encoding powers for clean sequences.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct theory predecessor: proves that max-margin shallow quadratic solutions for modular addition and finite-group composition use Fourier/irreducible-representation features.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Morwani et al. characterize endpoint implicit bias for binary composition, with strong assumptions including real irreps in the group theorem. The target analyzes temporal multi-phase acquisition for arbitrary finite groups (handling complex pairs through C_rho), k-way composition, and width/depth, but relies on AGF/alignment assumptions rather than max-margin convergence.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2024 spotlight conference version; OpenReview last modified 2024-04-12

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking Group Multiplication with Cosets
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct competing mechanistic formalism: completely reverse-engineers grokked one-hidden-layer S5/S6 models as subgroup-coset circuits and validates them with causal interchange interventions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stander et al. argue for coset rather than the earlier GCR account on binary permutation groups and emphasize causal faithfulness. The target uses irrep/Fourier dynamics on general k-way groups; Appendix E notes later unification between rank-one irrep factors and rho-sets, but the target does not perform comparable causal interventions on its learned networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fourier Circuits in Neural Networks and Transformers: A Case Study of Modular Arithmetic with Multiple Inputs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest k-input shallow-network predecessor: characterizes Fourier max-margin solutions for modular addition with multiple inputs and examines analogous one-layer Transformer attention mechanisms.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. remain cyclic and give a sufficient width proportional to 4^k(p-1), with empirical k=4,p=47 training. The target extends to arbitrary finite groups, improves its explicit exponential factor to 2^k (within the stated construction), and predicts full temporal irrep order, but provides no own Transformer evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards a unified and verified understanding of group-operation networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct binary group-operation interpretation/verification predecessor: identifies approximate bi-equivariance and rho-set structure and converts explanations into compact performance certificates.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. focus mainly on S5 one-hidden-layer models and verify >=95% accuracy bounds for 45% of trained models, unifying irrep and coset views. The target's rank-one factor construction is closely related to rho-sets but adds k-way small-init dynamics and architecture scaling; it lacks Wu et al.'s quantitative faithfulness certification.

reviewed_competitors.title: Alternating Gradient Flows: A Theory of Feature Learning in Two-layer Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Immediate methodological predecessor by overlapping authors: introduces AGF and applies it to quadratic modular addition, predicting Fourier features in decreasing coefficient magnitude.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kunin et al. provide the general dormant/active framework and a complete quadratic modular-addition dynamics case, plus a convergence result only for diagonal linear networks. The target applies AGF to k-way arbitrary finite groups, derives the dimension-sensitive irrep score and multi-irrep cost construction, while adding the new unproved alignment/coordination assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Learn Shortcuts to Automata
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct sequence-architecture theory and empirical predecessor: constructs logarithmic-depth Transformer simulators for all finite semiautomata, constant-depth shortcuts for solvable cases, and trains Transformers/RNNs on 19 synthetic automata.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. cover the more general semiautomata setting, provide depth lower bounds tied to solvability/complexity, run replicated Transformer and RNN comparisons, and audit OOD brittleness. The target gives finer shallow irrep feature dynamics for group products and explicit RNN/tree weights, but only discusses Transformers and does not test sequence generalization or equal-architecture baselines.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uncovering a Universal Abstract Algorithm for Modular Addition in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current deep modular-addition mechanistic competitor: proposes approximate-CRT/coset abstractions spanning neurons, clusters, full networks, MLPs, Transformers, and depth, and empirically validates O(log n) learned features.
reviewed_competitors.difference: McCracken et al. focus on binary cyclic modular addition and unifying learned mechanisms across architectures/hyperparameters, including trained deep networks. The target addresses arbitrary groups and sequence length k, provides AGF dynamics and exact associativity constructions, but has no trained deep-MLP or Transformer evidence and its O(log k) result concerns construction depth rather than O(log n) learned feature count.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2025 Main Conference camera-ready, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Mechanism and Dynamics of Modular Addition: Fourier Features, Lottery Ticket, and Grokking
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent/current dynamics competitor: analyzes two-layer modular-addition Fourier-feature competition, phase coupling, lottery-ticket initialization, diversification, and grokking through gradient-flow tools.
reviewed_competitors.difference: He et al. study cyclic binary modular addition and emphasize the first winning frequency, phase symmetry, frequency diversification, and three-stage grokking. The target's current v2 explicitly positions itself as extending a similar regime to full multi-phase irrep acquisition, arbitrary finite groups, k inputs, and depth constructions; He was submitted after the target's v1 but before its v2 revision.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks

reviewed_competitors.title: Approximating Likelihood Ratios with Calibrated Discriminative Classifiers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cranmer, Pavez, and Louppe show that a calibrated discriminative classifier output can preserve and recover likelihood ratios after dimensionality reduction, directly treating classification as a route to likelihood-ratio tests. The present paper shifts from learning a ratio for scientific inference to tracking class-conditional KL during ordinary classifier training and proving ideal one-vs-rest representation sufficiency; its broad claim that direct neural hypothesis-test interpretations were absent is therefore too strong.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Neural Networks for Likelihood/Density Ratio Estimation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Moustakides and Basioti derive neural-network training objectives whose population solutions are likelihood or density ratios for detection and hypothesis testing, including conditional ratios. This is closer to an explicit neural LRT than the present paper, which studies ordinary cross-entropy post hoc and contributes a training-trajectory diagnostic rather than a new ratio-training objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Likelihood Ratios with Neural Network Classifiers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rizvi, Pettee, and Nachman empirically compare classifier losses and output parameterizations for finite-data neural likelihood-ratio approximation on Gaussian and particle-physics distributions. The present work instead estimates KL between learned class representations across epochs and proposes the Evidence-Error plane; it does not benchmark how accurately its logits recover the true ratio.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Neural Network Approach for Online Nonlinear Neyman-Pearson Classification
reviewed_competitors.difference: Can and Ozkan explicitly train a single-hidden-layer neural classifier with a Lagrangian objective to maximize detection power at a user-controlled false-positive rate in an online stream. Unlike the present paper, it actually enforces the defining Neyman-Pearson constraint; it does not analyze retained representation KL or training trajectories.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neyman-Pearson classification under a strict constraint
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rigollet and Tong construct classifiers that control type-I error with high probability while approaching minimum type-II error. This formalizes the constraint the Evidence-Error plane omits; the present paper's novelty lies in representation divergence, not Neyman-Pearson learning guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Opening the Black Box of Deep Neural Networks via Information
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shwartz-Ziv and Tishby visualize I(X;T) against I(T;Y) and propose fitting/compression phases. The present paper replaces mutual information with one-vs-rest KL and an operational error coordinate, avoiding some deterministic-network pathologies but inheriting difficult high-dimensional estimation and overinterpreting its diagonal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Representations for Neural Network-Based Classification Using the Information Bottleneck Principle
reviewed_competitors.difference: Amjad and Geiger show that deterministic information-bottleneck objectives can be infinite or piecewise constant and invariant to bijections that alter desirable geometry. The present KL-between-class-conditionals quantity remains finite only under additional support/noise assumptions and is decision-focused, but its estimator and reparameterization choices still require care.

reviewed_competitors.title: Caveats for information bottleneck in deterministic scenarios
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kolchinsky, Tracey, and Van Kuyk analyze degeneracies of IB when labels or representations are deterministic. The present work explicitly injects noise to avoid singular class conditionals and uses class-conditional divergence rather than I(X;T), but the need for that intervention limits claims about the original data channel.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Variational Information Bottleneck
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alemi et al. optimize a stochastic variational bottleneck to trade prediction against compressed representation and evaluate generalization and robustness. The present paper does not introduce a training regularizer or stochastic encoder; it diagnoses ordinary cross-entropy training with class-conditional KL.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Generalized Information Bottleneck Theory of Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Westphal, Hailes, and Musolesi replace standard IB quantities with synergy-based interaction information and report compression dynamics across CNNs and Transformers. The present paper supplies a simpler class-separation quantity with a likelihood-testing interpretation, but evaluates a narrower architecture and dataset range and lacks a valid finite-n error region.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Guide to Constraining Effective Field Theories with Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Brehmer et al. train several neural estimators of likelihood ratios using simulator-side information and compare them on a high-dimensional inference problem. This reinforces that neural discriminants as hypothesis-test statistics predate the present paper, whose distinct object is internal divergence preservation during supervised classification.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval
reviewed_competitors.difference: Weller et al. introduce LIMIT, prove the normalized positive-margin packing lower bound, and report failed free-embedding and learned-model experiments. Crucially, current v2 also records the Alon construction giving sign rank at most 2k and one extra dimension for normalized vectors. The present paper adds MED/RMED terminology, the exact linear min(2k,m-1) Radon result, an explicit squared-polynomial query, Euclidean transfer, a sharp finite-m margin ceiling, centroid upper witnesses, and counter-controls; it does not overturn Weller's margin lower bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Strengths and Limitations of Single-Vector Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.difference: Archish et al. independently use Alon sign-rank results to show 2k+1 normalized dimensions suffice for top-k retrieval and then isolate domain shift, task-similarity misalignment, finetuning, catastrophic forgetting, and multi-vector advantages on LIMIT. The present paper appeared earlier and proves a sharper exact linear constant plus robust margin theorems, but its empirical analysis is much narrower and does not study finetuning or generalization tradeoffs.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Limits Does Quantization Place on Dense Top-k Retrieval? A Theoretical Study
reviewed_competitors.difference: Okajima and Yoshida keep the same arbitrary top-k realizability problem but prove that B-bit coordinates require B d = Omega(k log N) and identify precision regimes where no dimension suffices. This formalizes the present paper's qualitative finite-precision caveat and shows its corpus-independent dimension is specific to infinite precision; the present work instead analyzes real-valued normalized score margins.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-Vector Embeddings are Provably More Expressive than Single Vector Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jayaram proves a strong dimension separation when single vectors must approximate multi-vector Chamfer similarity matrices, using a NAND pattern-matrix construction. That does not contradict low-dimensional exact subset ordering here: approximating all similarity values is a stronger and different requirement. It shows why practical multi-vector gains can coexist with favorable exact MED.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sign rank versus VC dimension
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alon, Moran, and Yehudayoff study sign rank at fixed VC dimension and use moment-curve upper-bound techniques. Their general matrix theory underlies later 2k+1 top-k observations; the present paper specializes the geometry to retrieval, proves the exact affine linear MED constant with Radon, and adds normalized-margin analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hierarchical Retrieval: The Geometry and a Pretrain-Finetune Recipe
reviewed_competitors.difference: You et al. analyze dual encoders when each answer set is the ancestor set of a node in a hierarchy and give dimension bounds tied to hierarchy depth and corpus size plus a practical pretrain-finetune method. MED covers the much larger family of every arbitrary subset up to k but supplies no trainable encoder; neither theorem directly bounds the other answer family.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Curse of Dense Low-Dimensional Information Retrieval for Large Index Sizes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reimers and Gurevych show theoretically and empirically that dense low-dimensional retrieval accumulates false positives faster as an index grows and can be overtaken by sparse retrieval. Their concern is noisy practical similarity distributions, not existential realization of every chosen subset. The present exact result does not remove that drowning effect; its robust and random-control analyses only begin to separate the mechanisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: MUVERA: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings
reviewed_competitors.difference: MUVERA compresses multi-vector Chamfer-style retrieval into asymmetric fixed-dimensional encodings with approximation guarantees and reports recall/latency gains. It targets efficient approximation of an existing multi-vector scoring function, whereas MED asks only whether some single-vector ordering can realize arbitrary answer sets and provides no indexing or latency result.

reviewed_competitors.title: ColBERT: Efficient and Effective Passage Search via Contextualized Late Interaction over BERT
reviewed_competitors.difference: ColBERT retains token-level query and document vectors and scores them with late interaction, trading storage and retrieval cost for learned fine-grained matching. The present paper studies single-vector existential capacity and excludes multi-vector baselines from its capacity comparison; ColBERT illustrates that practical expressivity and learnability can favor a richer score family despite low single-vector MED.

reviewed_competitors.difference: EGGROLL uses rank-r perturbations, proves high-dimensional consistency properties, and reaches near-inference throughput while remaining competitive with GRPO. The target studies dense full-parameter perturbations; therefore its density and forgetting diagnosis need not transfer to low-rank population members.

reviewed_competitors.title: ESSA: Evolutionary Strategies for Scalable Alignment
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct gradient-free LLM-alignment competitor that restricts the ES search subspace
reviewed_competitors.difference: ESSA evolves only singular values of LoRA adapters and supports INT4/INT8 inference, reporting task and scaling gains over GRPO up to 32B. The target evolves all weights at 1–1.5B and studies retention, so it contributes a distinct failure audit but not a verdict on parameter-efficient ES.

reviewed_competitors.title: RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior analysis of why on-policy RL retains old capabilities during new-task fine-tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shenfeld et al. compare RL with SFT across language and robotic models and argue that on-policy RL selects KL-minimal solutions, with theory and broader retention evidence. The target contrasts GRPO with ES and adds weight-space density/norm plots, but its explicit-KL GRPO versus unanchored ES design does not isolate the claimed optimizer mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reinforcement Learning Finetunes Small Subnetworks in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct antecedent for the GRPO update-sparsity diagnostic used as the target paper's mechanism comparator
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mukherjee et al. test seven RL algorithms and ten LLMs, find only 5–30% of parameters change materially, and validate that tuning the identified subnetwork recovers performance. The target transfers one fixed-threshold diagnostic to ES versus GRPO but does not perform the causal subnetwork or threshold-robustness tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fine-Tuning Language Models with Just Forward Passes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational inference-memory gradient-free LLM fine-tuning competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: MeZO uses two in-place zeroth-order forward passes, scales experiments to 66B, and evaluates classification, multiple choice, and generation with full and parameter-efficient tuning. It establishes the broader memory-efficiency premise but does not study online reward optimization or forgetting; the target's ES-specific retention audit is complementary and much smaller-scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Model Editing at Scale Leads to Gradual and Catastrophic Forgetting

The target shares authors and transfers the forgetting lens to ES, but its evidence is continued optimization on one task rather than sequential edits and does not demonstrate the same two-phase phenomenon.

The target's distinctive addition is fixed-beta phase-diagram, probe, and path language, but its claim that prior work did not systematically study beta is too broad and its related-work section omits this NeurIPS 2024 predecessor.

reviewed_competitors.title: KL Penalty Control via Perturbation for Direct Preference Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Epsilon-DPO perturbs and adapts beta per preference pair using policy/reference logits and reports gains over direct-alignment baselines. It provides a mechanism and broad benchmark comparison for beta control; the target instead diagnoses fixed-grid capability responses and a path effect but does not compare adaptive control or specify its preference data.

reviewed_competitors.title: Minor DPO Reject Penalty to Increase Training Robustness
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct prior analysis of beta's differing role in DPO versus the underlying RL objective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xie et al. analyze beta semantics and DPO's likelihood dynamics, then add a rejected-response penalty for stability. That directly anticipates the need to disentangle beta from a generic pressure knob; the target contributes cross-beta probe maps but no objective-level control or robust baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mitigating Reward Over-optimization in Direct Alignment Algorithms with Importance Sampling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest direct predecessor for DPO proxy improvement with downstream degradation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nguyen et al. show offline direct-alignment performance can deteriorate as the policy drifts, especially under low regularization, and propose clipped reference-distribution importance weighting. The target visualizes margin/probe anticorrelation across beta but does not measure policy drift or compare a mitigation, and its beta direction is described inconsistently with low-regularization semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Disentangling Length from Quality in Direct Preference Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct DPO metric-artifact and proxy-exploitation antecedent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. isolate length exploitation in DPO across summarization/dialogue and introduce a principled regularizer, with length-controlled evaluation. The target uses length-normalized fixed-probe margins and asserts sign/path effects are not length artifacts, but does not test generation-length, prompt, or other probe-construction artifacts.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Deep Dive into the Trade-Offs of Parameter-Efficient Preference Alignment Techniques

The target offers much denser beta resolution and probe decomposition, but far thinner data/model reporting and no instruction-tuned or alternative-method control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
reviewed_competitors.difference: Birth of a Transformer already tracks fast global-bigram learning and slower induction-head formation in a simplified two-layer model on synthetic mixtures of global and context-specific bigrams. The reviewed paper's narrower advance is a simultaneous multilayer early-step formula for every attention-only parameter on arbitrary empirical text; it does not match the prior work's later phase formation of an induction mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scan and Snap: Understanding Training Dynamics and Token Composition in 1-layer Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scan and Snap proves how a one-layer reparameterized Transformer trained for next-token prediction promotes distinct co-occurring tokens, suppresses common ones, and freezes after a learning-rate-dependent phase transition, assuming long sequences and a faster decoder. The reviewed work removes that staged-speed premise and covers L layers plus positions and values, but only near initialization and without a snapping or convergence account.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Do Transformers Learn Topic Structure: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding
reviewed_competitors.difference: This prior work already connects co-occurrence-defined semantics to block structure in embeddings, value matrices, and attention using an LDA-like topic model, masked prediction, Wikipedia experiments, and analyses of optima under frozen or constrained components. The reviewed paper substitutes arbitrary natural-language corpus statistics and simultaneous early gradients across layers, but offers a weaker semantic evaluation and no topic-recovery guarantee.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Transformers Learn Causal Structure with Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: The ICML camera-ready prior shows that gradients in a simplified two-layer Transformer encode mutual information and recover a latent causal graph, including induction heads for in-context Markov chains. The reviewed paper handles unstructured empirical text and all attention-only weight classes, but its distributional association maps do not identify causal structure or prove task solution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mechanics of Next Token Prediction with Self-Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mechanics of Next Token Prediction characterizes the trained one-layer self-attention solution as hard retrieval of high-priority strongly connected components followed by soft composition. The reviewed paper instead identifies finite early updates for output, value, attention, and position matrices in a residual multilayer model; it neither reaches the learned automaton nor provides the prior's implicit-bias characterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Dynamics of Transformers to Recognize Word Co-occurrence via Gradient Flow Analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: This NeurIPS work jointly analyzes three softmax-attention matrices and an MLP from random initialization, proving two-phase gradient-flow behavior and near-minimum loss for a designated-word co-occurrence classification task. The reviewed paper is closer to autoregressive language modeling and covers depth and relative position, but its early leading terms do not supply an end-to-end loss-convergence result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Non-asymptotic Convergence of Training Transformers for Next-token Prediction
reviewed_competitors.difference: The NeurIPS paper proves rates toward max-margin directions and linear cross-entropy convergence for a one-layer attention-plus-feed-forward model under a designed two-stage training procedure, with a dataset-shift result. The reviewed work analyzes standard simultaneous full-batch updates and arbitrary corpus statistics across multiple layers, while giving up convergence, max-margin, and distribution-shift guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepNet: Scaling Transformers to 1,000 Layers
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepNorm already modifies Post-LN to LN(αx+F(x)), derives depth-dependent α and initialization scaling, and trains Transformers beyond 1,000 layers. Keel's defensible difference is α=L plus an inner RMSNorm and first-layer exceptions, with decoder-only 3B LLM evidence and no DeepNorm weight rescaling; therefore thousand-layer Post-LN and residual scaling themselves are prior art.

reviewed_competitors.title: Peri-LN: Revisiting Normalization Layer in the Transformer Architecture
reviewed_competitors.difference: Peri-LN also places normalization around Transformer sublayers and analyzes activation variance and gradient propagation, with experiments up to 3.2B parameters. It preserves an unscaled residual topology rather than Keel's L-multiplied shortcut; Keel offers much deeper decoder-only runs, while Peri-LN supplies a broader variance analysis and a more standard peripheral-normalization interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mix-LN: Unleashing the Power of Deeper Layers by Combining Pre-LN and Post-LN
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mix-LN addresses ineffective deep layers by using Post-LN in an early fraction and Pre-LN later, reporting models through 7B plus SFT/RLHF transfer. Keel instead applies a common dual-normalized Post-LN-style equation through most sublayers and targets 512-1,024 depth; it removes Mix-LN's layer-transition ratio but introduces fixed α=L and first-layer exceptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: HybridNorm: Towards Stable and Efficient Transformer Training via Hybrid Normalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: HybridNorm combines QKV normalization in attention with Post-Norm in FFNs and evaluates dense and sparse large models, retaining a uniform intralayer hybrid without depth-scaled shortcuts. Keel normalizes the entire F input and post-residual output for both attention and FFN and adds α=L; its extreme-depth evidence is stronger, but the reviewed paper only compares HybridNorm on subjective MaxLR, not downstream quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Curse of Depth in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This NeurIPS work diagnoses Pre-LN variance growth and near-identity deep blocks, then scales LayerNorm output inversely with depth to improve layer use while keeping a Pre-LN residual path. Keel shares the effective-depth motivation but returns to Post-LN and scales the shortcut upward; its 1,024-layer/1T-token panels extend scale, while LayerNorm Scaling is a simpler alternative that the Keel experiments do not directly compare.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding the Difficulty of Training Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Admin attributes Post-LN instability to amplification from residual-branch dependence and uses adaptive initialization to stabilize early training, rather than treating vanishing shortcut gradients as the sole central failure. Keel replaces an initialization remedy with a permanent α=L plus inner RMSNorm topology; a direct controlled comparison would test these competing diagnoses, but Admin is absent from Keel's reported panels.

reviewed_competitors.title: Normalization in Attention Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: This NeurIPS theory unifies Post-LN, Pre-LN, Mix-LN, Peri-LN, nGPT, and LN Scaling as speed regulators and analyzes token clustering/representation collapse, identifying Peri-LN as a favorable balance under its assumptions. It omits MLPs and parameter-gradient training, but highlights a representational axis absent from Keel's shortcut-only derivation. Keel contributes an actual ultra-deep architecture and training runs rather than that paper's idealized attention ODE.

reviewed_competitors.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Agarwal et al.'s GKD already trains a student on its own generated sequences while a teacher supplies token feedback, directly supplying SDFT's on-policy distillation mechanism. SDFT's narrower addition is to make the same model a query-specific demonstration-conditioned teacher and study continual acquisition rather than model compression with a separate teacher.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning by Distilling Context
reviewed_competitors.difference: Snell et al. already condition a model on instructions or scratchpads and fine-tune that same model to reproduce the gain without context. Their training uses synthetic inputs and context-derived targets rather than correcting current student rollouts; SDFT adds on-policy output sampling and per-query expert demonstrations, not the basic contextual self-teacher idea.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Distillation Bridges Distribution Gap in Language Model Fine-Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. previously introduced a method also named Self-Distillation Fine-Tuning (SDFT), using model-generated data to stay near the original LLM distribution and preserve instruction following/safety during task fine-tuning. The present SDFT instead distills a demonstration-conditioned teacher on current student trajectories; its name and broad anti-forgetting claim are therefore not novel even if the mechanism differs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Retaining by Doing: The Role of On-Policy Data in Mitigating Forgetting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. systematically attribute RL's lower forgetting to on-policy data across Llama/Qwen families and show approximately on-policy data can suffice. SDFT operationalizes that principle when only demonstrations are available, but does not originate the on-policy-retention finding and tests a narrower sequential stream.

reviewed_competitors.title: RL's Razor: Why Online Reinforcement Learning Forgets Less
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shenfeld et al. argue that on-policy RL selects new-task solutions close to the base policy in KL and validate lower forgetting in language and robotic models. The current paper replaces an explicit reward with privileged demonstration context, but its KL-minimal continual-learning premise and authorship directly continue this antecedent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Distilled Reasoner: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhao et al.'s OPSD has the same central construction: one LLM is teacher and student under different contexts, the teacher sees privileged verified traces, and token divergence is minimized on student rollouts. OPSD focuses on mathematical reasoning and token efficiency, whereas the target paper's defensible distinction is continual skill/knowledge retention and EMA implementation; broad priority for on-policy contextual self-distillation is shared.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reinforcement Learning via Self-Distillation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hübotter et al.'s SDPO conditions the current model on rich environment feedback and distills its feedback-aware predictions into the policy, likewise avoiding an external teacher and producing dense token supervision. It addresses RLVR credit assignment with runtime/judge feedback, while SDFT addresses demonstration-only continual learning; both independently occupy the conditioned-self-teacher design space.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Projection Memory for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: GPM already performs a single-shot SVD of prior-task neural activations, stores subspace bases, and projects later gradients orthogonally to those important directions. LRCP's narrow possible advance is RADL-based restriction to selected LLM circuits; the target paper's claim that GPM continuously recomputes SVD every training step is contradicted by GPM's official record.

reviewed_competitors.title: Orthogonal Gradient Descent for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: OGD already restricts new-task updates to a subspace where outputs on previous tasks do not change, using stored gradient directions rather than historical activation SVD. LRCP changes the protected object and localizes application to selected transformer circuits, but not the core orthogonal-complement update principle.

reviewed_competitors.title: Preserving Principal Subspaces to Reduce Catastrophic Forgetting in Fine-tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Franke et al. already use SVD to protect principal weight-matrix subspaces during LLM fine-tuning without old training data, directly anticipating low-rank orthogonal preservation in this domain. LRCP instead builds bases from historical activations and selects circuits via drift diagnostics; a fair novelty test would compare these choices head-to-head, which the target paper does not do or cite.

reviewed_competitors.title: LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less
reviewed_competitors.difference: Biderman et al. quantify that low-rank LLM adaptation preserves out-of-domain capabilities better but learns less than full fine-tuning across instruction tuning and 20B-token continued pretraining, including the rank gap of learned updates. LRCP reports a better single-table trade-off than rank-16 LoRA, but does not match that study's scale, domains, budgets, or uncertainty and supplies no rank-matched LoRA sweep.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Model Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. directly connect LLM forgetting to loss-landscape flatness and mitigate it with sharpness-aware minimization on three fine-tuning datasets and multiple scales. The target paper claims attention/MLP/routing mechanisms and localized projection instead, but does not compare against SAM or provide sufficient controlled evidence to distinguish its mechanism from this prior one.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lottery Ticket Adaptation: Mitigating Destructive Interference in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: LoTA identifies and updates a sparse LLM subnetwork to reduce destructive interference across instruction, reasoning, math, and summarization tasks and supports task-vector merging. LRCP likewise activates only 1.62% of parameters but chooses them through drift localization and constrains directions rather than optimizing a sparse ticket; the target omits the closest sparse-update baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Retaining by Doing: The Role of On-Policy Data in Mitigating Forgetting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. compare SFT and RL across Llama/Qwen tasks and causally isolate on-policy data as the main driver of reduced forgetting, including approximately on-policy alternatives. The target evaluates only supervised-style parameter interventions; without on-policy training baselines it cannot show LRCP is preferable to a change in learning paradigm.

reviewed_competitors.title: Overcoming Catastrophic Forgetting in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: EWC protects parameters in proportion to estimated old-task importance and is the principal regularization baseline in Table 4. LRCP protects low-rank activation directions only in selected circuits and reports lower overhead/better retention, but the absence of tuning ranges, uncertainty, and equal-compute details prevents the single result from establishing superiority.

reviewed_competitors.title: CPMobius: Iterative Coach-Player Reasoning for Data-Free Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest current primary competitor: a coach proposes reasoning tasks and is rewarded from changes in a player's performance in an iterative cooperative RL loop.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CPMobius directly overlaps the broad coach/teacher-by-student-improvement idea and is an accepted ICML 2026 paper. It claims no external training data during co-evolution and uses difficulty/player-success shaping, whereas SOAR deliberately uses progress on a fixed answer-keyed fail@128 target set as the grounding signal, short replicated inner trainings, and thresholded student promotion.

reviewed_competitors.title: Absolute Zero: Reinforced Self-play Reasoning with Zero Data
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct zero-data self-play reasoning system in which a model proposes and solves its own tasks with RLVR.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Absolute Zero uses a code executor to validate proposed tasks and verify answers and rewards task learnability without a fixed target-failure reward. SOAR targets math domains lacking synthetic-question verification and accepts noisy proposed answers, but consumes labeled hard target questions to measure actual student progress.

reviewed_competitors.title: R-Zero: Self-Evolving Reasoning LLM from Zero Data
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A challenger-solver co-evolution framework that autonomously generates a near-frontier curriculum without pre-existing tasks or labels.
reviewed_competitors.difference: R-Zero trains distinct challenger and solver roles around intrinsic edge-of-capability rewards and evaluates multiple general/math backbones. SOAR instead anchors generator utility to post-update accuracy on a pre-existing hard target set and emphasizes escape from a screened sparse-reward plateau.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Questioning Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: An asymmetric proposer-solver self-play system that generates its own questions and answers for reasoning improvement.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SQLM rewards proposer questions for intermediate difficulty and uses majority vote as the solver's correctness proxy, with unit tests in code. SOAR directly ablates this learnability style and replaces it with measured progress on labeled hard target problems, at far greater bilevel compute cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: SeRL: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning for Large Language Models with Limited Data
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A self-instruction/self-rewarding RL system that evolves a reasoning curriculum from a limited seed set and filters for quality, diversity, and difficulty.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SeRL uses majority-vote pseudo-rewards and online filters and was run by SOAR as a direct MATH/HARP baseline. SOAR uses the seed set only as a hidden downstream progress evaluator and reports higher pass@k on its selected Llama-3.2-3B fail@128 setup.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Self-Play For Data-Free Training
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A game-theoretic language self-play method for improving instruction following, math, and coding without additional data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Language Self-Play casts capabilities as competitive language-game performance and does not optimize generated curricula against a fixed target failure set. SOAR is a specialized teacher-student data-generation loop whose outer signal is supervised target-domain improvement.

reviewed_competitors.title: SAGE: Multi-Agent Self-Evolution for LLM Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later multi-agent self-evolution system with challenger, planner, solver, and critic roles, explicit curriculum generation, and verifier-based quality control.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAGE adds planning and criticism to prevent curriculum drift and uses a small seed plus external verifiers across math and code. SOAR has only teacher/student roles and allows wrong synthetic answers, but its target-progress reward directly tests whether a short student update helps the fixed hard distribution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Adapting Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A bilevel self-adaptation method that trains a model to generate finetuning data/update directives using downstream performance after adaptation as the RL reward.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SEAL is the closest conceptual precedent for rewarding self-generated updates by post-update task performance, but it conditions self-edits on provided knowledge or examples and studies SFT-based adaptation. SOAR generates standalone math curricula without seeing target questions and uses nested RLVR plus a promoted student baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Elements of Differentiable Programming
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest current comprehensive tutorial/book on differentiable programming, spanning autodiff, optimization, probability, implicit differentiation, and program design.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Elements v4 is much broader and more systematic about the mathematical/programming foundations and is the source this paper repeatedly leans on. The reviewed tutorial narrows to duality plus first-order cone optimization and supplies application/code sketches, but it does not match Elements' breadth or rigor and contains several equation errors.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Optimize: A Primer and A Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A primary survey and reproducible benchmark devoted specifically to learned optimizers for continuous optimization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The JMLR article defines model-based/model-free L2O taxonomies, studies generalization and failure boundaries, and releases Open-L2O benchmarks. The reviewed paper instead mostly implements classical solvers and differentiable layers, with no cross-instance learned-optimizer benchmark; its unique emphasis is pairing cone/Fenchel duality with tutorial case sketches.

reviewed_competitors.title: End-to-End Constrained Optimization Learning: A Survey
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct conceptual survey of integrating constrained/combinatorial optimization and machine-learning architectures end to end.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kotary et al. organize learning approaches around feasibility, optimality, solver integration, and structural inference. The reviewed tutorial is more elementary and continuous/conic, includes software walkthroughs and derivations, but does not provide a comparable taxonomy or critical evidence synthesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers in Neural Architectures: Foundations and Perspectives
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A focused survey on the foundations, evolution, and applications of differentiable convex optimization layers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Katyal centers the neural-architecture optimization-layer literature and its mathematical proofs. The reviewed paper adds classical first-order algorithms, GPU-oriented snippets, duality, and domain examples, but much of its differentiable-layer overview overlaps and its case-study validation is thinner.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiable Convex Optimization Layers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The foundational CVXPYLayers/DPP primary paper for general differentiable disciplined convex programs used throughout the tutorial.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Agrawal et al. contribute ASA canonicalization, analytical cone-solver differentiation, implementations, and timed applications. The reviewed tutorial reuses this machinery in small examples and adds exposition around first-order dual methods, but contributes neither a replacement layer nor a technical extension to DPP.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient and Modular Implicit Differentiation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A primary framework paper for solver-agnostic automatic implicit differentiation through user-specified optimality conditions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Blondel et al. make the implicit-differentiation mechanism modular, benchmark it, and show bilevel applications. The reviewed tutorial gives only the textbook implicit-function formula and delegates implementation to CVXPYLayers, while focusing more on duality and explicit PDG/ADMM/PDHG unrolling.

reviewed_competitors.title: BPQP: A Differentiable Convex Optimization Framework for Efficient End-to-End Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A modern differentiable convex-optimization framework that turns the backward pass into a decoupled QP solvable with first-order methods.
reviewed_competitors.difference: BPQP provides a concrete new backward algorithm and reports order-of-magnitude runtime improvements on simulated and real tasks. The reviewed paper cites it but neither implements nor benchmarks against it; its claim of efficient first-order differentiable optimization is therefore pedagogical rather than competitive.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Fully First-Order Layer for Differentiable Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest current method claiming a fully first-order differentiable optimization layer with finite-time hypergradient guarantees and a library.
reviewed_competitors.difference: FFOLayer explicitly avoids Hessian/KKT linear solves via an active-set Lagrangian bilevel oracle and gives complexity guarantees. The reviewed tutorial merely notes that classical first-order solvers can be unrolled or embedded; it proposes no first-order hypergradient method and presents no comparison to FFOLayer despite sharing the headline framing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational direct predecessor for progressive sharpening and edge of stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cohen et al. directly track the largest training-loss Hessian eigenvalue under full-batch gradient descent and establish the 2/eta edge-of-stability phenomenon. The target uses that phenomenon as validation but substitutes an update-direction loss crossing that scales to 7B checkpoints; it adds scale and forward-only accessibility, not discovery of progressive sharpening or EoS.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct predecessor for Adam and preconditioned sharpness
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cohen et al. measure the maximum eigenvalue of the preconditioned Hessian and show adaptive optimizers equilibrate near optimizer-specific stability thresholds in full and sufficiently large batches. The target derives a weight-decay shift and estimates an optimizer-direction crossing without HVPs; its 7B evidence is cheaper but does not retain the predecessor's worst-case spectral meaning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Warmup the Learning Rate? Underlying Mechanisms and Improvements
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest methodological predecessor for critical-rate line search
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kalra and Barkeshli already use empirical critical learning-rate search, relate warmup/catapults to (preconditioned) sharpness, and choose an initial learning rate from that boundary. The target generalizes the search initialization/exit rule, repurposes the quantity as a scalable trajectory diagnostic, and introduces a cross-loss version for data mixtures. The core forward-pass crossing estimator is therefore inherited rather than new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stepping on the Edge: Curvature Aware Learning Rate Tuners
reviewed_competitors.difference: Roulet et al. analyze lambda_dir, closed-loop interactions between learning-rate tuning and curvature, and propose CDAT to favor long-term curvature stabilization. The target explicitly adopts the directional-sharpness formula as the quadratic approximation to lambda_c but uses empirical crossings to analyze rather than control training and extends the diagnostic to cross-dataset updates.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Loss Curvature Perspective on Training Instability in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gilmer et al. directly examine Hessian evolution across architectures, initialization, normalization, clipping, and warmup and argue that successful choices escape poor conditioning. The target narrows to a cheap optimizer-direction proxy compatible with modern LLM kernels and supplies 7B checkpoint curves, but it has less intervention breadth and no direct 7B Hessian validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: High dimensional analysis reveals conservative sharpening and a stochastic edge of stability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct stochastic sharpness alternative and batch-size challenge
reviewed_competitors.difference: Agarwala and Pennington show that small-batch dynamics can be governed by a stochastic edge tied to an NTK-trace quantity rather than the largest Hessian eigenvalue, and that stochasticity slows sharpening. The target instead treats an update-direction loss crossing as the proxy across batches; this competitor makes the target's 60-times-smaller OLMo analysis batch a substantive change of regime, not only a shifted threshold.

reviewed_competitors.title: Edge of Stochastic Stability: Revisiting the Edge of Stability for SGD
reviewed_competitors.difference: Andreyev and Beneventano define Batch Sharpness, expected mini-batch Hessian curvature along corresponding stochastic gradients, and show it rather than full-batch lambda_max stabilizes near 2/eta for SGD. Both works emphasize update-direction curvature, but the target estimates an empirical loss crossing, covers AdamW/LLMs, and does not model the expectation or batch-size dependence that Batch Sharpness makes explicit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling the Basin-Like Loss Landscape in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: overlapping LLM fine-tuning-basin and retention analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al.'s current revision studies random-direction and optimized worst-case perturbation landscapes around Qwen models, capability-specific basins, fine-tuning directions, and robustness bounds. The target instead measures the first pretraining-loss increase along one actual mixture update and uses it for rehearsal selection. Its relative measure is cheaper and optimizer-specific but does not establish a basin neighborhood or capability bound; the target cited this work under its earlier title.

reviewed_competitors.title: ARC Is a Vision Problem!
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct predecessor and strongest implementation baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: VARC supplies the canvas representation, RE-ARC offline expansion, per-task test-time training, 510-view voting, ViT/U-Net backbones, and the 54.5/60.4 ARC-1 baselines adopted here. The target mainly replaces the backbone with controller/context tokens, structured second-pass attention, and recurrence; because its successful blocks preserve a dense pass, the novelty is an architectural bias layered onto VARC rather than a new ARC protocol.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: HRM couples slow high-level and fast low-level recurrent modules and reports ARC alongside Sudoku and mazes without pretraining or chain-of-thought supervision. The target instead uses synchronous controller/workspace token roles inside a vision transformer, inherits VARC-style offline augmentation and TTT, and reports higher ARC scores, but it does not isolate its claimed hierarchy from dense global mixing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Less is More: Recursive Reasoning with Tiny Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: TRM simplifies HRM to one two-layer 7M-parameter network that recursively updates latent solution features and reports 45 percent ARC-AGI-1 and 8 percent ARC-AGI-2. The target is a 28M vision model with demonstration-derived controller tokens, dense/structured attention, and test-time optimization; its claim is role separation rather than TRM's minimal recurrence.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Akyurek et al. establish supervised test-time parameter updates on few-shot demonstrations for ARC and BBH, reaching 53.0 percent ARC with an 8B language model and 61.9 percent with program synthesis. The target applies the same broad adaptation principle inside VARC's much smaller visual model and changes token routing; TTT itself and the idea of adapting to demonstrations are not new here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Searching Latent Program Spaces
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct neural ARC test-time search alternative
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Latent Program Network learns a continuous distribution over programs and explicitly searches latent program space at test time, doubling out-of-distribution performance when search is enabled. The target instead optimizes model parameters/task tokens and never decodes a program or rule, so its controller should not be equated with an explicit latent program without additional evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: H-ARC: A Robust Estimate of Human Performance on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.relationship: human benchmark directly used for the headline comparison
reviewed_competitors.difference: H-ARC measures 1,729 humans across all 800 public ARC tasks and distinguishes first, second, and up-to-three-attempt accuracy: 47.8, 60.2, and 64.2 percent on the evaluation set. The target selects 60.2 for comparison with a 510-view, adapted, ensemble pass@2 system; H-ARC therefore narrows the human-level claim and exposes the protocol mismatch.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Measure of Intelligence
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chollet introduces ARC to assess skill-acquisition efficiency under explicit priors and emphasizes controlling experience and priors in comparisons. The target demonstrates task accuracy after large procedural expansion, offline cross-task training, per-task TTT, multiview voting, and ensembling; those resources should be reported as system skill and compute rather than direct evidence of human-like intelligence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Structural Inference: Interpreting Small Language Models with Susceptibilities
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baker et al. define the susceptibility response matrix and connect its low-rank structure to known functional modules in a 3M attention-only model. The present paper scales the estimator to Pythia, adds conductance clustering and a mode interpretation, but inherits the localized-posterior estimator and still lacks causal validation. The current official record is v3, revised after this paper's v1.

reviewed_competitors.title: Embryology of a Language Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. apply UMAP to per-token susceptibilities across checkpoints of a 3M model and report induction and spacing structures. The present paper replaces primarily visual discovery with conductance extraction on a larger model and a 510-cluster catalogue, but does not add a causal test of the resulting structures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Modes of Sequence Models and Learning Coefficients
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen and Murfet formalize conditional-distribution modes and their relationship to effective loss-landscape geometry. The present paper derives token susceptibilities in that basis and hypothesizes that clusters are spectral signatures, but does not compute the real-data modes required to test that hypothesis directly.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Quantization Model of Neural Scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Michaud et al. decompose token-loss gradients into candidate skills or quanta and connect their frequency distribution to scaling laws. Susceptibility clustering instead uses localized-posterior covariances and emphasizes component response, but offers no controlled comparison showing that its 510 themes are more faithful than gradient clusters.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. learn overcomplete sparse activation features and provide automated interpretability and causal IOI evidence. Susceptibility clustering assigns each example to one disjoint response cluster and avoids training a dictionary, but its SAE consistency check is searched cross-model and has no causal behavior test.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantifying Feature Space Universality Across Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct source of the SAE family used for cross-model comparison
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lan et al.'s current v4 studies analogous feature-space universality by matching SAE features and comparing relational geometry across models; the present paper uses an earlier form of those Pythia-70M SAEs as a target-token match bank for Pythia-14M clusters. The current official title and version postdate the citation form in this paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marks et al. combine gradient-discovered behaviors with SAE features to build and edit causal graphs, including intervention-based downstream use. The present paper finds a much broader descriptive pattern catalogue, but its linked-cluster networks lack measured edges and causal editing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Paulo et al. generate and evaluate explanations for millions of SAE features, including intervention scoring and explicit discussion of scoring pitfalls across two open models. The present paper labels 510 clusters with an LLM plus manual review, but its purported random validation is internally inconsistent and lacks blinded or intervention-based scoring.

reviewed_competitors.title: MSign: An Optimizer Preventing Training Instability in Large Language Models via Stable Rank Restoration
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ren et al., published after the reviewed v1, identify declining matrix stable rank and adjacent-layer Jacobian alignment before collapse, prove a mechanism for depth-amplified gradients, and intervene with MSign from 5M to 3B parameters. StabilityBench is broader across RL and LMs but supplies neither a comparable mechanism nor a validated intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: SPAM: Spike-Aware Adam with Momentum Reset for Stable LLM Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. quantify gradient spikes across architectures and datasets and test momentum reset plus spike-aware clipping from 60M to 1B, including RL. The reviewed paper offers a taxonomy and latent monitoring story, but no optimizer baseline or stabilization result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spike No More: Stabilizing the Pre-training of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Takase et al. analyze sublayer Jacobian spectral norms, derive small-sublayer/large-shortcut conditions, and test architectures that prevent spikes. StabilityBench calls gradient-coherence collapse a shared boundary without formally defining it or comparing these established mechanistic indicators.

reviewed_competitors.title: Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wortsman et al. reproduce known large-scale instabilities in small Transformers, sweep learning rate and mitigations, and predict some failures through scale trends in activation and gradient norms. The reviewed paper's GPT-2 protocol is less transparent and does not benchmark its meta-state against those simpler predictors.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stabilizing Transformer Training by Preventing Attention Entropy Collapse
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhai et al. track attention entropy, prove a spectral-norm-dependent lower bound, and test sigma-Reparam across vision, language, and speech tasks. StabilityBench's latent aggregate could be broader, but it neither compares attention entropy nor supplies an interpretable formal precursor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Methods of improving LLM training stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rybakov et al. force divergence in an 830M LM, localize growth in QKV, projection, and FC2 outputs, and compare normalization/capping remedies. The reviewed paper also induces failures at small scale but does not localize its signals to components or report comparable intervention ablations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Catapults in SGD: spikes in the training loss and their impact on generalization through feature learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhu et al. explicitly measure spikes in the low-dimensional top-eigenspace of the tangent kernel and show that smaller-batch stochasticity can increase beneficial catapults and feature learning. This is a crucial counterpoint to treating abrupt spikes as universally catastrophic and provides substantially more concrete low-dimensional evidence than StabilityBench.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cohen et al. relate non-monotone loss to Hessian sharpness near 2/step-size and show stable long-run descent despite short-run instability. The reviewed paper's binary recover/collapse framing and generic dynamical notation do not distinguish this established regime from destructive failure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding and Diagnosing Deep Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Korkmaz analyzes correlated instability directions and how sample shifts remodel sensitive directions in neural policy landscapes on ALE. StabilityBench provides a broader perturbation vocabulary, but its one-environment RL evidence lacks comparable directional diagnostics and statistical detail.

reviewed_competitors.title: Proximal Policy Optimization Suffices for On-Policy Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bouftini and Benzaouia, published after the reviewed v1, attribute PPO instability to coupled surrogate-optimization hyperparameters and propose a stabilized on-policy design with explicit empirical comparisons. StabilityBench observes PPO fragility but does not isolate PPO's mechanism or tune a within-PPO control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Structural Inference: Interpreting Small Language Models with Susceptibilities
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baker et al. define the posterior linear-response susceptibility, its per-token attribution, and the low-rank component/data response matrix in the same 3M Transformer. Patterning's new step is to pseudo-invert that already-measured map and retrain on the resulting direction; it therefore extends rather than originates susceptibility-based structural inference.

reviewed_competitors.title: Embryology of a Language Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. follow the same susceptibility geometry through training, identify induction-linked PC2 and the spacing fin, and use UMAP to describe emerging organization. The target turns those descriptive developmental signatures into fixed corpus interventions and adds an algorithm-selection study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Interpretation Predict Behavior on Unseen Data?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. introduce the parentheses distribution and train hundreds of Transformers whose in-distribution attention predicts Nested versus Equal-Count OOD behavior, while causal ablations show that predictive patterns need not implement the rule. Patterning reuses that task and model population but intervenes on susceptibility-selected in-distribution samples to shift the population of OOD outcomes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Spectroscopy: Susceptibility Clusters in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gordon et al. theoretically decompose susceptibility by data modes and cluster Pythia-14M token responses into 510 interpretable groups, with 50% matching SAE features. It remains a read/cluster method; the target uses mode inversion and retraining to attempt to write a chosen structure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bayesian Influence Functions for Hessian-Free Data Attribution
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kreer et al. use local posterior statistics and stochastic-gradient MCMC to build Hessian-free Bayesian influence functions that predict retraining effects at billion-parameter scale. Their target is prediction/data attribution, whereas Patterning targets component or LLC observables and designs a reweighting; a compute- and retraining-matched comparison is absent.

reviewed_competitors.title: LESS: Selecting Influential Data for Targeted Instruction Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: LESS performs optimizer-aware low-rank gradient-similarity selection from a reusable datastore and reports that 5% selected instruction data can beat the full set on target skills, including transfer from smaller to larger models. Patterning instead uses expensive posterior covariances to target internal structure rather than downstream validation behavior and does not benchmark against LESS-like gradients.

reviewed_competitors.title: TRAK: Attributing Model Behavior at Scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: TRAK approximates training-data influence with random-projected after-kernel features from a handful of trained models across image, vision-language, and language settings. It attributes prediction-level behavior efficiently; Patterning targets posterior internal observables and uses the inverse response for control, but its small-model evidence costs roughly 500 training runs in forward-pass equivalents.

reviewed_competitors.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dziri et al. study the same dynamic-programming and multi-digit-multiplication regimes, model tasks as computation graphs, and attribute rapid degradation to linearized subgraph matching and limited systematic composition. The target instead fits a thresholded correlated-noise law, includes explicit algorithms to reduce discovery demands, and argues expressive incapacity is unnecessary; it does not reproduce Dziri et al.'s computation-graph or mechanistic analyses.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Illusion of Thinking: Understanding the Strengths and Limitations of Reasoning Models via the Lens of Problem Complexity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shojaee et al. manipulate puzzle complexity, inspect reasoning traces and token effort, and report low-, medium-, and high-complexity regimes culminating in complete collapse, including Tower of Hanoi. The target gives a randomized-label Tower algorithm and models the accuracy cliff as accumulated execution noise, but does not test the distinctive decline in reasoning effort or compare standard and reasoning models under matched inference compute.

reviewed_competitors.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nikankin et al. use causal circuit and neuron analysis to argue arithmetic answers arise from an unordered bag of input-pattern heuristics rather than a robust algorithm or memorization. The target posits a nearby ideal algorithm plus parameter noise and explains Pro's failure by possible algorithm switching, but measures no arithmetic circuit or heuristic neurons, so its latent mechanism remains observationally distinguishable only in future work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tokenization counts: the impact of tokenization on arithmetic in frontier LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh and Strouse show that number tokenization direction causally changes frontier-LLM arithmetic, that right-to-left comma separation improves performance, and that left-to-right errors follow systematic patterns. The target absorbs prompt/token effects into r and q and assumes a small effective alphabet, but never ablates tokenizer segmentation or tests whether its curve parameters predict the known directionality effect.

reviewed_competitors.title: Positional Description Matters for Transformers Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shen et al. causally modify positional encoding or arithmetic representation and train a 100M model that extrapolates far beyond standard multiplication/addition baselines. The target's polynomial prompt similarly exposes place information at inference time and reports one Flash gain, but offers no training intervention, positional ablation, or near-perfect extrapolating solver.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Numerical Precision Affects Arithmetical Reasoning Capabilities of LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feng et al. prove precision-dependent size lower bounds for tokenized iterated addition and multiplication and experimentally vary numerical precision. The target instead posits prompt/model-specific parameter noise and fits output accuracy on hosted models; without manipulating precision or measuring perturbations it cannot separate finite-precision limitations from its generic sigma parameter.
