title: Engram

reviewed_competitors.title: STEM: Scaling Transformers with Embedding Modules
reviewed_competitors.difference: STEM replaces selected SwiGLU up-projections with one vocabulary-indexed vector per token while retaining the contextual gate and down-projection. Engram instead retrieves hashed compressed suffix 2/3-grams through multiple heads, adds short convolution, injects at two internal layers, and explicitly reallocates a MoE sparse budget; STEM's lookup is collision-free at the token row level but has no multi-token key unless context enters through its gate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Embedding Layers in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct prior offloaded N-gram embedding scaler
reviewed_competitors.difference: SCONE learns contextual embeddings for frequent N-grams with a separate model, precomputes them, and serves them from off-accelerator memory at the input representation while keeping a 1B accelerator-resident model. Engram jointly trains hashed tables inside the language model, covers suffixes through collisions rather than a frequent exact dictionary, and places gated memory deeper to overlap transfer, but its training includes table communication and optimizer cost absent from an inference-only FLOP comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Over-Tokenized Transformer: Vocabulary is Generally Worth Scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Over-Tokenized Transformer decouples enlarged multi-gram input vocabulary from the output vocabulary and reports a log-linear input-vocabulary trend with no extra inference computation. Engram keeps the base tokenizer/output vocabulary, hashes compressed suffix N-grams into internal memory, and context-gates their contribution; this adds collision and transfer questions but avoids making multi-grams explicit input tokens.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory Layers at Scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: Berges et al. learn content-addressed key/value memory with top-k retrieval, scale it to 128B memory parameters and 1T pretraining tokens, and compare against matched dense and MoE systems. Engram uses deterministic N-gram addresses with no learned nearest-neighbor search, enabling prefetch and host lookup, but can retrieve only patterns represented by its local token suffix and hash/gate path.

reviewed_competitors.title: UltraMemV2: Memory Networks Scaling to 120B Parameters with Superior Long-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: UltraMemV2 puts learned memory in every Transformer block, uses single-projection value expansion and PEER-style FFN value processing, and reports parity with 8-expert MoE up to 120B total/2.5B active parameters plus dedicated long-context memorization gains. Engram retrieves fewer deterministic local N-gram rows at selected layers and reports host prefetch; its simpler lookup is predictable but less content-adaptive.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory Grafting: Scaling Language Model Pre-training via Offline Conditional Memory
reviewed_competitors.difference: Memory Grafting constructs exact longest-match N-gram values offline from frozen hidden states of a separate pretrained model and uses a hash-based Engram fallback. It directly targets the cost and under-training of learning huge Engram tables from scratch and reports 53.86 average versus 52.43 for vanilla Engram and 51.95 for MoE at 2.8B scale; Engram's values are jointly optimized but require the full pretraining budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Collision-Free Hot-Tier Extension for Engram-Style Conditional Memory: A Controlled Study of Training Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later direct negative-result and collision-control study
reviewed_competitors.difference: Engram-Nine adds a minimal-perfect-hash hot tier while retaining hashed cold lookup and, under iso parameters, finds that collision removal does not consistently improve validation loss; it also reports a hot-to-cold advantage flip and persistent gate preference for higher-loss hot routes. This directly tests collision/gating behavior that the target assumes multi-head hashing and context gating will manage but never stratifies.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond N-gram: Data-Aware X-GRAM Extraction for Efficient Embedding Parameter Scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: X-GRAM explicitly addresses Zipfian tail under-training, layer-demand heterogeneity, and redundant slot collapse with hybrid hashing, alias mixing, normalized SwiGLU ShortConv, and depth-aware injection into attention values and residuals. It reports up to +3.2 average over retrieval baselines with substantially smaller tables; Engram uses uniform multi-head hash tables and a scalar context gate without frequency-stratified evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tokenizer-Agnostic Engram Module
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tokenizer-Agnostic Engram replaces disjoint token-N-gram XOR hashes with polynomial hashing over byte-equivalent sequences in one joint space across N and reports comparable performance plus cross-tokenizer hash equivalence. The target's normalized token IDs are bound to one tokenizer and cannot reuse a trained table after retokenization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Embedding Layers in Language Models

reviewed_competitors.title: Over-Tokenized Transformer: Vocabulary is Generally Worth Scaling

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory Layers at Scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: Memory Layers at Scale use learned content-addressed key/value retrieval, complement dense FFNs, reach 128B memory parameters and 1T tokens, and compare with parameter/compute-matched MoE. STEM uses O(1) exact token indexing and replaces part of the FFN, making prefetch simpler but sacrificing semantic lookup across different tokens and depending on a tokenizer-specific row.

reviewed_competitors.title: UltraMemV2: Memory Networks Scaling to 120B Parameters with Superior Long-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: UltraMemV2 combines learned sparse retrieval in every block with PEER-style FFN value processing and reports parity with 8-expert MoE up to 120B total/2.5B active plus memorization and in-context-learning gains. reviewed_competitors.difference: DYNOTEARS jointly estimates contemporaneous and lagged linear DBN structure through a penalized score and smooth acyclicity constraint. reviewed_competitors.difference: Adaptive Transformer Programs extends RASP/Transformer Programs with more expressive categorical and numerical attention plus a smooth discrete reparameterization—the transition mechanism reused by the reviewed paper. It covers broader NLP/algorithmic evaluations; the reviewed method instead specializes functional roles and uses symbolic regression to obtain compact algebra over continuous scalars.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: OpenReview forum W8K8slZ73R, ICLR 2025 published paper

reviewed_competitors.title: Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tracr compiles human-written RASP into standard decoder-only Transformer weights, yielding exact known program ground truth and exposing superposition. The reviewed paper tackles the inverse learned-model-to-program direction but only after imposing a more restrictive scalar architecture; Tracr offers a natural testbed for measuring whether extraction is faithful.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thinking Like Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: RASP supplies the programming abstraction that maps attention and feed-forward computation to sequence-processing primitives and bounds layers/heads for tasks. The reviewed architecture inherits this decomposition but adds continuous scalar variables, annealed learned pointers, and empirical symbolic regression rather than starting from a written RASP specification.

reviewed_competitors.title: Finite State Automata Inside Transformers with Chain-of-Thought: A Mechanistic Study on State Tracking
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work identifies finite-state representations and circuits inside more ordinary Transformer+CoT models and tests noise, skipped steps, and length generalization, but does not emit a whole executable program. It provides stronger state-tracking/OOD diagnostics than the reviewed fixed-length benchmark and weaker end-to-end symbolic extraction.

reviewed_competitors.title: TracrBench: Generating Interpretability Testbeds with Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: TracrBench provides 121 human-validated RASP programs and compiled Transformer weights as interpretability ground truth, explicitly finding that even frontier LLMs generate many invalid RASP programs. The reviewed paper uses a smaller task benchmark without exact internal program ground truth; TracrBench could test extraction fidelity rather than only output accuracy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering Interpretable Algorithms by Decompiling Transformers to RASP
reviewed_competitors.difference: This subsequent ICML 2026 work faithfully reparameterizes trained small Transformers as RASP and uses causal interventions to select a sufficient subprogram, directly targeting ordinary trained models and length-generalizing tasks. The reviewed paper more easily supports continuous algebra because its architecture is discrete/scalar by design, but it cannot claim the same standard-Transformer decompilation scope.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explaining Attention with Program Synthesis
reviewed_competitors.difference: This subsequent method prompts an LLM to synthesize executable programs approximating attention heads in GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Llama-3B and validates programmatic replacement, scaling to ordinary language models but only component-level approximate behavior. The reviewed method assembles whole-task programs with far higher control, at the price of a purpose-built model and hand-coded router taxonomy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Validating Mechanistic Interpretations: An Axiomatic Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: Palumbo et al. define compositional axioms for approximate mechanistic interpretations and validate a Transformer 2-SAT interpretation, emphasizing fidelity criteria rather than code generation. Applying those axioms or formal replacement tests would strengthen the reviewed paper's unseparated task-correctness and model-fidelity claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Decomposition Polyhedra of Piecewise Linear Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Brandenburg, Grillo, and Hertrich characterize the polyhedron of convex CPWL decompositions and conditions for irreducible or minimal decompositions. This paper instead applies one nonminimal layerwise decomposition to pretrained networks and develops numerical attribution heuristics; it does not study decomposition complexity or uniqueness.

reviewed_competitors.title: CDiNN -Convex Difference Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: CDiNN already learns a target as the difference of two polyhedral convex networks and exploits DCA/linear programs for optimization. The present work's distinct contribution is post-hoc splitting and attribution of an arbitrary pretrained ReLU model, plus qualitative factual/counterfactual MNIST variants.

reviewed_competitors.title: Input Convex Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: ICNN constrains weights to make a scalar network convex in selected inputs for optimization-based inference and analyzes representational power. This paper combines two such monotone/convex streams to recover nonconvex pretrained functions and targets attribution rather than convex inference.

reviewed_competitors.title: Piecewise Linear Regression via a Difference of Convex Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Siahkamari and colleagues fit two max-affine convex functions directly with a DC seminorm, statistical risk analysis, and quadratic programming. This paper decomposes the exact function of an existing deep ReLU network and studies saliency, without statistical guarantees for the explanation maps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantus: An Explainable AI Toolkit for Responsible Evaluation of Neural Network Explanations and Beyond
reviewed_competitors.relationship: evaluation framework used by the paper
reviewed_competitors.difference: Quantus standardizes many faithfulness, localization, robustness, complexity, and randomization metrics and emphasizes that explanation quality is multi-dimensional. The present paper selects a subset and tunes layers/configurations against them, so its contribution is a method result inside that framework rather than a new evaluation protocol.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adebayo and colleagues introduce cascading and independent parameter/data randomization tests and show visually plausible methods can be model-independent. The present work performs only a last-three-FC-layer VGG perturbation and obtains a severe negative result for SplitLRP.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shortcomings of Top-Down Randomization-Based Sanity Checks for Evaluations of Deep Neural Network Explanations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: primary critique of a key diagnostic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Binder and colleagues show top-down randomization can reward uninformative maps and should not rank explanation methods by itself. The present paper cites that caveat but still makes strong model-dependence language from a partial top-down test; its faithfulness metrics therefore need to carry the substantive burden.

reviewed_competitors.title: Finer-CAM: Spotting the Difference Reveals Finer Details for Visual Explanation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Finer-CAM improves class-discriminative detail by contrasting the target logit with similar classes and supports multimodal models without doubling every network stream. SplitCAM instead changes the internal representation through DC splitting and tests ordinary ImageNet object localization, but incurs much larger runtime and is not evaluated on fine-grained or multimodal tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Meta-Learning Strategies through Value Maximization in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: This earlier work by overlapping authors already optimizes discounted cumulative performance minus control effort using tractable average learning dynamics and studies curricula and resource allocation; the present paper's narrow addition is the scalar-rate closed form and episodic terminal-performance approximation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Protocols for Continual Learning via Statistical Physics and Control Theory
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mori and colleagues optimize task-selection protocols from exact low-dimensional dynamics to balance current performance and forgetting; this paper controls scalar learning speed and cumulative effort, without multi-task forgetting dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Statistical Physics Framework for Optimal Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mignacco and Mori optimize curricula, dropout, and noise protocols through order-parameter dynamics for final generalization objectives; the present paper derives a simpler architecture-agnostic feedback law for a cumulative performance-minus-rate-cost objective, conditioned on terminal performance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bilevel Programming for Hyperparameter Optimization and Meta-Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bilevel programming optimizes validation-defined outer objectives through approximate inner dynamics and provides convergence conditions for the approximation; the present work targets a cumulative normative utility and avoids full trajectory differentiation only in the undiscounted feedback derivation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient-based Hyperparameter Optimization through Reversible Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reversible learning differentiates exact cross-validation performance through all SGD-with-momentum steps and can optimize thousands of rate and momentum values; the present paper trades that expensive offline calculation for a two-scalar feedback rule under a narrower continuous-time objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Nonstochastic Control Approach to Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen and Hazan cast learning rate, momentum, and preconditioner selection as online nonstochastic control and obtain regret to the best offline method across problem sequences; the present controller instead solves one finite episode with known-form gradient-flow dynamics and an effort utility.

reviewed_competitors.title: AutoLRS: Automatic Learning-Rate Schedule by Bayesian Optimization on the Fly
reviewed_competitors.difference: AutoLRS forecasts validation loss for candidate rates with Bayesian optimization and reports ResNet, Transformer, and BERT speedups; this paper predicts only terminal performance and applies an analytic effort controller, but lacks comparable large-network evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaLRS: Loss-Guided Adaptive Learning Rate Search for Efficient Foundation Model Pretraining
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaLRS searches online using observed loss-descent velocity and reports LLM and VLM transfer across sizes and schedulers; the present paper's controller optimizes cumulative performance minus effort through an expected-terminal-performance signal and is not validated at foundation-model scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Theory of Optimal Learning Rate Schedules and Scaling Laws for a Random Feature Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon and Mori derive horizon-, task-spectrum-, and phase-dependent schedules for minimizing loss, jointly study batch and momentum, and test ResNet and GPT-2 regimes; this paper instead optimizes cumulative reward with an explicit effort penalty and emphasizes biological interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Do Near-Optimal Learning Rate Schedules Look Like?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Naganuma and colleagues separate shape from base rate and search reusable finite-horizon schedules across linear regression, CIFAR-10, and WikiText-103; this paper supplies a per-trajectory feedback policy for a different cumulative-effort objective and does not search conventional schedule families.

reviewed_competitors.title: Round and Round We Go! What Makes Rotary Positional Encodings Useful?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barbero et al. already show that Gemma uses high RoPE frequencies to construct positional attention and low frequencies for semantics, and propose p-RoPE. The present paper extends this line to thresholded fixed-offset heads across three models, random-token controls, Q/K low-rank origins, large offsets, and a staged ICL theorem, while inheriting the central frequency-specialization mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rotary Offset Features in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jonasson studies large rotary offset features in queries and keys across layers and architectures and derives frequency/angle bounds. The present paper focuses on attention-map diagonals, prompt invariance, rank-one composition, and gradient-based emergence rather than bounding individual rotary feature activations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Massive Values in Self-Attention Modules are the Key to Contextual Knowledge Understanding
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jin et al. trace concentrated massive Q/K values to RoPE and connect their removal or quantization to contextual-knowledge behavior. This paper instead explains fixed relative-offset attention through low-rank directions and frequency interference, but does not causally evaluate downstream behavior for the detected heads.

reviewed_competitors.title: DoPE: Denoising Rotary Position Embedding
reviewed_competitors.difference: DoPE identifies outlier frequency bands through truncated matrix entropy and reparameterizes them for training-free long-context extrapolation. The slash-pattern paper groups fixed coordinate bands and studies existing-head geometry; it neither optimizes extrapolation nor uses an entropy-selected intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Resonance RoPE: Improving Context Length Generalization of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Resonance RoPE modifies interpolated phases to improve train-short-test-long position recognition and downstream long-context performance. The present paper tests random-token invariance at fixed context length and explains pretrained offset heads, not position extrapolation or phase-resonance scaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. prove gradient-flow emergence of generalized induction heads on n-gram Markov data in a two-attention-layer model with relative position embeddings, multi-head softmax attention, normalization, and an MLP. The present theorem isolates a RoPE-created offset copier in a sparser staged regression model and connects it to pretrained slash geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
reviewed_competitors.difference: Olsson et al. supply causal evidence in small attention-only models and correlational evidence in larger models that induction heads accompany in-context learning. The present paper targets the preceding fixed-offset slash component, attributes it to RoPE frequency alignment, and proves it only in a stylized regression setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: LeRoPE: Learnable RoPE Frequencies Improve Language Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: LeRoPE, released after the reviewed paper, directly learns RoPE frequencies and evaluates language-model quality rather than diagnosing fixed bands after training. It makes the slash paper's static high/medium/low intervention less complete as a current design treatment, while not replacing its head-level low-rank and emergence analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Spectral Condition for Feature Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang, Simon, and Bernstein derive the sqrt(fan-out/fan-in) spectral scaling of weights and updates and connect it to maximal-update parametrization. SSO turns that condition into an explicit fixed-radius optimizer with retraction and a tangent matrix-sign step; the scaling law itself is inherited rather than novel.

reviewed_competitors.title: Old Optimizer, New Norm: An Anthology
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bernstein and Newhouse recast Adam, Shampoo, and related updates as steepest descent under tensor-role-specific norms and motivate modular optimizer geometry. SSO specializes this view to the spectral norm while additionally constraining the current weights to a sphere.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Deep Learning Models with Norm-Constrained LMOs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pethick et al. develop stochastic norm-ball linear-minimization-oracle methods, including Scion, with architecture-aware norms and model-size hyperparameter transfer. The SSO paper itself describes MuonSphere as similar to Scion; its narrower addition is simultaneous top-spectral-radius control and a tangent lambda solver at larger LLM scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training
reviewed_competitors.relationship: primary empirical baseline and systems predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. scale Muon to a 3B/16B MoE trained on 5.7T tokens using weight decay, per-parameter update scaling, and distributed implementation. SSO explicitly fixes weight spectral radii and reports smaller 100B-token experiments, while incurring a root-solver overhead and changing hidden-weight decay.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Polar Express: Optimal Matrix Sign Methods and Their Application to the Muon Algorithm
reviewed_competitors.difference: Amsel et al. design GPU-friendly, minimax polynomial polar iterations and test them inside Muon. SSO uses Polar Express coefficients as a subroutine but adds repeated lambda-dependent matrix signs, power iteration, module sharding, and sphere retraction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon Optimizes Under Spectral Norm Constraints
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct theoretical challenge to the half-aligned framing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen, Li, and Liu analyze Muon with decoupled weight decay as implicitly solving a spectral-norm-constrained optimization problem through the Lion-K framework. SSO enforces an explicit per-step target-radius equality, but this prior result narrows the claim that Muon leaves weights wholly unconstrained or that explicit sphere geometry is the unique constrained interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Extending muP: Spectral Conditions for Feature Learning Across Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Released after SSO, Gupta et al. derive and empirically test spectral muP rules for AdamW, ADOPT, LAMB, Sophia, Shampoo, and Muon, including width and depth transfer. This weakens SSO's current claim to uniquely preserve muP learning-rate transfer, while not supplying its explicit sphere retraction or tangent solver.

reviewed_competitors.title: Enhancing LLM Training via Spectral Clipping
reviewed_competitors.difference: SPECTRA applies efficient pre/post spectral clipping to several optimizers, interprets post-clipping through composite Frank-Wolfe, and reports uniform validation-loss improvements without forcing every weight to a fixed-radius equality. It is a lower-commitment current alternative to SSO's nonconvex sphere and scalar root search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shape of Thought: When Distribution Matters More than Correctness in Reasoning Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest current conceptual competitor argues that the distributional match of synthetic reasoning traces can matter more than final-answer correctness and tests model-generated, human, paraphrased-human, and deliberately corrupted traces across several domains and 1.5B-9B models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shape of Thought directly manipulates trace distribution and correctness without a molecular or attention-energy theory. The reviewed paper offers a specific four-state transition statistic, teacher-mixture conflict study, and transition-guided synthesis, but its semantic-isomer thesis overlaps substantially with this distribution-first account and uses a coarser operational measure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling the Key Factors for Distilling Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A broad controlled CoT-distillation study of granularity, format, and teacher choice using four teachers, seven students, and seven math/commonsense datasets; it independently finds that stronger teachers do not always produce stronger students.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The ACL study isolates conventional data factors and emphasizes student-dependent granularity/diversity/complexity. The reviewed paper proposes behavior-transition topology and Mole-Syn, but its full-table negative teacher results are consistent with rather than prior to this established teacher-student compatibility finding.

reviewed_competitors.title: OpenThoughts: Data Recipes for Reasoning Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct reasoning-data-recipe competitor that performs more than one thousand controlled pipeline experiments and scales verified QwQ-32B traces to a 1.2M-example OpenThoughts3 dataset and 7B model.
reviewed_competitors.difference: OpenThoughts emphasizes source curation, verification, scaling, and benchmark performance and supplies the corpus sampled by the reviewed paper. Mole-Syn instead compresses 20K teacher traces into a behavior controller and delegates surface realization to weak models; it is cheaper in generated-data scale but is not compared with OpenThoughts' controlled filtering recipes.

reviewed_competitors.title: LIMO: Less is More for Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A data-efficient reasoning-SFT competitor showing that a carefully selected small set of demonstrations can elicit strong mathematical reasoning from a capable pretrained model.
reviewed_competitors.difference: LIMO attributes gains to knowledge already present in pretraining plus high-quality cognitive templates and uses orders of magnitude fewer samples; the reviewed paper trains on 20K-35K traces and attributes learnability to matched transition topology. A direct quality-versus-transition-matching comparison is absent.

reviewed_competitors.title: s1: Simple test-time scaling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct small-data Long-CoT and test-time-control competitor that curates 1,000 difficult, diverse, high-quality traces and uses budget forcing to extend or truncate reasoning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: s1 validates data difficulty/diversity/quality and directly controls thinking length; Mole-Syn controls a sampled behavior sequence and later shows length alone is insufficient. The reviewed paper covers more student/teacher combinations but does not benchmark against the far smaller s1K recipe or budget forcing.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: EMNLP 2025 official ACL Anthology edition, pages 20275-20321, 4-9 November 2025

reviewed_competitors.title: 1.4 Million Open-Source Distilled Reasoning Dataset to Empower Large Language Model Training
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A large-scale direct-distillation competitor that cleans and verifies 1.4M reasoning traces with answer checks, code tests, or reward-model filtering and reports strong Qwen-32B/72B students.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The 1.4M dataset transfers verified teacher outputs at scale; Mole-Syn transfers a coarse transition controller and uses weak generators at much smaller scale. The reviewed paper's novelty lies in structural compression/synthesis, but it does not compare cost, contamination control, or accuracy against this verified-scale alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Continuous Autoregressive Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest pre-existing continuous-AR competitor replaces discrete next-token prediction with continuous next-vector prediction and develops a likelihood-free training/sampling framework.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CALM compresses K-token chunks through a learned autoencoder and reduces the number of generative steps, targeting performance-compute efficiency. Projected AR predicts one token embedding at a time, uses nearest-neighbor projection, preserves streaming, and studies a mutable causal suffix; its novelty is token-level delayed commitment rather than continuous AR in general.

reviewed_competitors.title: Soft-Masked Diffusion Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A particularly close current competitor that retains predictive information before commitment by blending a retained mask embedding with top-k predicted token embeddings from the previous denoising step.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Soft-Masked DLM refines masks across a globally revisable diffusion sequence and demonstrates perplexity, MAUVE, and coding gains at 169M and 7B; Projected AR refines a strictly causal local suffix and commits left-to-right. Both exploit continuous embedding mixtures before discrete resolution, so the reviewed paper's distinct contribution is the streaming AR interface, not the general idea of soft pre-commitment token state.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, revised 2 March 2026; ICLR 2026 accepted version

reviewed_competitors.title: TiDAR: Think in Diffusion, Talk in Autoregression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A hybrid competitor that keeps autoregressive final output while using diffusion-style parallel drafting within one structured-attention forward pass.
reviewed_competitors.difference: TiDAR drafts discrete sequence hypotheses and verifies/samples AR outputs, targeting measured throughput and AR-level quality at 1.5B/8B with 4.71x-5.91x speedups. Projected AR instead maintains token embeddings as the generative state and reports no throughput or standard task quality; it offers a different continuous control surface but much weaker efficiency validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Coconut is an established continuous-state language-model interface that feeds hidden states back as future input embeddings to defer discrete reasoning commitments and represent multiple possible next reasoning steps.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Coconut uses continuous states only as an internal reasoning substrate and eventually emits ordinary tokens; Projected AR makes continuous prediction the primary interface for every output token and projects each to the vocabulary. Coconut evaluates reasoning accuracy/search, whereas the reviewed paper evaluates open-ended surface statistics.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v3, revised 3 November 2025; COLM 2025 accepted version

reviewed_competitors.title: Simple and Effective Masked Diffusion Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A strong alternative to strict next-token AR that iteratively resolves masked discrete states, supports arbitrary-length semi-autoregressive generation, and approaches AR perplexity.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Masked diffusion revises a broader sequence in parallel and trains a Rao-Blackwellized masked-token objective; Projected AR keeps an immutable prefix, continuous token vectors, and nearest-neighbor commitment. The competitor has language-modeling benchmarks and likelihood evaluation that the reviewed empirical section lacks.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, revised 10 November 2024; NeurIPS 2024 version

reviewed_competitors.title: Dream 7B: Diffusion Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A 7B discrete-diffusion alternative that performs iterative full-sequence refinement, arbitrary-order generation, infilling, and quality-speed control across general, math, and code tasks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dream gives up strict streaming and immutable prefixes for global planning and revisability, while Projected AR restricts refinement to a causal local suffix. Dream evaluates broad capabilities at larger scale; Projected AR's advantage is streaming-compatible local commitment, not demonstrated task quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: DiffuCoder: Understanding and Improving Masked Diffusion Models for Code Generation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A 7B alternative-generation study that analyzes refinement order and trains a masked diffusion code model on 130B tokens, including diffusion-native RL and quantitative coding benchmarks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DiffuCoder globally denoises discrete masks and can choose causal or noncausal generation order; Projected AR uses a Granite code backbone but evaluates general web continuations through a strictly causal continuous suffix. DiffuCoder provides task accuracy and large-scale training evidence, while Projected AR provides token-embedding geometry and K=1 interface ablations.

The present work cites and operationalizes that perspective in a specific end-to-end computation, adding sparse tilings, causal count patches, attention-head twists, and adversarial delimiters rather than originating the manifold hypothesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pre-trained Large Language Models Use Fourier Features to Compute Addition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. show Fourier-sparse number features with complementary MLP/attention roles in addition. The present paper studies non-numeric character position learned from natural text and relates ringing to low-rank Fourier structure, while its boundary comparison uses QK offset alignment rather than arithmetic addition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Addition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kantamneni and Tegmark causally identify generalized helices and a Clock addition algorithm in three mid-sized LLMs. The present paper finds a related rippled/helical scalar geometry for character counting in one model and contributes a naturalistic line-boundary circuit rather than the first causal manipulation of helical numeric representations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding In-context Learning of Addition via Activation Subspaces
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu et al. localize addition ICL to a few attention heads and six-dimensional periodic/magnitude subspaces with causal analysis. The present paper likewise decomposes low-dimensional head computations but targets perceptual character counting, uses sparse crosscoder features for discovery, and emphasizes QK twisting and distributed newline-sink offsets.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Need Inductive Biases to Count Inductively
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chang and Bisk compare architectures and positional biases on train-short/test-long counting, finding Transformers rely on positional embeddings for OOD counting. The present work reverse engineers an approximate character counter learned in pretraining, but does not test inductive extrapolation beyond its 15-150 width regime or across architectures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Length Representations in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Moon et al. study hidden units and attention mechanisms that represent and causally control requested output sequence length. The present paper instead tracks within-line character position and implicit document width, contributing a finer end-to-end linebreak mechanism while leaving broader output-length control outside scope.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Description Length of Deep Learning models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Blier and Ollivier already apply variational and incremental/prequential codes to deep networks and show that learning-curve-based codes can compress data well. EDL reuses the online code but subtracts the achieved final test codelength to summarize absorbed predictive improvement; the prequential neural-network communication mechanism is prior work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Information-Theoretic Probing with Minimum Description Length
reviewed_competitors.difference: Voita and Titov use online and variational MDL to measure how efficiently pretrained representations support label prediction, incorporating both final quality and learning effort. EDL targets fine-tuning trajectories and subtracts a final test-loss floor, but its operational framing of teaching labels with an evolving predictor has this direct antecedent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evaluating representations by the complexity of learning low-loss predictors
reviewed_competitors.difference: Whitney et al. introduce Surplus Description Length and epsilon sample complexity from loss-data curves to quantify data needed to recover low-loss predictors. EDL is algebraically the same prequential area referenced to the achieved finite-data test loss rather than the optimal loss; computability improves, while algorithm and checkpoint dependence increase.

reviewed_competitors.title: Small Data, Big Decisions: Model Selection in the Small-Data Regime
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bornschein et al. estimate neural-network MDL in small-data regimes and use it for principled model selection. EDL instead fixes an algorithm/model and interprets the gap to its final test floor as learned predictive information, without demonstrating model-selection performance or minimizing over candidate codes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Information-theoretic analysis of generalization capability of learning algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu and Raginsky derive generalization bounds using mutual information between training data and the learned hypothesis. EDL is easier to compute from loss logs but is not mutual information and gives only a trajectory identity under its assumptions; claims about information stored in weights should be distinguished from this rigorous antecedent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning About Generalization via Conditional Mutual Information
reviewed_competitors.difference: Steinke and Zakynthinou use conditional mutual information to unify compression, stability, privacy, VC, and other generalization arguments. Their measure obeys information inequalities that the EDL hypothesis-collapse discussion violates; EDL offers a simple operational loss statistic but not an equivalent information-theoretic bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning and Occam's Razor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Elmoznino et al. directly connect next-token in-context learning loss to prequential coding and implicit model complexity. EDL studies parameter-updating fine-tuning and adds a final-test-floor subtraction plus teaching/elicitation interpretation, but the broader claim that sequential prediction loss operationalizes learned-rule complexity is not unique.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Blake et al. combine muP with unit scaling so activations, weights, and gradients start near unit scale, default hyperparameters are near-optimal, and FP8 training works out of the box, with loss equal to or below comparable muP models. LRMs instead learn scales from data and encounter bfloat16 symmetry drift requiring decay; no FP8, matched-sweep, or larger-scale u-muP comparison is supplied.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Salimans and Kingma explicitly decouple each weight vector's learned magnitude g from a normalized direction v/||v|| to improve conditioning and convergence without batch dependence. LRMs retain an unnormalized decayed W and multiply global or row/column factors to explain a noise-WD mechanism in LLMs; the new paper cites but does not experimentally compare this direct learned-norm baseline.

Learnable Multipliers frames bad scale as a lazy/feature-learning issue and learns factors, but provides no depth-transfer theorem, actual training-efficiency metric, or CompleteP baseline and remains confined to a 0.5B hybrid model.

The present paper shows LRMs add about 1.10 benchmark points to Muon at 0.5B, but it does not test whether the gain survives Muon's full large-scale recipe or compare quality per FLOP.

The present note gives a procedural BPE definition and an unproved Zipf/IID interpretation; it neither connects its entropy to compression utility nor addresses the formal counting variants.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Predictive V-information/V-entropy already makes information relative to a constrained predictive family and shows familiar information laws can fail. reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring Information Transfer in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work uses prequential coding to quantify information transfer from representations and models. reviewed_competitors.difference: Surrogate description length evaluates how quickly low-loss task predictors can be learned from a representation. It is downstream-task conditional and rewards lower learning complexity, whereas the target interprets a larger learned dataset code as more structural information and separately accounts for residual uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Modeling Is Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Delétang et al. evaluate language models as compressors for text, images, and audio and establish broad empirical links between prediction and compression. They measure total compression under pretrained models, not a time-bounded separation between program/training cost and irreducible data entropy; their cross-modal results also underscore representation-normalization issues for the target's modality claims.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: same-line theoretical competitor connecting compute, quantization, information, and generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work proves generalization behavior for compute-optimal language models through information/precision arguments. It concerns trained-model generalization under scaling rather than an intrinsic bounded-observer decomposition of a data distribution, but it supplies a more direct generalization target than treating high epiplexity as broadly useful.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Size of Teachers as a Measure of Data Complexity: PAC-Bayes Excess Risk Bounds and Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Teacher size near a target risk is used as a task-specific data-complexity measure with PAC-Bayes excess-risk bounds and scaling laws. The target instead counts a bounded generative/predictive program and residual log loss, including a training-replay code; it offers a structural/random split but lacks the competitor's direct risk-bound interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Curve Theory
reviewed_competitors.relationship: theoretical competitor for interpreting and extrapolating learning curves
reviewed_competitors.difference: Viering and Loog study mechanisms and variability that can generate diverse learning-curve shapes. That work does not propose an information decomposition, but it cautions against treating finite power-law curves as a uniquely identified structural code and supplies alternative explanations for the target's scaling extrapolations.

It narrows any current claim that the target uniquely introduces learnable structural information; the target remains earlier and distinctive in its formal bounded-program MDL split, cryptographic proofs, and requential coding construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States
reviewed_competitors.difference: TTT establishes the broader fast-weight recipe of making the recurrent state a model updated by a self-supervised gradient step on every test sequence. Trellis specializes that recipe to two fixed-slot KV regressors, a shared slot target, and explicit state decay.

reviewed_competitors.title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: Titans updates a deep neural long-term memory with per-token surprise, momentum, and retention and combines it with local attention. Trellis instead learns two shallow fixed-slot KV compressors with a shared latent code and no momentum, making it closer to bounded attention than to Titans' deep memory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gated DeltaNet provides state-dependent targeted replacement plus adaptive forgetting in a single fixed matrix state with an exact hardware-efficient algorithm. Trellis cascades two nonlinear slot regressors and uses a stale-gradient approximation, trading more complex compression for stronger reported perplexity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Test-time regression: a unifying framework for designing sequence models with associative memory
reviewed_competitors.difference: Test-time regression formalizes memorization as weighted regression and derives attention and online learners from the regressor, weights, and optimizer choices. Trellis is a concrete two-stage bounded regressor, so regression-based associative memory is prior while its cascade and shared slot code are more specific.

reviewed_competitors.title: ATLAS: Learning to Optimally Memorize the Context at Test Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: ATLAS publicly precedes the current Trellis record and uses a gated window of associations, lifted features, deep memory, and Muon-style updates. Trellis uses one-token online descent in a two-pass fixed-slot KV compressor; its simpler target is bounded attention rather than context-window refitting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gated DeltaNet-2: Decoupling Erase and Write in Linear Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gated DeltaNet-2 separately controls channel-wise erasure and writing and reports matched 1.3B/100B evidence. It remains a single linear-attention state rather than Trellis's nonlinear two-pass slot compression, but directly targets the retention failure Trellis observes.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Hyper-Connections expands and dynamically mixes multiple residual streams to improve depth-wise information flow. reviewed_competitors.difference: mHC constrains expanded connection matrices to restore identity mapping and adds systems optimization for scale. DDL enforces an identity limit through a scalar erase/write gate and edits one normalized feature direction, with much smaller-scale evidence.

reviewed_competitors.difference: RMT replaces the vector residual stream with an outer-product memory matrix and directly studies scaling residual capacity independently of model compute. reviewed_competitors.difference: LAuReL learns lightweight augmented residual pathways as near-drop-in replacements and reports vision and billion-parameter language results. reviewed_competitors.difference: MUDDFormer generates token-dependent dense connections separately for query, key, value, and residual streams across depth. reviewed_competitors.title: DenseFormer: Enhancing Information Flow in Transformers via Depth Weighted Averaging
reviewed_competitors.difference: DenseFormer learns depth-weighted averages of current and earlier representations to reuse information across layers. DDL instead edits the current persistent state toward a learned readout target and, in expanded form, increases storage channels rather than explicitly averaging past layer outputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Sequence-to-Sequence Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alpha-entmax supplies a tunable family between softmax and sparsemax while preserving normalized sparse distributions. reviewed_competitors.title: DuoAttention: Efficient Long-Context LLM Inference with Retrieval and Streaming Heads
reviewed_competitors.difference: DuoAttention separates retrieval and streaming heads and keeps sinks inside a memory-efficient inference policy, with measured latency and cache savings. reviewed_competitors.title: Spectrum Dependent Learning Curves in Kernel Regression and Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon, Canatar, and Pehlevan already derive approximate mode-resolved KRR learning curves using Gaussian-process and replica methods, predict successive acquisition of higher spectral modes, and validate on synthetic data, MNIST, NTK regression, and wide networks. Eigenlearning largely recovers the same omniscient risk expression but contributes the exact learnability trace law, a shorter cavity-style derivation, a more compact variable choice, predictor-covariance formulas, and new applications.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral Bias and Task-Model Alignment Explain Generalization in Kernel Regression and Infinitely Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Canatar, Bordelon, and Pehlevan use the replica method to express KRR generalization through kernel eigenvalues, target coefficients, noise, sample count, and an implicit effective regularization; they already analyze spectral bias, task-model alignment, and nonmonotonic learning curves on real and synthetic data. The reviewed paper's novelty is therefore not the underlying risk law but its exact conserved-overlap interpretation, simplified derivation and notation, covariance expression, and downstream vignettes.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v6 (2022-02-04), full primary PDF and record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Kernel Alignment Risk Estimator: Risk Prediction from Training Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jacot et al. derive a signal-capture threshold and predictor mean/variance using finite-size random-matrix analysis, then construct KARE, a risk estimator computed from the training Gram matrix and labels without knowing the population eigensystem or target coefficients. Eigenlearning offers a more transparent omniscient formula and exact finite-sample conservation identity, but it is less directly deployable for kernel selection and its approximate covariance differs by a target-dependent order-1/n term discussed in Appendix A.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1 (2020-06-17), full primary PDF and record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Curves for SGD on Structured Features
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon and Pehlevan derive expected test-loss dynamics for stochastic gradient descent from feature second and fourth moments, including batch-size, learning-rate, compute-budget, and fixed-training-set effects, and test the theory on MNIST and CIFAR-10. That work treats optimizer dynamics directly, whereas eigenlearning studies the fitted KRR solution and represents time only indirectly through a ridge proxy; it therefore covers important minibatch and trajectory effects absent from the reviewed framework.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v5 (2022-03-15), full primary PDF and record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Failure and success of the spectral bias prediction for Kernel Ridge Regression: the case of low-dimensional data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tomasini, Sclocchi, and Wyart rigorously and numerically show that the Gaussian/self-averaging spectral-bias prediction can fail for low-dimensional, nonuniform Laplace-kernel classification at sufficiently small ridge: predictor fluctuations persist near a low-density decision boundary and the ridgeless learning-curve exponent can be wrong outside high dimension. This does not challenge eigenlearning's exact trace conservation, but it sharply limits the universality of its approximate risk and covariance equations.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 (2022-02-16), full primary PDF and record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign, Tempered, or Catastrophic: A Taxonomy of Overfitting

reviewed_competitors.difference: CPR maximizes final-classifier entropy to promote wide minima and applies the patch across several regularization-based CL methods. GRACE distributes entropy terms across intermediate heads and replay, but its actual positive raw-entropy penalty minimizes entropy and its wide-minimum claim is not measured, making the sign-level distinction central.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uncertainty-based Continual Learning with Adaptive Regularization
reviewed_competitors.difference: UCL performs genuine variational Bayesian continual learning and derives node-wise uncertainty regularizers that freeze important old parameters while preserving plasticity. GRACE uses predictive entropy and an empirical z-score rule instead of weight uncertainty; its simpler replay integration is practical, but the Bayesian-inference novelty language is much weaker than UCL's executed posterior objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving Plasticity in Online Continual Learning via Collaborative Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: CCL explicitly targets online underfitting and introduces an entropy-reducing distillation chain from less confident to more confident predictions, with a quantitative stability-plasticity analysis. GRACE instead uses multiple depths as feedback units; CCL is cited but not included as a full method baseline, leaving an important entropy/plasticity comparator absent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving the Trainability of Deep Neural Networks through Layerwise Batch-Entropy Regularization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This prior work explicitly regularizes information flow at every hidden layer and studies trainability across very deep CNNs, residual networks, autoencoders, and transformers. It is not continual learning, but it narrows GRACE's layerwise-entropy novelty and offers direct trainability analyses missing from the continual benchmark narrative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Equi-angular Representations for Online Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: EARL also frames online continual learning as an underfitting problem but induces a fixed equiangular representation geometry and evaluates disjoint plus boundary-free streams through ImageNet-1K. GRACE uses adaptive head entropy on smaller task-bounded datasets and omits this strong underfitting-oriented baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Online-LoRA: Task-Free Online Continual Learning via Low Rank Adaptation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Online-LoRA adapts pretrained ViTs without replay under unknown gradual task boundaries and consolidates parameters from detected distribution shifts. GRACE beats its adapted CUB-200 table result but trains with explicit tasks, replay, and historical validation; this is not an apples-to-apples demonstration of superior task-free continual learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Enhancing Online Continual Learning with Plug-and-Play State Space Model and Class-Conditional Mixture of Discretization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This CVPR 2025 method uses class-conditional state-space routing and contrastive discretization to balance stability and plasticity and plugs into several OCL learners on the same CIFAR/Tiny-ImageNet family. It predates GRACE but is absent from the comparison, so the state-of-the-art claim does not cover a current strong competitor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Layers Matter: Why Continual Learning Regularization Should Be Layer-Adaptive
reviewed_competitors.difference: This subsequent analysis derives layer sensitivity from top Hessian eigenvalues, proves limits of diagonal-Fisher summaries, and adapts EWC/SLCA by protecting early layers more strongly. GRACE uses cheap online entropy and probe-accuracy signals instead of curvature; the later work provides a clearer theorem-to-algorithm link and a competing direction that need not equalize head uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.difference: K-FAC approximates the Fisher with Kronecker factors built from activations and backpropagated derivatives, then preconditions parameter updates toward natural-gradient geometry. It addresses cross-sample/layer curvature without changing the forward function, at higher cost; Bird instead proposes almost-free structural maps but only exactly aligns a restricted local Euclidean activation criterion.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Does Batch Normalization Help Optimization?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Santurkar et al. reject internal-covariate-shift as the main explanation and link BatchNorm to a smoother loss landscape and more predictive gradients using broad experiments. Bird instead proposes local activation-update scaling as a mechanism and derives new maps, but does not compare the two explanations through smoothness or mediation measurements.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond BatchNorm: Towards a Unified Understanding of Normalization in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lubana et al. analyze forward signal diversity, exponential activation growth, and gradient instability across BatchNorm, LayerNorm, GroupNorm, and InstanceNorm in deep residual networks. Bird offers a distinct induced-update geometry and a new affine map, but its single-layer theory explicitly excludes residual paths and its empirical scope is much narrower.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers without Normalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dynamic Tanh replaces normalization with a learned bounded elementwise map and matches or exceeds norms across vision, language, speech, diffusion, and genomic transformers. Like Bird, it supports an activation-function view of normalization without relying on scale invariance, but it predates the affine-divergence paper, includes learned scales, and supplies far broader modern-architecture evidence without the claimed update-alignment derivation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm
reviewed_competitors.difference: Large et al. recursively define a natural norm for a module tree and normalize any optimizer's updates so learning rates transfer across width and depth in ResMLPs, ResNets, and GPT. Bird normalizes the input-dependent forward map to target a local activation step; Modula keeps the architecture intact, handles composition and residual structure explicitly, and focuses on scalable update magnitudes rather than per-sample identity alignment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Root Mean Square Layer Normalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct normalization baseline and theoretical prior
reviewed_competitors.difference: RMSNorm removes mean centering while retaining learned gain, sqrt(n) scaling, rescaling invariance, and implicit learning-rate adaptation, with experiments across multiple tasks and architectures. Bird's norm-like equation is parameterless unit L2 normalization and its affine-like alternative preserves radial information, but its experiments handicap the published RMSNorm form by deleting learned scaling.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Favero, Sclocchi, and Wyart were publicly submitted one day earlier and independently report the same core law tau_mem proportional to dataset size, the competition between generalization and memorization times, early-stopping guidance, and a phase diagram across image and language diffusion. The present paper adds a random-feature two-bulk spectral analysis, U-Net width scaling, full-batch and Adam controls, and Gaussian-mixture checks, so the dataset-linear headline is not uniquely novel.

reviewed_competitors.title: Denoising Score Matching with Random Features: Insights on Diffusion Models from Precise Learning Curves
reviewed_competitors.difference: George, Veiga, and Macris derive asymptotically precise train/test learning curves and generalization-memorization regimes for random-feature denoising score matching as functions of sample, feature, and noise-sample ratios. The present paper starts from that random-feature setting but resolves finite gradient-flow time and interprets separated spectral bulks as tau_gen and tau_mem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Taking a Big Step: Large Learning Rates in Denoising Score Matching Prevent Memorization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu, Marion, Biau, and Boyer also make irregularity of the small-noise empirical score central, but prove that sufficiently large SGD steps cannot stably approach arbitrarily small excess risk in a one-dimensional two-layer setting. The present paper instead studies finite training duration and slow spectral modes, mostly at a fixed small learning rate, so learning-rate regularization and early stopping are distinct but interacting mechanisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memorization and Regularization in Generative Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baptista et al. analyze why the empirical score produces memorization in conditioned and unconditioned diffusion and numerically study Tikhonov, consistency, underparameterization, and early-stopping regularizers. The present paper's added claim is the quantitative dataset-linear delay and its random-feature spectral mechanism, not the general proposition that early stopping avoids the empirical minimizer.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Generalization Properties of Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. provide training-dynamics-dependent early-stopping generalization bounds polynomial in dataset size and model capacity, including a mode-shift analysis. The present paper focuses on the onset of sample reproduction, empirical time collapse, and a solvable random-feature spectrum rather than a generalization-gap upper bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization in diffusion models arises from geometry-adaptive harmonic representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kadkhodaie et al. attribute non-memorizing diffusion to architecture-aligned harmonic shrinkage and show score agreement across disjoint training subsets above a data threshold. The present paper explicitly separates that architectural phase from a finite-time dynamical phase that can exist even when the architecture can eventually memorize.

reviewed_competitors.title: An analytic theory of creativity in convolutional diffusion models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kamb and Ganguli explain creativity through locality and equivariance, deriving local-score machines that predict convolutional diffusion outputs. Their mechanism constrains the converged function class; the present paper explains why an expressive class can temporarily approximate population structure before learning dataset-specific detail.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Memorization in Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gu et al. define effective model memorization and map how dataset size, distribution, architecture, and training choices affect approximation to the memorizing optimum, including random-label conditioning. The present work concentrates on the temporal onset law and offers spectral dynamics rather than a broad factor survey.

reviewed_competitors.title: Progressive Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Progressive neural networks freeze one column per learned task and add a new column with lateral transfer, making retention structural at growing capacity. Parity-MTF likewise buys exact retention with task-specific parameters, but shares a frozen middle scaffold and stores about 67% of a model per task; it should be compared directly on transfer, routing, and memory rather than characterized as the opposite of expansion.

reviewed_competitors.title: PackNet: Adding Multiple Tasks to a Single Network by Iterative Pruning
reviewed_competitors.difference: PackNet iteratively prunes and fixes weights so several tasks occupy disjoint subsets of one network. It also assumes task identity, but its masks and weight allocation can be much smaller than storing a 67%-of-model flow snapshot for every task, making it a necessary memory-matched baseline for the stability claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Piggyback: Adapting a Single Network to Multiple Tasks by Learning to Mask Weights
reviewed_competitors.difference: Piggyback freezes a shared pretrained backbone and learns a binary weight mask per task. Its scaffold-plus-small-task-state pattern is operationally close to Parity-MTF but substantially more storage-efficient; Urysohn Ladder adds quotient and homology language without evaluating whether full flow snapshots outperform masks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting with hard attention to the task
reviewed_competitors.difference: HAT learns task-conditioned hard attention masks that protect previously used units while allowing unused capacity to remain plastic. It operationalizes stability-plasticity separation within one network and exposes capacity saturation directly; Parity-MTF instead freezes a scaffold and adds task flows, avoiding overwrites by linear storage growth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Continual learning with hypernetworks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Continual-learning hypernetworks generate task-model weights from compact task embeddings and regularize old outputs, offering another way to isolate behaviors without storing a large explicit flow for each task. The Urysohn paper neither compares memory/accuracy nor shows that quotient tokens provide a better context representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Supermasks in Superposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: SupSup stores multiple tasks as supermasks over one fixed random network and studies both supplied and inferred task contexts. It directly targets the two largest Parity-MTF confounds—linear per-task parameter storage and oracle task identity—yet is absent from the evaluation and related-work positioning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Prompt for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: L2P freezes a pretrained transformer and learns a pool of compact prompts selected from the input, enabling continual adaptation without explicit task identity at inference. That is a stronger modern comparator for shared-scaffold routing and memory than EWC, whereas Parity-MTF stores large task snapshots and assumes the correct one is known.

reviewed_competitors.title: CODA-Prompt: COntinual Decomposed Attention-based Prompting for Rehearsal-Free Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: CODA-Prompt learns decomposed attention-based prompt components over a frozen pretrained model for rehearsal-free continual learning. It supplies compact modular specialization and input-conditioned composition, a close operational alternative to shared scaffold plus fibers that the Urysohn paper does not benchmark.

reviewed_competitors.title: RanPAC: Random Projections and Pre-trained Models for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: RanPAC freezes pretrained features, expands them through a random projection, and updates class statistics analytically without replay. Although it uses expansion rather than contraction, it is a strong fixed-feature continual baseline with explicit accuracy and memory behavior; the Urysohn paper's small Permuted-MNIST study cannot support dismissal of such expansion methods without comparison.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: gated sparse-dictionary competitor evaluated in the paper

reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct SAE architecture and interpretability baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: JumpReLU directly optimizes L0-like sparsity through a learned discontinuous threshold and reports reconstruction fidelity plus interpretability on Gemma activations. The reviewed difference-clustering method is simpler and stronger on its probe suite, but supplies no fidelity measurement and tunes the JumpReLU coefficient using probe loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: BatchTopK Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: adaptive-sparsity SAE competitor cited but omitted from the main table
reviewed_competitors.difference: BatchTopK relaxes fixed per-sample sparsity to a batch budget, improving reconstruction while directly specifying average active latents. It addresses heterogeneous concept demand across samples; the reviewed method fixes dictionary width and scores individual directions but never evaluates adaptive coding or reconstruction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: Matryoshka SAEs train nested dictionaries to preserve both broad and specific features and evaluate sparse probing, feature absorption, and targeted erasure. The reviewed method obtains better aggregate probe rank at one flat width, but it does not test hierarchical recovery and configures only four Matryoshka groups up to 3,072 despite evaluating its own 6,144 centroids.

reviewed_competitors.title: Archetypal SAE: Adaptive and Stable Dictionary Learning for Concept Extraction in Large Vision Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest stability- and geometry-focused vision baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: Archetypal and relaxed archetypal SAEs constrain atoms near the data convex hull and introduce explicit plausibility and identifiability benchmarks. The reviewed centroids also stay tied to observed pairwise geometry and often improve probe loss, but its MPPC evidence is weaker than its prose suggests and it lacks ground-truth identifiability tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Projecting Assumptions: The Duality Between Sparse Autoencoders and Concept Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work shows that each SAE objective recovers only concept geometries compatible with its inductive assumptions. The reviewed method is cheaper and transparent but assumes one flat linear direction per concept and offers no hierarchy or nonlinear-accessibility benchmark.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamic Mixture of Experts: An Auto-Tuning Approach for Efficient Transformer Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: DynMoE already adjusts both the number of available experts and the number activated by each token across vision, language, and vision-language tasks. MASS replaces token-coverage growth with a gradient/weight drift heuristic and uses cumulative-mass routing, but does not isolate either change and improves selected downstream averages only modestly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Gating in Mixture-of-Experts based Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adaptive Gating lets the expert probability distribution choose a variable count per token and reports up to 22.5% training-time savings plus token-difficulty analysis. MASS uses a related probability-mass idea, adds structural growth, and reports active counts but no measured training or inference time.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct confidence-based dynamic-routing source adopted by MASS
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. activate a variable expert count from routing confidence and evaluate complexity-sensitive allocation with explicit parameter-use savings. MASS explicitly takes inspiration from this routing strategy and contributes the separate gradient-triggered pool-expansion mechanism rather than originating Top-p expert selection.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaMoE: Token-Adaptive Routing with Null Experts for Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaMoE inserts zero-FLOP null experts so a fixed top-k operator yields a variable number of real experts and demonstrates a 14.5% FLOP reduction with a 1.69-point ARC-C gain on Mixtral-8x7B. MASS grows real experts and uses Top-p, but its BERT-scale evidence reports no FLOPs and does not compare against this simpler adaptive mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: DA-MoE: Towards Dynamic Expert Allocation for Mixture-of-Experts Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: DA-MoE derives token importance from attention and chooses a variable top-k, reporting GLUE improvements. MASS uses router confidence rather than attention importance and also adapts total K, but evaluates on overlapping GLUE territory without a direct comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Expert Choice reverses assignment so each expert selects a fixed token bucket; tokens naturally receive variable expert counts while load is controlled, with matched-compute convergence and downstream comparisons. MASS keeps token-choice routing and dynamically grows the pool, but omits an expert-choice baseline and does not measure load or hardware efficiency.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepSeekMoE promotes specialization through fine-grained routed experts plus isolated shared experts and validates language-model scaling to billions of parameters. MASS instead tries to discover task-specific K online through drift-triggered duplication, but its specialization metric is router-only and its real language experiment is BERT classification fine-tuning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts are Domain Generalizable Learners
reviewed_competitors.difference: GMoE supplies the pretrained-ViT expert architecture and DomainBed evidence used by the paper. MASS adapts K from an initial pool, but its 72.8 average merely ties the GMoE K=6 row and trails the strongest static value on two datasets, so the vision result supports competitiveness rather than a consistent gain.

reviewed_competitors.title: Maximum Score Routing For Mixture-of-Experts
reviewed_competitors.relationship: contemporary cost- and capacity-aware routing competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: MaxScore formulates routing as minimum-cost maximum-flow with SoftTopk and reports comparisons at equivalent FLOPs while retaining GPU-compatible capacity. MASS targets semantic pool growth and variable active count, but ignores token dropping, capacity constraints, dispatch padding, and equivalent-FLOP routing comparisons.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Findings of ACL 2025 official ACL Anthology edition, pages 12619-12632, DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.findings-acl.653

reviewed_competitors.title: From Pseudo-Balancing to True Specialization: Memory-Aware Routing for Mixture-of-Experts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Memory-Aware Routing uses persistent expert preference memories to reduce knowledge overlap while retaining load balance and reports direct specialization, downstream accuracy, and half-expert efficiency results. MASS predates it and offers adaptive growth, but its synthetic router JSD does not measure stable expert knowledge or functional overlap.

reviewed_competitors.difference: STGC measures token-level conflict inside existing experts and trains the router to move conflicting tokens, with large vision-language experiments. CDSP instead claims to reshape the physical parameter topology, but tests only a small MNIST-family stream and does not match STGC's task scale or conflict ablations.

reviewed_competitors.title: DSelect-k: Differentiable Selection in the Mixture of Experts with Applications to Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: DSelect-k supplies a continuously differentiable sparse gate with explicit cardinality control and evaluates up to 128 tasks. CDSP retains hard top-r coordinate selection and only a scalar gradient bridge, while moving the learned choice from predefined experts to coordinates of a shared backbone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixture-of-Experts with Expert Choice Routing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Expert Choice gives experts fixed-capacity token buckets and directly controls load balance in scaled MoE training. CDSP removes fixed expert tensors and auxiliary balancing in favor of conflict-shaped sharing, but reports neither utilization guarantees nor comparable throughput and scale evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepSeekMoE combines fine-grained routed experts with explicit shared experts and validates specialization from 2B through preliminary 145B scales. CDSP's overlap is learned rather than designed, but its broad specialization and efficiency claims are unsupported beyond an approximately 32k-parameter vision setup.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: PCGrad projects conflicting task gradients while leaving architecture fixed and demonstrates gains across supervised and reinforcement-learning problems. CDSP's narrower possible novelty is using conflict to change sharing topology, but it lacks a PCGrad or other optimizer-level conflict baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaShare: Learning What To Share For Efficient Deep Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaShare jointly learns task-specific layer-execution policies with an explicit resource-efficiency objective. CDSP searches a finer coordinate topology using gradient conflict instead of a policy over layers, but does not quantify the resource trade-off that AdaShare makes part of its objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Universal Weight Subspace Hypothesis
reviewed_competitors.difference: The predecessor provides empirical spectral evidence for shared low-dimensional subspaces across more than 1,100 trained models. CDSP turns that observation into a much stronger axiom of unique sparse task masks and a trainable MoE topology; the uniqueness and coordinate-wise mask assumptions are not consequences established by the predecessor.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Bilen and Vedaldi already show that domain-specific scaling or instance normalization lets one network cover many visual problems.
