reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies a gradient-descent representation-learning guarantee without Bayesian mean field or ARD. The reviewed theorem's sparse-direction benefit therefore sits in an established line; its proposed novelty is explaining finite SGLD with a minimal static mean-field correction.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Merged-Staircase Property: A Necessary and Nearly Sufficient Condition for SGD Learning of Sparse Functions on Two-Layer Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Characterizes when SGD learns sparse Boolean functions with two-layer networks, directly overlapping the parity/sparse-function setting.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It concerns algorithmic learnability and the structure of sparse functions, not a posterior mean-field approximation. It provides important negative task-structure context absent from the two favorable teachers in the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Theoretical Analysis on Feature Learning in Neural Networks: Emergence from Inputs and Advantage over Fixed Features
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Studies emergence of input-dependent features and their advantage over fixed-feature kernels.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes gradient-based feature learning directly, whereas the reviewed paper uses equilibrium SGLD and mean-field self-consistency. It establishes that input-aligned feature emergence predates the paper's IFS terminology.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Kernel Predictors from Feature-Learning Infinite Limits of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Derives adaptive kernel predictors from infinite-width feature-learning limits and is a direct current alternative to a fixed NNGP baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It makes the learned predictor adaptive through an infinite-limit kernel description rather than coordinate-wise empirical-Bayes precisions. The reviewed paper's distinction is its finite-neuron IFS diagnosis, but it does not benchmark this stronger adaptive-kernel baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamical Decoupling of Generalization and Overfitting in Large Two-Layer Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Provides a current dynamical account in which feature learning, generalization, and later overfitting can decouple in large two-layer networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its negative late-time feature-unlearning behavior challenges a purely static equilibrium interpretation. It postdates the reviewed arXiv submission and does not negate its historical claim, but it narrows the current usefulness of an equilibrium-only explanation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Width-Robust Learnability in Mean-Field Bayesian Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later current work studies learnability and width robustness in Bayesian mean-field neural networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is a post-submission theoretical competitor focused on width-robust learnability rather than ARD reconstruction of SGLD feature-selection curves. Its existence limits present-day uniqueness of the broader Bayesian mean-field framing but not chronological novelty at submission.

reviewed_competitors.title: Random Feature Models with Learnable Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The direct model predecessor by the same authors, introducing RFLAF, its shared basis-parameterized activation, expressivity results, and initial feature-complexity analysis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The reviewed paper contributes the leverage-weighted oracle analysis and pool-resampling algorithm. Its model and activation-approximation lemma are inherited, so novelty should be assessed as a sampling/generalization extension rather than a new model family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards a Unified Analysis of Random Fourier Features
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest theoretical precursor for squared and Lipschitz risk bounds, effective dimension, exact ridge-leverage sampling, and a practical approximate-score scheme.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. analyze fixed Fourier features and supply the proof template that the reviewed paper explicitly adapts. The reviewed contribution is to handle a shared learnable activation, but its ideal-to-practical kernel-learning step and importance-weight generalization argument require new justification that is not inherited automatically.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization Properties of Learning with Random Features
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational statistical-learning analysis showing that kernel-ridge rates can be preserved with substantially fewer than n random features and that problem-dependent sampling can improve the tradeoff.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rudi and Rosasco establish the modern sample-feature-risk framework for fixed random features. The reviewed work specializes the effective-dimension idea to RFLAF and claims sharper spectrum-conditioned width rates, without providing matching lower bounds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Random Fourier Features for Kernel Ridge Regression: Approximation Bounds and Statistical Guarantees
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier ridge-leverage treatment of random Fourier features through regularized spectral approximation of kernel matrices.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Avron et al. give tight fixed-data spectral-approximation bounds and connect them to KRR risk. The reviewed paper instead targets population risk for a kernel whose activation is learned, but does not compare its empirical resampling algorithm against this established leverage-RFF line.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Equivalence between Kernel Quadrature Rules and Random Feature Expansions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Provides eigenvalue-based upper and lower bounds for nonuniform random-feature sampling and Lipschitz-loss learning, connecting optimal feature distributions to kernel quadrature.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bach supplies a genuine near-matching optimality story for kernel approximation, whereas the reviewed paper's 'sharpest' RFLAF counts are only sufficient. Its lower-bound methodology is a natural missing comparator for any statistical-limit claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data-dependent compression of random features for large-scale kernel approximation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A close practical precursor that begins with a large random-feature set and compresses it to a much smaller weighted set while preserving approximation guarantees.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Agrawal et al. already frame and test large-pool data-dependent compression, including a dataset with over 50 million observations. The reviewed algorithm adapts this pattern to a jointly learned activation but evaluates only four modest datasets and omits a direct compression baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalized Leverage Score Sampling for Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Extends leverage-score sampling beyond Fourier kernels and connects leverage initialization of neural networks with random-feature and neural-tangent-kernel ridge regression.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. cover a broader neural-kernel class and optimization-to-kernel equivalence. RFLAF learns a shared activation and resamples after fitting, but its own optimizer-to-kernel link is assumed rather than established.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Nonlinearities Improve Generalization Performance of Random Features
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct alternative for adapting the activation of random-feature models to improve task generalization, including regression, classification, and CIFAR-10 experiments.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Demir and Dogan derive optimal nonlinearities from an asymptotic Gaussian-equivalent model and study double descent, while RFLAF learns a flexible shared basis at finite sample and focuses on feature compression. The reviewed experiments do not compare the learned activation or accuracy-compute tradeoff against this alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Expressive Random Feature Models via Parametrized Activations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The later peer-reviewed UAI 2026 version of the same authors' core RFLAF model line, with expanded sample/feature theory, basis comparisons, and first-layer unfreezing.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It validates RFLAF expressivity and learned activations more broadly but does not replace the leverage-specific proof needed here. Read together, the leverage paper is best viewed as a width-compression branch of the larger parametrized-activation program.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Rates for Random Fourier Features
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Establishes finite-sample optimal approximation rates for random Fourier features in uniform and L-r norms, including growing domains and kernel derivatives.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sriperumbudur and Szabo analyze kernel-approximation quality rather than learned-activation population risk, but their precise use of 'optimal' illustrates the lower- and upper-bound standard absent from the reviewed statistical-limit wording.

reviewed_competitors.title: Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Introduces random Fourier features as an explicit low-dimensional approximation to shift-invariant kernels and demonstrates scalable linear learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rahimi and Recht provide the fixed-activation foundation. RFLAF replaces the fixed nonlinearity by a shared learned basis and then uses data-dependent selection, trading the original method's simplicity for task adaptivity and a harder nonconvex/statistical analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Not All Neuro-Symbolic Concepts Are Created Equal: Analysis and Mitigation of Reasoning Shortcuts
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational prior and closest theoretical predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: The NeurIPS 2023 paper introduces the formal concept-remapping view, deterministic shortcut count, four root causes, mitigation analysis, and four-dataset experiments. The present overview largely restates and integrates that substance with later identifiability, statistical-learning, awareness, RL, and concept-based-model work; its incremental contribution is breadth and tutorial synthesis rather than a replacement theorem or new experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analysis for Abductive Learning and Neural-Symbolic Reasoning Shortcuts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. directly define shortcut risk, relate it to knowledge complexity, sample size, and hypothesis space, and analyze how abductive distance choices reduce risk with empirical validation. The overview translates that line into a common vocabulary and contrasts it with identifiability theory, but does not add a tighter risk bound or new abductive result.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Neuro-Symbolic Benchmark Suite for Concept Quality and Reasoning Shortcuts
reviewed_competitors.difference: RSBench contributes customizable arithmetic, visual-logic, and autonomous-driving tasks, concept-quality metrics, and formal shortcut-verification procedures, then evaluates neural and neuro-symbolic models. The overview uses those tasks and findings as evidence and explains their theoretical context, but contributes neither a new benchmark split nor a new measured model comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: BEARS Make Neuro-Symbolic Models Aware of their Reasoning Shortcuts
reviewed_competitors.difference: BEARS derives an ensemble objective that makes concept uncertainty track alternative shortcut groundings and demonstrates improved awareness and active annotation. The overview generalizes the lesson into mitigation-versus-awareness terminology and compares BEARS with diffusion-based awareness; it does not introduce a new awareness algorithm or calibration experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shortcuts and Identifiability in Concept-based Models from a Neuro-Symbolic Lens
reviewed_competitors.relationship: prior extension to learned inference layers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bortolotti et al. extend fixed-inference reasoning shortcuts to joint shortcuts in concept-based models, derive identification conditions for both concepts and the inference layer, and empirically show standard mitigations often fail. The overview summarizes this extension and exposes open gaps, while keeping its central formal development focused on fixed-knowledge NeSy predictors.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Learnability Analysis on Neuro-Symbolic Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: He and Li characterize learnability through uniqueness of a derived CSP, give a finite-sample bound under a restricted hypothesis space, bound asymptotic concept error by disagreement among CSP solutions, and test MNIST-family tasks. The overview places this beside shortcut counts and risk analysis, but offers no stronger DCSP algorithm or error theorem and notes that the approach only enumerates in-distribution concept disagreement.

reviewed_competitors.title: Constraint-Based Analysis of Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct contemporary verification and repair framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: Takemura et al. formulate shortcut freedom as uniqueness in an explicit CSP, prove complexity and label-query bounds, supply a sound and complete ASP verifier, and greedily repair constraints across eight RSBench domains. The overview cites this as complementary task-level certification; it does not contribute an executable verifier, repair algorithm, or complexity classification.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiable Logic Programming to Mitigate Reasoning Shortcuts in Neurosymbolic Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Takemura and Inoue use unified matrix-based differentiable logic programming and one-to-one neural-output/atom grounding to reduce constraint-satisfaction and cognition shortcuts. Their MNIST/USPS and MNIST-Half experiments separate literal satisfaction from genuine digit learning and compare LTN, Semantic Loss, DeepProbLog, DeepStochLog, NeurASP, and other baselines. The overview offers a broader mitigation taxonomy but does not discuss this explicit-grounding design or its July 2026 experiments despite the record predating arXiv v3.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning Shortcuts and Value Symmetries: What Symmetry Permits, Architecture Realizes, and Optimization Selects
reviewed_competitors.relationship: post-cutoff direct theoretical refinement and critique
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu shows that a single global value permutation is not natively defined for the heterogeneous domains in four evaluated RSBench tasks, introduces global/typed/componentwise symmetry readings, reports an encoding-dependent 90.91% false-pathology example, proves structural and complexity results, and separates symbolic permission, architectural realizability, and optimizer selection using 94 observed shortcuts and controls. It appeared five days after the overview's v3 revision, so it does not negate the overview's tutorial contribution but materially narrows any claim that the v3 theory map is exhaustive or that formal shortcut counts alone predict learned failures.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest direct competitor and reported baseline (BSBM)
reviewed_competitors.difference: BranchSBM learns branched stochastic dynamics by explicitly parameterizing one velocity field and one growth field per target branch with unbalanced Schrödinger-bridge matching, requiring the branch decomposition to be specified; Y-Flows keeps a single deterministic velocity field and induces branching implicitly through a concave action, and reports beating BSBM on W1/W2/MMD across Tedsim and Paul15 dimensions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Theory and Approximate Solvers for Branched Optimal Transport with Multiple Sources
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior branched-transport solver the paper positions itself against
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lippmann et al. solve discrete BOT for finite sources/sinks by alternating O(nd) geometric optimization of branch points with combinatorial topology rewiring; it outputs a transport network, not a generative model, and cannot sample continuous distributions, which is exactly the gap the velocity-space formulation targets.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalized Schrödinger Bridge Matching
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior task-cost-augmented dynamic transport framework; source of the potential-energy penalty reused in the LiDAR experiment
reviewed_competitors.difference: GSBM generalizes bridge matching to task-specific state costs (obstacles, congestion) via conditional stochastic optimal control but keeps a convex kinetic energy, so mass still moves along effectively independent paths; Y-Flows changes the kinetic term itself to a sub-additive power to make shared trunks energetically favorable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving and generalizing flow-based generative models with minibatch optimal transport
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Representative V-shaped baseline (CFM/OT-CFM) used in the biology tables
reviewed_competitors.difference: OT-CFM straightens independent conditional paths by sampling endpoint pairs from mini-batch OT plans within a simulation-free regression objective; it optimizes the coupling but keeps constant-speed straight per-pair trajectories, whereas Y-Flows pays simulation cost to reshape the trajectories themselves into merge-then-branch structures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Few-step generation competitor and FFHQ baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: MeanFlow attacks step count by learning the average velocity over an interval via an identity linking average and instantaneous velocities, achieving strong 1-NFE ImageNet results; Y-Flows instead reduces steps as a side effect of concentrating transport into shared trunks, and only matches or narrowly beats MeanFlow at 2 steps on ALAE-latent Frechet distance while losing at 1 step to FM.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bayesian Influence Functions for Hessian-Free Data Attribution
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kreer et al. introduce the local BIF estimator, motivate stochastic-gradient MCMC as a Hessian-free alternative, and benchmark prediction of retraining effects. The reviewed paper's novelty is the temporal phase interpretation and interventions, not the BIF estimator itself; it provides a weaker independent approximation audit because it tunes on its leave-one-out trace.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Data Attribution via Approximate Unrolled Differentiation
reviewed_competitors.difference: SOURCE approximates unrolled differentiation and explicitly handles non-converged models, optimizer implicit bias, and multi-stage pipelines, with counterfactual retraining evaluation. The reviewed method preserves checkpoint-local trajectories to avoid temporal cancellation, but does not estimate the cumulative causal effect SOURCE targets.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: If Influence Functions are the Answer, Then What is the Question?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bae et al. decompose five sources of error between practical influence functions and leave-one-out retraining and show that estimates may instead track a proximal Bregman response. The reviewed paper motivates BIF from singularity but does not perform an equally granular out-of-sample decomposition of its covariance-estimation error.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: TRAK: Attributing Model Behavior at Scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: TRAK uses random projections and a handful of trained models to approximate retraining-based attribution at ImageNet, CLIP, BERT, and mT5 scale. It targets final behavior efficiently, whereas stagewise BIF targets dense local trajectories but is demonstrated only on targeted subsets of very small language models.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: HYDRA: Hypergradient Data Relevance Analysis for Interpreting Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: HYDRA unrolls hypergradients through the entire optimization trajectory, gives an approximation-error bound, and evaluates noisy-label detection and data contribution. The reviewed paper retains when influence matters rather than collapsing the path, but its assertion that attribution is generally static must be read in light of this explicit trajectory predecessor.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v7 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimating Training Data Influence by Tracing Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: TracIn accumulates gradient interactions at saved training checkpoints and is architecture-agnostic and simple to implement. Stagewise BIF instead treats the trajectory itself as the output and can show sign cancellation, but requires approximate posterior sampling and has not matched TracIn's scale.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v3 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Koh and Liang adapt classical inverse-Hessian influence to modern differentiable models and demonstrate training-point explanations. The reviewed paper replaces a point estimate and inverse Hessian with a local posterior covariance, primarily to handle singular intermediate checkpoints and temporal changes.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v3 primary record and abstract checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Studying Large Language Model Generalization with Influence Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Grosse et al. use EK-FAC to scale influence functions to language models up to 52B parameters and study cross-lingual, abstraction, math, and code influence patterns. The reviewed method avoids Hessian fitting and adds timing, but its largest language model is 14M and its estimator is query-costly across checkpoints.

reviewed_competitors.title: Structural Inference: Interpreting Small Language Models with Susceptibilities
reviewed_competitors.difference: Structural Inference already treats a small language model as a Bayesian statistical-mechanical system, estimates local SGLD susceptibilities, factorizes per-token contributions, and identifies induction and multigram modules in a 3M transformer. The reviewed paper's distinct addition is stagewise tracking and timed intervention, not the susceptibility-to-structure connection.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning of Stochastic Differential Equations with Foundation Inference Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Seifner et al. supply the FIM-SDE model that this paper freezes, and by the current version evaluate zero-shot and finetuned drift/diffusion estimation against symbolic, GP, and neural-SDE baselines. The coarse-graining paper's novelty is therefore the learned sensing map around an existing estimator; it does not independently establish the estimator's scope or calibration on learned, potentially off-prior coordinates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data-driven discovery of coordinates and governing equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Champion et al. jointly train an autoencoder and sparse SINDy equations and test three high-dimensional systems. The FIM wrapper replaces sparse equation fitting with an amortized SDE estimator and one loss, which may reduce target optimization, but the present paper tests fewer systems, returns non-symbolic coefficients, and does not run the direct baseline it uses for its video construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning interpretable continuous-time models of latent stochastic dynamical systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Duncker et al. jointly infer continuous latent paths from noisy, unevenly sampled high-dimensional outputs and use a GP drift structured by fixed points and local Jacobians. Their target-specific variational inference is slower than a frozen FIM, but it directly handles regimes this paper declares unsupported and gives interpretable phase portraits with uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.title: State estimation of a physical system with unknown governing equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Course and Nair jointly estimate hidden states and unknown symbolic or neural dynamics with calibrated posterior uncertainty, including noisy indirect measurements and systems up to 1,024 states. Their method requires target optimization and priors, whereas the FIM approach aims for speed; the latter does not yet test uncertainty, partial observability, noise, or quantitative equation recovery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Variational Gaussian Process Diffusion Processes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Verma et al. develop a site-based variational Gaussian diffusion process with a principled objective and fast convex-style optimization while explicitly diagnosing pathologies of earlier variational parameterizations. It is not an observation-space coordinate learner, but it supplies a proper probabilistic alternative for latent diffusion inference against which Equation 2's sampled MSE should be tested.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Langevin Dynamics: Towards Interpretable Neural Stochastic Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Koop et al. train a VAE whose latent SDE is restricted to Langevin dynamics, yielding an energy landscape tied to metastable states and residence times. The FIM method is less target-specific and potentially faster, but its generic drift/diffusion curves lack this structural interpretability and are not validated through state occupancy or transition observables.

reviewed_competitors.title: Expressive dynamics models with nonlinear injective readouts enable reliable recovery of latent features from neural activity
reviewed_competitors.difference: ODIN shows that non-injective readouts can invent misleading latent dynamics and builds an injective nonlinear observation map to improve ground-truth feature recovery. The FIM paper uses unconstrained MLP encoder-decoder maps, so ODIN identifies a direct failure mode and a missing control for its claim that learned coordinates capture the underlying physics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causal Representation Meets Stochastic Modeling under Generic Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ren, Wang, and Huang develop identifiability results plus a VAE with time-adaptive stochastic transitions for continuous-time latent processes. MUTATE targets point processes rather than pixel SDEs and is more complex, but it makes the geometry and identifiability problem explicit; the FIM wrapper offers speed without a corresponding guarantee or empirical identifiability test.

reviewed_competitors.difference: ODEFormer maps one noisy, irregular trajectory to an explicit multidimensional symbolic ODE and introduced the 63-system ODEBench benchmark. FIM-ODE instead returns a queryable neural vector field, accepts multiple context trajectories, and is much smaller, but the present study compares them only on FIM-ODE's in-distribution polynomial set and does not recover symbolic laws.

reviewed_competitors.title: DDOT: A Derivative-directed Dual-decoder Ordinary Differential Equation Transformer for Dynamic System Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: DDOT extends symbolic ODE transformers with an auxiliary derivative decoder and a state-space divergence metric, reporting gains over symbolic baselines on ODEBench and an anesthesia dataset. It remains equation-generating and single-trajectory oriented, whereas FIM-ODE conditions a continuous neural operator on one or more trajectories; DDOT supplies precisely the grid-level dynamics evaluation missing from FIM-ODE's qualitative field comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Foundation Inference Models for Stochastic Differential Equations: A Transformer-Based Approach for Zero-Shot Function Estimation
reviewed_competitors.difference: FIM-SDE establishes the same simulation-based, Transformer-and-neural-operator program for stochastic drift and diffusion estimation. FIM-ODE adapts that architecture to deterministic dynamics, where trajectories explore less of state space, but offers only a preliminary low-dimensional polynomial evaluation rather than the broader uncertainty-bearing SDE task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Manifold-Constrained Gaussian Process Inference for One-shot Learning of Unknown Ordinary Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: MAGI-X couples a neural vector field to a Gaussian-process trajectory prior and ODE manifold constraint, targeting scarce noisy and partially observed data with uncertainty and real flu forecasting. It performs per-system inference rather than amortized zero-shot prediction; its partial-observation and uncertainty evidence covers deployment conditions not tested by FIM-ODE.

reviewed_competitors.title: Verifier-Guided Model Discovery for Physical Dynamical Systems with Pretrained Symbolic Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This subsequent workflow pools ODEFormer candidates across trajectories and selects equations with executable dynamical and physical-admissibility checks, including transfer to vortex shedding. FIM-ODE natively combines trajectories but lacks symbolic auditability or verifiers; the later work shows that reconstruction fidelity alone does not establish physical discoverability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Critical Learning Periods in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Achille, Rovere, and Soatto introduced the deficit-window protocol and explained lasting impairment through information-plasticity dynamics measured with Fisher information. The reviewed paper mainly reproduces and broadens the corruption study, then argues that a phase-boundary learning-rate restart makes much of the effect reversible.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Warm-Starting Neural Network Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ash and Adams established stationary warm-start generalization gaps and proposed Shrink-and-Perturb. The reviewed paper supplies a simpler learning-rate-reset comparison and reframes subset warm-starting as an early information deficit, but omits a direct equal-compute comparison with Shrink-and-Perturb.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2020 proceedings version, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33

reviewed_competitors.title: A Study on the Plasticity of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Berariu et al. systematically examine how prior tasks reduce later learnability under fine-tuning and study optimization/generalization accounts. The reviewed paper is narrower—one vision stack and a boundary restart—but explicitly links this plasticity literature to the critical-period corruption protocol.

reviewed_competitors.title: DASH: Warm-Starting Neural Network Training in Stationary Settings without Loss of Plasticity
reviewed_competitors.difference: DASH attributes stationary warm-start loss to noise memorization and selectively shrinks parameter directions to forget noise while preserving features. It is a mechanism-targeted alternative with broader warm-start evaluation; the reviewed paper instead applies a global schedule restart and studies corruption type/severity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Loss of plasticity in deep continual learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dohare et al. demonstrate long-horizon plasticity loss across continual supervised and reinforcement-learning settings and maintain it by continually replacing low-utility units. That evidence challenges generalizing a successful one-transition learning-rate reset to indefinite continual learning and provides dormant-unit, stable-rank, and weight-growth diagnostics absent here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Critical Learning Periods Emerge Even in Deep Linear Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kleinman, Achille, and Soatto recover critical-period behavior in analytically tractable deep linear networks, locating it in training dynamics rather than nonlinear architectural quirks. The reviewed paper offers a practical recovery intervention but no theoretical account of when an LR restart should undo those dynamics.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv version associated with the ICLR 2024 paper

reviewed_competitors.title: One Period to Rule Them All: Identifying Critical Learning Periods in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fukase et al. estimate the end of critical periods online via layer-rotation dynamics and use it to stop costly augmentation or begin pruning. This addresses detection and compute reduction, whereas the reviewed paper assumes a known phase boundary and asks whether a restart repairs earlier deficient exposure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zeng et al. compare simple DLinear/NLinear models against multiple Transformer forecasters on nine real long-horizon datasets and find the linear panel stronger. Zhou et al. seek a formal explanation, but only in a known-order synthetic AR setting with LSA; they do not validate that their label-slot bottleneck explains Zeng et al.'s real-model results.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Time Series is Worth 64 Words: Long-term Forecasting with Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: PatchTST uses subseries patches and channel-independent shared Transformer weights to preserve local structure, extend receptive fields, and achieve strong supervised forecasting and representation learning. Those design choices lie outside the raw LSA label-slot feature class and directly test the paper's suggestion that attention compression necessarily obscures local predictive signal.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Decoder-only Foundation Model for Time-Series Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.difference: TimesFM pretrains a patched decoder attention model on real and synthetic corpora and reports competitive zero-shot accuracy across unseen domains, horizons, and granularities. It addresses cross-task transfer—the empirical phenomenon an ICL framing should explain—whereas Zhou et al. train on fixed synthetic AR processes and analyze neither pretraining nor zero-shot task shifts.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chronos tokenizes scaled and quantized values, trains 20M-710M T5-family models with cross-entropy on diverse real series plus synthetic Gaussian-process data, and evaluates probabilistic zero-shot forecasts on 42 datasets. Its success can arise from cross-domain pretraining, nonlinear features, softmax, MLPs, and distributional output, none covered by the LSA AR(p) lower bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unified Training of Universal Time Series Forecasting Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Moirai's any-variate attention, multi-patch sizes, distributional heads, and LOTSA pretraining over 27B observations target arbitrary variate counts, frequencies, and domains. Zhou et al.'s univariate known-p Hankel LSA excludes all of these mechanisms and therefore cannot adjudicate Moirai's empirical setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Trained Transformers Learn Linear Models In-Context
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang, Frei, and Bartlett prove gradient-flow convergence of a one-layer LSA model to a global population optimum on task-distributed linear-regression prompts and characterize covariate-shift brittleness, with larger nonlinear Transformer experiments. Zhou et al. instead use temporally dependent Hankel examples from a fixed AR process and focus on a label-slot representational lower bound; they do not analyze whether training finds their optima or adapts across rho tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: How do Transformers Perform In-Context Autoregressive Learning?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sander et al. train Transformers on vector next-token sequences s_{t+1}=Ws_t, identify in-context estimation and application of W, characterize one-layer multihead minima, and show positional encodings capture process structure. Their orthogonal-matrix setting is different from noisy scalar stable AR(p), but their multihead and trained-algorithm results undercut Zhou et al.'s unsupported speculation that heads over one source are unlikely to add expressivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning of Linear Dynamical Systems with Transformers: Error Bounds and Depth-Separation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest linear-dynamics lower-bound and depth competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cole et al. give a non-diminishing lower bound for a single-layer linear Transformer but construct logarithmic-depth Transformers with error comparable to least squares over a noisy linear-dynamical-system task family. Zhou et al. generalize the scalar process order and propose a Schur gap, yet their multi-layer appendix proves only trivial nesting and does not establish the depth separation or task-uniform approximation that Cole et al. analyze.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Learn to Implement Preconditioned Gradient Descent for In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ahn et al. characterize the one-layer population optimum as a distribution- and finite-data-aware preconditioned gradient step and identify multi-layer critical points implementing multiple steps. Zhou et al. borrow the LSA abstraction but study dependent Hankel features and a restricted label readout; their result is a projection lower bound, not an analysis of the algorithm training discovers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Transformers for Time Series Forecasting: A Case Study on Moirai
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. prove existence constructions in which Transformer layers rearrange raw univariate or arbitrary-variate histories and iteratively approximate AR least squares, then add dependent-data pretraining bounds under a Dobrushin condition and synthetic Moirai experiments. The work postdates Zhou et al.'s submission and covers softmax-capable practical architectures; it is complementary rather than a refutation because existence and generalization bounds do not prove training always finds the construction, but it sharply narrows any broad claim of inherent Transformer incapacity.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Pethick et al.'s Scion emphasizes norm-constrained LMOs and uses sign descent for non-matrix parameters. The reviewed work embeds Scion in a broader product-norm taxonomy and adds regularized and MoMo-capped variants.

reviewed_competitors.title: PolarGrad: A Class of Matrix-Gradient Optimizers from a Unifying Preconditioning Perspective

reviewed_competitors.title: MoMo: Momentum Models for Adaptive Learning Rates
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schaipp et al. derive and test truncated momentum models for SGD-M and Adam across vision, recommendation, translation, and diffusion. The reviewed paper generalizes the closed-form step to arbitrary norms and applies it to Muon product geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon Optimizes Under Spectral Norm Constraints
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen, Li, and Liu place Muon with decoupled weight decay in the Lion-K family and show implicit spectral-norm constraints. The reviewed paper derives explicit steepest-descent norms for practical hybrid updates and explores product scaling rather than implicit regularization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uniform Spectral Growth and Convergence of Muon in LoRA-Style Matrix Factorization

reviewed_competitors.difference: Kang et al. analyze equal-rate singular-value growth and convergence in a simplified LoRA factorization. It probes Muon's spectral dynamics, whereas the reviewed paper treats the polar update as a component in a system-level optimizer design space.

reviewed_competitors.difference: AutoSGD introduced the same increase-or-decrease family in stochastic and deterministic forms; the present paper's defensible addition is the revised deterministic controller with diffuse initialization, Armijo filtering, counterexamples, stronger convergence results, and a much broader deterministic evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Gradient Descent without Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdGD adapts from consecutive gradients without function values or line search and proves local-smoothness convex guarantees; AutoGD spends proposal objective evaluations instead and is designed to remain robust when finite-difference curvature changes rapidly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning-Rate-Free Learning by D-Adaptation
reviewed_competitors.difference: D-Adaptation estimates the distance-to-solution scale with no line search or extra evaluations and includes SGD and Adam experiments on large vision and language tasks; AutoGD instead targets deterministic objectives with direct local proposal comparisons and stronger nonconvex critical-point analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: DoG is SGD's Best Friend: A Parameter-Free Dynamic Step Size Schedule
reviewed_competitors.difference: DoG uses distance from initialization and accumulated gradient norms, supports stochastic convex theory with locally bounded gradients, and evaluates transfer learning; AutoGD uses current function-value probes and has no stochastic deep-learning evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: DoWG Unleashed: An Efficient Universal Parameter-Free Gradient Descent Method
reviewed_competitors.difference: DoWG adapts to smooth and nonsmooth convex objectives through distance-weighted gradient accumulation and matches tuned GD up to logarithms without trial evaluations; AutoGD offers different nonconvex safeguards but pays for proposal values.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tuning-Free Stochastic Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work defines tuning-free comparison to optimally tuned SGD, supplies impossibility results on unbounded domains, and allows loose parameter hints; AutoGD makes a narrower deterministic claim and should not be described as fully parameter-free under that stronger definition.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Free is Parameter-Free Stochastic Optimization?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Attia and Koren show that gradient-only fully parameter-free stochastic convex optimization is impossible without additional knowledge and that simple search can be strong; AutoGD escapes that oracle model by using deterministic function values, so its evaluation budget must be counted explicitly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Directional Smoothness and Gradient Methods: Convergence and Adaptivity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Directional-smoothness analysis explains Polyak and normalized-GD adaptivity through path-dependent curvature and implicit step equations; AutoGD instead discretely samples neighboring rates and proves a rate under gradient-ray unimodality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stochastic Polyak Step-size for SGD: An Adaptive Learning Rate for Fast Convergence
reviewed_competitors.difference: SPS computes a closed-form stochastic rate from a sample loss gap and gradient norm, usually assuming sample-optimum information or interpolation; AutoGD avoids the optimum-value oracle but evaluates several actual next points per deterministic step.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Dalvi et al. operationalize redundancy by neuron subsampling, critical mass, and performance-compression Pareto curves across pretrained representations. This paper uses covariance eigenvalue entropy, which need not track removable task-preserving neurons.

reviewed_competitors.title: Barlow Twins: Self-Supervised Learning via Redundancy Reduction

reviewed_competitors.title: VICReg: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bardes et al. separate invariance, per-dimension variance, and covariance penalties so redundancy reduction does not collapse the representation. This paper compresses those distinct effects into one spectral entropy and does not isolate collapse from beneficial dependence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Pairwise Correlations: The Role of Higher-Order Interactions in Self-Supervised Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: The SSLPM work measures feature predictability beyond pairwise correlation and reports that reducing higher-order redundancy improves representations. This paper's evaluated proxy sees only covariance and its general f-divergence is not estimated experimentally.

reviewed_competitors.title: RedTest: A Practical Redundancy Testing Framework for Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: RedTest scores redundancy across layers and architectures and validates it through pruning-related use cases. This paper studies coordinate dependence within one latent representation and offers no architectural compression test.

reviewed_competitors.difference: That work builds an energy-distance coupling-matrix index and evaluates it across multiple datasets and latent models, generally favoring lower redundancy. This paper proposes covariance effective rank and infers an intermediate optimum from four models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Auto-Compressing Networks

reviewed_competitors.title: The Entropy Mechanism of Reinforcement Learning for Reasoning Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cui et al. derive token-level entropy change from probability-logit covariance and introduce Clip-Cov and KL-Cov to restrict high-covariance updates. AER instead applies an explicit entropy bonus, routes it by prompt group accuracy, and controls its aggregate coefficient against an initial-relative target; Table 1 shows only a 0.4/0.8-point 8B average lead over Clip-Cov on pass@1/pass@32.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning with Exploration: An Entropy Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ent-Adv identifies high-entropy reasoning regions and adds entropy to the advantage to encourage longer, deeper trajectories. AER uses standard sequence entropy as a regularizer, assigns it only to low-success prompts, and dynamically regulates a run-level target rather than shaping every response advantage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking Entropy Regularization in Large Reasoning Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: SIREN argues naive global entropy bonuses create entropy explosion and selectively regularizes top-p, peak-entropy action/state regions with a self-anchor. AER is selective across prompts through difficulty gating but remains uniform across token positions within a selected response, making the two methods direct alternatives at different granularities.

reviewed_competitors.title: Asymmetric Advantage Modulation Calibrates Entropy Dynamics in RLVR
reviewed_competitors.difference: AsymGRPO separates positive and negative outcome channels, aiming to preserve productive entropy on successes while suppressing noisy entropy on failures and adapting emphasis by prompt difficulty. It directly challenges AER's use of undifferentiated entropy magnitude as the controlled state while remaining compatible enough to motivate a factorial combination.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding and Preventing Entropy Collapse in RLVR with On-Policy Entropy Flow Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: OPEFO measures entropy-increasing and entropy-decreasing token updates and adaptively balances their contributions under strict on-policy training. AER controls a coarse global entropy level via an auxiliary regularizer; OPEFO instead controls directional entropy flow at token level, offering a sharper mechanism test for collapse prevention.

reviewed_competitors.title: PAEC: Position-Aware Entropy Calibration for LLM Reasoning in RLVR
reviewed_competitors.difference: PAEC constructs a soft token-position mask from local top-p entropy and top-two competition, then applies an anchor-based lower-bound penalty only to decision-sensitive positions. AER chooses prompts rather than positions and regulates mean sequence entropy, so PAEC targets the central failure mode that AER may spend entropy on nondiagnostic tokens.

The target has a sharper riddling mechanism and local exponent, while using a much smaller and specially symmetric deep model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chaotic Dynamics are Intrinsic to Neural Network Training with SGD
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct cited predecessor connecting loss curvature to chaotic SGD dynamics and measuring divergence of nearby training trajectories.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Herrmann, Granz, and Landgraf establish local and long-run chaotic divergence and show suppressing negative-curvature chaos harms performance. The target adds multiple-attractor basin geometry and transverse stability, which is necessary to claim outcome-level riddling rather than trajectory chaos.

reviewed_competitors.title: Nondeterminism and Instability in Neural Network Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical predecessor showing that one-bit initialization changes can induce model diversity comparable to multiple extrinsic nondeterminism sources.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Summers and Dinneen isolate sources of run-to-run variability and propose mitigation but do not explain the scale insensitivity geometrically. The target proposes riddled basins as that mechanism and measures uncertainty scaling, while not matching the predecessor's breadth of ordinary architectures and datasets.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stochastic Collapse: How Gradient Noise Attracts SGD Dynamics Towards Simpler Subnetworks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct cited predecessor for convergence toward sparse or redundant symmetry-induced invariant sets under SGD.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. derive stochastic attractivity from curvature-noise competition and connect collapse to simplification and generalization. The target treats invariant sets as hosts for competing chaotic attractors and uses deterministic as well as stochastic training, so it extends collapse geometry toward outcome unpredictability rather than explaining the attraction itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimization on multifractal loss landscapes explains a diverse range of geometrical and dynamical properties of deep learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Immediate same-author predecessor offering a different unified fractal account of neural optimization dynamics and generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ly and Gong's multifractal model explains edge-of-stability, anomalous diffusion, and attraction to smoother regions through landscape roughness. The target instead studies basin boundaries and symmetry-driven competing destinations; the two frameworks overlap in chaos and fractality but neither paper empirically adjudicates whether one mechanism explains the other's signatures.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Xiao independently derives a space-frequency eigenspace decomposition and high-dimensional generalization theory for infinite-width deep CNNs, including curse-breaking claims. The thesis analyzes a fixed-dimension, large-sample asymptotic with receptive-field sectors and emphasizes the negative result for globally supported matched hierarchical teachers.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Deep Networks Learn Sparse and Hierarchical Data: the Sparse Random Hierarchy Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Sparse RHM adds spatial sparsity and discrete transformation invariance, quantifying how both sparsity and hierarchy affect CNN sample complexity. It directly relaxes one missing ingredient of the thesis's regular dense RHM, but still retains a synthetic hierarchical generator rather than resolving irregular or context-sensitive natural data.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamical Regimes of Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Biroli et al. derive speciation and memorization-collapse transitions from optimally trained empirical scores in high dimension and connect them to covariance spectra and excess entropy. The thesis's RHM transition instead targets hierarchical root reconstruction, low-level feature persistence, and a finite-time susceptibility peak that Gaussian mixtures do not reproduce.

reviewed_competitors.title: U-Nets as Belief Propagation: Efficient Classification, Denoising, and Diffusion in Generative Hierarchical Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mei proves that U-Nets can implement or approximate belief-propagation denoising in tree generative models and supplies efficient sample-complexity bounds. This supports the thesis's architectural analogy, while separating representability/learnability guarantees from its empirical claim that gradient training discovers the RHM grammar level by level.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Analytic Theory of Creativity in Convolutional Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kamb and Ganguli explain combinatorial novelty through locality and equivariance preventing optimal score matching and obtain a patch-mosaic predictor with high output correlation on convolution-only denoisers. The thesis attributes local-to-global coherence to hierarchical context clustering and higher-order latent grammar, while its own early kernel chapters also identify locality as a distinct inductive bias.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Edge of Memorization in Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Buchanan et al. predict a model-size crossover between generalizing and memorizing solutions in an underparameterized laboratory. The thesis instead holds models heavily overparameterized and predicts a training-time window, with memorization onset scaling approximately linearly in dataset size; together they imply distinct capacity and optimization-time phase boundaries.

reviewed_competitors.title: Localizing Task Information for Improved Model Merging and Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. find mostly non-overlapping parameter supports, introduce TALL masks, recover more than 99% of single-task accuracy from a merged vector, and identify selfish/catastrophic weights. This operationalizes localization in parameter space, whereas the thesis defines functional localization over input domains and diagnoses pretrained NTK eigenfunctions.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Task Vectors and Gradients
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. prove exact one-epoch task-vector/negative-gradient equivalence and bound a second-order multi-epoch error, reframing arithmetic as approximate multitask learning. That explains how task vectors form during early fine-tuning, while the thesis's weight-disentanglement condition explains when their functional effects do not interfere; neither alone derives the other.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding and Enforcing Weight Disentanglement in Task Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. explicitly argue that weight disentanglement describes the desired non-interfering outcome but not its underlying cause, introduce task-feature specialization as a sufficient cause, connect it to update orthogonality, and enforce it with OrthoReg. This directly sharpens the thesis's open question about the pretraining origin of disentanglement and its causal status.

reviewed_competitors.title: PENCIL: Long Thoughts with Short Memory
reviewed_competitors.difference: PENCIL already adds a learned-token-triggered reduction rule to autoregressive reasoning, simulates Turing machines with O(T) generated tokens and O(S) maximum context, and empirically trains from solver traces on SAT, QBF, and Einstein puzzles. AP-MDM generalizes the memory-reuse idea to bidirectional parallel generation, arbitrary remask/insert/delete controls, and PRAM time-space analysis; its overwrite advantage over a strictly append-only ARM therefore should not be conflated with an advantage over PENCIL-style editable autoregression.

reviewed_competitors.title: Levenshtein Transformer
reviewed_competitors.difference: LevT alternates parallel deletion, placeholder insertion, and token filling with a shared Transformer, trains the complementary policies by imitation learning, changes length dynamically, and unifies generation with refinement on translation, summarization, and post-editing. AP-MDM adds remasking, masked-diffusion framing, parallel-complexity theorems, and solver-trace tasks, but insert/delete sequence generation and learned loop termination were demonstrated six years earlier.

reviewed_competitors.title: Remasking Discrete Diffusion Models with Inference-Time Scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: ReMDM derives a non-Markovian remasking posterior and plug-in schedules that reuse pretrained masked-diffusion weights, improving text, image, molecule, and LLaDA inference-time scaling without learning an edit head. AP-MDM learns remask controls and combines them with insertion/deletion plus formal memory-reuse claims, but supplies no comparable natural-language or large-model remasking evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Any-Order Flexible Length Masked Diffusion
reviewed_competitors.difference: FlexMDM starts from the empty string, learns an insertion expectation and unmasking posterior through a joint stochastic interpolant, proves target-distribution and any-order sampling guarantees, and retrofits LLaDA-8B with gains on GSM8K and code infilling. AP-MDM offers the broader remask/insert/delete operation set and computational expressivity analysis; FlexMDM has stronger probabilistic grounding and real 8B evidence for variable length but does not address arbitrary memory rewrite or PSPACE simulation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Edit Flows: Flow Matching with Edit Operations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Edit Flows defines insertion, deletion, and substitution rates in a sequence-level CTMC, trains them tractably with auxiliary alignments and flow matching, and evaluates 280M-1.3B models on captions, text, and code. AP-MDM's mask-centric operations, learned backtracking, and PRAM analysis are distinct, but Edit Flows predates its all-edit framing and provides substantially stronger scaled generative evidence; AP-MDM instead excels on controlled algorithm-trace tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fine-Tuning Masked Diffusion for Provable Self-Correction
reviewed_competitors.difference: PRISM learns a calibrated per-token quality scalar with a lightweight adapter and a provable likelihood target, then remasks low-quality tokens in the current state; current results cover Sudoku, 170M text, and 8B code. AP-MDM's remask bit is part of a more general edit controller and supports global formal simulations, but its proposed corruption-detection remask loss is not tested and has no explicit current-state quality guarantee. PRISM itself acknowledges that marginal token quality cannot capture global reasoning errors.

reviewed_competitors.title: LLaDA2.1: Speeding Up Text Diffusion via Token Editing
reviewed_competitors.difference: LLaDA2.1 trains a joint mask-to-token and token-to-token editor, revisits prior blocks, adds diffusion-specific RL, and demonstrates configurable speed-quality tradeoffs at 16B and 100B across 33 benchmarks. It lacks AP-MDM's variable-length insert/delete operations and complexity separations, but is decisive current evidence that direct rewriting scales far beyond AP-MDM's synthetic models and narrows any practical claim that learned token correction is unique to the proposed framework.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learn from Your Mistakes: Self-Correcting Masked Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: ProSeCo trains one MDM to correct samples from its own denoiser, interleaves full-token corrective loops with unmasking, and improves speed-quality tradeoffs on large math/code models, molecules, and unconditional text. AP-MDM covers insertion/deletion and stronger abstract computation claims, while ProSeCo supplies a much more realistic on-policy error distribution and extensive current evidence for learned rewriting; its main cost is a second training forward pass.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Veit et al. rewrite ResNets as paths and support the shallow-ensemble view through gradient and lesion experiments. The present paper adds a lambda-Taylor formula and scaling argument, but its nonlinear hierarchy is local rather than the fully exact infinite expansion implied by its prose.

reviewed_competitors.title: Jet Expansions of Residual Computation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. use jets, which generalize truncated Taylor series, to systematically disentangle residual computational paths for data-free interpretability and expose super-exponential recursive path structure. The present paper uses a simpler common-scale expansion to derive trainability and capacity claims rather than model-analysis tools.

reviewed_competitors.title: Batch Normalization Biases Residual Blocks Towards the Identity Function in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: De and Smith derive an order-1/sqrt(depth) initialization effect from BatchNorm and introduce SkipInit, supported by a detailed optimization study. The present paper instead derives 1/n from fixed-order functional term counts, then empirically returns toward 1/sqrt(n) for accuracy and interprets the scale as capacity control.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Loss Surface of Residual Networks: Ensembles and the Role of Batch Normalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Littwin and Wolf analyze a dynamic residual ensemble whose effective depth changes during training and identify BatchNorm scaling as the controlling mechanism using generalized spin-glass models. The present work emphasizes a direct functional lambda expansion and normalization-free branch scaling rather than critical-point statistics and ensemble dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Deep ResNet Blocks Sequentially using Boosting Theory
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. prove a multi-channel telescoping-sum boosting theory and an exponential training-error decay under a weak-learning condition, while also proposing sequential block training. The present paper's first-order sum resembles that view but studies jointly trained shared-parameter residual towers, higher-order interactions, and normalization-free scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Time Transfer: On Optimal Learning Rate and Batch Size In The Infinite Data Limit
reviewed_competitors.difference: Time Transfer already jointly studies learning rate, batch size, token horizon, critical-batch growth, loss sensitivity, and preservation under muP model scaling. The reviewed paper adds an output-operator-norm coordinate, Scion-specific exponents, depth and normalization ablations, and groupwise rates, but its joint-scaling setup and several questions directly continue this predecessor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Optimal LR Across Token Horizons
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bjorck et al. establish that longer token horizons require smaller optimal learning rates and fit a transferable horizon law. The reviewed paper jointly varies batch size and horizon and asks whether those optima share a layer norm, but it does not displace the earlier learning-rate-horizon result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Predictable Scale: Part I, Step Law -- Optimal Hyperparameter Scaling Law in Large Language Model Pretraining
reviewed_competitors.difference: Step Law fits optimal learning rate as a function of model and dataset size and optimal batch size primarily as a function of data, validated over thousands of models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, and multiple recipes. The reviewed work is narrower empirically but offers a candidate norm-based diagnostic and direct Scion measurements; it provides no matched predictive-accuracy or tuning-cost comparison to Step Law.

reviewed_competitors.title: Power Lines: Scaling Laws for Weight Decay and Batch Size in LLM Pre-training
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct batch-size and regularization scaling competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Power Lines models optimal weight decay through an AdamW timescale and reports that optimal and critical batch sizes scale with dataset size independently of model size. The reviewed paper removes weight decay in its main regime, fits a compatible batch-horizon law for Scion, and studies output norm; its raw norm target therefore does not cover the regularized regime central to Power Lines.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Deep Learning Models with Norm-Constrained LMOs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pethick et al. introduce the Scion family, layer-specific norm-ball linear minimization oracles, and model-size hyperparameter transfer. The reviewed paper uses that optimizer almost unchanged in its main experiments and contributes data/depth scaling observations, a measured norm trajectory, groupwise tuning, and a distributed implementation rather than a new optimization rule.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm
reviewed_competitors.difference: Large et al. define an architecture-composed modular norm and use it to normalize base-optimizer updates so learning rates transfer across both width and depth. The reviewed paper instead monitors a particular layer's induced norm under Scion and extends the empirical question to token horizons; its claim of depth transfer is therefore not the first norm-based width/depth transfer result.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Spectral Condition for Feature Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang, Simon, and Bernstein derive fan-out/fan-in spectral scaling of weights and updates as a condition for feature learning and recover maximal-update parameterization. The reviewed paper empirically searches for a constant trained output norm associated with minimum loss; it neither derives that value from the spectral condition nor proves that the observed configurations uniquely characterize feature learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Autoregressive Generative Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Henighan et al. fit a power law plus constant and interpret the floor through data entropy and KL divergence across several modalities; that established constant-floor explanation competes with attributing CE slowdown specifically to changing Error-Entropy share.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Neural Scaling Laws in Language and Vision
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alabdulmohsin et al. evaluate scaling laws by held-out extrapolation loss and reliable parameter estimation across 90 tasks; the reviewed paper selects its preferred component using in-sample R-squared and exponent similarity, so it does not meet this stronger predictive protocol.

reviewed_competitors.title: Broken Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Caballero et al. model bends and multiple regimes with a smoothly broken power law and benchmark extrapolation across many tasks; the reviewed paper instead seeks a component with one straight log-log regime and does not compare predictive accuracy against BNSL.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Quantization Model of Neural Scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Michaud et al. explain loss power laws through a frequency distribution over learned skills and test a gradient-based behavioral decomposition; the reviewed paper supplies an exact output-statistic decomposition but no generative theory for its exponent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Scaling Laws for Language Models: The Role of Data Quality and Training Strategies
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. show that data quality and training strategy alter observed language-model scaling; the reviewed paper pools released models without controlling those factors and therefore cannot distinguish component mechanics from training-mixture confounding.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws Are Unreliable for Downstream Tasks: A Reality Check
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lourie et al. find predictable downstream scaling in only a minority of compiled cases and emphasize setting sensitivity; the reviewed paper remains at next-token corpus metrics and offers no evidence that its cleaner component predicts downstream behavior.

Wave-PDE adds learned physical coefficients and multi-step integration; without a FNet ablation, the reported result cannot show whether the PDE structure helps beyond generic FFT mixing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tensor Programs V defines muTransfer through the full maximal-update parameterization and demonstrates widthwise hyperparameter transfer on ResNets and Transformers up to billions of parameters. AM-muP instead proposes a depth-dependent global rate for idealized CNNs and ResNets, but does not specify or test the complete per-parameter muP scaling needed to establish joint width transfer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Depth Dependence of muP Learning Rates in ReLU MLPs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jelassi et al. already derive the L^(-3/2) maximal-update rate for fully connected ReLU MLPs. This paper's potential contribution is extending that exponent to convolution and residual structure via an arithmetic-mean budget; the exponent itself and much of the sensitivity-counting template are prior work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs VI: Feature Learning in Infinite-Depth Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tensor Programs VI classifies residual block multipliers and learning-rate scalings, identifies Depth-muP for one-layer residual blocks, and finds fundamental limitations when blocks are deeper. AM-muP offers a simpler L^(-3/2) scalar law but its general m=o(L) block claim is only a proof sketch and does not engage this direct adverse result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Depthwise Hyperparameter Transfer in Residual Networks: Dynamics and Scaling Limit
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon et al. combine 1/sqrt(depth) residual branches with muP, derive a joint infinite-width/infinite-depth feature-learning limit using dynamical mean-field theory, and demonstrate depth and width transfer for convolutional ResNets and ViTs on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. AM-muP instead predicts a changing global LR and tests custom shallow blocks, so it must compare transfer error and model quality against this already validated alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Principled Architecture-aware Scaling of Hyperparameters
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. derive initialization and maximal learning rates from full DAG topology, including depth, width, convolutional kernels and path connectivity, and validate on complex NAS graphs. AM-muP deliberately reduces heterogeneous updates to one mean and often to minimal depth alone; its cleaner rule is useful only if distant-target regret beats PathSum under matched training, which is not shown. The target paper also miscites this ICLR paper as a single-author technical report.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Feature Speed Formula: a flexible approach to scale hyper-parameters of deep neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Feature Speed Formula relates feature-update magnitude at any training time to loss decay, backward magnitude and an alignment angle, recovering depth rules for MLPs and 1/sqrt(depth)-scaled ResNets. AM-muP uses a cheaper initialization-time arithmetic energy target, but does not show that this target predicts later feature speed or full-training optima.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Everett et al. study three optimizers, four parameterizations, multiple alignment assumptions and models up to 27B parameters, finding that all parameterizations can transfer and that a per-layer standard-parameterization prescription can outperform muP. AM-muP studies one global SGD rate on small homogeneous vision models, so universal practical positioning requires optimizer, per-layer-rate and scale comparisons against this broader evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Function-Space Learning Rates
reviewed_competitors.difference: FLeRM measures layerwise function-space learning rates with a few extra backward passes and transfers across width, depth, initialization scale and LoRA rank in residual MLPs and normalized transformers. AM-muP avoids measurement overhead and offers a closed-form exponent, but its unweighted hidden-state mean is less directly tied to output-function change and its distant transfer accuracy is much weaker documented.

reviewed_competitors.title: Don't be lazy: CompleteP enables compute-efficient deep transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: CompleteP argues that learning-rate transfer alone can coexist with lazy internal layers, derives a parameterization that preserves both transfer and nontrivial feature learning, and reports 12-34 percent compute-efficiency gains in large transformer training. AM-muP validates only one-epoch LR slopes in CNNs and ResNets and never measures whether deeper layers learn useful non-linear features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hyperparameter Transfer Laws for Non-Recurrent Multi-Path Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The 2026 successor retains arithmetic-mean muP and the -3/2 claim while introducing graph-based effective depth and extending experiments to Transformers. It includes the same CNN and ResNet slopes, making the present paper best viewed as an earlier architecture-limited version; current novelty claims should be assessed against what the successor adds and whether it repairs the mean-control, proof and validation gaps identified here.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Huh and colleagues argue that capable vision and language models converge toward shared relational geometry and provide the target paper's main conceptual foundation. The target adds inference-time SEE and HEAR steering plus autoregressive state pooling, but geometric similarity in either work is not by itself a causal perceptual mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Objective drives the consistency of representational similarity across datasets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ciernik and colleagues show that objective strongly shapes cross-dataset representational-similarity consistency and that correspondence with behavior is dataset-dependent. Their result motivates cross-dataset stability and cue-to-task mediation tests missing from the target's within-dataset bootstrap analysis.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This human-norm study finds that language-only models recover non-sensorimotor concept features better than sensory and motor features, with visual training improving vision-related alignment. It permits language-mediated sensory relations but cautions against relabeling the target's sensory-encoder-like neighborhood geometry as unqualified perception or human sensorimotor grounding.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Abdou and colleagues find correspondence between text-derived color-word geometry and perceptual color structure, partly mediated by collocation and syntax. The target extends this question to vision and audio encoders and actively changes geometry through generation, while the predecessor supplies a direct language-statistics explanation for the effect.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mapping Language Models to Grounded Conceptual Spaces
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work gives text-only models a few grounded examples in structured domains such as direction and color and evaluates generalization to unseen related concepts. reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct prior for explicit linear symmetry discovery
reviewed_competitors.difference: LieGAN adversarially learns interpretable Lie-algebra matrices whose transformations preserve a data distribution and demonstrates rotation and Lorentz symmetries plus reuse in equivariant models. Its representation acts linearly in observation space and its basis dimension is supplied in the reviewed experiments; LieNLSD instead handles nonlinear point-action coefficients through a feature library and derives the entire thresholded null space, while relying on differential structure and hand-tuned spectral thresholds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Latent Space Symmetry Discovery

reviewed_competitors.title: Symmetry Discovery Beyond Affine Transformations

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest earlier multiplication-specific interpretability work, already attributing failure to successive carries and cached intermediate results and reporting more than 99.9% accuracy for five-digit multiplication after targeted changes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. describe parallel digit subtasks, sequential subtask learning, carry/cache weaknesses, and formatting/architectural improvements. The target paper studies a failed matched SFT against a successful ICoT circuit, specifies a two-layer attention-cache DAG, adds Minkowski/Fourier geometry, and tests a running-sum latent target. Its broad failure explanation therefore overlaps substantially with prior carry/cache analysis even though the mechanistic objects differ.

The target holds its reversed fixed-length positional format constant and locates failure in learning partial-product dependencies; it does not compare digit-position embeddings or recurrence, so long-range optimization is not isolated from positional inductive bias.

The target explains in-distribution optimization and one learned four-digit circuit. The two accounts address distinct axes, and the target's mechanism remains untested on the length regimes central to the ACL work.

It shows that regularization can activate a succinct Transformer circuit without explicit process targets. The target studies decimal multiplication and uses ICoT or direct running-sum supervision; it does not test delayed grokking or complexity regularization as an alternative escape route.

The target's tiny models use one textual format and learn a columnar partial-product cache. The later results question whether that circuit explains real pretrained-model routing or only one trained-from-scratch solution.
