reviewed_competitors.title: Language Model Inversion
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational learned inversion from next-token probability vectors.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Morris et al. train a T5-based inverter and demonstrate exact prompt leakage from probability outputs, including 27% exact recovery for Llama-2-7B. SODA replaces amortized learning with per-example white-box search and is much stronger on short random tokens with full logits, at vastly higher per-example compute.

reviewed_competitors.title: Better Language Model Inversion by Compactly Representing Next-Token Distributions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct contemporary logprob-sequence competitor published as NeurIPS 2025.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PILS exploits the low-dimensional subspace of next-token distributions across generation steps, reaches 2-3.5 times prior exact recovery and up to 60%, handles system prompts, and supports cross-family transfer. It preceded the target's arXiv submission by 12 days, uses a more realistic multi-step logprob channel, and remains an amortized learned method rather than exact white-box token search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Extracting Prompts by Inverting LLM Outputs
reviewed_competitors.difference: output2prompt uses only normal generated text, a sparse encoding, and demonstrates cross-model zero-shot transfer. SODA achieves much higher exactness only when given weights, gradients, and logits; its text-only result remains 3.6%.

reviewed_competitors.title: DORY: Deliberative Prompt Recovery for LLM
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Black-box prompt-recovery predecessor using uncertainty and deliberation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DORY extracts prompt clues from limited outputs through a single LLM and uncertainty-guided deliberation without target gradients. It prioritizes plausible semantic recovery in an API setting rather than exact recovery of short token strings from full internal logits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reverse Prompt Engineering
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li and Klabjan use a genetic algorithm under strict zero-shot black-box conditions and target useful natural prompts from limited text outputs. This is operationally broader but does not claim SODA's token-exact reconstruction.

reviewed_competitors.title: PTP: Previous-Token Prediction based LLM Inversion for Near-Exact Prompt Reconstruction
reviewed_competitors.difference: PTP trains a model to predict previous tokens from synthetic target outputs and frames reconstruction sequentially, moving near exactness toward black-box text access. It is later than SODA and does not require differentiating through the target model, but depends on training an auxiliary inverter.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Invariant Latent Space Perspective on Language Model Inversion
reviewed_competitors.difference: Inv2A learns a lightweight inverse encoder with source and cycle invariance and combines multiple outputs in representation space, reporting gains over nine user/system-prompt datasets. It emphasizes semantic prompt recovery and amortization rather than SODA's exact short-token search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prompting Complexity: Shortest Prompts for Texts and Behaviors in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication formalization of observable prompt preimages.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cosma explicitly treats deterministic visible outputs as having a preimage set and asks for the shortest plausible generating prompt rather than assuming a unique historical cause. This formal lens directly exposes why SODA's text-output equality cannot certify original-prompt exactness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models are Injective and Hence Invertible
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication exact inversion from internal hidden states with a formal guarantee.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SIPIT proves almost-sure injectivity under stated decoder/parameter assumptions and sequentially recovers exact tokens from per-position hidden states in at most T times vocabulary trials. Its observation is far more internal than output logits, but it supplies the kind of uniqueness theorem and linear sequential structure SODA lacks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Recovering Input Text from Hidden States: Study of Gradient-Based Inversion of Decoder-Only Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication continuous optimization study for exact hidden-state inversion.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Slowikowski and Majewski retain continuous search until token commitment and use discrete commit loss to make failures observable, reaching 97.5% exact recovery on 10-token C4 prompts with a wider candidate window. The signal is hidden states rather than generated outputs, but its failure diagnostics and near-miss analysis are directly relevant to SODA.

reviewed_competitors.title: Automatically Auditing Large Language Models via Discrete Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: ARCA jointly optimizes prompts and outputs for specified auditing behaviors and was already used to reverse fixed suffixes. SODA narrows the goal to original-input recovery and replaces coordinate approximations with relaxed one-hot Adam search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Greedy Coordinate Gradient search baseline and adversarial-prompt predecessor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: GCG uses token-coordinate gradients to find suffixes that induce target behaviors and can transfer across models. SODA's relaxed joint variables are much stronger for exact short-input logit inversion, although the target implements GCG under a custom matched loss and wall-time budget rather than its original jailbreak task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hard Prompts Made Easy: Gradient-Based Discrete Optimization for Prompt Tuning and Discovery
reviewed_competitors.difference: PEZ repeatedly projects continuous prompt embeddings to vocabulary tokens and optimizes controllable hard prompts. SODA instead relaxes one-hot vocabulary coordinates and matches a known LM output, adding decay and optimizer resets to improve exact recovery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient-based Adversarial Attacks against Text Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: GBDA parameterizes a distribution over text and uses gradient optimization for adversarial examples, establishing the relaxed-discrete technique family. SODA specializes it to causal-LM inversion and attributes gains to its custom Adam decay and reset dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Was it Slander? Towards Exact Inversion of Generative Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct author-team predecessor and motivating application.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The earlier work uses genetic algorithms and particle-swarm optimization to ask whether a reported output has a causal prompt, concluding exact reconstruction is rare. SODA is the stronger white-box successor, but still cannot turn heuristic failure into a proof of nonexistence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uncovering Hidden Intentions: Exploring Prompt Recovery for Deeper Insights into Generated Texts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Give et al. study recovering likely intent from generated text in an open task setting. Its semantic objective better fits explainability, while SODA's exactness target requires much stronger access and short inputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: PRSA: Prompt Stealing Attacks against Real-World Prompt Services
reviewed_competitors.difference: PRSA targets deployed prompt services and iteratively reconstructs valuable prompts through service interactions. It is operationally realistic but optimizes semantic/function similarity rather than exact historical tokens; SODA's UI discussion should not be conflated with this black-box setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prompt Stealing Attacks Against Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prompt-service theft predecessor using black-box interactions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sha and Zhang infer protected prompts through queries to an LLM service, focusing on prompt assets and downstream performance. SODA focuses exact token causality under white-box gradients and full output information.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prompt Inversion Attack against Collaborative Inference of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prompt reconstruction from split collaborative-inference leakage.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qu et al. reconstruct prompts from shared intermediate information in collaborative inference, a distinct deployment threat with stronger internal leakage than output APIs. SODA instead consumes output signals plus the complete model and provides no split-computing defense evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Input Reconstruction Attack against Vertical Federated Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Input reconstruction from intermediate federated representations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zheng studies reconstructing private text from vertical-federated intermediate states. That leakage channel is not generated output and permits different inversion strategies; it demonstrates why SODA's output-access threat should remain separate from representation leakage.

reviewed_competitors.title: InversionView: A General-Purpose Method for Reading Information from Neural Activations
reviewed_competitors.difference: InversionView samples inputs that produce similar activations to characterize a representation's equivalence class rather than identify one historical cause. Its set-valued interpretation is a useful conceptual corrective to SODA's unique-prompt framing.

reviewed_competitors.title: InverseScope: Scalable Activation Inversion for Interpreting Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: InverseScope learns a conditional generator for distributions of activation-matching inputs and quantitatively tests feature consistency. It targets interpretable neighborhoods rather than exact output causality, and its current v3 postdates SODA with broader scaling analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Information Leakage in Embedding Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational text-reconstruction privacy attack on continuous representations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Song and Raghunathan demonstrate that text embeddings leak sensitive inputs and use relaxed token distributions for inversion. SODA transfers related optimization ideas to decoder outputs, but full logits and embeddings are distinct security boundaries.

reviewed_competitors.title: IPAD: Inverse Prompt for AI Detection - A Robust and Interpretable LLM-Generated Text Detector
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication application of prompt inversion to AI-text detection.
reviewed_competitors.difference: IPAD predicts a plausible generating prompt and uses prompt-text alignment as interpretable detection evidence, reporting robust detector gains. It shows a useful application for approximate inverse prompts, whereas SODA's exact-token criterion and white-box access are unnecessary for that goal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Trojan Detection in Large Language Models: Insights from The Trojan Detection Challenge
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Backdoor-detection benchmark underlying the target's six-trigger demonstration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maloyan et al. analyze the challenge and its detection setting across backdoored LLMs. SODA uses one released Pythia checkpoint for qualitative exact-trigger recovery but does not rerun the challenge protocol or report detector-level recall and false positives.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equilibrium Propagation: Bridging the Gap Between Energy-Based Models and Backpropagation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Equilibrium Propagation derives a local two-phase rule that computes the gradient of a well-defined global objective through physical relaxation. It is a crucial methodological comparator because HPN also claims an exact local global gradient, but HPN's displayed derivative omits the effect of W_ij on R_j.

reviewed_competitors.title: Supervised learning in physical networks: From machine learning to learning machines
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stern et al. derive physically plausible local coupled-learning rules for disordered flow and elastic networks in equilibrium or steady state. This predates HPN's plastic conductance framing and supplies direct flow-network baselines, though it optimizes externally specified input-output tasks rather than a conservation residual during a PDE solve.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physical learning beyond the quasistatic limit
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work experimentally and numerically sweeps the ratio of learning to physical relaxation rates in resistor networks, finding a critical threshold and oscillatory dynamics beyond it. That is the missing kind of evidence for HPN's eta_w invariance and adiabatic-band claims; it suggests timescale ratios can change behavior rather than merely reparameterize a path.

reviewed_competitors.title: How to Train Your Resistive Network: Generalized Equilibrium Propagation and Analytical Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Generalized Equilibrium Propagation unifies several Hebbian physical-learning rules and gives graph-theoretic exact gradients for resistor networks with strictly limited readout. It sharpens the standard HPN would need to meet for an exact local-gradient claim and offers analytical handling of the global dependencies carried through a physical network.

reviewed_competitors.title: Coercivity and Local Convergence of Physical Learning in Linear Circuits
reviewed_competitors.difference: McGinnis et al. formulate coercivity as an incidence-structure rank condition, prove local exponential convergence for specific physical-learning dynamics, and exhibit a circuit where coercivity degenerates. HPN instead assumes coercivity axiomatically and does not show that its adaptive graph satisfies or preserves it.

reviewed_competitors.title: OnsagerNet: Learning Stable and Interpretable Dynamics using a Generalized Onsager Principle
reviewed_competitors.difference: OnsagerNet explicitly separates learned free energy, positive-semidefinite diffusion, conservative skew motion, and forcing to obtain stable interpretable dynamics. HPN claims this structure emerges from its update, but does not parameterize or test positive definiteness and reciprocity of the assembled operator.

reviewed_competitors.title: PDE-Net: Learning PDEs from Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: PDE-Net learns discrete differential operators and nonlinear responses with moment/sum-rule constraints that make the recovered stencil interpretable as a derivative. HPN adapts per-edge coefficients during one solve without data, but its claim to learn constitutive geometry would benefit from PDE-Net-style consistency constraints and operator-identification tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning data driven discretizations for partial differential equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bar-Sinai et al. learn local derivative approximations end-to-end and quantify accuracy versus standard finite differences at 4-8 times coarser resolution. It is a direct empirical baseline for whether adaptive local transport coefficients improve a discretization; HPN reports no equal-resolution accuracy or cost comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: MeshGraphNets learns message passing and adaptive mesh resolution across aerodynamics, structural mechanics, and cloth, with resolution transfer and reported 1-2 order-of-magnitude speedups. It is amortized data-driven simulation rather than per-instance local relaxation, but substantially exceeds HPN's breadth, transfer, and efficiency validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics-Embedded Neural Networks: Graph Neural PDE Solvers with Mixed Boundary Conditions
reviewed_competitors.difference: PENN uses an E(n)-equivariant graph model, explicit mixed-boundary treatment, and an implicit nonlinear solver to handle long-range interactions, then reports speed-accuracy performance on flow geometries. It directly addresses boundary fidelity and global propagation, both under-specified in HPN's cavity demonstration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Graph Neural PDE Solvers with Conservation and Similarity-Equivariance
reviewed_competitors.difference: FluxGNN derives necessary architectural conditions for local conservation, connects message passing to finite-volume fluxes, preserves physical similarity symmetries, and tests generalization to unseen domains. Its antisymmetric flux construction is the most direct baseline for HPN, whose cavity update explicitly omits the outgoing conservative term.

reviewed_competitors.title: A hyperbolic relaxation system of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with artificial compressibility
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. formulate a local hyperbolic artificial-compressibility relaxation and rigorously prove its asymptotic limit to incompressible Navier-Stokes with energy error estimates. HPN's pressure update belongs to this established solver family but provides no relaxation-parameter limit, divergence error, or convergence-rate analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics Informed Deep Learning (Part I): Data-driven Solutions of Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: PINNs impose PDE residuals through a global training objective and differentiable function approximation, the top-down approach HPN contrasts against. A matched PINN baseline would reveal whether local per-edge relaxation improves conservation, accuracy, or cost rather than only changing where the residual optimization is implemented.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Structure-Preserving Graph Neural Solver for Parametric Hyperbolic Conservation Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: This graph solver learns reconstruction and numerical fluxes while enforcing local conservation and upwinding, then evaluates long-horizon stability, broad geometry/boundary variations, accuracy, and runtime speedups on supersonic flows. It illustrates the validation and discrete-structure standard needed to turn HPN's adaptive-locality idea into a competitive transport solver.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deeply-Supervised Nets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. add companion classification objectives to hidden layers to improve gradient flow and training, analyze a restricted convergence setting, and evaluate MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and SVHN. Ghost categories are cheaper output-only auxiliary parameters with no extra labels, but the reviewed evidence is far narrower and does not isolate its approach from the established general idea of training-only auxiliary supervision.

reviewed_competitors.title: New Paradigm of Adversarial Training: Breaking Inherent Trade-Off between Accuracy and Robustness via Dummy Classes

Its dummy categories have semantic training targets and a robustness purpose; ghost categories are always zero-target and intended only to perturb optimization, but the reviewed paper does not compare against this broader extra-class design space.

This is a closer empirical test of training-only architectural perturbations; ghost nodes use a simpler zero-target softmax penalty and an ergodic narrative but lack matched-capacity and mechanism controls.

This supplies concrete counterexamples to monotonic deliberate refinement while also showing how diverse guesses can strengthen the model.

The reviewed paper treats general L of moments and infers global symbolic convergence from diagonal terms without comparable convexity or feasibility conditions.

Their result does not say that a neural parameter velocity becomes equivariant or that symbolic moment optimization globally converges, which are additional claims made here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The empirical origin of delayed generalization on modular arithmetic that motivates explaining symbolic structure emergence during training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Power et al. measure how dataset size and optimization time affect generalization. The reviewed paper offers an idealized moment-flow story but performs no grokking experiment and does not connect its order parameters to delayed test generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct empirical account of structured Fourier mechanisms emerging in transformers trained on modular addition.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nanda et al. reverse engineer the learned circuit, validate it with Fourier-space ablations, and track continuous progress through memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. The reviewed paper proposes moments as progress variables but never measures or intervenes on them.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking modular arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A closely matched study of two-layer networks learning modular arithmetic and identifiable task-structured feature maps.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gromov gives analytic solution weights and empirical evidence that vanilla gradient descent and AdamW find the predicted feature maps. The reviewed paper generalizes more abstractly but offers neither a realizable equivariant architecture nor empirical evidence that its target measure solutions are found.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature emergence via margin maximization: case studies in algebraic tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A competing theory for why Fourier and representation-theoretic features emerge on modular addition, sparse parity, and finite-group operations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Morwani et al. derive learned features from margin maximization and cover general finite groups through irreducible representations. The reviewed paper instead invokes a measure semiring and equivariant flow, but its exact symmetry prevents the odd target moments from emerging.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Do You Grok? A Theoretical Analysis of Grokking Modular Addition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A formal and empirical explanation of modular-addition grokking for the same two-layer quadratic model family.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mohamadi et al. separate an early kernel regime from later feature learning, prove a sample barrier for permutation-equivariant kernel-like models, and analyze bounded-norm quadratic networks trained with regularization. reviewed_competitors.difference: Cao et al. operationalize the learned-interface/formal-backend route on 18,000 instruction pairs and expose separate task accuracies. reviewed_competitors.title: Stress-Testing the Reasoning Competence of Language Models With Formal Proofs

reviewed_competitors.difference: ProofGrid supplies adversarially diagnostic tasks and detailed empirical failure modes for contemporary reasoning models. The target paper provides a theory for why any finite distributional benchmark can miss rare errors, suggesting ProofGrid should be paired with exhaustive generators or proof certificates rather than treated as exactness evidence.

It is more directly testable than an all-input exact-risk objective, but it still cannot prove equivalence outside the observed dependency suite.

This weakens any generic curriculum prescription and supports the target paper's narrower point that teaching data must depend on the target and learner rather than difficulty alone.

reviewed_competitors.difference: STA uses hardware-aware sliding 3D tiles and an optimized kernel, reaching stronger raw latency in Table 1 but worse dense-output similarity. It provides a simpler locality prior without Radial's logarithmic far-frame sampling or flawed decay theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient-vDiT: Efficient Video Diffusion Transformers With Attention Tile
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier video-specific static tiled-attention and distillation system.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Efficient-vDiT identifies repeating tile patterns with frame-linear attention and combines them with few-step consistency distillation, reporting 7.4-7.8x end-to-end acceleration. Radial isolates sparse attention and length LoRA, but does not compare against the joint architecture-sampling alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: DSV: Exploiting Dynamic Sparsity to Accelerate Large-Scale Video DiT Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: DSV uses two-stage dynamic sparsity plus sparsity-aware context parallelism and reports up to 3.02x training throughput. It directly targets training and communication heterogeneity that Radial's static mask and hours-only accounting leave unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse VideoGen: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Spatial-Temporal Sparsity
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct dynamic sparse-attention predecessor and main baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SVG profiles heads online and switches between spatial and temporal masks, achieving up to 2.33x end-to-end acceleration. Radial avoids online classification and supports training, but Table 1 shows near-tied or weaker quality-latency results and no variance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training-free and Adaptive Sparse Attention for Efficient Long Video Generation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier online adaptive long-video sparse-attention competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaSpa caches log-sum-exp information across denoising steps and performs head-adaptive hierarchical block search without fine-tuning or offline profiling. It trades mask-decision overhead for input and head adaptation, directly challenging Radial's uniform static-mask assumption.

reviewed_competitors.title: SpargeAttention: Accurate and Training-free Sparse Attention Accelerating Any Model Inference
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Generic dynamic sparse-and-quantized attention competitor evaluated on video.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SpargeAttention predicts blocks online and applies a softmax-aware second filter across language, image, and video models. Radial is structurally cheaper and training-compatible, while SpargeAttention is more input-adaptive and model-general.

reviewed_competitors.title: XAttention: Block Sparse Attention with Antidiagonal Scoring
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary block-importance competitor covering video generation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: XAttention scores block antidiagonals as a cheap importance proxy and reports up to 13.5x attention acceleration across long-context tasks. It adapts blocks to actual scores, whereas Radial commits to a video-prior mask before seeing content.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalized Neighborhood Attention: Multi-dimensional Sparse Attention at the Speed of Light
reviewed_competitors.difference: GNA unifies sliding, strided, and blocked neighborhoods, supplies a hardware simulator, and reports 28-46% end-to-end gains on Cosmos, HunyuanVideo, and FLUX on B200. It offers native multidimensional geometry and performance modeling absent from Radial's flattened-index construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: VSA: Faster Video Diffusion with Trainable Sparse Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: VSA learns block-friendly critical-token selection end to end, reports a 2.53x training-FLOP reduction in a 60M-1.4B scaling sweep, and retrofits Wan2.1. It appeared five weeks before Radial and provides much stronger scaling evidence for training-time sparsity, at the cost of a learned selector.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse VideoGen2: Accelerate Video Generation with Sparse Attention via Semantic-Aware Permutation
reviewed_competitors.difference: SVG2 clusters and permutes semantically similar tokens, uses dynamic top-p budgets, and reports up to 2.30x speedup. It addresses the failure of position-only neighborhoods to capture semantic blocks, precisely the risk in Radial's fixed flattened-index bands.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training-Free Efficient Video Generation via Dynamic Token Carving
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jenga combines dynamic block carving along 3D space-filling curves with progressive latent resolution and reports up to 8.83x end-to-end speedup. Its broader system changes complicate attribution but give a stronger measured frontier than Radial's attention-only optimization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse-vDiT: Unleashing the Power of Sparse Attention to Accelerate Video Diffusion Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sparse-vDiT profiles diagonal, multi-diagonal, vertical-stripe, and skippable-head patterns offline and performs hardware-aware per-head search, reporting 1.58-1.85x actual speedups on three backbones. It retains static execution while adapting pattern choice across heads and layers, a middle ground Radial omits.

reviewed_competitors.title: FPSAttention: Training-Aware FP8 and Sparsity Co-Design for Fast Video Diffusion
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct pre-submission training-aware sparsity and quantization competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: FPSAttention jointly trains denoising-step-aware 3D tile sparsity and FP8 kernels and reports 4.96x end-to-end Wan speedup. It shows that precision and sparsity interactions can dominate a fixed BF16 mask comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: VMoBA: Mixture-of-Block Attention for Video Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Immediate post-submission video-native trainable block-routing successor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: VMoBA adds recurrent 1D/2D/3D block partitioning, global block selection, and cumulative-similarity thresholds, reporting 2.92x training FLOPs and 1.48x training latency reduction plus training-free inference gains. It directly addresses head-specific and spatial-layout heterogeneity.

reviewed_competitors.title: PowerAttention: Exponentially Scaling of Receptive Fields for Effective Sparse Attention
reviewed_competitors.relationship: O(n log n) static sparse baseline adapted by the paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PowerAttention attends at power-of-two distances to grow receptive fields exponentially across LLM layers. Radial adds video-specific spatial-temporal geometry and performs better in the target's point estimates, but the baseline was designed for causal language modeling rather than bidirectional video diffusion.

reviewed_competitors.title: LongLoRA: Efficient Fine-tuning of Long-Context Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: LongLoRA combines shifted sparse training attention with improved LoRA while retaining dense global inference. The target adapts it to video as a baseline; at Hunyuan 4x it trains slightly faster than Radial and has better imaging quality but lower VisionReward.

reviewed_competitors.title: RIFLEx: A Free Lunch for Length Extrapolation in Video Diffusion Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: RIFLEx modifies one intrinsic RoPE frequency and enables 2x extrapolation without training, with minimal tuning for 3x. It does not accelerate attention, but exposes how much of length extension can be obtained without Radial's new mask or training data.

reviewed_competitors.title: LinGen: Towards High-Resolution Minute-Length Text-to-Video Generation with Linear Computational Complexity
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier architectural alternative for long-video scaling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: LinGen replaces self-attention with a linear Mamba-plus-temporal-window block and reports minute-length single-GPU generation with up to 11.5x latency reduction. It requires training a new backbone rather than retrofitting dense models, but offers true joint token-linear architecture evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Frame Context Packing and Drift Prevention in Next-Frame-Prediction Video Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Alternative constant-context route to long video.
reviewed_competitors.difference: FramePack compresses history into a fixed context and adds anti-drift sampling, making workload invariant to generated length. It changes generation factorization and can stream, whereas Radial preserves bidirectional full-sequence DiTs and retains growing O(n log n) work.

reviewed_competitors.title: SANA: Efficient High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Linear Diffusion Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Linear-attention architecture baseline adapted by the paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SANA combines aggressive latent compression and linear DiT attention, designed and trained end to end for images. The target's poor SANA fine-tuning results do not establish that linear video architectures fail, because the replacement is applied post hoc to a softmax-trained video model.

reviewed_competitors.title: VBench-2.0: Advancing Video Generation Benchmark Suite for Intrinsic Faithfulness
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary evaluation benchmark that narrows the target's metric claims.
reviewed_competitors.difference: VBench-2.0 adds physics, commonsense, anatomy, composition, controllability, and creativity because earlier metrics capture superficial faithfulness. Radial reports only three VBench-Long dimensions, leaving many intrinsic failures unmeasured.

reviewed_competitors.title: FG-Attn: Leveraging Fine-Grained Sparse Attention in Video Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: FG-Attn skips M-by-1 slices with an asynchronous gather-load kernel and reports up to 1.65x speedup. It demonstrates that Radial's coarse block granularity leaves exploitable vector-level sparsity, while requiring more irregular hardware support.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention Sparsity is Input-Stable: Training-Free Sparse Attention for Video Generation via Offline Sparsity Profiling and Online QK Co-Clustering
reviewed_competitors.difference: SVOO profiles intrinsic per-layer sparsity offline and co-clusters Q and K online, reporting up to 1.93x speedup across seven models. It keeps most static execution benefits while addressing the layer heterogeneity and query-key coupling ignored by Radial.

reviewed_competitors.title: VecAttention: Vector-wise Sparse Attention for Accelerating Long Context Inference
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later vector-granularity competitor for video generation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: VecAttention selects informative vertical vectors and reports 2.65x over full attention and 1.83x over sparse baselines on video tasks. Its observed vertical-vector structure directly challenges a single diagonal-band prior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Veda: Scalable Video Diffusion via Distilled Sparse Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: Veda explicitly reconstructs dense tile geometry using statistics-aware scores and head-aware tiling and reports 5.1x end-to-end acceleration for 720p ten-second Waver generation. It turns mask quality into a supervised reconstruction objective rather than assuming an average decay law.

reviewed_competitors.title: LVSA: Training-Free Sparse Attention for Long Video Diffusion
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later long-video static-pattern and evaluation successor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: LVSA uses a structured window with rotating global anchors and introduces VQeval because looped videos can score well on VBench-Long. It reports up to 3.33x compute reduction and directly exposes the target's missing loop-sensitive validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: HEART: Exploiting Head Heterogeneity in Sparse Attention for Video Diffusion
reviewed_competitors.difference: HEART reuses masks based on query-key drift and allocates per-head budgets using measured model-output error, improving XAttention and SVG2 up to 1.93x. Its design directly addresses the head heterogeneity and error-budget calibration absent from Radial.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sol-Attn: Accelerating Video Generation Inference via On-the-Fly Attention Sparsification
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sol-Attn fuses threshold routing with online softmax and reuses proxy scores to approximate dropped blocks, reporting 2.1x video-generation acceleration. It reduces the routing-overhead argument for choosing a fully static mask and preserves information from rejected blocks.

reviewed_competitors.title: DSA: Efficient Serving For Video Generation Models via Distributed Sparse Attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: DSA co-designs sparse spatial and temporal patterns with communication and sequence parallelism, reporting up to 1.43x over an existing distributed method and 10.79x over single-GPU dense inference on eight GPUs. Radial reports eight-GPU long-video latency but does not analyze communication or scaling efficiency.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2026 conference paper, official OpenReview PDF checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: SPADE: An Input-Adaptive Sparse Attention Engine for Fast Video Diffusion Models Inference
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Latest pre-cutoff input-adaptive video sparse-attention engine.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SPADE specifies 3D candidate blocks, synthesizes runtime schemes, groups kernels, and reports 1.49-1.80x end-to-end gains across Hunyuan and Wan models. It represents the current hardware-aware adaptive alternative to Radial's fixed mask.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention-based clustering
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maulen-Soto et al. analyze a simplified two-head attention layer on Gaussian mixtures, prove population-risk alignment with mixture centroids, and study training-free in-context quantization. The target instead gives an explicit encoder-decoder circuit for exact iterative Lloyd updates and a separately trained update rule, but lacks the competitor's population-risk learning analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Set Transformer: A Framework for Attention-based Permutation-Invariant Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Set Transformer supplies permutation-invariant attention encoder-decoder modules and learned inducing points for set tasks, including clustering-style outputs. It learns generic set functions and does not provide an exact Lloyd circuit or a component-wise map to classical clustering updates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Clustering Processes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural Clustering Processes learn to sample well-defined posterior cluster labels for arbitrary dataset size and potentially unbounded component count. The target executes deterministic centroid iterations with fixed k and optimizes k-means objective rather than approximating a generative-model posterior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Sets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Deep Sets characterizes invariant and equivariant set functions through pooled representations and demonstrates several set tasks. The target uses explicit point and center token types to unroll a specific algorithm, trading universality for interpretability and exact update semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Set2Graph: Learning Graphs From Sets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Set2Graph universally approximates continuous set-to-graph functions and treats clustering as learned pairwise or hypergraph structure. The target maintains explicit centers and assignments and reproduces iterative k-means rather than predicting a relation graph in one generic learned map.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spatial Transformer K-Means
reviewed_competitors.difference: Spatial Transformer K-Means learns transformation-invariant similarity while preserving clustering in input space and convergence guarantees. The target learns the update circuit itself and studies multiple algorithm variants, but its learned model loses to Lloyd on every reported real dataset and has no analogous convergence guarantee.

reviewed_competitors.title: The emergence of clusters in self-attention dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geshkovski et al. prove asymptotic clustering of token particles under fixed self-attention dynamics and characterize limiting objects from the value-matrix spectrum. The target instead supplies separate center tokens and exact finite-iteration Lloyd semantics; it does not analyze spontaneous representation clustering.

reviewed_competitors.title: A mathematical perspective on Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work develops an interacting-particle framework in which clusters emerge at long depth. The target's clusters are solutions to an externally defined k-means problem with explicit initialization and center registers, not emergent attractors of generic token dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers learn in-context by gradient descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Von Oswald et al. construct linear self-attention equivalent to a regression gradient step and show trained weights can match that mesa-optimizer. The target extends exact algorithm realization to unsupervised Lloyd updates with standard selective attention, but its learned weights do not match its construction as closely.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Execution of Graph Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural Execution trains graph networks to imitate intermediate steps of breadth-first search, Bellman-Ford, and Prim and studies transfer among algorithms. The target analytically programs a transformer for Lloyd before learning, yielding exact semantics but a much narrower task family and no algorithm-transfer experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context learning and Occam's razor
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior with the same central claim
reviewed_competitors.difference: Elmoznino et al. prove that next-token loss is equivalent to prequential coding and thus jointly pressures fit and learned-model complexity. The target instead directly tests inference-time selection between explicit nested classes in Markov, regression, PCFG, and Boolean settings.

reviewed_competitors.title: What and How does In-Context Learning Learn? Bayesian Model Averaging, Parameterization, and Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work derives Bayesian model averaging, regret, approximation, and pretraining generalization bounds for latent-variable ICL. The target contributes an empirical ambiguity test over nested complexity classes but lacks comparable finite-sample or optimization guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning through the Bayesian Prism
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Bayesian Prism already trains on unions of multiple linear and nonlinear function families and compares transformers with tractable Bayesian predictors. The target isolates strict nesting and asks which sufficient class is selected under exact prompt ambiguity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring Inductive Biases of In-Context Learning with Underspecified Demonstrations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Si et al. use demonstrations where two NLP features are equally predictive to measure which feature GPT-3 selects and how instructions or label words alter that choice. The target studies parameterized complexity classes and Bayesian penalties rather than semantic feature preferences.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Can Transformers Learn In-Context? A Case Study of Simple Function Classes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Garg et al. show transformers can match task-specific estimators for linear, sparse linear, neural-network, and tree classes. The target places nested classes in one pretraining mixture and focuses on class selection when multiple estimators interpolate the same context.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper traces a uniform-to-unigram-to-bigram training phase transition and identifies statistical induction heads on first-order Markov tasks. The target mixes different true orders and studies selection among complexity classes, without an equally detailed head-level mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: ICLL evaluates regular-language generation and attributes transformer performance to higher-order n-gram heads, including natural-language-model improvements from hard-wiring them. The target's PCFG case instead tests simple-versus-complex grammar inference and is much smaller and distribution-shifted.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pretraining task diversity and the emergence of non-Bayesian in-context learning for regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Raventos et al. vary the number of pretraining regressors and observe a transition from a finite-prior Bayesian estimator to ridge regression over new tasks. The target holds a mixture of two nested dimensions and asks which class-specific interpolator is selected per prompt.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dual Operating Modes of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dual Operating Modes derives exact task-group posteriors and distinguishes pretrained-skill retrieval from learning a new task, including early ascent. The target's class hierarchy is nested by expressivity and its core stress test gives both classes zero training error.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning Is Provably Bayesian Inference: A Generalization Theory for Meta-Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later paper bounds Bayes Gap and Posterior Variance for diverse task mixtures and shows exponential disappearance of task-mixture uncertainty with context. It supplies finite-sample theory absent from the target but does not test least-complex sufficient class selection under the target's ambiguity construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: DPOT: Auto-Regressive Denoising Operator Transformer for Large-Scale PDE Pre-Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: DPOT predates PhysiX with autoregressive denoising pretraining of operators up to 0.5B parameters on more than ten PDE datasets and over 100,000 trajectories, including downstream 3D transfer. PhysiX scales parameters much further and imports video priors/discrete tokens, but omits this direct foundation-model baseline from experiments and remains 2D-only.

reviewed_competitors.title: Poseidon: Efficient Foundation Models for PDEs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Poseidon uses a multiscale operator transformer, continuous-time conditioning, and semigroup-based data augmentation, then evaluates sample-efficient transfer on 15 downstream tasks including unseen physics. It is smaller and operator-centric, while PhysiX emphasizes a 4.5B video-token route; matched accuracy, transfer, and inference efficiency are not reported.

reviewed_competitors.title: PDE-Transformer: Efficient and Versatile Transformers for Physics Simulations
reviewed_competitors.difference: PDE-Transformer trains across 16 PDE types using channel-wise spatiotemporal tokens and reports transfer gains over other physics foundation architectures. It targets continuous regular-grid fields without video-style discrete quantization; its contemporaneous ICML 2025 evidence makes PhysiX's unqualified 'first foundation model' wording defensible only under a narrow large-scale/autoregressive definition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Foundation Models for Scientific Machine Learning: Characterizing Scaling and Transfer Behavior
reviewed_competitors.difference: Subramanian et al. systematically vary pretrained size, downstream data, out-of-distribution physics parameters, and mixed-physics transfer, finding stronger fine-tuning gains with scale. PhysiX reaches a much larger backbone and broader benchmark domains but offers only three non-monotonic scratch sizes and two fully fine-tuned held-out tasks.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2023 proceedings version, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36

reviewed_competitors.title: PDE-Refiner: Achieving Accurate Long Rollouts with Neural PDE Solvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: PDE-Refiner diagnoses loss of nondominant spatial frequencies, uses multistep diffusion-style refinement, evaluates spectral fidelity and predictive uncertainty, and compares with neural, numerical, and hybrid solvers. PhysiX's refinement is a deterministic pixel-space corrector and its Well comparison omits these physics/uncertainty diagnostics.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Well: a Large-Scale Collection of Diverse Physics Simulations for Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Well provides 15TB across 16 simulation datasets and the FNO/TFNO/U-Net baselines used by PhysiX. PhysiX trains on only eight 2D datasets and explicitly inherits unresolved baseline reproducibility issues, so conclusions should be tied to that subset and code version.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks proceedings version; DOI 10.52202/079017-1430

reviewed_competitors.title: Cosmos World Foundation Model Platform for Physical AI
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cosmos supplies the causal FSQ tokenizer and 4B autoregressive video checkpoint that make PhysiX's scale affordable and provides broad video world-model priors. PhysiX's contribution is domain adaptation to numerical fields, heterogeneous channels, and task-specific precision refinement rather than a new large-scale transformer from scratch.

reviewed_competitors.title: Walrus: A Cross-Domain Foundation Model for Continuum Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Walrus trains a 1.3B transformer on nineteen 2D and 3D scenarios, adds harmonic-analysis-based rollout stabilization and compute-adaptive tokenization, and reports stronger short/long-horizon transfer than prior foundation models. It directly addresses PhysiX's 2D, fixed-tokenization, and stability limitations with fewer parameters.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards a Physics Foundation Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: GPhyT is trained on 1.8TB across fluid-solid, shock, convection, and multiphase dynamics and claims in-context zero-shot generalization to unseen physical systems with stable 50-step rollouts. That is the train-once capability PhysiX explicitly lacks and is a more stringent foundation-model validation than full tokenizer/backbone fine-tuning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differential learning kinetics govern the transition from memorization to generalization during in-context learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work models memorizing and generalizing subcircuits as largely independent learners with different rates and derives a memorization scaling law. The target instead fits posterior odds from loss and compressed predictor complexity without identifying or intervening on circuits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Strategy Coopetition identifies ICL and context-constrained in-weights learning, shows shared subcircuits, and proposes a minimal interaction model. The target's two Bayesian endpoints give a stronger quantitative behavioral fit but no shared-circuit mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Competition Dynamics Shape Algorithmic Phases of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper decomposes behavior on finite mixtures of Markov chains into four retrieval-or-inference by unigram-or-bigram algorithms. The target supplies a top-down loss-complexity posterior for two endpoints but does not validate its proposed extension to four strategies.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamics of Transient Structure in In-Context Linear Regression Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work explains transient ridge behavior through Bayesian internal model selection and measures architecture-dependent complexity with the local learning coefficient. The target adds a quantitative three-parameter prediction across three tasks but relies on external code compression and a manual exception.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Transient Nature of Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper establishes that ICL can emerge and then yield to in-weights learning and tests regularization as a stabilizer. The target attempts to predict the transition time and diversity boundary with loss-complexity odds rather than only documenting transience.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pretraining task diversity and the emergence of non-Bayesian in-context learning for regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work reports a diversity threshold where transformers leave the Bayes estimator under the finite pretraining prior and behave like ridge regression over unseen tasks. The target reframes both finite-prior and continuous-prior behaviors as Bayesian under different candidate assumptions and predicts their posterior weighting.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context learning and Occam's razor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Elmoznino et al. connect next-token loss to prequential coding and an Occam objective over in-context models. The target operationalizes a related loss-complexity idea as fitted posterior odds over two explicit strategies and tests training-time crossovers.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning through the Bayesian Prism
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Bayesian Prism studies hierarchical mixtures of linear and nonlinear function families and when transformers mimic or depart from Bayes prediction. The target narrows to two tractable predictors and adds a fitted theory of how their preference changes during pretraining.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dual Operating Modes of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work derives a closed-form posterior for task retrieval and task learning within multi-group linear regression and explains early ascent as mistaken retrieval. The target models memorizing-generalizing selection across pretraining time and diversity rather than context-length-dependent retrieval error.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning Is Provably Bayesian Inference: A Generalization Theory for Meta-Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later work gives finite-sample Bayes-Gap and Posterior-Variance bounds for task mixtures and a uniform-attention transformer. It provides statistical guarantees absent from the target, while not modeling the target's empirical memorization-generalization crossover or implementation-complexity prior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Progressive Neural Networks

reviewed_competitors.title: Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks

reviewed_competitors.title: Continual Learning Through Synaptic Intelligence

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory Aware Synapses: Learning what (not) to forget
reviewed_competitors.difference: MAS estimates parameter importance online from output-function sensitivity using unlabeled samples, then penalizes important changes. KappaTune requires no samples but substitutes matrix conditioning for functional sensitivity; the target paper never tests whether that substitution preserves the same parameters or capabilities.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Explanation of In-context Learning as Implicit Bayesian Inference
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor for latent-concept inference from a mixture of HMMs under next-token pretraining, including the same short-context ascent that the reviewed paper calls the KL bump.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xie et al. prove and test ICL emergence under a prompt/pretraining mismatch and evaluate GINC accuracy; they do not build the 12,288-task compositional MetaHMM oracle or a diffusion-sampled mitigation. Because the reviewed paper explicitly says Xie et al.'s Figure 7 already noticed the transient bump, the bump itself is not new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory-Based Meta-Learning on Non-Stationary Distributions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Omitted direct predecessor for testing neural sequential predictors against known Bayes-optimal algorithms under log-loss meta-learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Genewein et al. study piecewise-stationary Bernoulli sources with latent switches and show Transformers, LSTMs, and RNNs can approximate exact Bayesian predictors, including out-of-distribution tests. MetaHMM instead fixes one latent HMM per sequence and focuses on an early ambiguity gap plus a sampled retrofit; the earlier paper already occupies the broad claim of an exact-oracle sequence meta-learning benchmark.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Bayes-optimality: meta-learning what you know you don't know
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct conceptual predecessor for ambiguity-sensitive meta-learning motivated by bounded and non-Bayes-optimal behavior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Grau-Moya et al. train R2D2 ensembles and a meta-policy to distinguish familiar risk from novel-task ambiguity in reward-driven urn and grid-world decisions. Their ambiguity is support novelty and controls action preference, whereas the reviewed paper treats within-support posterior entropy during passive next-token prediction and varies Monte Carlo samples.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct benchmark predecessor for probabilistic sequence meta-learning over unknown finite automata and for comparing sequence architectures on next-token distributions; also the subject of a factual related-work error in the reviewed paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Akyürek et al. define the integrated Bayes predictor but explicitly say no general efficient computation is known. Their evaluated baselines are in-context n-grams and Baum–Welch, and TVD is to the sampled language, not the integrated oracle; thus MetaHMM genuinely adds a tractable exact posterior predictive, but the reviewed paper is wrong that RegBench already compared models with a Bayesian oracle. RegBench otherwise emphasizes architectures and n-gram heads rather than ambiguity-adaptive sampling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Competition Dynamics Shape Algorithmic Phases of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Omitted, especially close predecessor using a finite mixture of Markov chains, next-token KL, context-length sweeps, and explicit inference-versus-retrieval algorithms.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. explain early ascent and other non-monotonic context effects as phase competition among unigram/bigram retrieval and inference strategies, validated by KL to candidate algorithms. The reviewed paper instead attributes its bump to underallocated latent-posterior computation without testing those alternative algorithms; MetaHMM's compositional HMMs and diffusion retrofit remain different, but the causal interpretation is narrowed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Constrained Belief Updates Explain Geometric Structures in Transformer Representations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous direct analysis of next-token Transformers on a tractable HMM family through Bayesian belief updates.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Piotrowski et al. derive how attention's architectural constraints yield partial Bayesian updates and predict attention, OV-vector, embedding, and belief-simplex geometry. They do not study a posterior over thousands of task generators or adaptive sampling, but their constrained-update account provides another architecture-level explanation for departures from the optimal predictor that MetaHMM does not distinguish.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does learning the right latent variables necessarily improve in-context learning?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct same-team predecessor for explicitly extracting a task latent through a Transformer bottleneck and testing whether a downstream predictor can use that representation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mittal et al. find that their bottleneck recovers task-relevant latents but downstream processing often cannot use them for robust prediction, so correct latent extraction alone does not generally improve out-of-distribution ICL. Their tasks are conditionally independent regression and classification examples rather than autoregressive HMM sequences, and their latent is not diffusion-sampled or Monte Carlo marginalized; nevertheless, the result is a particularly relevant alternative explanation for why MetaHMM's sampled proxy can fail at larger scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: We're Afraid Language Models Aren't Modeling Ambiguity
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct natural-language predecessor showing that next-token language models fail to preserve genuine semantic ambiguity in their predictive distributions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. compare model distributions with ambiguous linguistic interpretations and human uncertainty rather than using a known latent generator and exact Bayesian oracle. Their evidence is closer to deployed language, while the reviewed paper supplies mechanistic synthetic control; the latter does not test whether its retrofit repairs the natural-language failures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Clarify When Necessary: Resolving Ambiguity Through Interaction with LMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct alternative that estimates intent entropy and allocates clarification actions to reducible ambiguity instead of passively averaging hypotheses.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang and Choi decompose clarification into deciding when to ask, what to ask, and how to use the answer; their intent-sim selector doubles the gain of random selection when only 10% of examples may be clarified across QA, translation, and NLI. That changes the evidence state and evaluates natural language, whereas the reviewed method cannot act, assumes a fixed prefix, and spends researcher-selected diffusion samples.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor for difficulty-conditioned allocation of language-model test-time compute and for compute-matched comparison against parameter scaling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Snell et al. adapt search or response-distribution updates per prompt, report more than 4x efficiency over best-of-N, and show a smaller model can beat a 14x larger one in a FLOPs-matched regime where the small model has nontrivial success. Their signal is problem difficulty and verifier/search performance rather than a latent-task posterior; the reviewed paper offers a Bayesian sampling interpretation but neither learns a budget rule nor performs the corresponding FLOPs-matched test.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning How Hard to Think: Input-Adaptive Allocation of LM Computation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Especially direct predecessor for learning an input-conditioned computation budget rather than sweeping one global sample count.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damani et al. predict the reward distribution for each input and budget, then allocate adaptive best-of-k samples or route between cheap and expensive decoders. Across programming, mathematics, and dialogue they reduce compute by up to 50% at unchanged quality or improve quality by up to 10% at fixed budget. They do not use a latent-task posterior or exact oracle, but they implement the adaptive allocator that the reviewed paper motivates without demonstrating.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning Strategies Emerge Rationally
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-concurrent resource-rational account of Transformer next-token behavior under latent task mixtures and computational constraints.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wurgaft et al. use a hierarchical Bayesian observer over memorizing and generalizing strategies, with a loss-versus-complexity tradeoff that predicts model outputs throughout training. They do not propose an ambiguity-triggered predictor or MetaHMM, but their strategy-complexity account is a concrete alternative to the reviewed paper's unmeasured claim that the bump reflects too little per-token capacity.

reviewed_competitors.title: What does a Bayes-filtered transformer believe? A predictive Monte Carlo approach
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication direct continuation combining Bayes-filtered sequence meta-learning, latent-task posteriors, and predictive Monte Carlo.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Aswadi, Ma, and Wei roll out an already trained Transformer and use sufficient statistics of completions to recover its implicit prior and posterior over 0-Markov and 1-Markov task families; their Monte Carlo is an interpretability diagnostic, not a diffusion sampler used to improve next-token predictions. They also show why prediction-space agreement cannot uniquely identify latent beliefs, directly delimiting what MetaHMM's Div metric establishes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Dynamic Compute Allocation in Recurrent Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication direct work on token-level variable compute with synthetic tasks whose underlying complexity and ambiguity can be controlled.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Moosa et al.'s ANIRA recurrent Transformer varies depth per token and finds that allocation can align with task complexity without explicit difficulty labels; on grammar tasks, recurrent depth tracks parse-space ambiguity rather than a latent-generator posterior. It also finds that aligned allocation does not ensure extrapolation and distinguishes early static-cue decisions from online halting. Unlike fixed-S MetaHMM sweeps, ANIRA actually executes a per-token compute policy, but it lacks an exact Bayesian predictive target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring in-context algorithmic reasoning in language models against an exact Bayes-optimal standard
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-publication exact-oracle sequence-ICL benchmark and the closest current expansion from a small synthetic HMM family to broad algorithmic hypotheses and served foundation models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zenil and Ozelim's F-ICL exhaustively enumerates 1.5 billion bounded Turing programs, computes a closed-form Bayes posterior under a bounded universal prior, and compares served distributions from 105 configurations over 37 open models plus frontier systems. It finds 45 of 46 distribution-exposing models farther from the optimum than a keystroke reference, 6,545 solved-to-unsolved updates, and no scale closure. It has no diffusion mitigation or compute allocator, but it provides the real-model exact-oracle validation absent from MetaHMM.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploring the Limits of Feature Learning in Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct preliminary version from substantially the same author group.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The NeurIPS 2024 workshop paper already reports the core empirical claims: gamma_0-controlled lazy/rich interpolation, increasing feature drift with forgetting, an optimum near 0.1 that transfers across widths, width helping only through laziness, and task-similarity shifts. The ICML paper's clearest additions are the two-layer DMFT treatment, infinite-width simulations, deeper appendices, and expanded depth/landscape analysis, rather than the empirical headline itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Wide Neural Networks Forget Less Catastrophically
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical predecessor on width and catastrophic forgetting.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mirzadeh et al. report that wider networks forget less and discuss lazy dynamics, gradient orthogonality, and sparsity. The target paper's useful refinement is to show that this trend appears under NTP but largely disappears when muP preserves feature updates across widths; it does not overturn the earlier result under its original parameterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Disconnect Between Theory and Practice of Neural Networks: Limits of the NTK Perspective
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct counterevidence on the practical relevance of width-induced NTK behavior, including continual learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wenger et al. show that practical architectures and longer training do not retain the expected NTK advantages. The target paper reinterprets the continual-learning result as longer training inducing richer dynamics, but its own gamma_0 experiment couples richness to the learning rate and explicitly leaves that confound unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Theoretical Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting through the NTK Overlap Matrix
reviewed_competitors.difference: Doan et al. characterize forgetting through NTK overlap and analyze projected-gradient mitigation in the fixed-feature regime. The target paper extends the dynamical variables to evolving feature and gradient kernels at infinite width, but only for a one-hidden-layer fixed-data model and without a clean closed-form rich-regime forgetting result.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Joint Effect of Task Similarity and Over-Parameterization on Catastrophic Forgetting — An Analytical Model
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct analytical competitor on task similarity, scale, and forgetting.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goldfarb et al. derive an exact finite-dimensional expression for two-task linear regression and show that similarity interacts non-monotonically with overparameterization. The target paper studies nonlinear feature-learning dynamics and convolutional experiments, but its Appendix E ultimately recovers only the known lazy linear dependence on similarity and stops before a rich correction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Order Parameters and Phase Transitions of Continual Learning in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent statistical-mechanics theory of task relations, architecture, and phase transitions in deep continual learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shan, Li, and Sompolinsky use a Gibbs formulation and task-relation order parameters, covering deep wide networks, single- versus multi-head behavior, forgetting, anterograde interference, width/depth, and similarity-driven phase transitions. The target instead models fixed-data gradient-descent dynamics and varies feature-learning strength; the scopes are complementary, so broad claims of the first unified scale/similarity theory need qualification.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature Learning beyond the Lazy-Rich Dichotomy: Insights from Representational Geometry
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Same-venue conceptual competitor on how feature learning should be measured and classified.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chou et al. argue that a binary lazy/rich axis hides distinct learning strategies and use task-relevant manifold geometry to resolve them. The target uses gamma_0 and average CKA drift as essentially scalar richness measures; combining the approaches could determine whether destructive and transferable feature changes occupy different geometric subtypes.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Theory of Continual Learning with Gradient Descent for Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later current competitor deriving explicit train- and test-time forgetting guarantees for neural networks under gradient descent.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Taheri, Ghosh, and Mazumdar analyze a one-hidden-layer quadratic network on XOR-cluster tasks and obtain explicit dependencies on samples, iterations, tasks, and width plus an algorithmic-stability test bound. It is more distribution-specific and kernel-oriented than the target's implicit feature-learning DMFT, but it supplies the finite-sample/generalization guarantees and training-horizon dependence absent from the target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability

reviewed_competitors.difference: This later work uses normalized Transformer dynamics to transfer learning rates across width, depth, and token horizon. Those dimensions and a direct Transformer mechanism are absent from LVP's fixed-time linear embedding-projection derivation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Function-Space Learning Rates
reviewed_competitors.difference: FLeRM measures and matches layerwise function changes in arbitrary networks and transfers across width, depth, initialization, and LoRA rank. It offers an empirical functional controller alternative to LVP's disputed parameter-scaling proof and one global embedding multiplier.
