reviewed_competitors.title: TanhExp: A Smooth Activation Function with High Convergence Speed for Lightweight Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: exact prior work and direct novelty collision
reviewed_competitors.difference: TanhExp defines f(x) = x tanh(exp(x)), exactly TeLU's formula, and predates it by more than four years. It already claims simplicity, efficiency, robustness, convergence speed, and accuracy across lightweight vision networks, so TeLU's durable incremental value would need to come from corrected theory or broader reproducible evaluation rather than the function itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Searching for Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work discovers Swish, x sigmoid(beta x), through exhaustive and reinforcement-learning search and validates ImageNet gains on deep architectures. It supplies a stronger discovery methodology than TeLU's hand-selected fixed expression, while TeLU/TanhExp uses a tanh-of-exponential gate and emphasizes a broader but inconsistent task suite.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mish: A Self Regularized Non-Monotonic Activation Function
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mish uses x tanh(softplus(x)), sharing TeLU's smooth self-gated non-monotone form but replacing exp(x) with softplus(x). It reports controlled ImageNet and COCO comparisons and has broader deployment evidence; TeLU is closer to the positive identity and faster in the manuscript's naive microbenchmarks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Activate or Not: Learning Customized Activation
reviewed_competitors.difference: ACON generalizes smooth Maxout/Swish-style gating and meta-ACON learns when to activate, with ImageNet, detection, and segmentation evaluations. It trades TeLU's zero-parameter fixed simplicity for adaptability to layer, architecture, and data.

reviewed_competitors.title: Padé Activation Units: End-to-end Learning of Flexible Activation Functions in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: PAUs learn compact rational activations end to end and can approximate existing activations, directly addressing the fact that the best nonlinearity depends on architecture, hyperparameters, and dataset. TeLU avoids learned coefficients but assumes one exact fixed formula transfers broadly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gaussian Error Linear Units (GELUs)
reviewed_competitors.difference: GELU weights inputs by a Gaussian CDF and has extensive adoption in transformers. TeLU reports closer positive identity behavior and faster naive evaluation, but the manuscript does not show that these properties beat optimized GELU kernels or modern tuned transformer recipes.

reviewed_competitors.title: ReLU Strikes Back: Exploiting Activation Sparsity in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work reports negligible LLM convergence/performance loss from ReLU while exploiting exact activation sparsity for up to threefold inference-compute reduction. It challenges TeLU's claim that smooth dense activation is the preferable scalable default and highlights a system benefit absent from TeLU's elementwise timing analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Three Decades of Activations: A Comprehensive Survey of 400 Activation Functions for Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The survey catalogs 400 functions and explicitly identifies redundancy and unintentional rediscovery as a field problem. It is not a model competitor, but it establishes the prior-art screening standard that would likely have surfaced TanhExp before TeLU was framed as a new activation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct foundational baseline that EXAdam modifies
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adam derives bias corrections for exponential moment estimates and supplies an online-convex regret analysis. EXAdam keeps Adam's state but adds heuristic cross-conditioned multipliers and a current-gradient term; it does not provide a comparable theorem or isolate whether gains come from a larger effective step.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Convergence-critical Adam variant cited by EXAdam
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reddi et al. construct a convex counterexample for Adam, identify failures caused by its exponential second-moment memory, and propose AMSGrad-style long-term memory with convergence guarantees. EXAdam neither tests the counterexample nor introduces a monotone second-moment maximum, so its cross-rescaling does not by itself address that established failure mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest established attempt to couple current-gradient information with adaptive moment scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaBelief replaces Adam's uncentered second moment with the EMA of squared gradient prediction error (g-m)^2, giving an explicit innovation-based interpretation and evaluations spanning image classification, language modeling, and GANs. EXAdam instead rescales unchanged Adam moments and adds g directly; its claimed covariance/curvature interpretation is not represented by the stored statistic.

reviewed_competitors.difference: AggMo combines velocity buffers at several decay rates to damp oscillations and analyzes quadratic convergence, at the cost of extra state. TAM keeps one momentum buffer and adds one scalar state, but supplies no comparable theorem and does not test whether its angle gate outperforms a memory-timescale mixture under equal tuning and compute.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdamP: Slowing Down the Slowdown for Momentum Optimizers on Scale-invariant Weights
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdamP and SGDP detect scale-invariant weights and remove the radial component of a momentum update, preserving the functionally relevant tangent direction with analysis and 13 benchmarks. TAM instead gates the new gradient by temporal alignment and applies beyond normalized weights; AdamP shows that directional optimizer geometry and preserved convergence were already studied with more explicit invariance assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaBelief Optimizer: Adapting Stepsizes by the Belief in Observed Gradients
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaBelief treats momentum as a prediction of the next gradient and reduces coordinatewise step sizes when the observed gradient deviates from that prediction, with convergence analysis and broad experiments. TAM uses only the global angular component of the same mismatch and rescales the incoming first moment; omitting AdaBelief from the baseline panel leaves the claimed stability/generalization mechanism weakly isolated.

reviewed_competitors.title: Positive-Negative Momentum: Manipulating Stochastic Gradient Noise to Improve Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: PNM maintains two approximately independent momentum states and takes their controlled difference to shape anisotropic stochastic-gradient noise, with theoretical convergence and generalization results for SGD and Adam variants. TAM is cheaper and targets directional conflict, but its claims about enhanced exploration and generalization lack both a noise characterization and a comparison to this established momentum alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: AngularGrad: A New Optimization Technique for Angular Convergence of Convolutional Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: AngularGrad uses the angle between consecutive gradients to control an Adam-style step and reports an Adam-like regret bound. TAM argues that momentum-current alignment is the more relevant temporal comparison and does include AngularGrad, but only on image classification; it does not isolate consecutive-gradient versus momentum-gradient information under a shared update and learning-rate scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: The AdEMAMix Optimizer: Better, Faster, Older
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdEMAMix mixes short and very long gradient EMAs and reports that old gradients remain useful for tens of thousands of steps, including a 1.3B-parameter 101B-token language-model study. TAM instead suppresses gradients that conflict with one buffer and evaluates only continued pretraining of at most 355M parameters; AdEMAMix is a stronger current baseline for claims about preserving valuable historical information.

reviewed_competitors.title: Cautious Optimizers: Improving Training with One Line of Code
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cautious optimizers suppress coordinate updates whose momentum and current gradient signs disagree and now provide a Lyapunov analysis plus large-scale pretraining results. Its first arXiv version appeared one month before TAM's arXiv version, although TAM's OpenReview submission predates it, so priority is concurrent; current novelty is the smooth globally smoothed cosine gate rather than the general idea of rejecting momentum-gradient conflict.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grams: Gradient Descent with Adaptive Momentum Scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Grams takes update direction from the current gradient and uses momentum only to scale magnitude, explicitly avoiding a stale momentum direction, and supplies a global convergence guarantee plus comparisons with cautious optimizers. It was posted three days before TAM's arXiv version but after TAM's OpenReview submission; its opposite design choice is an essential stress test for TAM's premise that the old direction should dominate conflict.

reviewed_competitors.title: MARS: Unleashing the Power of Variance Reduction for Training Large Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: MARS combines scaled stochastic recursive momentum with AdamW, Lion, or Shampoo preconditioning and evaluates GPT-2 training at fixed token budgets, with a formal variance-reduction motivation. TAM is simpler and explores vision and distribution shifts, but its masked-language fine-tuning does not support competitive large-model optimizer claims without token-, FLOP-, and wall-time-controlled comparisons like MARS.

reviewed_competitors.title: MGUP: A Momentum-Gradient Alignment Update Policy for Stochastic Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: MGUP ranks coordinatewise momentum-gradient alignment and applies larger versus smaller nonzero steps to fixed proportions of parameters, integrates with AdamW, Lion, and Muon, and gives a stochastic convergence guarantee for its AdamW variant. It postdates TAM and validates the broader alignment-control direction, while also highlighting TAM's missing coordinate resolution, nonzero-floor design analysis, and theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational demonstration that overcomplete SAEs can recover more interpretable features than native neurons from transformer activations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It establishes the generic SAE recipe and language-model evidence that InterPLM transfers to proteins. InterPLM's novelty is the biological evaluation stack, structural visualization, annotation mining, and PLM intervention rather than the sparse-autoencoder mechanism itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Preceding work on SAE scaling, TopK sparsity, dead latents, reconstruction-sparsity frontiers, and multiple feature-quality metrics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies training and evaluation controls that the reviewed L1 SAEs largely omit, including explicit scaling behavior and dead-latent handling. InterPLM contributes a domain-grounded Swiss-Prot benchmark and protein tools but does not study dictionary scaling or reproducibility.

reviewed_competitors.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A near-contemporary ground-truth audit showing that apparently monosemantic SAE latents can split or absorb features.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its controlled first-letter task diagnoses missing activations and shows that dictionary size or sparsity alone does not solve feature absorption. This directly cautions against interpreting InterPLM's 2,548 qualifying latents as 2,548 distinct, complete biological features without duplication and recall audits.

reviewed_competitors.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier protein-transformer interpretability across structure, binding sites, biophysical properties, layers, architectures, and datasets.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes native attention heads across BERT, ALBERT, and XLNet, rather than learning a new feature basis. InterPLM is broader in unsupervised feature discovery and annotation tooling but narrower in subject-model scale and architecture diversity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformer protein language models are unsupervised structure learners
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier evidence that native PLM attention maps encode residue contacts and support accurate unsupervised structure readout.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It evaluates a specific structural signal quantitatively and across model capacity, whereas InterPLM discovers a wide feature dictionary and mostly uses annotations/illustrations. InterPLM does not show that its individual features causally implement contact prediction.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology: Training, Evaluating, and Interpreting Sparse Autoencoders on Protein Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest independent PLM-SAE study, developed concurrently and later published at ICML 2025.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adams et al. emphasize generic versus family-specific features, coevolution, downstream probes for thermostability/localization, and the InterProt visualizer. InterPLM appeared publicly earlier and emphasizes Swiss-Prot residue/domain scoring, LLM descriptions, annotation completion, and steering; the two provide complementary rather than unique evidence that ESM-2 admits biologically aligned sparse features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models through Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later direct replication/extension on ESM-2-8M that maps SAE latents to UniProt labels and performs iterative sequence generation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It uses intrinsic dimension for layer selection and generates 180 candidate sequences, finding 24 zinc-finger matches when steering two latents versus zero for base/random controls. This is stronger evidence for nontrivial sequence generation than InterPLM's short periodic-glycine MLM-probability intervention, although InterPLM provides broader feature coverage and annotation analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Interpretable Protein Structure Prediction with Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later scale and capability extension from ESM-2-8M to ESM2-3B and ESMFold using TopK and Matryoshka SAEs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It reports broader Swiss-Prot coverage at 3B scale, checks contact and structure reconstruction, and steers predicted solvent accessibility while holding sequence fixed. It directly addresses several future directions in InterPLM, though its structure-steering evidence is still a small case study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Antibody Language Models Using SAEs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later domain-specific PLM study that explicitly separates concept correlation from causal steering quality.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It finds TopK features can be biologically interpretable yet poorly steerable, whereas Ordered SAEs improve control at the cost of more complex activation patterns. That result challenges any general inference from InterPLM's annotation F1 to causal controllability and motivates architecture-aware intervention tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: ProtSAE: Disentangling and Interpreting Protein Language Models via Semantically-Guided Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later protein-specific alternative that builds annotation labels and ontology structure into SAE training to target semantic disentanglement.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ProtSAE gives up InterPLM's fully unsupervised dictionary-training claim in exchange for concept-aligned directions and improved interpretable probing. It is a direct design alternative when reliable known-concept manipulation matters more than discovering unanticipated features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring Progress in Dictionary Learning for Language Model Interpretability with Board Game Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A contemporary framework for evaluating dictionary learning where the complete ground-truth feature set is better specified.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It motivates supervised recovery metrics and p-annealing on chess/Othello states, avoiding the incomplete-label problem that complicates Swiss-Prot false positives. InterPLM contributes a richer real scientific domain but needs withheld-label, completeness, and feature-duplication tests to approach the same falsifiability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor for defining how many parameter-space degrees of freedom are needed to solve a task through restricted-subspace training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. use random subspaces prospectively and scale across supervised and reinforcement-learning tasks; the focal paper uses a trajectory-specific post hoc SVD space that is more diagnostic but far more expensive and circular for training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent Happens in a Tiny Subspace
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor for the claim that neural-network gradients concentrate in a small persistent subspace.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gur-Ari et al. identify an online top-Hessian eigenspace from gradients; the focal paper studies the full initialization-to-final sensitivity map and finds both useful stable and chaotic directions outside a large bulk.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does SGD Really Happen in Tiny Subspaces?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest cited challenge to identifying an active training space from gradient-Hessian alignment.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Song et al. show that projecting onto the dominant Hessian space can stall while removing it can still train across practical optimizers; the focal paper proposes a different post hoc operator but needs comparable anti-spuriousness controls.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization Guarantees for Neural Networks via Harnessing the Low-rank Structure of the Jacobian
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior theory linking a function Jacobian's information and nuisance subspaces to optimization and generalization on structured versus noisy data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Oymak et al. analyze the parameter-to-output Jacobian and provide generalization guarantees; the focal paper analyzes initialization-to-trained-parameters and only hypothesizes an inductive-bias connection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chaotic Dynamics are Intrinsic to Neural Network Training with SGD
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct prior work on perturbation growth, local chaotic directions, and the temporal confinement of chaos in SGD training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Herrmann et al. connect negative curvature to chaos and track long-term divergence; the focal paper labels singular values above one chaotic from a final training map but does not study time-resolved Lyapunov behavior or cite this close precedent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning versus Kernel Learning: An Empirical Study of Loss Landscape Geometry and the Time Evolution of the Neural Tangent Kernel
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior empirical evidence for an early chaotic transient followed by a stable training phase across larger neural-network settings.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fort et al. track loss geometry and function-kernel evolution over time; the focal paper compresses the complete trajectory into a final parameter-map Jacobian and does not resolve phases.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linear Mode Connectivity and the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior perturb-and-retrain evidence for a transition from initialization-sensitive to SGD-noise-stable network states.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Frankle et al. use functionally meaningful mode connectivity and scale through ResNet-50 on ImageNet; the focal paper gives a local differential parameter-space decomposition on much smaller networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient-based Hyperparameter Optimization through Reversible Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational prior for exact differentiation through an entire SGD-with-momentum training procedure, including sensitivities to initialization and hyperparameters.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maclaurin et al. use reversible reverse-mode dynamics to make hypergradients practical; the focal paper materializes the full initialization Jacobian and interprets its SVD without situating that operator in the established hypergradient framework.

reviewed_competitors.title: Forward and Reverse Gradient-Based Hyperparameter Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior general treatment of forward and reverse differentiation through iterative optimization dynamics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Franceschi et al. develop algorithmic tradeoffs for hypergradient computation and validation objectives; the focal paper applies forward differentiation to every initialization coordinate and studies spectral geometry rather than optimization of outer variables.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational function-space Jacobian/kernel account of linearized neural-network training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jacot et al. study infinite-width prediction dynamics and generalization through the output Jacobian Gram matrix; the focal paper linearizes the finite training algorithm as a parameter-to-parameter map.

reviewed_competitors.title: Wide Neural Networks of Any Depth Evolve as Linear Models Under Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior large-width theory and experiments for when function evolution is captured by a first-order linearization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. linearize network outputs around initialization and test wide architectures; the focal paper differentiates final weights with respect to initial weights and demonstrates finite perturbation linearity in only two directions.

reviewed_competitors.title: ReLoRA: High-Rank Training Through Low-Rank Updates
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Practical competing evidence that useful training updates can be composed from low-rank phases at billion-parameter scale.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ReLoRA is a deployable optimizer strategy evaluated up to 1.3B parameters and does not need an oracle trajectory Jacobian; the focal paper provides a richer local sensitivity diagnostic but does not scale beyond a small LeNet spectrum.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Much Does Initialization Affect Generalization?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior theory and empirical study of initialization components that survive training and affect function behavior and generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramasinghe et al. connect retained high-frequency initialization components to generalization on practical architectures; the focal paper maps locally preserved weight directions but does not test a generalization consequence.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Butterfly Effect: Neural Network Training Trajectories Are Highly Sensitive to Initial Conditions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct subsequent work testing infinitesimal initialization sensitivity and the early chaotic phase with several parameter, function, representation, and alignment metrics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Altintas et al. broaden perturbation evidence across models and distinguish raw, permutation-aligned, functional, barrier, and representation divergence; this directly addresses the focal paper's symmetry and scale limitations without computing a full training Jacobian.

reviewed_competitors.title: New Evidence of the Two-Phase Learning Dynamics of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct subsequent perturbation study of a transition from chaotic sensitivity to stable refinement, coupled to empirical-NTK cone stabilization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. inject perturbations at multiple training times and measure a phase transition; the focal paper studies only the final initialization-to-end map and cannot localize when amplification occurs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Leveraging Chaotic Transients in the Training of Artificial Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct subsequent work measuring positive maximum Lyapunov exponents and relating learnable chaos to faster optimization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jimenez-Gonzalez et al. sweep learning rates, architectures, datasets, activations, and regularization and test a constructive role for chaos; the focal paper labels expansion directions chaotic but does not establish Lyapunov chaos or utility.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Map Behind the Flow: Finite-Step Gradient Descent as a Dynamical System
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current exact analysis of finite-step gradient-descent maps, bifurcations, edge-of-stability behavior, and representation selection.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hofmann derives solvable discrete maps and shows learning rate changes attractors and dynamics, supplying theoretical machinery for optimizer-specific expansion that the focal paper's quadratic gradient-flow example lacks.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Perez-Corral et al. track activation-pattern change online across fully connected, convolutional, and transformer models; the focal paper's full-Jacobian diagnostic is much costlier and does not resolve temporal regime change.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimizing Neural Networks with Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature
reviewed_competitors.difference: K-FAC derives layer blocks of a Fisher or generalized Gauss–Newton approximation as Kronecker products of activation and backpropagated-gradient covariances, with damping and inversion machinery. SNGD also works layerwise but replaces this derivation with E(v_f)E(xxᵀ) and a detached inverse-square-root layer; it claims lower overhead without establishing equal natural-gradient fidelity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tractable Structured Natural-Gradient Descent Using Local Parameterizations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lin et al. rigorously use local parameter coordinates and matrix-group structure to obtain tractable natural gradients for structured distributions across variational inference, evolution strategies, and deep learning. SNGD borrows the local-parameterization framing but applies a much less specified layer statistic and does not analyze the error caused by changing detached coordinates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scalable Second Order Optimization for Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Distributed Shampoo demonstrates full-matrix-AdaGrad-style Kronecker preconditioning on ResNet-50, BERT, translation, and recommendation workloads with heterogeneous hardware and end-to-end wall-clock gains. It is not a Fisher natural gradient, but it supplies the large-scale systems evidence and strong matrix-preconditioner baseline absent from SNGD.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Normal Training for Deep Learning Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: TNT derives a Kronecker-separable Fisher approximation from a tensor-normal model of sampling-based gradients and compares with K-FAC and Shampoo, reporting near-first-order overhead. SNGD likewise seeks cheap layerwise factors but offers neither an equivalent distributional derivation nor contemporary second-order comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fisher-Legendre Optimization of Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: FishLeg learns the inverse-Fisher vector product online through Legendre–Fenchel duality, avoiding layer-specific inverse algebra, and provides convergence results under a PL condition plus second-order benchmarks. SNGD instead explicitly estimates and square-roots local matrices; it may be simpler per layer but lacks a fidelity or convergence theorem for its approximation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eva: A General Vectorized Approximation Framework for Second-Order Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Eva compresses Kronecker curvature factors to stochastic vectors and uses Sherman–Morrison updates, reporting up to 2.42× end-to-end speedup over K-FAC/Shampoo across models. It is a particularly relevant efficiency competitor that SNGD does not evaluate despite making the same low-overhead second-order claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Layer-Wise Natural Gradient Optimizer for Training Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: LNGD uses block-diagonal Fisher structure, layerwise sampling, a trace-preserving Kronecker/diagonal approximation, adaptive layer learning rates, and a stated global convergence analysis, with image-classification and machine-translation tests. It directly competes on layerwise NGD cost while providing a more explicit Fisher approximation and broader baseline suite.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaFisher: Adaptive Second-Order Optimization via Diagonal Block-Kronecker Fisher Approximation
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaFisher, published at ICLR 2025, uses a diagonal block-Kronecker Fisher approximation and evaluates image classification and language modeling with explicit stability and hyperparameter-robustness claims. It is the kind of current natural-gradient-like optimizer against which SNGD's effectiveness, overhead, and approximation fidelity now need direct testing.

reviewed_competitors.title: SOAP: Improving and Stabilizing Shampoo Using Adam
reviewed_competitors.difference: SOAP interprets Shampoo as adaptive optimization in a preconditioner eigenbasis and reports 35%+ wall-clock gains over AdamW on 360M/660M language models. Although not a Fisher method, it demonstrates that matrix-coordinate transformations require continual statistics, infrequent basis updates, and large-model time-to-quality evidence—issues left untreated by SNGD's changing detached Fisher coordinates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Theoretical Limitations of Ensembles in the Age of Overparameterization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest contemporaneous direct theory on random-feature ensembles versus a single model at matched parameter budget.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dern, Cunningham, and Pleiss prove pointwise infinite-ensemble equivalence and rapid finite-width convergence, exactly for ridgeless and approximately for small-ridge overparameterized RF models, and reinterpret member variance. The reviewed paper appeared later, cites this work, and adds strict optimal-ridge monotonicity for its deterministic equivalent plus underparameterized allocation scaling laws.

reviewed_competitors.title: More is Better in Modern Machine Learning: when Infinite Overparameterization is Optimal and Overfitting is Obligatory
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct single-random-feature monotonicity foundation extended by the reviewed paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Simon et al. prove that optimally tuned single-model RF risk decreases with width and samples and develop the spectral task conditions; the reviewed work extends the risk formula to homogeneous ensembles and studies fixed-budget K versus N allocation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dimension-free deterministic equivalents and scaling laws for random feature regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary finite-size foundation for translating deterministic-equivalent RF risk to actual risk.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Defilippis, Loureiro, and Misiakiewicz give a nonasymptotic dimension-free multiplicative approximation for a single RFRR model; the reviewed theorem needs but does not prove an analogous K>1 result.

reviewed_competitors.title: When are ensembles really effective?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: General classification theory identifying disagreement and competence conditions for ensemble improvement.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Theisen et al. relate majority-vote gains to disagreement relative to error and distinguish interpolating from noninterpolating models; the reviewed paper instead optimizes squared risk under a fixed homogeneous RF feature budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: Ensemble linear interpolators: The role of ensembling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct contrasting theory in which bagging improves overparameterized linear prediction through implicit regularization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu and Sun analyze multiplier-bootstrap and sketched least-squares bagging and show bounded risk around interpolation; the reviewed setup gives every same-data RF member explicit oracle ridge, eliminating the implicit-regularization advantage that resampling can create.

reviewed_competitors.title: Asymptotically free sketched ridge ensembles: Risks, cross-validation, and tuning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest ridge-ensemble theory addressing realistic tuning and randomized sketches.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Patil and LeJeune prove generalized cross-validation consistency, optimize sketch size, construct prediction intervals, and use ensembles to estimate unsketched ridge risk; the reviewed paper assumes an oracle ridge and optimizes only accuracy over homogeneous feature maps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Curves for Noisy Heterogeneous Feature-Subsampled Ridge Ensembles
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Same-author predecessor allowing unequal member sizes and feature subsampling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ruben and Pehlevan analyze heterogeneous widths as a way to shift and smooth double descent and expose a subsampling-noise versus variance trade-off; the reviewed theorem deliberately fixes homogeneous widths and optimal ridge to establish a sharper single-model optimum.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multiple Descent in the Multiple Random Feature Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: Meng et al. concatenate heterogeneous random-feature types and derive multiple-descent curves in proportional limits; the reviewed work averages separately fitted homogeneous predictors and focuses on optimally regularized fixed-budget monotonicity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Ensembles Work, But Are They Necessary?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical deep-network comparison of ensembles and single larger models beyond accuracy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abe et al. test uncertainty and distribution-shift claims and find that larger single networks can often replicate ensemble gains; the reviewed paper provides a tractable RF allocation theorem but no end-to-end deep-network or OOD evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational deep-ensemble baseline defining uncertainty and shift objectives omitted by the MSE theorem.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lakshminarayanan et al. train learned neural members with a proper scoring rule and evaluate predictive uncertainty and OOD behavior; the reviewed work freezes random features and optimizes mean squared accuracy only.

reviewed_competitors.title: BatchEnsemble: An Alternative Approach to Efficient Ensemble and Lifelong Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Efficient shared-parameter ensemble alternative that changes the relevant budget.
reviewed_competitors.difference: BatchEnsemble shares a full weight matrix and gives each member rank-one factors, reporting accuracy, uncertainty, OOD, memory, and speed across vision and translation; the reviewed theorem assumes disjoint frozen feature budgets and independent member maps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse MoEs meet Efficient Ensembles
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Large-scale specialized and parameter-sharing ensemble competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: E3 combines sparse experts with efficient ensembles and evaluates likelihood, robustness, few-shot learning, and uncertainty up to 2.7B parameters; its functional specialization and active-parameter routing lie outside homogeneous RFRR.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Feature Learning Can Improve Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct beyond-kernel scaling theory named as the main route by which deep networks can violate RF laws.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon, Atanasov, and Pehlevan show that feature learning changes scaling on hard tasks and the compute-optimal allocation of parameters and training; the reviewed paper freezes features and treats spectral alignment as fixed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Loop Corrections to the Training Error and Generalization Gap of Random Feature Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current finite-width correction to mean-kernel random-feature risk approximations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kim and Ringel derive error contributions from higher-order random-kernel fluctuation statistics beyond the mean-kernel approximation; the reviewed monotonicity proof operates on a Gaussian deterministic equivalent and lacks an ensemble finite-size ordering bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature Bagging Provides Stability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current theory showing an ensemble benefit under a utility omitted by MSE-only allocation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sun and Cheng prove that feature bagging improves feature and instance stability and that modest rounds approach infinite-bagging stability; the reviewed result asks only which homogeneous allocation minimizes oracle-ridge squared error.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior theoretical and empirical competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ilbert et al. also analyze a toy linear forecasting problem where attention fails to reach the true solution, but connect the failure to bad minima and show that sharpness-aware optimization plus channel-wise attention repairs it across real multivariate benchmarks. The reviewed paper proposes a different output-sign asymmetry on an engineered residual SSM and conditioned OOD task, offers a longer NTK proof, but supplies no new experiment and its central proof chain has the contradictions documented here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linear Transformers as VAR Models: Aligning Autoregressive Attention Mechanisms with Autoregressive Forecasting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lu and Yang interpret one linear-attention layer as a dynamic VAR, diagnose a structural mismatch between deeper Transformers and autoregressive objectives, and redesign the flow into an interpretable mixture-of-VAR forecaster with empirical gains. That work locates the problem in architecture-objective alignment rather than fixed-output sign dynamics and validates a constructive model; it also concerns linear rather than softmax attention.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Closer Look at Transformers for Time Series Forecasting: Understanding Why They Work and Where They Struggle
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. compare point-, patch-, and variate-wise tokenization, use mutual information and synthetic data, and find that benchmark success is dominated by intra-variate self-dependence, stationarity, normalization, and skip connections, with additional healthcare validation. This broader diagnosis challenges treating one sign-conditioned residual-feature mechanism as the general explanation and provides original tests absent from the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Do Transformers Fail to Forecast Time Series In-Context?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. study linear self-attention as an in-context learner on AR(p) processes, prove it cannot beat the classical linear expected-MSE optimum, characterize convergence to that optimum with context length, analyze mean collapse under chain-of-thought inference, and validate the results experimentally. Its model and question differ, but it provides a cleaner classical-process comparator and empirical theorem checks rather than a sign-selected SSM risk claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Analysis of Linear Time Series Forecasting Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Toner and Darlow characterize the function classes of popular normalized linear forecasters, show several are equivalent to unconstrained linear regression on augmented features, and use closed-form fits that win across 72 percent of dataset-horizon settings. Their identifiability and closed-form analysis is a stronger basis for the linear side of the comparison than the reviewed paper's singular claimed-unique residual solution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational empirical premise and residual-linear baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zeng et al. introduce DLinear and NLinear, compare them with Transformer forecasters on nine real datasets, and attribute shortcomings to temporal-information loss and evaluation design. The reviewed paper is motivated by those results and seeks a first NTK explanation, but its residual predictor and conditioned one-step task are much narrower than DLinear's multi-horizon benchmark setting.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical precursor for facts-per-parameter scaling in language models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Allen-Zhu and Li train broader transformer families on multiple controlled factual datasets and report about two knowledge bits per parameter plus architecture, quantization, sparsity, duration, and noise effects. Nichani et al. supply explicit shallow associative-memory constructions and bounded-information lower bounds for a narrower atomic lookup model rather than estimating a universal empirical constant.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Associative Memories
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest theoretical precursor for outer-product associative-memory scaling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cabannes, Dohmatob, and Bietti analyze high-dimensional associative memories under heavy-tailed token distributions and compare estimators and optimization. The target extends the primitive to two-layer MLPs and a subject-relation transformer lookup construction, while relying on the precursor's fixed-random-embedding perspective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Mechanistic and optimization precursor connecting transformer weights to associative memory.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bietti et al. study global versus context-specific bigrams and the staged emergence of induction heads in a simplified two-layer transformer. The target studies random factual pairs, one shallow block, explicit capacity bounds, and a different relation-first gradient trajectory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memorization Capacity of Multi-Head Attention in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mahdavi, Liao, and Thrampoulidis bound how many input sequences multi-head attention can memorize under linear-independence conditions, emphasizing head and context scaling. The target instead exploits subject-relation token structure, disjoint answer sets, and value-matrix superposition to obtain a fact-count bound and an attention-MLP tradeoff.

reviewed_competitors.title: Next-token prediction capacity: general upper bounds and a lower bound for transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct upper-and-lower-bound competitor for decoder-only next-token memorization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Madden, Fox, and Thrampoulidis characterize interpolation of arbitrary next-token distributions and highlight self-attention injectivity, with matching bounds up to constants in their setting. Nichani et al. target a structured factual dictionary, random embeddings, bounded bits, and explicit attention-versus-MLP associative mechanisms rather than arbitrary context distributions.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 71(9), 2025; arXiv:2405.13718v3

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Optimal Memorization Capacity of Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent optimal-capacity construction using a different parameter-sharing regime.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kajitsuka and Sato show that N arbitrary labeled sequences can be memorized with roughly square-root-N parameters in next-token prediction, optimal up to logs, by exploiting shared parameters and high bit complexity; sequence-to-sequence capacity scales differently. The target deliberately favors near-linear facts per bounded-precision parameter constructions and argues that square-root parameter schemes hide at least linear total bits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do LLMs dream of elephants (when told not to)? Latent concept association and associative memory in transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest concurrent constructive account of value matrices as associative memories in a shallow transformer.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jiang et al. study latent concept association, include context manipulations in open-source LLMs, and prove that self-attention gathers evidence while the value matrix recalls concepts. The target focuses on exact random subject-relation facts, adds an MLP storage route, quantifies parameter capacity, and analyzes bounded-information optimality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixture of Parrots: Experts improve memorization more than reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Architecture-level competitor on how parameter allocation changes memorization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jelassi et al. show that adding routed experts at fixed active parameters improves synthetic and closed-book memorization more than reasoning and evaluate pretrained MoE and dense models. The target analyzes one dense shallow layer and a continuous attention-MLP storage tradeoff, without conditional routing or natural language pretraining.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct real-model mechanistic alternative for factual retrieval.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geva et al. use attention-edge interventions in pretrained autoregressive LMs and propose subject enrichment by early MLPs, relation propagation, and attention-mediated attribute extraction. That evidence is closer to natural recall mechanism but does not provide capacity bounds; the target provides rigorous capacity constructions but never tests whether real models implement them.

reviewed_competitors.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Causal-editing alternative to construction-only storage claims.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Meng et al. causally trace and rank-one edit factual associations in middle-layer GPT MLPs, testing specificity and generalization on real prompts. The target gives mathematical reasons attention values or MLPs can store random facts but lacks causal necessity or fact-edit evidence in trained language models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Finetuning for Factual Knowledge Extraction
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct alternative account of plausible-but-wrong factual outputs during training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghosal, Hashimoto, and Raghunathan show theoretically and on Llama-2 and Mistral QA that fine-tuning lesser-known facts can make a model ignore subjects and emit generic plausible answers. Their setting better supports a practical hallucination connection, while the target proves a cleaner relation-first stage in a much more restrictive synthetic gradient-flow model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometric Factual Recall in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Most direct successor and assumption-level competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ravfogel et al. replace fixed random embeddings with learned fact-bearing geometry, prove logarithmic embedding dimension for random bijections, interpret a small ReLU MLP as a relation-conditioned selector rather than key-value memory, show gradient descent finds that structure, and extend to multi-hop capacity-depth tradeoffs. This directly demonstrates that the target's associative-memory allocation is not unique once embeddings learn, though the task families and accounting differ.

reviewed_competitors.title: Factual recall in linear associative memories: sharp asymptotics and mechanistic insights
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct sharp-capacity successor for the paper's linear associative-memory core.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Giorlandino, Goldt, and Maillard characterize a decoupled model and report the sharp threshold p_c log p_c divided by d squared equal to one half, extend it to linear two-layer architectures, and explain how optimized margins differ from naive Hebbian storage. The target supplies high-probability polylog bounds and a simple outer-product construction but no sharp constant or comparable learned-weight mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers, Parallel Computation, and Logarithmic Depth
reviewed_competitors.relationship: prior expressivity theory underlying the claimed parallel-search circuit
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sanford, Hsu, and Telgarsky connect constant transformer depth to rounds of massively parallel computation and show logarithmic depth suffices for several basic problems. It supports treating parallel reachability as a natural transformer algorithm, but it addresses representability rather than whether gradient training discovers that algorithm. The reviewed paper supplies empirical learning and circuit evidence, while its fixed-depth width sweep cannot by itself test the theory's depth prediction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Transformer Reasoning Capabilities via Graph Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior graph-algorithm theory and benchmark
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sanford et al. derive a hierarchy over depth, width, and auxiliary execution tokens, prove logarithmic depth necessary and sufficient for graph connectivity in their regime, and evaluate a broader GraphQA suite. The reviewed paper focuses more sharply on learnability and reverse-engineers a compatible merge circuit, but tests far fewer architectural scaling axes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stream of Search (SoS): Learning to Search in Language
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gandhi et al. train a transformer on flattened search streams containing fruitful mistakes and multiple strategies, report 25% higher Countdown accuracy than optimal-trajectory training, and further improve with policy optimization. That is a genuine generated search process, unlike the reviewed paper's one-step teacher-forced DFS/selection tasks, though it studies a different domain and does not establish unbounded graph-size generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causal Language Modeling Can Elicit Search and Reasoning Capabilities on Logic Puzzles
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shah et al. train causal transformers on logically ordered solver steps and report 94.21% fully solved Sudoku and 92.04% Zebra puzzles, while models without logical steps fail. It shows that explicit trajectories can teach complex search in other controlled settings. The reviewed paper contributes a cleaner graph-size diagnosis, but its conclusion that chain-of-thought does not help is much narrower than this contrasting evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fan et al. tie transformer weights across adaptive execution steps and obtain strong length generalization on tasks with iterative RASP-L solutions. This directly targets the mismatch between fixed network depth and variable algorithmic horizon; the reviewed paper mentions looped transformers as future work but does not test them.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers meet Neural Algorithmic Reasoners
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bounsi et al. combine a language transformer with a graph-neural algorithmic reasoner and report more than 20-point absolute gains in several out-of-distribution CLRS-Text algorithm families. It accepts stronger structural bias and a two-phase procedure, whereas the reviewed paper deliberately probes a plain transformer; it is therefore an important practical alternative to interpreting the observed failure as unavoidable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models, Graph Searching, and Supervision Adulteration: When More Supervision is Less and How to Make More More
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct subsequent analysis of path-star learnability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Frydenlund shows that decoder-only path-star failure can arise because teacher forcing gives a trivial edge-following shortcut most of the supervision, leaving one critical planning token under-supported. Online data and small task modifications that induce subtask decomposition let standard decoder models solve the task, although scaling to larger graphs remains difficult. This strengthens the reviewed paper's data-sensitivity result while weakening paradigm-level interpretations of small-task failure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Provably Learn Algorithmic Solutions for Graph Connectivity, But Only with the Right Data
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct subsequent theory of the reviewed training phenomenon
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ye et al. prove that an L-layer Disentangled Transformer can implement adjacency-matrix powering through diameter 3^L and analyze how training examples within that capacity favor the exact algorithm while beyond-capacity examples favor a degree heuristic. They empirically recover the exact solution in both standard and disentangled transformers by restricting training to within-capacity data. This gives a sharper capacity-curriculum account than the reviewed paper's broad claim that scale does not help.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discrete Diffusion Models Exploit Asymmetry to Solve Lookahead Planning Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct subsequent architecture and curriculum competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Trainin et al. identify the asymmetry between difficult forward branching and often deterministic reverse decoding. Both autoregressive and nonautoregressive models reach perfect accuracy on their lookahead task, but discrete diffusion models use future tokens to decode backward with exponentially fewer examples and shallower networks; autoregressive models often require curriculum adjustments. This supports the reviewed paper's optimization diagnosis but contradicts a fundamental transformer-inability reading.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Depth Ceiling: On the Limits of Large Language Models in Discovering Latent Planning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu, Jettkant, and Ruis separate discovering a multi-step latent plan from executing it once learned. Tiny scratch models discover up to three latent steps, fine-tuned GPT-4o and Qwen3-32B reach five, and GPT-5.4 reaches seven under few-shot prompting; learned strategies execute to eight. This later evidence supports a real discovery bottleneck while replacing the reviewed paper's parameter-only inference with controlled tests of contemporary pretrained models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can RL Teach Long-Horizon Reasoning to LLMs? Expressiveness Is Key
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later RL and curriculum counterexample to architectural fatalism
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. introduce ScaleLogic, independently control proof horizon and logical expressiveness, and find RL training compute follows a high-fit power law in depth whose exponent depends on expressiveness. Curricula improve scaling efficiency and expressive environments transfer better to downstream reasoning, leading the authors to argue that long-horizon shortcomings are trainable rather than fundamental. The domain and objective differ, but the study directly tests several missing axes from the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uncovering Graph Reasoning in Decoder-only Transformers with Circuit Tracing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dai et al. apply circuit tracing to decoder-only graph reasoning and identify token merging plus structural memorization across path and substructure tasks, then vary density and model size. It independently supports merge-like mechanisms while broadening the candidate circuit beyond pure reachable-set merging; comparative causal validation between the two interpretability pipelines remains open.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest competing explanation of hierarchical generalization through training objective, coexisting subnetworks, and grammar simplicity.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ahuja et al. compare five objectives on five synthetic tasks, identify prunable linear and hierarchical subnetworks, and provide a Bayesian grammar account. The target isolates center embedding and syntax-tree count with more seeds, but infers competition behaviorally without circuit or grammar-complexity measurements.

reviewed_competitors.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases

reviewed_competitors.difference: Mueller and Linzen use child-directed, Wikipedia, and web pretraining and find that corpus genre and depth matter beyond parameter count. reviewed_competitors.difference: FiCT spans many linguistic phenomena in filtered corpora and shows surprisingly strong indirect-evidence generalization. reviewed_competitors.title: Attribute Diversity Determines the Systematicity Gap in VQA

reviewed_competitors.title: Editing Models with Task Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational task-vector method and the direct arithmetic baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Task Arithmetic flattens and adds full task updates with a scalar coefficient. TSV-M preserves layer matrices, truncates their SVDs, and transforms concatenated singular factors before reconstruction.

reviewed_competitors.title: TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: TIES trims small coordinate updates and resolves sign conflicts before merging; TSV-M instead works with low-rank layer subspaces and removes cross-task factor correlations. TIES is listed but omitted from the main comparison.

reviewed_competitors.difference: DARE randomly drops and rescales delta coordinates and is demonstrated on language models. TSV-M deterministically keeps leading matrix singular components and polar-transforms their bases, but does not test LLMs or compare DARE in Table 2.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Adaptive coefficient-merging competitor on the same CLIP task family.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaMerging optimizes task- or layer-wise coefficients by entropy minimization on unlabeled test data. TSV-M is static and data-free after checkpoint access; its only direct comparison is a seven-task appendix result, where the two approaches are also complementary.

reviewed_competitors.title: Localizing Task Information for Improved Model Merging and Compression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest direct benchmark, compression baseline, and source of Consensus Task Arithmetic.
reviewed_competitors.difference: TALL-Mask localizes sparse coordinate supports and Consensus Merging removes weights selected as catastrophic; TSV-C stores low-rank factors and TSV-M decorrelates singular subspaces. reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary tuning-free merger with lightweight task-specific modulators.
reviewed_competitors.difference: EMR elects a unified model and stores masks and rescalers to recover each task, spanning vision, NLP, PEFT, and multimodal settings. TSV-M constructs a single static low-rank polar merge; EMR is acknowledged but absent from the main empirical panel.

reviewed_competitors.title: Twin-Merging: Dynamic Integration of Modular Expertise in Model Merging
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct low-rank compression and interference competitor with dynamic task-specific routing.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Twin-Merging separates shared and exclusive knowledge, compresses modules with SVD, and routes exclusive expertise per input across vision and language. TSV-M avoids routing for merging and instead orthogonalizes low-rank task factors, while TSV-C separately assumes task identity.

reviewed_competitors.title: SMILE: Zero-Shot Sparse Mixture of Low-Rank Experts Construction From Pre-Trained Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest pre-existing SVD/subspace treatment of interference and low-rank experts.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SMILE explicitly formulates linear-layer interference and expands fine-tuned updates into a routed sparse mixture of low-rank experts across CLIP, Flan-T5, Mistral, full fine-tuning, and LoRA. TSV-M instead compresses all task updates into one polar-transformed model with no input routing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Model Merging with SVD to Tie the Knots
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Independent ICLR 2025 SVD-based alignment method and very close contemporary competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: KnOTS jointly SVD-transforms task updates into a shared aligned space before applying existing merge operators, focusing especially on LoRA models and warning that flattened task-vector orthogonality alone does not ensure mergeability. TSV-M separately decomposes each update, truncates it, and enforces factor decorrelation.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Matters for Model Merging at Scale?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Large-scale empirical stress test of standard mergers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The study merges 1B-64B language models and up to eight experts, finding model size, base quality, and heterogeneity central and methods increasingly similar at scale. TSV-M's evidence instead grows task count only within homogeneous CLIP vision experts.

reviewed_competitors.title: LoRE-Merging: Exploring Low-Rank Estimation For Large Language Model Merging
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct successor using dominant singular structure to reduce interference in LLM merging.
reviewed_competitors.difference: LoRE formulates low-rank task-vector merging as an optimization problem and can operate without the base model, targeting language models. TSV-M uses a closed-form polar reconstruction from a known common base and supplies the earlier homogeneous-vision evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Modeling Multi-Task Model Merging as Adaptive Projective Gradient Descent

reviewed_competitors.difference: Adaptive projective gradient descent argues that conflicting task-specific information can still be performance-critical and optimizes modifications outside a shared subspace. TSV-M treats overlap as interference and fully decorrelates retained factors, making this a direct challenge to its causal story.

reviewed_competitors.title: No Task Left Behind: Isotropic Model Merging with Common and Task-Specific Subspaces
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct subspace successor that distinguishes common and task-specific geometry.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Iso-C constructs common and task-specific subspaces and isotropically normalizes their contributions rather than forcing complete cross-task orthogonality. It targets the same imbalance/interference problem and offers a more nuanced treatment of potentially useful shared directions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Whoever Started the Interference Should End It: Guiding Data-Free Model Merging via Task Vectors
reviewed_competitors.relationship: ICML 2025 data-free successor focused explicitly on task-vector interference.
reviewed_competitors.difference: WUDI derives an approximate task-vector input subspace for linear layers and removes interference under task-vector guidance across vision and language without a scaling coefficient. TSV-M uses singular-factor overlap and polar decorrelation, with narrower modality evidence and a heuristic STI definition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Weight Averaging for Model Merging
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-simultaneous low-rank task-vector merger on vision and language benchmarks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CART centers task vectors around the weight average and truncates the centered updates, arguing that centering reduces interference and top singular directions concentrate knowledge. reviewed_competitors.title: A Systematic Study of In-the-Wild Model Merging for Large Language Models

reviewed_competitors.difference: The TMLR study finds simple Task Arithmetic is the only method that reliably improves as heterogeneous real-world LLM experts are added, while TSV-Merge and other subspace methods decline. This does not negate the CLIP result but sharply bounds its scaling and generality claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: STAR: Spectral Truncation and Rescale for Model Merging
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct spectral-truncation successor for data-free language-model merging.
reviewed_competitors.difference: STAR removes small components in task matrices' spectral spaces and automatically rescales to preserve nuclear norm, reporting robustness across Flan-T5 sizes and twelve merged models. TSV-M keeps leading components but transforms their singular bases, without the explicit norm-preservation step or NLP evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Superpose Task-specific Features for Model Merging

reviewed_competitors.difference: STF formulates preservation of task-specific linear features as a linear system and superposes them in the merged model. TSV-M instead modifies parameter singular bases to make them independent, so STF tests a constructive feature-preservation view of overlapping transformations.

reviewed_competitors.title: DELLA-Merging: Reducing Interference in Model Merging through Magnitude-Based Sampling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary data-free interference competitor for large language models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DELLA ranks delta coordinates and applies magnitude-dependent stochastic pruning and rescaling, reporting gains over TIES and DARE on language, math, and code experts. TSV-M operates deterministically in matrix singular subspaces but lacks those LLM comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaRank: Adaptive Rank Pruning for Enhanced Model Merging

reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaRank reports that dominant singular components themselves can cause critical cross-task interference and learns which singular directions to prune through test-time entropy minimization. TSV-M always preserves an equal top-rank budget per task and is data-free, making AdaRank both a competing method and a direct failure-mode study.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Izmailov et al. establish stochastic weight averaging with a constant or cyclic learning rate and a uniform average, linking it to wider optima on CIFAR and ImageNet. The target isolates dense EMA, early trajectory dynamics, batch-normalization handling, label noise, consistency, calibration, and transfer, but its own clean results do not show a clear advantage over SWA.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Trajectories, Mini-Batch Losses and the Curious Role of the Learning Rate
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sandler et al. model how learning rate shapes training trajectories and connect EMA and SWA to generalization, with ImageNet validation. The target cites this mechanism and adds a focused downstream property audit, but offers less causal or theoretical isolation of the learning-rate effect.

reviewed_competitors.title: Early Weight Averaging Meets High Learning Rates for LLM Pre-training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sanyal et al. apply layer-wise adaptive weight averaging to 125M-12B-parameter language-model pretraining at high learning rates and report advantages over EMA and SWA. This predates and qualifies the target's image-only early-averaging story at much larger scale, while using a different adaptive averaging mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Road Less Scheduled
reviewed_competitors.difference: Defazio et al. derive schedule-free optimization by combining interpolation and averaging so training can avoid a conventional learning-rate schedule, then evaluate it across broad workloads and AlgoPerf. It operationalizes the target's schedule-versus-average motivation inside the optimizer and at broader scale, while the target supplies detailed diagnostics of an ordinary offline EMA.

reviewed_competitors.title: When, Where and Why to Average Weights?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ajroldi et al. test averaging over seven AlgoPerf architectures and datasets, report roughly 12% lower GPU-hours and mild generalization gains, and find that averaging plus learning-rate annealing is best. Their broader controlled benchmark supports a compute benefit but narrows any claim that averaging should replace annealing; the target contributes earlier granular BN, calibration, transfer, and label-noise evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding SGD with Exponential Moving Average: A Case Study in Linear Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li and Gu give instance-dependent high-dimensional linear-regression risk bounds in which EMA reduces variance while retaining an exponentially decaying bias in each eigensubspace, and compare it with tail and beginning averaging. This supplies a mechanism-level theory absent from the target, but only under a linear regression model far from the target's deep vision setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: EMA Without the Lag: Bias-Corrected Iterate Averaging Schemes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Block and Zhang target EMA's lag from overweighting old iterates, introduce bias-corrected averaging schemes, and test them in language-model fine-tuning with accompanying theory. Their intervention directly addresses a failure mode the target observes but does not correct, while the target offers broader empirical diagnostics for conventional EMA.

reviewed_competitors.title: ScheduleFree+: Scaling Learning-Rate-Free & Schedule-Free Learning to Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: ScheduleFree+ extends interpolation-and-averaging optimization to large-language-model training and reports gains without a hand-designed learning-rate schedule. It demonstrates the current scale and adaptive-optimizer frontier beyond the target's fixed-decay image EMA, although it changes the training algorithm rather than auditing an untouched SGD trajectory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Editing Models with Task Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ilharco et al. introduce task vectors, addition, negation, and scalar-controlled editing across vision and language. Tao et al. do not invent Task Arithmetic; they specialize its multi-task addition case, expose an exact one-round FedAvg form, and use that form to motivate heterogeneity analysis and alternative aggregators.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dataless Knowledge Fusion by Merging Weights of Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jin et al.'s RegMean formulates layer merging as a closed-form regression problem using intermediate features and explicitly notes that model merging is an extreme single-communication-round federated-learning case. It therefore precedes the broad bridge claim, although it does not develop FedAvg heterogeneity theory or transfer the four federated aggregators studied by Tao et al.

reviewed_competitors.title: Task Arithmetic in the Tangent Space: Improved Editing of Pre-Trained Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ortiz-Jimenez et al. explain success through weight disentanglement and localized NTK eigenfunctions, then improve merging by fine-tuning in a linearized tangent space. Tao et al. instead use distributed-optimization heterogeneity and post-hoc aggregation; they need no new expert training but do not directly test whether the FL view predicts more than disentanglement.

reviewed_competitors.title: TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: TIES trims small updates, elects a dominant sign, and merges only sign-aligned coordinates, addressing redundancy and sign conflict across modalities and scales. FedGMA shares the sign-agreement intuition and Median/CCLIP address outliers, but Tao et al. compare only to vanilla Task Arithmetic, leaving the stronger purpose-built TIES baseline untested.

reviewed_competitors.title: Localizing Task Information for Improved Model Merging and Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. find mostly non-overlapping task supports, introduce TALL masks, and filter selfish/catastrophic weights with Consensus Merging across vision and NLP with up to 20 tasks. It offers a model-merging-specific diagnosis and data-free variant that competes directly with generic FedGMA/Median/CCLIP but is omitted from Tao et al.'s experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tackling the Objective Inconsistency Problem in Heterogeneous Federated Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. establish objective inconsistency under heterogeneous local computation and introduce FedNova to normalize it over federated rounds. Tao et al.'s training-heterogeneity analysis and FedNova merger are adaptations of this result to a single checkpoint aggregation, so novelty lies in transfer and evaluation rather than the theory or normalization mechanism itself.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2020 proceedings version, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33

reviewed_competitors.title: The Limits and Potentials of Local SGD for Distributed Heterogeneous Learning with Intermittent Communication
reviewed_competitors.difference: Patel et al. prove an existential hard-instance lower bound and min-max limitations of first-order heterogeneity, while also motivating higher-order notions. Tao et al. substitute one communication round into that rate, but print the lower bound with a minimum over problems; checking the primary COLT theorem exposes that quantifier error.

reviewed_competitors.title: Twin-Merging: Dynamic Integration of Modular Expertise in Model Merging
reviewed_competitors.difference: Twin-Merging decomposes shared and exclusive knowledge and trains a router to compose it conditionally at inference, directly targeting heterogeneous test mixtures. It reports much broader vision/language evaluation and larger gains, but pays router-training, storage, and inference complexity that violate Tao et al.'s strict no-additional-training/static-model criteria.

reviewed_competitors.title: No Task Left Behind: Isotropic Model Merging with Common and Task-Specific Subspaces
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marczak et al. connect performance to singular-component alignment, flatten task-matrix spectra, and preserve common plus task-specific subspaces across vision, language, full fine-tuning, and LoRA without additional training. This is a later model-specific competitor to scalar effective-step normalization and coordinate-robust aggregation, especially for the PEFT/full-finetune mismatch Tao et al. leave open.

Its standardized evidence that stronger bases, tuned coefficients, and sparsification matter provides a much broader test bed for Tao et al.'s hypotheses than their three 13B checkpoints, while also documenting the remaining gap to multi-task training.
