reviewed_competitors.title: Recon: Reducing Conflicting Gradients from the Root for Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest direct predecessor for proactively changing the shared parameter space to reduce conflicts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Recon scores conflict per shared layer and converts high-conflict layers to task-specific copies, explicitly interpreting the change as coordinate projection. PSN avoids per-task conflict profiling and architectural expansion by freezing a common magnitude-selected subset. That is cheaper and simpler, but it is task-agnostic and lacks Recon's conflict-targeting rationale; the core 'remove conflict from the root by projection' idea predates this paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: MTLoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation Approach for Efficient Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct contemporary parameter-efficient visual MTL competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: MTLoRA adds task-agnostic and task-specific low-rank modules to disentangle shared interaction from specialization and reports a parameter/accuracy Pareto frontier. PSN adds no modules and can wrap gradient optimizers, but supplies only one common scalar mask, no task-specific adaptation, and no matched efficiency comparison despite MTLoRA predating it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Sparse Sharing Architectures for Multiple Tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sparse Sharing learns a partially overlapping subnetwork for every task and subsumes hard/hierarchical sharing, directly adapting overlap to task relatedness. PSN freezes one shared subset for all tasks, preserving the original architecture and avoiding search, but cannot isolate task-specific conflict inside the encoder.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaShare: Learning What To Share For Efficient Deep Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: learned task-specific routing and sharing competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaShare jointly learns task-specific policies for executing or skipping layers, explicitly trading recognition accuracy against resources. PSN is far cheaper to select and applies at scalar resolution, but its task-independent mask cannot learn which representations should be shared by which tasks and has no FLOP benefit demonstration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient-based Parameter Selection for Efficient Fine-Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: GPS selects a small distributed subset using downstream gradients and reports matched PEFT comparisons across visual tasks. PSN replaces task-aware gradient selection with initial weight magnitude and applies one common subset to MTL, making selection cheaper but less targeted. The paper cites GPS yet does not compare it against PSN even on pretrained vision backbones.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Effectiveness of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: theoretical and algorithmic sparse-fine-tuning precursor used by the paper
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fu et al. analyze sparse fine-tuning through stability/generalization and propose a task-data-aware second-order selector. This paper imports the regularization explanation but applies a simpler magnitude rule to MTL and random initialization without checking the prior theorem's assumptions or comparing selection methods.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Surgery for Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational task-gradient projection method and source of the conflict framing
reviewed_competitors.difference: PCGrad modifies each conflicting task gradient and motivates detrimental interference using conflict together with high curvature and norm imbalance. PSN does not inspect gradients and projects all tasks into a fixed coordinate subspace before/after aggregation; it is cheaper to combine but offers no condition ensuring alignment and reduces the conflict definition to cosine sign alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conflict-Averse Gradient Descent for Multi-task Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: principled conflict-aware optimizer included as a baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: CAGrad chooses an update that protects worst local task improvement within a ball around the mean gradient and supplies convergence analysis. PSN changes capacity before applying CAGrad and empirically improves its aggregate scores, but its own theory neither preserves CAGrad's guarantees under hard masking nor targets the directional derivatives CAGrad optimizes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Just Pick a Sign: Optimizing Deep Multitask Models with Gradient Sign Dropout
reviewed_competitors.relationship: gradient-coordinate masking predecessor included as a baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: GradDrop stochastically masks conflicting gradient signs at an activation layer using current task consistency, changing masks through training. PSN deterministically masks weight coordinates once based on magnitude and can wrap GradDrop. Both can act as regularizers, but only GradDrop is task-gradient aware; neither alone establishes that binary sign consistency is the causal target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-Task Learning as a Bargaining Game
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nash-MTL derives a unique bargaining solution under assumptions and convergence guarantees for combining task gradients. PSN is an orthogonal capacity constraint that improves reported NashMTL aggregate scores, but frequently changes individual task trade-offs and does not analyze whether hard projection preserves the bargaining solution's properties.

reviewed_competitors.title: FAMO: Fast Adaptive Multitask Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: FAMO uses loss history to balance progress with O(1) task-gradient space/time, directly addressing the scaling cost that motivates PSN. The appendix shows PSN can improve FAMO, but there is no conflict-incidence or systems-efficiency analysis for the combination and no proof that weight sparsity adds complementary causal benefit.

reviewed_competitors.title: In Defense of the Unitary Scalarization for Deep Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: critical evidence that standard regularization can explain specialized MTL optimizer gains
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kurin et al. find equal-weight scalarization plus ordinary stabilization/regularization matches or beats complex MTL optimizers and interpret many as regularizers. PSN's broad improvement is consistent with that thesis, but the paper frames gains mainly as proactive conflict reduction and does not compare against matched dense regularization or test mediation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do Current Multi-Task Optimization Methods in Deep Learning Even Help?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: large-scale evaluation warning about MTL optimizer attribution and tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xin et al. report that specialized optimizers do not beat well-tuned traditional approaches and document evaluation pitfalls. PSN offers a simple traditional capacity constraint that improves many named methods, but its different learning rates, unclear K tuning, single-run results, and lack of strong PEFT/dense-regularization controls leave the same attribution concern unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantifying Task Priority for Multi-Task Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Connection-strength optimization uses parameter magnitude together with task-specific backpropagation paths to infer priority and modify gradients toward Pareto solutions. PSN also elevates large-magnitude connections but merely freezes the rest with one common mask. The omitted comparison would help test whether task-aware magnitude information is necessary.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Consistent Multi-Task Learning: Unlocking the Potential of Task-Specific Parameters
reviewed_competitors.difference: ConsMTL uses bilevel optimization so task-specific parameters shape the gradients reaching shared parameters, reporting results from 2 to 40 tasks. It postdates PSN and does not affect priority, but it is now a stronger current comparator for proactive conflict reduction because it targets both shared and task-specific optimization rather than freezing a task-independent shared subset.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rep-MTL: Unleashing the Power of Representation-level Task Saliency for Multi-Task Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: postdating alternative to conflict-centric optimizer design
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rep-MTL argues pure gradient-conflict solving is inconsistent and regularizes representation-level task saliency to preserve task learning and complementarity. It postdates this preprint, but its current evidence reinforces the need to compare PSN's conflict explanation against representation and regularization mechanisms rather than treating cosine incidence as the sole target.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Piggyback freezes a pretrained network and learns a binary weight mask per task at one bit per backbone parameter, preventing cross-task overwriting with much lower mask storage. Soft-TF uses dense real masks on selected Transformer attention projections, starts exactly at the unmasked function, integrates class-incremental task inference, and gains continuous rescaling capacity at substantially higher bits per masked parameter.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Prompt for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: L2P introduces a prompt pool and key-based retrieval for rehearsal-free, task-agnostic class-incremental learning with a frozen pretrained model and tiny memory. Soft-TF reuses its selector and prompts but adds full weight-level masks to improve specialization, changing the resource profile from kilobyte-scale prompt growth to millions of floats per task.

reviewed_competitors.title: DualPrompt: Complementary Prompting for Rehearsal-free Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: DualPrompt separates shared general and task-specific expert prompts and supplies most of Soft-TF's training and retrieval scaffold. Soft-TF retains both prompt types but multiplies selected Q/K/V/O matrices by a routed task mask, increasing expressive capacity, storage, and the degree to which performance depends on modular routing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hierarchical Decomposition of Prompt-Based Continual Learning: Rethinking Obscured Sub-optimality
reviewed_competitors.difference: HiDe-Prompt explicitly decomposes within-task prediction, task-identity inference, and task-adaptive prediction and handles supervised versus self-supervised pretraining with prompt ensembles and feature statistics. Soft-TF plugs into its selector and demonstrates an additional fixed-selector gain from weight rescaling; HiDe-Prompt remains much more storage-efficient and already identifies routing as an independent bottleneck.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixture of Experts Meets Prompt-Based Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: NoRGa interprets prefix prompting as adding task-specific linear experts to a pretrained attention mixture and improves gates with nonlinear residual structure. Soft-TF uses NoRGa's strong prompts and TII selector, then adds dense multiplicative weight experts; the combination performs best in its tables, but the marginal mask gain costs roughly 6.93M values per task.

reviewed_competitors.title: InfLoRA: Interference-Free Low-Rank Adaptation for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: InfLoRA interprets low-rank adapters as a fine-tuning subspace and designs that subspace to avoid new-task interference with old tasks, targeting the stability–plasticity tradeoff without full elementwise matrices. Soft-TF instead isolates stored per-task rescalings and relies on routing; its paper compares only a simpler task-specific LoRA baseline, not this interference-aware method.

reviewed_competitors.title: RanPAC: Random Projections and Pre-trained Models for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: RanPAC freezes a random nonlinear projector and accumulates decorrelated class prototypes, avoiding explicit task inference and training rapidly with bounded head storage. It sacrifices per-task backbone specialization; Soft-TF beats the reproduced RanPAC rows on the chosen splits but trains longer and pays linear full-mask memory and routing complexity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Parameter-Level Soft-Masking for Continual Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: SPG soft-masks gradients according to old-task parameter importance so every task continues using one full shared network, explicitly targeting knowledge transfer and fixed capacity rather than storing a separate task subnetwork. Soft-TF masks the forward weights of a frozen pretrained Transformer per task, giving stronger isolation but linear memory and a discrete routing problem; the target paper cites but does not empirically compare SPG.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stolfo et al. establish the early-attention transport and later-MLP result-processing architecture through causal mediation across arithmetic questions. The reviewed paper reproduces and narrows that circuit, then contributes a neuron-level rule taxonomy and prompt-conditioned causal knockout intended to explain what the MLPs compute.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Addition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kantamneni and Tegmark find a generalized helical number representation and propose a causal Clock algorithm for addition across three mid-sized LLMs, modeling heads, MLP outputs, and neuron preactivations. This challenges a flat no-algorithm reading, although helix features could be the shared numerical basis from which the reviewed paper's local heuristics read and write; a head-to-head intervention is needed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.difference: McLeish et al. add digit-position embeddings and train on at most 20-digit inputs yet reach up to 99% accuracy on 100-digit addition, with gains on sorting and multiplication. Their controlled models are not pretrained LLMs, but they show that transformer arithmetic can length-generalize when tokenization and positional structure support an algorithm—the exact regime excluded by the reviewed study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Arithmetic Heuristic Neurons Form-Invariant? A Mechanistic Analysis of Symbols, Text, and Code in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Naganna et al. identify a compact neuron set shared across symbolic arithmetic, word problems, and Python in three Llama-3 models; targeted necessity/sufficiency tests and cross-format activation transfer recover over 97% of failed addition/subtraction cases. This supports the reviewed paper's heuristic-neuron premise while addressing its format restriction, though it remains within one model family and is under review.

reviewed_competitors.difference: WSINDy moves derivatives onto test functions in a convolutional weak form, avoiding noisy pointwise high-order differentiation and providing fast threshold selection for large libraries. reviewed_competitors.difference: Sun et al. also compute derivatives from spline bases and jointly use equation residuals, but add Bayesian posterior approximation, iterative L0-like sparsity, uncertainty propagation, and comparisons with prior methods. KAN-PISF's primitive proposals could complement it, yet the reviewed work returns no structural or coefficient uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.difference: D-CODE combines a variational objective that avoids observed derivatives with symbolic regression and proves the objective proxies ODE estimation error, evaluating high-noise and infrequent sampling. KAN-PISF handles higher-order targets through explicit spline derivatives but supplies neither an identifiability argument nor comparative automation.

reviewed_competitors.title: D-CIPHER: Discovery of Closed-form Partial Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: D-CIPHER searches a broad variational class of higher-order ODEs and PDEs without estimating derivatives, using constrained symbolic optimization and explicit prior encoding. KAN-PISF may be more visually collaborative, but its manually constructed library and strong-form derivatives are less general and less robustly benchmarked.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovery of Partial Differential Equations from Highly Noisy and Sparse Data with Physics-Informed Information Criterion
reviewed_competitors.difference: PIC combines genetic library generation, moving-horizon parsimony, and PINN precision scoring, evaluating seven PDEs, sparse data, up to very high Gaussian noise, hyperparameter sensitivity, and a real multiscale application. KAN-PISF's four selected demonstrations do not substantiate comparable robustness or practical model selection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symmetry-Informed Governing Equation Discovery
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. compress sparse-regression and genetic-programming search spaces with known or learned symmetries and report recovery probabilities over 100 noisy runs plus long-horizon prediction. KAN-PISF uses no symmetry or dimensional prior and reports only selected runs, leaving reliability far less established.

reviewed_competitors.difference: SKANODE embeds KAN in a structured neural ODE, performs virtual sensing of latent displacement and velocity, recovers Duffing/Van der Pol nonlinearities, and studies real F-16 hysteresis against black-box and ARX/NARX baselines. reviewed_competitors.title: Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gurnee et al. use labeled concepts and k-sparse probes across seven models to quantify which neurons carry known features, supplying external targets and scale comparisons. The reviewed method is unsupervised and can surface unknown modes, but lacks that label-grounded accuracy and model-scale evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary SAE baseline and target application.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. learn overcomplete sparse directions, score automated interpretability, and localize causally responsible IOI features. The reviewed paper instead characterizes examples for one existing unit and proposes an auxiliary compactness loss; its MNIST evaluation never matches the baseline's language or causal validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: Makelov et al. compare unsupervised dictionaries with supervised task features along approximation, control and interpretation axes and reveal feature occlusion and oversplitting. That external causal scaffold directly addresses the reviewed paper's circularity from optimizing and evaluating the same geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous large-scale SAE architecture and evaluation competitor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gao et al. use TopK sparsity, control dead latents, derive scaling laws, and evaluate feature recovery, explainability and downstream-effect sparsity up to a 16-million-latent GPT-4 SAE. The reviewed work offers a cheap additional metric but only tests one 512-unit MNIST SAE and worsens its reconstruction-sparsity frontier.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gated SAEs separate support selection from magnitude estimation to avoid L1 shrinkage and obtain a better fidelity-sparsity frontier on LMs through 7B parameters. The reviewed prototype regularizer targets within-unit compactness but quadruples active density and lacks a matched-fidelity comparison, so the methods address different failure modes.

reviewed_competitors.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Ground-truth stress test of monosemantic-looking SAE features.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chanin et al. use known first-letter features and hundreds of SAEs to show apparently monosemantic latents can fail to fire because parent features are absorbed into children. A tight characteristic-example cluster would not detect these missing positives, demonstrating why the reviewed geometry needs coverage and recall tests as well as coherence.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v6 / NeurIPS 2025 oral record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking Evaluation of Sparse Autoencoders through the Representation of Polysemous Words
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct semantics-focused successor for SAE polysemanticity evaluation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Minegishi et al. build evaluations around known senses of polysemous words and find improvements on MSE-L0 do not necessarily improve monosemantic representation. Their labeled sense contrast measures semantic separation more directly than unlabeled point-cloud compactness, though it covers a narrower predefined concept family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Successor challenging atomistic and complete SAE feature interpretations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Leask et al. use SAE stitching to demonstrate incompleteness and meta-SAEs to decompose apparently atomic latents, showing feature granularity changes with dictionary scale. This directly qualifies the reviewed premise that one dense cluster should be equated with one canonical semantic behaviour.

reviewed_competitors.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: SAEBench compares more than 200 SAEs across architectures using interpretability, disentanglement and practical applications and finds proxy improvements do not reliably transfer. Neuron-embedding compactness could be added as one unsupervised diagnostic, but the reviewed paper's claim that it directly measures monosemanticity is not supported without correlations to these independent axes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Sparse Autoencoders Useful? A Case Study in Sparse Probing
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Downstream-utility stress test for SAE representations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kantamneni et al. evaluate data scarcity, imbalance, label noise and covariate shift with strong non-SAE probes and find no consistent ensemble advantage. It exemplifies the independent practical validation absent from the reviewed MNIST geometry, while leaving open whether clusters help human hypothesis generation.

reviewed_competitors.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.difference: MIB evaluates whether methods recover task-relevant causal variables and pathways across tasks and models; supervised DAS wins its causal-variable track and SAE features are not better than neurons. The reviewed clusters organize examples but never show recovery of a causal variable, making MIB a natural external endpoint.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fereidouni et al. use concept-conditioned activation distributions, Jensen-Shannon separability, five datasets, two LMs and targeted suppression to connect semantic separation with intervention utility. This is more directly label- and behavior-grounded than weighted input compactness, though it requires predefined concepts.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Price of Amortized inference in Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current theoretical and empirical successor on SAE pathologies.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sun et al. connect feature absorption, splitting, dead and dense latents to global amortized encoding and mitigate them with semi/non-amortized inference. Their analysis suggests a single global prototype penalty may trade one pathology for another; it also supplies the kind of mechanism and multi-pathology evaluation missing from the reviewed unexplained dead-unit result.

reviewed_competitors.difference: LEO already learns a low-dimensional stochastic latent and performs differentiable task adaptation there rather than in the high-dimensional parameter space. It decodes the latent into classifier weights and targets few-shot classification, whereas LPN conditions a shared input-output decoder directly on an implicit-program latent, trains with leave-one-pair-out reconstruction, and tests structured program induction and ARC.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Synthesize Programs as Interpretable and Generalizable Policies
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest prior continuous latent program search
reviewed_competitors.difference: LEAPS learns a continuous embedding of executable DSL programs and uses gradient-free cross-entropy search to find reward-maximizing interpretable policies. This more directly predates the phrase and concept of searching a latent program space; LPN removes the DSL and executable-program decoder, instead optimizing a neurally implicit transformation by demonstration likelihood and allowing gradient search, gaining flexibility but losing explicit program interpretability and execution guarantees.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v4 (2022-01-31), full primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Combinatorial Optimization with Policy Adaptation using Latent Space Search
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct precursor inference-time latent policy search
reviewed_competitors.difference: COMPASS, which shares an author with LPN, trains a conditioned policy whose 16-dimensional latent regions specialize to instance subdistributions and searches them with CMA-ES at inference time. It already establishes that anticipating latent search during training can beat full-policy adaptation on combinatorial optimization; LPN transfers that principle to input-output program induction, amortizes an initialization from demonstrations, and differentiates through gradient-based search.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 (2024-05-28), full primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Combining Induction and Transduction for Abstract Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: contemporaneous direct ARC induction and transduction competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. train matched neural architectures on synthetic variants of Python programs and show complementary strengths between explicit program induction and direct transduction, with their ensemble later combined with stronger TTT for 61.9 percent public validation accuracy. LPN avoids explicit Python generation and searches only a compact latent, making adaptation cheaper and domain-language-free but scoring 15.5 percent on its ARC evaluation protocol and offering no executable explanation.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v4 (2024-12-02), full primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Test-Time Training for Few-Shot Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Akyurek et al. update all or selected LM parameters per task and, with augmentation and hierarchical voting, report 53.0 percent ARC public-validation pass-at-2 and 61.9 percent with a program-synthesis ensemble. LPN's 256-value latent update is much smaller and wins its matched 178-million-parameter comparison at low-to-medium FLOPs, but it does not demonstrate competitive absolute accuracy against the later 8-billion-parameter TTT system and the benchmark splits and compute are not directly aligned.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 (2025-03-25), full primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: CodeIt: Self-Improving Language Models with Prioritized Hindsight Replay
reviewed_competitors.difference: CodeIt iterates explicit program sampling, execution, hindsight relabeling, and prioritized replay and reports 15 percent on ARC evaluation. It produces executable programs and improves a model across tasks, while LPN performs continuous per-task latent adaptation with a fixed decoder; their similar headline accuracy conceals large differences in interpretability, training data, parameter count, and inference budget.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 (2024-07-01), full primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Improving Language Models for Evolutionary Program Synthesis: A Case Study on ARC-AGI
reviewed_competitors.relationship: subsequent evolutionary search and self-improvement competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: SOAR alternates evolutionary sampling and refinement of explicit programs with hindsight fine-tuning, reaching 52 percent on the ARC-AGI public test set. It uses far larger language models and a more expensive outer self-improvement loop but demonstrates that discrete executable search, cross-task learning from search traces, and refinement scale well beyond LPN's reported ARC coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: ARC-AGI-2: A New Challenge for Frontier AI Reasoning Systems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: current successor benchmark and external-validity boundary
reviewed_competitors.difference: ARC-AGI-2 preserves the few-shot grid interface but increases compositional complexity and was constructed after strong ARC-AGI-1 progress. LPN is evaluated only on ARC-AGI-1 and its observed three-primitive composition failure makes transfer to ARC-AGI-2 an open question rather than an established general-reasoning result.

reviewed_competitors.title: ARC Prize 2025: Technical Report
reviewed_competitors.relationship: current field-level result and systems competitor audit
reviewed_competitors.difference: The 2025 report identifies iterative refinement loops as the dominant ARC-AGI-2 pattern, reports a 24 percent private-set winner at about 0.20 dollars per task, documents competitive zero-pretraining test-time gradient methods with roughly seven-million-parameter networks, and reports application-layer frontier-model refinement above 50 percent on ARC-AGI-1. These results support LPN's general thesis that per-task iterative adaptation matters, while superseding its absolute ARC-AGI-1 performance and showing that latent-only search is one of several viable refinement spaces.

reviewed_competitors.title: Position: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: the central convergence hypothesis challenged and refined by the reviewed paper
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huh et al. synthesize and demonstrate representational convergence across model scale and modalities and propose a shared statistical model of reality. Ciernik et al. make the evaluation stimulus explicit and show that relative vision-model alignment depends on objective and dataset; however, their final-layer observational statistic does not directly test whether models encode the same underlying content.

reviewed_competitors.title: Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational CKA method and representation-comparison baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kornblith et al. motivate CKA, characterize its invariances, and show it can align layers across random initializations. The reviewed work builds a second-order correlation over CKA dyads across datasets, adding stimulus consistency but inheriting the need to justify what CKA's geometry means functionally.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grounding Representation Similarity with Statistical Testing
reviewed_competitors.relationship: functional sensitivity and specificity audit for representation metrics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ding et al. evaluate CKA and alternatives by whether they respond to changes that alter functional behavior and ignore changes that do not, finding disagreements and shared failures. Ciernik et al. compare metric trends and linear-probe gaps but do not apply these sensitivity/specificity tests to their cross-dataset consistency statistic.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deconfounded Representation Similarity for Comparison of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct input-population confound and missing metric baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cui et al. show that input population structure can spuriously increase RSA and CKA even for random networks and propose covariate-adjusted deconfounded similarity that better tracks OOD accuracy. Because Ciernik et al. deliberately vary the input dataset, repeating the atlas with deconfounded CKA is a decisive missing baseline for separating stimulus geometry from model geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Wild Comparisons: A Study of How Representation Similarity Changes When Input Data Is Drawn from a Shifted Distribution
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest contemporaneous precursor on stimulus-distribution sensitivity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Brown et al. directly vary in-distribution, shifted, and subpopulation inputs and report that absolute similarity changes while relative comparisons remain fairly robust in a smaller setting. Ciernik et al. scale this question to 64 models and 23 datasets and attribute heterogeneity to model/dataset groups, but do not inherit a formal distribution-shift scalar or uncertainty model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Getting aligned on representational alignment
reviewed_competitors.relationship: cross-disciplinary taxonomy of alignment measurements and behavior
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sucholutsky et al. distinguish measurement, mutual information, bridging, and causality across machine learning and neuroscience and foreground when alignment should imply behavior. Ciernik et al. instantiate one geometric, stimulus-conditioned cell of this taxonomy; the broader framework highlights that consistency alone is not causal or semantic alignment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Equivalence between representational similarity analysis, centered kernel alignment, and canonical correlations analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: mathematical dependence among purported robustness metrics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Williams shows that mean-centered RSA and CKA are largely equivalent and connects them to CCA. This makes Ciernik et al.'s similar conclusions under linear CKA and RSA useful implementation robustness but weaker evidence of construct robustness than agreement among unrelated measures would be.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Representational Similarity Measures Imply about Decodable Information
reviewed_competitors.relationship: theoretical interpretation of similarity through linear decoding
reviewed_competitors.difference: Harvey et al. derive how CKA, CCA, and other measures correspond to average alignment of optimal linear readouts. Their results provide a more precise interpretation for Ciernik et al.'s geometry, while also showing that a single CKA coefficient does not identify which tasks or features are shared.

reviewed_competitors.title: Not all solutions are created equal: An analytical dissociation of functional and representational similarity in deep linear neural networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: analytical counterexample to inferring function from representation alignment
reviewed_competitors.difference: Braun et al. prove and simulate that representational and functional similarity can dissociate in both directions and that generalization error need not constrain representation. This directly limits interpretation of Ciernik et al.'s performance-gap correlations and motivates functional or causal tests beyond geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: A large-scale examination of inductive biases shaping high-level visual representation in brains and machines
reviewed_competitors.relationship: large-scale factor analysis emphasizing training-data effects
reviewed_competitors.difference: Conwell et al. analyze many vision networks and report that training data is a key driver of high-level representational geometry, potentially beyond architecture, objective, or metric. Ciernik et al. cite this challenge and reproduce a strong training-domain effect only in Appendix I, which qualifies their main coarse claim that data size is less important than objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Similarity of Neural Network Models: A Survey of Functional and Representational Measures
reviewed_competitors.relationship: current comprehensive map of metric properties and failure modes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Klabunde et al. organize functional and representational measures, their invariances, robustness issues, and application tradeoffs. The reviewed paper supplies a new stimulus-consistency application but evaluates a narrow subset of this design space and omits several functional and deconfounded controls highlighted by the survey.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causes and Consequences of Representational Similarity in Machine Learning Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct current controlled study of causes and downstream consequences
reviewed_competitors.difference: This ICLR 2026-era work varies task and dataset overlap across models and modalities and evaluates consequences of the resulting alignment, moving from observational zoo stratification toward controlled causes. It is a close successor and a stronger template for testing whether objective or shared data actually creates consistency.

reviewed_competitors.title: Position: An Empirically Grounded Identifiability Theory Will Accelerate Self-Supervised Learning Research
reviewed_competitors.relationship: current theoretical account of SSL convergence and non-identifiability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reizinger et al. argue that finite samples, data diversity, augmentations, architecture, initialization, optimization, and dynamics all condition whether SSL representations are identifiable or converge. These are precisely the uncontrolled variables inside Ciernik et al.'s heterogeneous SSL group, so high group consistency is evidence to explain rather than an isolated objective effect.

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimating Neural Representation Alignment from Sparsely Sampled Inputs and Features
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chun et al. analyze CKA bias from sampling both inputs and representation features and introduce a corrected estimator. Ciernik et al. use unbiased CKA and bootstrap input subsets, a strong start, but do not test feature-sampling or dimension-dependent correction across checkpoints with radically different widths.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convergence Without Understanding: When Language Models Agree on Representations but Disagree on Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: current empirical dissociation between alignment, correctness, and causal reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Usama and Chang report high cross-model CKA even on collectively failed problems, sharp alignment changes across generation stages, and weak causal influence of shared decodable information. Although their domain is language reasoning, the results directly caution against interpreting Ciernik et al.'s stable final-layer vision geometry as shared understanding without causal tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-Task Pretraining Drives Representational Convergence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: current controlled mechanism for objective/task-diversity-driven convergence
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park uses small transformers on controlled geometric tasks and finds increasing task diversity drives CKA convergence and dominant world-map structure. This provides a causal, factorial test of one Platonic mechanism, whereas Ciernik et al.'s heterogeneous pretrained zoo cannot distinguish task diversity from data, architecture, family, or optimization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reliability of CKA as a Similarity Measure in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct reliability audit of the primary metric
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work studies when CKA behaves reliably across layer widths, architectures, initializations, and sample regimes and documents important sensitivity conditions. Ciernik et al. address stimulus count carefully on ImageNet, but a broader CKA reliability panel across model widths and representation dimensions remains a relevant missing diagnostic.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lossless and Near-Lossless Compression for Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: The April 2024 precursor (largely the same authors) establishes model compressibility and byte grouping and adds a tunable near-lossless variant; ZipNN supersedes it with the Huffman-only design justified by the shuffle control, clean/regular model auto-detection, delta auto codec selection, multi-worker throughput engineering, and end-to-end hub/serving measurements, while dropping the lossy variant.

reviewed_competitors.title: NeuZip: Memory-Efficient Training and Inference with Dynamic Compression of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: NeuZip also exploits low-entropy exponent bits but compresses them with ANS on the GPU to shrink live training/inference memory (Llama-3 8B training 31GB to under 16GB), keeping weights compressed in device memory; ZipNN targets at-rest storage and network transfer with CPU Huffman streams, clean-model byte grouping, and delta compression, and does not address in-memory training footprints.

reviewed_competitors.title: FM-Delta: Lossless Compression for Storing Massive Fine-tuned Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: FM-Delta (NeurIPS 2024) maps fine-tuned and pre-trained parameters to same-width integers and entropy-codes the integer delta, with theoretical analysis of fine-tune drift, purpose-built for cloud storage of fine-tune families; ZipNN's delta mode is a simpler XOR plus Huffman/Zstd auto-selection evaluated mainly on training checkpoints, but ZipNN additionally covers standalone models, gradients/optimizers, and throughput engineering.

reviewed_competitors.title: Huff-LLM: End-to-End Lossless Compression for Efficient LLM Inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huff-LLM keeps Huffman-compressed weights compressed through the entire inference pipeline including on-chip buffers, targeting latency/energy on edge and hardware architectures; ZipNN decompresses fully before serving and optimizes storage/transfer, demonstrating that the same entropy-coding observation supports both at-rest and in-pipeline designs.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Barakat and Bianchi construct a non-autonomous continuous Adam ODE, prove weak approximation of interpolated stochastic iterates, establish existence and convergence under stated conditions, and analyze fluctuations. reviewed_competitors.difference: Belotto da Silva and Gazeau derive a general non-autonomous differential system for adaptive algorithms and study critical-point convergence, saddle avoidance, and convex rates. The reviewed work is narrower but connects its modified equation to practical beta-gamma sweeps and nested adaptivity; its claim of a continuous-time foundation should remain secondary to this prior general and rigorous framework.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the SDEs and Scaling Rules for Adaptive Gradient Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Malladi et al. derive and validate SDE approximations for RMSprop and Adam with correctness guarantees and use them to obtain practical batch-size scaling rules on vision and language tasks. The reviewed paper obtains a different deterministic max-update geometry and an optimizer hypothesis, but its omission of stochasticity and approximation error makes its practical generalization claims weaker.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noether's Learning Dynamics: Role of Symmetry Breaking in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor for normalization as implicit adaptive optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tanaka and Kunin already use continuous Lagrangian symmetry analysis to show that normalization-induced scale invariance creates an RMSprop-like implicit adaptive effect. The reviewed paper's extension to Adam and proposal of explicit nested normalization are useful, but the central normalization-as-adaptivity interpretation is inherited, and the explicit 2-Adam mapping is only heuristic after coarse-graining.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdamP: Slowing Down the Slowdown for Momentum Optimizers on Scale-invariant Weights
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Omitted direct optimizer competitor for scale-invariant weights
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdamP identifies radial momentum growth and premature effective-step decay on scale-invariant weights, removes the radial update component, and reports gains across 13 vision, retrieval, detection, language, and audio benchmarks. k-Adam instead adds repeated moment normalization and is evaluated on two small settings; a direct comparison is essential because both claim to improve Adam specifically through normalization-induced scale geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rotational Equilibrium: How Weight Decay Balances Learning Across Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous detailed theory of scale-invariant weight norms under AdamW
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kosson et al. analyze norm and angular-update equilibria across Adam, Lion, and momentum SGD, connect weight decay to balanced rotation, and validate the mechanism broadly. The reviewed paper focuses on an EMA interpretation of the norm and nested adaptivity, but does not compare its approximation or optimizer against this more directly quantified eta-lambda-weight-norm theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Everett et al. test tens of thousands of models up to 27B parameters, show Adam epsilon must scale correctly to avoid underflow, and introduce epsilon-free Adam-atan2. The reviewed work omits epsilon from its theory and defaults k-Adam to 10^-30 without ablation, so this primary result directly challenges its unqualified numerical-stability framing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Bias of AdamW: l-infinity-Norm Constrained Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Discrete-time AdamW dynamics and cumulative-update comparator
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xie and Li analyze AdamW's discrete cumulative updates and establish an l-infinity constrained implicit-bias interpretation. The reviewed paper cites their bounding technique but shifts to instantaneous approximate max updates; Xie-Li illustrates why update geometry and optimization outcome require a discrete, loss-aware analysis beyond bounded step size.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Convergence of Adam for Stochastic Optimization under Relaxed Assumptions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Rigorous stochastic stability and convergence comparator
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hong and Lin prove high-probability stationary-point rates for vanilla Adam under affine-variance noise, unbounded-gradient-compatible generalized smoothness, and specified hyperparameters. The reviewed paper cites it but substitutes a loss-independent update envelope for convergence; the two results should not be conflated, because bounded u_n alone is substantially weaker than stochastic optimization stability.

reviewed_competitors.title: ODE Approximation for the Adam Algorithm: General and Overparametrized Setting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dereich, Jentzen, and Kassing rigorously treat fixed momentum parameters and vanishing step size through a fast-slow Adam vector field and asymptotic pseudo-trajectories, then distinguish zeros of that field from objective critical points. This postdates the reviewed paper but supplies the kind of controlled fixed-momentum limit and convergence semantics missing from its formal Taylor argument.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Delétang and collaborators organize formal-language tasks by the Chomsky hierarchy and empirically train 20,910 models on 15 tasks to relate computational requirements to architecture and out-of-distribution length generalization. Algebraic circuit divergence covers richer polynomial structure, but the prior work already instantiates a theory-of-computation framework with extensive predictive experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou and collaborators use simplicity of RASP-L programs as a hypothesis for when transformers will length-generalize and support it with experiments and scratchpad interventions. Circuit divergence describes problem representations independently of a transformer, while RASP-L is architecture-linked and empirically predictive; the two frameworks need head-to-head predictive evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Faith and Fate represents multi-digit multiplication, logic puzzles, and dynamic programming as computation graphs, measures complexity through subprocedures, and reports empirical and theoretical degradation with composition depth. The reviewed Perspective generalizes the graph vocabulary to algebraic-circuit properties but its claim that prior reasoning evaluations lack verifiable complexity frameworks is too broad.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Expressive Power of Transformers with Chain of Thought
reviewed_competitors.difference: Merrill and Sabharwal formally characterize how logarithmic, linear, and polynomial intermediate-generation lengths change decoder-only transformer expressivity under stated precision and normalization assumptions. The Perspective suggests checking chain-of-thought against circuit paths but supplies no theorem or experiment connecting its circuit depth to generated reasoning length.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analyzing the Nuances of Transformers' Polynomial Simplification Abilities
reviewed_competitors.difference: Agarwal, Aditya, and Goyal generate polynomials with unique simplification proof steps, vary coefficient and representation choices, train transformer baselines, and test curricula and calculator delegation. It is narrower than the circuit-divergence agenda but directly implements the proposed polynomial transduction and intermediate-reasoning setting three years earlier.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.difference: McLeish and collaborators isolate digit-position encoding, input injection, and recurrence and report up to 99 percent accuracy when training on 20-digit addition and testing at 100 digits, plus multiplication and sorting. Their results show why token position and architecture can dominate a nominally fixed algebraic circuit class, exposing costs omitted by the Perspective's field-element divergence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Circuit Complexity Bounds for RoPE-based Transformer Architecture
reviewed_competitors.difference: Submitted four days after the reviewed paper, Chen and collaborators prove that, unless TC0 equals NC1, constant-layer polynomial-precision RoPE transformers of bounded width cannot solve arithmetic formula evaluation or Boolean formula value. This is a concrete architecture-to-circuit result with explicit assumptions; the Perspective's depth-to-layers mapping is an untested intuition and should be grounded in results of this kind.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fan and collaborators formalize iterative n-RASP-L tasks and train weight-shared looped transformers whose inference depth adapts with problem length. Their empirical design directly tests a resource mapping and shows why fixed network layers need not correspond to algorithm depth; the circuit-divergence proposal does not model recurrent or test-time computation.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang and collaborators give an identifiable-in-the-limit framework for causal transformers with learnable absolute positions, prove positive results for a family of tasks, and experimentally test success and failure predictions. Its assumptions are idealized and its scope is length generalization rather than algebraic circuits, but it demonstrates the theorem-plus-validation standard needed to turn the reviewed agenda into a predictive science.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evaluating Compositionality in Neural Models Using Arithmetic Expressions
reviewed_competitors.difference: CobA procedurally generates addition-and-multiplication expressions and controlled partitions for localism, substitutivity, productivity, and systematicity, then compares transformer, sequential, and tree-structured encoders. Its arithmetic and model scope is limited, but it directly implements several split concepts the Perspective presents as future circuit benchmarks and documents severe compositional extrapolation failures.

It instead specifies desired log-density evolution for deterministic and stochastic flow sampling and controls detail over a range, making it the more direct practical density-control method while relying on the reviewed density-change identity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Probing the Geometry of Diffusion Models with the String Method
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct current follow-on for high-density modes, typical paths, and learned-density geometry.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The string method connects endpoints through transport, zero-temperature minimum-energy paths, and finite-temperature principal curves, reproducing cartoon-like high-likelihood image interiors and adding protein paths. It studies path geometry and an energy-entropy continuum, whereas the reviewed paper studies single-sample conditional modes and likelihood tracking.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inverse problems with diffusion models: MAP estimation via mode-seeking loss
reviewed_competitors.difference: VML-MAP minimizes a variational mode-seeking loss at each reverse step for measurement-conditioned inverse problems and is analytic for linear measurements. reviewed_competitors.title: D-Flow: Differentiating through Flows for Controlled Generation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct prior art for post-training optimization through diffusion and flow samplers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: D-Flow differentiates arbitrary objectives through a deterministic generative flow and optimizes the source noise while regularizing it toward the Gaussian typical shell. It is more general for controlled tasks and explicitly avoids collapse to the Gaussian mode; the reviewed method provides density-specific stochastic identities and conditional mode dynamics without backpropagating an external loss through the whole flow.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Autoguidance subtracts a smaller or undertrained model to improve quality without reducing variation and motivates avoiding low-density outliers. reviewed_competitors.difference: DEER is a direct omitted decision-training prior with stronger tool generalization; AWL contributes model-relative relabeling and scientific knowledge distillation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive-RAG: Learning to Adapt Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models through Question Complexity
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Automatically derives outcome labels and trains a complexity router among no retrieval, single retrieval, and iterative retrieval.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This is the structurally closest omitted TUA prior; AWL replaces an external classifier with model-relative correctness labels and extends routing to scientific simulators plus internalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: LLM and Simulation as Bilevel Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Scientific-discovery method coupling LLM hypotheses with differentiable simulation feedback, cited by AWL.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It targets iterative discovery/optimization; AWL targets QA, knowledge distillation, and selective calls but validates primarily against synthetic evaluator outcomes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Tool-augmented Large Language Models be Aware of Incomplete Conditions?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Studies whether agents refrain when questions or tools lack conditions needed for valid execution.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AWL's binary failure-derived labels assume hard implies use; they do not represent impossible, missing-input, unreliable-tool, or abstain cases.

reviewed_competitors.title: Query Routing for Homogeneous Tools: An Instantiation in the RAG Scenario
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predicts both performance and cost to route queries to cost-effective retrieval tools.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It operationalizes utility and cost, whereas AWL treats fewer calls as efficient and does not estimate marginal outcome gain.

reviewed_competitors.title: WTU-EVAL: A Whether-or-Not Tool Usage Evaluation Benchmark for Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct whether-or-not benchmark and fine-tuning dataset showing that incorrect tool use can hurt performance.
reviewed_competitors.difference: WTU-Eval is a major omitted pre-v1 benchmark/training prior; AWL contributes dynamic model-relative labels and scientific domains but uses a less causal necessity definition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Toolken+: Improving LLM Tool Usage with Reranking and a Reject Option
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Adds an explicit reject/no-tool action and reduces false-positive calls 17 days before AWL v1.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Toolken+ is a direct omitted selective-use prior based on reranking; AWL instead alters training data and internalizes scientific tool knowledge.

reviewed_competitors.title: ChemToolAgent: The Impact of Tools on Language Agents for Chemistry Problem Solving
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent scientific-tool study finding that tools do not consistently improve base-model chemistry performance.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is evaluation-focused and chemistry-specific; its mixed tool treatment effects reinforce the need for utility labels beyond AWL's hard-equals-tool assumption.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Training Large Language Models for Tool-Use Without Demonstrations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Post-AWL method that synthesizes its own tool traces and studies SFT and preference tuning without demonstrations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its mixed out-of-domain results show that synthetic tool traces do not automatically generalize; AWL does not test comparable unseen-domain transfer.

reviewed_competitors.title: SMART: Self-Aware Agent for Tool Overuse Mitigation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Trains step-level rationales for switching between parametric reasoning and tools and evaluates out-of-distribution generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SMART has a finer-grained switching target and stronger routing generalization tests; AWL uniquely combines routing with scientific solver distillation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Tool Use in Large Language Models with Meta-Cognition Trigger
reviewed_competitors.relationship: MeCo derives a latent metacognitive trigger for tool use without AWL-style fine-tuning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MeCo offers a cheaper inference-time alternative to repeated sampling and adaptive retraining; AWL targets knowledge internalization as well as routing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Alignment for Efficient Tool Calling of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Uses probabilistic knowledge-boundary estimation and multi-objective alignment over accuracy, speed, and cost.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It provides a more explicit efficiency objective than AWL's binary label and call-count proxy; AWL covers scientific simulator knowledge transfer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Distilling Tool Knowledge into Language Models via Back-Translated Traces
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Close post-publication WKL competitor translating tool calls into coherent natural-language reasoning before distillation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It focuses on tool-free internalization quality; AWL jointly trains a selective policy for retaining tool access on harder items.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaTIR: Adaptive Tool-Integrated Reasoning via Difficulty-Aware Policy Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-direct successor combining difficulty-aware policy optimization, adaptive budgets, and reasoning internalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaTIR optimizes an explicit efficiency reward and analyzes reward-sign failure, whereas AWL imitates static easy/hard targets without utility or cost calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Tool-Overuse Illusion: Why Does LLM Prefer External Tools over Internal Knowledge?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Causal analysis linking tool overuse to misestimated knowledge boundaries and outcome-only rewards.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It uses balanced rewards and DPO to correct knowledge-boundary errors; AWL's self-correctness labels can inherit precisely those miscalibrations.

reviewed_competitors.title: To Call or Not to Call: A Framework to Assess and Optimize LLM Tool Calling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Separates tool necessity, utility, and affordability and optimizes budgeted call allocation with latent estimators.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its taxonomy directly exposes AWL's conflation of direct-answer failure with tool desirability and supplies a more causal evaluation target.

reviewed_competitors.title: LLM Agents Already Know When to Call Tools - Even Without Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: When2Tool builds controlled necessity boundaries and reads them with a linear-probe controller.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It offers cleaner necessity ground truth and a lightweight controller; AWL derives labels from model failure and adapts the full model on domain tools.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Tools Always Beneficial? Learning to Invoke Tools Adaptively for Dual-Mode Multimodal LLM Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: AutoTool jointly explores tool-assisted and text-only modes under mode-specific reinforcement-learning rewards.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It learns from outcome differences rather than fixed failure labels and extends to multimodal reasoning; AWL provides scientific-domain distillation and iterative supervised relabeling.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Effectiveness and Efficiency of Agentic Tool-calling and RL Training
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Shows agentic tool-call results are highly sensitive to seed, system prompt, conversation construction, and history handling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its controlled sensitivity study highlights missing robustness dimensions in AWL's single-run evaluation; AWL focuses on scientific environment adaptation.

reviewed_competitors.title: ToolFailBench: Diagnosing Tool-Use Failures in LLM Agents
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Diagnoses tool skipping, unnecessary calls, result ignoring, fabrication, and other distinct failure types.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AWL's binary call/no-call metric cannot observe these failure types and can reward a call on a hard item even when the result is unused or harmful.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Empirical Interpretation of Internal Circuits and Properties in Grokked Transformers on Modular Polynomials

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Mechanism and Dynamics of Modular Addition: Fourier Features, Lottery Ticket, and Grokking

It supplies stronger circuit-selection dynamics for a different architecture; the reviewed clustering-head stationarity result still lacks such reachability theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cohen et al. establish progressive sharpening and the 2/eta edge-of-stability phenomenon; Central Flows attempts to predict the smoothed trajectory and residual covariance once that regime begins.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Gradient Methods at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work documents effective-Hessian equilibration for Adam-like methods at full and large batch sizes; Central Flows derives time-averaged equations for Scalar RMSProp and momentum-free RMSProp but does not cover full Adam.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damian et al. analyze cubic self-stabilization and a constrained trajectory primarily with one unstable eigenvalue; Central Flows generalizes the time-averaged covariance construction to multiple critical directions and adaptive preconditioners.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rod Flow: A Continuous-Time Model for Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rod Flow represents neighboring iterates as an extended one-dimensional object, gives a principled quartic derivation, and reports comparable neural-network accuracy with an explicit cheaper flow, directly targeting Central Flow's cubic failure and computational cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Rod Flow Model for Adam at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: This extension models heavy-ball, Nesterov, RMSProp, Adam, and NAdam in joint parameter-momentum state, covering the momentum and full-Adam regimes that Central Flows explicitly leaves open.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability: Free Energy Model and Kinetic Description of the Two-Layer Network
reviewed_competitors.difference: The free-energy model also couples averaged weights to fast-fluctuation covariance, but tracks oscillation envelopes without requiring timescale separation and derives a mean-field kinetic limit for wide two-layer networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Edge Flow: A Tractable and Predictive Continuous-Time Model for Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Edge Flow explicitly evolves the center, oscillation direction, and magnitude using two gradients and one Hessian-vector product, resolving onset oscillations and offering a cheaper state-space alternative to covariance-constrained Central Flow.

reviewed_competitors.title: LayerSkip: Enabling Early Exit Inference and Self-Speculative Decoding
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary scalable alternative for converting intermediate predictions into verified speedups.

The reviewed work contributes an observational rank signal on GPT-2 XL, but offers much narrower efficiency evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: FitNets: Hints for Thin Deep Nets
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Canonical predecessor for using a fixed teacher's intermediate representations to make a difficult student easier to optimize.
reviewed_competitors.difference: FitNets regresses selected student features onto a trained teacher through learned adapters for model compression; guidance uses dimension-invariant sample geometry across many layers and, crucially, studies cross-family random guides to isolate effects available without learned knowledge.

reviewed_competitors.title: Similarity-Preserving Knowledge Distillation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct loss-level predecessor that distills pairwise minibatch similarities between heterogeneous teacher and student activations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It uses a trained teacher and normalized Gram-matrix matching for vision compression; guidance changes the normalization to CKA, applies alignment layerwise across broader architecture families, and treats random guides and ill-suited targets as the scientific intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Functional Transfer Methods Capture Simple Inductive Biases?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier direct study of whether functional and representational matching actually transfers an architectural inductive bias across networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nix et al. give a negative result: ordinary distillation and representational-distance learning need not transfer even shift equivariance, then learn an explicit equivariance model for regularization. Guidance reports task gains and CKA/error-pattern changes but does not directly verify transfer of a formal invariant property, so the earlier result narrows its causal interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Random Teachers are Good Teachers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior evidence that a frozen randomly initialized teacher can improve a student without dark knowledge.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies self-distillation dynamics, normally with the same architecture, a student initialized near the random teacher, and downstream linear probes. Guidance combines supervised task loss with layerwise CKA between deliberately different architecture families and does not require near-teacher parameter initialization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning from Randomly Initialized Neural Network Features
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier formalization of architecture-dependent random features as a neural-network prior kernel and evidence that trained structure is echoed at initialization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: NNPK averages features from many independently randomized networks and trains a classifier on the resulting fixed embedding; guidance uses one frozen random guide's per-layer batch geometry as an auxiliary loss to change all parameters of a separate target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking Centered Kernel Alignment in Knowledge Distillation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A pre-target-paper CKA distillation method and theory that makes CKA itself non-novel as a teacher-student training loss.
reviewed_competitors.difference: RCKA decomposes CKA through an MMD bound and dynamically customizes relation alignment for efficient trained-teacher vision distillation. Guidance's novelty lies in cross-family untrainable targets and random-guide interventions, not the use of CKA for distillation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deconfounded Representation Similarity for Comparison of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Negative diagnostic work directly challenging causal interpretations of CKA and RSA between random networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows input-population structure can create spuriously high similarity for completely random networks and proposes covariate-adjusted CKA/RSA. Guidance optimizes ordinary CKA and interprets random-guide alignment as architecture-prior transfer without applying this deconfounding control.

reviewed_competitors.title: InBiaseD: Inductive Bias Distillation to Improve Generalization and Robustness through Shape-awareness
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier method explicitly framed as distilling an inductive bias through feature- and decision-alignment objectives.
reviewed_competitors.difference: InBiaseD specifies the desired shape bias, constructs edge-derived inputs, and jointly trains paired networks for robustness; guidance seeks implicit architectural priors from a fixed guide and can operate without knowing or naming the transferred property.

reviewed_competitors.title: Network of Theseus (like the ship)
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later same-author extension that turns whole-network guidance into progressive component replacement for architectural conversion.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Network of Theseus replaces and aligns target modules stage by stage, reports large cross-family conversions such as ResNet-to-MLP and GPT-2-to-RNN, and aims to preserve guide functionality at deployment. It directly addresses the reviewed paper's large guide-target gaps and simultaneous-alignment bottlenecks, while retaining the unresolved question of what random-guide property is causally transferred.

reviewed_competitors.title: Representation Alignment for Generation: Training Diffusion Transformers Is Easier Than You Think
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A closely concurrent representation-alignment regularizer, submitted seventeen days before the reviewed paper's first arXiv version, that uses a frozen external guide to make a difficult training problem easier.
reviewed_competitors.difference: REPA projects noisy diffusion-transformer states toward clean representations from a pretrained visual encoder and reports large generative-training speedups. It transfers learned semantic features in one task family rather than isolating random architectural priors across arbitrary guide-target graphs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Knowledge distillation through geometry-aware representational alignment
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later direct theoretical and empirical critique of CKA as a feature-distillation loss.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves that projection MSE and CKA can fail to preserve teacher feature structure even at zero loss, then obtains better language-model distillation with Procrustes and feature-Gram losses. This directly weakens the inference that a low guidance CKA necessarily means faithful prior transfer, although it does not test random-guide rescue.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Are Born Biased: Structural Inductive Biases at Random Initialization and Their Practical Consequences
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later independent mechanistic evidence that random Transformer initializations contain stable, architecture-mediated structural biases.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It identifies seed-dependent representation contraction, extreme token preferences, persistence through training, and attention-sink effects inside Transformers. It corroborates the existence of initialization bias but does not show that layerwise CKA transfers that bias into a different architecture or that the transferred property is beneficial.

reviewed_competitors.title: Signal-to-Noise Ratio and Sample Size Govern Representational Alignment in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current negative evidence against treating greater representational alignment as a general proxy for better generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It controls signal-to-noise ratio and sample size across linear and nonlinear networks, finding non-monotonic sample-size effects and that stronger alignment need not imply lower generalization error. Guidance optimizes alignment directly, so it needs task and functional checks beyond its CKA curves to validate mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.difference: ISAAC builds an approximate conditioner from inputs to a neural-network layer and applies it to parameter-gradient training; Newton Losses instead uses exact or empirical curvature of the external loss with respect to model outputs and leaves the network optimizer first-order.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning with Algorithmic Supervision via Continuous Relaxations
reviewed_competitors.difference: AlgoVision smooths control flow by perturbing accessed variables and approximating expectations, creating one of the hard-to-optimize losses tested here; Newton Losses is a wrapper intended to improve such an existing relaxation rather than a new relaxation of the algorithm itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalizing Stochastic Smoothing for Differentiation and Gradient Estimation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Generalized stochastic smoothing focuses on differentiating black-box functions and reducing estimator variance across distributions; Newton Losses consumes such estimated gradients and sometimes Hessians to build a preconditioned target, adding a second optimization layer whose low-sample instability is visible in Table 3.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning with Differentiable Perturbed Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Perturbed optimizers make discrete optimizer outputs differentiable and pair them with Fenchel-Young losses, with theoretical properties and good few-sample behavior. Newton Losses wraps their loss with curvature; its Hessian variant improves some Warcraft means, while its empirical-Fisher variant adds essentially no value in this formulation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiation of Blackbox Combinatorial Solvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Blackbox differentiation defines a surrogate backward pass through existing linear-objective combinatorial solvers and introduced the Warcraft benchmark; Newton Losses does not replace that differentiation mechanism, but attempts to precondition the resulting output-space loss signal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Limitations of the Empirical Fisher Approximation for Natural Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kunstner et al. show that the empirical Fisher generally does not represent the Hessian or true Fisher and can be pathological. Newton Losses acknowledges this distinction but still treats the uncentered output-gradient moment as a cheap preconditioner, so its Fisher route is a heuristic whose value must be established per loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Practical Second-Order Optimizers in Deep Learning: Insights from Fisher Information Analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: The 2025 AdaFisher thesis uses a diagonal block-Kronecker Fisher approximation to precondition network-parameter gradients across image and language tasks. Newton Losses instead confines a dense empirical-Fisher solve to model-output space and targets algorithmic losses, trading broader optimizer scope for lower-dimensional curvature.
