reviewed_competitors.difference: Ripken et al. benchmark MGN, BSMS, and MGN+Tree on the same PDEBench Darcy and electric-motor datasets and provide the graph implementations and defaults reused here. The reviewed paper's concrete additions are the graded U-bend, direct image models on Motor, a reduced Darcy sample set, and TTE; its graph side is application and comparison rather than a new solver.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Learning of Mesh-Based Physical Simulation with BSMS-GNN
reviewed_competitors.difference: BSMS-GNN contributes the breadth-first bi-stride pooling and multiscale message passing used by the reviewed paper's best graph baseline, with its own accuracy and computational-efficiency evaluations. The reviewed study does not modify BSMS; it evaluates a reused implementation on three steady-field datasets.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: MeshGraphNets is one of the reviewed paper's model families and demonstrates adaptive, resolution-independent mesh dynamics plus measured 1-2-order solver speedups. Its broader multi-system, adaptive-mesh evaluation makes it the necessary reference point for claims about graph limitations; the reviewed study uses a small default MGN without testing resolution transfer or inference speed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Message Passing Neural PDE Solvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: MP-PDE targets generalization across topology, geometry, boundary conditions, discretization regularity, resolution, and dimension, with stability-motivated autoregressive training. Those controlled variation axes are largely absent from the one-dataset-per-topology comparison here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformer for Partial Differential Equations' Operator Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: OFormer natively accepts nonuniform input points and arbitrary output queries through self- and cross-attention. The reviewed paper cites it but benchmarks generic natural-image DINOv2 and DeiT encoders instead, so its poor transformer results do not represent the established PDE-transformer design space.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fourier Neural Operator with Learned Deformations for PDEs on General Geometries
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geo-FNO learns a deformation from meshes, point clouds, or design parameters to a regular latent grid, retaining physical geometry while exploiting FFT efficiency. It directly offers the structured-to-unstructured bridge that arbitrary node-order image reshaping lacks and reports speed against numerical solvers.

reviewed_competitors.title: MAgNet: Mesh Agnostic Neural PDE Solver
reviewed_competitors.difference: MAgNet combines implicit neural representations and graphs for continuous spatial queries, zero-shot nonuniform-mesh transfer, and resolutions up to four times training resolution. Those tests directly probe mesh agnosticism, whereas the reviewed paper fixes array size and never permutes or remeshes its evaluation domains.

reviewed_competitors.title: PDEBench: An Extensive Benchmark for Scientific Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: PDEBench supplies diverse PDEs, numerical-solver and ML baselines, standardized APIs, and holistic physical metrics. The reviewed paper takes one Darcy subset but reduces evaluation to aggregate RMSE and TTE, omitting the benchmark's broader controls and metric philosophy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convolutional Neural Operators for robust and accurate learning of PDEs
reviewed_competitors.difference: CNO is designed as a discretization-consistent continuous operator, proves universality, and evaluates a suite of multiscale PDEs against operator baselines. It is a stronger test of the reviewed paper's image-model thesis than a large generic diffusion U-Net, but is mentioned only as related work and not benchmarked.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometry-Informed Neural Operator for Large-Scale 3D PDEs
reviewed_competitors.difference: GINO combines graph operators on point clouds with a regular latent Fourier grid, is discretization-convergent, tests unseen geometry/boundary-condition combinations, and measures cost against CFD. It offers a principled hybrid alternative to flattening unstructured nodes into an arbitrary image and directly addresses geometry and solver-speed claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transolver: A Fast Transformer Solver for PDEs on General Geometries
reviewed_competitors.difference: Transolver compresses mesh points into learned physics-aware slices, reports linear complexity and state-of-the-art results across six benchmarks plus industrial geometries. It is a direct transformer control that preserves geometry rather than importing frozen natural-image features and globally pooling them.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Physics Transformers: A Framework For Efficiently Scaling Neural Operators
reviewed_competitors.difference: UPT provides one latent-space architecture across meshes, particles, fluid simulation, steady RANS, and Lagrangian dynamics, with continuous space-time queries. It directly challenges the premise that model families must be chosen categorically by discretization and supplies a PDE-native transformer comparison absent here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Poseidon: Efficient Foundation Models for PDEs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Poseidon pretrains a multiscale operator transformer on fluid equations and evaluates sample efficiency, scaling, and transfer on 15 downstream PDE tasks, including unseen physics. It is the appropriate current comparator for the reviewed paper's foundation-model claims; DINOv2 and DeiT were pretrained on natural images and adapted through a confounded pooled decoder.

reviewed_competitors.title: Artificial intelligence and illusions of understanding in scientific research
reviewed_competitors.difference: Messeri and Crockett also warn that AI can make scientists believe they understand more than they do, but develop a social-epistemic taxonomy of illusions and scientific monocultures rather than Hogg and Villar's two statistical mechanisms. Their analysis broadens the risk from local estimator and emulator failure to community-level narrowing of questions and methods.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang and colleagues survey AI across hypothesis generation, experimental design, simulation, and data analysis, with concrete examples of self-supervision, geometric learning, and generative design alongside data-quality and stewardship risks. It supplies the cross-domain evidence and more graded discovery taxonomy missing from the position paper's physics-centered breakthrough claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Decoding complexity through machine learning is redefining scientific discovery
reviewed_competitors.difference: This 2026 perspective organizes ML-enabled discovery by the amount of available mechanistic knowledge and treats bias, interpretability, overfitting, and validation as design challenges. It updates the debate beyond a data-versus-latents dichotomy and offers a continuum in which the scientific role of ML changes with prior theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: The frontier of simulation-based inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cranmer, Brehmer, and Louppe survey neural likelihood, likelihood-ratio, and posterior estimation for simulator-based inverse problems. Their framework distinguishes learned inferential objects and validation requirements instead of treating all simulator emulation as point regression, directly narrowing the scope of the no-safe-emulator claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benchmarking Simulation-Based Inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lueckmann and colleagues provide public simulator tasks and multiple posterior-quality metrics, show that metric choice changes conclusions, and use benchmarks to expose algorithm-specific weaknesses. This does not make finite validation complete, but demonstrates concrete diagnostic infrastructure between trusting held-out loss and rerunning every first-principles analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Validating Bayesian Inference Algorithms with Simulation-Based Calibration
reviewed_competitors.difference: Talts and colleagues introduce simulation-based calibration to detect inaccurate posterior computation and implementation inconsistencies through repeated prior-predictive simulation and rank diagnostics. SBC cannot validate whether a simulator describes nature, but it directly contradicts the implication that only exhaustive phase-space testing can reveal inferential failure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Treatment and Causal Parameters
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chernozhukov and colleagues show that good nuisance prediction does not automatically yield valid causal estimates: naive plug-in ML can fail through regularization bias, while orthogonal scores and cross-fitting can recover root-n inference under explicit conditions. This supplies the missing qualification to the position paper's claim that more expressive confounder models are inherently more conservative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics-informed machine learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Karniadakis and colleagues review methods that combine noisy observations with differential equations, invariants, operator structure, and uncertainty for forward and inverse problems. The field is a direct counterexample to the claim that ML's ontology contains only data, while its stated need for robust benchmarks supports the position paper's caution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Characterizing possible failure modes in physics-informed neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Krishnapriyan and colleagues show that physics-informed neural networks can fail on modestly harder convection, reaction, and diffusion problems because soft PDE penalties make optimization ill-conditioned, then test curriculum and sequence-to-sequence mitigations. It supports the paper's demand for scientific validation while showing that physical structure is not automatically a safe remedy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering Symbolic Models from Deep Learning with Inductive Biases
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cranmer and colleagues distill sparse symbolic relations from graph neural networks, recover known force laws and Hamiltonians, and report a new analytic relation for dark-matter halo concentration. The work exemplifies the hybrid latent-structure route the position paper endorses and shows why 'no important discoveries' needs an explicit threshold rather than assertion.

reviewed_competitors.title: AI Feynman: a Physics-Inspired Method for Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Udrescu and Tegmark combine neural fitting with symmetry, separability, and dimensional reasoning to recover all 100 tested Feynman equations and outperform prior symbolic-regression software on a harder set. It is a concrete bridge between predictive fitting and interpretable law recovery, although benchmark rediscovery is not itself proof of novel natural science.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine learning and the physical sciences
reviewed_competitors.difference: Carleo and colleagues review two-way exchange between physics and ML across particle physics, cosmology, quantum many-body systems, chemistry, materials, and computing architectures, reporting successes and domain-specific challenges. This earlier map provides the breadth needed to test whether Hogg and Villar's role taxonomy covers the actual field.

reviewed_competitors.title: Infinite Attention: NNGP and NTK for Deep Attention Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hron et al. rigorously show that standard-scaled single-head attention remains non-Gaussian and obtain GP behavior by taking the number of heads to infinity, deriving NNGP/NTK kernels with positional encoding and normalization. Tiberi et al. instead fix Q/K and keep finite H while taking sample size proportional to value width, producing a label-dependent Bayesian kernel beyond the GP limit; it gains feature renormalization but uses a much less standard attention stack.

reviewed_competitors.title: Globally Gated Deep Linear Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest methodological precursor for finite-width kernel renormalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li and Sompolinsky already derive task-dependent matrix kernel-shape renormalization in the same finite-width Bayesian thermodynamic regime for nonlinear networks with fixed global gates, and compare qualitatively with gradient descent. The attention-path paper specializes that machinery to softmax-derived gates organized as head sequences and turns the matrix entries into path-overlap and pruning interpretations; its general theoretical mechanism is therefore an architectural extension, not a wholly new finite-width principle.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Phase Transition between Positional and Semantic Learning in a Solvable Model of Dot-Product Attention
reviewed_competitors.relationship: contemporaneous statistical-mechanics theory of learned attention
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cui et al. tightly characterize the global empirical-risk minimum of a one-head, one-layer teacher-student model with trainable tied low-rank Q/K and reveal a sample-complexity phase transition between positional and semantic mechanisms. It directly analyzes acquisition of attention features, which Tiberi et al. leave fixed, but has no depth, multi-head path interplay, Bayesian posterior, or realistic data and acknowledges that gradient descent must be initialized near the predicted minima.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Understanding Inductive Bias in Transformers: A View From Infinity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lavie et al. solve simplified Transformer kernels in the infinitely overparameterized GP limit and use permutation-group representations to derive context-length sample-complexity scaling laws. Their symmetry account is sharper about architectural inductive bias but explicitly omits finite-size feature learning; Tiberi et al. supply a label-dependent finite-width correction and path decomposition, at the cost of fixed Q/K and exponentially many path-pair variables.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 (2024-05-28), ICML 2024, full 27-page primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamical Mean-Field Theory of Self-Attention Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Poc-López and Aguilera map recurrent self-attention with one-bit tokens and weights to an asymmetric Hopfield system and derive large-size mean-field dynamics exhibiting periodic, quasi-periodic, and chaotic regimes with memory beyond a four-token window. It analyzes temporal dynamics rather than supervised generalization and uses manually explored tiny configurations; Tiberi et al. analyze equilibrium learning and task kernels but cannot describe optimizer or autoregressive dynamics.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v1 (2024-06-11), full 13-page primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Infinite-Width Limit of a Single Attention Layer: Analysis via Tensor Programs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sakai et al. rigorously derive the hierarchical non-Gaussian infinite-width law of a standard-scaled single attention layer with finite heads, correcting the Gaussian simplification inherent in infinite-head or 1/n-scaled theories and validating it down to finite widths. This is more faithful to realistic Q/K score randomness than Tiberi et al.'s fixed-attention treatment, but it covers initialization of one layer rather than supervised learning, depth, generalization, or path selection.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v3 (2026-01-02), NeurIPS 2025, full 28-page primary PDF and current record checked

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Sixteen Heads Really Better than One?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Michel et al. measure per-head loss sensitivity, greedily prune heads on WMT translation and BERT tasks, and show that 20 percent and 40 percent of heads can be removed from their translation and BERT models without statistically significant degradation, while examining speed and memory. Tiberi et al. offer a task-kernel interpretation of head importance but test only tiny image models, without matched established scores, uncertainty, or systems measurements, so the pruning evidence does not supersede this older baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Complementary Attention Head Pruning for Efficient Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: CAHP clusters attention-head behavior and keeps salient representatives from complementary groups, automatically chooses retention through a knee criterion, then fine-tunes. On BERT Base/Large over SST-5 and MNLI it reports multiple seeds, matched DSP/PASS/attribution baselines, fewer than 20 percent retained heads with modest losses, stability, and runtime. Its scope is standard pretrained encoders and practical pruning rather than theory, but its controls make it the stronger current pruning result; Tiberi et al.'s U may motivate a complementarity graph yet is computationally exponential and unbenchmarked.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: The direct motivating work reports full-gradient convergence to a class-count top-Hessian subspace and suggests that gradient descent happens there.

reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Trains networks inside fixed random parameter subspaces to estimate how many degrees of freedom a task needs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Intrinsic-dimension subspaces are randomly oriented and selected by success, not the local sharp Hessian eigenspace that Song et al. find unproductive.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Develops changing and layerwise random bases for practical low-dimensional training and reports memory/speed gains.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: SubGD restricts adaptation to a low-dimensional update-autocorrelation space learned across related tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent for Low-Rank Functions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Formalizes functions that vary along a few significant directions and exploits them with low-rank gradient descent.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its guarantees assume the identified low-rank directions contain objective variation; Song et al. show that top curvature alone need not identify the progress-bearing directions of deep-network training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral alignment of stochastic gradient descent for high-dimensional classification tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Proves SGD alignment with emerging low-rank Hessian and gradient-matrix outlier spaces in stylized high-dimensional classification models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It establishes when spectral alignment arises, whereas Song et al. ask whether the aligned component causes loss progress in practical finite networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Identifying Policy Gradient Subspaces
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Finds low-dimensional update structure for policy-gradient reinforcement learning and uses identified spaces to analyze learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It extends the subspace question beyond supervised Hessian geometry; Song et al. do not test RL or whether policy-gradient subspaces suffer the same alignment-versus-progress split.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compressible Dynamics in Deep Overparameterized Low-Rank Learning & Adaptation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Proves invariant low-dimensional weight dynamics for deep low-rank recovery and exploits them in compressed models and Deep LoRA.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its useful spaces follow problem/weight low-rank structure and can support exact compressed dynamics; Song et al.'s local top-Hessian space is neither invariant nor sufficient for progress.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Derives SAM's gradient-norm-dependent stability edge and verifies that SAM trains near it.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Analyzes how mini-batch stochasticity changes sharpening and yields a trace-sensitive stochastic stability boundary.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Its counterexample reinforces the need to separate expected-gradient structure from stochastic-update behavior, a distinction left unmeasured in Song et al.'s SGD headline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Jaynes Machine: The universal microstructure of deep neural networks

reviewed_competitors.difference: It formulates feature conditions for softmax regression and recursive feature learning rather than entropy of weight-bin occupancy, undercutting the target's novelty framing around maximum entropy and robustness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Entropy-SGD: Biasing Gradient Descent Into Wide Valleys
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor using local entropy as an explicit optimization objective for generalizable neural solutions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Entropy-SGD defines an executable optimizer, analyzes stability under assumptions, and tests generalization; the target does not connect its occupancy potential to actual training updates or outcomes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Self-Regularization in Deep Neural Networks: Evidence from Random Matrix Theory and Implications for Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor studying universal-looking microstructure and implicit regularization in trained weight matrices.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes empirical spectral densities, identifies several heavy-tailed training phases, and intervenes on batch size; the target fits individual absolute-weight histograms and assumes one lognormal equilibrium.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Heavy-Tailed Theory of Stochastic Gradient Descent for Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor deriving optimizer-dependent heavy-tailed gradient-noise behavior in deep learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It starts from stochastic-gradient dynamics and tests tail indices across architectures, losses, sizes, and data, offering a causal alternative to the target's optimizer-free utility postulate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multiplicative noise and heavy tails in stochastic optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor deriving heavy-tailed stationary parameter behavior from multiplicative optimization noise.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows dependence on step size, batch size, data variability, and optimizer in linear and broader nonlinear settings, variables that the target's universal checkpoint fit does not model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Heavy Tails in SGD and Compressibility of Overparametrized Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor connecting a stationary weight law to a concrete network property and generalization bounds.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It links step-size/batch-size-induced heavy tails to l_p compressibility and pruning error; the target neither compares heavy-tail families nor validates a downstream consequence of its lognormal fit.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Mean Field View of the Landscape of Two-Layers Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor treating neurons as a population and deriving a distributional training limit.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its nonlinear PDE is derived from SGD on an explicit risk and supports convergence results in a specified scaling limit; the target declares a population game without establishing dynamical equivalence to SGD.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor offering a mathematically explicit theory of wide-network gradient-descent dynamics and generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: NTK derives function-space evolution and convergence from the network and loss in an infinite-width regime, directly contradicting the target's suggestion that gradient descent cannot support predictive neural theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Entropy, Free Energy, and Work of Restricted Boltzmann Machines
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor explicitly analyzing entropy and free energy during Boltzmann-machine training.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It calculates thermodynamic entropy, free energy, internal energy, correlations, and work across epochs, providing direct primary evidence against the target's assertion that Boltzmann models omit entropy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Heavy-Tailed Regularization of Weight Matrices in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor turning heavy-tailed spectral observations into explicit differentiable regularizers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It compares regularization outcomes and models weight-matrix spectra with power-law and Frechet priors; the target fits scalar magnitudes without testing whether its distribution improves performance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Posterior and variational inference for deep neural networks with heavy-tailed weights
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-contemporaneous theoretical alternative using heavy-tailed weight priors in Bayesian deep learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves adaptive posterior-contraction and variational results under explicit probabilistic assumptions, whereas the target offers a descriptive checkpoint histogram and an unsupported robustness analogy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stable extrapolation of analytic functions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest classical stability and minimax predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Demanet and Townsend derive an asymptotically optimal regularized polynomial extrapolant and explicit noise-dependent accuracy region for analytic functions sampled on an interval. NExT instead amortizes a fixed finite-space inverse under a synthetic prior, but does not compare against their degree truncation or distinguish average prior risk from worst-case attainable stability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stable soft extrapolation of entire functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Batenkov, Demanet, and Mhaskar give a weighted least-squares polynomial method with noise- and length-scale-dependent guarantees and asymptotic minimaxity for windowed entire functions. It demonstrates that carefully regularized least squares is a much stronger baseline than the unregularized LS used by NExT.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantifying the ill-conditioning of analytic continuation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Trefethen separates ill-posed continuation from conditionally stable continuation under explicit boundedness assumptions and quantifies geometry-dependent digit loss. NExT's finite-space kappa is a loose basis-coordinate bound and does not characterize the intrinsic continuation operator or attainable error under noise.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conditional Neural Processes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Conditional Neural Processes learn a prior-conditioned mapping from arbitrary context pairs and target coordinates, supporting varying observation sets and off-grid predictions. NExT uses a fixed ordered sample vector and returns explicit coefficients for one known basis, gaining exact structural bias but losing set/discretization flexibility and uncertainty modeling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Processes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural Processes amortize posterior-like prediction over distributions of functions and explicitly model latent uncertainty from variable context sets. NExT shares prior-data training but predicts a deterministic coefficient vector on a fixed grid and reports no calibrated uncertainty, making the Bayesian linear and neural-process comparisons especially relevant.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepONet: Learning nonlinear operators for identifying differential equations based on the universal approximation theorem of operators
reviewed_competitors.difference: DeepONet separates a branch network over sensor values from a trunk network over output coordinates, learning nonlinear operators with continuous query locations. NExT's branch-like coefficient predictor is simpler and exploits a fixed known output basis, but the paper does not position this as a restricted operator-learning architecture or test discretization changes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric Partial Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: FNO learns mesh-transferable maps between fields through Fourier-domain integral kernels and demonstrates zero-shot super-resolution for PDE operators. NExT also exploits spectral coefficients but for one fixed restriction inverse with known basis; its spherical example does not show resolution invariance or operator generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Operator: Learning Maps Between Function Spaces With Applications to PDEs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kovachki et al. formulate discretization-invariant neural operators and analyze multiple kernel parameterizations. NExT is a finite-dimensional coefficient map tied to fixed sensor locations; treating it as an operator-learning special case makes its retraining and grid-dependence limitations clearer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Extrapolation and learning equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Martius and Lampert introduce equation-learning networks with a small library of analytic units to recover compact formulas that extrapolate beyond the training domain. NExT assumes the basis explicitly and estimates coefficients; saying EQL reduces to LS under the exact supplied basis does not replace an empirical EQL comparison under realistic basis uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Equations for Extrapolation and Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sahoo, Lampert, and Martius extend equation learning with division and a model-selection strategy and test recovery of interpretable dynamics. NExT is more direct when a correct linear basis is already known, while equation learning addresses discovery of the analytic form that NExT takes as input.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks Fail to Learn Periodic Functions and How to Fix It
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu, Hartwig, and Ueda give the Snake activation a periodic inductive bias for direct coordinate regression. NExT's lower errors arise with exact basis and prior access unavailable to Snake in the comparison, so the experiment does not decide between the methods under matched information.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: SIREN supplies sinusoidal activations and principled initialization for continuous signals and boundary-value problems and can combine with hypernetworks to learn function priors. It is a stronger periodic-neural comparator than a generic ReLU MLP, though it still solves a coordinate representation problem rather than NExT's labeled coefficient inverse.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Self-Supervised Framework for Function Learning and Extrapolation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Segert and Cohen learn representations invariant to topological distortions and adapt them few-shot across scalar function tasks. NExT uses explicit basis knowledge and synthetic labels rather than learning a reusable representation, so cross-family and limited-data transfer remain untested.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Neural Networks Extrapolate: From Feedforward to Graph Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu et al. analyze when ReLU and graph networks extrapolate through their asymptotic linear regions and task features. NExT avoids direct coordinate-to-value extrapolation by learning an inverse into a prescribed function family, but consequently inherits fixed-grid and prior-misspecification constraints rather than solving identifiability generically.

reviewed_competitors.title: Extrapolation and Spectral Bias of Neural Nets with Hadamard Product: a Polynomial Net Study
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest omitted polynomial and spherical-harmonic neural competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. study Hadamard-product polynomial networks, NTK spectral bias, direct polynomial extrapolation, and spherical harmonics. NExT prespecifies those basis functions and predicts their coefficients; a matched comparison would test whether supervised inverse amortization is needed once the architecture already expresses the relevant polynomial family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Periodic Extrapolative Generalisation in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: This study stress-tests architectures and training schemes on periodic signals and finds that periodic activations alone are often insufficient. It makes the paper's single selected Snake comparison too narrow and motivates matched tuning, held-out frequencies, and prior-shift evaluation for NExT.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data-driven extrapolation via feature augmentation based on variably scaled thin plate splines
reviewed_competitors.difference: VSK thin-plate splines use feature augmentation and regularized meshfree approximation without a large prior-matched meta-training phase. They are a relevant classical-data-driven control for irregular sampling, whereas NExT consumes a fixed ordered grid and known finite basis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Matérn Gaussian Processes on Riemannian Manifolds
reviewed_competitors.difference: Borovitskiy et al. construct Matérn and squared-exponential Gaussian processes from Laplace-Beltrami spectra and return posterior uncertainty on manifolds. For NExT's Gaussian spherical-harmonic generator, the analogous finite spectral GP/Bayesian linear regression is especially close and analytically available but untested.

reviewed_competitors.title: Just One Layer Norm Guarantees Stable Extrapolation
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later work proves bounded infinite-width NTK extrapolation after adding LayerNorm and validates finite networks. Boundedness is not identification or accuracy, while NExT obtains accuracy from a matched explicit prior; together they separate architectural stability from prior-driven recovery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Cannot Neural Networks Master Extrapolation? Insights from Physical Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dakhmouche and Gorji formalize structural properties behind extrapolation and contrast statistical models with physical-law commitments. It is later than NExT and reinforces that NExT succeeds by injecting a correct function space and target-domain loss, not by learning extrapolation from in-domain evidence alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does Your Neural Network Extrapolate? Feature Engineering as Identifiability Bias for OOD Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Aguilar et al. argue that extrapolation from one in-domain window is non-identifiable without a correct structural commitment and test representation changes across scientific settings. This later result provides a sharper framing for NExT: its known basis, coefficient prior, anchors, and Xi loss are the commitments doing the work and must be stress-tested under misspecification.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Neural Networks as Gaussian Processes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. derive the infinite-width deep-network Gaussian process and evaluate Bayesian prediction on MNIST/CIFAR; the reviewed paper takes that prior correspondence as input and analyzes its full spherical spectrum as depth then diverges, without inference or training experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exponential expressivity in deep neural networks through transient chaos
reviewed_competitors.difference: Poole et al. connect correlation dynamics to exponential manifold curvature and depth separation in the chaotic phase; the reviewed work refines the correlation map into a harmonic law and derivative hierarchy but does not prove computational expressivity or task benefit.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Impact of the Activation Function on Deep Neural Networks Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hayou et al. study initialization hyperparameters, signal propagation, and training acceleration along the edge of chaos; the reviewed sparse regime shares the critical endpoint slope but separates L2 mass from derivative energy through the whole angular spectrum.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Equals Shallow for ReLU Networks in Kernel Regimes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bietti and Bach show that deep and shallow fully connected ReLU kernels have the same tail eigendecay and equivalent approximation spaces; the reviewed paper's main novelty is to show that the finite-body distribution of this spectrum can still change sharply with depth.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Spectral Analysis of Dot-product Kernels
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scetbon and Harchaoui derive eigendecay regimes and statistical risk tradeoffs for compositional dot-product kernels; the reviewed paper instead normalizes the entire spectrum as a depth-indexed law and studies long-depth moments, but stops short of statistical estimation bounds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectrum Dependent Learning Curves in Kernel Regression and Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon et al. combine kernel eigenvalues with target-mode coefficients to predict sample-dependent generalization and validate trained wide networks; the reviewed C_alpha and D_alpha are target-free prior summaries and therefore cannot by themselves support its overfitting interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Future is Log-Gaussian: ResNets and Their Infinite-Depth-and-Width Limit at Initialization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. show that when depth and width grow proportionally, finite-width ReLU ResNets have log-Gaussian rather than GP behavior and expose failures of the sequential Gaussian limit; the reviewed work uses a fully connected sequential width-then-depth limit and leaves this finite-ratio regime open.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Tangent Kernel Beyond the Infinite-Width Limit: Effects of Depth and Initialization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Seleznova and Kutyniok quantify NTK dispersion and training-regime dependence when depth is comparable to width; the reviewed NNGP angular law is more detailed in spherical frequency but does not describe finite-width NTK training dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Can Be Learnt With Wide Convolutional Neural Networks?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cagnetta et al. characterize spectra and generalization for hierarchical convolutional kernels and show target-locality-dependent learning rates; the reviewed analysis is restricted to isotropic fully connected kernels but offers sharper full-distribution depth asymptotics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-layer random features and the approximation power of neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Takhanov links NNGP RKHS norm to constructive finite-width approximation and supervised last-layer learning, while noting theory can be vacuous on realistic tasks; the reviewed paper supplies a depth-sensitive prior statistic but no construction or approximation-error guarantee from C_alpha.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fractal and Regular Geometry of Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Di Lillo et al. extend the spectral/random-field program to excursion-boundary volumes and fractal dimensions across activations, providing a geometric observable closer to the future-work program; it remains an initialization-prior analysis rather than trained generalization evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning as Neural Low-Degree Filtering: A Spectral Theory of Hierarchical Feature Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dandi et al. model layerwise gradient-driven selection of label-correlated low-degree features and compare against random-feature baselines on fully connected and convolutional networks; this addresses the training and target alignment absent from the reviewed random NNGP complexity claim, albeit in its own stylized limit.

reviewed_competitors.difference: DTR evicts activations online and recomputes them on demand, supporting dynamic models through runtime interception. MemSave has no recomputation when its dependency rule applies, but does not provide DTR's graph-generic budget control.

reviewed_competitors.difference: ActNN substitutes layers and quantizes necessary activations to about two bits, trading gradient variance and compression work for broad savings and larger batches. MemSave seeks exact deletion of unnecessary operands and is therefore orthogonal but narrower.

reviewed_competitors.title: GACT: Activation Compressed Training for Generic Network Architectures
reviewed_competitors.difference: GACT uses runtime sensitivity estimates to assign compression across generic architectures and reports up to 8.1x activation reduction with convergence analysis. MemSave avoids approximation for selected derivative masks but lacks a generic optimizer and end-to-end accuracy study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rockmate: an Efficient, Fast, Automatic and Generic Tool for Re-materialization in PyTorch
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rockmate rewrites PyTorch models into blocks and controls activation memory with about 10%-20% recomputation overhead. It is broader and budget-aware; MemSave's local exact-elimination rules could reduce the graph Rockmate must schedule.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tempo: Accelerating Transformer-Based Model Training through Memory Footprint Reduction
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tempo supplies memory-aware GELU, LayerNorm, and attention replacements and evaluates training throughput plus accuracy on BERT, GPT-2, and RoBERTa. MemSave focuses on selective gradients and reports more architectures, but does not validate task training and its LLM replacements contain correctness defects.

reviewed_competitors.title: LoRA-FA: Efficient and Effective Low Rank Representation Fine-tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: LoRA-FA freezes one LoRA factor so full-rank activations need not be retained for that factor's gradient and adds low-rank gradient corrections. It changes the adaptation parameterization, whereas MemSave aims to preserve a user's chosen training method while optimizing operator tape storage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Make Pre-trained Model Reversible: From Parameter to Memory Efficient Fine-Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: MEFT inserts reversible adapters so intermediate activations can be reconstructed and reports downstream task quality. It requires an architectural transformation and recomputation; MemSave seeks local exact deletion without changing the model's mathematical forward pass.

reviewed_competitors.title: LISA: Layerwise Importance Sampling for Memory-Efficient Large Language Model Fine-Tuning
reviewed_competitors.difference: LISA repeatedly trains sampled layers and freezes most others, directly creating the selective-differentiation pattern where MemSave should help, while also reducing optimizer state. LISA validates downstream quality up to 70B; the present paper cites it but does not benchmark their composition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory-Efficient Fine-Tuning via Low-Rank Activation Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: LoRAct compresses necessary activations online into low-rank factors and reports about 80% activation-memory reduction relative to LoRA across language and vision. It introduces approximation and decomposition cost; MemSave's exact dependency pruning should be evaluated before and in combination with it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rigorous data-driven computation of spectral properties of Koopman operators for dynamical systems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct post-review resolution of the spectral-pollution gap
reviewed_competitors.difference: Colbrook and Townsend introduce ResDMD, using infinite-dimensional residuals and resolvent calculations to compute spectra, pseudospectra, and smoothed spectral measures without spectral pollution. The review carefully describes why EDMD operator convergence does not imply spectral convergence; ResDMD turns that caveat into a verified computational method.

reviewed_competitors.title: The mpEDMD Algorithm for Data-Driven Computations of Measure-Preserving Dynamical Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Colbrook introduces an orthogonal-Procrustes truncation that preserves measure-preserving structure and whose eigendecomposition converges to spectral quantities for general measure-preserving systems. It directly strengthens the review's discussion of continuous spectra, noise, and the insufficiency of generic finite Galerkin eigenvalues.

reviewed_competitors.title: Another look at Residual Dynamic Mode Decomposition in the regime of fewer Snapshots than Dictionary Size
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Scalable extension of verified spectral DMD
reviewed_competitors.difference: Colbrook derives a dual least-squares formulation that applies residual verification when snapshots are fewer than dictionary functions without requiring a separate quadrature dataset. This addresses a practical scaling regime left open by the review's distinction between large expressive dictionaries and reliable spectra.

reviewed_competitors.title: Error bounds for kernel-based approximations of the Koopman operator
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Finite-data theory for the review's RKHS route
reviewed_competitors.difference: Philipp et al. derive variance expressions, probabilistic estimation bounds, observable-prediction bounds, and full approximation bounds under RKHS invariance for stochastic dynamics sampled along ergodic trajectories. The review introduces RKHS regularity and calls convergence active; this paper quantifies one important sampling regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Error analysis of kernel EDMD for prediction and control in the Koopman framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: Philipp et al. prove kEDMD prediction-error bounds for i.i.d. samples from application-defined distributions and extend them to control-affine systems through approximately affine Koopman operators at small sampling times. It narrows the review's broad control promise to explicit kernels, domains, sampling, invariance, and control-affinity assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: L-infinity error bounds for approximations of the Koopman operator by kernel extended dynamic mode decomposition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Pointwise-error refinement of kernel Koopman approximation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Köhne et al. establish pointwise kEDMD error bounds using invariant Wendland RKHSs and interpolation estimates. This directly answers the review's warning that Lp equivalence classes and finite point samples do not automatically support pointwise claims, while remaining conditional on smoothness, kernels, and invariant domains.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analytic Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mauroy and Mezić preserve a triangular Taylor structure in an analytic RKHS to avoid spectral pollution and obtain strong eigenfunction convergence and spectrum error bounds near hyperbolic equilibria. The method gains rigor by accepting a narrower analytic, equilibrium-centered regime than the review's general-purpose DMD narrative.

reviewed_competitors.title: ResKoopNet: Learning Koopman Representations for Complex Dynamics with Spectral Residuals
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Learned-dictionary successor with a spectral objective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pan and Duraisamy train a neural dictionary by minimizing Koopman spectral residuals rather than only reconstruction or prediction error, and compare on pendulum, turbulence, and biological dynamics. This is a direct response to the review's unresolved question of how neural observables can be validated as spectral coordinates, although its empirical coverage does not replace general guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Course Correcting Koopman Representations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct audit of long-horizon neural Koopman rollouts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fathi et al. show that pure latent linear unrolling can drift off the decoded state manifold, intersect itself, and mishandle multiple fixed-point regimes; periodic decode-and-reencode steps improve long-horizon forecasts. The result operationalizes topology and closure problems that the review explains theoretically, but the nonlinear correction also weakens a claim of globally autonomous latent linear evolution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Koopman Data-Driven Predictive Control with Robust Stability and Recursive Feasibility Guarantees
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closed-loop guarantee follow-up to the review's MPC gap
reviewed_competitors.difference: de Jong et al. learn multi-step subspace predictors, use an interpolated initial state and terminal ingredients for recursive feasibility, and prove input-to-state stability with respect to prediction error. This advances beyond the review's three illustrative MPC examples by making model error part of a conditional closed-loop theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: An overview of Koopman-based control: From error bounds to closed-loop guarantees
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current successor survey focused on control guarantees
reviewed_competitors.difference: Strässer et al. reorganize the post-2021 control literature around finite-data approximation errors, linear and bilinear surrogates, robust control, stability, performance, and closed-loop guarantees. It supersedes the dated control frontier of the reviewed article without replacing its broader coverage of spectral theory, DMD, geometry, and applications.

reviewed_competitors.title: Task-Oriented Koopman-Based Control with Contrastive Encoder
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Task-first alternative to model-identification-first Koopman control
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lyu et al. jointly learn the embedding, operator, and controller with reinforcement learning and a contrastive encoder, evaluating pixel inputs and a real robot. Their task cost explicitly reduces reliance on a faithful identified model, making the approach a useful counterpoint to the review's own observation that control success and Koopman fidelity are separable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Koopman Representations with Controllability Guarantees
reviewed_competitors.difference: Miao et al. parameterize neural Koopman dynamics in a controllability-preserving canonical form and add Gramian regularization, proving a transfer from latent to nominal controllability under their representation. This tackles an explicit open question on pages 87-88 of the review, while its guarantees remain tied to the stipulated model form and nonlinear benchmark setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: MetaKoopman: Bayesian Meta-Learning of Koopman Operators for Modeling Structured Dynamics under Distribution Shifts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Selim, Bhat, and Johansson learn a structured Bayesian prior over Koopman operators and perform closed-form posterior adaptation from recent trajectory segments under changing dynamics. This directly extends the review's relatively limited stochastic and nonautonomous treatment toward calibrated rapid adaptation rather than a single fixed fitted operator.

reviewed_competitors.title: DySLIM: Dynamics Stable Learning by Invariant Measure for Chaotic Systems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Non-Koopman adjacent baseline for chaotic learned dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schiff et al. regularize learned chaotic simulators by matching invariant measures, targeting stable long-run statistics when trajectory errors inevitably grow. It is an important competing evaluation philosophy for the review's broadband and chaotic regimes: a finite Koopman matrix should be compared on invariant statistics, not only short-horizon states or discrete modes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data-driven optimal control of unknown nonlinear dynamical systems using the Koopman operator
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zeng et al. allow nonlinear state-control observables, combine the learned operator with neural PDE solvers, and prove iterative convergence of value functions and controls under their assumptions. This attacks the review's linear-control-input restriction and optimality gap, while the reported scale remains modest at systems up to nine dimensions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Distributional Properties Drive Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chan et al. introduce the bursty Omniglot setup and causally vary class rarity, dynamic meanings, within-class variation, and Zipf structure. The target narrows to an ICL-required exact-match regime and adds head/subcircuit interventions, but its C/L sweep is less factorial than the predecessor's data study.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
reviewed_competitors.difference: Olsson et al. define match-and-copy induction heads, connect their arrival to an ICL phase change, and provide strong causal evidence in small attention-only models plus correlational evidence in larger language models. The target's main increment is redundancy analysis and activation clamping throughout formation, not discovery of the head or phase coincidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bietti et al. track global-bigram memory followed by slower induction-head formation in a controlled two-layer transformer and relate gradients to associative memories. The target offers finer causal activation decomposition on classification, while Birth supplies a sequence-modeling setting and weight-level learning account.

reviewed_competitors.title: The mechanistic basis of data dependence and abrupt learning in an in-context classification task
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reddy identifies precursor measures, reconstructs data dependencies in a two-parameter induction model, and explains abrupt learning with three nested logits and an intrinsic curriculum. The target adds through-training causal clamps and a copy subcircuit, but its three-factor toy claim is not a transformer-derived dynamical model and should not erase this prior three-stage account.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Evolution of Statistical Induction Heads: In-Context Learning Markov Chains
reviewed_competitors.difference: Edelman et al. show uniform, unigram, and abrupt bigram phases on a Markov-chain task and combine empirical analysis with theory of statistical induction heads. The target identifies different operational subcircuits in exact-label copying, while this work shows that phase structure also reflects competition with a simpler algorithm.

reviewed_competitors.title: Induction Heads as an Essential Mechanism for Pattern Matching in In-context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Crosbie and Shutova ablate induction heads and specific induction patterns in Llama-3-8B and InternLM2-20B across abstract and NLP tasks, extending causal relevance beyond the toy network. They inspect finished pretrained models rather than formation, but provide scale and task evidence the target lacks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling Induction Heads: Provable Training Dynamics and Feature Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. prove gradient-flow convergence of a two-attention-layer transformer with softmax attention, normalization, an MLP, and relative positions to a copier-selector-classifier mechanism on n-gram Markov data. The theorem is narrower and modified, but links subcomponents to actual optimization more formally than the target's toy analogy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Competition Dynamics Shape Algorithmic Phases of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. decompose a finite-mixture Markov model into four retrieval/inference and unigram/bigram algorithms whose dominance changes with context, diversity, and training. This directly limits a single-circuit explanation of ICL phases; the target remains more causal at the activation level for one exact-copy circuit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differential learning kinetics govern the transition from memorization to generalization during in-context learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nguyen and Reddy explain sharp diversity transitions and transience through largely independent memorizing and generalizing subcircuits with different learning rates. The target studies interacting prerequisites inside one induction circuit; the later work provides a quantitative alternative in which competition between solutions, not only multiplicative subcomponents, controls phase timing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Which Attention Heads Matter for In-Context Learning?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yin and Steinhardt causally compare induction and function-vector heads in twelve language models and find few-shot ICL is driven primarily by function-vector heads, especially at scale; many function-vector heads begin as induction heads. This makes the target's formation result potentially developmental rather than an account of the mature mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh et al. extend the intervention toolkit to ICL versus context-constrained in-weights learning and find shared subcircuits create both cooperation and competition. It broadens formation beyond a single induction head and shows that the target's circuit can be scaffolded or displaced by another strategy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Induction Heads: In-Context Meta Learning Induces Multi-Phase Circuit Emergence
reviewed_competitors.difference: Minegishi et al. require inference of a task whose answer is not already present in context and observe multiple distinct circuit phases. Their setting exposes the target's exact-copy scope: induction formation alone cannot explain practical meta-learning ICL, though the later paper is still controlled rather than natural language pretraining.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Happens During the Loss Plateau? Understanding Abrupt Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gopalani and Hu find partial solutions, repetition bias, representation collapse, and slowly improving attention during plateaus, intervene on attention, and observe related signatures in early Pythia and OLMo pretraining. This adds natural-model evidence and hidden progress beyond the target's perfect-clamp decomposition.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Emergence of Induction Heads for In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Musat et al. prove a 19-dimensional invariant training subspace, empirically localize emergence to three dimensions, and derive quadratic context-length scaling of emergence time. Their transformer is modified and minimal, but the result is a falsifiable dynamical reduction and scaling law absent from the target's three-subcircuit analogy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Predicting the Emergence of Induction Heads in Language Model Pretraining
reviewed_competitors.difference: Aoyama et al. report that batch and context size predict emergence timing and that bigram repetition frequency and reliability define an effective formation boundary across synthetic and natural training data. This directly tests the prediction promise left speculative by the target and weakens any implication that full training is necessarily required to forecast formation.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Shortcut to Induction Head: How Data Diversity Shapes Algorithm Selection in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kawata et al. prove and empirically validate that trigger-position diversity selects between a generalizing induction head and a positional shortcut, including a context-length/OOD tradeoff. Their one-layer trigger task is narrower, but the explicit shortcut boundary is a stronger control than the target's fixed-position data sweep.

reviewed_competitors.title: Emergent Capabilities Arise Randomly from Learning Sparse Attention Patterns
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baherwani et al. attribute abrupt capabilities to stochastic arrival of sparse task-relevant attention patterns and vary context length, sparsity, head count, head dimension, alternative mixers, and Pythia scale. As a current preprint it needs independent replication, but it supplies architecture and stochastic controls absent from the target's deterministic three-factor story.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dong models circuit completion as a driven rare event, reports prospective held-out arrival prediction, and intervenes on data mixtures and query-key slices up to 1.4B parameters. It is a single current preprint with a different conjunction-circuit theory, but it most directly extends the target's causal-through-training ambition to prediction, plasticity, and larger scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Disentangling Neuron Representations with Concept Vectors
reviewed_competitors.difference: O'Mahony et al. separate a polysemantic neuron into concept vectors formed from linear combinations in activation space and let users choose the desired granularity. PURE instead clusters target-conditioned incoming attribution vectors, arguing that raw activations retain features irrelevant to the selected neuron; it does not provide a matched causal comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. learn an overcomplete sparse dictionary over model activations and include counterfactual causal localization in a language model. PURE requires no auxiliary training and stays attached to one image neuron's incoming connectivity, but its centroids only partition examples and receive no reconstruction or intervention test.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Feature Circuits: Discovering and Editing Interpretable Causal Graphs in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marks et al. build causally implicated graphs over sparse learned features and demonstrate feature ablation and downstream editing, including automated discovery at scale. PURE is simpler and training-free for a selected CNN neuron, but calling its one-layer attribution clusters circuits is weaker because graph structure, causal implication, and editing are not evaluated.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transcoders Find Interpretable LLM Feature Circuits
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later sparse computation and circuit competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dunefsky et al. train sparse replacements for dense MLP transformations, factorize feature-to-feature computation, and analyze models up to 1.4B parameters. PURE avoids fitting a replacement model and targets CNN polysemanticity, but stops at sample clustering rather than a faithful sparse approximation of the original computation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Steering Llama 2 via Contrastive Activation Addition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Introduces the exact contrastive activation-addition method and seven-behavior evaluation transferred by this paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It evaluates fixed Transformer interventions, open-ended behavior, capability preservation, and mechanism analyses; the present paper tests residual transfer to RNNs and adds recurrent-state steering but uses post-hoc layer extrema and fewer side-effect controls.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Introduces per-layer affine translators for decoding latent next-token trajectories and validates them on Transformers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It includes reliability, bias, malicious-input, and causal-feature tests up to 20B parameters; the present paper demonstrates predictive fit on Mamba/RWKV but leaves metric units, held-out evaluation, and causal faithfulness unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eliciting Latent Knowledge from Quirky Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Creates the Alice/Bob quirky benchmark, probing suite, and anomaly detector reproduced here on Mamba.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It reports the original Transformer study with broader methodological details and higher best transfer/anomaly scores; the present work primarily asks whether the same benchmark behaves similarly in a recurrent architecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in Mamba
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A near-simultaneous direct study transferring causal tracing, rank-one editing, linear relation analysis, and information-flow interventions from Transformers to Mamba.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes a concrete Mamba mechanism and compares causal effects with a similar Transformer, going beyond residual-level probes; this paper covers three broader representation tools and introduces state steering but explicitly omits circuit methods.

reviewed_competitors.title: MambaLRP: Explaining Selective State Space Sequence Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Develops an architecture-specific relevance-conserving explanation method for selective SSM components.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It modifies relevance propagation where naïve Transformer-style attribution becomes unfaithful and evaluates explanation quality across datasets; the present paper uses shared residual interfaces and does not test attribution faithfulness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Investigating the Indirect Object Identification circuit in Mamba
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Directly tests whether circuit-style mechanistic interpretability transfers by partially reverse-engineering Mamba's IOI computation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It identifies a layer-39 bottleneck, convolutional name shifting, linear SSM storage, and an attribution-patched circuit; this paper's architecture-specific work is limited to non-causal state addition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Patchscopes: A Unifying Framework for Inspecting Hidden Representations of Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Unifies projection and activation-patching methods and addresses expressivity and early-layer weaknesses of vocabulary lenses.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It elicits natural-language explanations through target-model patching and supports richer causal inspections; the present work uses lightweight affine vocabulary translators and does not adapt Patchscopes to recurrent state.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpreting and Steering State-Space Models via Activation Subspace Bottlenecks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later identifies causal activation bottlenecks in seven SSMs and turns them into both test-time steering and a retrained Stable-Mamba architecture.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It evaluates six benchmarks and reports an 8.27% mean improvement with a mechanistically localized scalar intervention; this paper's state steering uses contrastive means, selected behavior maxima, and qualitative examples without causal localization.

reviewed_competitors.title: WriteSAE: Sparse Autoencoders for Recurrent State
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later learns interpretable rank-one atoms for matrix-valued recurrent writes and validates them by direct cache replacement and steering.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It works at the recurrence-native write tensor and tests causal replacement fidelity across Gated DeltaNet, Mamba-2, and RWKV-7; the present paper represents all states as generic vectors and does not measure intervention fidelity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lost in State Space: Probing Frozen Mamba Representations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Tests the tempting claim that compressed Mamba state provides a strong semantic summary under strict frozen-feature probing.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It finds patch-boundary states do not consistently beat mean pooling and documents extreme anisotropy and state collapse; this directly cautions against treating compression as inherently easier to interpret or steer, an assumption motivating the present paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Detection vs. Execution: Single-Bucket Probes Miss Half the Mamba-2 State Sink
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Shows directly that a Mamba probe can recover a strong representational signature while missing or conflating the heads that causally execute the behavior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It separates detection and execution with class-conditional aggregation and ablation, including a 1.00-to-0.00 retrieval collapse; the present paper relies on AUROC and predictive lenses without comparable causal validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Task Structure Reverses Layerwise State Encoding in Sequence Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Demonstrates across Transformers, Mamba, Mamba-2, LSTMs, and GRUs that layerwise probe profiles depend jointly on task and architecture and need not locate causal bottlenecks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It combines formal tasks, out-of-distribution lengths, ablation, and activation patching, finding highly readable directions can be functionally diffuse; the present paper generalizes from three probe suites without task-structure or causal controls.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Mathematical foundation that defines the geometric-data-set observable-diameter dimension specialized by this paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hanika, Schneider, and Stumme provide the axiomatic feature-family framework and experiments, while this paper contributes the binary-formal-context specialization and support-based approximation rather than a new dimension axiom system.

reviewed_competitors.title: Intrinsic Dimension for Large-Scale Geometric Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Same observable-diameter family and a direct scalability alternative for large geometric data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stubbemann, Hanika, and Schneider derive a computationally feasible finite-data formula and incorporate neighborhood/graph features for Open Graph Benchmark studies; the reviewed paper instead uses all supported formal concepts of a binary context, whose enumeration remains exponential and miner-bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Intrinsic Dimension Estimation for Discrete Metrics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary discrete-data intrinsic-dimension estimator applicable to binary and categorical observations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Macocco, Glielmo, Grilli, and Laio model local neighbor statistics in discrete metric spaces and validate on benchmark and metagenomic data; it requires a meaningful discrete metric but avoids formal-concept enumeration and supplies a point-cloud estimator rather than FCA-semantic probes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Complexity: An FCA-Based Approach
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest FCA-based alternative for measuring the structural complexity of binary tabular data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Buzmakov, Dudyrev, Kuznetsov, Makhalova, and Napoli use distributions of intents, generators, pseudo-intents, premises, and lattice linearity/distributivity; their outputs are interpretable FCA complexity indices rather than an axiomatic observable-diameter dimension, but share the same concept-lattice computational burden.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unsupervised Detection of Semantic Correlations in Big Data
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strongest post-publication direct competitor for intrinsic dimension of extremely high-dimensional binary data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Acevedo, Rodriguez, and Laio fit the global Hamming-distance distribution of binary hypercube samples and report dimensions around 10^5 from 2,500 samples with tests up to one million bits, spin-system phase transitions, and neural image/text representations. It sacrifices FCA concept semantics and assumes binary-hypercube geometry, but directly addresses scale and validates against CD, MLE, GRIDE, I3D, and FCI more broadly than the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Disentangling deep neural networks with rectified linear units using duality
reviewed_competitors.difference: This same research line already introduces DLGN as a deep-linear preactivation/gating network masking a separate value network, describes primal and dual linearities, and evaluates CIFAR-10/100. It makes the 2024 architecture claim incremental; the newer paper chiefly adds active-path regions, overlap visualizations, and the simple-region allocation hypothesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explicitising The Implicit Intrepretability of Deep Neural Networks Via Duality
reviewed_competitors.difference: This follow-up already motivates DLGN by making the feature network linear, feeding ones to the value network, and studying an interpretability-accuracy tradeoff on CIFAR. The piecewise-constant and disentanglement elements in Half-Space Feature Learning therefore have substantial direct precedent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Path Features and Neural Path Kernel : Understanding the role of gates in deep learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lakshminarayanan and Singh already encode ReLU gate states as neural path features, separate neural path values, define the neural path kernel, and show learned gates matter on MNIST/CIFAR. The 2024 overlap kernel is a closely related co-activation count specialized to its MoE framing and DLGN geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks as Kernel Learners: The Silent Alignment Effect
reviewed_competitors.difference: Silent alignment gives a quantitative mechanism in which an evolving tangent kernel learns eigenstructure early and later grows in scale, with analytical treatment for homogeneous linear networks and explicit initialization/data conditions. Half-Space Feature Learning offers a geometric path-gate narrative but does not establish that gate motion causes the observed NTK evolution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Regularization via Neural Feature Alignment
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baratin et al. quantify tangent-feature alignment and compression toward task-relevant directions along optimization paths. It provides spectral and complexity measures against which the DLGN paper's qualitative trace-normalized overlap heatmaps should be compared.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang and Hu classify parameterizations into feature-learning and kernel regimes and derive computable infinite-width feature-learning limits. This replaces the paper's two-extremes setup with a formal continuum and shows that feature learning is not inherently a finite-width phenomenon.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Theoretical Analysis on Feature Learning in Neural Networks: Emergence from Inputs and Advantage over Fixed Features
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shi, Wei, and Liang prove emergence of effective features from structured inputs and a separation from polynomial-size data-independent features. The DLGN paper cites this direction but offers only visual evidence on a toy target and no analogous learning or sample-complexity guarantee.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks can Learn Representations with Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damian, Lee, and Soltanolkotabi prove that gradient descent on a two-layer network learns low-dimensional relevant directions with better sample complexity and transfer than kernel methods for a broad polynomial family. Half-Space Feature Learning seeks a more visual multilayer mechanism but does not demonstrate a controlled advantage over a tuned kernel baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Does Gradient Descent Learn Features -- A Local Analysis for Regularized Two-Layer Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou and Ge prove ground-truth direction recovery both early and after loss becomes small under an explicit regularized objective. It demonstrates the kind of optimization theorem and late-stage control missing from the DLGN resource-allocation conjecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Feature Learning Can Improve Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bordelon, Atanasov, and Pehlevan formalize hard, easy, and super-easy targets by membership in the initial NTK RKHS and show analytically when feature learning changes compute scaling exponents. This supplies an operational task-difficulty definition and scaling tests absent from the paper's frequency/cluster labels.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Networks Learn Features From Local Discontinuities in the Label Function
reviewed_competitors.difference: The later ICLR 2025 work develops DLGN with explicit sigmoid relaxation for trainable gates, formalizes label-function discontinuity scores, adds architecture variants and decision-tree extraction, and evaluates broader binary tasks. It both extends the half-space hypothesis and exposes the 2024 paper's missing hard-gate training specification.
