reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset
reviewed_competitors.difference: MATH supplies 12,500 competition problems with step-by-step solutions and train/test splits, establishing the large-scale final-answer benchmark on which later process work builds. CHAMP is far smaller and lacks a training split, but uniquely adds reusable concepts, problem-specific hints, controlled context interventions, and author-labeled first errors in model outputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Let's Verify Step by Step
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct prior in process supervision and step verification
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work releases PRM800K with 800,000 human step labels and demonstrates that process-supervised reward models outperform outcome supervision on a representative MATH subset. CHAMP contributes a much smaller diagnostic FWS corpus and prompt-based verifier test rather than training a reward model, but adds concept/hint interventions absent from PRM800K.

reviewed_competitors.title: FELM: Benchmarking Factuality Evaluation of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: FELM labels factuality at text-segment granularity, adds error types and supporting or contradicting references, and includes math and reasoning alongside world knowledge. CHAMP narrows to competition mathematics, localizes only the first objective error, and connects errors to problem-level concepts and hints rather than retrieval evidence.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, 2023-11-28; NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: construct-validity challenge for written reasoning traces
reviewed_competitors.difference: Turpin et al. causally manipulate biasing input features and show that generated chains can rationalize answers without mentioning the true influence. CHAMP checks whether emitted math steps are valid but does not test causal faithfulness, so its full-solution metric is best interpreted as explanation/output quality rather than direct access to internal reasoning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Large Language Models: A Focus on Error Identification and Correction
reviewed_competitors.difference: This concurrent Findings paper defines four examiner tasks, labels error steps and types, evaluates identification and correction, and studies error-type prompts across eleven models. CHAMP instead combines solver, side-information, whole-solution, and FWS-verifier analyses on a single concept-linked competition corpus, but has no comparable correction task or error taxonomy.

reviewed_competitors.title: CriticBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Critique-Correct Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: CriticBench compiles 15 datasets across mathematical, commonsense, symbolic, coding, and algorithmic domains and evaluates 17 models on generation, critique, and correction. CHAMP offers deeper, human-written concept and hint structure within one math collection, while CriticBench supplies broader domains, more response families, and an explicit correction axis.

reviewed_competitors.title: OlympiadBench: A Challenging Benchmark for Promoting AGI with Olympiad-Level Bilingual Multimodal Scientific Problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: OlympiadBench contains 8,476 bilingual multimodal mathematics and physics problems with expert step-by-step annotations and a richer difficulty/domain range. CHAMP has only 270 text problems but enables interventions on per-problem concepts and hints and evaluates first-error verification, dimensions OlympiadBench does not center.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stepwise Verification and Remediation of Student Reasoning Errors with Large Language Model Tutors
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work collects 1,002 teacher-annotated student reasoning chains and shows that explicit verification can improve targeted tutoring responses under automatic and human evaluation. CHAMP's errors come from four language models rather than students and it stops at diagnosis, but its competition-level concept/hint annotations support controlled side-information studies.

reviewed_competitors.title: ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: ProcessBench provides 3,400 expert-annotated competition- and Olympiad-level cases and evaluates both process reward models and generative critics on earliest-error identification. It scales and modernizes CHAMP's verifier axis and exposes PRM generalization failure, but does not test how concepts, hints, or misleading context affect solving.

reviewed_competitors.title: LLMs cannot spot math errors, even when allowed to peek into the solution
reviewed_competitors.relationship: subsequent direct test of reference-assisted first-error localization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Using VtG and PRM800K, this study independently confirms that even a reference solution does not make first-error localization reliable and improves it by generating an intermediate corrected student solution. CHAMP first documented the reference-assisted failure on its own small corpus but did not test alignment-through-correction mechanisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hard2Verify: A Step-Level Verification Benchmark for Open-Ended Frontier Math
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hard2Verify spends more than 500 hours on human annotation of recent, open-ended frontier mathematics and evaluates 29 generative critics and process reward models, including verification-compute and self-verification analyses. CHAMP's compact, older, mostly checkable-answer problems are more interpretable for hint ablations but no longer represent the frontier verifier regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Challenging the Boundaries of Reasoning: An Olympiad-Level Math Benchmark for Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: OlymMATH provides 350 parallel English/Chinese Olympiad problems, 200 objectively scored numerical tasks, 150 Lean 4 formalizations, expert verification, and 582,000-plus trajectories. It addresses contamination and process validation more directly than CHAMP's rewritten one-book sample and LLM grader, while CHAMP retains the more granular concept/hint intervention design.

reviewed_competitors.title: Kernel and Rich Regimes in Overparametrized Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational direct predecessor for solvable kernel-to-rich transitions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It already gives analytic initialization-scale transitions and width effects in depth-D diagonal linear networks; the target adds a dense arbitrary-width scalar-data factorization and its layer-cosine taxonomy, not the first solvable two-regime model.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Implicit Bias of Initialization Shape: Beyond Infinitesimal Mirror Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor on relative layer scales and implicit bias.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows that initialization shape, not just total scale, controls rich/lazy behavior and derives closed-form implicit regularizers; the target supplies a different exact time trajectory with explicit layerwise rates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks as Kernel Learners: The Silent Alignment Effect
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest predecessor for an alignment-then-rescaling mechanism.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes early NTK eigenstructure alignment followed by overall kernel rescaling in linear networks; the target studies a different signed layer-to-layer cosine, but its broad composite-mechanism novelty is narrowed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Phase diagram for two-layer ReLU neural networks at infinite-width limit
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor phase diagram for initialization-controlled regimes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It maps hyperparameters to linear, critical, and condensed infinite-width ReLU regimes; the target adds finite hidden width and correlated initialization but only for one-dimensional linear data.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixed Dynamics In Linear Networks: Unifying the Lazy and Active Regimes
reviewed_competitors.difference: It gives a learned-matrix formula and almost complete width/variance phase diagram with mode-wise mixed lazy/active behavior on general MSE tasks; it appeared after target v1 but before v3 and substantially broadens the one-dimensional picture.

reviewed_competitors.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It solves all-initialization gradient flow for a one-neuron two-layer linear net, separates alignment and fitting phases, and extends to more neurons, outputs, layers, and piecewise-linear nets; the target retains an arbitrary-width exact scalar formula.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Lazy to Rich: Exact Learning Dynamics in Deep Linear Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives representation and NTK trajectories across the lazy-rich spectrum for deep linear networks under lambda-balanced initializations; it is broader in depth/task structure but more restricted in initialization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent Converges Linearly to Flatter Minima than Gradient Flow in Shallow Linear Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct finite-step successor on the same shallow factorized family.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It treats true discrete gradient descent, proves rates, and shows its selected flatter solution can differ from gradient flow, directly delimiting the target's transfer from continuous time to finite-step experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Impact of Anisotropic Covariance Structure on the Training Dynamics and Generalization Error of Linear Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives two-phase dynamics and generalization for a two-layer linear regressor with spiked anisotropic covariance, filling the target's one-dimensional data and weak generalization analysis gaps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Balancing Learning Rates Across Layers: Exact Two-Step Dynamics and Optimal Scaling in Linear Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It gives exact one- and two-step GD/test-loss analysis for two- and three-layer linear nets and finds unequal layer rates can be optimal initially and equal later, refining the target's asymptotic exponent advice.

reviewed_competitors.title: Alternating Gradient Flows: A Theory of Feature Learning in Two-layer Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Successor formalizing alignment and norm-growth mechanisms.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It predicts alternating direction-alignment plateaus and norm-growth loss drops across diagonal/fully connected linear nets, attention-only Transformers, and quadratic tasks, turning qualitative motifs into feature-order and timing predictions.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Spectral Condition for Feature Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor for parameterization-level feature-learning criteria.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies spectral-norm scaling conditions and an elementary muP derivation that are more architecture relevant, while the target offers an exact finite-width path only in its scalar model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational predecessor classifying kernel and feature-learning parameterizations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves tensor-program limits for broad architectures and parameterizations; the target trades scope for a finite-width scalar closed form.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Lazy Training in Differentiable Programming
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational predecessor for scale-induced finite-width lazy behavior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves that output/model scaling induces lazy dynamics and documents degraded CNN performance; the target expands power-counting in one tractable factorized model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exact solutions to the nonlinear dynamics of learning in deep linear neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives exact task-mode dynamics, plateaus, rapid transitions, and special orthogonal or aligned initializations; the target's distinction is arbitrary initialization and hidden width for rank-one data.

reviewed_competitors.title: An analytic theory of generalization dynamics and transfer learning in deep linear networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes train/test dynamics versus sample size, task signal-to-noise, network size, and initialization; the target's Appendix D only tracks a fitted slope on one input direction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient descent aligns the layers of deep linear networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves asymptotic rank-one inter-layer alignment and max-margin direction for separable logistic training; the target adds finite-time monotone alignment or disalignment for scalar squared loss, but not the first layer-alignment result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Regularization via Neural Feature Alignment
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor connecting alignment to implicit regularization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies task-relevant tangent-feature alignment, compression, and complexity; the target's parameter-layer cosine is different and receives no comparable generalization theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: High-dimensional Asymptotics of Feature Learning: How One Gradient Step Improves the Representation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor validating target alignment and risk after one step.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves rank-one target alignment and computes risk improvement in proportional asymptotics with rich data; the target covers an all-time scalar trajectory but lacks a comparable held-out-risk theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Two-Layer Neural Networks Learn, One (Giant) Step at a Time
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor and current direct theory of sequential feature acquisition.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives sample complexity and direction specialization across multiple steps; the target's single sufficient statistic cannot model acquisition order among task features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Asymptotics of feature learning in two-layer networks after one gradient-step
reviewed_competitors.difference: It computes generalization of spiked random features after one step, complementing the target's exact time path and showing why NTK movement alone is weaker than measured risk improvement.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamics of Finite Width Kernel and Prediction Fluctuations in Mean Field Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor on finite-width kernel evolution and fluctuations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives coupled O(width^-1/2) kernel/prediction fluctuations nonperturbatively in feature-learning strength and tests CIFAR; the target is exact in hidden width but only for rank-one data.

reviewed_competitors.title: The large learning rate phase of deep learning: the catapult mechanism
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor solvable phase model for finite learning rates.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes nonlinear uv dynamics and a small/large-learning-rate transition relevant to discrete practice; the target deliberately restricts to gradient flow and therefore cannot validate its discrete instability language.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quadratic models for understanding catapult dynamics of neural networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor on large-rate nonlinear dynamics and generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It captures behavior beyond linearized NTK in quadratic models; the target omits the large-rate axis despite extrapolating its phase labels to SGD experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Catapults in SGD: spikes in the training loss and their impact on generalization through feature learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It connects minibatch catapults to gradient-feature alignment and test performance; this directly limits transfer from the target's deterministic gradient flow to minibatch SGD.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs IVb: Adaptive Optimization in the Infinite-Width Limit
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Predecessor extending kernel/feature limits to adaptive optimizers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves optimizer-dependent infinite-width limits for broad architectures; the target's phase theorem only treats continuous gradient flow.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: It runs tens of thousands of experiments across optimizers, scales, and parameterizations and weakens assumed alignment scalings; its empirical scope far exceeds the target's unreplicated plots.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Optimization Landscape of SGD Across the Feature Learning Strength
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Successor practical phase map across feature-learning strength.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It maps output scale and learning rate jointly, derives depth-dependent optimal-rate scaling, and studies ultra-rich plateaus across tasks; the target's map is a small-rate scalar limit.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Feature Learning Can Improve Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Successor linking feature learning to conditional generalization benefits.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It provides task-difficulty-dependent scaling-law improvements, replacing the target's speculative claim that a trainable kernel generally improves test performance with a conditional analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Kernels to Features: A Multi-Scale Adaptive Theory of Feature Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Successor sharpening the definition of feature learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It separates directional kernel adaptation from mere kernel rescaling, directly addressing the target's own admission that output rescaling may not represent acquisition of actual features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Microscopic and collective signatures of feature learning in neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It distinguishes weight-level and representation-manifold signatures and notes the lack of a consensus definition, showing why a changing parameter NTK or layer cosine alone is not a sufficient feature-learning construct.

reviewed_competitors.title: A simple mean field model of feature learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies finite-width symmetry-breaking alignment with quantitative generalization and self-reinforcing input-feature selection, providing a stronger task-feature mechanism than factorization cosine alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral Dynamics in Deep Networks: Feature Learning, Outlier Escape, and Learning Rate Transfer
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current frontier successor in deep spectral feature dynamics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It develops joint bulk/outlier dynamical mean-field theory for nonlinear muP and deep-linear proportional limits, explaining width-stable mode growth and when small-output scalar pictures fail for large-output tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Investigating the Limitations of Transformers with Simple Arithmetic Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strict arithmetic-transformer predecessor studying extrapolation and surface representation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nogueira et al. show that formatting and position representations can support very long arithmetic outputs, whereas the target studies a small fixed-format model's internal carry allocation rather than optimizing length extrapolation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thinking Like Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Theoretical predecessor for expressing algorithms as transformer programs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Weiss et al. use RASP to construct and reason about symbolic transformer computations; the target infers a learned decimal circuit from weights and activations without proving RASP-style equivalence.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Neural Data Router: Adaptive Control Flow in Transformers Improves Systematic Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Architectural predecessor for systematic generalization on algorithmic tasks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Neural Data Router modifies control flow to improve systematic extrapolation, while the target diagnoses ordinary transformer circuitry and observes that its zero-shot length transfer fails.

reviewed_competitors.title: Grokking: Generalization Beyond Overfitting on Small Algorithmic Datasets
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Training-dynamics predecessor for delayed algorithmic generalization and weight-norm changes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Power et al. establish grokking on modular and algorithmic tasks; the target reports an earlier QK/attention transition in ordinary addition and calls it non-grokking without a formal phase analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Mechanistic predecessor for abrupt attention-head circuit formation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Olsson et al. document phase changes associated with induction heads across training; this prior weakens broad novelty for the target's visually abrupt QK staircase while addressing a different computation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior mechanistic training study of an addition-like transformer circuit.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nanda et al. identify and causally test a Fourier circuit for modular addition; the target studies ordinary decimal carry routing and MLP correction but provides weaker circuit reconstruction and intervention robustness.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Arithmetic Reasoning in Language Models using Causal Mediation Analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strict predecessor for causal localization of arithmetic in pretrained language models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stolfo et al. use causal mediation to separate early attention transport from later result processing across arithmetic tasks; the target uses visual head scans and zero pair ablations in three 7B fine-tunes after developing a more detailed toy carry hypothesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Randomized Positional Encodings Boost Length Generalization of Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strict positional-encoding predecessor for length generalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ruoss et al. randomize positions during training to improve extrapolation; the target uses a fixed custom rotary scheme and longer-example priming, then explains why unprimed OOD positions deteriorate.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strict systematic study of position encodings and sequence-length extrapolation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kazemnejad et al. compare positional schemes across tasks and highlight the importance of architecture/encoding choices; the target contributes circuit observations but does not compare its nonstandard rotary implementation to alternatives.

reviewed_competitors.title: Length Generalization in Arithmetic Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct arithmetic length-generalization predecessor cited by the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jelassi et al. evaluate addition beyond trained widths and show that a tiny set of longer examples can transform extrapolation; the target reproduces priming behavior and adds an internal analysis showing that the clean fixed-width module allocation changes.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct cautionary predecessor about algorithm diversity in trained addition networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhong et al. find Clock, Pizza, mixed, and other modular-addition algorithms across seeds and hyperparameters; the target's six-run qualitative consistency and shifting three-layer roles do not exclude comparable diversity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning or Reciting? Exploring the Capabilities and Limitations of Language Models Through Counterfactual Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strict predecessor advocating counterfactual tests of apparent reasoning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. alter task rules to distinguish reusable reasoning from familiar-pattern recitation; the target does not test counterfactual bases, symbols, order, or carry rules despite making algorithmic claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Teaching Arithmetic to Small Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. study data format, training phase changes, and length failure in small arithmetic transformers; the target's distinctive addition is a proposed attention/MLP carry decomposition and task-conditioned causal diagnostics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Arithmetic with Language Models: from Memorization to Computation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Strict arithmetic-learning predecessor separating internal encoding, computation, and decoding.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maltoni and Ferrara analyze learned arithmetic computation and generalization under alternative encodings; the target focuses more narrowly on decimal carry components and tries to bridge them to fine-tuned 7B models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Addition in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest direct pre-v1 paper, reverse-engineering ordinary n-digit addition in a small transformer.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Quirke and Barez identify parallel digit streams, local carry predicates, and a bounded-carry failure in a one-layer decoder; the target extends the question to a canonical two-layer encoder allocation, final-MLP carry correction, priming, and suggestive pretrained-LLM evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-concurrent framework relating learned algorithms to length extrapolation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. use formal program structure and length generalization to ask which algorithms transformers learn; by that stronger criterion the target's unprimed circuit is a fixed-position motif because its zero-shot longer-width behavior collapses.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Addition and Subtraction in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Quirke et al. analyze 49 models across addition, subtraction, and mixed operations with stronger systematic ablation and node constraints, greatly broadening and tightening the target's smaller two-layer case study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later architectural counterexample to weak length extrapolation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: McLeish et al. use digit-relative embeddings and related architectural changes to report up to 99% accuracy on 100-digit addition after training on at most 20 digits; the target supplies richer internals but far weaker zero-shot scaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Position Coupling: Improving Length Generalization of Arithmetic Transformers Using Task Structure
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later task-structured position method and theoretical addition baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cho et al. couple corresponding digit positions and extrapolate from lengths up to 30 to tests at 200 digits with a theoretical construction; the target's custom rotary positions fail without priming and have no formal scaling result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 2.1, Grade-School Math and the Hidden Reasoning Process
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later broad study of language-model grade-school arithmetic and hidden computation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Allen-Zhu and Li investigate data, representation, and hidden reasoning processes at a broader task/model scale; the target offers a more compact component narrative for one addition format but little scaling evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpreting and Improving Large Language Models in Arithmetic Calculation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later pretrained-LLM arithmetic interpretation and intervention work.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work pairs mechanistic analysis with methods intended to improve calculation, while the target's 7B section is a small same-sample head search and does not demonstrate a complete or improving intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpreting Arithmetic Mechanism in Large Language Models through Comparative Neuron Analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later neuron-level arithmetic mechanism study in large models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The comparative-neuron approach searches for arithmetic-selective internal units across conditions, providing a different localization route from the target's broad small-model MLP partition and attention-pair ablations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Algorithmic Capabilities of Random Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later control on how much algorithmic structure architecture supplies before learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Random-transformer results caution that decodable algorithmic features or useful routing geometry need not uniquely identify a learned human algorithm; the target does not include untrained or label-randomized circuit controls.

reviewed_competitors.title: Arithmetic Transformers Can Length-Generalize in Both Operand Length and Count
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later stronger multi-axis arithmetic extrapolation result.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work targets both operand length and number of operands, broadening the generalization criterion beyond the target's three-to-six-digit two-operand setup and showing that architecture/data design can overcome its failure mode.

reviewed_competitors.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later direct competing account of arithmetic computation in pretrained language models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nikankin et al. causally identify sparse operand-range and answer heuristics across LLMs and argue that their combination explains arithmetic behavior; this directly cautions against inferring the toy model's clean human carry algorithm from staircase heads in three 7B models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Use Trigonometry to Do Addition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later competing representation-level and causal account of addition in LLMs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kantamneni and Tegmark identify generalized helical number representations and a Clock-style addition mechanism across mid-sized models; this is a more explicit alternative to the target's qualitative residual similarity and attention-head story.

reviewed_competitors.title: Arithmetic in the Wild: Llama uses Base-10 Addition to Reason About Cyclic Concepts
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current successor connecting arithmetic representations to non-arithmetic cyclic reasoning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work tests a broader causal abstraction of base-10 addition inside Llama on cyclic concepts, moving beyond the target's one-format four-digit prompts and visually analogous residual states.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Arithmetic Heuristic Neurons Form-Invariant? A Mechanistic Analysis of Symbols, Text, and Code in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current cross-format causal successor for arithmetic mechanisms.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Naganna et al. test necessity, sufficiency, and activation transfer for neurons shared across symbolic arithmetic, word problems, and code in Llama-3 models; this directly addresses the format restriction and weak causal validation of the target's 7B section.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploring Hidden Semantics in Neural Networks with Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: SRNet evolves Cartesian genetic-programming expressions to reproduce individual layers and the whole network; symbolic gradients instead identifies a scalar concept only up to invertible output transforms and targets level-set fidelity rather than activation-value fidelity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symbolic Metamodels for Interpreting Black-boxes Using Primitive Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: The metamodel approach combines Kolmogorov-style primitive-function trees with gradient-optimized genetic search to approximate black-box outputs. It can explain feature effects globally but may replicate an equivalent predictor rather than reveal the particular classifier's encoded level sets.

reviewed_competitors.title: AI Feynman 2.0: Pareto-optimal symbolic regression exploiting graph modularity
reviewed_competitors.difference: AI Feynman uses gradients of a neural fit to discover separability, symmetry, and modularity of an unknown data-generating formula. The reviewed method instead uses normalized gradients as the primary invariant for explaining a fixed classifier whose output scale is non-identifiable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Closed-Form Interpretation of Neural Network Latent Spaces with Symbolic Gradients
reviewed_competitors.difference: The follow-on applies the same equivalence-class machinery to Siamese latent spaces and recovers matrix invariants and conserved quantities, extending the reviewed classifier-only toy evidence but not independently testing a competing mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Toy Models of Superposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Elhage et al. study how more sparse features than available dimensions can be represented through nonorthogonal geometric codes and phase changes. The reviewed paper's distinctive claim is that coordinate sharing can instead arise with m at least n because sparsity pressure and random initialization select colliding privileged-basis neurons; its evidence is narrower and does not test realistic learned features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Polysemanticity and Capacity in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scherlis et al. formalize feature capacity and show how sparsity, importance, kurtosis, and architecture yield represented, partially represented, or ignored features and block semi-orthogonal structure. That broader capacity geometry is a stronger comparator than a simple features-greater-than-neurons story; the reviewed work isolates initialization collisions in a neuron-aligned basis but does not quantify capacity in real networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Emergence of Sparse Representations from Noise
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bricken et al. derive implicit regularization from Gaussian input or data noise and demonstrate sparse activations, high-variance feature selection, and biological-style receptive fields including on noisy CIFAR-10. The reviewed paper instead injects iid noise into a linear hidden space, where only non-Gaussian excess kurtosis selects coordinate axes; this yields a clean moment calculation but much weaker real-data validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. train sparse autoencoders on transformer activations, score learned features for interpretability, and causally analyze an IOI circuit. It supplies the real-model semantic and causal measurements missing here, though it focuses on extracting feature directions after training rather than explaining which training dynamics caused neuron polysemanticity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gao et al. scale k-sparse autoencoders to as many as 16 million latents on a production language model and develop reconstruction, sparsity, interpretability, and downstream-evaluation metrics with released artifacts. This raises the empirical bar for the reviewed paper's suggested real-network study, while also showing that a learned decomposition rather than raw neurons may be the more tractable measurement unit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Leask et al. show SAE latents can be incomplete and non-atomic through feature stitching and meta-SAEs, challenging the assumption that one sparse latent is a canonical semantic unit. Any proposed test of incidental polysemanticity using SAE features must therefore demonstrate decomposition stability and causal sufficiency rather than treating feature count or sharing labels as ground truth.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational predecessor for executable stress tests of explanation methods.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adebayo et al. randomize model parameters and labels to ask whether a saliency method depends on the learned model or data at all. The reviewed paper instead holds the trained model fixed, builds simplified internal proxies, and evaluates cross-distribution behavioral fidelity; it omits analogous random-projection and matched-perturbation controls.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention is not Explanation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct antecedent questioning whether attention patterns are faithful explanations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jain and Wallace construct alternative attention distributions with similar outputs and compare attention with feature attribution across NLP tasks. The reviewed work changes model-generated key/query representations through a fixed simplification and asks whether agreement transfers across input distributions, a different but complementary failure of attention-based interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Attention is not not Explanation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Methodological counterpoint defining stronger tests for attention explanations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wiegreffe and Pinter argue that explanation validity depends on the definition and the whole trained model, proposing uniform-attention, seed-variance, diagnostic, and end-to-end adversarial tests. That critique limits any inference from a deliberately altered proxy to the validity of a hypothesis tested on the original network and motivates controls absent from the reviewed study.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Interpretability Illusion for BERT
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest conceptual predecessor and source of the interpretability-illusion framing.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bolukbasi et al. show that neurons and linear combinations can look monosemantic on a narrow corpus yet encode more complex concepts across datasets, tracing the illusion to representation geometry and dataset coverage. The reviewed paper advances from activation examples to executable proxy interventions and systematic generalization, but its representative-IID control is weaker than the framing suggests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent formal framework for grading whether a simplified high-level mechanism is faithful to a neural network.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geiger et al. define faithfulness through causal abstraction and interventions, providing a way to operationalize an interpretation rather than equating it with a compressed executable network. The reviewed paper supplies valuable distribution-shift counterexamples but does not express or test the proposed human-level mechanism as a causal abstraction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does Circuit Analysis Interpretability Scale? Evidence from Multiple Choice Capabilities in Chinchilla
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Very close contemporaneous study of compressed query/key/value explanations beyond their discovery distribution.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lieberum et al. compress a correct-letter head in a 70B model without loss on ordinary multiple-choice labels, then find the 'Nth item' explanation is only partial on randomized labels. The reviewed work generalizes that warning across SVD, clustering, hard attention, Dyck, code, and SCAN, but at much smaller scale and without the predecessor's large-model evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers are uninterpretable with myopic methods: a case study with bounded Dyck grammars
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct Dyck-task predecessor showing that component-local interpretations are non-identifiable.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wen et al. theoretically characterize rich sets of Dyck solutions and show that a single layer's attention can be nearly randomized without changing the network function, challenging myopic inspection even on one distribution. The reviewed paper asks a distinct generalization question: whether one fixed simplification continues to match one trained model across shifts.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Circuit Behavior and Generalization in Mechanistic Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later direct study of whether a known circuit and its component mechanisms generalize across prompt variants.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nainani et al. intervene on the established GPT-2 Small IOI circuit and find that its components are reused with added edges and adaptive behavior across variants. This supplies a positive, circuit-level complement to the reviewed paper's mostly negative proxy-fidelity results and illustrates why whole-circuit causal tests can outperform fixed local simplifications.

reviewed_competitors.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later benchmark formalizing comparative evaluation of causal pathways and causal-variable features.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MIB evaluates precision and concision in recovering task-relevant causal pathways or variables across four tasks and five models, and finds supervised DAS stronger than SAE features for causal-variable localization. It provides standardized causal targets missing from the reviewed proxy-agreement setup, though cross-distribution validity is not its sole focus.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometry-Adaptive Explainer for Faithful Dictionary-Based Interpretability under Distribution Shift
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Recent direct successor that formalizes and mitigates OOD fidelity loss for learned feature dictionaries.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lim et al. model shift as rotation between an ID dictionary and the OOD-active subspace, derive a bound relating that geometry to causal faithfulness loss, and adapt the dictionary with unlabeled OOD activations. This directly addresses the reviewed paper's diagnostic concern for modern sparse dictionaries and supplies the missing geometric and mitigation machinery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Classification without labels: Learning from mixed samples in high energy physics
reviewed_competitors.difference: CWoLa proves that classifying two mixtures with different class proportions recovers the fully supervised decision boundary without instance labels or known proportions. FORCE replaces the need for two externally defined mixtures with two nominally factorized variable groups inside one sample, but gains much stricter independence and target-mean assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Anomaly Detection for Resonant New Physics with Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: CWoLa Hunting learns from a signal mass window versus sidebands and requires localization in one known direction. FORCE can in principle detect a nonresonant factorized species, but its only realistic demonstration is the same kind of resonant dijet benchmark and still relies on a bump fit for statistical interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine Learning Templates for QCD Factorization in the Search for Physics Beyond the Standard Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work learns data-driven conditional QCD templates from a background-rich region under a factorization assumption and uses them to predict backgrounds. FORCE instead treats violation of a within-species kinematics/substructure factorization as the anomaly score, avoiding a generator but not producing a complete background estimate for nonresonant use.

reviewed_competitors.title: Classifying Anomalies THrough Outer Density Estimation (CATHODE)
reviewed_competitors.difference: CATHODE learns a conditional background density in sidebands, samples it in a signal region, and trains a data-versus-background classifier; on the LHC Olympics benchmark it reports near-optimal performance and robustness to feature correlations. It requires a localized signal region and a generative model, whereas FORCE is cheaper and potentially nonresonant but more fragile to factorization leakage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Disentangling Quarks and Gluons with CMS Open Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Komiske, Kryhin, and Thaler apply topic-mixture reasoning and ROC-endpoint regression to extract latent quark/gluon categories in unfolded real CMS data; FORCE explicitly credits this as a prior regression route to an optimal classifier. The earlier method uses two observed mixed samples plus reducibility assumptions, while FORCE uses a cross-scale conditional mean in one mixture.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Interplay of Machine Learning--based Resonant Anomaly Detection Methods
reviewed_competitors.difference: This primary benchmark tests whether resonant anomaly methods select the same background and signal events and finds gains from combining complementary detectors. FORCE presents itself as a complementary assumption class, but does not enter such a matched benchmark; its residuals could be combined with sideband and density scores to reduce method-specific false positives.

reviewed_competitors.title: Full Phase Space Resonant Anomaly Detection
reviewed_competitors.difference: Buhmann et al. extend sideband-generated backgrounds to variable-length particle clouds and the full event phase space, trading substantially greater modeling and compute for broader representation. FORCE is a seven-feature scalar regression with a clear theorem, but can miss signals outside its hand-selected factorized observables.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Anomaly Detection at the LHC: Transforming Optimal Classifiers and the DDD Method
reviewed_competitors.difference: DDD trains a standard discriminator against synthetically distorted background events and evaluates multiple channels and four-top production, offering a broad nonresonant inductive bias with no factorization theorem. FORCE has a more interpretable physics assumption and analytic optimum, while DDD covers richer event representations and explicitly compares several anomaly baselines.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inferring correlated distributions: boosted top jets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alvarez et al. extend Bayesian collider mixture models to correlated within-class observables, using imperfect simulator correlations as priors that data corrects. This directly addresses a central FORCE failure mode at the cost of simulation dependence and a more structured probabilistic model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine-learning techniques for model-independent searches in dijet final states
reviewed_competitors.difference: The CMS Collaboration reports anomaly-detection methods used with 13 TeV collision data, compares their sensitivity, and demonstrates model-agnostic recovery of boosted top jets. It supplies the detector-systematics and real-data benchmark absent from FORCE's Delphes-only study; a mature FORCE validation should be tested within this kind of experimental workflow.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Probst and Boulesteix already show theoretically and across 306 OpenML datasets that Brier, log, and squared losses avoid the classification-error nonmonotonicity seen as tree count grows. The reviewed paper lifts those metric-specific observations to a general exchangeable convex-loss theorem and adds local nonconvex and tail analyses.

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimating a sharp convergence bound for randomized ensembles
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lopes quantifies stabilization of majority-vote error through sharp algorithmic-variance bounds and estimators, whereas the reviewed work targets the sign of every or eventual K-to-K+1 change. The reviewed paper correctly notes that low-order convergence expansions alone do not imply monotonicity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Uphill Roads to Variational Tightness: Monotonicity and Monte Carlo Objectives
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mattei and Frellsen study monotone tightening of Monte Carlo objectives, correlation, and nonuniform weights using stochastic orders. The reviewed paper transfers the leave-one-out convexity logic to predictive ensembles and develops nonconvex loss and classification-tail cases.

reviewed_competitors.title: When are ensembles really effective?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Theisen et al. bound relative classification improvement through disagreement versus error and test interpolating and non-interpolating models. The reviewed paper instead asks monotonicity with ensemble size across arbitrary convex losses and supplies local-curvature conditions, but has much narrower empirical coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Are Two Scores Better Than One? Investigating Ensembles of Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This follow-up shows that score ensembling can improve convex score-matching loss and likelihood without consistently improving nonconvex perceptual quality such as FID, directly extending the reviewed paper's metric-dependence message beyond supervised prediction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Mixtures and Products for Ensemble Aggregation: A Likelihood Perspective on Generalized Means
reviewed_competitors.difference: The follow-up moves beyond arithmetic means to normalized generalized means and identifies r in [0,1] as the range with systematic log-likelihood improvement over individuals. It addresses an aggregation question explicitly left open here, while focusing on improvement over members rather than consecutive-size monotonicity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Finding Alignments Between Interpretable Causal Variables and Distributed Neural Representations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct method predecessor: Distributed Alignment Search
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geiger et al. introduce DAS and evaluate alignment through distributed interchange intervention accuracy under a causal-abstraction framework. The reviewed paper does not replace DAS; it shows that an optimized alignment with the desired end-to-end counterfactual can exploit output-null variation and a dormant causal channel unless the representation's ordinary mechanistic role is separately validated.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Reply to Makelov et al. (2023)'s 'Interpretability Illusion' Arguments
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. argue that Makelov et al.'s nullspace-based illusion definition can reject intuitive desirable representations and that the reported pathologies depend on training and evaluation choices. Their independent IOI experiments agree that the MLP activation has about 4% IIA while the layer-8 residual direction reaches about 70%, and trace the signal through attention heads. This makes the reviewed paper's empirical warning strong but its normative label contested.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
reviewed_competitors.relationship: manual-circuit ground for the IOI case study
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. identify S-inhibition, name-mover, backup, duplicate-token, and negative heads using multiple interventions and quantify faithfulness, completeness, and minimality. The reviewed paper leverages that component-level circuit as a prior to distinguish a plausible residual feature from an MLP subspace, but the manual circuit is itself incomplete and does not constitute formal ground truth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Locating and Editing Factual Associations in GPT
reviewed_competitors.difference: Meng et al. combine causal tracing with the ROME rank-one editor and evaluate rewrite, paraphrase, and neighborhood behavior on CounterFact. The reviewed paper gives a useful variance-minimization reformulation and dormant-pathway account, but its 40-pair correspondence tests only rewrite-oriented outputs and therefore do not reproduce ROME's broader locality/generalization evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does Localization Inform Editing? Surprising Differences in Causality-Based Localization vs. Knowledge Editing in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct empirical motivation and competing explanation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hase et al. show on hundreds of facts and multiple robustness variants that causal-tracing localization adds little predictive value for the best editing layer beyond layer identity. The reviewed paper proposes dormant pathways and rank-one controllability as a mechanistic explanation, but tests a much smaller fact set and does not establish that its mechanism quantitatively explains Hase et al.'s full localization-editing mismatch.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang and Nanda systematically vary patching metrics and corruption/patch choices, demonstrating that localization conclusions depend strongly on experimental design. The reviewed paper contributes a distinct algebraic failure mode inside learned subspaces; together they imply that both the intervention operator and its measurement protocol must be audited.

reviewed_competitors.title: How to use and interpret activation patching
reviewed_competitors.difference: Heimersheim and Nanda synthesize what activation patching can support, metric pitfalls, corruption choices, and circuit-level interpretation. It operationalizes the reviewed paper's caution for practitioners but is guidance rather than a benchmark with known mechanisms or a formal dormant-pathway detector.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformer Circuit Faithfulness Metrics Are Not Robust
reviewed_competitors.difference: Miller, Chughtai, and Saunders show that circuit faithfulness scores vary substantially under reasonable ablation implementations, including on IOI. Their result generalizes the reviewed paper's central lesson from subspace mixing to circuit evaluation: measured faithfulness is partly a property of the intervention distribution and replacement rule.

reviewed_competitors.title: InterpBench: Semi-Synthetic Transformers for Evaluating Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques
reviewed_competitors.difference: InterpBench creates realistic semi-synthetic transformers whose intended circuits are known and whose non-circuit nodes are prevented from affecting outputs. It directly addresses the reviewed paper's acknowledged ground-truth problem and could measure whether subspace methods recover normal mechanisms rather than only successful interventions, although planted models may not capture all natural-model degeneracies.

reviewed_competitors.title: Identifying Functionally Important Features with End-to-End Sparse Dictionary Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Braun et al. train sparse dictionaries to preserve the model's output distribution when inserted end to end, explicitly targeting functional importance rather than activation reconstruction. This reduces one proxy gap but does not by itself rule out dormant or off-manifold intervention features; the reviewed paper suggests adding normal-use and reader/writer diagnostics to such objectives.

reviewed_competitors.title: Combining Causal Models for More Accurate Abstractions of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pislar et al. combine multiple simple high-level causal models and expose a trade-off between coverage and interchange-intervention faithfulness. This addresses hypothesis misspecification and input-dependent algorithms, while the reviewed paper highlights a different identifiability issue: even high intervention agreement can be achieved by a low-level alignment that is mechanistically perverse under the chosen decomposition.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sutter et al. prove that sufficiently expressive alignment maps can map essentially any network to any algorithm, making unconstrained causal abstraction trivial. Their impossibility result complements the reviewed paper's constructive linear counterexample and sharpens why alignment classes need simplicity, geometry, and normal-use constraints.

reviewed_competitors.title: Certified Interventional Fidelity: Anytime-Valid, Adaptive Evaluation of Causal Claims in Mechanistic Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Asiaee defines bounded interventional fidelity estimands over explicit input and intervention distributions and supplies confidence sequences robust to adaptive sampling, with IOI experiments. It directly fixes the reviewed paper's missing uncertainty and intervention-distribution specification, but statistical certification of a patching effect cannot alone certify that the chosen subspace is the model's normal mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretability at Scale: Identifying Causal Mechanisms in Alpaca
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. replace DAS's remaining discrete search with learned boundaries and report robust high-level boolean alignments in Alpaca-7B across inputs and instructions. It extends the method to a much larger model, but the reviewed paper implies that held-out interchange accuracy still needs ordinary-pathway and nullspace diagnostics before being interpreted as a unique internal mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Conmy et al.'s ACDC greedily prunes model edges under activation patching and validates recovery of known circuit component types. It searches architectural graph structure rather than arbitrary activation bases, which supplies a stronger parsimony prior, but it remains sensitive to the metric, corruption, replacement distribution, and incompleteness of reference circuits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causal Differentiating Concepts: Interpreting LM Behavior via Causal Representation Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goyal et al. learn sparse behavior-changing latent concepts without predefined labels and test ground-truth recovery in synthetic and semi-synthetic settings plus LM refusal. Their constrained representation-learning objective attacks label and supervision limitations, while the reviewed paper warns that any behavior-changing direction still needs natural-use and off-manifold checks.

reviewed_competitors.title: pyvene: A Library for Understanding and Improving PyTorch Models via Interventions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. provide a unified implementation layer for static and trainable interventions, causal abstraction, and localization across PyTorch modules. This improves reproducibility and makes intervention semantics explicit in code, but software unification does not resolve which counterfactual replacements are scientifically identifying.

reviewed_competitors.title: CausalGym: Benchmarking causal interpretability methods on linguistic tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: CausalGym evaluates DAS-style distributed interventions alongside simple representation baselines on controlled linguistic variables and includes selectivity and arbitrary-mapping controls. It provides the matched random/simple-direction protocol absent from the reviewed IOI and one-pair factual studies, though controlled linguistic tasks do not resolve natural-mechanism ground truth in open-ended behavior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Everything, Everywhere, All at Once: Is Mechanistic Interpretability Identifiable?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Meloux et al. enumerate circuits, algorithms, and alignment subspaces in small networks and find multiple incompatible explanations satisfying standard criteria for both where-then-what and what-then-where strategies. This generalizes the reviewed paper's basis-dependent counterexample: even without a null-plus-dormant splice, output faithfulness need not identify a unique explanation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. learn an overcomplete sparse dictionary and identify finer-grained causally relevant IOI features, rather than directly optimizing a source-to-base control direction. Sparsity and reconstruction offer a different natural-activation prior, but SAE features can still split, combine, or control behavior without a stable context-general downstream function.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Interpretability Illusion for BERT
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bolukbasi et al. show that apparently simple neuron or direction concepts can arise from BERT embedding geometry and narrow corpus slices, motivating tests across datasets. The reviewed paper's narrower novelty is causal: its patched direction splices an output-null correlate with a dormant output-effective direction, so it can control behavior despite mislocalizing normal mediation.

reviewed_competitors.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Karvonen et al. evaluate more than 200 sparse autoencoders across interpretability, disentanglement, and practical control metrics and find proxy gains do not reliably predict practical utility. This reinforces the reviewed paper's proxy warning and supplies breadth it lacks, while focusing on SAE dictionaries rather than direct dormant-pathway detection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Encode Both Concepts and Functions: The Downstream Geometry of Feature Effects
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hoang et al.'s FEGA removes the same active SAE feature across contexts and studies the cloud of resulting logit changes, finding stable one-dimensional effects rare and distinguishing value-like from context-dependent pointer-like features. It operationalizes the reviewed paper's control-versus-reusable-function distinction beyond a single source/base pair.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causal Abstraction: A Theoretical Foundation for Mechanistic Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Geiger et al. formalize causal abstraction for arbitrary mechanism transformations and unify patching, tracing, scrubbing, concept erasure, DAS, sparse autoencoders, and steering. The reviewed paper supplies a concrete warning that graded interventional faithfulness is not by itself a human-readable or decomposition-invariant identification criterion.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Theory for Length Generalization in Learning to Reason
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct successor by the same authors, explicitly flagged by arXiv for text overlap, that develops the program into the later ICLR 2025 paper on generalizing reasoning problems.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It replaces the target's finite-R emphasis with a stronger (n,r)-consistency framework and adds representations that report perfect length generalization for parity, addition, and multiplication; it should be treated as the current version of this research line rather than independent corroboration.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Far Can Transformers Reason? The Globality Barrier and Inductive Scratchpad
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A more developed theoretical account of when task distributions are locally learnable and how supervised intermediate states can lower autoregressive locality.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves a negative result under explicit technical assumptions, distinguishes agnostic, educated, and inductive scratchpads, and reports multi-seed extrapolation; the target offers a simpler operand-distance heuristic but its key locality proof and learning assumptions are weaker.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A transformer-specific identifiability theory that characterizes functions selected from long-prefix evidence under absolute position embeddings and norm regularization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It models an explicit architecture and inference bias and validates predictions across algorithmic/formal-language tasks; the target claims architecture independence by assuming exhaustive table coverage, leaving actual learner selection unexplained.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A nearly contemporaneous framework linking successful length extrapolation to short all-length RASP programs and testing that conjecture across algorithmic tasks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: RASP length captures implementability by a fixed Transformer program, whereas the target's R captures operand proximity in a chosen serialization; the two expose distinct architectural and representational bottlenecks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Position Coupling: Improving Length Generalization of Arithmetic Transformers Using Task Structure
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct method competitor that injects arithmetic structure by assigning shared position IDs to digits of the same significance.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves a one-layer construction and reports generalization from 30- to 200-digit addition plus multiplication and two-dimensional tasks; the target encodes locality through multi-line CoT state rewriting and reports a much smaller synthetic comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Another direct alternative showing that digit-relative embeddings, input injection, and recurrence can unlock arithmetic length extrapolation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It reaches up to 99% on 100-digit addition after training on 20 digits and evaluates sorting and multiplication; the target emphasizes a task-agnostic DAG abstraction but does not isolate positional encoding and architectural recurrence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Randomized Positional Encodings Boost Length Generalization of Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A strong empirical competitor demonstrating that positional-distribution shift itself is a major cause of failure across 15 algorithmic tasks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It evaluates 6,000 models and reports a 12-point average gain by randomizing ordered positions; the target uses relative positions without an ablation and attributes outcomes primarily to causal-domain finiteness and R.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evaluation of Neural Architectures Trained with Square Loss vs Cross-Entropy in Classification Tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hui and Belkin compare explicit square loss against cross-entropy over major vision, NLP, speech, and Transformer settings with computational resources controlled. ISBE instead avoids scalar evaluation and tests manual score-error gradients only on MNIST; its plotted MSE is not its training gradient for nonlinear scores.

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimating or Propagating Gradients Through Stochastic Neurons for Conditional Computation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bengio, Leonard, and Courville explicitly study derivative-bypassing estimators and name the straight-through estimator. ISBE's hard-activation variants similarly bypass local derivatives, but for deterministic classifier outputs and without estimator-bias or convergence analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Softmax to Sparsemax: A Sparse Model of Attention and Multi-Label Classification
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sparsemax derives an alternative simplex-valued transformation, its exact Jacobian, and a matching smooth convex classification loss. ISBE permits arbitrary bounded monotone scores and bypasses their Jacobians, gaining simplicity but giving up sparsemax's explicit probabilistic and optimization semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are All Losses Created Equal: A Neural Collapse Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. analyze when cross-entropy, MSE, focal loss, and label smoothing share neural-collapse solutions and test objective choice beyond one accuracy number. ISBE reports near-equal MNIST accuracy but does not analyze representations or identify the implicit objectives of its activation-specific gradients.

reviewed_competitors.title: $f$-Divergence Based Classification: Beyond the Use of Cross-Entropy
reviewed_competitors.difference: Novello and Tonello derive a principled family of alternative classification objectives from variational f-divergences and evaluate image and signal tasks. This broadens cross-entropy through explicit statistical objectives, whereas ISBE focuses on directly prescribing logit gradients and gives no risk or calibration interpretation for most variants.

reviewed_competitors.title: BCE vs. CE in Deep Feature Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Xiao, and Shen explicitly analyze one-vs-all binary cross-entropy against multiclass cross-entropy and show different absolute-versus-relative score geometry. ISBE's sigmoid rule has exactly the BCE-with-logits gradient, so this later work supplies an objective and feature-learning interpretation absent from ISBE's loss-unnecessary framing.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. show that small randomly initialized Transformers benefit from arithmetic-aware formatting and chain-of-thought-style intermediate results across addition, multiplication, and square root, emphasizing sample complexity and phase transitions. reviewed_competitors.title: Length Generalization in Arithmetic Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jelassi et al. use relative positional embeddings to extrapolate addition from 5 to 15 digits and train-set priming with 10-50 long examples when relative positions fail for multiplication, reaching 5-by-3 to 35-by-3 extrapolation. The reviewed paper changes layouts or injects random tags, reaches only 10-to-12-digit addition robustly in its table, and evaluates direct multiplication within trained lengths.

reviewed_competitors.title: Randomized Positional Encodings Boost Length Generalization of Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ruoss et al. sample an ordered subset of position indices from a longer virtual range, exposing training sequences to the position distribution expected at longer lengths, and evaluate about 6,000 models on 15 algorithmic tasks. The reviewed random embedding instead injects freshly sampled Gaussian token tags without ordered positional semantics and studies a much narrower arithmetic suite.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kazemnejad et al. systematically compare absolute, T5-relative, ALiBi, RoPE, and no positional encoding across mathematical and reasoning tasks and analyze how causal NoPE models recover positional behavior. The reviewed paper offers arithmetic-specific format and random-tag interventions rather than a broad controlled positional-encoding comparison.

reviewed_competitors.difference: MathGLM obtains near-perfect multi-digit arithmetic with a 2-billion-parameter model and sufficient specialized data, then fine-tunes a larger pretrained model for textual mathematics. reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. combine reversed answers, index hints, randomized positions, and FIRE embeddings to reach 2.5-times addition extrapolation, but repeated runs reveal large variance from initialization and data order. reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Length Generalization with Turing Programs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Turing Programs express computation as a chain of text-copying steps with small local modifications, length-generalize on addition, multiplication, and in-context SGD, and come with a RASP construction simulating arbitrary Turing machines. This gives up the reviewed paper's direct no-scratchpad multiplication objective in exchange for a task-general and theoretically universal decomposition.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. retain the standard Transformer, position encoding, and input format while iteratively generating, filtering, and retraining on harder examples, reporting addition extrapolation from 10 to 100 digits without apparent saturation. reviewed_competitors.difference: O'Brien et al. remove dual-use material during pretraining and report 6.9B models that resist up to 10,000 adversarial fine-tuning steps and 300M biothreat-related tokens, over an order of magnitude beyond post-training baselines. This supports the target paper's conclusion that robust removal may require intervention before ordinary fine-tuning, while also showing context-provided knowledge can bypass internal ignorance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fine-Tuning Without Forgetting via Loss-Adaptive Learning Rates
reviewed_competitors.difference: FINCH bounds per-step forgetting by learning rate times square-root loss and adapts the rate to high-loss batches, reporting 93% average forgetting reduction while matching target-task performance. It operationalizes the target paper's learning-rate sensitivity on contemporary LLM benchmarks but focuses preservation rather than mechanistic wrapper identification.
