reviewed_competitors.difference: NeuSA projects PDE dynamics onto a learned spectral representation, integrates it with a Neural ODE, and uses classical-method initialization to address both spectral bias and temporal causality. Its integrated multi-frequency treatment avoids MSNN's single-peak residual heuristic and evaluates temporal consistency directly.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2025 official OpenReview poster record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 Small
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The principal manual language-model circuit predecessor and methodological template for activation/path patching, functional head classes, and backup behavior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It targets a 117M open model and aims at a more complete algorithmic circuit with explicit faithfulness and minimality tests; the Chinchilla study establishes much larger-model feasibility but analyzes only a late cross-section and is not reproducible outside DeepMind.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Automated Circuit Discovery for Mechanistic Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A contemporaneous method competitor that automates circuit edge selection through ACDC instead of manually ranking and categorizing components.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ACDC focuses on scalable search and comparison with known small-model circuits; the target demonstrates infrastructure-level application at 70B but retains labor-intensive manual semantics and does not benchmark search quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Hydra Effect: Emergent Self-repair in Language Model Computations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A near-contemporaneous same-lab causal study directly explaining why ablation and total effects can be smaller than direct effects through downstream self-repair and late-MLP counterbalancing.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It makes compensation itself the object of controlled study across language-model computations; the target observes likely backup/calibration artifacts, including its B-label anomaly, but leaves them unresolved in the selected circuit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A systematic evaluation of precisely the corruption, metric, and patching choices on which the target's localization depends.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows that methodological hyperparameters can yield disparate localization results and recommends controlled choices; the target acknowledges many variants but reports one narrow ABCD-relative/resampling configuration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Is This the Subspace You Are Looking for? An Interpretability Illusion for Subspace Activation Patching
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct challenge to interpreting behavior-changing low-dimensional patches as evidence that a model normally represents the proposed semantic feature in that subspace.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It constructs and empirically demonstrates dormant-pathway illusions and specifies additional faithfulness evidence; the target's SVD projection is less aggressively optimized than DAS, but preservation plus partial OOD transfer still cannot uniquely validate its enumeration semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: AtP*: An efficient and scalable method for localizing LLM behaviour to components
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct same-author successor addressing the computational scaling bottleneck of exhaustive activation patching.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AtP* develops fast gradient attribution, repairs saturated-attention and cancellation false negatives, and provides a probabilistic residual-error diagnostic; the target proves that selected brute-force analyses can run at 70B but offers no systematic localization-cost or missed-component guarantee.

reviewed_competitors.title: Have Faith in Faithfulness: Going Beyond Circuit Overlap When Finding Model Mechanisms
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A method/evaluation competitor arguing that circuits should be judged by retained behavior after ablating everything outside them, not component overlap or independent effects.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It introduces integrated-gradient edge attribution and explicitly evaluates circuit faithfulness; the target patches its 45 selected nodes into an otherwise intact model, which establishes a causal cross-section but leaves outside-component sufficiency untested.

reviewed_competitors.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct empirical answer to the target's broader scale question across 154 training checkpoints and model sizes from 70M to 2.8B, with supplementary larger models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It finds role/algorithm consistency despite individual-head turnover and increasing circuit size using open Pythia checkpoints; the target reaches a much larger 70B endpoint but provides only one proprietary snapshot, one capability, and no cross-scale circuit comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: InterpBench: Semi-Synthetic Transformers for Evaluating Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A benchmark response to the lack of ground truth when judging whether a discovered circuit or feature explanation is actually correct.
reviewed_competitors.difference: InterpBench supplies realistic semi-synthetic models with known circuits and compares discovery techniques; the Chinchilla analysis has realistic frontier scale but no ground-truth circuit, so recovered performance cannot establish completeness or semantic correctness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adversarial Circuit Evaluation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct evaluation alternative that searches for inputs where published circuits diverge maximally from their full models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows that high average performance can conceal benign in-distribution failures and derives sampling bounds for tail behavior; the target reports averages, sees large prompt variance, and does not characterize worst-case or subgroup fidelity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hypothesis Testing the Circuit Hypothesis in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A statistical framework for testing preservation, localization, and minimality across six previously proposed circuits.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It makes the idealized circuit criteria explicit and finds mixed support in learned Transformers; the target uses descriptive patch recovery and knowingly retains ambiguous nodes without statistical minimality or localization tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: MIB: A Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The current standardized competitive benchmark for circuit and causal-variable localization methods across tasks and models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MIB compares complete faithfulness-versus-size curves and finds attribution/mask optimization strongest for circuits and supervised DAS strongest for variables, with SAE features no better than neurons; the target's one chosen 45-node cutoff and rank-three SVD case cannot support method-level comparative claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Min et al. test 12 models and report that independently randomizing demonstration labels often barely hurts classification or multiple-choice performance, emphasizing label space, input distribution, and format. Halawi et al. instead use a coherent cyclic wrong mapping, measure explicit copying of that mapping, and inspect internal depth and components; the contrast also shows that conclusions about label correctness depend on the corruption construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Ground-Truth Labels Matter: A Deeper Look into Input-Label Demonstrations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yoo et al. already quantify label-correctness sensitivity across 17 classification datasets and show strong dependence on task, prompt verbosity, calibration method, inference formulation, and model size, including GPT-J and GPT-NeoX. Halawi et al. add the layerwise divergence and component interventions, but their own prompt and calibration heterogeneity should be interpreted in light of this prior conditionality result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Larger language models do in-context learning differently
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wei et al. study flipped and semantically unrelated labels across GPT-3, InstructGPT, Codex, PaLM, and Flan-PaLM and find that overriding semantic priors emerges with scale. Halawi et al. analyze smaller open models internally and show a late-depth override pattern, but do not test the much larger API-model scaling regime that motivates Wei et al.'s claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
reviewed_competitors.difference: Olsson et al. define match-and-copy induction heads and connect their training-time emergence to in-context loss improvement, with strong causality in small attention-only models but mainly correlational evidence in larger models with MLPs. Halawi et al. adapt that hypothesis to false class-label copying and provide a GPT-J cross-task lesion, while leaving formation dynamics and architecture-general causal evidence unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eliciting Latent Predictions from Transformers with the Tuned Lens
reviewed_competitors.difference: Belrose et al. show that raw logit lenses can be biased and unreliable because intermediate representations drift, train per-layer universal affine translators, test causal fidelity, and directly reproduce the overthinking pattern on BLOOM-560M and GPT-Neo models. This supports the phenomenon while weakening any interpretation that treats Halawi et al.'s untrained intermediate logits as literal beliefs; the current tuned-lens record also develops prompt-injection detection beyond the target paper's preliminary appendix.

reviewed_competitors.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh et al. use controlled synthetic training and optogenetics-inspired activation clamping to identify three interacting subcircuits behind induction-head formation and its phase change. Their work studies how induction circuits arise rather than harmful false-label following, but provides a stronger formation-level causal framework than post-training zero lesions alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mechanistic Fine-tuning for In-context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cho et al. turn attention-to-label mechanisms into an attention-behavior fine-tuning objective that promotes attention to correct label tokens and suppresses wrong ones, evaluating nine modern language models and eight datasets. Halawi et al. supply the diagnostic and sparse lesion motivation; Cho et al. target a trainable, broader robustness intervention rather than deleting five GPT-J heads.

reviewed_competitors.title: Safe and Efficient In-Context Learning via Risk Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wynn et al. use harmful demonstrations as the same safety problem but add dynamic early exit, exclusion of late heads that attend to unsafe inputs, and distribution-free control of degradation below a zero-shot baseline, with both theory and empirical tests. That work converts Halawi et al.'s post hoc early-exit opportunity into an explicit risk-control objective; it does not replace the target paper's original mechanistic localization evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Survey of Small Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nguyen et al. supply a structured taxonomy of architectures, training, compression, pruning, quantization, benchmarks, metrics, and open challenges. The reviewed article is earlier and more advocacy-oriented, with stronger emphasis on open-source participation and the adaptability-controllability-affordability frame but far less systematic technical coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Small Language Models in the Era of Large Language Models: Techniques, Enhancements, Applications, Collaboration with LLMs, and Trustworthiness
reviewed_competitors.difference: This survey explicitly tackles definition, acquisition, application, enhancement, LLM collaboration, and reliability, and defines SLMs through specialized-task capability and resource constraints rather than a nominal 10B cutoff. It directly develops areas that the reviewed paper raises only qualitatively, especially trustworthiness and the unstable definition of smallness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Small Language Models (SLMs) Can Still Pack a Punch: A survey (updated 2026)
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mehta et al. review roughly 160 papers, focus on general and task-specific models in the 1-8B range, cover construction techniques, and introduce effective size as capability relative to LLMs. It preserves the reviewed paper's core smaller-can-compete thesis but supplies a much later and larger evidence base and a more explicit account of capability versus nominal scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Small Language Models: Architectures, Techniques, Evaluation, Problems and Future Adaptation
reviewed_competitors.difference: This survey organizes SLM architecture, training, model compression, pruning, quantization, evaluation datasets, efficiency-quality trade-offs, and future directions. The reviewed work offers a historically useful early ecosystem narrative, but not this later taxonomy or evaluation coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Small Language Models for Agentic Systems: A Survey of Architectures, Capabilities, and Deployment Trade offs
reviewed_competitors.difference: The agentic-systems survey evaluates the compact-model case through schema validity, executable calls, cost per successful task, latency, energy, routing, guided decoding, and verifier cascades, while preserving LLM fallback for open-domain or long-horizon work. It operationalizes the reviewed paper's affordability and controllability themes for a narrower workload instead of treating smallness as a general advantage.

reviewed_competitors.title: TinyLlama: An Open-Source Small Language Model
reviewed_competitors.difference: TinyLlama trains a 1.1B model on roughly one trillion tokens and releases checkpoints and code, providing an empirical, artifact-backed example well inside the reviewed paper's nominal size range. It demonstrates a concrete compact-model build rather than surveying heterogeneous assistants derived from larger backbones.

reviewed_competitors.title: OpenELM: An Efficient Language Model Family with Open Training and Inference Framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: OpenELM releases public-data training and evaluation code, logs, multiple checkpoints, configurations, weights, and MLX conversion support. Its component-level artifact directly addresses the reviewed paper's under-specified binary openness labels and demonstrates that weights alone need not define an open model release.

reviewed_competitors.title: MiniCPM: Unveiling the Potential of Small Language Models with Scalable Training Strategies
reviewed_competitors.difference: MiniCPM reports 1.2B and 2.4B non-embedding-parameter models, model/data scaling experiments, the Warmup-Stable-Decay scheduler, and comparisons to 7B-13B systems. It directly tests resource-efficient compact-model capability and scaling, whereas the reviewed paper infers that capability from separate project reports.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine learning and the physical sciences
reviewed_competitors.relationship: An earlier broad expert review of the interface between machine learning and physical sciences, including physics-motivated ML, particle physics, cosmology, quantum systems, chemistry, and materials.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Carleo et al. cover a broader traditional-physics landscape and ML concepts as of 2019; the reviewed survey goes deeper on 3D equivariance and extends the scale taxonomy through proteins, molecular interactions, modern generative models, and learned PDEs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Provides the most direct competing unification around geometric priors, symmetries, representations, and equivariant architectures.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bronstein et al. develop a deeper and more general geometric blueprint across grids, groups, graphs, manifolds, and gauges; the reviewed survey uses a narrower symmetry tutorial as one bridge inside a much larger catalog of scientific domains, datasets, and application-specific failure modes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scientific discovery in the age of artificial intelligence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A contemporary broad review of how representation learning, geometric deep learning, generative models, and AI-assisted experimentation enter the scientific process.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. organize around discovery functions and cross-disciplinary breakthroughs in a compact perspective; the reviewed paper narrows to quantum, atomistic, and continuum systems and supplies much more mathematical and benchmark-level technical detail.

reviewed_competitors.title: Modern applications of machine learning in quantum sciences
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A comprehensive book-length treatment of machine learning for quantum phases, many-body states, control, circuits, generative modeling, and quantum machine learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dawid et al. offer substantially broader depth within quantum science, including quantum control and circuits; the reviewed survey covers a more selective neural-wavefunction slice so it can connect quantum problems to atomistic and continuum modeling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine Learning Force Fields
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A focused review of learned force fields, their construction, applications, chemical interpretation, and validation challenges.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Unke et al. provide a practical step-by-step force-field treatment and deeper atomistic detail; the reviewed survey situates force fields within molecular representation, dynamics, materials, cross-scale modeling, and shared symmetry/OOD concerns.

reviewed_competitors.title: AI for Science: Current progress and pathways forward
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later field-level assessment of AI adoption in high-impact natural and health science and proposed workflows for broader AI4Science integration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yu and Jin emphasize adoption barriers, usable tools, proactive AI researchers, and ecosystem interventions based on publication analysis; the reviewed survey emphasizes mathematical foundations, domain methods, and benchmark taxonomies rather than scientometric uptake.

reviewed_competitors.title: From AI for Science to Agentic Science: A Survey on Autonomous Scientific Discovery
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later survey reframing AI for science around autonomous agents that generate hypotheses, design and execute experiments, analyze results, and iterate across several scientific domains.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wei et al. organize around degrees of agency and the scientific workflow, especially LLM-enabled systems; the reviewed survey is centered on scientific objects, physical scales, geometric priors, domain predictors, generative models, and simulators rather than autonomous research loops.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Estella Aguerri and Zaidi formulate the multi-encoder DIB problem, characterize discrete and Gaussian information-rate regions, and give iterative algorithms. Murphy and Bassett repurpose that communication-theoretic objective for neural scientific interpretation with arbitrary data and feature-value visualizations; the DIB principle itself is not new here.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Distributed Information Bottleneck reveals the explanatory structure of complex systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: This 2022 preprint already introduces the explanatory DIB, Boolean-circuit subset recovery, and localization of plastic-rearrangement information in sheared glass. The reviewed PNAS work refines mutual-information estimation, threshold/value inspection, and per-particle analysis, but substantially overlaps its method, systems, and principal claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretability with full complexity by constraining feature information
reviewed_competitors.difference: The ICLR 2023 paper develops essentially the same per-feature compression path as a general tabular explanation and feature-selection framework. The PNAS paper specializes the framework to scientific micro-macro analysis, adds circuit ground truth and detailed amorphous-material interpretations, but should be understood as an application/refinement within one research program.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Explain: An Information-Theoretic Perspective on Model Interpretation
reviewed_competitors.difference: L2X learns instancewise subsets maximizing mutual information with a model response. It offers local selection and direct predictive-model explanation, whereas DIB gives a global continuous rate path and within-value compression; neither by itself establishes causal scientific relevance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Partial Information Decomposition for Data Interpretability and Feature Selection
reviewed_competitors.difference: PIDF assigns each feature target-shared, synergy-contribution, and redundancy quantities and tests genetics and neuroscience cases. reviewed_competitors.title: Surveying the space of descriptions of a composite system with machine learning

reviewed_competitors.title: The Causal Information Bottleneck and Optimal Causal Variable Abstractions
reviewed_competitors.difference: The causal information bottleneck preserves intervention-relevant structure in abstractions rather than observational predictive information alone. It targets a central limitation of using DIB discoveries as scientific mechanisms, at the cost of requiring causal structure or interventional semantics unavailable in the reviewed glass dataset.

DIB is more general and reveals graded feature-value distinctions, while the softness work asks whether simpler stable physical descriptors can outperform black-box decompositions in transfer and experimental usability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Dynamics of In-Context Learning in Linear Attention

reviewed_competitors.difference: Jin and Wu establish positivity of differential NTKs for shallow and deep networks, broad activations, and linear differential operators. It represents the current rigorous physics-informed kernel direction absent from the reviewed notes.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: A large empirical characterization of naturally circulated jailbreak prompts and their evolution across communities and models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: JailbreakHub studies 1,405 in-the-wild prompts, 131 communities, and 107,250 evaluation samples, greatly expanding ecological and longitudinal coverage beyond this paper's 32 curated and 317 synthetic prompts, while offering less emphasis on a training-failure taxonomy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Jailbreaking Black Box Large Language Models in Twenty Queries
reviewed_competitors.relationship: An automated black-box adaptive attack using an attacker language model to refine a semantic jailbreak from target feedback.
reviewed_competitors.difference: PAIR specifies an executable adaptive policy that often succeeds within twenty queries, whereas this paper's adaptive result is retrospective success by any attack in a fixed panel and does not control query budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: HarmBench: A Standardized Evaluation Framework for Automated Red Teaming and Robust Refusal
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A standardized large-scale framework for comparing automated red-team attacks, target models, and defenses.
reviewed_competitors.difference: HarmBench compares 18 methods and 33 targets or defenses with open artifacts and standardized behavior/evaluator infrastructure, addressing this paper's small bespoke panel, absent artifact package, and incomparable adaptive budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: A StrongREJECT for Empty Jailbreaks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A benchmark and evaluator focused on whether a jailbreak yields useful harmful information rather than merely bypassing refusal.
reviewed_competitors.difference: StrongREJECT directly exposes the principal weakness of this paper's BADBOT label: existing success metrics can overstate attack efficacy when jailbreaking reduces output capability. It releases code and data with stronger human-judgment agreement.

reviewed_competitors.title: JailbreakBench: An Open Robustness Benchmark for Jailbreaking Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: An open, evolving benchmark designed to make attack and defense results comparable and reproducible.
reviewed_competitors.difference: JailbreakBench publishes 100 behaviors, adversarial artifacts, threat-model details, templates, scoring, an over-refusal evaluation, and a leaderboard, explicitly addressing withheld prompts, closed code, and evolving proprietary APIs that constrain reproduction here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Jailbreaking Leading Safety-Aligned LLMs with Simple Adaptive Attacks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later study of target-adaptive jailbreaks across open and closed models, including system-specific log-probability search, transfer, and prefilling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It operationalizes safety-capability parity through attacks adapted to each model and API, reports later model families and defenses, and releases code, logs, and JailbreakBench artifacts; its judge-based 100% rates still require evaluator scrutiny.

reviewed_competitors.title: Best-of-N Jailbreaking
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A simple black-box best-of-many attack that repeatedly samples augmented prompts across text, vision, and audio systems.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It turns the multiple-tries effect into the main object of study, reports success as a function of N up to 10,000 and extends beyond text. This sharpens the budget-scaling issue left implicit by this paper's oracle best-of-28 adaptive score.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Attacker Moves Second: Stronger Adaptive Attacks Bypass Defenses Against Llm Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A defense-aware evaluation study that scales and adapts gradient, reinforcement-learning, random-search, and human-guided attacks to the specific safeguard under test.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It generalizes this paper's safety-capability-parity warning into an evaluation rule: the attacker must move second and receive enough optimization budget. Its adaptive attacks bypass 12 recent defenses, usually above 90% success, despite most originally reporting near-zero rates.

reviewed_competitors.title: GuidedBench: Measuring and Mitigating the Evaluation Discrepancies of In-the-wild LLM Jailbreak Methods
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A current benchmark for resolving evaluation disagreement through case-specific harmful-response guidelines.
reviewed_competitors.difference: GuidedBench audits 37 jailbreak studies and reports that its guideline-based evaluator reduces inter-evaluator variance by at least 76.03%. It advances beyond this paper's unblinded three-way author labels by making response-specific judging criteria the central reproducibility object.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Mechanics: Symmetry and Broken Conservation Laws in Deep Learning Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct prior symmetry-based account of conservation laws and their finite-step breaking.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kunin et al. start from known continuous parameter symmetries, derive gradient/Hessian constraints and conservation laws, and use modified gradient flow to predict finite-learning-rate drift on VGG-16. The reviewed paper instead starts from an architecture reparametrization and Lie-closes its Jacobian fields to count all local independent laws, but does not model realistic finite-step training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noether: The More Things Change, the More Stay the Same
reviewed_competitors.difference: Głuch and Urbanke derive path restrictions and balancedness from model, data-augmentation, and time symmetries. The reviewed method does not require a symmetry to be supplied and adds a maximal local count through Lie algebra and Frobenius theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noether's Learning Dynamics: Role of Symmetry Breaking in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior mechanics-based treatment of broken symmetries under practical learning dynamics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tanaka and Kunin generalize Noether-charge dynamics using a Lagrangian formulation and apply kinetic symmetry breaking to normalization and implicit adaptive optimization. The reviewed paper focuses on exact first-order Euclidean gradient-flow invariants and their complete local count.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on Reparametrized Models: On Equivalence to Mirror Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior direct analysis of when overparameterized gradient flow admits an intrinsic lower-dimensional geometry.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. characterize commuting parametrizations that make gradient flow equivalent to continuous mirror descent, a stronger global structural property than merely having conservation laws. The reviewed paper uses weaker Frobenius conditions to count invariants and obtains only a local initialization-dependent positive-semidefinite metric flow.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symmetries, flat minima, and the conserved quantities of gradient flow
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior connection among parameter symmetries, conserved quantities, initialization, and low-loss valleys.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhao et al. construct continuous symmetries from activation equivariances and use their conserved coordinates to analyze flat minima, convergence, and robustness. The reviewed paper is complementary: it can discover and count local laws directly from model Jacobians even when a generating symmetry is not known, but offers far less empirical evidence about optimization outcomes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Keep the Momentum: Conservation Laws beyond Euclidean Gradient Flows
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct follow-up by the same authors extending the framework beyond the reviewed dynamic.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The follow-up characterizes conservation laws for momentum and non-Euclidean flows, including time-dependent laws, fewer linear-network momentum laws, and no ReLU momentum laws. It directly resolves one of the reviewed paper's stated extensions and shows exact Euclidean-gradient-flow invariants are not optimizer-robust.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformative or Conservative? Conservation laws for ResNets and Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct architecture-level successor by the same authors.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marcotte et al. extend completeness analysis to shallow convolutional blocks, residual blocks, and single attention layers, introduce subset-supported laws, and study persistence under SGD. This covers several modern-architecture and discrete-dynamics gaps explicitly left open in the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Intrinsic training dynamics of deep neural networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct successor developing the reviewed paper's local intrinsic-flow application.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The later work gives kernel-inclusion criteria for intrinsic dynamics, proves path-lifting reductions for arbitrary-depth ReLU networks on a dense initialization set, and characterizes relaxed balanced linear initializations. It turns the reviewed paper's short local proposition into a dedicated architecture-level theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conservation Law Breaking at the Edge of Stability: A Spectral Theory of Non-Convex Neural Network Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct follow-up on the finite-step failure mode.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Medeiros analyzes how balancedness laws drift under discrete gradient descent near the edge of stability and proposes a spectral eta-dependent account validated across linear and ReLU experiments. The reviewed paper only states that finite steps break exact laws and leaves approximate conservation open.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conservation Laws from Data Symmetry in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current complementary extension from architecture-universal laws to data-dependent laws.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Galley et al. ask whether training-data symmetries add integrals of motion, prove generic nonexistence for analytic nonpolynomial losses, and find MSE exceptions for tensorizable networks including Lightning Attention. The reviewed definition intentionally seeks laws common to every dataset and therefore excludes this data-dependent layer of structure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conservation Laws for Modern Neural Architectures
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current direct competitor applying conservation-law analysis to contemporary components.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tran et al. treat GELU, SiLU, SwiGLU, multihead attention with sinusoidal or rotary position encodings, and mixture-of-experts gating, supported by invariant-tracking experiments. This substantially broadens architecture coverage beyond the reviewed paper's linear and ReLU emphasis, while the reviewed paper remains the more general Lie/Frobenius counting template.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Represent n-gram Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Svete and Cotterell construct transformer language models that exactly represent any n-gram model using hard or sparse attention. The present paper instead constructs a one-layer recurrent SSM with softmax epsilon-approximation and an explicit nilpotent finite-memory mechanism; it does not compare resource requirements or optimization between the two constructions.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Expressive Capacity of State Space Models: A Formal Language Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sarrof, Veitsman, and Hahn characterize positive and negative capabilities of practical SSM families over star-free regular languages, counters, and bounded hierarchy, with Mamba experiments and finite-precision considerations. The present paper gives a narrower finite n-gram distribution construction with an explicit |P|-unit bound but does not characterize the wider language class or modern gate constraints.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Illusion of State in State-Space Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Merrill, Petty, and Sabharwal prove circuit-complexity limits for bounded-depth SSMs and show Mamba-style models struggle with state tracking such as permutation composition. Those limits concern length-growing sequential computation; they do not contradict memorizing a fixed finite n-gram context set, but they sharply limit extrapolating the present construction to general state tracking.

reviewed_competitors.title: Repeat After Me: Transformers are Better than State Space Models at Copying
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jelassi and colleagues prove and measure a transformer advantage over fixed-state generalized SSMs on copying and retrieval as sequence length grows. The present paper studies local finite-context rules, where deliberate forgetting is sufficient; it therefore cannot support a broad claim that SSMs dominate attention on sequence expressivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Expressivity of Selective State-Space Layers: A Multivariate Polynomial Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cohen-Karlik and colleagues analyze the input-selective S6 layer through multivariate polynomial degree and compare it with linear attention, including empirical checks on simplified Mamba variants. The present paper analyzes a fixed linear recurrence plus ReLU readout and n-gram interpolation, so its proof does not cover the selectivity mechanism responsible for modern Mamba expressivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploring Length Generalization in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Anil et al. test pretrained and scratch-trained autoregressive language models across algorithmic tasks and show that scratchpad and scale alone often fail to extrapolate. Jelassi et al. move to controlled noncausal encoders, positional variants, and joint target-length mixing, gaining stronger arithmetic results at the cost of a less LLM-like setup.

reviewed_competitors.title: Teaching Algorithmic Reasoning via In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. restructure prompts and intermediate computation so autoregressive models can extrapolate further on addition and related algorithms. Jelassi et al. instead modify encoder positions and training support, with no generated scratchpad; the two approaches alter different parts of the inductive bias and are not directly compute-comparable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Show Your Work: Scratchpads for Intermediate Computation with Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nye et al. externalize intermediate states so a causal model can reuse a local algorithm over longer inputs. Jelassi et al. predicts the complete result in parallel without an execution trace; priming supplies target-length occupancy instead of decomposing the computation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Train Short, Test Long: Attention with Linear Biases Enables Input Length Extrapolation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Press et al. introduce ALiBi to extrapolate language models to longer contexts without learned absolute embeddings. Jelassi et al. studies digit-position OOD behavior with Shaw/Huang RPE inside padded arithmetic layouts and does not compare ALiBi directly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Randomized Positional Encodings Boost Length Generalization of Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ruoss et al. randomize ordered positional subsets to simulate longer positions and evaluate roughly 6,000 models across 15 algorithmic tasks, finding even relative encodings can become OOD. This is much broader and more robustly sampled than Jelassi et al.'s PE grid, while train-set priming targets task data rather than positions.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Impact of Positional Encoding on Length Generalization in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kazemnejad et al. compare APE, T5-relative, ALiBi, RoPE, and NoPE on decoder-only reasoning tasks and often find NoPE strongest, while showing scratchpad format can help or hurt. Jelassi et al. finds RPE essential in its encoder/padded-addition setting, underscoring architecture and formatting dependence rather than one universal PE ranking.

reviewed_competitors.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dziri et al. analyze multi-digit multiplication as a computation graph and find LLM performance resembles linearized subgraph matching with error compounding. Jelassi et al.'s isolated success at explicitly primed lengths is compatible with this warning and does not demonstrate systematic compositional execution across unprimed lengths.

reviewed_competitors.title: Teaching Arithmetic to Small Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. show that representation changes and explicit intermediate results sharply improve small autoregressive transformers' arithmetic sample efficiency, convergence, and accuracy, while examining length challenges. Jelassi et al.'s priming is simpler but requires target-length support and a parallel encoder head.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Algorithms Can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. propose that tasks with short length-uniform RASP-L programs and sufficiently diverse data are likely to extrapolate, and design scratchpads accordingly. This framework predicts why position/format complexity matters and offers a stronger algorithmic criterion than Jelassi et al.'s simultaneous-digit-learning heuristic.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Interpolation to Extrapolation: Complete Length Generalization for Arithmetic Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Duan and Shi calibrate targeted attention biases connected to relative-position mechanisms and report near-perfect extrapolation on addition and parity without inserting target arithmetic examples in the same way. Their two-stage task-specific intervention trades genericity for more direct attention control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Positional Description Matters for Transformers Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shen et al. modify positional descriptions or arithmetic formatting and train a roughly 100M model with 300k samples to perform direct 12-15 digit multiplication, plus 10-to-12 digit addition extrapolation. It attacks the representation failure directly rather than anchoring a chosen long length with priming.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Achieve Length Generalization But Not Robustly
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. combine FIRE, randomized positions, reversed digits, and index hints to reach about 98% on 100-digit addition after training to 40 digits, but find large seed and data-order variance. Their robustness audit highlights the missing per-seed uncertainty behind Jelassi et al.'s three-seed averages and sharp thresholds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Can Do Arithmetic with the Right Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.difference: McLeish et al. introduce Abacus embeddings that reset positions within each number, combine them with input injection and recurrent layers, and report up to 99% 100-digit addition after training on 20 digits, with sorting and multiplication gains. This encodes digit significance more explicitly than generic pairwise RPE and avoids relying on a few target-length arithmetic templates for the addition result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Position Coupling: Improving Length Generalization of Arithmetic Transformers Using Task Structure
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cho et al. assign the same position ID to equal-significance digits, reach 200-digit addition after training through 30 digits, extend to Nx2 multiplication, and prove a one-layer representability result. It makes the alignment Jelassi et al. hopes RPE will infer explicit and supplies theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explicitly Encoding Structural Symmetry is Key to Length Generalization in Arithmetic Tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sabbaghi et al. use modified number formatting and custom positional encodings to extrapolate five-digit addition and multiplication to 50 digits without long target data, and give a necessity result for structural encoding. This directly supersedes the claim that multiplication needs priming under ordinary RPE, while remaining task-specific.

reviewed_competitors.title: Arithmetic Transformers Can Length-Generalize in Both Operand Length and Count
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cho et al. combine task-specific scratchpads with multilevel position coupling to achieve roughly 2-3x extrapolation for multi-operand addition and multiplication while growing both operand length and count/length, with a one-layer theorem. Jelassi et al. grows only one operand and requires every desired target length in the priming support.

reviewed_competitors.title: Looped Transformers for Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fan et al. use an adaptive number of applications of a shared Transformer for tasks with iterative RASP-L solutions and train length-generalizing programs. Jelassi et al. motivates Universal Transformer sharing but keeps a fixed number of layers and target-sized parallel outputs, so computation does not scale naturally with operand length.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Formal Framework for Understanding Length Generalization in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. characterize functions identifiable in the limit under a minimum-norm idealization with learnable APE and validate predictions across algorithms/formal languages. It replaces Jelassi et al.'s descriptive PE explanation with explicit assumptions about hypothesis selection and identifiability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Principled Understanding of Generalization for Generative Transformer Models in Arithmetic Reasoning Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct theoretical explanation of this paper's anomalies
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu et al. develop a unified theory around translation invariance, RPE alignment, task structure, and base mismatch, explicitly addressing inconsistent multiplication and modulo-100 versus modulo-101 behavior. It supplies the mechanism Jelassi et al. leaves as empirical hypotheses and tests causal decoder-style models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Non-Asymptotic Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen, Ma, and Li define a computable training-length threshold needed to identify a target function, derive optimality for a minimum-complexity interpolator, and bound DFA/C-RASP cases. Jelassi et al.'s 'scaling laws' are empirical target-priming thresholds without an identifiability guarantee or held-out prediction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Length Generalization Bounds for Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. prove that computable generalization bounds do not exist for general two-layer CRASP/transformers, while positive CRASP/fixed-precision fragments admit optimal exponential bounds. This sharply limits how broadly any empirical arithmetic priming curve can be promoted to a universal length-scaling principle.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural GPUs Learn Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kaiser and Sutskever build a recurrent convolutional architecture whose computation scales with sequence length and demonstrate algorithm learning including binary multiplication. Jelassi et al. chooses shared-layer encoders for a similar recursive bias but uses fixed-depth parallel prediction and decimal target-layout priming.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Arithmetic Logic Units
reviewed_competitors.difference: Trask et al. hard-code arithmetic-friendly additive/multiplicative pathways to extrapolate numerical functions outside the training range. Jelassi et al. deliberately tests generic Transformers; its weaker but less specialized inductive bias requires position engineering or target support.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning About Generalization via Conditional Mutual Information
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational predecessor for the dissertation's supersample generalization framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: Steinke and Zakynthinou define conditional mutual information between the learned algorithm output and a supersample selection mask, connect it to VC dimension, compression, privacy, and generalization, and establish the paired-sample setting. Chapter 4 replaces the full output with predictions on paired examples, making deterministic black-box bounds finite and much easier to estimate but still dependent on repeated supersample training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Shapley: Equitable Valuation of Data for Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing notion of per-example value adjacent to smooth functional sample information
reviewed_competitors.difference: Data Shapley averages each datum's marginal utility over all training subsets and is uniquely characterized by cooperative-game axioms, naturally accounting for redundancy better than a single leave-one-out effect. The dissertation's F-SI has an information/stability interpretation and an NTK closed form that scales lightly with parameter count, but measures only unique contribution and can require iterative recomputation during deletion.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tighter Information-Theoretic Generalization Bounds from Supersamples
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct follow-on that tightens the same supersample prediction/loss-information line
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang and Mao project each train/test loss pair to one scalar and correlate it with Rademacher or shifted variables, deriving square-root, fast-rate, variance, sharpness, and interpolation bounds reported tighter than prior supersample information bounds. f-CMI uses raw prediction pairs and emphasizes black-box deterministic applicability; the follow-on exploits evaluated losses more aggressively but remains a supersample expected-generalization framework.

reviewed_competitors.title: Slicing Mutual Information Generalization Bounds for Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Alternative current route to computable nonvacuous information bounds for neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Slicing operates in random lower-dimensional parameter subspaces and uses disintegrated or k-sliced mutual information plus rate-distortion/compressibility terms, yielding nonvacuous neural bounds and a regularizer. The dissertation's f-CMI is architecture-agnostic and black-box because it observes predictions, but requires extensive retraining; slicing changes or assumes structure in the learning algorithm and model compression geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exactly Tight Information-theoretic Generalization Bounds via Binary Jensen-Shannon Divergence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current theoretical competitor that directly improves prediction/evaluated-loss information bounds
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dong et al. use a binarized Jensen-Shannon divergence to reduce conditioning, derive prediction-based bounds that surpass evaluated-loss mutual-information bounds, and obtain exactly tight bounds for randomized algorithms with bounded loss. This weakens the case that f-CMI is the final tight prediction-space formulation, while f-CMI's dissertation contribution remains the earlier, empirically demonstrated black-box construction and its explicit limits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Limitations of Information-Theoretic Generalization Bounds for Gradient Descent Methods in Stochastic Convex Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Independent limitation result complementary to Chapter 5
reviewed_competitors.difference: Haghifam et al. show that input-output MI, CMI variants, PAC-Bayes, and noisy-surrogate analyses fail to recover minimax rates for gradient methods in stochastic convex optimization. Chapter 5 instead rules out universal one-sample squared, PAC-Bayes, and single-draw bounds via high-order information even outside gradient descent. The two negative results target different ambitions: rate optimality for a realistic algorithm class versus strength of per-sample information for arbitrary learners.

reviewed_competitors.title: Knowledge Distillation in Wide Neural Networks: Risk Bound, Data Efficiency and Imperfect Teacher
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior NTK-based theory of knowledge distillation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ji and Zhu analyze KD in a wide-network linearization, derive a transfer-risk bound, define data inefficiency, and explain why soft labels help with a perfect teacher while hard labels correct an imperfect one. Chapter 6 instead centers student-relative supervision complexity, decomposes teacher error/margin/complexity, and turns the analysis into a checkpoint curriculum with multi-architecture image experiments; both inherit wide/linearized-network assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring the Intrinsic Dimension of Objective Landscapes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. define an operational parameter-space dimension by finding the smallest random subspace in which a model can be trained. The reviewed paper instead compresses already observed prediction trajectories; its explained stress is not the same intrinsic-dimension estimator and does not construct a trainable low-dimensional parameterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent Happens in a Tiny Subspace
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gur-Ari, Roberts, and Dyer show that gradients align with a small Hessian-eigenvector subspace after early training. That is a parameter-gradient and curvature statement with a class-count prediction; the reviewed paper studies output probabilities across architectures and does not identify its axes with a Hessian subspace.

reviewed_competitors.title: Large Scale Structure of Neural Network Loss Landscapes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fort and Jastrzebski propose high-dimensional connected loss-landscape wedges and demonstrate low-loss subspaces connecting multiple solutions. Their object is weight-space loss geometry and optimizer path selection; the reviewed paper avoids parameter correspondence and embeds finite prediction distributions instead.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prevalence of Neural Collapse during the terminal phase of deep learning training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Papyan, Han, and Donoho identify a highly structured terminal geometry of class means, classifiers, and within-class variability across common networks. Neural collapse is a representation and endpoint phenomenon with specific simplex predictions; the reviewed work spans complete probability trajectories and offers compression rather than the same terminal law.

reviewed_competitors.title: A picture of the space of typical learnable tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The same team already applies information geometry to low-dimensional manifolds of probabilistic models trained across supervised, meta-, semi-supervised, and contrastive tasks. The reviewed paper deepens the within-task, across-architecture trajectory analysis and adds random-corner and synthetic experiments; it does not originate the team's prediction-space manifold toolkit.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Effective Gram Matrix Characterizes Generalization in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang and Chaudhari derive a differential equation for the generalization gap using contraction between training trajectories on perturbed datasets and an effective Gram matrix, then test loss predictions. This supplies a more mechanistic trajectory-to-generalization analysis, whereas the reviewed paper's common-manifold geometry is descriptive and uses fixed datasets.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Analytical Characterization of Sloppiness in Neural Networks: Insights from Linear Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Griniasty and collaborators analytically decompose linear-model trajectory covariance and identify data-spectrum, initialization-scale, horizon, and stochastic-noise regimes controlling low-dimensional hyper-ribbons. It directly targets the reviewed empirical phenomenon, but only in linear squared-loss and fixed-kernel surrogates rather than the nonlinear prediction geometry measured here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Trajectory-Restricted Optimization Conditions and Geometry-Aware Linear Convergence

reviewed_competitors.difference: Hess et al. address chaotic long-horizon training by proving bounded gradients for generalized teacher forcing and evaluate invariant geometrical and temporal reconstruction with interpretable recurrent models. reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen and Wu combine short trajectory data with explicitly measured long-term statistics through hybrid gradient-based and derivative-free calibration in a space-time-continuous neural operator, including KS and Navier-Stokes. reviewed_competitors.difference: DySLIM regularizes a learned map by comparing distributions after pushing data and model samples through the dynamics, producing a tractable invariant-measure residual that composes with existing objectives. It more directly tests invariance under the learned transition than the reviewed paper's h=1 matching of expert summaries or trajectory-instance features, and reports both pointwise and long-run gains.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Park, Yang, and Chandramoorthy define statistical generalization through physical invariant measures and analyze why small regression error can coexist with wrong moments or Lyapunov exponents; they show how Jacobian information improves statistical accuracy across several neural model classes. reviewed_competitors.title: Is your batch size the problem? Revisiting the Adam-SGD gap in language modeling
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct present-day re-evaluation of directional sharpness and clipping.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It finds tuned momentum SGD can approach or beat Adam at small batches, imports the target's alignment and sharpness diagnostics, and concludes they track success but do not explain the batch cause; adaptive clipping only partially repairs large-batch SGD.

reviewed_competitors.title: Small Batch Size Training for Language Models: When Vanilla SGD Works, and Why Gradient Accumulation Is Wasteful
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies when ordinary SGD succeeds in language modeling and separates microbatch updates from gradient accumulation. The target's batches of roughly 1,000 and 1,024 leave this key regime untested.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benchmarking Optimizers for Large Language Model Pretraining
reviewed_competitors.difference: It carefully tunes recent optimizers across model size, batch, and training duration and finds many claimed speedups shrink with scale. The target uses two small models, unmatched schedules, and no validation or compute metric.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them
reviewed_competitors.difference: It evaluates modern scalar and matrix optimizers under contemporary pretraining protocols. This supplies the multi-family, carefully normalized comparison absent from the target's local proxy study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Muon Outperforms Adam in Tail-End Associative Memory Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current heavy-tail and optimizer-geometry mechanism study.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It localizes Muon's advantage to matrix associative-memory parameters and an isotropic singular spectrum under heavy-tailed data. The target's coordinate Rayleigh quotient does not analyze parameter role or matrix singular geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adam Reduces a Unique Form of Sharpness: Theoretical Insights Near the Minimizer Manifold
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives an implicit Adam sharpness functional near a minimizer manifold and distinguishes it from SGD's trace bias. That optimizer-specific stochastic theory differs from the target's instantaneous signed update-direction curvature.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting the Adam-SGD Gap in LLM Pre-Training: The Role of Large Effective Learning Rates
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Latest effective-step and clipping account before the cutoff.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It attributes much of the gap to SGD's inability to sustain Adam-like effective learning rates because of output imbalance and spikes; simple clipping closes most of the gap on a 1B LLaMA run. It tests the practical large-step hypothesis far beyond the target's local scans.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond a Single Explanation of the Adam--SGD Gap
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Latest controlled synthesis of competing causal hypotheses.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Across language, vision, genomics, and graphs it finds no single data, architecture, or optimization factor consistently explains the gap and models a batch-size crossover. This directly contradicts the target's singular causal conclusion.

reviewed_competitors.title: Directional Curvature from Armijo Backtracking: A Low-Cost Sharpness Probe and a Calibration-Free Learning-Rate Safeguard for Adam
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Latest direct directional-curvature method before the cutoff.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It estimates directional curvature through Armijo backtracking and turns it into an Adam learning-rate safeguard with explicit overhead and architecture sweeps. The target computes exact HVPs post hoc and does not validate an online curvature-controlled step rule.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Principles Behind Neural Network Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Latest comprehensive Adam/Hessian treatment before the cutoff.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The thesis combines Adam convergence, near-block-diagonal heterogeneous Hessian evolution, matrix-product origins, Adam-mini, and Muon. It places directional curvature as one hypothesis within a broader structural account rather than a universal explanation.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Marginal Value of Adaptive Gradient Methods in Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It separates optimization speed from the often different solutions and generalization behavior of adaptive methods. The target reports training loss only, so faster optimization cannot establish broader practical value.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Convergence of Adam and Beyond
reviewed_competitors.difference: It exposes Adam convergence failures and develops AMSGrad with global guarantees. The target instead offers a local directional diagnostic and an invalid clipping theorem without addressing known adaptive-method failure conditions.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Empirical Comparisons of Optimizers for Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows optimizer rankings can reverse under fair and sufficiently broad hyperparameter searches. The target gives neither search grids nor equal-budget tuning, and changes learning rates and schedule classes between clipped pairs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Disentangling Adaptive Gradient Methods from Learning Rates
reviewed_competitors.difference: Update grafting explicitly combines one optimizer's direction with another's step magnitude to isolate causal components. The target normalizes counterfactual directions locally but does not graft them into actual paired training trajectories.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Large Batch Optimizer Reality Check: Traditional, Generic Optimizers Suffice Across Batch Sizes
reviewed_competitors.difference: It finds strong generic optimizers remain competitive after disciplined tuning across batch sizes. The target fixes large batches, provides no tuning budget, and therefore cannot separate optimizer mechanism from baseline quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Provable Adaptivity of Adam under Non-uniform Smoothness
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves Adam adaptivity under explicit non-uniform smoothness conditions. The target's related coordinate-submatrix argument does not connect clipped gradient coordinates to the low-curvature subset and fails its own constant comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Directional Smoothness and Gradient Methods: Convergence and Adaptivity
reviewed_competitors.difference: It turns path-dependent directional smoothness into actual convergence and adaptivity bounds. The target measures a one-point signed Rayleigh quotient and extrapolates global speed without a valid pathwise theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Convergence of Adam under Non-uniform Smoothness: Separability from SGDM and Beyond
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives rate separations under stated non-uniform-smoothness assumptions. This provides the kind of explicit global condition and valid comparison missing from the target's clipped-gradient theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Optimization and Generalization of Two-layer Transformers with Sign Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes staged SignGD dynamics and generalization in a simplified Transformer model. The target measures signSGD directions empirically but provides no architecture-linked optimization or generalization account.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exact Risk Curves of signSGD in High-Dimensions: Quantifying Preconditioning and Noise-Compression Effects
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its high-dimensional risk dynamics separate effective learning rate, preconditioning, compression, and noise reshaping. The target collapses these effects into local alignment and curvature and does not test their independent contributions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hyperparameter Transfer Enables Consistent Gains of Matrix-Preconditioned Optimizers Across Scales
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies width/depth transfer and matrix-preconditioned optimizers from 190M to 1.4B parameters. The target supplies no scale sweep and no transferable tuning procedure, so its small-model ranking cannot establish scaling behavior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws of SignSGD in Linear Regression: When Does It Outperform SGD?
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives exact regimes where normalized drift and noise reshaping make signSGD preferable and adds Transformer scaling experiments. The target gives neither a scaling law nor a compute-aware regime map for its clipping hypothesis.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Papyan, Han, and Donoho formalize within-class collapse, simplex class means, classifier alignment, and nearest-center decisions near the penultimate layer. The tunnel paper extends the depthwise and transfer view but does not originate class-conditional compression.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Origins of the Block Structure Phenomenon in Neural Network Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nguyen, Raghu, and Kornblith already find contiguous similar-layer blocks that emerge early and tie them to seed-specific dominant datapoints. The tunnel paper adds rank, transfer, and continual-task consequences and interprets the late block as source-task compression.

reviewed_competitors.title: Head2Toe: Utilizing Intermediate Representations for Better Transfer Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Evci et al. select and combine features across all pretrained layers and outperform fine-tuning on OOD VTAB transfer. That is a stronger actionable baseline than selecting one tunnel-entry layer, but it does not diagnose compression or continual forgetting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Limitations of Neural Collapse for Understanding Generalization in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hui, Belkin, and Nakkiran show training collapse need not extend to test data and that terminal training can harm transfer features. The tunnel paper localizes a related transfer decline across depth but still cannot infer generalization from source compression alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature learning in deep classifiers through Intermediate Neural Collapse
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rangamani et al. analyze covariance and weight/class-mean subspaces across hidden layers, finding progressive intermediate collapse and configuration-dependent failures. The tunnel work adds an explicit probe boundary, OOD transfer curves, and sequential-task swaps.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Variables Affect Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Pretrained Models?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Harun et al. broaden architectures, resolution, data, and augmentations and conclude that late compression harming transfer is not universal; high-resolution many-class pretraining weakens it. This is the decisive external-validity correction to the reviewed CIFAR/CINIC regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Controlling Neural Collapse Enhances Out-of-Distribution Detection and Transfer Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Harun et al. separate a tradeoff in which stronger collapse aids OOD detection but hurts transfer, then use entropy regularization and fixed simplex projectors at different layers. It turns the tunnel's observational compression link into controllable layerwise objectives.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unpacking Softmax: How Temperature Drives Representation Collapse, Compression, and Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Masarczyk et al. identify a softmax-logit-norm rank-deficit bias and manipulate temperature to trade compression against OOD performance across broader models and datasets. It proposes a concrete control variable missing from the tunnel paper's descriptive capacity account.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Forward-Forward Algorithm: Some Preliminary Investigations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The originating method paper defining positive/negative passes, local goodness, layer normalization, and label-conditioned image classification.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hinton establishes feasibility and motivates temporal separation and biological plausibility on small tasks. The target contributes a multi-dataset representation audit and the key BP/FF objective control, but inherits the label-conditioning and shallow-task limitations.

reviewed_competitors.title: A theory for the sparsity emerged in the Forward Forward algorithm
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct theoretical follow-up explaining the target's principal empirical phenomenon.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang derives single-layer predictions for how goodness reduction and the complete positive/negative update change one sample's sparsity and checks them on MNIST. The target is broader empirically across layers and datasets but does not supply a causal derivation of its ensemble or bias/weight results.

reviewed_competitors.title: Layer Collaboration in the Forward-Forward Algorithm
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A contemporaneous analysis of information-flow limitations created by training FF layers independently.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lorberbom et al. argue vanilla FF is suboptimal because layers cannot collaborate and propose a no-extra-compute collaboration mechanism with theoretical and objective evaluations. The target characterizes the resulting layerwise representations, including declining/deviant deep-layer sparsity, but does not test a collaborative FF variant.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Convolutional Neural Networks with the Forward-Forward algorithm
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct extension beyond the target's fully connected models that also audits learned visual features and label shortcuts.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scodellaro et al. introduce spatially extended labels for CNNs, scale to CIFAR-10/100, and use class-activation maps; the current revision explicitly reports morphology labels preventing shortcut solutions. The target provides richer sparsity statistics but its corner-label ensemble analysis lacks that shortcut control.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeeperForward: Enhanced Forward-Forward Training for Deeper and Better Performance
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A peer-reviewed post-target method addressing the failure of vanilla FF to improve with depth.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sun et al. redesign goodness and feature transport to train deeper models and test performance at ICLR scale. The target's three-layer analysis reveals representation changes but cannot establish whether its sparse ensembles persist in deeper, higher-performing FF systems.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scalable Forward-Forward Algorithm
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A current scaling competitor for FF on modern convolutional and residual architectures.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Krutsylo trains MobileNetV3 and ResNet18 layerwise or by locally backpropagated blocks, reporting accuracy and speed comparable to backpropagation plus transfer-learning results. The target offers finer representation descriptions but no modern architecture, transfer task, speed, memory, or scale evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Forward-Forward Algorithm: Characterizing Training Behavior
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later mechanistic study of layerwise FF learning dynamics rather than only final representations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adamson tracks accuracy throughout training, perturbs system characteristics, and finds delayed learning in deeper layers plus strong shallow-layer correlation with total accuracy. The target measures richer final sparsity and overlap, while leaving the training-time formation and replacement of its selected sets to future work.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the correspondence between thermodynamics and inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: LaMont and Wiggins establish the sample-size-as-inverse-temperature correspondence and learning-capacity concept used by the target. The reviewed paper's contribution is a new cross-validation estimator and broad deep-learning application, not the original definition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Deep Models: Effective Dimensionality Revisited
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maddox, Benton, and Wilson use Hessian effective dimensionality for posterior contraction, model selection, generalization, and double descent, with released code. It predates and undermines the target's priority language about effective dimensionality resolving double descent; the target differs by differentiating over sample size and including nonparametric models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does the Data Induce Capacity Control in Deep Learning?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang, Mao, and Chaudhari study data-dependent capacity using sloppy Hessian or Fisher spectra and PAC-Bayes effective dimension. The target replaces direct curvature with a sample-size learning-curve derivative while retaining the same broad capacity-control program.

reviewed_competitors.title: Effective dimension of machine learning models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abbas et al. define a local and global effective dimension from Fisher information and derive a generalization bound before the target. Their object measures local model geometry, while learning capacity differentiates predictive performance over sample size; this further limits any claim to introducing effective dimensionality or its generalization connection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nakkiran et al. formalize effective model complexity and empirical double descent across model size, data, and training time. The target proposes learning capacity as one alternate horizontal axis but evaluates a much narrower subset of the phenomenon.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fantastic Generalization Measures and Where to Find Them
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jiang et al. benchmark many generalization measures across controlled interventions and expose frequent failures of correlation. The target evaluates far fewer architecture families and does not subject learning capacity to an equivalent intervention matrix.

reviewed_competitors.title: Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep (Stochastic) Neural Networks with Many More Parameters than Training Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dziugaite and Roy optimize stochastic neural-network posteriors to obtain nonvacuous PAC-Bayes bounds. The target uses a looser analytic analogy and an approximate Hessian comparison rather than computing a full bound for its model suite.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Training Process of Many Deep Networks Explores the Same Low-Dimensional Manifold
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mao et al. measure a low-dimensional prediction manifold across deep networks using information geometry. Submitted earlier in May 2023, it offers a more direct geometric capacity notion; the target instead infers a scalar dimension from sample-size response.

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimating Real Log Canonical Thresholds
reviewed_competitors.difference: Imai develops numerical estimation of real log canonical thresholds, the asymptotic singular-model quantity invoked in Appendix C. reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning is Singular, and That's Good

reviewed_competitors.title: EikoNet: Solving the Eikonal equation with Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: EikoNet already learns a continuous grid-free Eikonal travel-time field from differential residuals and evaluates multiple heterogeneous velocity models and sampling schemes. Short and Straight generalizes the residual to a Riemannian metric on differentiable manifolds and adds curvature-biased sampling and geodesic flow, while its empirical validation is much smaller.

reviewed_competitors.title: Manifold-augmented Eikonal Equations: Geodesic Distances and Flows on Differentiable Manifolds
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kelshaw and Magri subsequently publish a paper centered on the manifold-augmented Eikonal distance field and globally minimizing flows. It separates that contribution from the earlier preprint's symplectic-shooting critique, making the 2023 target best read as a broader preliminary combination rather than the final standalone account of the Eikonal method.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Riemannian Take on Distance Fields and Geodesic Flows in Robotics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Qiu, and Calinon develop neural Riemannian Eikonal solvers conditioned on boundary data or spatially varying metrics and validate them across robot tasks, including a seven-axis Franka energy metric. This extends the same PDE idea toward arbitrary queries and higher-dimensional application evidence that Short and Straight leaves open.
