reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct successor and efficiency competitor from an overlapping author team
reviewed_competitors.difference: Edge Attribution Patching linearly approximates the activation-patching effect of every edge with two forward passes and one backward pass, then ranks edges globally. It reports higher average circuit-recovery AUC than ACDC and is far cheaper than one patched forward evaluation per edge, but its first-order approximation can degrade for large perturbations and does not remove dependence on the task metric or corruption baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: InterpBench: Semi-Synthetic Transformers for Evaluating Mechanistic Interpretability Techniques
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Benchmark that directly addresses ACDC's unreliable manual-circuit ground truth
reviewed_competitors.difference: InterpBench uses Strict Interchange Intervention Training to produce more realistic transformers whose intended circuits are known and whose non-circuit nodes are prevented from influencing output, then evaluates circuit-discovery methods. ACDC instead reconstructs tiny Tracr graphs or treats human analyses as truth; InterpBench improves validation realism but is a benchmark/training construction rather than a discovery algorithm.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v3 / NeurIPS 2024 Datasets and Benchmarks, 2025-10-11

reviewed_competitors.title: EAP-GP: Mitigating Saturation Effect in Gradient-based Automated Circuit Identification
reviewed_competitors.difference: EAP-GP replaces a fixed integrated-gradient path with an adaptive GradPath intended to avoid zero-gradient and saturation regions. It evaluates six tasks through GPT-2 XL and reports faithfulness improvements up to 17.7%, extending scale beyond ACDC; it remains attribution- and patching-dependent and does not itself establish semantic completeness or corruption-invariant circuits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering Transformer Circuits via a Hybrid Attribution and Pruning Framework
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Hybrid approach that explicitly trades attribution speed against pruning faithfulness
reviewed_competitors.difference: HAP first uses fast Edge Attribution Patching to restrict the candidate graph, then performs edge pruning on that subgraph. It reports a 46% speedup without losing tested faithfulness and preserves IOI S-inhibition components that pure attribution can drop. ACDC performs expensive greedy pruning over the full graph; HAP is more scalable but inherits shortlist-recall risk and its evidence is narrower than ACDC's six-task study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Formal Mechanistic Interpretability: Automated Circuit Discovery with Provable Guarantees
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Verification-based alternative to heuristic circuit recovery
reviewed_competitors.difference: The formal approach uses neural-network verification to certify input-domain agreement, robustness under continuous patching perturbations, and notions of circuit minimality. This directly targets ACDC's finite-sample, threshold-sensitive evidence, but experiments focus on vision models where verification is tractable rather than GPT-scale language-model circuits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Descriptor Fields: SE(3)-Equivariant Object Representations for Manipulation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural Descriptor Fields learn continuous SE(3)-equivariant descriptors and optimize poses for object manipulation, giving a stronger guarantee inside known rigid-body symmetry. Bilinear transduction is potentially broader, including scale and non-equivariant repeated relations, but depends on empirical difference coverage and low-rank structure rather than an exact architectural symmetry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Additive Decoders for Latent Variables Identification and Cartesian-Product Extrapolation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Additive decoders turn out-of-support image generation into novel Cartesian-product combinations of observed latent factors and prove block identifiability under exact reconstruction. This is a close structural alternative: additive object-factor decomposition replaces anchor-relative differences, exact bilinear transducibility, and supervised or imitation prediction.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Use of Anchoring for Training Vision Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: This NeurIPS 2024 work scales reference-residual anchoring to large vision models and identifies shortcut learning as a failure of ordinary anchored training, then adds reference masking. It validates the relative-coordinate principle more broadly while showing that anchor construction alone can introduce new shortcuts; it does not use the original low-rank completion theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Understanding Extrapolation: a Causal Lens
reviewed_competitors.difference: The causal approach identifies invariant semantic variables and sparse changing mechanisms from as little as one off-support target sample under a minimal-change model. It replaces difference-support coverage and bilinear low rank with latent causal identifiability; neither assumption family subsumes the other.

reviewed_competitors.title: Known Unknowns: Out-of-Distribution Property Prediction in Materials and Molecules
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work adapts bilinear transduction to materials compositions and molecular graphs and evaluates precision and recall for extreme property screening against domain models. It is evidence that the mechanism transfers beyond the original toys and robotics, but remains dependent on analogical representations and favorable property differences rather than resolving the original assumption audit.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work links length generalization to short RASP-L programs and alters scratchpads to make the intended algorithm simpler. It uses algorithmic and architectural alignment instead of low-rank anchor completion and offers a stronger validation pattern across increasing lengths, although its broad RASP generalization statement is empirically supported rather than a universal theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Graph neural networks extrapolate out-of-distribution for shortest paths
reviewed_competitors.difference: The 2026 COLT paper proves that a sparsity-regularized GNN optimizer implements K Bellman-Ford steps, with an approximate-minimization error guarantee, and then tests OOD graph sizes. Its result is narrow and task-specific, but identifies the learned computation and its scaling behavior more directly than a generic population-risk transfer bound plus nearby held-out bands.

reviewed_competitors.title: Complexity of Linear Regions in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hanin and Rolnick already develop a general expected-boundary framework for random piecewise-linear deep networks, proving that average region count along one-dimensional subspaces grows linearly with total neurons and studying distance to the nearest boundary. Holmes gives elementary exact laws for one shallow scalar architecture and reveals a √width exception under a globally coupled weight prior, but is far narrower and does not discuss this direct predecessor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep ReLU Networks Have Surprisingly Few Activation Patterns
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work bounds average activation patterns at initialization by total-neuron count raised to input dimension and tests tightness during training, including memorization. The reviewed paper instead derives exact breakpoint probabilities for a one-dimensional shallow model and compares parameter measures, without training evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Effective Number of Linear Regions in Shallow Univariate ReLU Networks: Convergence Guarantees and Implicit Bias
reviewed_competitors.difference: Safran, Vardi, and Lee analyze the same broad shallow-univariate geometry under gradient flow with labeled data, proving convergence to classifiers with O(r) effective regions under assumptions. Holmes isolates exact unconditioned prior laws for random parameters, making distribution geometry transparent but leaving the training-conditioned claim conjectural.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Number of Regions of Piecewise Linear Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goujon, Etemadi, and Unser cover arbitrary possibly multivariate piecewise-linear activations and bound expected region density along one-dimensional paths by depth, width, and activation complexity. Holmes is more exact for three special first-layer priors but does not handle depth or multivariate activations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks Fail to Learn Periodic Functions and How to Fix It
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ziyin, Hartwig, and Ueda prove and empirically demonstrate poor periodic extrapolation for standard activations and propose x+sin²(x) as a periodic inductive bias. Holmes uses periodic sawtooth functions only as a motivating mismatch between description length and random-breakpoint geometry; it neither trains on periodic data nor tests the proposed geometric explanation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning Generalizes Because the Parameter-Function Map Is Biased Towards Simple Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Valle-Pérez, Camargo, and Louis argue empirically and theoretically for an Occam-like parameter-to-function bias using information-theoretic complexity. Holmes challenges the sufficiency of that notion with an analytically tractable geometric statistic, but does not measure both complexity notions on a common distribution of fitted functions.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct prior theory for instance-dependent success of random exploration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu and Brunskill derive sufficient random-exploration conditions through covering and reachability properties and PAC analysis. The reviewed work demonstrates that a covering-length instantiation is often far too pessimistic on benchmark-derived deterministic MDPs, and replaces visit-everything coverage with short lookahead plus random return evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Guarantees for Epsilon-Greedy Reinforcement Learning with Function Approximation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior guarantee for naive exploration with function approximation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dann et al. formalize the myopic exploration gap and give guarantees for epsilon-greedy learning with function approximation. The reviewed paper argues that the gap becomes exponentially pessimistic in the presence of distracting reward paths and is difficult to compute, while effective horizon is empirically calculable from full tabular instances; unlike Dann et al., however, its original theorem excludes function generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sample Efficient Reinforcement Learning in Continuous State Spaces: A Perspective Beyond Linearity
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior shallow-planning and function-approximation complexity result.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Malik et al. obtain sample-efficient continuous-state RL under structural conditions that limit the effective planning window and support nonlinear value approximation. The reviewed paper's rollout leaf evaluation can exploit delayed rewards beyond a short window and empirically produces much tighter bounds, but only after complete deterministic tabulation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hardness in Markov Decision Processes: Theory and Practice
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior benchmark connecting computable MDP hardness measures with empirical agents.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Conserva and Rauber survey hardness theory, introduce Colosseum with controlled diversity over multiple measures, and evaluate tabular and non-tabular agents. BRIDGE scales exact tabulation to benchmark-derived Atari, Procgen, and MiniGrid tasks and proposes one highly predictive metric, but lacks Colosseum's controlled orthogonal variation and independent stress axes.

reviewed_competitors.title: MDP Playground: Controlling Orthogonal Dimensions of Hardness in Toy Environments
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing benchmark methodology for causal difficulty analysis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: MDP Playground varies delayed reward, rewardable sequence length, sparsity, stochasticity, irrelevant features, time scale, and action branching independently in fast synthetic environments. BRIDGE sacrifices such factorial control for recognizable benchmark-derived MDPs and exact instance-level bounds. Combining both designs would test whether effective horizon changes causally rather than merely correlating across games.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimistic PAC Reinforcement Learning: the Instance-Dependent View
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary instance-dependent exact or near-best-policy identification theory.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tirinzoni, Al-Marjani, and Kaufmann analyze an optimistic PAC algorithm with refined gaps and show near instance-optimality for deterministic transitions up to a horizon factor. Their complexity is tied to strategic exploration and near-optimal identification, whereas the reviewed work targets the empirical behavior of random-exploration deep agents and validates predictions at scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond No Regret: Instance-Dependent PAC Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior instance-dependent PAC policy-identification framework with active coverage.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wagenmaker, Simchowitz, and Jamieson derive instance-dependent lower bounds and Learn2Explore-style active data collection for epsilon-optimal policies. This handles approximate performance and strategic coverage more rigorously; the reviewed work instead asks why simple random exploration works in common deep-RL benchmarks and obtains a far more empirically predictive but hindsight-dependent statistic.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Effective Horizon Explains Deep RL Performance in Stochastic Environments
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct post-publication extension by the same research line.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Laidlaw et al. introduce SQIRL, extend k-step random-Q reasoning to stochastic MDPs, and incorporate a regression class with in-distribution generalization, then test correlations with PPO and DQN on stochastic environments. It directly addresses the reviewed paper's two largest exclusions—transition noise and function generalization—while retaining the central effective-horizon hypothesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Effective Horizon Challenge
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current follow-up benchmark deliberately selecting long-effective-horizon environments.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Laidlaw et al. construct 43 small deterministic planning and game MDPs after filtering out tasks solvable by GORP or random guessing within ten million steps; PPO solves only 8 and DQN 12. This is a prospective challenge derived from the reviewed hypothesis and strengthens its falsifiable consequence, though selection on GORP difficulty makes it unsuitable as an unbiased validation of the metric itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting the Arcade Learning Environment: Evaluation Protocols and Open Problems for General Agents
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary evaluation-protocol standard exposing deterministic Atari shortcuts.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Machado et al. show that deterministic ALE protocols can reward brute open-loop solutions and recommend sticky actions, standardized reporting, and clearer protocol identity. BRIDGE intentionally removes stochasticity to enable exact tables, so its surprising GORP performance must be interpreted alongside this known determinism shortcut rather than as evidence about standard robust Atari learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hyperparameters in Reinforcement Learning and How To Tune Them
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary methodology for fair and reproducible RL tuning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Eimer, Lindauer, and Raileanu show that RL hyperparameter landscapes depend strongly on tuning seeds and recommend separating tuning from test seeds with principled optimization. The reviewed study minimizes over two sensitive settings on the same five seeds and environment collection used for analysis, so its empirical sample complexities would benefit from this stricter protocol.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Jackstraw inserts a small number of permuted synthetic-null variables, recomputes PCs, and obtains an empirical null that accounts for PCA overfitting before FDR control. reviewed_competitors.title: Forecastable Component Analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct prior definition of unsupervised signal through temporal structure rather than variance or labels.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ForeCA formalizes signal as forecastability and optimizes a convergent projection that separates predictable components from orthogonal white noise on ordered time series. The reviewed paper uses an indirect correlation-length interpretation of random sample thinning and extrapolates to zero samples, even for unordered patients.

reviewed_competitors.title: Automatic PCA Dimension Selection for High Dimensional Data and Small Sample Sizes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Directly contradicts the suggestion that PCA dimensionality in the high-dimensional small-sample regime must be chosen by a subjective variance threshold.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives an improved Bayesian evidence criterion whose high-dimensional fixed-ratio limit agrees with frequentist testing. It selects the number of signal components rather than individual variables, but demonstrates that automatic objective component selection existed long before the reviewed framing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiable Unsupervised Feature Selection based on a Gated Laplacian
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A modern target-free selector that defines informative features by preservation of latent manifold or cluster structure under heavy nuisance dimensions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It learns continuous feature gates and recomputes the graph Laplacian on selected inputs, with mathematical motivation and multiple real-data baselines. The reviewed method uses loading-tail outliers and one synthetic plus one genomic dataset, with no baseline or downstream clustering evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Unsupervised Feature Selection by Discarding Nuisance and Correlated Features
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A competing unsupervised selector designed for simultaneous nuisance rejection and redundancy control.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It combines gated Laplacian structure preservation with autoencoder reconstruction and evaluates against related methods on ten real datasets. The reviewed persistence rule neither controls redundancy nor tests whether its selected features preserve a useful structure out of sample.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-modal Differentiable Unsupervised Feature Selection
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A contemporary biology-oriented framework for finding shared and modality-specific latent structures without labels.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It exploits paired modalities as internal cross-validation, learns nuisance-masking gates, and tests single-cell multi-omics. The reviewed work has only one expression modality and uses cancer labels to choose the purportedly intrinsic component.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stability Selection
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The foundational error-controlled framework for turning subsample selection frequencies into high-dimensional variable selections.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stability selection ties frequency thresholds and regularization paths to finite-sample false-positive bounds under explicit assumptions. The reviewed method uses dramatically different 1% and 99.5% frequency thresholds chosen for a positive extrapolation and provides no corresponding error control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adapted Tensor Decomposition and PCA Based Unsupervised Feature Extraction Select More Biologically Reasonable Differentially Expressed Genes than Conventional Methods
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The direct methodological predecessor by Taguchi and Turki for the optimized-scale PCA/TD loading-outlier test reused here.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It already standardizes samples, chooses biologically aligned components, fits the loading Gaussian scale, applies chi-square tails and BH correction, and benchmarks differential genes. The reviewed paper's algorithmic novelty is therefore mainly repeated thinning plus the intrinsic zero-sample interpretation, not the core feature test.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unsupervised Feature Selection via Nonnegative Orthogonal Constrained Regularized Minimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A current optimization-based alternative with explicit robustness and convergence analysis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: NOCRM embeds selection into nonnegative spectral clustering, regularizes against overfitting, proves convergence to a stationary point, and compares broadly on benchmark datasets. It uses a declared clustering notion of utility rather than claiming a goal-independent signal definition, but offers much stronger algorithmic validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fortuitous Forgetting in Connectionist Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. unify iterative training as forget-and-relearn and introduce later-layer forgetting to preferentially remove undesirable information. SEAL adopts that framing but replaces later-layer reinitialization with low-rate early-layer ascent and contributes transfer evidence showing LLF can damage downstream features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Knowledge Evolution in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Knowledge Evolution repeatedly reinitializes a reset hypothesis while preserving a fit hypothesis and targets small-data accuracy plus a slim inference model. SEAL retains every parameter and perturbs the early hypothesis through ascent, so its novelty is the update direction and layer placement rather than the generation-based training template.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Impact of Reinitialization on Generalization in Convolutional Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alabdulmohsin et al. compare reinitialization across 12 image datasets and propose bottom-up layerwise rescale-and-reset training, with matched-compute curves, margins, and perturbation flatness. SEAL avoids hard resets and shows broader transfer from one source dataset, but its causal and compute controls are weaker.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Does Re-initialization Work?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: large-scale competing audit of iterative reinitialization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zaidi et al. train more than 15,000 image models and find reinitialization helps without other regularization but adds little after data augmentation, cosine schedules, and weight decay are carefully tuned, except under label noise and for hyperparameter robustness. SEAL reports sizable gains despite several regularizers, but does not tune the conventional baseline comparably enough to resolve this tension.

reviewed_competitors.title: RIFLE: Backpropagation in Depth for Deep Transfer Learning through Re-Initializing the Fully-connected LayEr
reviewed_competitors.difference: RIFLE periodically resets the classifier during fine-tuning so strong new gradients reach deeper pretrained layers, and explicitly contrasts the reset with cyclic learning rate. SEAL perturbs early layers during source pretraining and evaluates frozen-feature transfer, but lacks an equally targeted separation from its own optimizer and schedule restarts.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learn, Unlearn and Relearn: An Online Learning Paradigm for Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: LURE uses data-dependent parameter-importance masks and reinitialization as new data chunks arrive, evaluating replay, robustness, calibration, architectures, and few-shot learning. SEAL is simpler and stationary-data focused, but its fixed layer split cannot adapt forgetting to incoming data or connection importance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reset It and Forget It: Relearning Last-Layer Weights Improves Continual and Transfer Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Frati et al.'s zapping repeatedly resamples the classifier during pretraining and shows faster few-shot adaptation and continual-transfer gains with a very simple reset. Its mechanism is closer to LLF/RIFLE than SEAL, but it challenges the claim that damaging early layers is necessary for transferable representations.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Effectiveness of Random Forgetting for Robust Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later forget-and-relearn method for adversarial robustness
reviewed_competitors.difference: FOMO periodically reinitializes random subsets of later-layer parameters during adversarial training and consolidates relearned states in an exponential-moving-average model to reduce robust overfitting. SEAL operates on early layers without a stable model and targets ordinary and transfer generalization rather than adversarial robustness.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Weight Resampling and Optimizers Shape the Dynamics of Continual Learning and Forgetting in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later mechanism study of classifier resets and optimizer effects
reviewed_competitors.difference: Frati et al. show zapped models recover classifier alignment faster and that SGD versus Adam creates very different task-level learning and forgetting trajectories, while leaving the wider-basin story hypothetical. This later evidence makes SEAL's unablated optimizer resets especially important: optimizer dynamics can imitate or reshape a purported forgetting mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Deep Networks without Learning Rates Through Coin Betting
reviewed_competitors.difference: COCOB reduces optimization to coin betting, proves convex and quasi-convex rates, and evaluates a stochastic learning-rate-free optimizer. AGD instead derives architecture-specific relative updates for nonconvex deep compositions, but its guarantees require exact assumptions and do not cover its stochastic experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning-Rate-Free Learning by D-Adaptation
reviewed_competitors.difference: D-Adaptation estimates the distance-to-solution scale, has convex Lipschitz guarantees without extra gradient evaluations, wraps SGD and Adam, and reports more than a dozen vision/language tasks. AGD uses network width/depth semantics and no optimizer state, but supports fewer architectures and rests on stronger unmeasured neural assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prodigy: An Expeditiously Adaptive Parameter-Free Learner
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prodigy improves D-Adaptation's distance estimate and evaluates logistic regression, CNNs, ViTs, LSTMs, DLRMs, medical reconstruction, RoBERTa, and GPT. It is broadly architecture-agnostic and Adam-compatible; AGD offers an explicit compositional-architecture derivation but much narrower empirical coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mechanic: A Learning Rate Tuner
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mechanic automatically tunes the scale of any base optimizer and schedule and evaluates large-scale tasks, batch sizes, and optimizer families. It preserves mature optimizer machinery; AGD replaces that machinery with normed architecture-dependent updates and claims lower state memory, at the cost of restricted module support.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tuning-Free Stochastic Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Khaled et al. formalize tuning-free matching of optimally tuned SGD, prove impossibility on important unbounded convex settings, and give conditional stochastic and nonconvex results. This work places AGD's broad elimination rhetoric in a sharper problem-class and hint-dependent framework that the AGD paper does not address.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Majorization-Minimization Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Universal MM uses Taylor-mode automatic differentiation to derive majorizers for arbitrary problems automatically and claims convergence from any start without tuning. AGD hand-derives a simpler neural architecture bound and a cheap first-order rule, but only after conditional cancellations and restricted module assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scalable Optimization in the Modular Norm
reviewed_competitors.difference: Modular norm recursively assigns natural norms to general neural modules and normalizes any base optimizer for width/depth transfer, with a Modula package. It generalizes AGD's layer-matrix geometry beyond plain FCNs while shifting from complete rate elimination to transferable architecture-aware scaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Modular Duality in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Modular dualization maps gradients from dual to primal spaces using semantic layer norms and derives GPU-friendly Embed, Linear, and Conv2D updates linked to record-setting NanoGPT training. It develops AGD's architecture-geometry motivation into broader and faster practical optimizers, but does not eliminate all training hyperparameters.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Road Less Scheduled
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schedule-Free optimization removes dependence on a predetermined stopping horizon by unifying scheduling and iterate averaging, and its AdamW variant won the 2024 AlgoPerf self-tuning track. AGD derives an automatic per-batch scalar and needs no explicit schedule, but lacks comparable self-tuning benchmark evidence and mature AdamW regularization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Anytime Training with Schedule-Free Spectral Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: SF-NorMuon combines schedule-free training with matrix-spectral updates, reports one configuration across multiple language-model scales and 1-8 times Chinchilla horizons, and proves a stationarity guarantee. It operationalizes both norm-aware updates and horizon robustness on Transformers, two directions left open by AGD, while retaining a fixed hyperparameter configuration rather than claiming none.

reviewed_competitors.title: Riemannian Score-Based Generative Modelling
reviewed_competitors.difference: De Bortoli et al. extend score-based diffusion, time reversal, and score matching to smooth Riemannian manifolds without boundary. The reviewed paper reuses that framework and several authors but targets inequality boundaries through barrier or reflection; its formal and numerical difficulties arise precisely where the predecessor's complete-boundaryless assumptions stop applying.

reviewed_competitors.title: Riemannian Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. derive continuous-time diffusion, variational likelihood, divergence computation, and Riemannian score matching on smooth manifolds such as spheres, tori, hyperboloids, and orthogonal groups. It does not solve inequality-boundary feasibility; the target adds two boundary mechanisms but does not match that paper's likelihood benchmark coverage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reflected Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lou and Ermon were submitted one day earlier and independently develop reverse reflected SDEs, constrained denoising/score matching, likelihood training, diffusion guidance, and ODE sampling, scaling to high-dimensional simplices and image benchmarks. The target adds the distinct log-barrier route and scientific product/SPD examples, but reflected diffusion and its probability-flow extension are not unique to it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Metropolis Sampling for Constrained Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fishman et al. explicitly identify the reviewed barrier/reflection samplers as computationally burdensome or convex-Euclidean-only, then introduce a Metropolis discretization of reflected Brownian motion with substantial reported efficiency/performance gains and convex, nonconvex, geospatial, robotics, and protein tasks. It supersedes much of the original practical sampler claim while retaining the target's basic constrained-score motivation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mirror Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tae proposes mapping constrained continuous and categorical domains through mirror geometry, demonstrating simplex diffusion and suggesting image/text extensions. It is a short theoretical report without the target's scientific applications, but anticipates dual-space avoidance of explicit boundary reflection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mirror Diffusion Models for Constrained and Watermarked Generation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. map convex constrained sets to an unconstrained Euclidean dual space so transition kernels and scores remain tractable, derive efficient maps for simplices and l2 balls, and report improvements over prior constrained methods. It trades the target's direct barrier/reflection geometry and general manifold aspiration for analytic training and stronger convex-domain scalability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reflected Schrodinger Bridge for Constrained Generative Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Deng et al. add entropy-regularized optimal transport, reflected forward-backward SDEs, Neumann/Robin boundary conditions, likelihood training, and an approximate convergence account, with image-scale evaluation. The target supplies two simpler noising processes and earlier scientific examples but no transport optimality or comparable scale.

reviewed_competitors.title: Constrained Synthesis with Projected Diffusion Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Christopher et al. recast reverse diffusion as constrained optimization and certify convex, nonconvex, ODE, materials, motion, and planning constraints. It targets feasible synthesis from existing diffusion processes rather than learning a constraint-preserving forward process, covering broader constraint forms at the cost of a different distributional objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Score-based constrained generative modeling via Langevin diffusions with boundary conditions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nordenhog and Sharma introduce underdamped kinetic Langevin dynamics with specular velocity reflection, characterize its reverse boundary dynamics, and give optimally convergent discretizations while directly comparing local-time reflected models. This addresses sampler regularity and rate questions left open by the reviewed Brownian constructions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reflected Schrodinger Bridge Matching
reviewed_competitors.difference: Haggbom et al. give a partially simulation-free reflected bridge framework with a new regression target and report negligible extra wall-clock cost on high-dimensional image couplings. It directly attacks the full-path simulation and higher-derivative burden of earlier reflected bridge methods; the reviewed paper remains simpler but substantially less scalable and less rigorously benchmarked.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning ReLU Networks via Alternating Minimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jagatap and Hegde explicitly alternate ReLU activation-pattern estimation with least-squares weight updates and prove local linear recovery under well-initialized teacher-student assumptions. ANMIN broadens empirical regression settings and derives a different joint hidden-weight ridge system, but omits this work and provides weaker theoretical support, sharply narrowing high-level novelty.

reviewed_competitors.title: Global Convergence of Block Coordinate Descent in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zeng et al. split weights, preactivations, and activations into tractable blocks and prove convergence to a critical point at O(1/k) for broad deep-learning objectives. ANMIN's smaller shallow square-loss system is simpler and sometimes faster, but its unconstrained frozen-gate step lacks the consistency and convergence machinery central to the prior BCD framework.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks are Convex Regularizers: Exact Polynomial-time Convex Optimization Formulations for Two-layer Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pilanci and Ergen give an exact convex representation for weight-decay-regularized two-layer ReLU training using activation-pattern cone constraints. ANMIN avoids enumerating or optimizing all cones and can be cheap at small dh, but sacrifices global optimality and even omits the constraints for its selected local cone.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Hidden Convex Optimization Landscape of Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks: an Exact Characterization of the Optimal Solutions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Lacotte, and Pilanci characterize global solutions and activation-cone geometry through a convex program and provide global-minimum checks. This supplies a principled reference for assessing ANMIN's historical best; ANMIN supplies no certificate that its frozen-pattern surrogate reaches even a stationary point of the original loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: Vector-output ReLU Neural Network Problems are Copositive Programs: Convex Analysis of Two Layer Networks and Polynomial-time Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sahiner et al. treat the vector-output case featured by ANMIN and connect its global training problem to a convex copositive program, with exact algorithms under restricted rank or convolutional regimes. ANMIN is a pragmatic dense local heuristic with better nominal dependence in some dimensions but no approximation or optimality bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fast Convex Optimization for Two-Layer ReLU Networks: Equivalent Model Classes and Cone Decompositions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mishkin, Sahiner, and Pilanci develop accelerated proximal and augmented-Lagrangian solvers for cone-constrained convex and gated-ReLU models and scale them to MNIST and CIFAR-10. ANMIN is algebraically simpler for square regression but the paper does not empirically compare against this cited direct competitor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving Levenberg-Marquardt Algorithm for Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pooladzandi and Zhou evaluate a globalized Levenberg-Marquardt method with momentum, line search, and uphill-step acceptance against SGD, Adam, L-BFGS, Hessian-free methods, and K-FAC. It is a much stronger nonlinear-least-squares baseline than ANMIN's fixed-rate L-BFGS run and directly challenges the claim that ReLU nonsmoothness makes second-order competitors explode.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convex Relaxations of ReLU Neural Networks Approximate Global Optima in Polynomial Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kim and Pilanci bound the relative gap of tractable convex relaxations for random data and derive polynomial-time approximation guarantees. This subsequent work offers a principled accuracy-complexity tradeoff absent from ANMIN, although its guarantees and computational regime differ from ANMIN's small-d dense solves.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Structure-Guided Gauss-Newton Method for Shallow ReLU Neural Network
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cai et al. also alternate nonlinear hidden parameters with exact linear output solves, but update the hidden block using a damped structure-aware Gauss-Newton direction and analyze positive definiteness under assumptions. It preserves nonlinear least-squares geometry more faithfully than ANMIN's unconstrained stale-pattern solve and is now an essential head-to-head baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simplicity Bias and Optimization Threshold in Two-Layer ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Boursier and Flammarion show in a restricted setting that gradient training can converge to simpler noninterpolating solutions with better population loss beyond an optimization threshold. This supports the audit that a deeper ANMIN training minimum need not be desirable and that high-d lower test loss may reflect bias rather than superior optimization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convergence Analysis of Block Newton Methods for 1D Shallow Neural Network Approximation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cai et al. analyze local convergence for block Newton, nonlinear Gauss-Seidel/Jacobi, and reduced-neuron variants in one-dimensional shallow approximation. Its scope is narrower than ANMIN's datasets but it supplies the kind of block-update convergence statement and neuron reduction strategy that ANMIN leaves open.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Both Layers Learn: Training Dynamics of Representing Linear Models via ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tinaz, Xie, and Soltanolkotabi prove linear convergence of joint gradient descent from moderate random initialization for a realizable Gaussian linear target and track alignment, growth, and refinement phases. The stylized assumptions do not settle ANMIN's general regression regime, but they refute any blanket implication that ordinary joint layer training cannot reach good shallow-ReLU optima.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimizing Neural Networks with Kronecker-factored Approximate Curvature
reviewed_competitors.difference: K-FAC replaces a monolithic curvature matrix by invertible Kronecker factors and demonstrates faster progress than momentum SGD in stochastic regimes. It is not specific to shallow square loss, but its scalable structured-curvature tradeoff is directly relevant because ANMIN materializes a much larger dense (dh)-square system and compares only first-order methods and weak L-BFGS.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shampoo: Preconditioned Stochastic Tensor Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shampoo preserves tensor structure through per-axis preconditioners and scales curvature-informed updates to modern networks. It lacks ANMIN's exact layerwise solve but provides a better compute- and memory-scalable comparison for the claim that analytic curvature beats gradient optimization.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Parisi formula for mixed p-spin models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Panchenko proves the Parisi free-energy formula for general mixed p-spin models, including odd interactions. It is a theorem-level baseline for the lecture's mean-field claims, but it does not make the original replica continuation rigorous or resolve finite-dimensional Edwards-Anderson physics.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Parisi ultrametricity conjecture
reviewed_competitors.difference: Panchenko proves that random measures satisfying the Ghirlanda-Guerra identities are ultrametric almost surely. This precisely supports the mean-field hierarchy discussed in the lecture while showing that ultrametricity needs strong overlap identities, not just a visually broad P(q).

reviewed_competitors.title: Spin glass phase at zero temperature in the Edwards-Anderson model
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chatterjee rigorously proves several glassy properties for short-range ground states, including disorder chaos, low-cost macroscopic spin overturning, and growing critical droplets. The results establish nontrivial finite-dimensional glassiness without proving the full Parisi pure-state or ultrametric scenario summarized by the lecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: Critical Droplets and Replica Symmetry Breaking
reviewed_competitors.difference: Newman and Stein formulate a finite-dimensional discriminator: low-energy interfaces between incongruent ground states, as required by an RSB picture, are equivalent to critical droplets whose boundaries occupy a positive fraction of lattice edges. It narrows the lecture's qualitative finite-dimensional extrapolation to a falsifiable geometric condition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Experimental evidence of replica symmetry breaking in random lasers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghofraniha and colleagues measure a pulse-to-pulse optical analogue of the Parisi overlap and report a glassy-light transition compatible with RSB. It is direct evidence for the random-laser application highlighted by the lecture, but it validates that mapped photonic observable rather than magnetic-spin-glass ultrametricity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Survey propagation: an algorithm for satisfiability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Braunstein, Mezard, and Zecchina turn clustered-solution ideas from replica analysis into a message-passing and decimation algorithm for hard random K-SAT instances. It is a concrete algorithmic result behind the lecture's optimization lineage, not evidence that all NP-complete instances have the same equilibrium geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Replica symmetry breaking in dense neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Albanese and colleagues use transport PDE and Guerra-style interpolation to analyze replica symmetry breaking and storage in dense associative Hebbian networks. This is a mathematically specified continuation of the Hopfield lineage, substantially narrower and more testable than a generic claim about modern deep learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks as Spin Models: From Glass to Hidden Order Through Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barney, Winer, and Galitski map randomly initialized networks to layered SK-like models with RSB, then find that training rapidly destroys the spin glass and produces a hidden-order phase. The result supports a precise initialization mapping while warning against carrying the spin-glass label unchanged through learning dynamics.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Bietti, Venturi, and Bruna derive nonparametric kernel rates on spheres for finite isometric groups and geometric-stability sets, including the |G|-factor gain once sample size is sufficiently large. The reviewed paper's intended novelty is arbitrary compact manifolds and positive-dimensional Lie groups via quotient geometry, but the predecessor is more explicit that the improvement is asymptotic and group-spectrum-dependent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning with invariances in random features and kernel models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mei, Misiakiewicz, and Montanari characterize test error on spheres and hypercubes when dimension, samples, and random features scale together, finding a d^alpha saving and distinguishing invariant kernels, output symmetrization, and data augmentation. It is narrower geometrically but more directly addresses finite-width random features, high-dimensional scaling, and implementation choices absent from the reviewed fixed-manifold Sobolev asymptotics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Provably Strict Generalisation Benefit for Invariance in Kernel Methods
reviewed_competitors.difference: Elesedy proves a strictly positive KRR benefit under a compact group through feature averaging and an orthogonal invariant/non-invariant RKHS decomposition, with effective dimension determined jointly by kernel and group. It avoids identifying all benefit with quotient dimension and volume, making it better suited to arbitrary kernels whose spectra do not follow the reviewed Sobolev construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Benefits of Invariance in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lyle et al. compare augmentation with feature averaging, prove risk/gradient and PAC-Bayes improvements, and empirically show that learned augmentation invariance can fail outside the training distribution. This directly studies enforcement choice and misspecification behavior, whereas the reviewed theory assumes an exactly invariant kernel and target from the outset.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improved Generalization Bounds of Group Invariant / Equivariant Deep Networks via Quotient Feature Spaces
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sannai, Imaizumi, and Kawano already use quotient feature-space volume to improve invariant/equivariant deep-network bounds, include approximation theory, and report empirical support. Their leading gain for DeepSets is a square-root factorial in their bound rather than the reviewed KRR's effective m! sample multiplier, underscoring that the gain depends on algorithm, hypothesis class, and bound type.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the hardness of learning under symmetries
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kiani et al. prove superpolynomial or exponential correlational-statistical-query lower bounds for several equivariant neural classes, including GNNs, CNNs, invariant polynomials, and frame averaging. It shows why a favorable sample-complexity exponent for an ideal invariant RKHS does not imply efficient gradient-based learnability of the architectures invoked in Section 5.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sample Complexity Bounds for Estimating Probability Divergences under Invariances
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tahmasebi and Jegelka extend the dimension/normalized-quotient-volume thesis to Wasserstein distance, Sobolev IPMs, MMD, and L2/L-infinity density estimation. It broadens the statistical tasks beyond regression and is the most direct follow-on, but its shared quotient-spectral machinery makes careful checking of orbit weighting, local norms, and singular strata especially important rather than independent confirmation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning with Exact Invariances in Polynomial Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: Soleymani et al. ask how to realize exact kernel invariance computationally and give a polynomial-time method under oracle access to input geometry, framed through constrained convex quadratic programs. This addresses a missing axis of the reviewed work—computability of the invariant estimator—while making strong oracle assumptions that should be evaluated separately from statistical rates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reconciling Modern Machine Learning Practice and the Bias-Variance Trade-off
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Introduced and popularized the unified double-descent curve across model families and datasets.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Belkin et al. establish the broad empirical framing and posit a mechanism; Schaeffer et al. narrow to an elementary singular-mode explanation and targeted ablations for ordinary regression.

reviewed_competitors.title: Surprises in High-Dimensional Ridgeless Least Squares Interpolation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Derives rigorous asymptotic and non-asymptotic risk results for minimum-norm linear and random-feature regression.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It gives quantitatively precise double-descent conditions under explicit random-design assumptions; the target trades that rigor for a shorter pointwise SVD tutorial and small real-data demonstrations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Characterizes covariance effective-rank conditions under which a minimum-norm interpolator has near-optimal prediction accuracy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bartlett et al. explain when the far-overparameterized regime is benign; the target focuses on why residual error can blow up near interpolation and does not characterize eventual risk.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Generalization Error of Random Features Regression: Precise Asymptotics and Double Descent Curve
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Computes high-dimensional test-risk asymptotics for ridge regression on random nonlinear features, including the full double-descent curve.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies an analytically tractable nonlinear-feature model and joint width/sample/dimension limit; Schaeffer et al. only analogize fixed features to nonlinear networks and run no neural experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Double Descent in the Condition Number
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Shows that random rectangular linear systems are typically worst conditioned near the square interpolation point.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This is the closest spectral precursor to the target's inverse-smallest-singular-value intuition; the target adds residual and test-vector alignments, correctly showing why conditioning alone is not prediction error.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Demonstrates model-wise, epoch-wise, and sample-wise double descent in modern deep-learning tasks and proposes effective model complexity.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It provides the finite-network phenomenon the target seeks to make intuitive; the target analyzes only sample-wise linear regression and does not validate its mechanism for model- or epoch-wise neural curves.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Regularization Can Mitigate Double Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Proves monotonic sample- and model-size risk for optimally tuned ridge in specific isotropic linear models and demonstrates mitigation in neural networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies a practical regularization protocol and its assumptions; the target uses hard singular-value deletion as an explanatory ablation and does not evaluate tuned ridge.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multiple Descent: Design Your Own Generalization Curve
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Constructs linear-regression families with arbitrarily many controllable generalization peaks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves that curve shape is an interaction of data and inductive bias rather than an intrinsic two-descent law, limiting any universal reading of the target's generic three-factor threshold story.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memorizing without Overfitting: Bias, Variance, and Interpolation in Over-parameterized Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A same-coauthor predecessor derives analytic bias and variance in linear and nonlinear two-layer models, including no-label-noise overfitting.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is mathematically broader and already establishes variance divergence and nonlinear cases; the target's novelty is its elementary mode-wise pedagogy and visual ablation panel rather than the underlying phenomenon.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Double Descent Requires a Fine-Grained Bias-Variance Decomposition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Decomposes variance by sampling, initialization, and label randomness and finds interpolation divergence without label noise in random-feature kernel regression.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adlam and Pennington expose interactions among randomness sources that the target's single fixed-design residual sum does not separate; they also derive asymptotic curves and ensemble/bagging predictions.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Geometry of Over-parameterized Regression and Adversarial Perturbations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Develops a feature-space geometry for under- and overparameterized regression and explains double descent with and without label noise.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It provides geometric and bias-variance analyses across linear and nonlinear basis models; the target reorganizes a related view into three directly ablated singular-mode factors.

reviewed_competitors.title: Phenomenology of Double Descent in Finite-Width Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Analyzes finite-width neural networks through influence functions and Hessian spectra, including the effect of the loss function.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It directly targets the nonlinear finite-width and loss-dependent gap left by linear/kernel explanations; Schaeffer et al.'s deep-network extension remains an informal fixed-feature analogy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Least Squares Regression Can Exhibit Under-Parameterized Double Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A near-concurrent/later work constructs and proves least-squares peaks strictly inside the underparameterized regime through spectrum and target-eigenvector alignment.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its counterexamples show that peaks need not sit at interpolation and that prevailing threshold explanations are incomplete, sharpening the limits of the target's Marchenko-Pastur-centered intuition.

reviewed_competitors.title: A U-turn on Double Descent: Rethinking Parameter Counting in Statistical Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later critique shows that apparent second descents in several classical models coincide with switching between different parameter-growth mechanisms rather than inherently with p=n.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It replaces raw parameter count with a test-aware effective-parameter view and can fold curves back into classical shapes; the target treats N/P and the interpolation threshold as the main organizing axis.

reviewed_competitors.title: eGAD! Double Descent Is Explained by Generalized Aliasing Decomposition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later decomposition separates model insufficiency, data insufficiency, and generalized aliasing across random features, signal processing, differential equations, and materials prediction.
reviewed_competitors.difference: GAD is designed to explain double and multiple descents across broader linear-function settings and can inform design without labels; the target isolates label/residual amplification in OLS and three small datasets.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unified Neural Network Scaling Laws and Scale-time Equivalence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A same-author later work combines a linear double-descent analysis with scale-time equivalence and tests a joint size, training-time, and data-volume law on vision networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It begins to connect the target's linear intuition to finite neural architectures and multiple scaling axes, although its broader scaling claims require separate validation and are not evidence retroactively contained in the tutorial.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exact Expressions for Double Descent and Implicit Regularization via Surrogate Random Design
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Derives exact non-asymptotic mean-squared-error expressions for minimum-norm linear estimation under a surrogate random design and connects overparameterization to implicit ridge regularization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It predates the target and is theoretically sharper about expected risk and implicit regularization, while the target is more elementary and per-test-point but supplies no comparable risk theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectrum Dependent Learning Curves in Kernel Regression and Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Decomposes population generalization by kernel eigenmodes and analyzes the successive learning of spectral components in kernel regression and wide networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its eigenmode learning curves operate at the distribution/kernel level; the target uses an empirical design SVD and one test point's projections without deriving an expected learning curve.

reviewed_competitors.title: Double Trouble in Double Descent: Bias and Variance(s) in the Lazy Regime
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Separates sampling, label, and initialization variance in lazy/random-feature models and analyzes how averaging changes the interpolation peak.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It provides causal attribution among distinct randomness sources; the target compresses all unfit structure into u_r dot E, gaining simplicity while losing that source-level resolution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Triple Descent and the Two Kinds of Overfitting: Where & Why Do They Appear?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Distinguishes nonlinear/random-feature and linear/noise interpolation transitions and shows that two peaks can coexist as triple descent.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It demonstrates that visually similar peaks can occur at different effective transitions and respond differently to noise and regularization, limiting a single universal three-factor narrative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Early Stopping in Deep Networks: Double Descent and How to Eliminate It
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Explains epoch-wise double descent through components learned at different rates and shows how layerwise step-size control can remove it.
reviewed_competitors.difference: That is an optimization-dynamical mechanism for finite deep networks, entirely outside the target's converged static OLS factorization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Post-Hoc Reversal: Are We Selecting Models Prematurely?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later study that cites the target shows post-hoc temperature scaling can induce double descent while ensembling and stochastic weight averaging can flatten it.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It demonstrates that the observed curve depends on metric and post-hoc prediction transformation, variables absent from the target's raw squared-error OLS account.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lundberg and Lee formalize additive feature attribution and efficient SHAP approximations. Bertossi places one conditional-expectation version beside causal responsibility and logic, emphasizing exact complexity and counterfactual reasoning rather than approximation performance or user studies.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Many Shapley Values for Model Explanation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sundararajan and Najmi distinguish baseline, random-baseline, and conditional-expectation games and show the usual uniqueness argument does not choose among them. This directly qualifies the article's singular presentation of 'the Shap score' and makes the distribution/game choice central.

reviewed_competitors.title: Predictive and Causal Implications of Using Shapley Value for Model Interpretation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ma and Tourani analyze Shapley values in Bayesian networks and show feature attribution need not reflect causal relations or safe feature removal. Their result sharpens the distinction this exposition sometimes blurs between attribution under a distribution and actual causality under interventions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Abduction-Based Explanations for Machine Learning Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ignatiev et al. compile models to constraints and compute subset- or cardinality-minimal sufficient explanations with formal guarantees and benchmark evidence. This article explains the abduction connection more broadly and advocates ASP, but provides no new scalability evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Algorithmic Recourse under Imperfect Causal Knowledge: a Probabilistic Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: Karimi et al. prove guaranteed recourse is impossible without true structural equations and optimize probabilistic counterfactual or subpopulation interventions under causal uncertainty. Bertossi's ASP proposal is stronger for declarative constraints and queries but does not resolve causal-model uncertainty or validate action success.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Computational Tractability of the (Many) Shapley Values
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marzouk et al. separately map local/global conditional, interventional, and baseline SHAP complexity across model and distribution classes, including tractability under Hidden Markov distributions and new tree/neural hardness. This extends the article's complexity discussion beyond conditional SHAP and deterministic-decomposable circuits.

reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies nonasymptotic semiclassical analysis and explicit quantum-classical separations that do not rely only on barrier tunneling. That is a more rigorous answer to the quantum-advantage question than QHD's selected simulation and D-Wave rankings, though on defined function families rather than generic objectives.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Bau and colleagues align hidden units with a broad labeled ontology of objects, parts, scenes, textures, materials, and colors and compare training and architecture conditions. Interaction concepts capture input coalitions rather than individual units, but the paper omits Network Dissection's explicit external semantic labels, so recurrence cannot substitute for measured semantic alignment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
reviewed_competitors.difference: TCAV uses human-provided positive and random examples to test how sensitive a class score is to a named concept direction, including repeated statistical testing. Li and Zhang avoid concept-example supervision and expose combinatorial input interactions, but never validate that extracted subset identities correspond to consistently named human concepts.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Automatic Concept-based Explanations
reviewed_competitors.difference: ACE automatically segments and clusters visual examples, then evaluates concepts for meaningfulness, coherence, and importance with quantitative human experiments. The interaction paper's superpixel appendix is similarly automatic but supplies selected visual examples rather than ACE-style human coherence and importance evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Completeness-aware Concept-Based Explanations in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yeh and colleagues define predictive completeness, optimize concepts for completeness and interpretability, and validate on known-concept synthetic data, images, language, and user studies. Harsanyi efficiency gives Li and Zhang exact score accounting over all coalitions, but their small dictionary is evaluated by identity coverage rather than held-out completeness or human interpretability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Concept Bottleneck Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Koh and colleagues train an explicit human-labeled concept layer and test task accuracy, concept accuracy, and the benefit of correcting concepts at inference. This requires concept supervision and changes the model, unlike post-hoc interactions, but provides an operational intervention test that a local exact decomposition does not.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Shapley Taylor Interaction Index
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shapley-Taylor axiomatizes a k-order allocation of predictive effects and connects it to the multilinear Taylor series, avoiding enumeration of named concepts at every order. Li and Zhang use the full Harsanyi basis and exact all-order efficiency, but do not empirically compare whether their interaction allocation is more stable, meaningful, or concise for the same models.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Many Shapley Values for Model Explanation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sundararajan and Najmi show that Shapley explanations differ with how the model, data, context, and baseline are operationalized, and that uniqueness applies only after those choices are fixed. This directly qualifies Li and Zhang's appeal to Harsanyi axioms: the decomposition can be unique for one coalition game while the game itself changes under equally plausible absence definitions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sanity Checks for Saliency Maps
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adebayo and colleagues introduce parameter- and data-randomization tests showing that visually plausible explanations can be independent of the learned model. Li and Zhang include label noise and a shortcut, but omit the direct untrained and progressively randomized network tests needed before qualitative interaction visualizations can establish learned semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can We Faithfully Represent Absence States to Compute Shapley Values on a DNN?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ren and colleagues explicitly identify baseline masking as an unsolved absence-state problem and learn baselines intended not to inject signals. Li and Zhang cite this companion line but use several fixed modality-specific baselines without an ablation, leaving their cross-sample and cross-model interaction identities conditional on an unvalidated absence representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unifying Framework to the Analysis of Interaction Methods using Synergy Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lundstrom and Razaviyayn characterize game-theoretic and gradient interaction methods by how they distribute synergies and argue that method criteria must follow the explanation goal and context. Their framework makes explicit that algebraically justified interaction allocations are policy choices; Li and Zhang instead elevate one allocation's stable subsets to symbols without a task-specific comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Where We Have Arrived in Proving the Emergence of Sparse Symbolic Concepts in AI Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ren and colleagues prove sparsity of primitive interaction patterns under assumptions about high-order derivatives, masking behavior, and confidence on occluded samples. This strengthens the sparsity story conditionally, but still concerns functional mimicry on masked coalitions; it does not prove that a sparse primitive has human semantics, stable grounding, or symbolic syntax.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretable Neural-Symbolic Concept Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barbiero and colleagues reserve the symbolic claim for explicit syntactic rule structures executed on concept truth degrees, and evaluate rule recovery against known ground truth and counterfactual guidance. Li and Zhang recover local conjunction effects without rules, names, or truth semantics, so 'symbolic primitive interaction' is a narrower and less operational notion.

reviewed_competitors.title: Layerwise Change of Knowledge in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cheng and colleagues extend the same interaction ontology into intermediate layers to track emergence and forgetting through forward propagation. It addresses Li and Zhang's stated learning-dynamics direction, but explicitly notes that consensus on what constitutes DNN knowledge remains absent, so the subsequent extension does not resolve semantic validity.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Luo and colleagues use a positive-operator-valued-measure probability representation with autoregressive networks, exact sampling, string states, forward-backward time integration, and one- and two-dimensional spin benchmarks. Q-Flow transfers the probabilistic strategy to continuous bosonic Husimi-Q densities and off-the-shelf continuous flows, but its interacting scaling evidence is much narrower.

reviewed_competitors.title: Time-dependent variational principle for open quantum systems with artificial neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reh, Schmitt, and Garttner evolve deep autoregressive mixed-state representations under a Lindblad equation with TDVP and benchmark dissipative Heisenberg systems up to 40 spins. Q-Flow instead models continuous-variable Q densities and adds Euler-KL, but does not benchmark a comparably interacting many-site family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Variational Monte Carlo Approach to Partial Differential Equations with Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Reh and Garttner encode high-dimensional probability densities with neural networks and evolve parameters variationally on unbounded domains. Q-Flow applies that TDVP lineage to a Husimi-Q quantum PDE and contributes a first-order KL alternative; its claimed novelty therefore lies in the quantum representation and Euler-KL mechanism, not neural variational density evolution itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Solving time dependent Fokker-Planck equations via temporal normalizing flow
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feng, Zeng, and Zhou already use a time-conditioned normalizing flow and a physics residual to solve time-dependent Fokker-Planck equations without labeled data. Q-Flow uses separately optimized time slices and a Liouvillian Euler-KL or TDVP update specialized through the Husimi representation, so normalizing-flow probability-PDE evolution itself predates it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Probability flow solution of the Fokker-Planck equation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Boffi and Vanden-Eijnden learn an on-the-fly score and transport samples through a deterministic probability-flow ODE, with KL control and high-dimensional interacting-particle experiments. It offers a stronger theoretical and interacting classical comparator to Q-Flow's sequential explicit-Euler fit, although it applies to Fokker-Planck structure rather than arbitrary derived quantum-Q operators.

reviewed_competitors.title: Coherent-State Ladder Time-Dependent Variational Principle for Open Quantum Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schlegel, Minganti, and Savona represent an interacting many-boson density matrix as a superposition of photon-added coherent states and target several driven-dissipative modes with large occupation and cat states. Its structural ansatz is less generic than a universal flow but directly attacks the interacting bosonic regime that Q-Flow evaluates only at two sites.

reviewed_competitors.title: Real-time Dynamics of the Schwinger Model as an Open Quantum System with Neural Density Operators
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lin, Luo, Yao, and Shanahan evolve neural density operators for an interacting lattice gauge theory and study scaling to 32 spatial sites and three interacting strings. It returns a neural density-matrix object for discrete lattice physics rather than a continuous phase-space density, but provides stronger interacting size-scaling evidence than Q-Flow's separable 20-site oscillator.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simulating non-Markovian open quantum dynamics by exploiting physics-informed neural network
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cao and colleagues combine time-encoded PINNs with a dissipaton-embedded master equation and domain decomposition, validating against hierarchical equations of motion for a single-impurity Anderson model. It extends beyond Q-Flow's Markovian scope and openly reports failure from error accumulation at strongly non-Markovian low temperatures, but does not offer Q-Flow's normalized density likelihood and sampling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generative Modeling of Quantum Distribution with Functional Flow Matching
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hahm and colleagues use spin Wigner functions and functional flow matching to learn multi-qubit quantum distributions and evaluate trace, purity, and entanglement entropy. It advances modern flow matching and physical-property validation but learns static distributions rather than integrating an open-system Liouvillian trajectory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Flow-based Phase-space Tomography of Continuous-variable Quantum States
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dugan, Dangovski, Lu, and Luo extend the flow-based phase-space program to measured tomography: QST-QFlow models positive Husimi Q and QST-WFlow represents signed Wigner functions as a difference of flows, with non-Gaussian, multimode, and noisy-data tests. It strengthens static reconstruction evidence on difficult states but does not validate dynamical scaling or repair Q-Flow's sequential integration guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Criteria for Feasible Monte Carlo Stochastic Simulations of Bosonic Markovian Open Quantum Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yoneya, Fujimoto, and Kawaguchi derive conditions under which P, Wigner, or Husimi-Q phase-space equations admit positive-semidefinite diffusion and exact stochastic simulation. This sharpens when the sample-only baseline that Q-Flow calls restricted is feasible and necessary; Q-Flow remains useful when explicit density or derivatives are needed or those SDE conditions fail.

The reviewed paper uses an even smaller uv model for exact finite-width threshold calculations and contributes a broader empirical depth-width phase map, but its analytic model is less representative and it omits generalization tests.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Agarwala et al. analytically recover progressive sharpening and near-edge behavior in second-order regression models, addressing later nonlinear curvature evolution. reviewed_competitors.difference: Meltzer, Chen, and Liu prove catapult behavior for a broad class including quadratic and two-layer homogeneous networks and relate large loss to decreasing weight norm, with ReLU activation sparsity experiments. The reviewed paper instead resolves empirical loss and Hessian-sharpness subphases across depth and width and derives only a much narrower uv example. The competitor's current 2025 revision postdates the reviewed camera-ready.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Kalra, He, and Barkeshli extend the reviewed paper's uv direction into a fixed-point and vector-field account of sharpness reduction, progressive sharpening, edge-of-stability conditions, and period-doubling chaos, with real-network and language-model experiments. This supersedes the reviewed paper as the more complete dynamical-mechanism account, while the reviewed work retains the more systematic empirical depth-width boundary atlas.

It advances exact late-regime depth-dependent theory, whereas the reviewed uv analysis is shallow and early-regime and its empirical deep networks do not receive a comparable dynamical derivation.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Chiribella, D'Ariano, and Perinotti reconstruct finite-dimensional quantum theory from operational composition and purification principles, including transformations and systems. reviewed_competitors.difference: Auffèves and Grangier pursue a physically realist reconstruction of Hilbert-space quantum formalism from contextual and extravalence principles. reviewed_competitors.difference: Model Soups averages checkpoints fine-tuned from the same pretrained model, motivates success through a shared low-error basin, and focuses on selecting/averaging models for improved target performance. reviewed_competitors.difference: Fisher merging treats each fine-tuned model as a local posterior and weights parameters by estimated Fisher information instead of taking an unweighted centroid. reviewed_competitors.title: Editing Models with Task Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Task Arithmetic explicitly adds and subtracts fine-tuning displacement vectors to compose tasks, forget behavior, and create analogies. reviewed_competitors.title: TIES-Merging: Resolving Interference When Merging Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: TIES-Merging identifies redundant parameter changes and sign disagreement as causes of destructive task-vector merging, then trims small changes, elects a consensus sign, and merges only aligned values. That directly qualifies the assumption that a plain centroid is broadly representative: the region paper establishes useful geometric regularity, whereas TIES supplies a mechanism for cases where region vectors conflict coordinate by coordinate.
