reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent on Neural Networks Typically Occurs at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cohen et al. establish progressive sharpening, sharpness hovering just above 2/eta, and short-timescale non-monotone loss across practical full-batch neural training with released code. The reviewed paper answers that empirical challenge in tractable low-dimensional models and links it to threshold-bias learning, but has much narrower practical coverage and no code.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Stabilization: The Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damian et al. use a cubic local expansion to model divergence along the top Hessian eigenvector and implicit projected motion toward lower sharpness, with predictions checked in standard settings. The reviewed work instead gives a more elementary global analysis of exact toy recurrences and a specific bias-learning phase transition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Edge-of-Stability Training Dynamics with a Minimalist Example
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhu et al. rigorously construct a simple bifurcating objective whose endpoint sharpness is close to 2/eta within a large local region. The reviewed paper analyzes the structurally simpler ell(xy) class globally under its assumptions, derives loss-shape-dependent gaps, and connects the mechanism to an approximate ReLU bias model.

reviewed_competitors.title: SGD with Large Step Sizes Learns Sparse Features
reviewed_competitors.difference: Andriushchenko et al. study stochastic bouncing across valleys and show large-step schedules bias networks toward sparse predictors, with broader experiments and released code. The reviewed paper proves a sharper deterministic threshold in a mean model, but its link from negative bias to useful sparse features and generalization remains largely illustrative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Trajectory Alignment: Understanding the Edge of Stability Phenomenon via Bifurcation Theory
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct follow-up named by the authors
reviewed_competitors.difference: Song and Yun align reparameterized GD trajectories on a common bifurcation diagram and prove progressive sharpening plus EoS for a two-layer linear network and a nonlinear neuron. It extends the reviewed paper's low-dimensional phase-transition intuition toward richer models, while not targeting sparse-coding bias learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stable Minima Cannot Overfit in Univariate ReLU Networks: Generalization by Large Step Sizes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nacson et al. prove that constant-rate-stable minima of univariate two-layer ReLU regression have learning-rate-controlled total variation and near-optimal nonparametric risk, with extensive simulations. This supplies an actual large-step generalization bound, whereas the reviewed paper offers a possible threshold-feature mechanism without a risk theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training on the Edge of Stability Is Caused by Layerwise Jacobian Alignment
reviewed_competitors.difference: MacDonald et al. use an exponential Euler control to avoid EoS and empirically attribute sharpness growth to layerwise Jacobian alignment, including dataset-size scaling. It studies a deep-network mechanism missing from the reviewed two-variable theory and questions whether one scalar bias coordinate explains practical EoS broadly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Sharpness Dynamics in NN Training with a Minimalist Example: The Effects of Dataset Difficulty, Depth, Stochasticity, and More
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work uses deep scalar linear networks to study how data difficulty, depth, step size, and optimizer stochasticity affect progressive sharpening, then checks transfer to practical settings. It directly covers several dimensions that the reviewed paper leaves open while trading away the threshold-neuron mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kuzborskij et al. model stochastic optimizers as random dynamical systems with fractal attractors, define sharpness dimension from the full Hessian spectrum, prove a corresponding generalization bound, and test MLPs and Transformers. This supersedes the reviewed paper's speculative bias-to-generalization bridge with a different, spectrum-wide complexity mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Bifurcation Theory Framework for Gradient Descent on the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. decompose motion normal and tangent to a minimizing manifold, characterize stable EoS as a flip bifurcation via a Lyapunov coefficient, and prove convergence under spectral/geometric assumptions for overparameterized networks. It directly generalizes beyond the scalar and low-dimensional structural forms acknowledged as the reviewed paper's main boundary.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Road Taken: The Role of Optimizers at the Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xie et al. show maximum-Hessian thresholds can miss realized stability by factors up to 21.1 across optimizers and replace 2/eta with directional Hessian and update-alignment diagnostics. The reviewed paper's 2/eta law is exact for plain GD in its toy geometry but should not be exported unchanged to the SGD and scheduled practical panels.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Franceschi et al. model the infinite-width discriminator through its NTK, explicitly repair ill-defined discriminator gradients in earlier idealized analyses, characterize trained critics for multiple losses, and derive distributional convergence insights. reviewed_competitors.difference: Mroueh and Nguyen derive a parametric kernelized MMD flow, an explicit condition for global convergence, and non-asymptotic rates under gradient regularization. The reviewed paper broadens the physical picture to generic discriminator gradients and mode-collapse phase diagrams, but gives heuristic rather than global convergence results.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sobolev Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sobolev Descent already simplifies adversarial generation to particles transported by a gradient-regularized critic and relates the flow to optimal transport, emphasizing smooth transitions and avoiding large gradients. The reviewed work adds an explicit generator-NTK coupling between particles and maps coupling-dependent collapse, but uses a narrower toy target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Functional Space Analysis of Local GAN Convergence
reviewed_competitors.difference: Khrulkov et al. represent local adversarial dynamics as PDEs, derive convergence from a differential operator's eigenvalues, and estimate useful spectra from target data to choose augmentation. The reviewed paper provides a more visually intuitive finite-particle mechanism for mode collapse, but lacks a corresponding local convergence theorem or real-data predictive test.

reviewed_competitors.title: WGAN with an Infinitely Wide Generator Has No Spurious Stationary Points
reviewed_competitors.difference: No et al. prove that a two-layer infinite-width-generator WGAN with a finite two-layer discriminator has no spurious stationary points and extend the safe region to wide finite generators. The reviewed paper instead demonstrates nonconvergent trajectories created by coarse NTK coupling; stationary-point absence and dynamic convergence are different questions, and their assumptions and objectives are not directly reconciled.

reviewed_competitors.title: Instability and Local Minima in GAN Training with Kernel Discriminators
reviewed_competitors.difference: Becker et al. analyze finite real and generated point sets with a kernel discriminator and precisely characterize good minima, approximate mode collapse, and divergence in an isolated-points model. The reviewed paper places the kernel on the generator and emphasizes collective motion, discriminator spectral bias, and regularization phase diagrams rather than local-minimum conditions.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Limitations of First-Order Approximation in GAN Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. rigorously analyze a two-Gaussian GMM-GAN, prove convergence with an optimal discriminator, and show first-order discriminator updates can cause instability and collapse. The reviewed paper reaches a compatible time-scale lesson in an eight-mode particle system and adds generator coupling, but its phase-boundary explanation is heuristic.

reviewed_competitors.title: Which Training Methods for GANs do actually Converge?

The reviewed paper's under/critical/over-damping analogy is closely related but applies an NTK-weighted generator-gradient penalty and focuses on mode-coverage trajectories.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Information Propagation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schoenholz et al. establish ordered and chaotic phases, signal-propagation depth scales, the divergent edge-of-chaos scale, and corresponding vanishing/exploding gradient regimes with mean-field theory. The reviewed paper reuses that phase framework, adds input-to-hidden coordinate correlations and a Gaussian information lower bound, but its claim that classic mean-field theory is invalid is much broader than its normalization-sensitive tail objection supports.

reviewed_competitors.title: Resurrecting the Sigmoid in Deep Learning Through Dynamical Isometry: Theory and Practice
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pennington et al. derive the full input-output Jacobian spectrum and show sigmoidal networks achieve dynamical isometry only with orthogonal weights, then demonstrate orders-of-magnitude faster learning. The reviewed paper adds a covariance lower-bound interpretation but labels Gaussian critical networks DI despite deriving depth-growing spectral spread and performs no learning experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gaussian Lower Bound for the Information Bottleneck Limit
reviewed_competitors.difference: Painsky and Tishby construct an optimal Gaussian embedding and a lower bound to the information-bottleneck curve while explicitly treating Gaussianization as a bounded surrogate problem. The reviewed paper transports that idea to layerwise initialization but then infers maxima of true mutual information from the lower-bound maximum without proving tightness or a shared optimizer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Initialization of ReLUs for Dynamical Isometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Burkholz and Dubatovka derive exact joint output distributions for Gaussian fully connected networks without a mean-field assumption, quantify deviations, and design a parameter-sharing ReLU initialization for dynamical isometry. This is a more constructive response to finite-width and distributional limits than the reviewed paper's arbitrary-input correction, which loses closed forms and is tested only with tanh covariance surrogates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Critical Initialization of Wide and Deep Neural Networks Through Partial Jacobians: General Theory and Applications
reviewed_competitors.difference: Doshi et al. use partial-Jacobian recurrences and a cheap numerical diagnostic across fully connected, convolutional, normalization, residual, ResNet, and MLP-Mixer settings. The reviewed paper gives a narrower homogeneous-MLP information interpretation and heatmaps but no implemented model-selection test or modern-architecture validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature Learning and Generalization in Deep Networks with Orthogonal Weights
reviewed_competitors.difference: Day et al. show orthogonal tanh initialization suppresses depth-growing finite-width preactivation and NTK-descendant fluctuations, then connect those measurements to MNIST and CIFAR-10 training and generalization. It supplies the finite-width feature-learning and task evidence absent from the reviewed paper's claim that lower-bound preservation makes an optimal channel.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Fyodorov and Khoruzhenko derive a topology-trivialization transition and exponentially many mostly unstable equilibria for a generic Gaussian nonlinear vector field using mean counts. The reviewed paper specializes to positive GLV abundances and invasion constraints and, importantly, replaces the annealed mean by a diversity-resolved quenched count.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Ben Arous, Fyodorov, and Khoruzhenko calculate annealed counts by the fraction of unstable directions in mixed gradient and solenoidal random dynamics. The reviewed work gains quenched typicality and ecological feasibility constraints but reports only a bulk stable-versus-unstable split rather than an instability-index distribution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Marginally Stable Equilibria in Critical Ecosystems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Biroli, Bunin, and Cammarota analyze gamma=1 random GLV through its energy landscape and numerical studies, finding exponentially many marginally stable equilibria and a spin-glass phase. It establishes both the reciprocity-dependent contrast with gamma=0 and the known need for replica-symmetry breaking that limits the reviewed RS ansatz.

reviewed_competitors.title: Properties of equilibria and glassy phases of the random Lotka-Volterra model with demographic noise
reviewed_competitors.difference: Altieri et al. use a symmetric noisy model, one-step replica-symmetry breaking, and numerical dynamics to find exponentially many stable equilibria and a Gardner marginal phase. It shows that equilibrium organization changes with reciprocity and demographic noise and supplies a kind of numerical validation absent from the reviewed gamma=0 theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: The effect of population abundances on the stability of large random ecosystems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gibbs et al. explicitly analyze the community matrix diag(N*)H for arbitrary feasible abundance distributions. For uncorrelated dense interactions they recover an abundance-independent May crossing while showing that abundances change relaxation and that matrix-level equivalence is not automatic. This supports the reviewed gamma=0 asymptotic threshold but exposes its missing Jacobian factor and proof step.

reviewed_competitors.title: Numerical implementation of dynamical mean field theory for disordered systems: application to the Lotka-Volterra model of ecosystems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Roy et al. derive and numerically solve DMFT for random GLV, directly characterizing chaos and aging in trajectories. The reviewed paper instead counts static roots and does not calculate Lyapunov exponents or attractors, so DMFT is the appropriate baseline for testing rather than inferring its dynamical claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Breakdown of random-matrix universality in persistent Lotka--Volterra communities
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baron et al. derive the actual reduced Jacobian and interaction matrix after extinction dynamics and show that persistence induces non-Gaussian, shared-index correlations that can defeat first-two-moment spectral universality. Their supplement makes the abundance diagonal and conditional threshold argument explicit; the reviewed work assumes a simpler root-conditioned elliptic bulk and does not test evolved-community correlations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quenched complexity of equilibria for asymmetric Generalized Lotka-Volterra equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ros et al. provide the 53-page derivation, generic saddle equations, and numerical solution strategy delegated by the reviewed Letter. It is essential implementation context but not independent validation: it retains replica symmetry, repeats H as the stability matrix, and reports saddle-equation solutions without finite-S equilibrium enumeration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Many-species ecological fluctuations as a jump process from the brink of extinction
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arnoulx de Pirey and Bunin derive an exact asymptotic jump-process theory and verify it in simulations: abundant species remain below the stability bound while rare species drive turnover. This supports a role for internally stable but invadable quasi-equilibria and is more precise than the reviewed inference that unstable uninvadable equilibria directly explain chaos.

reviewed_competitors.title: Non-reciprocal interactions and high-dimensional chaos: comparing dynamics and statistics of equilibria in a solvable class of models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fournier et al. combine DMFT and Kac-Rice in a solvable nonreciprocal model and show that magnetization and overlap on the chaotic attractor cannot be inferred from the numerous unstable equilibria. It directly narrows the reviewed paper's proposed equilibrium-to-dynamics interpretation even though the model is not GLV.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalized Lotka-Volterra model with sparse interactions: non-Gaussian effects and topological multiple-equilibria phase
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tonolo et al. solve a sparse symmetric random GLV using cavity and belief propagation, finding non-Gaussian abundance statistics and a topology-dependent glass phase tied to extinctions. It demonstrates that the reviewed dense fully connected Gaussian complexity is not automatically universal across more ecological network structures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fragile vs robust Multiple Equilibria phases in generalized Lotka-Volterra model with non-reciprocal interactions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Louis-Sarrola and Ros extend quenched Kac-Rice across gamma from zero to one and separate total, invadable, uninvadable, and internally stable equilibria. They predict a fragile phase at high asymmetry and a robust phase with exponentially many internally stable uninvadable equilibria at greater reciprocity, proving that the reviewed 'all unstable' conclusion is gamma=0-specific. The extension still assumes replica symmetry, reuses the H-as-J shortcut, and provides no finite-S enumeration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chaos in high-dimensional dynamical systems with tunable non-reciprocity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fournier and Urbani compute chaotic-attractor behavior and the maximal Lyapunov exponent while tuning away from reciprocal gradient dynamics, finding chaos for every nonzero nonreciprocity in their model. It supplies the direct dynamical observable missing from the reviewed static complexity analysis and shows that reciprocity effects should be tested through trajectories, not inferred from counts alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generative Adversarial Neural Operators
reviewed_competitors.relationship: An earlier neural-operator generative model learns probability measures over functions with an infinite-dimensional Wasserstein adversarial objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Infinity-Diff: Infinite Resolution Diffusion with Subsampled Mollified States
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Builds an infinite-resolution functional latent diffusion model with sparse-coordinate training and multiscale integral operators.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It prioritizes efficient high-fidelity image generation through latent compression and mollification; the reviewed paper operates on observed one-dimensional functions and develops measure/KL semantics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conditional Score-Based Diffusion Models for Bayesian Inference in Infinite Dimensions

reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes conditional-score blow-up and trains task-conditioned posteriors; this paper applies heuristic ILVR overwrites to a pretrained unconditional model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Score-Based Diffusion Models in Infinite Dimensions: A Malliavin Calculus Perspective

reviewed_competitors.difference: It avoids finite projections and semigroup-invertibility assumptions in its theoretical score expression; the reviewed paper builds a discrete Gaussian-measure ELBO and then approximates KL on observation grids.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Raff and Nicholas define the exact discrete LZ digest/Jaccard method with strong malware-scale practicality. reviewed_competitors.title: Hopfield Networks is All You Need
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramsauer et al. provide continuous modern Hopfield retrieval with large capacity and one-step updates. It gives LZ Networks the most faithful memory behavior in short tests, but its quadratic cost defeats the desired ultra-long scaling and motivates noisier fixed-size VSA memory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces
reviewed_competitors.difference: S4 provides a structured state-space memory with efficient convolutional training and strong Long Range Arena results through length 16k. LZ Networks instead uses data-dependent discrete phrase resets and associative writes, but does not compare to S4 or reach its benchmark lengths.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hyena Hierarchy: Towards Larger Convolutional Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hyena combines implicit long convolutions and gating, demonstrates associative recall through 131k and language scaling, and reports throughput. It attacks the same long-context bottleneck with parallel operators rather than an explicit phrase dictionary and supplies the scaling evidence missing from LZ Networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mamba makes recurrent state transitions input-dependent to selectively retain or forget information, provides a hardware-aware linear-time scan, and scales to million-length real data. It realizes a soft learned memory policy without discrete external writes and is a stronger modern comparator for the LZ reset idea.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shuffling Recurrent Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rotman and Wolf propose the Shuffle RNN and supply the addition/PS-MNIST/copy setup reused here. Saul et al. outperform that baseline on PS-MNIST but find that a carefully reimplemented ordinary LSTM is stronger, underscoring the paper's baseline-tuning message.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mad Max: Affine Spline Insights into Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Balestriero and Baraniuk rigorously formulate piecewise-affine deep networks as compositions of max-affine spline operators and connect their partitions to vector quantization. The reviewed paper repackages this geometry as a mechanistic-interpretability unit and adds semantic hypotheses, but does not add a comparable formal guarantee for its semantic metrics.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Hard to Soft: Understanding Deep Network Nonlinearities via Vector Quantization and Statistical Inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: This MASO extension replaces hard regions with probabilistic soft vector-quantization inference for smooth nonlinearities. The reviewed appendix cites it, but the GPT-2 experiments still use hard binary codes and omit attention and LayerNorm from any soft-region construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Traversing the Local Polytopes of ReLU Neural Networks: A Unified Approach for Network Verification
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu et al. explicitly traverse adjacent ReLU regions and recover the local topology, which directly measures regions rather than inferring crossings from endpoint codes. Their method is more exact but faces the same combinatorial scaling that motivates the reviewed paper's clustering heuristic.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cunningham et al. learn an overcomplete sparse dictionary, quantitatively score interpretability, and perform causal feature interventions. This realizes the decomposable k-greater-than-one direction program that the reviewed Discussion proposes but does not implement, while remaining primarily linear within activation space.

reviewed_competitors.title: Not All Language Model Features Are Linear
reviewed_competitors.difference: Engels et al. define irreducible multidimensional features, discover interpretable circular representations in GPT-2 and Mistral, and validate their causal role by intervention. It addresses failures of one-dimensional directions with explicit geometry and causal tests rather than discrete transformer gate patterns.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Do Not Find Canonical Units of Analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Leask et al. show SAE dictionaries are incomplete and non-atomic through stitching and meta-SAEs. This reinforces the reviewed paper's concern that no single global direction basis is canonical, but also warns that replacing directions with any purported atomic unit requires explicit stability and completeness tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Data Statistics to Feature Geometry: How Correlations Shape Superposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prieto et al. show in a controlled text-derived setting that correlated features can make interference constructive and yield semantic clusters and cycles, challenging the reviewed paper's motivating picture that nonlinear thresholds mainly silence harmful interference between nonorthogonal features.

reviewed_competitors.title: Subspace-Aware Sparse Autoencoders for Effective Mechanistic Interpretability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dalili and Mahdavi replace one-vector SAE features with learned sparse subspaces, prove why multidimensional features split under ordinary SAEs, and evaluate GPT-2 and Mistral-7B. This offers a decomposable continuous alternative to both global directions and exponentially many discrete polytope regions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Encode Both Concepts and Functions: The Downstream Geometry of Feature Effects
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hoang et al. analyze clouds of downstream logit changes caused by feature interventions and find stable one-dimensional effects rare. Their causal effect geometry directly operationalizes the reviewed paper's unmeasured question of whether similar representation codes actually implement similar transformations.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Sander and Yorke study how infinitely many cascades organize in broad parameterized maps, including forced damped systems. Their theory emphasizes robust paired and solitary cascades rather than reducing every damped-driven system to one logistic family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linearly-Recurrent Autoencoder Networks for Learning Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Otto and Rowley learn low-dimensional Koopman-invariant latent dynamics with an autoencoder. The representation is linear rather than logistic and does not claim topological conjugacy, providing a broader predictive alternative with different guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Asymmetric unimodal maps with non-universal period-doubling scaling laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kozlovski and van Strien construct strongly asymmetric unimodal families whose period-doubling scalings are super-exponential and map-dependent. This directly refutes any inference from unimodality alone to the quadratic logistic scaling law.

reviewed_competitors.title: Topological conjugacy for unimodal nonautonomous discrete dynamical systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Araujo makes kneading sequences explicit as complete invariants under stated hypotheses. This highlights the combinatorial conditions the target never measures before asserting a logistic conjugacy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Koopman Operator Dynamical Models: Learning, Analysis and Control
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bevanda, Sosnowski, and Hirche review structured and unstructured Koopman learning and emphasize finite-approximation and well-posedness issues. It supplies a broader model-learning framework without assuming a logistic prototype.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning of Conjugate Mappings
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bramburger, Brunton, and Kutz introduced the autoencoder conjugacy architecture and evaluated it on Rossler, Lorenz, Gissinger, Kuramoto-Sivashinsky, and Mackey-Glass dynamics. The target largely reuses its method and repository but does not add a trained damped-driven example.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning the Koopman Eigendecomposition: A Diffeomorphic Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bevanda et al. learn a conjugacy to a stable linearization with a normalizing flow, so the coordinate transformation is diffeomorphic by construction and the resulting model remains asymptotically stable. That architectural guarantee predates and is stronger than the target's claim that a one-sided reconstruction loss ensures a homeomorphism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning normal form autoencoders for data-driven discovery of universal,parameter-dependent governing equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kalia et al. learn parameter-dependent coordinate transformations constrained by local Hopf, pitchfork, transcritical, and saddle-node normal forms. It more carefully treats parameterized families, whereas the target proposes independent logistic fitting without a family-level experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Walking droplets as a damped-driven system
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rahman and Kutz develop the averaged droplet gain-loss recurrence and period-doubling figures reused in the target. The target broadens the narrative to many domains but does not strengthen this precursor into a general conjugacy theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Damped-driven system of bouncing droplets leading to deterministic diffusive behavior
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rahman later reports an experimental and theoretical annular-droplet study with Gaussian velocity changes and Brownian-like or Levy-like motion. It improves domain evidence but studies stochastic-looking transport rather than validating the target's blanket logistic conjugacy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Testing topological conjugacy of time series
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dlotko, Lipinski, and Signerska-Rynkowska give finite-sample conjugacy tests with convergence as sample size grows, plus robustness and Takens-embedding diagnostics. Their explicit tests directly address the gap between small empirical residuals and a global conjugacy that the target leaves unsupported.

reviewed_competitors.title: Identifying Equivalent Training Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Redman et al. use Koopman spectra to identify conjugate and non-conjugate learning dynamics. Their explicit negative-equivalence tests illustrate the need to measure invariants rather than assume a chosen latent prototype is valid.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thermodynamic limit in learning period three
reviewed_competitors.difference: Terasaki and Nakajima study when quadratic neural interpolation produces a post-learning bifurcation scenario consistent with logistic conjugacy. The qualification to quadratic interpolation and the analysis of unstable learned periods are narrower and more explicit than the target's universal physical claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient pseudometrics for data-driven comparisons of nonlinear dynamical systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bryan Glaz quantifies deviation from topological conjugacy using Koopman spectra and trajectory geometry. The pseudometrics provide the type of graded equivalence test missing from the target's schematic finite-sample losses.

reviewed_competitors.title: Characterizing Nonlinear Dynamics via Smooth Prototype Equivalences
reviewed_competitors.difference: Friedman et al. use invertible neural networks to learn smooth phase-space deformations to prototype dynamics and evaluate noisy sparse observations. Architectural invertibility directly addresses the target's unsupported claim that a reconstruction penalty ensures a homeomorphism.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Improved Autoencoder Conjugacy Network to Learn Chaotic Maps
reviewed_competitors.difference: Carney et al. improve the predecessor conjugacy autoencoder with a tent-map layer and explicit treatment of well-known versus defective conjugacies. Their stability-focused comparisons and public code sharpen precisely the numerical weaknesses the target leaves unevaluated.

reviewed_competitors.title: Topological Entropy for Power-Law Unimodal Maps
reviewed_competitors.difference: Benedicks and Rodrigues extend monotone kneading and entropy results to arbitrary power-law critical exponents. The nontrivial dependence on criticality shows why a generic physical loss curve cannot inherit quadratic-family structure from unimodality alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Recurrence, symbolic dynamics, and wild attractors for unimodal maps
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alvin and Činč construct high-critical-order unimodal families with wild attractors and varied recurrent combinatorics. This current theory reinforces that 'unimodal' contains far richer behavior than a single logistic normal-form claim suggests.

reviewed_competitors.difference: AI Feynman recursively exploits dimensional regularities, separability, symmetry, and neural fits to solve multivariate equations and uses an MDL-inspired selection rule. ESR sacrifices that reach for an exact low-node grammar scan and replaces its fixed real-number precision with Fisher-scaled parameter costs, although ESR's own code has a derived constant omission.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symbolic Regression by Exhaustive Search: Reducing the Search Space Using Syntactical Constraints and Efficient Semantic Structure Deduplication
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kammerer et al. enumerate a grammar under syntactic restrictions, fit constants by nonlinear least squares, use semantic deduplication, and prioritize promising expansions to reach good functions earlier. ESR instead systematically covers every fixed-node tree and retains full rankings, but is slower to first strong solution and similarly depends on grammar scope and numerical fitting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Contemporary Symbolic Regression Methods and their Relative Performance
reviewed_competitors.difference: SRBench evaluates 14 symbolic and seven conventional regressors over 252 ground-truth and black-box problems with noise and reproducibility guidance. ESR selects one SRBench task, so it supplies a useful exact local oracle but does not meet the breadth needed for a field-level superiority claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Symbolic Regression that Scales
reviewed_competitors.difference: NeSymReS pretrains a set-to-sequence Transformer on procedurally generated equations and amortizes inference across tasks, trading a learned equation prior and training distribution for rapid multivariate prediction. ESR is task-specific and exponentially bounded but can certify that every expression in its declared low-complexity grammar was considered.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unified Framework for Deep Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: The unified framework combines recursive simplification, neural-guided search, large-scale pretraining, genetic programming, and linear methods and evaluates 252 tasks. It targets higher recovery and scale without exhaustive guarantees; ESR offers exact low-complexity fronts that could serve as an oracle or initializer for such hybrids.

reviewed_competitors.title: End-to-end Symbolic Regression with Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kamienny et al. directly decode expression skeletons and constants with a Transformer, then optionally refine constants, achieving orders-of-magnitude faster inference on SRBench. ESR avoids reliance on a synthetic pretraining prior inside its small grammar but incurs fresh exhaustive enumeration and fitting per operator set.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Generative Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: DGSR learns equation invariances in a conditional generative model and refines it at inference, emphasizing scalability to more input variables and efficient reuse. ESR remains univariate and exact only under a fixed small grammar, but its result set is transparent and independent of a learned latent equation distribution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Science with PySR and SymbolicRegression.jl
reviewed_competitors.difference: PySR uses distributed populations with evolve-simplify-optimize loops, user-defined operators, and broad science-facing tooling, scaling to larger and multivariate expressions without completeness. ESR directly benchmarks PySR and can expose missed low-complexity optima, while PySR is far more practical outside ESR's node budget and now has a broader EmpiricalBench evaluation target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformer-based Planning for Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: TPSR inserts Monte Carlo tree search into Transformer decoding so actual fit and complexity feedback guide a pretrained proposal model. It reaches higher spaces and integrates non-differentiable goals but cannot certify full coverage; ESR is a clean oracle for the low-complexity portion TPSR traverses.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symbolic Regression with a Learned Concept Library
reviewed_competitors.difference: LaSR induces reusable textual concepts with zero-shot LLM queries and injects them into evolutionary search, reporting gains on Feynman and synthetic tasks and a new scaling law. It deliberately prioritizes a tiny knowledge-guided part of expression space; ESR covers its declared small space uniformly and exposes how priors versus completeness change discovery.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving Monte Carlo Tree Search for Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: This MCTS method adds extreme bandit allocation with finite-time assumptions and mutation/crossover state jumps to seek globally strong expressions without sequential-search stagnation. It offers favorable recovery and accuracy-complexity frontiers over broad datasets, whereas ESR gives a literal finite-space guarantee but becomes unusable at the larger complexities MCTS targets.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bayesian Symbolic Regression with Entropic Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: ERRLESS learns a maximum-entropy policy whose rollouts approximate a posterior over expression trees, directly representing structural uncertainty and natural priors. ESR ranks a finite catalogue with an approximate two-part score and only proposes posterior-style functional weighting; it does not sample a normalized Bayesian posterior or marginalize parameters.

reviewed_competitors.title: VaSST: Variational Inference for Symbolic Regression using Soft Symbolic Trees
reviewed_competitors.difference: VaSST replaces discrete operator and feature choices with distributions in soft symbolic trees and optimizes a variational posterior by gradients, enabling structural uncertainty over enormous spaces. ESR retains exact discrete coverage and auditable expressions only inside a much smaller grammar and provides no coherent posterior uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Bardone and Goldt analyze why nominally expensive pth-cumulant directions can become learnable sooner when latent variables shared across cumulant orders are correlated, deriving near-sharp online-SGD sample thresholds. reviewed_competitors.difference: Szekely et al. use a spiked-cumulant model to separate statistical distinguishability, low-degree computational limits, random features, and feature-learning neural networks. It supplies sample-complexity structure absent from the original curve-collapse study and shows that representation learning can access high-order signal in regimes where lazy methods fail.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang, Saxe, and Latham explain increasing functional complexity through visits to invariant manifolds and saddles, with rank, ReLU kinks, convolutional kernels, or attention heads added over time. It is not a moment hierarchy, but it offers an architecture-level mechanism that can produce staged learning and explicitly separates data- and initialization-induced effects.

reviewed_competitors.difference: JumpReLU directly learns discontinuous activation thresholds and an L0 sparsity target, improving the fidelity-sparsity frontier over vanilla, gated, and TopK SAEs. reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang and colleagues systematically show that standard stochastic training can fit random labels and random pixels without explicit regularization. reviewed_competitors.difference: Hardt, Recht, and Singer use algorithmic stability—sensitivity to replacing a training example—to derive generalization bounds for convex and nonconvex stochastic gradient methods under stated smoothness and iteration conditions. The reviewed paper instead uses local parameter flatness and supplies no population-risk or sample-replacement bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharp Minima Can Generalize For Deep Nets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dinh and colleagues construct functionally equivalent ReLU networks with arbitrarily different sharpness through parameter symmetries. That directly invalidates treating the reviewed paper's raw Euclidean parameter-stability radius or basin volume as an intrinsic property of the predictor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Flatness Does and Does Not Correlate with Generalization for Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang and colleagues show that parameter rescaling and optimizers including Adam can break popular flatness-generalization correlations, and propose the initialization-induced Bayesian function prior as a more robust predictor. The reviewed paper uses Adam experimentally but does not test whether its stability measure survives either challenge.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign Overfitting without Linearity: Neural Network Classifiers Trained by Gradient Descent for Noisy Linear Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Frei, Chatterji, and Bartlett prove that nonlinear two-layer networks trained by gradient descent can interpolate adversarially corrupted labels while achieving minimax-optimal test error under explicit distributional separation. This refutes the reviewed paper's broad heuristic that reaching a global or interpolating solution is generally undesirable.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Implicit Regularization of Dynamical Stability in Stochastic Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu and Su distinguish linear and loss stability, derive Hessian constraints, and obtain model-specific generalization results for two-layer ReLU and diagonal linear networks. Crucially, they prove stability-induced regularization of deterministic GD is too weak for satisfactory generalization while SGD can be stronger, directly opposing the reviewed paper's universal GD conclusion.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stable Minima Cannot Overfit in Univariate ReLU Networks: Generalization by Large Step Sizes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiao and colleagues prove a nearly optimal generalization rate from constant-step minima stability for a specific univariate two-layer ReLU regression problem, connecting step size to bounded function variation. It demonstrates what a valid stability-to-risk theorem needs while sharply limiting architecture, dimension, loss, and data assumptions absent from the reviewed proof.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization Below the Edge of Stability: The Role of Data Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liang and colleagues derive generalization bounds that adapt to intrinsic dimension and show that easily shattered spherical data can favor memorization. reviewed_competitors.title: Stable Minima of ReLU Neural Networks Suffer from the Curse of Dimensionality: The Neural Shattering Phenomenon
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liang, Qiao, Wang, and Parhi prove upper and lower bounds showing that flatness-based generalization rates for multivariate ReLU networks can deteriorate exponentially with input dimension and lag low-norm solutions. This is the opposite of the reviewed paper's informal claim that high dimension automatically makes stable generalizing attractors overwhelmingly dominant.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sparse autoencoders learn an overcomplete feature dictionary from language-model activations and report more monosemantic, interpretable directions plus finer causal localization on an indirect-object task. This moves beyond single neurons and CNNs, but automated interpretability remains extensional and reconstruction-sparsity choices do not guarantee concept identity.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Neural Activations to Concepts: A Survey on Explaining Concepts in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later survey covers extracting concept knowledge and inserting concepts into architectures across vision, language, neuro-symbolic learning, and reasoning. It is a substantially broader map of the field than the three-method philosophical perspective, though the source's extension-intension critique remains a useful lens for assessing its many methods.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, 2024-05-03; accepted in Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence

reviewed_competitors.title: Explainable Concept Generation through Vision-Language Preference Learning for Understanding Neural Networks' Internal Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: The ICML 2025 method frames concept-set construction as image generation and uses preference optimization to articulate difficult visual concepts, reducing manual guessing and collection for TCAV-like analysis. It expands candidate extensions rather than solving the source's deeper intension problem, and generative-model priors can introduce new artifacts.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evaluating Adversarial Robustness of Concept Representations in Sparse Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: This study operationalizes robustness with input-space optimization and finds that tiny perturbations can manipulate SAE concept interpretations while leaving base-model activations largely unchanged. It provides the kind of adversarial fidelity test absent from the source's proposed qualitative triangulation and shows that apparent interpretability can be fragile even for newer distributed-feature methods.

reviewed_competitors.title: Capturing Polysemanticity with PRISM: A Multi-Concept Feature Description Framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: PRISM explicitly rejects one-label-per-neuron assumptions and clusters then scores multiple concepts for a polysemantic LLM feature. It directly targets a failure mode the source recognizes but does not methodologically solve; its descriptions still depend on sampled activations, automated labels, and robustness evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Descriptive Collision in Sparse Autoencoder Auto-Interpretability: When One Explanation Describes Many Features
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper formalizes the inverse of familiar polysemanticity: many distinct SAE features receive the same natural-language description. Its discrimination metric and empirical collision rates make the source's extension-to-meaning underdetermination quantitatively testable for modern auto-interpretability, although it audits descriptions rather than establishing intensional content.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics-informed machine learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct prior review of physics-informed learning, operator regression, forward and inverse problems, applications, limitations, and benchmark needs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is narrower than Huang et al.'s four-decade neural-PDE history but offers a more explicit physics-data integration framework and limitations agenda. Because it appeared in 2021 and is cited by the reviewed paper, the claim that a comprehensive review was still lacking must be read as a claim about the authors' broader taxonomy, not absence of major reviews.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scientific Machine Learning through Physics-Informed Neural Networks: Where we are and What's next
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct prior PINN survey covering vanilla, conservative, variational, and other collocation-based variants, their applications, advantages, disadvantages, and unresolved theory.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cuomo et al. is narrower because it does not center neural operators, but it gives a more detailed PINN method taxonomy and a more candid limitations treatment. It was current before Huang et al.'s submission and further weakens any literal no-comprehensive-review claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine Learning for Partial Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later broad review of machine learning for PDE discovery, reduced coordinates and models, solution operators, and improvement of traditional numerical algorithms.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Brunton and Kutz organize the field by scientific task rather than mainly by PINNs versus neural operators, so they cover discovery and numerical augmentation more centrally and avoid presenting neural methods as a single replacement paradigm.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Survey on Solving and Discovering Differential Equations Using Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later DNN-DE survey that explicitly separates solving from discovery, proposes an application taxonomy, and supplies a DeepXDE tutorial.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jung et al. is less centered on operator learning but is more reproducible pedagogically because it demonstrates a concrete forward and inverse transport-equation workflow. Its task distinction repairs one of Huang et al.'s principal taxonomic conflations.

reviewed_competitors.title: From PINNs to PIKANs: Recent Advances in Physics-Informed Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A current review of PINN architecture, feature expansion, adaptive refinement, domain decomposition, optimization, uncertainty, applications, and software.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is substantially narrower than the historical PINN-plus-operator scope, but much more current and technically granular about why PINNs train poorly and how later architectures and tooling address those problems.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Physics-informed Neural Networks: A Survey
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A focused current survey of transfer-learning and meta-learning approaches for PINN convergence and rapid adaptation across PDE parameters.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It directly addresses the re-optimization limitation that Huang et al. identify but sometimes obscure with broad claims about neural transfer. Its scope is specialized, while its problem statement is more precise about when a PINN must be retrained.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conditional Physics Informed Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kovacs et al. already condition a PINN on parameters defining a class of eigenvalue problems and learn eigenfunctions and eigenvalues without labels, demonstrated for micromagnetic coercivity. The reviewed paper specializes this conditional-eigenproblem idea to an all-electron molecular Coulomb Hamiltonian and adds atomic-orbital cusps, LCAO asymptotics, inversion symmetry, and force differentiation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Quantum Eigenvalue Problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jin, Mattheakis, and Protopapas develop the immediate PINN predecessor, including normalization, orthogonality, parity, multiple eigenstates, and hydrogen-atom tests. The H₂⁺ paper extends that family to a geometry-conditioned molecular surface and explicit Coulomb/LCAO features, but narrows evaluation to one ground-state system.

reviewed_competitors.title: Ab-Initio Solution of the Many-Electron Schrödinger Equation with Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: FermiNet uses an antisymmetric neural ansatz and variational Monte Carlo to reach high accuracy on atoms, molecules, and difficult dissociation curves with many electrons. It is vastly more chemically general and variationally safe, but expensive and historically optimized per geometry; the reviewed PINN is cheap and continuously conditioned on R, yet only proves the one-electron case.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Neural Network Solution of the Electronic Schrödinger Equation
reviewed_competitors.difference: PauliNet embeds Hartree-Fock structure, antisymmetry, cusps, and variational Monte Carlo into a many-electron wavefunction with near-exact small-molecule results. Both approaches emphasize physical priors, but PauliNet addresses fermionic correlation and variational energies while the reviewed method targets a label-free PDE residual and a single differentiable geometry surface.

reviewed_competitors.title: Ab-Initio Potential Energy Surfaces by Pairing GNNs with Neural Wave Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: PESNet predates the reviewed work's submission and jointly solves many-electron Schrödinger equations across continuous geometries using a geometry GNN plus variational neural wavefunction, reporting up to 40× multi-geometry training speedups. The H₂⁺ PINN offers direct differentiable energy inference without Monte Carlo and exact single-electron cusp features, but its broad parametric-surface positioning overlaps substantially and its evidence is much narrower.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sampling-Free Inference for Ab-Initio Potential Energy Surface Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: PlaNet pairs a variational neural wavefunction with an energy surrogate to avoid Monte Carlo at inference and reports seven-order inference acceleration plus improved PESNet++ errors on larger molecules. It tackles the same cheap energy-surface goal with many-electron evidence; the reviewed energy head is simpler and differentiable but can violate the variational bound and lacks a consistency-training mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalizing Neural Wave Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Globe and Moon extend generalized neural wavefunctions across molecules with different atoms and enforce size consistency, reporting 4.5× fewer steps or lower energies. This directly addresses composition and scaling dimensions left open by the fixed-composition H₂⁺ PINN, though it retains variational Monte Carlo cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: Variational Monte Carlo on a Budget — Fine-Tuning Pre-Trained Neural Wavefunctions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scherbela et al. pretrain a self-supervised equivariant neural wavefunction across chemically diverse molecules, demonstrate zero-shot transfer, and improve accuracy further with brief fine-tuning. It supplies the broad held-out-system evaluation absent here, while the reviewed PINN remains appealing for cheap continuous derivatives if its one-electron formulation can be generalized.

reviewed_competitors.difference: NCA directly optimizes a stochastic leave-one-out nearest-neighbor objective and learns an explicit low-rank linear transform, with quantitative comparisons and out-of-sample projection. GDR instead moves the labeled training samples themselves, has no predictive objective or inductive map, and does not compare against NCA.

reviewed_competitors.title: Distance Metric Learning for Large Margin Nearest Neighbor Classification
reviewed_competitors.difference: LMNN learns a positive semidefinite Mahalanobis metric that pulls target neighbors together while separating impostors by a margin and evaluates held-out kNN accuracy across datasets. GDR has only within-class attraction, no between-class margin, no learned test-time metric, and no held-out evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Joint Dimensionality Reduction and Metric Learning: A Geometric Take
reviewed_competitors.difference: DRML learns a low-dimensional mapping and metric jointly on a Riemannian optimization domain, reporting runtime and predictive accuracy against major metric-learning baselines. GDR uses geometry terminology but fixes PCA to three dimensions, does not learn the metric tensor, and supplies neither a joint objective nor quantitative comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction
reviewed_competitors.difference: UMAP defines attractive and repulsive neighborhood objectives from an explicit manifold-learning construction, scales to real datasets, supports general embedding dimensions, and has supervised and transform extensions in its implementation lineage. GDR uses only same-class attraction and can manufacture separation by destroying intra-class geometry, without measuring neighborhood preservation or out-of-sample quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Steering Distortions to Preserve Classes and Neighbors in Supervised Dimensionality Reduction
reviewed_competitors.difference: ClassNeRV explicitly balances class separation against false- and missed-neighbor distortions and compares against nine alternatives. That tradeoff directly addresses GDR's unmeasured destruction of within-class structure; GDR optimizes contraction alone and offers no neighbor-preservation control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Force2Vec: Parallel force-directed graph embedding
reviewed_competitors.difference: Force2Vec operationalizes attractive and repulsive layout forces as a graph-embedding objective, maps computation to parallel linear algebra, reports up to billion-edge scaling, and evaluates visualization plus downstream tasks. It demonstrates that physical-force-inspired embeddings predate GDR and that such an analogy can be paired with scalability and quantitative validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Enhancing Supervised Visualization through Autoencoder and Random Forest Proximities for Out-of-Sample Extension
reviewed_competitors.difference: This RF-PHATE extension uses an autoencoder to learn a label-free map for unseen points, quantitatively evaluates alternative reconstruction targets, and reports consistent quality using a subset of training data. It directly addresses the out-of-sample limitation GDR leaves as future work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Boosting Mapping for Dimensionality Reduction and Feature Extraction
reviewed_competitors.difference: GBMAP learns explicit low-dimensional supervised features from simple weak learners, evaluates prediction and distance quality, detects distribution shift, and reports million-sample timing. It is a current alternative when the goal is discriminative, human-inspectable coordinates rather than transductive collapse of labeled samples.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Koopman Operator of Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dietrich, Thiem, and Kevrekidis treat gradient descent, Nesterov, Newton, and other algorithms with data-driven Koopman analysis and acceleration. This establishes that the optimizer-as-Koopman-system framing predates QuACK; it does not address variational quantum circuits, shots, noisy candidate selection, or hardware query savings.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv:1907.10807v3; SIAM Journal on Applied Dynamical Systems 2020

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimizing Neural Networks via Koopman Operator Theory
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dogra and Redman predict neural-network weights and biases over a training window and report more than 10x acceleration versus several optimizers. QuACK transfers that trajectory-skipping idea to VQAs and introduces quantum-query accounting and blockwise measured selection, but does not establish a general long-horizon advantage over this prior paradigm.

reviewed_competitors.title: Accelerating Training in Artificial Neural Networks with Dynamic Mode Decomposition
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tano, Portwood, and Ragusa already run a few exact backpropagation steps, fit POD/DMD, extrapolate toward a converged state, resume exact training, and refit. That is the closest pre-QuACK alternating exact-update/DMD-jump/restart skeleton. QuACK's distinct contribution is VQA adaptation, measured candidate selection, QNG motivation, and quantum resource analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Using models to improve optimizers for variational quantum algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sung et al. reuse noisy VQA evaluations in local quadratic trust-region models for model gradient and policy-gradient optimization, and emphasize experimentally relevant cloud cost models and hyperparameter tuning. It lacks DMD trajectory rollout but is a stronger direct baseline for whether QuACK beats generic history reuse under realistic noise and wall-clock accounting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stochastic Gradient Line Bayesian Optimization for Efficient Noise-Robust Optimization of Parameterized Quantum Circuits
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tamiya and Yamasaki combine stochastic-gradient directions with Bayesian step-size selection, adaptive shots, and suffix averaging. They directly optimize shot efficiency and noise robustness without long recursive trajectory forecasts. This is a pre-QuACK baseline for the same scarce-measurement objective that the paper cites but does not compare empirically.

reviewed_competitors.title: Surrogate-based optimization for variational quantum algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shaffer, Kocia, and Sarovar reconstruct local patches of noisy variational objectives with kernel approximations and optimize the surrogate on QAOA and molecular ground-state tasks. The method models the loss rather than a raw optimizer trajectory and provides a natural trust-region/uncertainty comparison missing from QuACK.

reviewed_competitors.title: Faster variational quantum algorithms with quantum kernel-based surrogate models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Smith, Paige, and Kim posted this hours before QuACK v1 and use a Gaussian-process surrogate with a classically evaluated quantum kernel to reduce VQE quantum queries under noiseless and noisy simulation. It forecasts objective structure rather than optimizer steps and reports less than an order-of-magnitude query reduction, making it a close contemporary alternative omitted from QuACK's comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: Koopman Analysis of Quantum Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Klus, Nueske, and Peitz develop data-driven Koopman and stochastic-control tools for quantum systems, including stationary and imaginary-time Schrodinger problems. It establishes the quantum/Koopman/imaginary-time connection before QuACK, but does not learn VQA outer-loop parameter trajectories or quantify gradient-query savings.

reviewed_competitors.title: DyPP: Dynamic Parameter Prediction to Accelerate Convergence of Variational Quantum Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kundu and Ghosh exploit regular trends in VQA parameters with naive and adaptive prediction, reporting roughly 2-3x acceleration and fewer shots across QNN, VQE, and QAOA tasks including hardware noise. It is simpler than DMD and directly tests whether generic dynamic parameter prediction suffices, but does not provide Koopman motivation or QuACK's blockwise candidate search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Observation Cost Control for Variational Quantum Eigensolvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Anders et al.'s SubsCoRe uses a Gaussian-process surrogate to keep an updated subspace within a confidence region and allocates the minimum observations needed for prescribed accuracy. It addresses the candidate-uncertainty and shot-allocation problems left uncontrolled by QuACK, though it is built around sequential minimal optimization rather than trajectory rollout.

reviewed_competitors.title: PALQO: Physics-informed Model for Accelerating Large-scale Quantum Optimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: clearest direct successor and partial independent benchmark
reviewed_competitors.difference: PALQO fits a PDE-informed neural model to short VQA trajectories, scales experiments to 40 qubits, reports up to 30x acceleration and 90% resource reduction, and independently implements a QuACK DMD baseline. Its reported shot counts favor PALQO on 20-qubit TFIM/Heisenberg and 14-qubit BeH2, and it explicitly criticizes QuACK's energy evaluation at every predicted step. It does not faithfully reproduce all five QuACK variants or the original headline claims and remains simulation/shot-estimate evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: TITAN: A Trajectory-Informed Technique for Adaptive Parameter Freezing in Large-Scale VQE
reviewed_competitors.difference: TITAN cites QuACK but uses early trajectory features to freeze inactive parameters, reporting up to 3x faster convergence and 40-60% fewer circuit evaluations through 30 qubits. It reduces future gradient dimension rather than forecasting full parameter blocks, so the methods are complementary and the evidence is not a QuACK replication.

reviewed_competitors.title: Accelerating Noisy Variational Quantum Algorithms with Physics-Informed Denoising Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu and Wang train a physics-informed denoiser to reproduce zero-noise-extrapolated expectations and gradient directions from noisy observations and history, reporting four- to six-fold fewer circuit executions and gradient cosine similarity above 0.95. It targets error-mitigation cost rather than gradient-block skipping and provides explicit directional validation absent from QuACK's noisy best-candidate study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Nested-Loop Trajectory-Informed Variational Quantum Solver for Interior-Point OPF
reviewed_competitors.difference: This application-specific method uses an LSTM on a short VQLS parameter prefix to jump toward a lower-cost region and then resumes optimization, reporting up to 95.2% fewer variational updates and a two-bus IBM demonstration. It does not cite QuACK and is evaluated only on 2-12-bus OPF systems, so it is conceptual convergence rather than replication.

reviewed_competitors.title: Computing Linear Restrictions of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: ExactLine computes the exact affine partition of a piecewise-linear network along an entire line segment and applies it to verification and attribution.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ExactLine certifies an existing network without changing it, whereas POLICE modifies biases during training to create one affine region over a higher-dimensional convex polytope.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linearly Constrained Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Guarantees that learned vector fields obey known linear differential-operator constraints by applying a null-space-compatible transformation to a neural potential.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It enforces a specified global physical operator identity, while POLICE constrains local input-output geometry to an unspecified affine map on one region.

reviewed_competitors.title: DC3: A Learning Method for Optimization with Hard Constraints
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Uses differentiable completion for equality constraints and iterative correction for inequalities so neural optimization surrogates return feasible solutions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DC3 enforces task-specific output feasibility and evaluates optimal power flow; POLICE instead restricts the functional form over an input region and has zero recurring inference correction after bias folding.

reviewed_competitors.title: RAYEN: Imposition of Hard Convex Constraints on Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Enforces combinations of linear, quadratic, second-order-cone, and matrix-inequality constraints on network outputs or latents for every input.
reviewed_competitors.difference: RAYEN covers rich convex feasible sets with measured optimization benchmarks; POLICE covers the orthogonal requirement that the entire mapping itself remain affine over a specified input polytope.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hard-Constrained Neural Networks with Universal Approximation Guarantees
reviewed_competitors.relationship: HardNet appends a differentiable projection layer for input-dependent affine and convex output constraints while proving retained universal approximation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: HardNet directly studies the constraint-capacity tradeoff and prescribed feasible outputs; POLICE eliminates all internal breakpoints within R and gives no universal approximation result for that restricted class.

reviewed_competitors.title: ENFORCE: Exact Nonlinear Constrained Learning with Adaptive-depth Neural Projection
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Uses adaptive differentiable local projections to satisfy nonlinear C1 equality constraints in both inputs and outputs to a requested tolerance.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ENFORCE broadens constraints beyond affine and convex forms at recurring projection cost; POLICE's narrower CPA-region guarantee can be folded into biases for zero inference overhead.

reviewed_competitors.title: CAffNet: Hard Constraint-Affine Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A current method inserts trainable constraint-affine layers into feedforward networks and transformers for arbitrary-cardinality input-dependent affine constraints.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CAffNet targets specified equality and inequality feasibility while preserving universal approximation; POLICE predates it and targets local affinity of the whole mapping through vertex-conditioned bias projection.

reviewed_competitors.title: POLICEd RL: Learning Closed-Loop Robot Control Policies with Provable Satisfaction of Hard Constraints
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Directly builds on POLICE by making a learned policy affine in a repulsive buffer near an unsafe set and deriving closed-loop safety conditions for black-box environments.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies the realistic downstream control semantics absent from the original paper: affinity is only one component, and additional repulsiveness, dynamics, and boundary conditions are required for an actual safety guarantee.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Happens after SGD Reaches Zero Loss? --A Mathematical Framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Wang, and Arora adapt Katzenberger's framework to characterize small-step SGD motion on minimizer manifolds with arbitrary covariance. Flatter, Faster extends that projection analysis to heavy-ball momentum and adds the competing relaxation times that produce the 2/3 rule.

reviewed_competitors.title: Label Noise SGD Provably Prefers Flat Global Minimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damian, Ma, and Lee derive an explicit sharpness-penalizing regularized loss, including finite-step and momentum extensions. Their focus is convergence and implicit regularization rather than optimizing the coupled eta-beta asymptotic transport speed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Inertia: Disentangling the Effects of Adaptive Learning Rate and Momentum
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xie et al.'s diffusion analysis argues conventional momentum mainly assists saddle escape and almost does not alter flat-minimum selection, motivating parameter-wise adaptive inertia. Flatter, Faster instead finds that momentum can dramatically accelerate label-noise transport toward flatter points after interpolation; the different noise and phase assumptions need a direct reconciliation.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Quasistatic Derivation of Optimization Algorithms' Exploration on Minima Manifolds
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ma, Kunin, and Ying derive intuitive effective dynamics for SGD, SGDm, and Adam under multiple covariance structures and argue joint learning-rate/batch scaling accelerates exploration without changing generalization. It covers more optimizers and noises, while Flatter, Faster supplies a more formal momentum-specific limit and a distinct 2/3 coupling claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does Momentum Help in Stochastic Optimization? A Sample Complexity Analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ganesh et al. account for both bias and variance on quadratics and show stochastic heavy-ball and accelerated SGD do not always beat vanilla SGD in sample complexity. This directly cautions against reading the post-interpolation 2/3 mechanism as a general stochastic-optimization acceleration theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: When and Why Momentum Accelerates SGD: An Empirical Study
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fu et al. compare SGD and SGDM at matched effective learning rate and batch size and attribute momentum's advantage to avoiding or delaying abrupt sharpening/edge-of-stability behavior. It studies practical from-scratch training and supplies an alternative mechanism; its ICLR 2024 submission was withdrawn.

reviewed_competitors.title: Large Catapults in Momentum Gradient Descent with Warmup: An Empirical Study
reviewed_competitors.difference: Phunyaphibarn et al. find that warmup plus heavy-ball momentum amplifies catapults and drives networks toward flatter minima through self-stabilization. That large-learning-rate transient mechanism lies outside Flatter, Faster's small-noise, small-eta, near-manifold diffusion regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Momentum Further Constrains Sharpness at the Edge of Stochastic Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Andreyev et al. report two batch-size-dependent momentum sharpness plateaus, 2(1-beta)/eta for small batches and 2(1+beta)/eta for large batches, which cannot be reduced to one momentum-adjusted threshold. Their finite-batch edge-of-stochastic-stability picture is a strong modern test of when the 2/3 label-noise scaling should or should not transfer.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Sukenik et al. show that beyond two layers or two classes, regularization's low-rank bias can beat deep neural collapse in the standard unconstrained-features model. It reinforces the need to monitor rank rather than interpreting falling pseudoinverse-based D as unambiguously better separation.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. report layer inequality, depth-dependent redundancy, and architecture-specific memorization behavior on clean and noisy data.
