reviewed_competitors.title: Path-SGD: Path-Normalized Optimization in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Path-SGD explicitly designs an optimization geometry invariant to neuron rescaling. RWF instead introduces an unconstrained scale symmetry and evaluates Euclidean effective-weight movement; Path-SGD is the stronger precedent for asking whether an update is parameterization invariant.

reviewed_competitors.title: Weight Normalization: A Simple Reparameterization to Accelerate Training of Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Weight normalization decouples learned magnitude and unit direction through w=g v/||v||. RWF removes the normalization, samples a positive per-neuron scale, and initializes the complementary factor to preserve W; it is related but not recovered merely by assigning s=||w||.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Optimization of Deep Networks: Implicit Acceleration by Overparameterization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arora, Cohen, and Hazan analyze how overparameterization can induce acceleration in matrix factorization under specified dynamics. It predates RWF's geometric motivation and illustrates the kind of trajectory-level theorem missing from the target's zero-distance argument.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rahaman et al. characterize frequency-dependent learning in neural networks and motivate direct Fourier-domain diagnostics. RWF cites this phenomenon but substitutes one final NTK eigenspectrum for a frequency-resolved or temporal test.

reviewed_competitors.title: Frequency Principle: Fourier Analysis Sheds Light on Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The frequency-principle work measures lower-to-higher frequency learning behavior directly. It supports the target's problem motivation but also highlights the absence of frequency-aligned measurements in RWF's causal claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive activation functions accelerate convergence in deep and physics-informed neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adaptive activations insert learned slopes into nonlinearities and are a direct baseline in the target. RWF instead scales weight vectors while preserving the effective initial W, but the comparison lacks matched search and seed analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: SIREN combines sine activations with a frequency multiplier and tailored initialization to represent signals and derivatives. RWF's appendix varies the multiplier but does not isolate it from the activation and initialization, so its claim that scaling is the crucial cause is unresolved.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fourier features reshape the effective kernel through an input embedding and supply many of the target's data sets. RWF is often evaluated on top of a selected Fourier map, so the reported result does not isolate output-weight scaling from input-spectrum design.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multiplicative Filter Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: MFNs use multiplicative filters and structured bases to represent high-frequency continuous signals. They provide an architectural alternative to RWF's optimizer-oriented scaling and were already established before the target's submission.

reviewed_competitors.title: BACON: Band-limited Coordinate Networks for Multiscale Scene Representation
reviewed_competitors.difference: BACON builds explicit multiscale band limits and intermediate outputs into a coordinate network. It attacks fine-detail and scale control through representational structure rather than a learned weight gauge, providing a direct alternative for several target tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding
reviewed_competitors.difference: Instant-NGP obtains major neural-field speedups through a multiresolution hash encoding and fused implementation. It is a stronger systems baseline for the target's acceleration language, though it changes representation and hardware implementation rather than only parameterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: MuP formalizes parameterization choices that permit hyperparameter transfer across width. It is not an INR method, but it is a relevant predecessor to broad drop-in and transfer claims because it distinguishes parameterization-specific learning-rate scaling with explicit theory and tests.

reviewed_competitors.title: Residual Multiplicative Filter Networks for Multiscale Reconstruction
reviewed_competitors.difference: Residual MFNs add skip connections and frequency-aware initialization for coarse-to-fine reconstruction and inverse problems. They were submitted four months before RWF and offer a targeted multiscale architecture rather than an unconstrained learned scale factor.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Activation Function Dependence of the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hong et al. theoretically connect ReLU spectral bias to finite-element behavior and propose Hat activations to remove it in tested settings. This predates the target by two months and offers activation-based theory and experiments rather than RWF's final-NTK inference.

reviewed_competitors.title: DINER: Disorder-Invariant Implicit Neural Representation
reviewed_competitors.difference: DINER learns a hash-table mapping to reduce dependence on spatial ordering and improve high-frequency fitting across inverse tasks. It followed RWF by about six weeks and changes the coordinate representation rather than the weight update geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: WIRE: Wavelet Implicit Neural Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: WIRE uses complex Gabor wavelet activations to combine spatial and frequency localization across imaging and 3D tasks. It is a direct post-target competitor for fine detail that changes the basis rather than factorizing every weight row.

reviewed_competitors.title: GaborPINN: Efficient physics informed neural networks using multiplicative filtered networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: GaborPINN embeds frequency-aware Gabor filters in multiplicative networks for Helmholtz wavefields and reports convergence improvements. It is a problem-structured PINN alternative whose mechanism is distinct from random neuron scales.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Expert's Guide to Training Physics-informed Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The same group later includes RWF-off ablations inside a stronger PINN training recipe, with task-dependent gains. This is valuable extension evidence but repeats the scalar theorem and is neither independent reproduction nor an isolation of RWF across the target's non-PINN tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: NeuRBF: A Neural Fields Representation with Adaptive Radial Basis Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: NeuRBF learns adaptive radial basis features for neural fields and evaluates geometry and appearance tasks. It offers localized adaptive capacity rather than a global dense-layer gauge and should be included in any current INR comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: FINER: Flexible spectral-bias tuning in Implicit NEural Representation by Variable-periodic Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: FINER uses variable-periodic activations to tune spectral bias and benchmarks multiple INR tasks. It directly targets the same high-frequency failure claim with an activation mechanism and later empirical scope.

reviewed_competitors.title: PirateNets: Physics-informed Deep Learning with Residual Adaptive Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: PirateNets incorporates RWF into residual adaptive PINNs with Fourier features and other training choices. It demonstrates that the factorization became part of a strong pipeline but does not independently verify the target's theory or full benchmark panel.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Alignment in Physics-informed Neural Networks: A Second-Order Optimization Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work diagnoses PINN training through gradient alignment and proposes second-order SOAP optimization while using PirateNet with RWF as a baseline ingredient. It offers a different optimization explanation and does not isolate RWF's contribution.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unified Theory of Sinusoidal Activation Families for Implicit Neural Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: The current TMLR version develops trainable sinusoidal activations, NTK-spectrum analysis, and broad INR experiments while explicitly concluding that periodic activations alleviate but do not eliminate spectral bias. It is a more current theory-and-benchmark alternative to RWF's SIREN attribution.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics-informed neural networks for solving moving interface flow problems using the level set approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: The level-set system uses PirateNet features including RWF, causal and sequence-to-sequence training, and Fourier embeddings. Its results show application uptake, but the composite architecture does not provide an RWF-on versus RWF-off validation of the target's mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: SMURF: Scalable method for unsupervised reconstruction of flow in 4D flow MRI
reviewed_competitors.difference: SMURF combines Fourier features and RWF in a likelihood-based continuous representation for segmentation and velocity reconstruction. It broadens application evidence but does not isolate random scales from the embedding, measurement model, or subsampling system.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical PINNs for Scientific Computing: A Multi-GPU Open-Source Framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: The current QPINNACLE framework includes RWF among Fourier features, strict boundaries, loss balancing, curricula, and second-order methods and emphasizes systematic compute benchmarking. Its present ablations do not reproduce the target's full RWF study, but it is a relevant current framework for the missing matched-cost validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Pitfalls of Simplicity Bias in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational simplicity-bias benchmark and failure result
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shah et al. construct settings where SGD-trained networks rely almost exclusively on a simple feature and fail extreme shifts. The target paper proposes feature replication as a reconciliation with evidence that backbones retain complex features, then intervenes at the classifier bottleneck.

reviewed_competitors.title: In Search of Lost Domain Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz introduce DomainBed and show that carefully tuned ERM is difficult to beat under controlled selection. The target paper uses this framework, but its conflicting SMA tables undermine the benchmark comparison that the protocol is meant to make auditable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fine-Tuning can Distort Pretrained Features and Underperform Out-of-Distribution
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kumar et al. show that linear probing before full fine-tuning can preserve pretrained OOD features and motivate LP-FT. FRR adopts that staging insight but changes the linear-probe objective to reconstruct features from logits and freezes the resulting head during backbone refinement.

reviewed_competitors.title: Last Layer Re-Training is Sufficient for Robustness to Spurious Correlations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kirichenko et al.'s DFR retrains the last layer on a small group-balanced set and demonstrates that ERM representations often retain core features. FRR avoids group labels and balanced data, but therefore lacks DFR's direct signal identifying which available features are robust.

reviewed_competitors.title: Evading the Simplicity Bias: Training a Diverse Set of Models Discovers Solutions with Superior OOD Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Teney et al. encourage models with diverse input-gradient explanations and use side information for model selection, explicitly emphasizing that IID data alone cannot identify the desired OOD solution. FRR returns one model from source data alone, but its reconstruction objective likewise cannot tell robust diversity from nuisance diversity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Overcoming Simplicity Bias in Deep Networks using a Feature Sieve
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tiwari and Shenoy iteratively identify learned features and prevent the network from reusing them so subsequent training exposes harder features. Feature Sieve operates through sequential feature suppression, while FRR tries to make a single classifier encode the frozen representation through its logits.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2023 PMLR volume 202 version of record

reviewed_competitors.title: Mitigating Simplicity Bias in Deep Learning for Improved OOD Generalization and Robustness
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vasudeva et al. first train a simple model and then use a conditional-mutual-information regularizer to make the final model exploit information beyond that model, with theoretical OOD analysis. This targets diversity relative to an explicit simple reference rather than reconstructing every backbone feature from logits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simplicity Bias via Global Convergence of Sharpness Minimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later theoretical support for replicated simple features
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gatmiry et al. prove in a narrow two-layer setting that label-noise SGD converges globally toward a network in which neurons replicate a single linear feature. This supplies a more explicit route to replication than the target paper, but does not validate FRR or its Adam-trained deep-network mechanism.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2024 PMLR volume 235 version of record

reviewed_competitors.title: Simplicity Bias of Two-Layer Networks beyond Linearly Separable Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tsoy and Konstantinov analyze two-layer gradient flow beyond separability and show hidden weights cluster around a small set of directions, with intermediate features sometimes generalizing better. Their result reinforces the need to study representation dynamics rather than infer a mechanism solely from final OOD accuracy.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2024 PMLR volume 235 version of record

reviewed_competitors.title: Complexity Matters: Feature Learning in the Presence of Spurious Correlations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later theory of core-versus-spurious feature learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qiu et al. vary relative feature complexity and correlation strength, finding separate core/spurious subnetworks and explaining both the success and limitations of last-layer retraining. Their controlled dynamics give alternative explanations for available-but-underused core features beyond coordinate replication.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2024 PMLR volume 235 version of record

reviewed_competitors.title: Infinitely deep neural networks as diffusion processes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Peluchetti and Favaro already establish that depth-scaled residual networks converge to diffusion processes and investigate their nondegenerate functional behavior. The reviewed paper applies a different iid-Gaussian architecture and develops explicit activation-dependent marginals, ReLU collapse, and norm laws; the core ResNet-to-SDE bridge itself is not new.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stable ResNet
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hayou et al. design depth-scaled Stable ResNets to control gradients and preserve expressivity, with infinite-width NNGP/NTK analysis and trained-image experiments. The reviewed paper moves to fixed finite width and a diffusion law, but its practical gradient and trainability evidence is far narrower.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Future is Log-Gaussian: ResNets and Their Infinite-Depth-and-Width Limit at Initialization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Nica, and Roy analyze the joint limit at fixed depth/width ratio, derive log-Gaussian behavior, quantify hypoactivation and interlayer correlations, and propose Balanced ResNets. The reviewed work instead takes depth first at fixed width and obtains activation-sensitive diffusions, so the regimes are complementary; it does not offer the competitor's architecture correction or joint finite-ratio fit.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Neural Covariance SDE: Shaped Infinite Depth-and-Width Networks at Initialization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Nica, and Roy derive an SDE for the random covariance matrix in a shaped joint depth-width limit and an if-and-only-if norm stability condition. That work directly treats multi-input covariance fluctuations, whereas the reviewed paper derives a fixed-width state SDE but leaves its correlation process essentially open.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling ResNets in the Large-depth Regime
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marion et al. characterize 1/sqrt(L) as the only nontrivial scaling under iid initialization, contrast it with 1/L under correlated smooth weights, and evaluate performance before and after training. The reviewed paper assumes rather than uniquely derives that iid scaling, provides finer fixed-width diffusion observables, and does not test trained performance.

reviewed_competitors.title: Width and Depth Limits Commute in Residual Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hayou and Yang explicitly prove that width and depth limits commute in 1/sqrt(depth)-scaled residual networks and that the same covariance structure arises independent of the route. It directly repairs or supersedes the reviewed v3's internally contradictory sequential-limit section while offering stronger simulations for arbitrary width-depth ratios.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural signature kernels as infinite-width-depth-limits of controlled ResNets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cirone, Lemercier, and Salvi extend finite-width depth limits and commutativity to controlled ResNets and Neural CDEs, derive path-indexed Gaussian kernels and PDEs, and distinguish shared from independent layer weights. The reviewed paper covers a simpler autonomous input setting and leaves its full kernel open.

reviewed_competitors.title: Commutative Width and Depth Scaling in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hayou formalizes commutative scaling for neural functions and proves covariance-kernel commutativity with non-stochastic-calculus methods under suitable branch scaling. This makes the reviewed paper best viewed as an earlier fixed-width diffusion analysis, not a settled comparison of sequential limits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs VI: Feature Learning in Infinite-Depth Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. classify depthwise block and learning-rate parameterizations under infinite-width-then-depth training limits, propose Depth-muP, and test feature learning and hyperparameter transfer including transformers. It addresses the training and parameterization questions the reviewed initialization-only finite-width paper explicitly leaves open, but in a different order of limits.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational activation-pattern enumeration and exact-ERM baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arora et al. already enumerate hyperplane-induced sign patterns and solve a polynomial convex subproblem for each pattern. The reviewed paper's defensible novelty is to expose the full oriented-arrangement and dual-zonotope incidence structure, not the combinatorial-convex decomposition itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tight Hardness Results for Training Depth-2 ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: hardness foundation directly modified by the reviewed paper
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goel et al. give worst-case exact and approximation hardness and proper-learning lower bounds using explicit set-cover-style constructions. The reviewed paper tries to extend one construction to general-position data, but its appendix omits the reverse implication required for the reduction.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Computational Complexity of ReLU Network Training Parameterized by Data Dimensionality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Froese et al. prove W[1]-hardness and ETH lower bounds matching the n^(O(d)) hyperplane-partition brute force across broad losses. This supplies a formal worst-case boundary for activation-pattern search; the reviewed paper instead proposes a geometric organization and an uncertified local heuristic.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Approximation Algorithm for Training One-Node ReLU Neural Network
reviewed_competitors.relationship: single-node activation-set search and approximation baseline
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dey, Wang, and Xie search candidate active sets using label information and prove approximation behavior for one ReLU. The reviewed GLS instead uses zonotope adjacency for multiple fixed-sign units but supplies neither an approximation ratio nor valid synthetic evidence of superiority.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks are Convex Regularizers: Exact Polynomial-time Convex Optimization Formulations for Two-layer Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pilanci and Ergen optimize all activation cones simultaneously through a group-l1 convex program for weight-decay-regularized two-layer networks, avoiding exponential dependence on hidden width but retaining rank or dimension dependence. This directly addresses trained output weights and stability that the reviewed fixed-v zonotope walk leaves outside its theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Hidden Convex Optimization Landscape of Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks: an Exact Characterization of the Optimal Solutions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Lacotte, and Pilanci use cone-constrained convex optimization to recover all global optima, test global optimality, and characterize widths without spurious valleys. Their framework treats jointly parameterized regularized networks; the reviewed paper offers a more elementary combinatorial picture but much weaker optimization guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Convex Geometry of Backpropagation: Neural Network Gradient Flows Converge to Extreme Points of the Dual Convex Program
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang and Pilanci relate nonconvex two-layer gradient flow to extreme points and KKT solutions of a dual convex program under explicit data conditions. This is a formal account of when gradient dynamics reach global solutions, whereas the reviewed paper's pseudo-annealing over zonotope vertices is only an informal hypothesis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fast Convex Optimization for Two-Layer ReLU Networks: Equivalent Model Classes and Cone Decompositions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mishkin, Sahiner, and Pilanci develop accelerated and augmented-Lagrangian solvers, gated-ReLU approximations, data-dependent bounds, runtime comparisons, and MNIST/CIFAR-10 experiments. It is a substantially stronger practical baseline than repeatedly calling a generic conic solver at neighboring vertices.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Global Optimization of Two-Layer ReLU Networks: Quadratic-Time Algorithms and Adversarial Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bai, Gautam, and Sojoudi provide ADMM and sampled-convex-program algorithms with convergence or approximate-global guarantees, quadratic per-iteration cost for the approximation, and adversarial-training extensions. The reviewed GLS has only per-step polynomiality and can take exponentially many costly steps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convex Relaxations of ReLU Neural Networks Approximate Global Optima in Polynomial Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kim and Pilanci bound the relative gap of regularized two-layer convex relaxations by O(sqrt(log n)) for random data and derive low-loss guarantees for local gradient methods. This offers a quantified average-case alternative to the reviewed paper's unproved suggestion that real activation-graph searches tend to be tractable.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convex Formulations for Training Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later exact copositive formulation and SDP relaxation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prakhya, Birdal, and Yurtsever exactly lift sufficiently wide or infinite-width training to a finite completely positive program, preserve the underlying NP-hardness, and evaluate a polynomial SDP relaxation on classification. It more cleanly separates convex representation from computational tractability than the reviewed paper's claim that a useful zonotope structure implies benign practical search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Simplicity Bias and Optimization Threshold in Two-Layer ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Boursier and Flammarion analyze an optimization threshold where overparameterized gradient dynamics favor a simpler noninterpolating solution with better test loss. This directly challenges the reviewed paper's reliance on exact training fit as the target and highlights why training-only mGLS gains cannot establish practical value.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Manifold Dimensions with Conditional Variational Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest concurrent theorem connecting globally optimal autoencoders to manifold dimension.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zheng et al. prove that global VAE minima can recover data-manifold dimension and extend the result to conditional unions of manifolds, with synthetic known-dimension and real experiments. Benign Autoencoders instead targets a task-utility-dependent decoded dimension controlled by Hessian signs; its object may differ from data intrinsic dimension, but its experiment never measures either support dimension or Hessian inertia.

reviewed_competitors.title: Least Volume Analysis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct operational competitor for learning and ordering an autoencoder's necessary latent dimensions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Least Volume regularizes latent volume while controlling decoder Lipschitzness, proves PCA as a linear special case, dynamically prunes coordinates, and validates on known-dimension and image benchmarks. It offers a trainable route to dimension discovery rather than a post hoc width grid; Benign Autoencoders remains more explicitly task-utility-dependent but supplies no algorithm for its Hessian count.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2 dated 2025-09-25, expanded from the ICLR 2024 Least Volume paper

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Value of Infinite Gradients in Variational Autoencoder Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct contrary theory for the paper's claim that bounded or smooth gradients are inherently desirable in compressed autoencoders.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dai, Wenliang, and Wipf prove a technical sense in which infinite gradients are required to avoid both over- and under-regularization while pruning latent dimensions. This does not refute W-monotonicity, but it shows that turning monotonicity into a blanket smooth-gradient benefit is not justified and motivates direct gradient diagnostics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fixing a Broken ELBO
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational rate-distortion comparator for representation quality and compression tradeoffs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alemi et al. derive mutual-information bounds and a rate-distortion plane, demonstrating that identical ELBO values can hide qualitatively different representations. Benign Autoencoders replaces information rate with a pointwise utility geometry, but never compares its width optimum with rate, distortion, mutual information, or effective latent usage.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Variational Information Bottleneck
reviewed_competitors.difference: Deep VIB trains a neural bottleneck by explicitly trading information about inputs against predictive information about labels and reports generalization and adversarial robustness. Benign Autoencoders proposes a different mechanism that can remove informative but utility-malignant directions, yet its supervised experiment does not compare to VIB or quantify information retained.

reviewed_competitors.title: Wasserstein Auto-Encoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct generative-autoencoder baseline exposing the aggregate-latent sampling requirement.
reviewed_competitors.difference: WAE explicitly regularizes the aggregate encoded distribution to match a chosen prior and evaluates FID. The Benign Autoencoders GAN code samples a Gaussian prior despite never matching E(x) to it, violating its own theoretical instruction to sample the encoded marginal and leaving a strong alternative explanation for high-width FID failure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adversarial Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior-matching autoencoder antecedent directly relevant to Gaussian latent generation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AAE adversarially matches the aggregate posterior to an arbitrary prior so that prior samples decode meaningfully. Benign Autoencoders cites AAE historically but does not implement any code-distribution match, making its standard-normal FID generation an out-of-distribution decoder test rather than the defined encoded-marginal generator.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Variational to Deterministic Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Deterministic generative-autoencoder alternative with explicit attention to latent sampling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Regularized Autoencoders replace VAE stochasticity with decoder regularization and fit an ex-post density model to actual codes for generation, with broad empirical comparisons. Benign Autoencoders gives a richer utility-dependent existence theory, but its released generator omits the ex-post or matched-prior step and its deterministic-existence proof has a partition-limit gap.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dimension Estimation Using Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor for turning autoencoder behavior into an intrinsic-dimension estimate.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bahadur and Paffenroth analyze architecture and regularization choices needed to estimate data intrinsic dimension from autoencoders. Benign Autoencoders instead defines task-specific compressibility via utility curvature, but its empirical procedure is merely a coarse performance grid and does not estimate effective dimension.

reviewed_competitors.title: Autoencoders with Intrinsic Dimension Constraints for Learning Low Dimensional Image Representations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing explicit regularization of global and local representation dimension.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zheng et al. add global and local intrinsic-dimension constraints to reconstruction and evaluate downstream classification and clustering on several image datasets. Their target is geometric preservation rather than utility-Hessian compression, but they provide an operational mechanism and downstream baselines absent from the BAE width sweep.

reviewed_competitors.title: Thinner Latent Spaces: Detecting dimension and imposing invariance through autoencoder gradient constraints
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current gradient-geometric method for detecting effective latent dimension.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Conformal autoencoders use orthogonality of latent gradients to infer local manifold dimension while learning coordinates and invariances. This is data-geometry rather than utility geometry, but it directly measures local tangent structure and supplies a concrete alternative to equating channel count with intrinsic dimension.

reviewed_competitors.title: Intrinsic Dimension Estimating Autoencoder (IDEA) Using CancelOut Layer and a Projected Loss
reviewed_competitors.difference: IDEA learns removable coordinates with reweighted CancelOut layers and a projected reconstruction loss, then validates dimension estimates on theoretical benchmarks before a scientific flow application. It is not task-utility-specific, but it illustrates the known-dimension validation and algorithmic estimator that a practical BAE successor needs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compression of Structured Data with Autoencoders: Provable Benefit of Nonlinearities and Depth
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current theory showing that architecture and optimization can dominate autoencoder compression outcomes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kogler et al. prove that gradient descent on a shallow autoencoder can ignore sparse structure and show how denoising nonlinearities and depth improve compression, with image validation. This directly supports architecture and optimization as competing explanations for BAE's width curves; BAE's nonparametric optimum abstracts those effects away.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Current arXiv record checked 2026-08-23; ICML 2024 paper

reviewed_competitors.title: A Geometric Perspective on Variational Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Alternative latent-geometry account with a geometry-aware sampling procedure.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chadebec and Allassonniere derive a Riemannian structure from the VAE and sample from its intrinsic volume, improving generation and low-data robustness. Benign Autoencoders instead studies geometry of decoded conditional means under utility; the comparison highlights why a principled sampler tied to learned geometry is necessary before interpreting FID.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning High Dimensional Wasserstein Geodesics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest earlier neural dynamic-OT geodesic solver and an explicit predecessor cited by GeONet.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It trains sample-based neural networks for one source-target pair through a bidirectional minimax problem and additionally estimates samples, the distance, and the OT map; GeONet trades that per-pair optimization for an endpoint-conditioned density operator amortized over a fixed family and grid representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Generate Wasserstein Barycenters
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier amortized prediction of pairwise and multi-measure Wasserstein barycenters on image grids.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its convolutional model is supervised by precomputed barycenters and tied to regular image grids, whereas GeONet uses endpoint-only PDE residuals and exposes arbitrary output coordinates but still fixes its branch-input grid.

reviewed_competitors.title: Meta Optimal Transport
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct amortized-OT competitor that predicts solutions for repeatedly changing measures.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Meta OT predicts static transport maps or warm starts in discrete and continuous settings using prior solved tasks; GeONet predicts the full density path and dual potential from PDE losses without labeled geodesics, but does not output a guaranteed map and has weaker input-resolution flexibility.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Optimal Transport
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary neural solver for continuous strong and weak transport maps and plans.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It targets static maps/plans for a given distribution pair and supports more general costs and sample access; GeONet amortizes a quadratic-cost density geodesic over many grid-sampled endpoint pairs but lacks its explicit map/plan output.

reviewed_competitors.title: Entropic Neural Optimal Transport via Diffusion Processes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct neural dynamic entropic-OT and Schrödinger-bridge alternative relevant to GeONet's proposed ER extension.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It solves one sample-accessible entropic transport problem through a diffusion-based saddle formulation and evaluates small regularization values; GeONet only sketches an amortized entropic residual, leaves the forward/backward drift convention unstated, and provides no ER experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A point-sample distribution-flow baseline used in GeONet's empirical-density comparison.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rectified flow fits an ODE by least squares to straighten paths under observed couplings and decreases convex transport costs, but does not generally recover the exact Wasserstein geodesic; GeONet directly predicts grid densities from endpoint functions and penalizes dynamic-OT PDEs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving and generalizing flow-based generative models with minibatch optimal transport
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Conditional-flow-matching baseline used by GeONet and a scalable dynamic-OT-adjacent sample-flow method.
reviewed_competitors.difference: OT-CFM trains a CNF by simulation-free velocity regression and approximates dynamic OT when a true OT coupling is available; it operates on samples and a learned vector field rather than an endpoint-conditioned density operator, so GeONet's histogram L1 comparison does not match the native task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multisample Flow Matching: Straightening Flows with Minibatch Couplings
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary flow method using minibatch couplings to obtain straighter, lower-cost transport paths.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It improves sample generation and transport cost with coupling-aware flow matching but neither promises an exact W2 geodesic nor amortizes over arbitrary pairs of input density functions; GeONet targets those properties through PDE residual operator learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do Neural Optimal Transport Solvers Work? A Continuous Wasserstein-2 Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary benchmark defining analytically known continuous W2 maps and documenting that downstream success need not imply OT correctness.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is not a solver, but supplies the kind of independent continuous ground truth absent from GeONet's POT-relative evaluation; applying its benchmark family would test path/map fidelity without circularly treating a tuned numerical solver as truth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural solver for Wasserstein Geodesics and optimal transport dynamics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest current post-GeONet primary competitor found by the 2026-08-24 audit.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is a sample-based per-pair minimax solver that recovers the geodesic, OT map, particle velocities, and a full velocity field and extends beyond quadratic cost; GeONet remains distinctive in amortizing density paths over an endpoint family, but is restricted by fixed-grid branches and does not recover a certified map.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Neural Optimal Transport
reviewed_competitors.relationship: closest direct variable-resolution neural OT and geodesic competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: UNOT uses a Fourier neural operator to predict entropic OT costs and plans for variable-resolution measures and directly evaluates Wasserstein geodesics against GeONet. Its reported geodesics are closer to ground truth without geodesic-specific or MNIST training, narrowing GeONet's distinction to endpoint-conditioned PDE-residual direct density-path amortization rather than variable-resolution neural OT or best demonstrated path accuracy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Optimal Transport with Lagrangian Costs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct dynamic and broader-cost neural alternative
reviewed_competitors.difference: This method amortizes spline-based geodesic paths for general Lagrangian costs and outputs an OT map without an ODE solver. It is not conditioned on a family of endpoint density pairs like GeONet, but directly competes on learned dynamic paths while extending beyond quadratic cost.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational source of the balanced-gradient-flow invariant used by the reviewed deep-chain analysis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Du, Hu, and Lee prove layer squared-norm differences are invariant for broad homogeneous fully connected and convolutional models. reviewed_competitors.title: Exponential Convergence Time of Gradient Descent for One-Dimensional Deep Linear Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct prior on depth and initialization slowdown in scalar product parameterizations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shamir studies objectives of products of scalar layer weights and proves iteration complexity can grow exponentially with depth. Once its internal ReLUs are positive, the reviewed width-one model has essentially this scalar-factorization structure plus one input direction; its angle bounds refine that special extension but the depth-slowdown mechanism predates it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning a Single Neuron with Bias Using Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary extension showing that a learned bias qualitatively changes even the one-neuron problem.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vardi, Yehudai, and Shamir characterize new critical points, failures, and positive guarantees when the ReLU threshold is trained. The reviewed two-coordinate system excludes bias and its claim that bias is equivalent to adding a constant coordinate does not preserve spherical symmetry, so this is a substantive missing regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Regularization in ReLU Networks with the Square Loss
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Complementary analysis of what gradient flow selects under the same regression loss.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vardi and Shamir show that even single-ReLU square-loss implicit regularization generally cannot be represented by a fixed explicit parameter regularizer. The reviewed paper instead tracks convergence to a unique teacher under spherical realizability and therefore does not resolve solution selection in underdetermined data.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Flow Dynamics of Shallow ReLU Networks for Square Loss and Orthogonal Inputs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-contemporary detailed phase analysis for actual multi-neuron ReLU networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Boursier, Pillaud-Vivien, and Flammarion analyze small-initialization alignment, saddle-to-saddle phases, zero loss, and variation-norm bias for a wide shallow network on orthogonal finite data. Their setting has real feature competition; the reviewed paper gives simpler closed norm-angle envelopes for one effective neuron under population symmetry.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Expressive Power of Neural Networks: A View from the Width
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lu et al. initiated the width phase-transition line: on all of R^dx they place the scalar ReLU L1 minimum between dx+1 and dx+4, while their compact-cube theorem excludes width at most dx-1. Cai targets the exact compact-domain threshold, arbitrary finite activation libraries for the lower bound, vector outputs, and a flow-based leaky-ReLU upper bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Approximating Continuous Functions by ReLU Nets of Minimal Width
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hanin and Sellke prove the exact scalar-output uniform ReLU width dx+1 and a dx+dy vector-output upper bound, with quantitative depth estimates through the modulus of continuity. Cai instead reaches a smaller activation-agnostic bottleneck only for Lp with leaky-ReLU or for uniform approximation with discontinuous or engineered activations, and supplies no depth rate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep, Skinny Neural Networks are not Universal Approximators
reviewed_competitors.difference: For scalar output and dx>=2, Johnson proves level-set obstructions for width at most dx under uniformly continuous activations approximable by continuous injections, yielding the dx+1 uniform lower bound. Cai uses a simpler affine-nullspace argument for an activation-independent Lp lower bound of dx, separately handles the scalar-input monotonicity case, and invokes the same homeomorphism intuition to explain why leaky-ReLU does not attain the critical width uniformly.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Approximation with Deep Narrow Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kidger and Lyons establish compact-domain uniform UAP at width dx+dy+2 for nonaffine continuous activations differentiable with a nonzero derivative somewhere, improved to dx+dy+1 when the activation is also nonpolynomial; their polynomial coverage uses the former bound. Cai optimizes width more aggressively but changes the norm to Lp for practical continuous activations or introduces FLOOR/UOE for uniform approximation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Minimum Width for Universal Approximation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. prove exact width max(dx+1,dy) for ReLU Lp approximation on R^dx and for ReLU+STEP uniform approximation, introduce the encoder-memorizer-decoder construction, and give general-activation upper bounds. Cai adopts that coding idea for FLOOR-based C-UAP but uses compact domains and neural-ODE flows to remove the extra input neuron for leaky-ReLU Lp-UAP.

reviewed_competitors.title: Expressiveness of Neural Networks Having Width Equal or Below the Input Dimension
reviewed_competitors.difference: Beise and Da Cruz prove a maximum principle and compact-set uniform non-universality for continuous monotone activations, while also showing width-one cosine networks can fit arbitrary finite sets. That finite-set contrast exposes why Cai's ambient-dimension lower bound requires domain geometry beyond the unrestricted compact-set wording.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2022 paper, last modified 2023-02-13; related arXiv:2011.04923v6

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning via Dynamical Systems: An Approximation Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Lin, and Shen give sufficient conditions for Lp universal approximation by continuous-time controlled flow maps and explain the dimension-one monotonicity obstruction. Cai imports a special case as its high-dimensional target-map approximator and then compiles those flows into ordinary width-d leaky-ReLU FNNs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Vanilla Feedforward Neural Networks as a Discretization of Dynamical Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Duan et al. prove that width-d leaky-ReLU FNNs can approximate flow maps through splitting-based single-coordinate transformations. Cai's central upper bound composes this result with Li et al.'s flow-map density; it does not independently prove the full discretization theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Minimum Width of Leaky-ReLU Neural Networks for Uniform Universal Approximation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al., including Cai, extend the topology-and-flow program to ordinary continuous leaky-ReLU uniform approximation. The current erratum-bearing arXiv v3 replaces the originally published closed form with max(dx,dy)+Delta(dx,dy), where Delta is a topological embedding quantity that remains unresolved in general; scalar output securely gives dx+1. This both addresses part of the practical continuous-activation C-UAP regime left open here and demonstrates that Cai's FLOOR/UOE critical width does not transfer directly to ordinary leaky-ReLU.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv:2305.18460v3, 2024-02-01, includes errata superseding the stale PMLR abstract; ICML 2023

reviewed_competitors.title: Minimum Width for Universal Approximation Using ReLU Networks on Compact Domain
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kim, Min, and Park prove the same compact-cube Lp minimum max(dx,dy,2) for ReLU, Softplus, leaky-ReLU, ELU, CELU, and SELU using a direct encoder-decoder construction; GELU, SiLU, and Mish are covered when dx+dy>=3. They also add a dy+1 uniform lower bound when dx<dy<=2dx. This strictly broadens Cai's practical activation coverage and avoids dependence on neural-ODE flow approximation, while retaining an explicit full cube domain.

reviewed_competitors.title: Minimum Width for Deep, Narrow MLP: A Diffeomorphism Approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hwang formalizes uniform approximation through embeddings and diffeomorphisms, derives activation-dependent upper bounds max(2dx+1,dy)+alpha(sigma), and obtains exact values such as w(2,2)=w(2,3)=4. Cai's diffeomorphism view is used for Lp density at the smaller bottleneck width but does not solve the ordinary-continuous-activation uniform geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Minimum Width for Universal Approximation Using Squashable Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shin et al. prove the compact-cube Lp minimum max(dx,dy,2) for squashable activations outside the potentially nonmonotone scalar exception and give checkable sufficient conditions covering every non-affine analytic activation plus broad piecewise classes. Monotone squashable scalar activations require width two, whereas the exact nonmonotone scalar value can remain one or two. This converts Cai's isolated leaky-ReLU and custom ABS examples into a much wider practical taxonomy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hamiltonian Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: HNN learns a Hamiltonian vector field in canonical coordinates and makes the learned energy a continuous first integral. Müller instead uses generalized coordinates and known configuration-space symmetries to obtain linear and angular Noether charges, but likewise relies on a separate numerical integrator.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lagrangian Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cranmer et al. introduced the arbitrary neural Lagrangian and Hessian-derived acceleration used here, including graph and field examples. The focal paper's novelty is the explicit invariant first layer and evaluation of non-energy Noether charges.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symplectic Recurrent Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: SRNN combines a learned Hamiltonian with symplectic integration, multistep training, and initial-state optimization for noisy trajectories. It addresses the discrete rollout geometry that Müller's RK4 evaluation leaves uncontrolled, but assumes Hamiltonian/canonical structure and focuses on energy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Variational Integrator Networks for Physically Structured Embeddings
reviewed_competitors.difference: VINs put a learned Lagrangian inside a variational integrator, yielding symplectic and discrete-momentum-preserving maps and supporting noisy phase-space or pixel observations. Müller learns a continuous Lagrangian and then rolls it out with non-geometric RK4.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Energy-Based Modeling of Discrete-Time Physics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Matsubara et al.'s automatic discrete differentiation and discrete-gradient model preserve specified energy, dissipation, and mass laws in discrete time. It directly exposes the continuous-versus-discrete exactness gap in Müller's RK4 pipeline, though it targets energetic structure rather than Noether momentum from group actions.

reviewed_competitors.title: SympNets: Intrinsic structure-preserving symplectic networks for identifying Hamiltonian systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: SympNets directly parameterize universal symplectic maps for separable and nonseparable Hamiltonian systems and avoid repeated Hessian inversion. They preserve symplectic structure rather than explicitly guaranteeing user-selected linear or angular momentum.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Poisson systems and trajectories of autonomous systems via Poisson neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Poisson neural networks learn coordinate changes around a structured symplectic map and can handle autonomous systems from noncanonical observations. Müller's formulation stays in known generalized coordinates and supplies selected configuration symmetries rather than learning Poisson geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noether Networks: Meta-Learning Useful Conserved Quantities
reviewed_competitors.difference: Noether Networks meta-learn a conservation loss and optimize it inside a sequential predictor, discovering useful inductive biases without a supplied physical group. Müller's charges are analytically interpretable and exact for its learned continuous Lagrangian, but the symmetry must be known.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scalars are universal: Equivariant machine learning, structured like classical physics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Villar et al. prove broad scalar-generator universality for O(d), Euclidean, Lorentz, and Poincare equivariance and discuss efficient structured outputs. Müller specializes scalar generators to an invariant Lagrangian and invokes Noether, with a dense implementation that does not inherit the broader scalability story.

reviewed_competitors.title: A simple equivariant machine learning method for dynamics based on scalars
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yao et al. use invariant scalars to build an equivariant forcing function and show accuracy and speed on chaotic dynamics. Müller correctly notes that force equivariance alone does not generally imply a Noether first integral; its invariant Lagrangian supplies that guarantee at the cost of Hessians.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning the Dynamics of Particle-based Systems with Lagrangian Graph Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: LGnn appeared in the same month and factorizes particle Lagrangians with graph structure, reporting constraint/drag handling and zero-shot rollouts to systems two orders of magnitude larger. Müller obtains hard global momentum charges but explicitly does not solve the many-particle scaling problem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Articulated Rigid Body Dynamics with Lagrangian Graph Neural Network
reviewed_competitors.difference: This concurrent LGNN handles ropes, chains, trusses, non-diagonal mass matrices, and unseen system sizes or hybrids. Müller's examples are only one or two point particles and use global dense Hessians, though its Noether charge construction is more explicit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discrete Lagrangian Neural Networks with Automatic Symmetry Discovery
reviewed_competitors.difference: SymDLNN learns a discrete Lagrangian and an affine Lie subgroup from position snapshots, derives discrete conserved quantities, and regularizes numerical solvability. It removes Müller's known-symmetry, velocity-observation, and non-geometric-integration assumptions, but was posted two months later.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hamiltonian Neural Networks with Automatic Symmetry Detection
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dierkes et al. jointly learn a Hamiltonian and Lie-algebra generators, recovering energy and continuous symmetries rather than requiring the group in advance. The price is canonical Hamiltonian structure and small proposed action families.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symmetry Preservation in Hamiltonian Systems: Simulation and Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vaquero et al. construct G-invariant Lagrangian submanifolds so learned symplectic or Poisson maps preserve the same momentum quantities as the original Hamiltonian system. This gives a discrete geometric guarantee closer to the title's promise than applying RK4 to a continuous invariant Lagrangian.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lie Group Forced Variational Integrator Networks for Learning and Control of Robot Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: LieFVIN learns discrete-time controlled Lagrangian or Hamiltonian flows on matrix Lie groups from position-only or position-velocity data while preserving group and symplectic structure. Müller is simpler and gives explicit scalar charges, but excludes controls and manifold-valued robot states.

reviewed_competitors.title: Forced Variational Integrator Networks for Prediction and Control of Mechanical Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: FVIN incorporates forcing, damping, and control through the discrete d'Alembert principle while retaining passive variational structure. Müller's hard conservation is narrower and would be misspecified for most actuated or dissipative systems.

reviewed_competitors.title: GFINNs: GENERIC Formalism Informed Neural Networks for Deterministic and Stochastic Dynamical Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: GFINNs architecturally enforce GENERIC degeneracy conditions for coupled conservative and dissipative dynamics and prove an expressivity result. Müller targets conservative point mechanics and linear/angular Noether charges, with no entropy or stochastic component.

reviewed_competitors.title: Port-Hamiltonian Neural Networks for Learning Explicit Time-Dependent Dynamical Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Port-HNN separates stationary energy, time-dependent forcing, and dissipation and supports non-autonomous chaotic systems. It sacrifices strict conservation where physics demands exchange, whereas Müller's autonomous invariant Lagrangian cannot express those regimes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Conservation Laws: A Divergence-Free Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Richter-Powell et al. parameterize universal divergence-free density-flux pairs with differential forms so continuity holds identically, extending exact architectural conservation to PDE-like fields. Müller instead derives finite-dimensional momentum maps from global action symmetries.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Physical Models that Can Respect Conservation Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: ProbConserv applies a Bayesian update based on an integral conservation law to generic SciML predictors and retains uncertainty quantification, including shocks and heteroscedasticity. Müller is mechanistically interpretable through Noether but deterministic and tied to regular Lagrangian ODEs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exactly conservative physics-informed neural networks and deep operator networks for dynamical systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cardoso-Bihlo and Bihlo append a Newton projection layer that maps any candidate PINN or DeepONet solution onto the manifold of known first integrals. It preserves the supplied physical integral itself rather than a learned shadow charge, but assumes those integrals are known and projection reaches the correct component.

reviewed_competitors.title: Direct Poisson neural networks: Learning non-symplectic mechanical systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Direct Poisson networks learn both energy and a Jacobi-satisfying Poisson bracket, distinguishing symplectic from degenerate non-symplectic mechanics. Müller assumes a regular Lagrangian and therefore excludes precisely the singular structures for which its Hessian inverse fails.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symplectic Neural Networks Based on Dynamical Systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tapley derives geometric-integrator SympNets with universality, exact quadratic-map representation, nonvanishing-gradient analysis, and symbolic regression through backward error analysis. This advances direct learned-map structure beyond Müller's small continuous LNN tests, but does not automatically encode arbitrary specified momentum maps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine Learning Symmetry Discovery for Classical Mechanics
reviewed_competitors.difference: MLSD learns conserved generators and their Lie-algebra structure coefficients, including non-abelian hidden Kepler symmetries. Müller enforces only supplied rotations and translations and therefore misses the Runge-Lenz-type hidden structure of its own Kepler benchmark.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Symmetry Discovery for Dynamical System Identification
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tahmasebi and Weber characterize how known equivariance reduces single-trajectory sample requirements and propose learning an unknown group with the same optimal trajectory length in their identification setting. It directly targets the focal paper's unmeasured sample-efficiency and known-symmetry assumptions, though it is theoretical and much later.

reviewed_competitors.difference: NeuralExecutor++ already shares a processor while retaining task-specific encoders and decoders, and uses paired related algorithms to transfer trace supervision to targets without hints. reviewed_competitors.title: The CLRS Algorithmic Reasoning Benchmark
reviewed_competitors.difference: CLRS supplies the thirty instrumented algorithms, typed graph interface, fixed train/validation/test splits, and Memnet/MPNN/PGN baselines. The generalist paper's major specialist gains combine a new processor with a materially different online and mixed-size training pipeline, not just multi-task sharing.

reviewed_competitors.title: EvoPrompting: Language Models for Code-Level Neural Architecture Search
reviewed_competitors.difference: EvoPrompting evolves code-level GNN architectures and reports beating then-current CLRS models on 21/30 tasks at similar size. It searches specialist architectures rather than proving one shared learner works, but challenges the hand-designed Triplet-GMPNN as the best processor family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Algorithmic Reasoning with Causal Regularisation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hint-ReLIC constructs causally equivalent inputs and regularizes identical next-step predictions, reporting up to threefold OOD gains on CLRS. It targets invariance of learned transitions, whereas the generalist paper relies mainly on generic online augmentation and parameter sharing.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Markov Property of Neural Algorithmic Reasoning: Analyses and Methods
reviewed_competitors.difference: ForgetNet removes historical embeddings and G-ForgetNet gates them away during training, arguing that the recurrent hidden state in Triplet-GMPNN conflicts with Markov traces. It reports a 30-task mean of 82.89% versus 75.98% for Triplet-GMPNN and also evaluates the multi-task setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Latent Space Representations of Neural Algorithmic Reasoners
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mirjanic et al. diagnose loss of latent resolution and failure outside the training numeric range, then add softmax aggregation and latent decay to improve a majority of CLRS-30 tasks. This exposes extrapolation failures left unresolved by the original generalist's max-aggregated shared space.

reviewed_competitors.title: Open-Book Neural Algorithmic Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Open-book NAR lets each query attend to stored training instances, including examples from other tasks, and uses attention weights to expose task relationships. It adds retrieval-time computation and memory but offers a more explicit, interpretable mechanism for cross-task transfer than one fully shared processor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discrete Neural Algorithmic Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rodionov and Prokhorenkova force execution through finite discrete node and edge states and report perfect single- and multi-task scores with correctness proofs on a narrower SALSA-CLRS task set. It trades the generalist paper's broad 30-task coverage for exact state transitions, graph-level success, and certifiability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficiently Learning Branching Networks for Multitask Algorithmic Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: AutoBRANE uses gradient affinity to learn a branching hierarchy that shares early layers and separates conflicting tasks, addressing the negative transfer visible in a fully shared processor. The KDD 2026 preprint reports 3.7% over the strongest single multitask GNN with lower runtime and memory across GNN and text reasoning benchmarks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational deep-network protocol reproduced and interpreted by the reviewed work.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nakkiran et al. establish model-, sample-, and epoch-wise double descent across vision and translation. The reviewed paper adds a local loss-geometry correlate but does not replace the original descriptive phenomenon with a causal theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sensitivity and Generalization in Neural Networks: an Empirical Study
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Key predecessor for input-space Jacobian diagnostics near data.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Novak et al. measure the input-output Jacobian on training and validation data, avoiding direct multiplication by a labeled cross-entropy residual. The reviewed work extends width/epoch and noisy-label coverage but changes the estimand to loss derivatives.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Universal Law of Robustness via Isoperimetry
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Theory the paper claims its experiments substantiate.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bubeck and Sellke prove a lower-bound tradeoff between parameter count and global Lipschitz robustness under isoperimetric distributions and smooth parameterization assumptions. The reviewed weak-direction, loss-gradient averages are not the theorem's Lipschitz quantity and cannot directly validate it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are All Linear Regions Created Equal?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor linking predictor variation and local region similarity to model-wise double descent.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gamba et al. contrast region counts with function-variation nonlinearity in VGG/ResNet models. The reviewed paper adds epoch-wise, label-stratified, and path-based analysis, but its loss-derived metric is more exposed to confidence saturation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Neural Nets Learn the Same Model Twice? Investigating Reproducibility and Double Descent From the Decision Boundary Perspective
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous function-space explanation using boundary geometry.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Somepalli et al. find fragmented, unstable, non-reproducible decision regions near interpolation and simpler reproducible regions at large width. That boundary-level evidence is complementary and can reveal irregularity that an average training-loss gradient misses.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why neural networks find simple solutions: the many regularizers of geometric complexity
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent predictor-Jacobian complexity account of double descent.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dherin et al. define geometric complexity from the logit-network Jacobian and connect it to explicit and implicit regularizers; they also observe width-wise double descent. It provides a cleaner sensitivity target than supervised-loss gradients, though it remains data-local and correlational.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unraveling the Enigma of Double Descent: an in-depth Analysis Through the Lens of Learned Feature Space
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later alternative mechanism centered on representation-level signal/noise separation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gu et al. argue noisy data makes the peak pronounced and that overparameterized representations separate robust information from noise. This shifts explanation from raw-input loss flatness to learned feature geometry and highlights that several co-moving diagnostics can fit the same test-error curve.

reviewed_competitors.title: Depth Uncertainty in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: DUN marginalizes predictions over shared subnetworks up to a user-specified maximum with single-pass inference. UDN removes that maximum and dynamically grows the active posterior support, at greater inference/training complexity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Variational Depth Search in ResNets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Variational Depth Search infers a posterior over depths within a fixed maximum ResNet and prunes from that supernet. UDN defines an unbounded generative model and creates deeper parameters when demanded by the optimized posterior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Networks with Stochastic Depth
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stochastic Depth drops residual blocks during training but deploys a predetermined deep network. UDN treats output depth as a Bayesian latent variable and marginalizes its posterior rather than using dropout as regularization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Ordinary Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neural ODEs tie depth to integration time in a continuous vector field. UDN retains ordinary discrete layers with separate weights and learns a posterior over finite truncations of an infinite sequence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks Fail to Learn Periodic Functions and How to Fix It
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct prior work proves standard ReLU/tanh/sigmoid extrapolation limitations and proposes the snake activation as a periodic inductive bias.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This paper's main empirical contribution is a broader negative evaluation of snake when period is unknown; it should be read as an optimization counterexample to that prescription, not a universal impossibility for periodic activations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Neural Representations with Periodic Activation Functions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: SIREN supplies a principled sinusoidal initialization and demonstrates high-fidelity continuous signal and derivative representation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is principally an interpolation/implicit-representation paper, but its initialization directly addresses optimization of periodic networks and is a conspicuous missing baseline before concluding that periodic activations themselves fail.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior work maps coordinates through Fourier features to convert an MLP's effective kernel into a tunable stationary kernel and overcome spectral bias.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its frequencies are generally supplied or sampled rather than recovered as a single master period, but the representation is directly relevant to known-period L2 and should be compared with hidden-layer sine/cosine activations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Periodic Activation Functions Induce Stationarity
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior theory connects periodic Bayesian neural-network activations to translation-invariant stationary Gaussian-process priors.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies function-space priors and uncertainty rather than point-estimate long-horizon frequency recovery, but provides a more precise account of what periodic activations guarantee and what they do not.

reviewed_competitors.title: BACON: Band-Limited Coordinate Networks for Multiscale Scene Representation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Published before this submission, BACON uses discrete sine frequencies and an analytically controlled spectrum, including a direct seamless-texture periodic-extrapolation demonstration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: BACON assumes a designed frequency grid/bandwidth and focuses on known-period spatial signals rather than recovering an unknown scalar period, but it directly contradicts the completeness of the surveyed architecture set for L2.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gaussian Process Kernels for Pattern Discovery and Extrapolation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Classical spectral-mixture Gaussian processes learn frequency structure from data and demonstrate long-range extrapolation on synthetic and real trend-plus-periodic series.
reviewed_competitors.difference: They are non-neural and scale differently, but are an essential period-discovery baseline once this paper permits Bayesian optimization and claims an expectation ceiling for machine-learning models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analytic Long-Term Forecasting with Periodic Gaussian Processes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior work explicitly develops probabilistic long-term forecasting for periodic processes with periodic Gaussian-process kernels.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It propagates uncertainty in dynamical forecasting rather than fitting arbitrary compositional waveforms, but exposes the benchmark's omission of calibrated classical long-horizon models and uncertainty metrics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Periodic Signal Recovery with Regularized Sine Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Near-concurrent later work uses diverse sine-frequency initialization and a non-convex sparsifying regularizer to recover multi-tone spectra and extrapolate beyond 100 periods.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It directly resolves several alias/interference failures diagnosed here and demonstrates that learned sine networks can succeed without population-wide modulo candidates, narrowing this paper's negative conclusion to its training recipe.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Functions for Learning Periodic Signal
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later work explicitly extracts periodic patterns and uses them in a neural representation, evaluating extrapolation on periodic differential-equation solutions and real time-series forecasting.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies the kind of end-to-end architecture and broader real-data validation this benchmark calls for, superseding the 2022 statement that no plausible periodic-extrapolation architecture exists.

reviewed_competitors.title: Does Your Neural Network Extrapolate? Feature Engineering as Identifiability Bias for OOD Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later theory formalizes finite-window OOD continuation as non-identifiable and explains success through a structural commitment in features, labels, and model class; Fourier coordinates turn periodic extrapolation into interpolation on a circle.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It gives the identifiability framework missing from the paper's dataset-period definition and clarifies that PerKit's modulo population advantage comes from injected structure rather than a generally stronger optimizer.
