reviewed_competitors.title: Least-squares finite elements for the Stokes problem
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jiang and Chang introduce the first-order velocity-pressure-vorticity least-squares formulation that the target explicitly adopts for Stokes and cavity flow. The target replaces finite-element trial spaces with a shared neural field and per-point dual weights; it does not originate the VVP reduction.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 78(3), 1990, version of record

reviewed_competitors.title: The Deep Ritz method: A deep learning-based numerical algorithm for solving variational problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: E and Yu optimize a variational energy with a neural trial function, avoiding strong-form high derivatives when a Ritz principle exists. It is an earlier neural PDE route to lower regularity requirements, whereas the target constructs first-order strong residuals and dual point constraints.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics Informed Deep Learning (Part I): Data-driven Solutions of Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Raissi, Perdikaris, and Karniadakis establish the continuous-time physics-informed residual framework that the target diagnoses and reformulates. It supplies the baseline training paradigm, while the target adds auxiliary fields and constrained optimization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conservative physics-informed neural networks on discrete domains for conservation laws: Applications to forward and inverse problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jagtap, Kharazmi, and Karniadakis use one PINN per subdomain and enforce interface flux continuity in strong form, including a twelve-network lid-driven-cavity study that the target directly discusses. This Conservative PINN is distinct from arxiv:2204.11144's Competitive PINN; its explicit interfaces provide a closer conservation baseline than the target's finite point penalties.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Computer Methods in Applied Mechanics and Engineering 365, 2020, version of record

reviewed_competitors.title: Weak Adversarial Networks for High-dimensional Partial Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zang et al. lower regularity requirements through a weak operator-norm objective and adversarial test network on irregular high-dimensional domains. It predates the target's strong first-order system and supplies a distinct mesh-free route around high derivatives.

reviewed_competitors.title: Variational Physics-Informed Neural Networks For Solving Partial Differential Equations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kharazmi et al. use Petrov-Galerkin residuals and integration by parts to lower differential order and training cost. This establishes that avoiding high-order automatic derivatives was already a PINN design principle, without auxiliary pointwise dual variables.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding and mitigating gradient pathologies in physics-informed neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Teng, and Perdikaris diagnose imbalanced backpropagated gradients across composite losses and use learning-rate annealing. The target instead attributes sensitivity to differential operators and replaces manual aggregate weights with first-order reformulation and per-point multipliers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimally weighted loss functions for solving PDEs with Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Van der Meer et al. analyze optimal scaling for well-posed linear PDEs and test the same convection-diffusion boundary-layer family. The target uses a harder alpha and avoids a single manually selected balance through pointwise dual weights.

reviewed_competitors.title: When and why PINNs fail to train: A neural tangent kernel perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Yu, and Perdikaris derive convergence-rate mismatch from the limiting PINN NTK and use eigenvalue-based weighting. It gives a formal conditioning analysis missing from the target's histogram perturbation study, but does not lower PDE order.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Adaptive Physics-Informed Neural Networks using a Soft Attention Mechanism
reviewed_competitors.difference: McClenny and Braga-Neto already maximize independent per-point nonnegative weights so hard regions receive attention, with an NTK interpretation. The target's pointwise multiplier mechanism is close in spirit but adds RMS-scaled updates, equality-constraint language, and first-order fields.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exact imposition of boundary conditions with distance functions in physics-informed deep neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sukumar and Srivastava embed Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin conditions into trial functions using approximate distance fields, including curved and higher-dimensional domains. Unlike the target's finite point penalties, this makes exact boundary satisfaction literal by construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Characterizing possible failure modes in physics-informed neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Krishnapriyan et al. characterize convection, reaction, and diffusion failures and propose curriculum and sequence-to-sequence remedies. The target reuses its convection benchmark but proposes first-order dual constraints; its Table 1 comparison is not a matched rerun.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics and Equality Constrained Artificial Neural Networks: Application to Forward and Inverse Problems with Multi-fidelity Data Fusion
reviewed_competitors.difference: Basir and Senocak's PECANN already frames PINNs as constrained optimization and uses an augmented Lagrangian for boundary and high-fidelity constraints. The target removes the quadratic augmentation from its final dual, adds first-order auxiliary fields, and uses RMS-scaled pointwise multipliers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient-enhanced physics-informed neural networks for forward and inverse PDE problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yu et al. add derivatives of the PDE residual and report better accuracy with fewer points, especially with adaptive refinement. This does not refute conditioning problems, but it shows that higher derivative order can add useful signal and is not universally contaminating.

reviewed_competitors.title: Respecting causality is all you need for training physics-informed neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Sankaran, and Perdikaris use causal weighting and time marching to prevent later residuals from dominating before earlier dynamics are learned. It addresses time-dependent training failure without auxiliary fields and is directly relevant to the target's convection benchmark.

reviewed_competitors.title: Competitive Physics Informed Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zeng et al. use an adversarial discriminator and argue that squared residual objectives square discretization condition numbers. Their min-max weak formulation reaches high accuracy without the target's first-order point-dual construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Networks with Augmented Lagrangian Relaxation Method (AL-PINNs)
reviewed_competitors.difference: Son, Cho, and Hwang treat initial and boundary conditions as constraints in a sequential max-min augmented-Lagrangian PINN and give convergence analysis for three PDE classes. It predates the target and provides a closer theoretical constrained baseline than the papers actually compared.

reviewed_competitors.title: Is $L^2$ Physics-Informed Loss Always Suitable for Training Physics-Informed Neural Network?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. use PDE stability to show that small L2 residual need not control solution error for broad HJB equations and propose an adversarial L-infinity objective. This supplies a theory-backed reason why residual norm, not only derivative order or scale, determines PINN validity.

reviewed_competitors.title: A mixed formulation for physics-informed neural networks as a potential solver for engineering problems in heterogeneous domains: comparison with finite element method
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rezaei et al. submitted before the target and predict gradients from auxiliary networks so physical losses require only first derivatives, explicitly targeting heterogeneous solids and diffusion. The target differs through a shared network and adaptive constrained optimizer, not the core mixed reformulation.

reviewed_competitors.title: FO-PINNs: A First-Order formulation for Physics Informed Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gladstone et al. submitted one month later and package first-order PDE losses, parameterized systems, timing gains, and exact distance-function boundary conditions. It independently corroborates the derivative-order idea while using hard ansatzes rather than pointwise dual ascent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixed formulation of physics-informed neural networks for thermo-mechanically coupled systems and heterogeneous domains
reviewed_competitors.difference: Harandi et al. extend mixed first-order PINNs to coupled thermo-mechanics, heterogeneous domains, hard boundaries, optimizer and architecture comparisons, and sequential versus joint training. It provides broader coupling ablations than the target's single shared-head choice.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Error Certification for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Eiras et al. use derivative-aware bound propagation to certify initial, boundary, and residual conditions over continuous domains. It directly addresses the gap between the target's finite point constraints and its claims of strict enforcement.

reviewed_competitors.title: PINNacle: A Comprehensive Benchmark of Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving PDEs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hao et al. benchmark about ten PINN methods on more than twenty PDEs spanning complex geometry, multiscale behavior, nonlinearity, and high dimension. Its breadth and standardized toolbox expose how little a six-problem manufactured suite can support universal claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Expert's Guide to Training Physics-informed Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. provide challenging benchmarks, fully reproducible architecture and training ablations, and a JAX library. It treats optimizer, architecture, normalization, causality, and sampling jointly and supplies the controlled evidence missing from the target.

reviewed_competitors.title: Challenges in Training PINNs: A Loss Landscape Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rathore et al. formally connect differential operators to loss ill-conditioning, compare Adam, L-BFGS, and their combination, and test a Nyström Newton-CG optimizer. It provides Hessian- and benchmark-based support for a narrower conditioning claim while showing optimization can mitigate it without first-order reformulation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for the Numerical Modeling of Steady-State and Transient Electromagnetic Problems with Discontinuous Media
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nohra and Dufour analyze first-order Maxwell PINNs with NTKs, smooth discontinuous material properties, and overlapping domain decomposition in three-dimensional electromagnetic settings. It turns the target's one manufactured interface illustration into a field-specific conditioning and decomposition study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conditionally adaptive augmented Lagrangian method for physics-informed learning of forward and inverse problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu, Basir, and Senocak add multiple augmented penalties, constraint aggregation for pointwise-memory efficiency, Fourier features, time windows, and conditionally adaptive penalty updates. The successor implicitly bounds the target's robustness and scalability claims and offers the most direct modern replacement.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hard-constrained Physics-informed Neural Networks for Interface Problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chung et al. embed interface continuity and flux balance through window or buffer ansatzes and test one- and two-dimensional interface geometries. Unlike the target's implicit smooth shared representation, interface fidelity is the explicit object of enforcement and measurement.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Risk-gap theory between kernel and feature learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghorbani et al. prove sample/prediction-risk separations among random features, neural tangent, and fully trained two-layer networks on structured distributions. This paper gives a complementary temporal and example-group account, but with a much less general theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang and Hu's maximal-update framework distinguishes parameterizations that retain feature learning at infinite width and supports hyperparameter transfer. It offers a scalable parameterization view beyond the finite alpha knob; the present paper instead focuses directly on which examples are learned first.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning sparse features can lead to overfitting in neural networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing account of when feature learning hurts

George et al. identify an orthogonal early-training hazard: rapid uptake of easy spurious correlations and minority delay.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mixed Dynamics In Linear Networks: Unifying the Lazy and Active Regimes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tu, Aranguri, and Jacot derive a mixed regime in which singular directions transition from lazy to active above a threshold, combining alignment and low-rank bias. This complicates a global lazy-versus-feature dichotomy and supplies a more general direction-wise theory than the paper's fixed two-regime quadratic example.

reviewed_competitors.title: Distributionally Robust Neural Networks for Group Shifts: On the Importance of Regularization for Worst-Case Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sagawa et al. benchmark Waterbirds/CelebA and optimize worst-group loss with regularization, directly targeting minority robustness. George et al. explain why ordinary feature-learning dynamics can initially worsen those groups, but do not turn the diagnosis into a robust training method.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine learning materials physics: Integrable deep neural networks enable scale bridging by learning free energy functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Teichert and collaborators introduced an Integrable Deep Neural Network trained to derivative data and recovered a free-energy representation used in phase-field simulation. It predates DNNI by more than three years and already demonstrates the core derivative-to-function paradigm in a multidimensional scientific application; DNNI broadens the example suite but does not originate that mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning for Symbolic Mathematics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lample and Charton train sequence models to emit symbolic integration and differential-equation solutions. Their output aims to be an exact expression that can be checked symbolically, whereas DNNI learns an implicit numeric function through collocation; citing symbolic integration does not make DNNI itself symbolic or closed form in that sense.

reviewed_competitors.title: AutoInt: Automatic Integration for Fast Neural Volume Rendering
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lindell, Martel, and Wetzstein explicitly instantiate and fit a network's derivative graph, reuse the original coordinate network as its antiderivative, and evaluate definite integrals with two calls, then show more than 10x rendering speedup. This is essentially DNNI's central algorithm before DNNI's submission, with more specialized architecture analysis and a large application; its omission invalidates a broad novelty claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-variable Integration with a Neural Network
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maître and Santos-Mateos extend derivative-loss primitive fitting to multiple integration variables and parametric loop integrals, reporting per-mil to percent accuracy and 40-125x repeated-evaluation speedups. DNNI handles one integration coordinate with auxiliary parameters and sketches broader extensions, but does not demonstrate true multivariable integration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural networks can be FLOP-efficient integrators of 1D oscillatory integrands
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sinha and Bryngelson train networks over parametric oscillatory function families and compare them to quadrature under FLOP budgets, reporting about 10^3 average FLOP gain at relative accuracy 10^-3. It directly addresses the weakest part of DNNI's oscillatory evaluation: matched computational budgets and learned cross-integrand structure rather than a few separately fitted cases.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Control Variates with Automatic Integration
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li and collaborators combine antiderivative networks with Monte Carlo control variates so residual integration remains unbiased even when the derivative network is not exact, and apply the method to walk-on-sphere PDE solvers. This explicitly fixes DNNI's lack of an accuracy guarantee while retaining expressive neural surrogates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Parametric Numerical Integration with (Differential) Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Leitao and Rafales learn parametric integral outputs with standard and differential-learning surrogates across statistical functionals, Chebyshev coefficients, and differential-equation integrals, reporting lower MSE and better sample efficiency from derivative information. Unlike DNNI's endpoint primitive, this work emphasizes systematic parametric generalization and comparative learning methodology.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Entezari et al. state the conjecture that motivates the reviewed paper and report evidence that many apparent barriers vanish after hidden-unit permutations. The reviewed work supplies a simple activation-matching witness, a systematic MLP width/depth study, the retrospective initialization result, and a CNN/learning-rate contrast rather than originating the conjecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimizing Mode Connectivity via Neuron Alignment
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tatro et al. already align neurons from intermediate activations and jointly optimize permutations with simple learned connectivity curves, including adversarially robust models and a theoretical upper-bound analysis. The reviewed paper focuses on unlearned straight segments, a cheaper independent Hungarian match, and transporting the learned permutation back to initialization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Model Fusion via Optimal Transport
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh and Jaggi align neurons with hard or soft optimal transport and demonstrate one-shot fusion across widths and non-IID data. Their objective is usable model fusion, whereas the reviewed paper uses hard feature matching primarily to test loss-landscape claims and uniquely examines aligned random initializations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Git Re-Basin: Merging Models modulo Permutation Symmetries
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ainsworth et al. independently develop weight matching, activation matching, and a straight-through estimator; demonstrate re-basing and merging including widened ResNets; and provide a finite counterexample. The reviewed paper's clearest additions are its systematic fully connected width/depth curves, CNN learning-rate dependence, and above-chance ancestral-initialization observation.

reviewed_competitors.title: REPAIR: REnormalizing Permuted Activations for Interpolation Repair
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jordan et al. show that alignment alone can leave a barrier because interpolated deep networks suffer activation-variance collapse, then repair preactivation moments. This supplies a concrete alternative explanation for the reviewed paper's CNN residual barriers and weakens any inference that those barriers necessarily mark genuinely distinct modes.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2023 conference paper, OpenReview forum gU5sJ6ZggcX

reviewed_competitors.title: Re-Basin via Implicit Sinkhorn Differentiation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pena et al. replace discrete, non-differentiable matching with an implicit-differentiation Sinkhorn re-basin module that can optimize task-specific objectives and support continual learning. It directly addresses the reviewed paper's acknowledged inability to know whether a residual barrier is due to a suboptimal permutation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analysis of Linear Mode Connectivity via Permutation-Based Weight Matching: With Insights into Other Permutation Search Methods
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ito et al. argue empirically that connectivity is not explained merely by reducing parameter distance; weight and activation matching align dominant singular-vector directions that preserve model functionality. This supplies a spectral mechanism missing from the reviewed paper and compares activation matching directly with weight matching and straight-through search.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICLR 2025 conference paper, corresponding to arXiv:2402.04051v5

reviewed_competitors.title: Analyzing the Role of Permutation Invariance in Linear Mode Connectivity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhan et al. formalize the width observation for two-layer ReLU teacher-student models: the modulo-permutation barrier exhibits double descent and decays at O(m^-1/2) when sufficiently wide, while learning-rate-driven sparsity changes the barrier. This turns two central empirical axes of the reviewed paper into a restricted but quantitative theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Linear Mode Connectivity between Multiple Models modulo Permutation Symmetries
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ito et al. show that permutation methods designed for two models can fail to move many models into one convex low-loss basin, then introduce STE-MM and test pairwise barriers, merged loss, and Hessian trace. This directly exposes the gap between the reviewed paper's pairwise evidence and its language about a shared basin or averaging more than two initializations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do We Really Need Permutations? Impact of Model Width on Linear Mode Connectivity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ito et al. report that sufficiently widening models can produce linear connectivity even without permutations when softmax temperature is calibrated, and propose layerwise exponentially weighted connectivity as an explanation. This challenges the reviewed paper's implicit attribution of the width trend primarily to finding better permutations and highlights calibration as a missing control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning Scaling is Predictable, Empirically
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hestness et al. establish empirical power-law data scaling across translation, language modeling, vision, and speech and motivate forecasting applications. The reviewed paper changes the validation target from fit quality to held-out extrapolation and introduces a pre-asymptotic transition form.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kaplan et al. fit loss against parameters, data, and compute across enormous scale spans and derive compute allocation. The reviewed paper focuses on one-dimensional held-out curve prediction across domains and shows why best fit alone need not identify a valid exponent.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hernandez et al. quantify effective transferred data with joint parameter and fine-tuning-data laws. The reviewed paper instead forecasts downstream few-shot error from upstream examples seen and supplies a flexible transition curve, without a joint causal transfer model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explaining Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bahri et al. distinguish variance- and resolution-limited mechanisms and relate data and model exponents theoretically. The reviewed paper is an empirical estimator-selection study: its sigmoid transition is functional rather than a derived regime model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Scaling Laws in NMT: The Effect of Noise and Architecture
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct NMT data and baseline source
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bansal et al. study how architecture and noise change NMT exponents and introduce the M3-style saturating form; their five architecture curves are reused here. The reviewed paper benchmarks alternative estimators on later NMT points rather than producing those runs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Broken Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Caballero et al. use smoothly broken power laws with multiple transitions, benchmark much more diverse phenomena, and represent double descent and delayed inflections that monotone M4 cannot. M4 is simpler, nests a standard offset power law, and was explicitly selected by held-out extrapolation on its 92-curve suite.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reproducible scaling laws for contrastive language-image learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cherti et al. release OpenCLIP models and an evaluation workflow for training-set, model, compute, and downstream scaling up to two billion image-text pairs, and show training distribution changes the law. This removes the reviewed paper's proprietary-JFT upstream reproducibility barrier but does not center estimator-family selection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Resolving Discrepancies in Compute-Optimal Scaling of Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Porian et al. reproduce conflicting compute-optimal laws and trace them to last-layer cost, warmup, and scale-dependent optimizer tuning. Their result shows that a better curve family cannot rescue extrapolation when the training protocol itself changes with scale, a confound largely abstracted away here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Predicting Downstream Performance in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. map FLOPs to pretraining loss and then loss to downstream performance, extending to mixtures with domain-specific losses and a neural map. This targets emergent downstream behavior at 7B-13B scale, whereas M4 directly fits each scalar task curve and cannot transfer information across losses or data mixtures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Establishing Task Scaling Laws via Compute-Efficient Model Ladders
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bhagia et al. train explicit small-model ladders and use a two-step task-loss-to-accuracy forecast for 7B/13B targets, with ablations on ladder compute and task metric variance. It offers target-model validation and design guidance absent from M4, while covering fewer task and architecture families.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Laws for Robust Comparison of Open Foundation Language-Vision Models and Datasets
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nezhurina et al. fit dense model-by-samples-seen surfaces for CLIP and MaMMUT across three open datasets, validate held-out prediction, and release code, raw data, models, and intermediate checkpoints. It operationalizes the reviewed paper's extrapolation-first principle with much stronger upstream openness and multidimensional comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Neural Scaling Laws
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hu et al. frame downstream scaling as time-series extrapolation using token-level losses and accuracy history, obtaining 2.04% MAE over 66 tasks, a 38% reduction from logistic laws at 3.29%, while generalizing to unseen families. It abandons M4's interpretable parametric asymptote to capture plateaus and degradation, but requires a learned cross-curve corpus and brings its own transfer risks.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Hitchhiker's Guide to Scaling Law Estimation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Choshen et al. fit more than 1,000 laws from 485 released pretrained models and test checkpoint choice, target proximity, and seed allocation. It turns the reviewed paper's extrapolation-first principle into broader estimation guidance with substantially more independent model evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bayesian Neural Scaling Law Extrapolation with Prior-Data Fitted Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. directly benchmark M1-M4-style point estimators against a prior-data fitted Bayesian forecaster, add posterior uncertainty and active selection, and improve data-limited extrapolation. These are precisely the uncertainty and sequential-design capabilities absent from M4.

reviewed_competitors.title: (Mis)Fitting Scaling Laws: A Survey of Scaling Law Fitting Techniques in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. compare how equation, optimizer, initialization, and reporting choices alter fitted laws. That directly frames the reviewed release's stale design column, beta constraint, learning-rate mismatch, and hidden tie rule as estimator-specification threats rather than incidental artifact details.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tokens-per-Parameter Coverage Is Critical for Robust LLM Scaling Law Extrapolation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kricheli et al. prove and empirically show that collinear tokens-per-parameter designs make common scaling-law parameters ill-conditioned and practically unidentifiable. It supplies the design-matrix diagnosis and coverage requirement missing from M4's one-dimensional curve fitting.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Rissanen, Heinonen, and Solin introduce stochastic inversion of the heat equation and expose a coarse-to-fine image bias, but directly predict prior blurred states with a heuristic scalar reverse variance. Blurring Diffusion reinterprets that process as coordinatewise Gaussian diffusion, derives Markov posteriors, adds a terminal noise schedule, and uses epsilon prediction to close much of the quality gap.

reviewed_competitors.title: Progressive Deblurring of Diffusion Models for Coarse-to-Fine Image Synthesis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lee et al. also define diffusion in a rotated coordinate system with frequency-dependent speeds and combine gradual blur with noise for coarse-to-fine synthesis, reporting gains on LSUN bedrooms and churches. It predates the target preprint and makes the high-level blur-diffusion idea concurrent rather than unique; the target emphasizes the IHDM equivalence, exact posterior parameterization, and broader invertible-basis derivation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Cold Diffusion: Inverting Arbitrary Image Transforms Without Noise
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bansal et al. generalize iterative restoration to arbitrary deterministic degradations such as blur and masking and argue that noise is not necessary for generative behavior. Blurring Diffusion instead restores a probabilistic Markov model and small-step reverse expressivity through Gaussian noise, yielding stronger unconditional FID but covering a narrower linear corruption family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Soft Diffusion: Score Matching for General Corruptions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Daras et al. derive Soft Score Matching for general linear corruptions, add a corruption-aware network objective and momentum sampler, and report CelebA-64 FID 1.85. It is broader over linear operators and uses a different reverse construction; Blurring Diffusion retains the standard epsilon U-Net by restricting the process to analytically diagonal Gaussian schedules.

reviewed_competitors.title: Score-based Denoising Diffusion with Non-Isotropic Gaussian Noise Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Voleti, Pal, and Oberman derive DDPM and score-matching models for general non-isotropic Gaussian noise and examine Gaussian free fields on CIFAR-10. Their covariance shapes the injected noise itself; Blurring Diffusion primarily shapes frequency-dependent signal attenuation while retaining scalar noise in its chosen basis and targets a heat/coarse-to-fine interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: gDDIM: Generalized denoising diffusion implicit models

reviewed_competitors.title: Relay Diffusion: Unifying diffusion process across resolutions for image synthesis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Relay Diffusion uses DCT analysis, blurring diffusion, and block noise to transfer a partially noised state across image resolutions so high-resolution generation need not restart. It converts the target's frequency bias into an explicit cross-model resolution relay and evaluates higher-resolution CelebA-HQ and ImageNet synthesis.

reviewed_competitors.difference: FNO learns a resolution-invariant operator by applying unconstrained complex weights to Fourier modes and is the exact architecture that CFNO modifies. Clifford Fourier layers add grade-aware geometric-product tying across coupled fields, improving the paper's fixed-grid low-data cases but sacrificing real FFTs, adding computation, and not demonstrating FNO's zero-shot resolution or parameterized-operator scope.

reviewed_competitors.title: Message Passing Neural PDE Solvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: MP-PDE builds learned message-passing updates that contain classical discretizations and generalize across topology, geometry, boundary conditions, irregular discretizations, and equation parameters. It addresses a much broader solver regime than the fixed regular-grid Clifford models, while lacking their explicit scalar/vector/bivector coupling rule and spectral efficiency.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lie Point Symmetry Data Augmentation for Neural PDE Solvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: LPSDA derives solution-preserving transformations from each PDE and improves sample complexity by roughly 4x to 16x without changing the base FNO/ResNet layer algebra. It encodes equation symmetries rather than field-component types and can complement Clifford layers, but requires deriving and interpolating valid transformations for each PDE.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometric Clifford Algebra Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: GCANs parameterize linear combinations of learnable Pin-group actions as geometric templates and evaluate 3D rigid dynamics plus large-scale fluid simulation. They move beyond fixed geometric-product convolution toward explicit learned transformations, whereas the reviewed work is simpler to drop into regular-grid CNN/FNO surrogates and uniquely supplies Clifford spectral layers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Clifford Group Equivariant Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: CGENNs construct O(n)- and E(n)-equivariant polynomial maps whose Clifford-group action preserves grades and the geometric product, with one implementation spanning three to five dimensions. This directly supplies the rotation/reflection equivariance absent from the reviewed convolution, but targets set/graph physical tasks rather than efficient regular-grid Fourier operators.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geometric and Physical Constraints Synergistically Enhance Neural PDE Surrogates
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang and Greenberg impose symmetry and conservation-compatible input/output constraints on staggered CFD grids, test their interaction across architectures and horizons, and evaluate out-of-range initial conditions plus real ocean currents. This is a more direct validation of physical constraint benefits than multivector tying alone, while being tailored to specific fluid-grid constraints rather than a general Clifford field representation.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: foundational empirical challenge to classical capacity explanations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. use controlled random-label and random-input experiments to show that standard networks can memorize while still generalizing on real labels. Rohlfs cites this line but incorrectly turns training behavior into a VC-dimension upper bound and offers a much broader conceptual taxonomy instead of a controlled capacity study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct theoretical survey and analysis predecessor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kawaguchi, Kaelbling, and Bengio focus on why over-capacity deep networks can generalize and on non-vacuous theoretical guarantees. The target is broader across six phenomena but is substantially less rigorous in its PAC and capacity treatment.

reviewed_competitors.title: In Search of Lost Domain Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct domain-generalization benchmark and methodology boundary
reviewed_competitors.difference: DomainBed standardizes datasets, algorithms, model-selection criteria, and conditions and finds that careful ERM is difficult to beat. That controlled design exposes why the target's heterogeneous PACS literature table cannot measure algorithmic progress.

reviewed_competitors.title: Domain Generalization: A Survey
reviewed_competitors.relationship: specialist survey of one central level in the target taxonomy
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. give a comprehensive DG definition, methodology taxonomy, datasets, applications, and research directions. Rohlfs sacrifices this depth to relate DG to five other meanings of generalization and uses a coarser feature-mapping/parameter-sharing/ensemble grouping.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Out-Of-Distribution Generalization: A Survey
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shen et al. systematically organize OOD problem definitions, datasets, methods, theory, and applications. Their framing provides more precise distribution-shift distinctions than the target's single abstraction spectrum, while the target additionally spans task, modality, scope, and neuroscience.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: broad foundation-model treatment adjacent to task and modality generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bommasani et al. analyze adaptation, architectures, training, evaluation, applications, and societal risks of broadly pretrained models at report scale. Rohlfs uses foundation models as one stage in a wider conceptual spectrum but offers neither comparable technical depth nor the risk and data-provenance analysis.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Bai et al. focus on meta-learning mechanisms for OOD and domain shifts, with a method-level treatment of transferable knowledge and fast adaptation. It cuts across the target's domain/task boundary and illustrates why those categories are not naturally exclusive.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Mayilvahanan et al. construct style-excluded LAION natural and rendition subsets and show that in-domain examples explain a substantial share of CLIP performance, arguing that web-scale data can create an illusion of OOD generalization. This directly qualifies the target's optimistic foundation-model narrative and makes training-domain contamination a first-class audit variable.

This is a controlled counterpart to the target's heterogeneous modality examples and reveals compositional generalization as a missing axis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Kernel Alignment Risk Estimator: Risk Prediction from Training Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jacot et al. derive KARE, an explicit training-data statistic for estimating kernel-ridge risk and selecting kernels without access to the true target posterior. Simon's posterior kernel has stronger oracle optimality and a simpler proof, but it is circular computationally and does not evaluate whether alignment alone selects the same kernels as KARE.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks as Kernel Learners: The Silent Alignment Effect
reviewed_competitors.difference: Atanasov, Bordelon, and Pehlevan show analytically and empirically that small-initialization homogeneous networks can first learn a low-rank, target-aligned kernel eigenstructure and then behave like regression with the final tangent kernel. Simon supplies an oracle reason alignment and low rank can be optimal, but does not derive the network dynamics or the whitening, depth, and initialization conditions that make silent alignment occur.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Regularization via Neural Feature Alignment
reviewed_competitors.difference: Baratin et al. document tangent-feature alignment and spectral anisotropy through training and connect them to a heuristic path-dependent Rademacher complexity. Simon's posterior construction makes the maximally aligned rank-one endpoint algebraically transparent, but its one CNN figure does not improve the predecessor's empirical breadth or furnish a learnable regularizer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Properties of the After Kernel
reviewed_competitors.difference: Long tests SVMs built from post-training neural tangent kernels across MNIST/CIFAR architectures and measures global structure, transformation invariance, learning-rate effects, and conjugate-kernel approximations. Simon narrows attention to label alignment and effective rank and provides a Bayesian ideal, but does not explain the richer invariance changes or show that its oracle statistics determine after-kernel accuracy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Limitations of the NTK for Understanding Generalization in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vyas, Bansal, and Nakkiran show that finite neural networks can have better data-scaling exponents than initial or briefly pretrained empirical NTKs and that the NTK can evolve through most of training. This directly limits any inference from Simon's qualitative early alignment match: an adaptive kernel can look more posterior-like yet still fail to reproduce network scaling or later feature learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mean-field Analysis on Two-layer Neural Networks from a Kernel Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Takakura and Suzuki optimize an intrinsic kernel in a two-timescale mean-field limit, prove convergence and discretization error, and show task alignment and advantages over fixed RKHS choices. This converts the broad idea of a good data-dependent kernel into tractable dynamics under restrictive two-layer assumptions, whereas Simon's posterior kernel remains the unattainable Bayes oracle.

reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive kernel predictors from feature-learning infinite limits of neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lauditi, Bordelon, and Pehlevan derive numerically computable task-adapted kernel predictors for Bayesian feature-learning and gradient-flow/weight-decay infinite-width limits, then show lower test loss than lazy kernels. Their kernels are model- and dynamics-derived rather than Bayes-optimal over an assumed target posterior, making them substantially more actionable than Simon's identity while less distribution-universal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training NTK to Generalize with KARE
reviewed_competitors.difference: Schwab et al. directly optimize a neural tangent kernel against KARE and report that the trained kernel can match or outperform both the source DNN and its after-kernel. This tests an implementable generalization objective rather than merely maximizing train-label alignment, highlighting the missing algorithmic and held-out-risk bridge in Simon's note.

reviewed_competitors.title: Normalization effects on shallow neural networks and related asymptotic expansions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yu and Spiliopoulos already develop the exponent-indexed asymptotic expansion, variance conclusion, learning-rate scaling, and MNIST/CIFAR-10 trend for one hidden layer. The target's defensible increment is the two-hidden-layer outer-first expansion, its layer-sensitivity decomposition, and empirical three-hidden-layer extension; the arXiv record itself carries an administrative text-overlap note with this precursor.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler establish an infinite-width frozen-kernel evolution and relate training convergence to positive definiteness for deep networks. The target interpolates away from the square-root/NTK endpoint and adds finite-width fluctuation powers, but its leading dynamics are likewise a frozen linear kernel and therefore do not establish feature learning or population generalization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mean Field Analysis of Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sirignano and Spiliopoulos rigorously analyze arbitrary hidden depth through sequential large-layer and large-training-step limits, obtaining deterministic integro-differential dynamics and conditional zero training loss. The target asks a different interpolation question between normalization exponents and derives fluctuation corrections, but its arbitrary-depth discussion is less complete and unproved.

reviewed_competitors.title: A mean-field limit for certain deep neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Araújo, Oliveira, and Yukimura prove a McKean-Vlasov mean-field limit for fixed arbitrary depth and equal growing layer widths, with fixed random-feature weights near the input and output. The target trains all of its represented groups and resolves exponent-dependent corrections, but only sends its outer layer width to infinity in the main proof.

reviewed_competitors.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang and Hu classify a broad abc-parameterization family containing standard, NTK, and mean-field choices and prove a dichotomy between feature-learning and kernel limits, introducing maximal-update scaling. The target studies a narrower exponent path and output variance; because its empirical measure freezes at leading order, it does not answer the feature-learning and widthwise-transfer objectives addressed by maximal update parameterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang and colleagues test whether optimal hyperparameters transfer from small to large models under μP on ResNets and Transformers, including billion-parameter language models. The target motivates learning-rate powers through a nontrivial limit but does not test cross-width hyperparameter transfer or compare with μP, leaving its practical learning-rate claim much less validated.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tensor Programs VI: Feature Learning in Infinite-Depth Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang, Yu, Zhu, and Hayou jointly classify depth multipliers and learning rates after the infinite-width limit, define Depth-μP for one-layer residual blocks, test depthwise hyperparameter transfer, and identify limitations for deeper blocks. The target merely states arbitrary-depth feed-forward rate formulas without proof and does not analyze residual networks, depth limits, or transfer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Principled Architecture-aware Scaling of Hyperparameters
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen, Wu, Wang, and Hanin derive initialization and maximal-learning-rate rules from equal mean-squared preactivation changes across width, depth, kernel size, connectivity, MLPs, and CNNs, then evaluate architecture rankings. This broader evidence challenges extrapolating the target's fully connected feed-forward formulas to heterogeneous modern architectures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Exponents Across Parameterizations and Optimizers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Everett and colleagues weaken alignment assumptions, cover three optimizers and four parameterizations, and train tens of thousands of models up to 26.8B parameters. They find hyperparameter transfer under multiple parameterizations, a strong layerwise standard-parameterization prescription, and a critical role for Adam epsilon. This shows that the target's SGD/MNIST ordering is not sufficient to claim a generally optimal exponent scheme.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Surprising Effectiveness of Large Learning Rates under Standard Width Scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Haas, Bordt, von Luxburg, and Vankadara identify a controlled-divergence infinite-width regime under cross-entropy, with stable hidden statistics and feature learning, that does not occur under MSE; they test multiple optimizers, architectures, and modalities. This is especially relevant because the target proves MSE dynamics but evaluates cross-entropy, so its theoretical ranking need not govern its own experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory from coupled instabilities in unfolded crumpled sheets
reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct prior from the same system
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shohat, Hexner, and Lahini establish largest-compression and return-point memory in unfolded crumpled sheets using 3D imaging, global mechanics, and a coupled-instability model. The reviewed paper's substantive addition is a two-cycle mechanical and acoustic readout that aims to work when the local structure cannot be imaged.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory formation in cyclically deformed amorphous solids and sphere assemblies
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adhikari and Sastry compare read protocols for single and multiple amplitude memories in simulated amorphous solids and sphere assemblies and distinguish loop from point reversibility. Their observables use configuration changes, whereas Shohat and Lahini target a scalar macroscopic dissipation proxy; the earlier work covers multiple-memory capacity that the proxy does not test.

reviewed_competitors.title: Networks and Hierarchies: How Amorphous Materials Learn to Remember
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mungan et al. map cyclically deformed amorphous solids to directed transition networks and connect return-point memory to interacting localized rearrangements and one-way transitions. That topology gives a more explicit state-space mechanism; the reviewed experiments infer the same kind of one-way transition from excess work without reconstructing the network.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multiple memory formation in glassy landscapes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lindeman and Nagel show that interactions between hysteretic rearranging clusters explain long transients, multi-period orbits, and persistent multiple memories. Shohat and Lahini use interacting hysterons as an interpretation but test a rapidly referenced, largest-amplitude scalar readout rather than those harder dynamical regimes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Competition between energy and dynamics in memory formation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hagh et al. show that even one dynamical hysteron can take many cycles to settle and that forcing time scale changes which state is selected. This directly limits the reviewed protocol's assumption that cycle two is a settled reference and shows why a dissipation kink can depend on drive rate rather than only stored amplitude.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory switching due to thermal noise in amorphous solids subject to cyclic shear
reviewed_competitors.difference: Majumdar and Regev show that thermal noise can trigger cascades of new plastic events and catastrophic memory loss, with non-Arrhenius temperature dependence and frequency-sensitive survival. The reviewed work is effectively athermal and does not establish how its global excess-dissipation detector separates threshold crossing from noise-triggered escape.

reviewed_competitors.title: Aging of amorphous materials under cyclic strain
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shohat et al. later measure logarithmic decay of dissipation across three amorphous materials and compare noninteracting, interacting hysteron, and structural bistable-network models. That result broadens dissipation as a probe but also makes age and cycle count explicit state variables that a two-cycle largest-memory readout must control.

reviewed_competitors.title: Student-t Processes as Alternatives to Gaussian Processes
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shah, Wilson, and Ghahramani derive proper Student-t processes through an inverse-Wishart-process hierarchy, with closed-form marginal likelihood and prediction, data-dependent predictive covariance, analytic model selection, and no extra asymptotic cost over a GP. reviewed_competitors.difference: Serra and Krivobokova select both smoothing penalty and order by empirical Bayes and study adaptive credible sets with frequentist coverage. reviewed_competitors.title: Adaptive Bayesian credible sets in regression with a Gaussian process prior
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sniekers and van der Vaart analyze empirical and hierarchical Bayes scale adaptation, posterior contraction, and credible-set coverage under explicit self-similarity conditions. SIP offers a symmetry-motivated scale-free heuristic but does not test coverage or establish contraction, so widening its bands is not comparable evidence of calibrated uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.title: Propriety of the reference posterior distribution in Gaussian Process modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Muré proves that a reference prior yields proper GP posteriors for smooth squared-exponential, Matérn, and rational-quadratic kernels and derives tail behavior. SIP argues from invariance but knowingly retains infinite mass; this work makes posterior propriety, not sampler pole avoidance, the relevant objective-Bayes standard.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can we trust Bayesian uncertainty quantification from Gaussian process priors with squared exponential covariance kernel?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hadji and Szabó show that GP scale selection can yield overconfident credible sets and analyze modifications that recover coverage under restrictions. SIP criticizes GP extrapolation visually, but supplies no analogous coverage audit and uses moments from an improper local branch, making this calibration framework a necessary competing standard.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gaussian Process Regression in the Flat Limit
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barthelmé, Amblard, Tremblay, and Usevich show that flat-limit GP regression converges to polynomial or polyharmonic-spline regression in both predictive mean and variance, and connect the limit to leave-one-out model choice. This predates SIP's submission and narrows its novelty: SIP offers a different symmetry and heavy-tail derivation, not the first Bayesian polyharmonic predictive process.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Sellier and Dellaportas combine an analytically tractable Student-t process with a Hilbert-space reduced-rank Laplacian representation and demonstrate prediction and training-time gains. reviewed_competitors.difference: Ambrogioni uses improper infinite-variance GP limits and non-positive kernels to obtain stationary, non-mean-reverting models with analytic corrected posterior formulas and synthetic and real experiments. SIP reaches non-mean-reverting polyharmonic behavior through output-scale hyperbolicity, but its noisy posterior remains unnormalized and sampled rather than analytically conditioned.

reviewed_competitors.title: Robust and Conjugate Gaussian Process Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Altamirano, Briol, and Knoblauch use generalized Bayes to robustify GP regression while preserving exact conjugate updates at virtually no additional cost, with applications including Bayesian optimization. It retains a kernel but directly delivers proper computational and robustness evidence absent from SIP's slow pole-avoiding sampler and outlier-sensitive marathon example.

reviewed_competitors.difference: RTD uses the one-to-one correspondence between examples to measure multiscale topological dissimilarity across different ambient spaces and validates on vision and NLP uses. That directly replaces the reviewed paper's cluster selection and visual cross-layer comparison with a scalar paired representation metric.

reviewed_competitors.title: Experimental Observations of the Topology of Convolutional Neural Network Activations
reviewed_competitors.difference: This study analyzes convolutional activations on image classification with multiple point-cloud constructions, diagram distances, representation-similarity comparisons, and mapper graphs. reviewed_competitors.title: The Topology and Geometry of Neural Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Topological RSA explicitly tunes the balance between geometry and topology and evaluates layer identification across model seeds plus brain regions across subjects. It addresses noise robustness and representation comparison rather than inferring homeomorphism from raw Rips lifetimes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Similarity of Neural Network Representations Revisited
reviewed_competitors.difference: CKA quantifies representation similarity across layers, widths, and seeds with explicit invariance analysis. reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Persistence: A Complexity Measure for Deep Neural Networks Using Algebraic Topology

reviewed_competitors.title: Convolutional Persistence as a Remedy to Neural Model Analysis
reviewed_competitors.difference: Convolutional Topology Representation studies persistent properties of filter space across training methods and relates them to generalization on convolutional models. It provides larger empirical validation and an explicit predictive endpoint rather than visual topology preservation alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: ReLU Neural Networks, Polyhedral Decompositions, and Persistent Homology
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work computes persistent homology from ReLU activation-pattern polyhedra and shows manifold signals can survive the induced coarse quantization across varied trained networks. It analyzes the exact ReLU partition rather than HDBSCAN clusters of activation coordinates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Topological Signatures of ReLU Neural Network Activation Patterns
reviewed_competitors.difference: The 2026 study works with the polyhedral dual graph and cellular homology, connecting partitions to decision boundaries and training loss. It offers architecture-native topology signals with operational correlates rather than treating Euclidean hidden activations as isolated clouds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Zigzag Persistence of Large Language Models Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zigzag persistence treats depth as one sequence of related point clouds, connects adjacent layers through neighborhood intersections, and validates the signal through block-pruning effects in language models. It directly tackles cross-layer feature tracking missing from the reviewed independent diagrams.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Topology Layer for Machine Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: The topology layer makes persistence differentiable and uses it for regularization, generative priors, and adversarial attacks. It enables causal interventions on whether preserving topology helps a task, whereas the reviewed paper only observes post hoc diagrams.

reviewed_competitors.difference: SIREN couples sine activations to a principled initialization and demonstrates images, audio, video, derivatives, wavefields, and PDE boundary-value problems. reviewed_competitors.title: BACON: Band-limited Coordinate Networks for Multiscale Scene Representation
reviewed_competitors.difference: BACON builds an analytically controllable Fourier spectrum and produces outputs at multiple scales for images, radiance fields, and signed-distance scenes. reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral Bias in Practice: The Role of Function Frequency in Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fridovich-Keil et al. measure learned-function frequency on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across architectures, augmentation, data size, and distillation, finding that useful frequency behavior is local and tied to generalization. This supplies the modern held-out classification evidence absent from the reviewed paper's noisy MNIST fitting diagnostic.

reviewed_competitors.difference: WIRE uses complex Gabor wavelet activations that are localized in both space and frequency, and evaluates denoising, inpainting, super-resolution, CT, image fitting, and NeRF. reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Neural Network Approximation Theory
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A directly competing comprehensive approximation-theory treatment covering Kolmogorov-optimal approximation, quantized weights, connectivity, Besov and modulation spaces, and exponential constructions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It makes encodability and nonzero-weight complexity central and covers substantially broader function classes; the present survey is more elementary and adds its residual-Fourier-to-ReLU route.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Network Approximation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct survey competitor relating ReLU approximation to classical nonlinear approximation, rate-distortion, construction time, and stability.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It emphasizes that space-filling parameterizations can improve rate-distortion while damaging numerical stability, a tradeoff largely absent from the present survey's custom complexity proxy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Expressivity of Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct review of approximation rates, structured depth advantages, and expressivity results for feed-forward, convolutional, residual, and recurrent networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its architectural and literature coverage is broader, whereas the present paper gives longer pedagogical constructions and a narrow original Fourier-to-ReLU theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Nonlinear Approximation and (Deep) ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The most direct conceptual predecessor for comparing deep ReLU networks with free-knot splines and n-term nonlinear approximation on self-similar univariate classes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It frames neural networks against matched nonlinear rather than generic traditional baselines and explicitly notes that a complete quantification is missing; the present survey borrows this theme but sometimes makes stronger untested claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal approximation of continuous functions by very deep ReLU networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A central optimal-rate result for arbitrary continuous functions that gives a width-depth phase diagram and necessary discontinuity of weight selection for the fastest rates.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies optimality and stability tradeoffs in total weights, while the present density proof has no function-class rate and Theorem 4 uses W L^{1/3} rather than total weights.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Approximation Rate of ReLU Networks in terms of Width and Depth
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct width-depth competitor deriving near-sharp constructive rates for Holder and arbitrary continuous functions on bounded subsets of R^d.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It gives explicit multidimensional modulus-of-continuity rates and optimality claims; the present survey's new rate targets a Fourier-extension class but leaves its d-dimensional construction and spectral cutoff implicit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Approximation Rates for Deep ReLU Neural Networks on Sobolev and Besov Spaces
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A contemporaneous and subsequently developed rate result giving sharp ReLU approximation across Sobolev and Besov classes and Lp norms.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It explicitly distinguishes optimal parameter rates from non-encodable parameters and proves matching lower bounds; the present theorem stresses weak regularity but lacks those optimality and encoding audits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal approximation of piecewise smooth functions using deep ReLU neural networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct theorem for genuinely discontinuous piecewise-smooth targets, with optimal nonzero-weight rates, minimum-depth results, and low-dimensional feature-map structure.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its discontinuity class and metric are mathematically compatible with jumps; the present paper's L1-Fourier class is not, despite using step functions as empirical motivation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal rates of approximation by shallow ReLU^k neural networks and applications to nonparametric regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A post-survey counterpoint showing optimal approximation and minimax learning rates for shallow ReLU^k variation spaces, including links to deep and convolutional models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It weakens any blanket depth-advantage narrative by identifying classes where shallow networks are optimal and couples approximation to statistical estimation, which the present survey excludes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Smaller generalization error derived for a deep residual neural network compared to shallow networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The direct primary predecessor for the residual Fourier architecture, optimal-control formulation, target-dependent frequency distributions, and 1/(W_F L_F) upper bound imported as Lemma 5.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The present survey specializes and explains that result, then compiles its bounded-frequency network to ReLU; its deep Fourier theorem is not independent new evidence beyond this source.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Learning without Global Optimization by Random Fourier Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A same-author follow-up that turns the random Fourier theory into a layerwise MCMC training algorithm and supplies the multiscale, image, and discontinuity experiments summarized in the survey.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It addresses learnability and empirical training more directly, but its no-Gibbs claims remain numerical and it still does not convert parameter count into bitrate or bring discontinuities into the survey theorem class.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fourier Features Let Networks Learn High Frequency Functions in Low Dimensional Domains
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A major competing Fourier approach that maps coordinates through tunable Fourier features and explains spectral-bias changes through the neural tangent kernel.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It focuses on trainable MLPs and empirical low-dimensional signal reconstruction rather than oracle residual Fourier best approximation; it is a necessary baseline for the survey's high-frequency and image claims.

reviewed_competitors.title: Representation Compression and Generalization in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shwartz-Ziv, Painsky, and Tishby propose the high-dimensional typical-set input-compression inequality evaluated here. Galloway et al. supply its first large empirical study but inherit its incomplete proof and hidden fixed-encoder assumption.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Official OpenReview paper and theorem assumptions checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: How Does Information Bottleneck Help Deep Learning?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kawaguchi et al. explicitly classify the source inequality as an incomplete conjecture, explain the learned-encoder counterexample, and derive bounds depending on conditional representation information plus the complexity of the learned encoder. Their experiments also show I(X;Z) alone can be held fixed while generalization varies.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2023 PMLR paper and supplement checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Information in Infinite Ensembles of Infinitely-Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shwartz-Ziv and Alemi introduce the analytically tractable Gaussian infinite-ensemble setting and search for information quantities correlated with generalization. The target adds the claimed ICB coverage test, more datasets, random labels, and perturbation ranking.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Variational Bounds of Mutual Information
reviewed_competitors.difference: Poole et al. derive and analyze variational upper and lower objectives, emphasizing bias-variance and batch-size limits. The target applies known-conditional-density forms to NTK Gaussian outputs, but converts expectation-level objectives into empirical population-MI estimates without adding concentration theory.

reviewed_competitors.title: Spectral Bias and Task-Model Alignment Explain Generalization in Kernel Regression and Infinitely Wide Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Canatar, Bordelon, and Pehlevan derive analytical learning curves from the kernel spectrum, task alignment, data distribution, sample size, and noise. It is less black-box than ICB but directly targets expected kernel-regression error and distinguishes class-pair difficulty.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Current arXiv and Nature Communications record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization Through the Lens of Leave-One-Out Error
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bachmann, Hofmann, and Lucchi use a closed-form kernel leave-one-out error to predict test performance, double descent, random-label behavior, and transfer. Unlike ICB, it is an algorithm-specific error estimator rather than a claimed universal confidence bound and should be compared on the same small-data trials.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv and ICLR 2022 OpenReview paper checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Information-Theoretic Analysis of Generalization Capability of Learning Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu and Raginsky control expected generalization using mutual information between the training sample and the learned hypothesis. This captures data-dependent parameter selection that representation-only I(X;Z) misses, though it can be difficult to estimate non-vacuously for large models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reasoning About Generalization via Conditional Mutual Information
reviewed_competitors.difference: Steinke and Zakynthinou measure how much the learned output reveals about membership in a supersample and show that bounded CMI implies several generalization notions. Their information object explicitly concerns the data-dependent algorithm output rather than only compression of a fresh input representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Estimating Information Flow in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goldfeld et al. give a rigorous noisy-representation framework, show deterministic-network I(X;T) is vacuous, reinterpret apparent compression as geometric clustering, and find evidence against a simple causal compression-generalization link. The target avoids deterministic divergence using stochastic infinite ensembles but does not isolate causality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fantastic Generalization Measures and Where to Find Them
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jiang et al. compare many complexity measures while controlling training error and diagnose confounding across hyperparameters. The target borrows rank-correlation methodology but often permits training accuracy to vary and uses it only as a baseline, leaving compression entangled with fit and regularization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Computing Nonvacuous Generalization Bounds for Deep (Stochastic) Neural Networks with Many More Parameters than Training Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dziugaite and Roy optimize a PAC-Bayes posterior and compute a valid numerical certificate for trained stochastic networks, using far more data and yielding looser bounds. ICB reports much smaller numbers from under 2,000 samples, but its representation-only theorem does not apply to the learned encoder used.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Improved Nearest Neighbour Classifier
reviewed_competitors.relationship: same-work precursor and closest direct overlap
reviewed_competitors.difference: The same authors posted this manuscript before the reviewed paper. It presents WNN, the same MNIST and EMNIST headline numbers, window pruning, a complexity analysis, and the local-approximation roots in an appendix. The reviewed paper reverses the emphasis toward interpolation theory but is not an independent algorithm or experiment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Pattern Recognition Using a New Transformation Distance
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tangent distance builds translation, rotation, scale, shear, and stroke-thickness invariance directly into a memory-based distance and validates on NIST characters. WNN instead approximates invariance through independent windows plus a huge finite augmentation set, without comparing the two distance constructions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Invariant Scattering Convolution Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Scattering networks use fixed wavelet convolutions, modulus, and averaging to obtain translation invariance and provable stability to deformations, with handwritten-digit experiments. This provides the kind of explicit representation guarantee that WNN's K-functional analogy does not establish for its class-patch score.

reviewed_competitors.title: Matching Networks for One Shot Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Matching Networks learn support-conditioned embeddings and attention over labeled examples with an episodic train/validation/test design. They preserve exemplar-based prediction while learning a transferable metric, whereas WNN fixes raw-pixel Euclidean distance and expands storage through hand-designed transformations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prototypical Networks for Few-shot Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prototypical Networks learn an embedding in which each class can be represented by a mean prototype. That supplies a compact metric classifier and explicit held-out-class evaluation, contrasting with WNN's millions of raw augmented exemplars and no learned feature geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Simple Cache Model for Image Recognition
reviewed_competitors.difference: The cache model retrieves class evidence from pretrained hidden representations, continuously weights all cached examples, and evaluates accuracy, cache size, layers, datasets, and adversarial robustness. WNN is training-free but searches raw local pixels and reports no memory-size or robustness study.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep k-Nearest Neighbors: Towards Confident, Interpretable and Robust Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: DkNN retrieves labeled neighbors at every learned representation layer and turns their agreement into nonconformity, confidence, and exemplar explanations, including out-of-manifold inputs. WNN asserts transparency but neither exposes patch explanations nor tests calibration, robustness, or failure detection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Nearest Neighbors Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: N3 replaces hard kNN selection with a differentiable relaxation and learns the feature space used for patch matching. Although evaluated mainly on correspondence and restoration rather than digit classification, it directly addresses fixed raw-patch metrics and offers a modular route to trainable local retrieval absent from WNN.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Local Descriptor Based Image-to-Class Measure for Few-shot Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: DN4 also classifies by summing local-descriptor nearest-neighbor evidence over a class, but learns convolutional local descriptors end to end and evaluates across multiple few-shot datasets with held-out classes. It is the closest structural precedent to WNN's independently minimized window score and is not cited.

reviewed_competitors.title: Emerging Properties in Self-Supervised Vision Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: DINO shows that self-supervised transformer features support a 78.3% ImageNet kNN classifier while also yielding localized semantic structure. It separates the value of nearest-neighbor inference from the quality of the representation, a comparison WNN cannot make in raw pixels on only normalized digits.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tip-Adapter: Training-free Adaption of CLIP for Few-shot Classification
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tip-Adapter constructs a key-value cache from labeled support examples in CLIP feature space, combines retrieval with zero-shot priors, and tests 11 datasets; optional cache tuning converges quickly. WNN's no-backprop appeal is similar, but it lacks pretrained semantics, broad benchmarks, and a compact cache analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Integrating kNN with Foundation Models for Adaptable and Privacy-Aware Image Classification
reviewed_competitors.difference: This 2024 work combines self-supervised foundation-model embeddings with kNN and evaluates benchmark and medical images, continual updates, data removal, privacy, and open-source reproducibility. It demonstrates modern nonparametric adaptability without raw-pixel augmentation libraries.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Adversarial Training and the 1 Nearest Neighbor Classifier
reviewed_competitors.difference: The paper proves a local robustness property for 1-NN under stated assumptions and tests 135 binary image problems plus robust-model comparisons. It illustrates how a mathematical claim about nearest-neighbor behavior can be tied to explicit threat models and broad experiments, which WNN's approximation motivation does not do.

reviewed_competitors.title: Leveraging Cross-Modal Neighbor Representation for Improved CLIP Classification
reviewed_competitors.difference: CODER represents each image by distances to a dense generated text-neighbor set and evaluates zero- and few-shot classification across datasets and CLIP models. It treats neighbor geometry itself as a representation design problem, while WNN fixes raw windows and only enlarges the exemplar set.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fast and Multiphase Rates for Nearest Neighbor Classifiers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This 2025 COLT work studies how nearest-neighbor classification error scales with training-set size and identifies multiple rate regimes. It is a theory-first comparator for the guarantees WNN would need to justify its dependence on original and synthetically expanded sample counts.
