reviewed_competitors.title: ModelDiff: A Framework for Comparing Learning Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporary alternative for isolating behavioral consequences of design choices.
reviewed_competitors.difference: ModelDiff compares distributions of trained models, surfaces coherent input subpopulations where feature use differs, and validates candidate transformations counterfactually. The reviewed error-difference game synthesizes a target function directly but lacks ModelDiff's explicit three-stage causal validation and demonstrated real-image comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Spectral Bias of Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Prior analytic and empirical characterization of the low-frequency effect recovered in several examples.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rahaman et al. explicitly measure Fourier-frequency-dependent learning and connect it to manifold geometry. Dorrell et al. require no predefined Fourier basis and can expose other task structures, but their qualitative smooth-function findings do not by themselves exceed this stronger spectral baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Exact Computation of Inductive Bias
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later information-theoretic quantification of task-relative inductive bias.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Boopathy et al. estimate the information required to specify well-generalizing hypotheses from the random-hypothesis loss distribution and give approximation-error bounds. It quantifies an amount of task-relative bias across hypothesis spaces, whereas Dorrell et al. discovers exemplar tasks but supplies neither a scalar measure nor estimation guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Teasing Apart Architecture and Initial Weights as Sources of Inductive Bias in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later large controlled meta-learning study of bias attribution.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bencomo et al. meta-train 430 MLP, CNN, LSTM, and Transformer models across three known bias-demanding tasks and show initialization can erase architecture gaps. Their controlled factorial result reinforces that Dorrell et al.'s discovered functions cannot be attributed to circuit architecture without separating initial weights and meta-training history.

reviewed_competitors.title: A software platform for real-time and adaptive neuroscience experiments
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later experimental infrastructure demonstrating a narrower real biological closed loop.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The improv platform uses Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization online during zebrafish two-photon imaging to choose among 576 binocular motion stimuli, reaching a stopping criterion within at most 30 stimuli. It validates practical adaptive stimulus search but optimizes immediate neural response, not a target that a living animal learns and generalizes, so the reviewed proposal's repeated teaching burden remains open.

reviewed_competitors.difference: FaceNet directly learns a Euclidean embedding with triplet constraints so distances encode similarity and support recognition, verification, and clustering. reviewed_competitors.title: Supervised Contrastive Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: SupCon explicitly attracts same-class examples and repels different-class examples across a batch, reports strong ImageNet-scale accuracy and robustness, and subsumes several metric losses. reviewed_competitors.title: ProofWriter: Generating Implications, Proofs, and Abductive Statements over Natural Language
reviewed_competitors.difference: ProofWriter already generated natural-language implications and checkable proof trees, including iterative one-step generation, depth generalization, and abduction. PrOntoQA narrows the calculus and language to make arbitrary prompted CoTs easy to parse while adding fictional/true/false and context-order controls; it should not be read as the first generated natural-language proof benchmark.

reviewed_competitors.title: FOLIO: Natural Language Reasoning with First-Order Logic
reviewed_competitors.difference: FOLIO uses human-authored, linguistically varied premises with first-order annotations and substantially richer logic. It sacrifices PrOntoQA's exact generated proof trace and tight factorial control, but exposes the semantic and calculus simplicity hidden by the latter's general 'first-order logic' framing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Selection-Inference: Exploiting Large Language Models for Interpretable Logical Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Selection-Inference alternates explicit premise selection and inference modules so each step is causally tied to selected facts and can be searched. PrOntoQA diagnoses failures of a single free-form CoT call; SI supplies a direct architectural alternative to the paper's conclusion that goal-relevant selection is the bottleneck.

reviewed_competitors.title: Faithful Reasoning Using Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Creswell and Shanahan chain separately trained selection and inference models and use beam search over reasoning traces whose causal structure mirrors the deduction. This is precisely the kind of implemented search that PrOntoQA's prompt-only DFS and indirect argument about beam search do not evaluate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Standard self-consistency samples diverse reasoning paths and marginalizes their final answers. PrOntoQA's appendix instead groups identical full logical-form sequences and weights them by length-normalized scores, so its null result does not directly replicate the method it cites.

reviewed_competitors.title: Testing the General Deductive Reasoning Capacity of Large Language Models Using OOD Examples
reviewed_competitors.difference: The authors' PrOntoQA-OOD follow-up adds six deduction rules and explicit depth, width, and compositional generalization. It is the appropriate source for broader deductive-capacity claims and tacitly confirms that the original paper's linear five-hop modus-ponens benchmark cannot support them alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dziri and colleagues analyze multiplication, logic-grid puzzles, and dynamic programming as computation graphs and argue that autoregressive models rely on linearized subgraph matching with error compounding. Their richer tasks and theoretical framing broaden the local-success/global-failure pattern beyond PrOntoQA's tiny linear ontologies.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tree of Thoughts explicitly maintains candidate states, evaluates alternatives, and runs BFS or DFS with lookahead and backtracking. It directly demonstrates why changing demonstrations to DFS-like prose is not equivalent to executing a search algorithm, though its reported tasks are not formal-logic proof benchmarks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Explicit Planning Helps Language Models in Logical Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: LEAP adds lookahead over future consequences to premise selection and deduction and reports significant gains over CoT on PrOntoQA with GPT-3.5. It is a direct empirical counterweight to any reading of the appendix as evidence that search cannot help and turns the diagnosed planning bottleneck into an explicit intervention.

reviewed_competitors.title: Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Logic-LM translates problems into symbolic form, delegates inference to a deterministic solver, and uses solver errors for self-refinement across five benchmarks including PrOntoQA. It avoids free-form proof planning after semantic parsing and reports large gains over ordinary and CoT prompting.

reviewed_competitors.title: LINC: A Neurosymbolic Approach for Logical Reasoning by Combining Language Models with First-Order Logic Provers
reviewed_competitors.difference: LINC confines the LLM to semantic parsing and executes deduction in a first-order theorem prover, obtaining large gains on ProofWriter and complementary behavior on FOLIO. It realizes the PrOntoQA conclusion's proposed neurosymbolic direction but also moves the bottleneck from proof search to faithful language-to-logic translation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Turpin and colleagues intervene with biasing features and show that models often rationalize biased answers without mentioning the true influence. Their causal evidence separates plausible or even valid-looking emitted explanations from internal decision causes, a distinction PrOntoQA's formal output checker does not make.

reviewed_competitors.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lanham and colleagues intervene on CoTs through truncation, mistakes, paraphrases, and other tests to measure whether answers condition on the rationale. This provides a necessary causal complement to PrOntoQA's proof-validity analysis and finds that faithfulness varies by task and can decrease with model capability.

reviewed_competitors.title: How to Think Step-by-Step: A Mechanistic Understanding of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work uses PrOntoQA-style fictional ontology traces to patch attention heads, probe relational information, and trace candidate answer pathways in Llama-2 7B. It attempts the internal-mechanism analysis absent from the original, although its attention, probe, and logit-lens evidence remains only partly causal and covers one templated model setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Chain-of-Thought Is as Strong as Its Weakest Link: A Benchmark for Verifiers of Reasoning Chains
reviewed_competitors.difference: REVEAL labels relevance, evidence attribution, and logical correctness for each step across open-domain QA and modern models, then measures verifier failures. PrOntoQA offers exact synthetic proofs; REVEAL trades exactness for broader language and shows that automated step verification itself is difficult outside a closed grammar.

reviewed_competitors.title: LogicBench: Towards Systematic Evaluation of Logical Reasoning Ability of Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: LogicBench evaluates 25 patterns spanning propositional, first-order, and non-monotonic logic with contemporary model families and explicit negation analysis. Its cases focus mostly on one rule at a time, while PrOntoQA focuses on multi-hop chaining of one rule; together they expose complementary rule breadth and depth gaps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Large Language Models Meet Symbolic Provers for Logical Reasoning Evaluation
reviewed_competitors.difference: ProverGen combines LLM linguistic generation with symbolic proving to create ProverQA, retaining verified intermediate reasoning while increasing scale, diversity, and first-order complexity. It directly addresses PrOntoQA's template simplicity and narrow ontology family, though its LLM-generated language introduces a different quality-control burden.

reviewed_competitors.title: Concise and Organized Perception Facilitates Reasoning in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: COP explicitly reorganizes and filters premises and reports improvements on ProofWriter, PrOntoQA, PrOntoQA-OOD, and FOLIO. Its results support premise perception and distractibility as an actionable alternative explanation for the original top-down degradation, rather than uniquely attributing it to abstract proof planning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantifying Logical Consistency in Transformers via Query-Key Alignment
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work identifies attention heads whose query-key alignment predicts valid versus invalid inference in a single forward pass and evaluates modern 1.5B-70B models on PrOntoQA-OOD, PARARULE-Plus, and MultiLogicEval. It replaces emitted-CoT parsing with an internal diagnostic, but still requires calibration and does not by itself prove faithful causal reasoning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Correctness: Exposing LLM-generated Logical Flaws in Reasoning via Multi-step Automated Theorem Proving
reviewed_competitors.difference: MATP translates free-form reasoning into first-order logic and applies automated theorem provers, evaluating 10,830 traces from ten general and reasoning models across PrOntoQA-OOD, ProofWriter, and FOLIO. It scales the original formal step-checking idea beyond one grammar and one 2022 API family, while semantic translation accuracy remains part of the verifier.

reviewed_competitors.title: FaithCoT-Bench: Benchmarking Instance-Level Faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: FaithCoT-Bench turns causal CoT faithfulness into an instance-level detection task with expert annotations, fine-grained causes, and counterfactual, logit-based, and judge baselines across four domains. It targets whether a specific trace reflects the model process, whereas PrOntoQA establishes only whether a synthetic trace is formally valid and target-reaching.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This work gives an equivalent convex program for sums of three-layer ReLU subnetworks with weight decay and fixed-width complexity conditions. It weakens QCNN's framing that practical convex training was confined to shallow or strongly planted settings, while applying to a different regularized architecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Hidden Convex Optimization Landscape of Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks: an Exact Characterization of the Optimal Solutions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Lacotte, and Pilanci characterize all global optima of ordinary two-layer ReLU networks via a cone-constrained convex program and map convex solutions back to networks. QCNN's novelty is the minimum-pooled quasiconcave function class, not the first global convex view of shallow ReLU training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling Convex Neural Networks with Burer-Monteiro Factorization
reviewed_competitors.difference: The ICLR 2024 work scales equivalent convex formulations for two-layer fully connected, convolutional, and self-attention networks through Burer-Monteiro factorization and gives verifiable global-optimality conditions. It directly addresses the practical scaling question that QCNN leaves unspecified.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convex Relaxations of ReLU Neural Networks Approximate Global Optima in Polynomial Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: This ICML 2024 work studies polynomial-time convex relaxations and bounds their relative optimality gap on random data. It trades exactness for a stated approximation guarantee, whereas QCNN claims exact bisection but does not establish the required feasible sets.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convex Formulations for Training Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prakhya, Birdal, and Yurtsever formulate infinite-width two-layer ReLU training as a finite completely positive program and use a polynomial-time semidefinite relaxation, explicitly acknowledging that the exact convex cone remains NP-hard. This separates convexity from computational tractability more carefully than QCNN's feasibility claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Input Convex Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: ICNNs constrain the network to be convex in selected inputs so inference can solve an optimization problem; their training weights remain nonconvex. QCNN instead seeks quasiconcavity in the weights themselves, so the two approaches constrain different variables and solve different problems.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Optimal Memorization Power of ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vardi, Yehudai, and Shamir construct ReLU networks with roughly sqrt(N) parameters, prove near-optimality via VC dimension, characterize depth tradeoffs, and show that large bit complexity is necessary for sublinear parameters. The focal paper trades that compact storage for an O(N)-node routing tree and omits precisely the bit-complexity axis highlighted by its baseline.

reviewed_competitors.title: Provable Memorization via Deep Neural Networks using Sub-linear Parameters
reviewed_competitors.difference: Park et al. use depth to memorize N separated pairs with O(N^(2/3)) parameters and include empirical support. The focal method improves active query work with hard routing but expands total storage to linear and provides no experiment, making the two methods complementary points on an unmeasured size-compute frontier.

reviewed_competitors.title: Small ReLU networks are powerful memorizers: a tight analysis of memorization capacity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yun, Sra, and Jadbabaie prove tight sqrt(N) width for three-layer networks under their setting, extend finite-sample expressivity through depth, and study SGD near a memorizing solution. The focal paper counts input-conditional operations instead of width and does not address whether its tree can be found by gradient training.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memory capacity of neural networks with threshold and ReLU activations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vershynin gives probabilistic sparse constructions for threshold and mixed threshold/ReLU networks. The focal compiler is motivated by exploiting inactive weights, but it does not compare total sparsity, precision, or execution against this established sparse-capacity line.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memorization capacity of deep ReLU neural networks characterized by width and depth
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang and Yang explicitly characterize a width-depth product under a separation distance delta and discrete labels, supplying matching upper/lower scaling in that regime. It sharpens two gaps in the focal analysis: robustness/separation is a first-class parameter and discrete labels are covered rather than justified through continuously random outputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conditional Computation in Neural Networks for faster models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bengio et al. use policy gradients to learn activation-dependent block dropout against an accuracy-compute objective and report empirical speed improvements. The focal paper replaces learned routing with a dataset-specific exact compiler, obtaining a clean bound but no generalization or systems evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sparsely gated MoE demonstrates a practical capacity-compute tradeoff at up to 137 billion parameters with trainable top-k routing and distributed language tasks. The focal theorem explains how conditional paths can decouple total and active capacity, but its unit-cost lookup tree does not model gate training, load balance, communication, or prediction quality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Switch routing activates one expert per token and measures pretraining speed, communication, stability, low-precision behavior, and multilingual quality. It shows why elementary operation counts are incomplete: practical sparse gains require explicit load, dispatch, and hardware engineering absent from the focal analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hash Layers For Large Sparse Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hash layers deterministically select token-specific weights without learned gates, load-balancing losses, or assignment algorithms and match or beat learned MoE variants empirically. They provide a direct practical alternative to the focal paper's claim that activation configurations must be compiled into a branching tree.

reviewed_competitors.title: Large Memory Layers with Product Keys
reviewed_competitors.difference: Product-key memory indexes up to a billion learned values with fast exact nearest-neighbor selection and reports accuracy and twofold inference speed gains. It tackles the same large-storage/small-active-compute goal while supporting approximate semantic lookup, not merely exact equality on stored real vectors.

reviewed_competitors.title: Memorizing Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Memorizing Transformers perform approximate k-nearest-neighbor lookup over non-differentiable key-value memories and show scaling gains through 262K tokens across text, code, mathematics, and theorem data. The focal work provides exact finite-pattern theory but no mechanism for approximate contextual keys or evidence that memorized relations improve a task.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fast Feedforward Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fast Feedforward Networks use hard binary routing to select logarithmically many nodes from an exponentially large leaf set and report up to 220x feedforward and 6x MoE speedups. This is the closest practical successor to the focal tree idea: it trains on real tasks and measures latency, though it does not provide the same exact memorization lower bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Case for Learned Index Structures
reviewed_competitors.difference: Learned indexes treat lookup as predicting record position and compare neural models with cache-optimized B-trees in both memory and wall-clock speed. They expose the missing systems baseline for a construction that is functionally a dataset-specific index but counts neither stored bytes nor cache behavior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Datamodels: Understanding Predictions with Data and Data with Predictions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Datamodels learn a map from training-subset membership to target predictions and validate counterfactuals, brittleness, leakage, and data embeddings. They demand many retrainings like the target, but use those runs to model interactions beyond a single inclusion-minus-exclusion score and expose a stronger predictive validation framework.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: cross-scale memorisation study in language models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Carlini et al. quantify memorisation over model scale, duplication, context, and prompt length in language models using extractability-oriented measures. It shows that scale trends depend sharply on the memorisation definition; the target's classification-stability score cannot support claims about verbatim storage or extraction.

reviewed_competitors.title: TRAK: Attributing Model Behavior at Scale
reviewed_competitors.difference: TRAK combines random projections and a small ensemble to approximate retraining-based data attribution across ImageNet, CLIP, BERT, and mT5, with explicit efficacy benchmarks against expensive datamodel scores. The target's 400-model estimator is closer to the counterfactual quantity but does not compare accuracy, uncertainty, or compute against this scalable alternative.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Neural Network Memorization Be Localized?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maini et al. use gradient accounting, layer rewinding, retraining, and example-tied dropout to localize noisy-label and low-C-score behavior to small neuron sets. The reviewed manuscript maps which examples change across architectures but does not identify where dependence resides or causally manipulate it.

reviewed_competitors.title: What do larger image classifiers memorise?

This successor is the closest current record and should supersede the anonymous manuscript for final scientific claims while retaining the original as provenance for its printed defects.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Memorization Estimation: Fast, Formal and Free

It is an ICLR 2025 submission rather than an accepted result, but it targets the exact runtime and estimation weaknesses left unresolved by the reviewed manuscript.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Cohen et al. establish the full-batch neural-network phenomenon across practical experiments: Hessian sharpness hovers near 2/eta while loss oscillates. reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Gradient Descent on the Edge of Stability in Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arora et al. analyze edge dynamics as an implicit sharpness-minimizing flow along a manifold of minima for normalized GD and a transformed loss. The reviewed paper instead derives a local period-two attractor from explicit quadratic parameter nonlinearity in squared-loss models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analyzing Sharpness along GD Trajectory: Progressive Sharpening and Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. organize neural-network training into sharpening phases and prove behavior for two-layer fully connected linear networks under assumptions, emphasizing output-weight norms. The reviewed work uses an unstructured quadratic regression family and nullcline coordinates to argue the behavior is not uniquely neural.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quadratic models for understanding catapult dynamics of neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhu et al. show neural quadratic models capture the catapult phase and parallel neural-network generalization, with a revised version accepted at ICLR 2024. The reviewed work is more focused on progressive sharpening and a provable edge attractor in a minimal indefinite quadratic model, but provides much less generalization evidence.

It moves beyond the reviewed constant quadratic-output model and addresses precisely the higher-order and stochastic gaps left open here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Poly-time universality and limitations of deep learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows that a carefully initialized polynomial-size neural network trained by SGD can emulate any polynomial-time sample learner, while noisy full or large-batch GD cannot learn high-degree monomial classes. The staircase paper deliberately rules out such algorithm-emulation designs through within-layer regularity and supplies a transparent structured learner instead; it does not exceed the general emulator's learnable class.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Power of Differentiable Learning versus PAC and SQ Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It characterizes when SGD/GD can simulate SQ or full PAC learning as a function of batch size and gradient precision. The staircase result is a concrete regular-network construction rather than a generic simulation, and its proposed truncated-staircase separation is specifically about the gap between such regular gradient learners and unrestricted SQ-emulating architectures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Failures of Gradient-Based Deep Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It identifies simple targets, including high-order parity-style problems, for which gradients carry too little identifying information. The staircase paper changes the target support by adding accessible lower-degree correlations and uses depth to bootstrap toward the hard monomial; its isolated-parity control empirically reproduces the negative side of that contrast.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Can ResNet Learn Efficiently, Going Beyond Kernels?
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves distribution-free hierarchical and kernel-separation results for a smooth residual-network concept class. The reviewed paper contributes an interpretable Boolean Fourier-support condition and a function-independent regular random topology, but replaces ordinary end-to-end ResNet training in the theorem with layerwise quadratic coordinate descent and pruning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Backward Feature Correction: How Deep Learning Performs Deep (Hierarchical) Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It analyzes end-to-end SGD on a deep quadratic compositional concept class and makes correction of lower-layer errors part of the mechanism. The staircase paper uses a more transparent sparse Fourier class and regular function-independent topology, but freezes lower layers and only conjectures backward feature correction could remove its asymmetric regularization device.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Implications of Local Correlation on Learning Some Deep Functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: It turns local input/intermediate-label correlations into strong learning guarantees for tree-structured Boolean functions using an architecture matched to the target circuit. The staircase paper moves structure into Fourier support and uses a random regular architecture independent of the target, at the cost of a much more artificial neuronwise optimizer.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Understanding Hierarchical Learning: Benefits of Neural Representations
reviewed_competitors.difference: It quantifies sample-complexity gains from a fixed random neural representation followed by a quadratic Taylor learner on low-rank polynomials. The staircase construction instead learns named Boolean monomials recursively, but under a narrower product distribution and a specialized train-freeze-prune process.

reviewed_competitors.title: The merged-staircase property: a necessary and nearly sufficient condition for SGD learning of sparse functions on two-layer neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: It replaces strict one-monomial staircases with merged batches of newly introduced coordinates and obtains necessity plus generic near-sufficiency for O(d)-sample two-layer mean-field SGD on low-dimensional Boolean targets. That is closer to standard shallow SGD and tighter structurally, but it studies a different high-dimensional asymptotic regime and generic-coefficient qualification rather than the reviewed paper's all-target deep constructive theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: SGD learning on neural networks: leap complexity and saddle-to-saddle dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: It grades hierarchical difficulty by leap size and connects full-trajectory two-layer SGD time to CSQ lower bounds, proving a version for isotropic Gaussian data under additional dynamics assumptions. It goes beyond leap one and replaces explicit depthwise monomial assembly with saddle-to-saddle support discovery, but does not subsume the reviewed Boolean all-staircase construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Two-Layer Neural Networks Learn, One (Giant) Step at a Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies actual feature specialization in a high-dimensional two-layer network and shows how multiple gradient steps with O(d) batch size sequentially learn Gaussian target directions satisfying a staircase property. It gives a sharper batch-size-versus-step account for shallow networks, whereas the reviewed paper proves complete Boolean-function approximation through a custom deep architecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: Iteratively reweighted kernel machines efficiently learn sparse functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: It uses predictor derivatives to detect influential coordinates, repeatedly reweights the input geometry, and proves that adaptive kernel refits learn finite-leap hierarchical polynomials. This challenges any broad claim that hierarchy exploitation is unique to neural networks, while remaining consistent with the staircase paper's narrower contrast against one-shot fixed kernels.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Net2Net establishes function-preserving widening and deepening through neuron replication; the reviewed method adds variance-aware rescaling, optimizer-state handling, multi-stage rate adaptation, and hardware-aware schedules.

reviewed_competitors.title: GradMax: Growing Neural Networks using Gradient Information
reviewed_competitors.difference: GradMax chooses new-neuron initialization by an SVD that maximizes initial gradient magnitude; this paper avoids auxiliary optimization and instead transfers variance and assigns persistent stage-specific rates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Firefly Neural Architecture Descent: a General Approach for Growing Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Firefly greedily selects width or depth changes from a Taylor-approximated functional neighborhood and can search architecture; the reviewed method assumes the final architecture and optimizes cheap transitions along a prescribed width path.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning to Grow Pretrained Models for Efficient Transformer Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: LiGO learns Kronecker-factorized width and depth maps for pretrained Transformers with a short auxiliary optimization and reports up to roughly 50% savings; this paper uses a gradient-free signed initialization and focuses on parameter-age optimization across many growth stages.

reviewed_competitors.title: Masked Structural Growth for 2x Faster Language Model Pre-training
reviewed_competitors.difference: MSG decouples arbitrary initialization from exact function preservation with external masks and explores depth, width, head, and feed-forward schedules for language-model pretraining; this paper couples signed feature pairs with variance and stage-wise learning-rate transfer and tests broader non-LLM architectures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Navigating Scaling Laws: Compute Optimality in Adaptive Model Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Anagnostidis et al. derive adaptive shape trajectories from scaling laws across modalities; the reviewed paper proposes exponential schedules empirically and contributes lower-level parameter and optimizer transitions.

reviewed_competitors.title: When and How to Grow? On Efficient Pre-training via Model Growth
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. estimate when to grow, use smoothed dimensional expansion and redundant layers, and test 1.3B-to-2.5B language-model growth; the reviewed paper does not derive timing but provides explicit variance, rate, and optimizer-state transfer across CNN and Transformer tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: (Machine) Learning amplitudes for faster event generation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest author-overlapping precursor using boosted trees to emulate a loop-induced gg to ZZ amplitude at sub-percent accuracy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It establishes the low-dimensional boosted-tree proof of concept that this paper broadens to 2D/4D/8D targets, dense networks, skip connections, and symmetry reductions; the present baseline is therefore an extension rather than a wholly new surrogate premise.

reviewed_competitors.title: A factorisation-aware Matrix element emulator
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct physics-informed matrix-element emulator that encodes Catani-Seymour singular factorization and evaluates pointwise and integrated accuracy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Maître and Truong explicitly control extrapolation toward singular regions and test cross-section errors and phase-space trajectories. This paper instead flattens a higher-order target by a correlated lower-order denominator and tests uniform random coverage, without singular-limit or integral validation.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Primary arXiv record and JHEP 11 (2021) 066 status checked 2026-08-24

reviewed_competitors.title: Loop Amplitudes from Precision Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct neural surrogate for expensive loop amplitudes with learned predictive uncertainties and boosted retraining of difficult regions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Badger et al. center uncertainty reliability and targeted improvement in critical phase-space regions. The present paper covers broader model-family and dimensional comparisons but supplies only point predictions and finite-sample error fractions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unweighting multijet event generation using factorisation-aware neural networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous end-to-end use of matrix-element surrogates inside Sherpa for realistic multijet event generation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Janßen et al. wrap the approximation in two-stage rejection sampling that yields unbiased unweighted events and report 16-350x end-to-end cost reductions. The present paper reports larger inferred raw evaluation speedups but does not integrate the surrogate into an unbiased generator workflow.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Primary arXiv record, current revision and publication status checked 2026-08-24

reviewed_competitors.title: Accurate Surrogate Amplitudes with Calibrated Uncertainties
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later direct amplitude-surrogate work focused on jointly learned systematic/statistical uncertainty and calibration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bahl et al. use heteroscedastic, Bayesian, and ensemble approaches and assess pull-distribution coverage. This paper provides no uncertainty estimate, so its 90% threshold cannot identify whether a particular new prediction is trustworthy.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Primary arXiv v2 and SciPost Physics Core 8, 073 (2025) status checked 2026-08-24

reviewed_competitors.title: Accelerating multijet-merged event generation with neural network matrix element surrogates
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later realistic multijet-merged deployment of neural matrix-element surrogates with end-to-end timing and physics validation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Herrmann et al. address biased sampling, subprocess mappings, partial unweighting, and total event-generation time, reporting over 10x speedup for the six-parton setup while retaining exact correction. The present paper studies raw function regression on uniform coordinates without these deployment constraints.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Primary arXiv record and SciPost Physics 20, 071 (2026) status checked 2026-08-24

reviewed_competitors.title: How to Trust Learned Loop Amplitudes
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current direct loop-amplitude surrogate study targeting phase-space-wide trust, error-region discovery, and reliable refinement.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bahl et al. make calibrated uncertainty, localized failure detection, and targeted improvement central evaluation objects. Those capabilities directly address the gap between this paper's finite random-sample coverage and its domain-wide language.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Primary arXiv current record and SciPost Physics 20, 165 (2026) publication checked 2026-08-24

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling laws for amplitude surrogates
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current systematic study of how amplitude-surrogate error scales with training data, model size, and compute across multiple physics processes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bahl et al. separate data, parameter, and compute scaling and relate exponents to external-particle count, with repeated process sweeps and fitted uncertainty. This paper shows one data-volume curve and confounded 2D/4D/8D targets, so it cannot support a general resource or dimensional scaling law.

reviewed_competitors.title: Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Net: Selective Forgetting in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct deep-network predecessor defining scrubbing through indistinguishability from retraining.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Golatkar et al. perturb weights and bound residual information under a retraining-reference notion; SCRUBS instead uses teacher divergence and empirical error tradeoffs without an information bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine Unlearning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: System-level exact-unlearning alternative based on sharding, isolation, slicing, and aggregation (SISA).
reviewed_competitors.difference: SISA changes the original training architecture so affected shards can be exactly retrained; SCRUBS applies post hoc to a monolithic network but provides only approximate empirical forgetting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Adversarial Evaluations for Inexact Machine Unlearning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct methodological competitor and evaluation critique used as a baseline source in the reviewed paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goel et al. argue ordinary accuracy and distance evaluations can fail and introduce interclass confusion plus EU-k and CF-k; SCRUBS contributes a stronger optimization method and later adopts the confusion test, but retains forget error as its central metric.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Bad Teaching Induce Forgetting? Unlearning in Deep Networks using an Incompetent Teacher
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent direct teacher-student competitor for class and subset unlearning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bad Teacher distills an intentionally incompetent teacher on forget data and proposes ZRF without retraining; SCRUBS directly maximizes divergence from the competent teacher and alternates retain repair, producing more consistent results in its own reimplementation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Unbounded Machine Unlearning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct successor by the same project team and the clearest primary-source update to this submission.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The successor renames the method SCRUB, adds rewind, organizes metrics by bias/confusion/privacy applications, and evaluates privacy with an adapted LiRA membership attack; those changes address major validation gaps in the archived SCRUBS paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inexact Unlearning Needs More Careful Evaluations to Avoid a False Sense of Privacy
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later direct evaluation challenge for approximate unlearning, including methods from this lineage.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hayes et al. show per-example unlearning membership attacks are substantially stronger than common population attacks and expose heterogeneous vulnerabilities; SCRUBS evaluates no membership attack at all and aggregates behavior through error rates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine Unlearning Fails to Remove Data Poisoning Attacks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later causal stress test of practical approximate-unlearning methods across vision models and LLMs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pawelczyk et al. use poisoning effects as measurable evidence of residual influence and find failures even when conventional evaluations pass; SCRUBS tests injected label confusion but not diverse poisoning, targeted effects, or language models.

reviewed_competitors.title: SALSA: A Secure, Adaptive and Label-Agnostic Scalable Algorithm for Machine Unlearning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Accepted 2025 classification-unlearning competitor emphasizing security, labels, retain-data access, and speed.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SALSA redistributes predicted probabilities, anchors parameters, requires neither labels nor retain data, and evaluates eight metrics plus black-box attacks; SCRUBS requires retain labels/data and its original evidence is dominated by classification error.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Reliable Cryptographic Framework for Empirical Machine Unlearning Evaluation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Accepted 2025 verification framework targeting the central problem of empirically proving deletion.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The cryptographic evaluation embeds auditable signals designed to distinguish genuine influence removal from metric gaming; SCRUBS relies on natural-example prediction errors that can be increased without erasing information.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Explaining the Regularization Effect of Initial Large Learning Rate in Training Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Wei, and Ma already prove that a large initial rate plus annealing can generalize better in a constructed two-layer problem and connect the effect to the order in which generalizable and memorizable patterns are learned. The reviewed paper replaces learning-order analysis with a noise-driven sparsification story and broader trajectory visualizations, but offers less rigorous theory for nonlinear networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Bias of SGD for Diagonal Linear Networks: a Provable Benefit of Stochasticity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pesme, Pillaud-Vivien, and Flammarion characterize stochastic gradient flow for diagonal linear networks and prove a sparsifying generalization advantage whose strength grows with slower loss convergence. The reviewed paper imports that intuition to large-step plateaus and nonlinear features but does not carry over an exact implicit-objective theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shape Matters: Understanding the Implicit Bias of the Noise Covariance
reviewed_competitors.difference: HaoChen et al. prove that parameter-dependent label noise, unlike spherical Gaussian noise, recovers sparse ground truth in a quadratic model and emphasize that covariance shape is decisive. That result supports the reviewed mechanism's motivation while making its replacement of the exact residual covariance by a scalar Jacobian diffusion a consequential untested approximation.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: COLT 2021 PMLR Volume 134 official record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Validity of Modeling SGD with Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs)
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li, Malladi, and Arora stress that conventional Ito approximations are formally justified only for tiny learning rates and propose a testable necessary condition plus an efficient limiting simulator. The reviewed paper applies an even coarser diffusion specifically in a large-step bouncing regime and validates it only after per-setting scale calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Label noise (stochastic) gradient descent implicitly solves the Lasso for quadratic parametrisation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pillaud-Vivien, Reygner, and Flammarion explicitly characterize the stochastic-flow solution as a Lasso program and give convergence and support-recovery conditions. The reviewed work seeks a more practice-like source of persistent noise—large-step loss stabilization—but its general ReLU conclusion remains qualitative.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: COLT 2022 PMLR Volume 178 official record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Implicit Bias of the Step Size in Linear Diagonal Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nacson et al. prove that large full-batch steps can move non-centered diagonal networks from kernel-like to sparsity-inducing rich behavior through dynamic stability. The reviewed paper shows a centered counterexample where GD is much less sparse and argues stochastic noise is crucial, so the two works delimit data regimes rather than one universally displacing the other.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2022 PMLR Volume 162 official record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: (S)GD over Diagonal Linear Networks: Implicit bias, Large Stepsizes and Edge of Stability
reviewed_competitors.difference: Even et al. prove convergence with macroscopic steps and characterize the recovered solutions through an implicit regularization problem, explaining why large steps help SGD but can hurt GD near the edge of stability. This provides the crisp diagonal-network theory that the reviewed paper's SDE conjecture and selected curves did not establish.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stochastic Collapse: How Gradient Noise Attracts SGD Dynamics Towards Simpler Subnetworks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. formalize stochastic attraction to invariant sets representing vanishing or redundant neurons, give a curvature-versus-noise sufficient condition, and explicitly explain why longer early large-rate training can help. It reaches almost the same high-level conclusion through a more architecture-aware local mechanism rather than the reviewed paper's scalar Jacobian SDE.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Effect of SGD Batch Size on Autoencoder Learning: Sparsity, Sharpness, and Feature Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghosh et al. prove that any non-full batch selects a sparse, initialization-orthogonal global minimum for a one-neuron autoencoder on orthogonal data, while full-batch GD finds a dense initialization-aligned solution. This isolates stochasticity and batch size cleanly, but on a far narrower model than the reviewed deep-network evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Where Do Large Learning Rates Lead Us?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sadrtdinov et al. map a narrow optimal rate range just above the convergence threshold, test feature relevance rather than only activation counts, and show that too-large rates fail to extract meaningful patterns. It corroborates sparse feature selection while sharpening the reviewed paper's vague definition of large and its underdeveloped overregularization boundary.

reviewed_competitors.title: SGD vs GD: Rank Deficiency in Linear Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Varre, Sagitova, and Flammarion prove that label-noise stochastic flow reduces rank in two-layer linear networks while gradient flow preserves initialized rank, derive an eigenvalue SDE, and report extensions beyond linear regression. This turns the reviewed paper's empirical Jacobian-rank observation into a more exact but differently parameterized rank-deficiency mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Implicit Bias: The Insignificance of SGD Noise in Online Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vyas et al. find that small batches confer no implicit-bias advantage in single-epoch online image and language learning, with noise providing mainly computational savings. Their regime differs from the reviewed paper's many-pass plateaus, but the result shows that the claimed noise benefit is not universal and depends on data reuse and training horizon.

reviewed_competitors.title: SGD with Weight Decay Secretly Minimizes the Ranks of Your Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Galanti et al. analyze low-rank weight bias across arbitrary-width and depth networks and find it strengthens with higher rates or smaller batches, but also conclude weight decay is essential in their mechanism and the generalization effect is noticeable yet marginal. This challenges both the reviewed no-explicit-regularization emphasis and any automatic equation of rank reduction with large accuracy gains.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Intrinsic Dimension of Images and Its Impact on Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pope et al. establish low image-dataset intrinsic dimension, connect dataset-level dimension to learning difficulty, and validate the estimator on controlled GAN samples. The reviewed paper moves from whole datasets to proposed components and adds disconnected-support and component-adaptive modeling claims, while inheriting the same nearest-neighbor estimator limitations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning disconnected manifolds: a no GANs land
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tanielian et al. already analyze the connected-support obstruction for continuous GAN generators, prove a precision limitation, and reject high-Jacobian bridge samples. The reviewed paper generalizes the support statement beyond GAN-specific assumptions and repurposes it as an empirical probe, but its FID comparison is less topology-specific than the predecessor's bridge-quality analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Push-forward Generative Models Fit Multimodal Distributions?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Salmona et al. quantify lower bounds in total variation and KL as functions of mode separation and generator Lipschitz constant and contrast stochastic multi-step diffusion models. That theory addresses approximate fitting and stability, the crucial gap between the reviewed paper's exact connected-support proposition and its finite-FID evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: Diagnosing and Fixing Manifold Overfitting in Deep Generative Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Loaiza-Ganem et al. prove manifold-overfitting pathologies for likelihood models and justify two-step dimension reduction plus density estimation. The reviewed paper composes that method per component and varies bottleneck widths, but observes no consistent real-image gain from the component-specific estimates.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Manifold Dimensions with Conditional Variational Autoencoders
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zheng et al. prove conditions under which VAE global optima recover manifold dimension and show that conditioning can adapt to a union of manifolds with varying dimensions. This supplies a shared conditional-model alternative to the reviewed paper's separate checkpoints and focuses on learned latent activation rather than externally estimated fixed widths.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unveiling the Latent Space Geometry of Push-Forward Generative Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Issenhuth et al. analyze how pushforward models arrange latent regions for multiple disconnected modes, prove a sufficient optimality condition, and introduce simplicial latent truncation. It targets the bridge problem inside one generator rather than requiring one separately stored model per component.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Geometric View of Data Complexity: Efficient Local Intrinsic Dimension Estimation with Diffusion Models

reviewed_competitors.difference: Dinh et al. show that function-preserving reparameterizations can arbitrarily alter common sharpness measures without changing generalization. This directly limits the reviewed paper's inference from symmetry-controlled ambient Hessian spectra to generalization.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Du et al. derive automatic layer and neuron balancing for homogeneous networks under gradient flow. The reviewed paper subsumes these laws in a broader Lie-symmetry presentation and adds radial and data-dependent cases, but balance conservation itself is established prior work.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Mechanics: Symmetry and Broken Conservation Laws in Deep Learning Dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kunin et al. connect differentiable neural symmetries to gradient/Hessian constraints and analyze how finite learning rate, regularization, and other dynamics break conservation. The reviewed work offers an accessible group-action taxonomy and new radial/data-dependent examples but underexplores symmetry breaking already treated here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noether: The More Things Change, the More Stay the Same
reviewed_competitors.difference: Głuch and Urbanke systematize neural parameter symmetries, conserved quantities, balance, and boundedness. The reviewed paper's transpose-closed Lie-algebra derivation is closely aligned, while its main distinct bet is the nonlinear input-dependent construction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noether's Learning Dynamics: Role of Symmetry Breaking in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tanaka and Kunin use a Lagrangian formulation to analyze conserved quantities, second-order dynamics, and explicit symmetry breaking. It covers optimizer dynamics beyond the exact Euclidean gradient-flow regime emphasized by the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal approximation and model compression for radial neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The earlier radial-network paper by overlapping authors develops the radial rescaling activation and its O(h)-structured architecture for approximation and compression. The reviewed paper repurposes that symmetry for landscape and convergence analysis rather than introducing the architecture itself.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Networks on Toroids: Removing Symmetries Reveals the Structure of Flat Regions in the Landscape Geometry
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pittorino et al. explicitly quotient continuous neural symmetries before analyzing mode connectivity and flat regions. That approach avoids conflating parameter gauge directions with meaningful function-space flatness, a central weakness of the reviewed Hessian discussion.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symmetry Teleportation for Accelerated Optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhao et al. move along loss-preserving symmetry orbits to alter curvature and accelerate optimization. The reviewed paper supplies related conserved-quantity and flatness analysis but does not cleanly isolate the claimed rate mechanism in its scale sweep.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improving Convergence and Generalization Using Parameter Symmetries
reviewed_competitors.difference: The follow-up operationalizes parameter symmetries as teleportation algorithms and evaluates convergence and generalization more directly. It is a stronger empirical vehicle for claims that the reviewed paper supports mainly with synthetic curvature and rate illustrations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Abide by the Law and Follow the Flow: Conservation Laws for Gradient Flows
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marcotte et al. compute maximal independent conservation laws for gradient flows without requiring the investigator to guess a symmetry first, and give completeness-oriented algorithms. This advances beyond the reviewed paper's hand-selected group actions and exposes conservation laws that need not arise from its Noether template.

reviewed_competitors.title: Symmetry Induces Structure and Constraint of Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kunin et al. study how weight decay and noise interact with mirror symmetries to induce sparsity, low rank, and ensembling structure. It addresses the practical nonconservative dynamics and structural consequences largely absent from the reviewed experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Parameter Symmetry and Noise Equilibrium of Stochastic Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work analyzes how stochastic gradient noise drives motion along degenerate parameter-symmetry directions toward a noise equilibrium. It replaces exact full-batch gradient-flow conservation with a more realistic stochastic picture for trained networks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Keep the Momentum: Conservation Laws beyond Euclidean Gradient Flows
reviewed_competitors.difference: Marcotte et al. characterize conservation beyond Euclidean gradient flow and show that momentum or non-Euclidean geometry can remove many apparent laws. This directly narrows where the reviewed paper's invariants should be expected in contemporary optimization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Mode Connectivity via Parameter Space Symmetry
reviewed_competitors.difference: The authors' later work makes parameter symmetry central to mode connectivity and basin topology. It shifts from local orbit flatness to global connectivity, while still requiring quotient-aware interpretation of functionally identical paths.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformative or Conservative? Conservation laws for ResNets and Transformers

reviewed_competitors.title: Symmetry in Neural Network Parameter Spaces

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Double Descent: Where Bigger Models and More Data Hurt
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational empirical account of model-wise and sample-wise deep double descent, including label-noise effects.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nakkiran et al. center the interpolation peak and effective model complexity; Xue et al. identify an additional high-width final ascent and relate it to a separately increasing label-noise variance term and density.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Double Descent Requires a Fine-Grained Bias-Variance Decomposition
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct theoretical precursor decomposing random-feature risk into sampling, initialization, and label-noise-related components.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adlam and Pennington emphasize that coarse bias-variance accounts hide distinct variance sources around interpolation; Xue et al. focus on the label-noise contribution's large-width growth and extend the story to random density and deep-network experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Universality of the Double Descent Peak in Ridgeless Regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Theory of interpolation peaks and noise amplification across broad ridgeless-regression feature maps.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Holzmuller establishes when noise forces a universal interpolation peak; Xue et al. study a distinct deterioration after the second descent at very large width and propose density/regularization effects beyond the peak.

reviewed_competitors.title: Contrasting random and learned features in deep Bayesian linear regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest competing analysis of width, depth, data density, prior mismatch, and label noise in random versus fully learned features.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zavatone-Veth et al. find intermediate optimal widths for random-feature models but widest-or-narrowest optima in their fully learned deep linear networks, directly cautioning against transferring Xue et al.'s fixed-feature width mechanism to end-to-end feature learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: Regularization-wise double descent: Why it occurs and how to eliminate it
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing study treating regularization strength itself as the axis of double descent under noisy labels.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yilmaz and Heckel analyze and empirically control nonmonotone risk over L2 strength and show elimination strategies; Xue et al. instead argue stronger L2 can make the width-wise final ascent more pronounced by depressing intermediate-width risk.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign Overfitting in Classification: Provably Counter Label Noise with Larger Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing theory in which increasing classification-model size can counter label noise and enable benign overfitting.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Frei et al. prove beneficial large-model regimes under specific high-dimensional classification assumptions; Xue et al. locate regimes where still larger width worsens risk, so the two results delimit rather than universally contradict one another.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign, Tempered, or Catastrophic: A Taxonomy of Overfitting
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Broader taxonomy of asymptotic noise-fitting regimes in high-dimensional models.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mallinar et al. classify whether excess risk vanishes, remains bounded, or grows with overparameterization across kernels and neural models; Xue et al. focus on a finite-width nonmonotone curve and a controllable density axis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign Overfitting in Two-layer Convolutional Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Feature-learning theory giving signal-to-noise conditions for benign versus harmful interpolation in convolutional networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cao et al. analyze gradient-trained nonlinear CNNs and a signal-to-noise phase transition; Xue et al. offer a more explicit width/density curve decomposition but only in random or linear features, then rely on empirical transfer to CNNs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Random Pruning Is All We Need to Start Sparse
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct sparse-network comparator studying random source networks, width-sparsity tradeoffs, and approximation after pruning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chang et al. give approximation-oriented conditions under which a sufficiently wide random sparse source contains a target; Xue et al. study generalization under label noise and random masks, but do not match signal scale or prove that wider/sparser experimental optima preserve the same functions.

reviewed_competitors.title: DSD^2: Can We Dodge Sparse Double Descent and Compress the Neural Network Worry-Free?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest empirical competitor on sparse double descent and interactions among pruning, noise, width, and depth.
reviewed_competitors.difference: He et al. study pruning trajectories and strategies to avoid sparse double descent during compression; Xue et al. use random masks as a density intervention and emphasize a large-density final ascent rather than a compression algorithm.

reviewed_competitors.title: Early-Learning Regularization Prevents Memorization of Noisy Labels
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary source for ELR, one of the two noisy-label methods evaluated by the reviewed paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. introduce an early-learning consistency regularizer to prevent noisy-label memorization; Xue et al. use ELR as a stress test for final ascent but do not show that ELR is equivalent to a scalar L2 penalty or representative of all robust methods.

reviewed_competitors.title: DivideMix: Learning with Noisy Labels as Semi-supervised Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Primary source for DivideMix, the other noisy-label method tested in the paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. dynamically partitions examples by mixture-model losses and performs semi-supervised co-training; its mechanism is not merely regularization, whereas Xue et al. group its selected final-ascent curve with a broad regularization interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Contrastive Representation Learning through Alignment and Uniformity on the Hypersphere
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Provides the alignment-and-uniformity interpretation that motivates the reviewed paper's added regularizer and directly optimizes those two properties.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Its uniformity is a population feature-distribution criterion on the unit hypersphere with asymptotic analysis; IOT-CL equalizes negative entries of a mini-batch matching plan and does not prove equivalence to hyperspherical uniformity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hard Negative Sampling via Regularized Optimal Transport for Contrastive Representation Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A prior direct OT-based contrastive method optimizes over couplings and studies entropic regularization as a way to control negative-sample hardness.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is a min-max negative-distribution design with a degeneracy result and regularized ground-cost analysis; IOT-CL is min-min/bilevel, supervises a positive-pair coupling, and varies marginal constraints to derive softmax loss families.

reviewed_competitors.title: Intriguing Properties of Contrastive Losses
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Also generalizes standard contrastive loss into a broader family and evaluates how loss choice affects representation learning.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It finds many generalized losses perform similarly with a nonlinear projection head and analyzes feature suppression; IOT-CL organizes alternatives by transport marginals but does not test projection-head invariance or shortcut suppression.

reviewed_competitors.title: Your contrastive learning problem is secretly a distribution alignment problem
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The closest later successor explicitly builds on IOT-CL to formulate generalized contrastive alignment with entropic OT and evaluates the reviewed IOT variants directly.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives proximal multistep forms for several contrastive losses, introduces unbalanced OT for noisy views, gives additional theory, and reports five-seed standard/extreme-augmentation results; its GCA-UOT exceeds both IOT variants in every displayed setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Contrasting Multiple Representations with the Multi-Marginal Matching Gap
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later OT contrastive loss treats all views collectively and directly addresses settings with three or more representations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: M3G contrasts the ground-truth tuple cost with a multi-marginal OT polymatching cost and scales generalized Sinkhorn to 3-6 views; IOT-CL is fundamentally two-set and supervises a pairwise coupling, with MoCo as an unbalanced two-set extension.

reviewed_competitors.title: OT-CLIP: Understanding and Generalizing CLIP via Optimal Transport
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A same-author follow-up extends the inverse-OT interpretation from unimodal SimCLR/MoCo to image-text contrastive pretraining and inference.
reviewed_competitors.difference: OT-CLIP treats CLIP's two directional InfoNCE objectives as modified entropic OT, explores fused Gromov and unbalanced variants, and uses OT at zero-shot inference; the reviewed work only covers vision augmentations and leaves cross-modal or graph-aware costs untested.

reviewed_competitors.title: SinSim: Sinkhorn-Regularized SimCLR
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later direct Sinkhorn-and-SimCLR competitor adds an entropy-regularized Wasserstein term to organize the global latent geometry.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SinSim regularizes SimCLR with a separate Sinkhorn loss intended to disperse features, whereas IOT-CL derives the contrastive normalization itself from an inverse-OT coupling and penalizes negative coupling probabilities. SinSim is a direct current mechanism comparator but does not supersede the five-seed GCA-UOT evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning With Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: STaR already iterates rationale generation and fine-tuning from a few demonstrations, but uses ground-truth answers to retain correct paths and to rationalize failed cases. LMSI removes those per-question answer labels by substituting self-consistency, trading stronger supervision for vulnerability to confidently shared errors and evaluating a much larger model across more task families.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. introduce sampling diverse rationales and marginalizing their final answers at inference. LMSI turns that vote into pseudo-supervision and then applies self-consistency again after training, so equal-compute and single-path comparisons are essential to distinguish distribution distillation from extra ensemble compute.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: current arXiv v4 record checked 2026-08-23; ICLR 2023 version

reviewed_competitors.title: Reinforced Self-Training (ReST) for Language Modeling
reviewed_competitors.difference: ReST separates a Grow sampling stage from repeated Improve steps using an explicit reward and offline RL, with data reuse and human evaluation on translation. LMSI is simpler supervised imitation of majority paths and needs no reward model, but provides neither an independently grounded reward nor repeated-policy analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Human Data: Scaling Self-Training for Problem-Solving with Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: ReST-EM repeatedly generates math and code solutions, filters them with scalar correctness feedback, and studies scaling with PaLM-2 on MATH and APPS. It requires verifiable answers but offers cleaner correctness signal and multiple iterations; LMSI covers non-verifiable classifications using only agreement but cannot distinguish consensus from truth.

reviewed_competitors.title: Math-Shepherd: Verify and Reinforce LLMs Step-by-step without Human Annotations
reviewed_competitors.difference: Math-Shepherd constructs step-level supervision automatically and uses a process reward model for reranking and reinforcement on GSM8K and MATH. It directly addresses LMSI's unverified intermediate steps, at the cost of math-specific rollout labeling and a separate verifier rather than answer-only plurality.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ACL 2024 Anthology version of record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Quiet-STaR: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Think Before Speaking
reviewed_competitors.difference: Quiet-STaR learns token-level latent rationales throughout ordinary internet text and improves future-token prediction without task fine-tuning. It targets the task-specific-question limitation of LMSI, but introduces much heavier tokenwise sampling and reports modest reasoning accuracy from smaller models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Rewarding Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yuan et al. use the model as an LLM judge to create pairwise rewards and iterate DPO, jointly improving instruction following and judging. This generalizes beyond answer-parsable benchmarks, but self-judgment can inherit bias and requires calibration just as LMSI's self-consistency vote does.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2024 PMLR volume 235 version of record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Play Fine-Tuning Converts Weak Language Models to Strong Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: SPIN trains a model to distinguish human demonstrations from outputs of its previous iteration and proves a distribution-matching optimum, then evaluates open LLM leaderboards and MT-Bench. Unlike LMSI it retains human demonstrations as a fixed target distribution and studies multiple rounds, so it is not label-free but has a clearer anti-self-copying anchor.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: ICML 2024 PMLR volume 235 version of record checked 2026-08-23

reviewed_competitors.title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. find that intrinsic post-hoc self-correction without external feedback often fails or degrades reasoning, while external feedback can help. It studies inference-time revision rather than LMSI's population-level pseudo-label training, but reinforces the need to distinguish internal agreement from independently informative feedback.

reviewed_competitors.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
reviewed_competitors.difference: Self-Refine alternates model-generated critique and revision without parameter updates across seven generation tasks. It can adapt per example and avoids training cost, whereas LMSI amortizes many solutions into weights; neither approach by itself guarantees that internal feedback is correct, making independent verification an important shared boundary.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: NeurIPS 2023 proceedings version of record checked 2026-08-23
