reviewed_competitors.title: Combining Predictive Distributions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gneiting and Ranjan analyze linear pooling, calibration, and dispersion of combined forecasts. The target instead fixes logarithmic pooling and learns geometric weights in an online adversarial game.

reviewed_competitors.title: Combining probability distributions: Extending the logarithmic pooling approach
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rufo et al. explicitly learn LogOP weights from data with a hierarchical Bayesian construction. It is offline and model-based rather than forecast-blind online regret, but directly narrows the target's unqualified novelty claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transductive Log Opinion Pool of Gaussian Process Experts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cao and Fleet optimize transductive Gaussian-process expert weights plus a diversity correction at each input. The target learns one sequence-level static-comparator weight vector before seeing each report and seeks adversarial regret.

reviewed_competitors.title: Using stacking to average Bayesian predictive distributions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bayesian stacking selects linear-pool weights by leave-one-out predictive performance. It is data-driven and offline, without calibration-adversary regret or geometric pooling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Robust Forecast Aggregation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Preexisting regret under unknown Bayesian information structures.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arieli, Babichenko, and Smorodinsky derive robust static aggregators for binary Bayesian experts under structural classes. The target instead learns LogOP weights across repeated adaptive rounds using individual calibration only.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning of Optimal Forecast Aggregation in Partial Evidence Environments
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest earlier repeated learning from Bayesian/calibrated experts.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Babichenko and Garber learn an optimal aggregator under structured partial-evidence information and repeated outcome feedback. The target has a different best-static-LogOP benchmark and adaptive joint-law adversary, but not the first broad use of learning with calibrated forecasts.

reviewed_competitors.title: Forecast Aggregation via Peer Prediction
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lichtendahl et al. infer relative expertise from peer forecasts and study Brier/log scores without a long outcome history. The target instead observes outcomes online and proves a worst-case claim for geometric weights.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Proper Scoring Rules to Max-Min Optimal Forecast Aggregation
reviewed_competitors.difference: It proves score-induced pooling and online weight concavity for bounded proper scores. Log loss is excluded by its bounded-gradient guarantee; the target attempts to handle exactly that unbounded case using calibration and Tsallis geometry.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are You Smarter Than a Random Expert? The Robust Aggregation of Substitutable Signals
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives zero-sample averaging/extremization under projective substitutes and squared loss. The target uses repeated outcome feedback, log loss, individual calibration, and learns geometric weights.

reviewed_competitors.title: Soft-Bayes: Prod for Mixtures of Experts with Log-Loss
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest earlier online unbounded-log-loss aggregation algorithm.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Soft-Bayes robustly aggregates expert probabilities and gives loss-independent and tracking regret without calibration. Its mixture is linear and its benchmark is expert/mixture oriented rather than the target's fixed geometric-pool weights.

reviewed_competitors.title: Non-exponentially weighted aggregation: regret bounds for unbounded loss functions
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work uses non-exponential FTRL and phi-divergences for broad unbounded losses under different loss-growth conditions. The target exploits calibrated forecast geometry specific to log loss and LogOP weights.

reviewed_competitors.title: Online Aggregation of Unbounded Losses Using Shifting Experts with Confidence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier unbounded and shifting expert-advice method.
reviewed_competitors.difference: V'yugin and Trunov combine confidence-rated experts under signed unbounded losses and shifting regret. They aggregate expert losses/predictions rather than learning fixed LogOP weight parameters under calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Online Learning in Case of Unbounded Losses Using the Follow Perturbed Leader Algorithm
reviewed_competitors.difference: Poland and Hutter obtain FPL guarantees using scaled one-step loss fluctuation assumptions. The target instead derives probabilistic gradient tails from calibration for a geometric probability pool.

reviewed_competitors.title: Precise Regret Bounds for Log-loss via a Truncated Bayesian Algorithm
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mourtada and Gaiffas study sequential probability assignment for a prediction class using truncated Bayesian methods and tight class-complexity bounds. The target's parameter class is a report-dependent LogOP and its central challenge is forecast-blind adversarial timing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sample Complexity of Forecast Aggregation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Batch learning alternative for unknown forecast aggregation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lin and Chen quantify labeled samples needed to learn a Bayesian aggregator, with exponential expert dependence generally and improved rates under conditional independence. The target is online, parameter-restricted, and assumes calibration rather than iid training samples.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient and Near-Optimal Online Portfolio Selection
reviewed_competitors.difference: Portfolio selection learns convex asset mixtures under log return with efficient barrier geometry. It is the linear-pool analogue; the target's normalized geometric pool creates different unbounded gradients and needs forecast calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Tight Bounds on Minimax Regret under Logarithmic Loss via Self-Concordance
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Minimax log-loss benchmark for arbitrary expert classes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bilodeau, Foster, and Roy use self-concordance and sequential entropy when the learner directly chooses predictive distributions. The target instead restricts predictions to pre-report-selected LogOP weights and conditions the adversary by calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Maximum Likelihood vs. Sequential Normalized Maximum Likelihood in On-line Density Estimation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Earlier parametric online log-loss regret theory.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kotłowski and Grünwald obtain logarithmic regret for exponential-family density estimation. Their parameter controls a predictive density directly; the target's parameter weights arbitrary observed expert reports and faces an adaptive calibrated law.

reviewed_competitors.title: Online Aggregation of Probability Forecasts with Confidence
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Online probabilistic expert aggregation with confidence.
reviewed_competitors.difference: V'yugin and Trunov use confidence-weighted experts and mixability across probabilistic scores. The target learns forecast-blind geometric weights and relies specifically on calibration to handle unbounded log loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unconstrained Online Learning with Unbounded Losses
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jacobsen and Cutkosky develop optimal static and dynamic regret without a bounded domain under gradient-growth conditions. The target has a simplex domain but unbounded forecast-induced gradients controlled probabilistically by calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: U-Calibration: Forecasting for an Unknown Agent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kleinberg et al. give O(sqrt(T)) guarantees across bounded scoring-rule consumers for one forecaster facing an unknown agent. The target assumes experts already satisfy a much stronger exact condition and learns their pool under unbounded log loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: "Calibeating": Beating Forecasters at Their Own Game
reviewed_competitors.difference: Foster and Hart construct procedures that simultaneously improve calibration and accuracy relative to forecasts under Brier decompositions. They do not learn fixed logarithmic-pool weights or address unbounded log loss.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Does Optimizing a Proper Loss Yield Calibration?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct calibration-assumption theory cited by the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Błasiok et al. show that local optimality for a proper loss implies smooth calibration and describe neural-network applicability as plausible. This is weaker and differently formulated than the target's exact full-vector conditional calibration at every adaptive round.

reviewed_competitors.title: Algorithmic Robust Forecast Aggregation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo et al. approximate minimax-regret aggregators over explicit information-structure classes. Their work is offline robust computation rather than temporal LogOP weight learning, but it provides an algorithmic alternative to choosing calibration as the sole restriction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Peer Expectation in Robust Forecast Aggregation: The Possibility/Impossibility
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work asks what elicited expectations about peers make robust Bayesian aggregation possible. It changes the information available to the aggregator rather than learning forecast-blind LogOP weights over repeated rounds.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Surprising Benefits of Base Rate Neglect in Robust Aggregation
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Robust aggregation under relaxed Bayesian behavior.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Arieli et al. model base-rate neglect and worst-case binary aggregation rather than assuming exact calibration. It illustrates a different behavioral restriction and static-regret objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Kairosis: A method for dynamical probability forecast aggregation informed by Bayesian change point detection
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kairosis adapts weights with Bayesian change-point detection and evaluates tournament-style forecasts for an eventual outcome. It emphasizes dynamic empirical performance rather than worst-case repeated-outcome LogOP regret.

reviewed_competitors.title: Refined Risk Bounds for Unbounded Losses via Transductive Priors
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work uses data-dependent priors to refine PAC-Bayes-style risk bounds for unbounded losses. It is statistical/transductive rather than adversarial pooling, but provides modern tail-control machinery absent from the failed bad-event proof.

reviewed_competitors.title: Online Mixture of Experts: No-Regret Learning for Optimal Collective Decision-Making
reviewed_competitors.difference: It studies online committee/expert weighting and LLM collective decisions under voting or bandit-style feedback. The target concerns full probability reports, log loss, exact calibration, and a geometric pool.

reviewed_competitors.title: Robust forecast aggregation via additional queries
reviewed_competitors.difference: The method overcomes forecast-only impossibilities with truthful structured queries. It expands observable information instead of constraining the adversary by calibration and learning static LogOP weights over time.

reviewed_competitors.title: Prior-Agnostic Robust Forecast Aggregation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen, Peng, and Tang derive generalized log-odds rules with near-tight minimax regret under conditional-independence, Blackwell, and general classes. It is a static unknown-prior problem, not repeated best-weight learning.

reviewed_competitors.title: When Individually Calibrated Models Become Collectively Miscalibrated
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct current challenge to individual-calibration sufficiency.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It shows individual calibration need not survive strategic or correlated aggregation and proposes online adaptive weighting under Brier-style criteria. The target assumes nonstrategic calibrated experts and optimizes log loss without guaranteeing aggregate calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: AdaWeather: Adaptively Mixing Probabilistic Weather Forecasts with Logarithmic Regret
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest current empirical logarithmic-regret mixture successor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: AdaWeather obtains logarithmic regret to a best static probability mixture and evaluates weather forecasts. It uses a linear probabilistic mixture and domain assumptions rather than geometric pooling with a calibration-restricted adaptive adversary.

reviewed_competitors.title: Robust Aggregation of Calibrated Forecasts
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest current calibration-only robust aggregation successor.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work characterizes robust benchmarks and online algorithms using calibrated forecast/state feedback under decision payoffs. It does not restrict itself to best fixed LogOP weights and exposes a broader calibration-only frontier.

reviewed_competitors.title: Algorithmic Expert Aggregation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tang and Zhang require output experts themselves to be calibrated and study Blackwell refinement with randomized efficiency and deterministic hardness. The target uses calibration only as an input-tail assumption and does not ensure its pool remains calibrated.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Guo et al. show modern classifiers are often miscalibrated and propose temperature scaling. Their finite-data confidence calibration is not the exact full-vector conditional property the target's adaptive theorem requires.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ovadia et al. document predictive uncertainty and calibration degradation under shift. The target assumes calibration afresh for every adversarially chosen round law, a substantially stronger robustness property.

reviewed_competitors.title: Verified Uncertainty Calibration
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kumar et al. develop verified calibration estimates and recalibration methods. Such certificates target measurable finite-sample notions, whereas the target assumes exact continuum conditioning without an audit protocol.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Language-model calibration evidence cited in the target's motivation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kadavath et al. evaluate P(IK) and related self-knowledge formats on selected tasks and report out-of-distribution limitations. It does not establish exact class-vector calibration for arbitrary model ensembles and adaptive environments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting the Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical calibration evidence cited by the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Minderer et al. revisit architecture, pretraining, and shift effects and explicitly report many miscalibration cases. The target turns selected empirical calibration into an exact theorem assumption without a bridge or verification step.

reviewed_competitors.title: Calibration of Pre-trained Transformers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Transformer calibration evidence cited by the target.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Desai and Durrett study BERT/RoBERTa on three tasks and find domain sensitivity plus gains from temperature scaling and label smoothing. This is much narrower than exact adaptive-round auto-calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scale-Free Online Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Adaptive-scale OMD/FTRL predecessor for unbounded loss vectors.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Orabona and Pál adapt online algorithms to unknown loss-vector norms and prove mirror-descent limitations. Their setting is linearized online optimization, whereas the target uses report-dependent log loss and calibration tails; the scale-free design is a direct alternative to its horizon-known, defective rare-event clamp.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universal Portfolio Selection
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Classic expert-recommended portfolio aggregation predecessor cited by the paper.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vovk and Watkins obtain logarithmic regret for weighting experts that recommend portfolios. The induced return is linear in expert weights, unlike the normalized geometric probability pool studied here.

reviewed_competitors.title: DeepQMC: an open-source software suite for variational optimization of deep-learning molecular wave functions

reviewed_competitors.title: Sorting Out Quantum Monte Carlo
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Competing determinant-free antisymmetrization mechanism for neural variational Monte Carlo.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Richter-Powell et al. introduce an O(N log N) sortlet layer and report chemical accuracy for first-row atoms and small molecules; the commentary treats determinants or Pfaffians as essentially the only affordable antisymmetric forms.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hopfield Networks is All You Need
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct energy-based attention predecessor connecting Transformer attention to modern Hopfield retrieval.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramsauer et al. derive exact associative retrieval dynamics against fixed stored patterns and provide convergence and capacity results. The reviewed paper targets evolving self-attention hidden states and a full block, but its central descent theorem fails.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sinkformers: Transformers with Doubly Stochastic Attention
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous attention-as-optimization predecessor deriving a genuine energy gradient flow after changing the normalization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sander et al. replace row-softmax with Sinkhorn normalization and prove an infinite-depth Wasserstein gradient-flow interpretation under symmetry assumptions. This makes explicit that a modified doubly stochastic attention law, rather than ordinary row-softmax alone, is what supports their energy-minimization result.

reviewed_competitors.title: Graph Neural Networks Inspired by Classical Iterative Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Same-author predecessor using IRLS and majorization-minimization to derive robust graph message passing.
reviewed_competitors.difference: TWIRLS grounds attention-like graph propagation in a graph-regularized objective and validates robust GNNs. The reviewed paper extends the motif to fully connected token interactions, but its normalization proof and Transformer composition are not valid as printed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimization Induced Equilibrium Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Contemporaneous explicit-objective framework for interpretable equilibrium layers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: OptEq derives implicit networks from convex optimization with well-defined fixed points and training machinery. It is more constrained than ordinary Transformers but has a coherent optimization object, unlike the reviewed paper's unsupported composition of a changing nonconvex surrogate with AIM.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Equilibrium Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational weight-tied equilibrium framework that includes self-attention Transformers.
reviewed_competitors.difference: DEQ solves for a fixed point and differentiates implicitly without requiring the update to descend a scalar energy. The reviewed paper seeks the stronger energy interpretation but only for a much narrower block and does not establish it.

reviewed_competitors.title: Energy Transformer
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct later architecture explicitly designed as gradient descent on an engineered attention-plus-memory energy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Energy Transformer changes the architecture so its iterations are true energy updates and evaluates image completion plus graph tasks. It offers a sounder construction-by-design route than retrofitting the reviewed simplified Transformer through invalid descent theorems.

reviewed_competitors.title: Energy-Based Transformers are Scalable Learners and Thinkers
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later boundary competitor using Transformer networks to parameterize learned prediction energies minimized at inference time.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gladstone et al. optimize candidate predictions against a learned compatibility energy across language and vision rather than derive each hidden-state Transformer block from one scalar token energy. Its scaling and inference-time-compute results test a broader energy-based modeling route, but not the reviewed paper's layerwise equivalence claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: White-Box Transformers via Sparse Rate Reduction: Compression Is All There Is?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later white-box Transformer derivation from an explicit representation-learning objective.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CRATE derives attention and sparsification layers from sparse rate reduction and demonstrates vision and language variants at substantially broader scale. Its objective and operators differ from hidden-state energy descent, but it is a stronger competitor for optimization-derived interpretability and empirical scope.

reviewed_competitors.title: Scaling White-Box Transformers for Vision
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Scaled successor to objective-derived white-box Transformer design.
reviewed_competitors.difference: CRATE-alpha preserves an interpretable optimization-derived structure while reaching 83.2% and 85.1% ImageNet top-1 at larger scales. The reviewed paper reports only energy curves for a tiny recurrent sentiment model and no task score.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hyper-SET: Designing Transformers via Hyperspherical Energy Minimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest accepted current successor designing a Transformer around explicit hidden-state energy minimization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hyper-SET uses a constrained hyperspherical energy with symmetric attention, feedforward updates, RMSNorm, and recurrent depth, then tests Sudoku, classification, masked image modeling, and energy trajectories. It retains constraints but offers a more complete construction and validation than the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: NRGPT: An Energy-based Alternative for GPT
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct accepted successor deriving a causal recurrent GPT-like block from tokenwise energy gradients.
reviewed_competitors.difference: NRGPT defines per-token causal energies whose gradients yield attention and feedforward updates, proves descent only under restricted inference-rate conditions, and evaluates Shakespeare, ListOps, and OpenWebText. It directly addresses autoregressive generation, which the reviewed bidirectional tied block does not, while retaining explicit architectural constraints and hyperparameter sensitivity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Revisiting Transformer Layer Parameterization Through Causal Energy Minimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current direct successor deriving weight-tied multihead attention and gated MLP updates from conditional energies.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Xu et al. separate an energy's semantics from its numerical realization, derive constrained causal Transformer layers with lightweight preconditioners and recursion, and evaluate moderate hundred-million-parameter language models against matched baselines. It is substantially closer to practical causal Transformers than the reviewed sentiment prototype, although it also requires within-layer weight sharing.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Learn In-Context by Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Influential alternative optimization interpretation of Transformer forward computation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: von Oswald et al. interpret attention as performing gradient updates to an implicit task model encoded in context, not as descending a scalar energy over hidden tokens. This separates two often-confused meanings of 'Transformer as optimization.'

reviewed_competitors.title: Dynamics of stochastic gradient descent for two-layer neural networks in the teacher-student setup
reviewed_competitors.difference: Goldt and colleagues prove asymptotically exact overlap ODEs for one-pass SGD at fixed hidden width and study how training only the first layer versus both layers changes overparameterized generalization. Veiga and colleagues extend the deterministic approximation across joint width, learning-rate, and time scalings, but retain only-first-layer training and inherit the teacher-student Gaussian scope.

reviewed_competitors.title: Mean-field theory of two-layers neural networks: dimension-free bounds and kernel limit
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mei, Misiakiewicz, and Montanari approximate noisy SGD by a distributional Wasserstein PDE with width requirements independent of ambient parameter dimension and recover a kernel limit. The phase-diagram paper instead tracks finite overlap matrices in a high-dimensional teacher-student model and exposes when a quadratic SGD correction survives, giving a different bridge between fixed-width and wide limits.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Global Convergence of Gradient Descent for Over-parameterized Models using Optimal Transport
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chizat and Bach prove global convergence of many-particle gradient flow under correct initialization for measure-convex models. Veiga and colleagues identify a scaling where online-SGD variance vanishes toward that gradient-flow behavior, but their finite-horizon ODE bound does not reproduce the prior's long-time global-convergence conclusion from typical random initialization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Tangent Kernel: Convergence and Generalization in Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jacot, Gabriel, and Hongler obtain linear function-space training under a width parameterization whose limiting kernel remains fixed. Veiga and colleagues analyze feature specialization through changing teacher-student overlaps and explicitly distinguish their unspecialized plateau from lazy training; this also underscores that their width-learning-rate phase boundary is not parameterization invariant.

reviewed_competitors.title: Online stochastic gradient descent on non-convex losses from high-dimensional inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ben Arous, Gheissari, and Jagannath derive nearly sharp sample thresholds from random initialization via an information exponent and show that the initial search for correlation can consume most data. That line directly targets the vanishing-overlap search phase left open by Veiga and colleagues, whose main controlled initialization begins already in the teacher span.

reviewed_competitors.title: High-dimensional limit theorems for SGD: Effective dynamics and critical scaling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ben Arous, Gheissari, and Jagannath prove ballistic ODE and diffusive SDE limits for chosen summary statistics and show a critical step-size correction can alter phase diagrams across several inference tasks and two-layer classifiers. Veiga and colleagues give a sharper model-specific overlap analysis for two-layer teacher regression, but stop at a no-ODE region rather than developing the competing stochastic effective limit.

reviewed_competitors.title: Classifying high-dimensional Gaussian mixtures: Where kernel methods fail and neural networks succeed
reviewed_competitors.difference: Refinetti and colleagues derive exact ODEs showing small feature-learning networks can beat kernels on high-dimensional Gaussian-mixture classification and that overparameterization speeds convergence without improving final performance. Veiga and colleagues instead vary width jointly with learning rate in teacher regression, isolating stochastic variance but not testing whether the phase diagram transfers to the mixture classification setting.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks can Learn Representations with Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.difference: Damian, Lee, and Soltanolkotabi prove that gradient descent learns few relevant directions for structured polynomial targets, improving over kernel sample complexity and enabling transfer. Their theorem targets task-relevant representation recovery, whereas Veiga and colleagues characterize online overlap dynamics and noise scaling but do not prove random-start feature recovery for their multi-neuron teacher.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks Efficiently Learn Low-Dimensional Representations with SGD
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mousavi-Hosseini and colleagues prove online SGD with weight decay aligns arbitrary-width first-layer weights to a Gaussian multiple-index target subspace and obtain width-independent generalization and near-linear-in-d sample complexity for ReLU single-index learning. This supplies random-start representation and sample guarantees absent from the phase diagram, though under a different algorithm, loss, and target class.

reviewed_competitors.title: Asymptotics of feature learning in two-layer networks after one gradient-step
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cui and colleagues give exact generalization asymptotics after one feature-learning step when samples, width, and dimension grow proportionally, using a spiked random-features surrogate and Gaussian universality. This subsequent work studies finite-data generalization beyond initialization in a proportional regime, while Veiga and colleagues study many online steps and a broader exponent plane but only a realizable Gaussian teacher and controlled overlaps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent for Two-layer Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cao, Guo, and Shi analyze last-iterate SGD convergence rates for overparameterized two-layer networks through NTK and RKHS approximation and reduce required width from exponential to polynomial dependence. Their optimization-statistical guarantees address finite iterates in a kernel-like regime, complementary to Veiga and colleagues' exact teacher-overlap dynamics and drift-variance phase transition.

reviewed_competitors.title: Emergence and scaling laws in SGD learning of shallow neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ren, Nichani, Wu, and Lee characterize sharp online-SGD transition times for recovering individual orthogonal teacher directions at extensive width and derive sample-, step-, and parameter-scaling laws for power-law teacher strengths. This directly advances the emergence and initialization-timescale gap that Veiga and colleagues flag, although it focuses on even activations with information exponent above two and a different coefficient structure.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Yu, and Perdikaris use the PINN NTK to expose unequal convergence rates among loss components and adapt weights using kernel eigenvalues. reviewed_competitors.title: Competitive Physics Informed Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zeng et al. avoid the squared condition number of the PINN residual formulation through an adversarial primal-dual objective and explicitly compare that conditioning view with Sobolev acceleration. Their method targets high-accuracy optimization rather than minimax early stopping and provides a distinct way to counteract PDE stiffness without the reviewed paper's non-self-adjoint spectral argument.

reviewed_competitors.title: Achieving High Accuracy with PINNs via Energy Natural Gradients
reviewed_competitors.difference: Muller and Zeinhofer use a Hessian-induced function-space metric whose parameter update approximates a Newton direction and demonstrate high-accuracy PINN and DRM optimization. This is a curvature-aware optimizer rather than a higher-order Sobolev loss, but it directly competes with the claimed conditioning-based acceleration mechanism on actual neural parameterizations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent Finds the Global Optima of Two-Layer Physics-Informed Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gao, Gu, and Ng prove convergence of gradient flow and standard gradient descent for overparameterized two-layer PINNs across linear second-order PDEs. They analyze the exact neural empirical loss rather than statistical early stopping in a commuting RKHS, addressing the actual parameter dynamics that the reviewed paper's experiments use but its theorem does not cover.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantifying Training Difficulty and Accelerating Convergence in Neural Network-Based PDE Solvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work quantifies PDE-solver training difficulty through kernel effective rank and accelerates PINN, DRM, and DeepONet using partition-of-unity and variance-scaled initialization. It targets architecture initialization rather than Sobolev loss order and validates across more solver families.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convergence Guarantees for Gradient-Based Training of Neural PDE Solvers: From Linear to Nonlinear PDEs
reviewed_competitors.difference: The later paper proves gradient-training convergence for PINN and DRM under NTK or random-feature regimes and extends from linear to nonlinear PDEs. It studies actual neural parameter dynamics and critical-point convergence, while the reviewed manuscript focuses on statistical early stopping in an idealized commuting RKHS inverse problem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sobolev acceleration for neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Oh, Lyu, and Son derive exact population gradients and Hessians for shallow ReLU student-teacher models and prove conditioning and gradient-flow improvements from derivative-supervised Sobolev training. Their assumptions differ and require target derivatives, but they provide a direct neural-network acceleration theorem rather than transferring an RKHS spectral argument to neural experiments.

reviewed_competitors.title: Curvature-Aware Optimization for High-Accuracy Physics-Informed Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jnini et al. develop scalable natural-gradient, self-scaling BFGS, and Broyden strategies for rapid high-accuracy PINN convergence across a broad PDE and ODE suite, including batched training. The work prioritizes practical curvature-aware optimization rather than minimax regularization, but it is a current direct comparator for the reviewed paper's iteration-acceleration claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Complexity of Linear Regions in Deep Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hanin and Rolnick derive the ambient-space expected boundary-volume and inverse-neuron distance results at initialization and empirically observe roughly linear region growth. The reviewed paper attempts to transfer that framework to data manifolds via tangent Jacobians and geodesic tubes, but its new geometry constants and curvature proof contain the audited gaps.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are All Linear Regions Created Equal?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent challenge to linear-region density as an effective-complexity proxy
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gamba et al. compare region density with a function-variation measure on trained VGG and ResNet models and find shortcomings in treating all regions equally. The reviewed paper assumes density proxies expressivity and studies support geometry, but does not measure how much adjacent affine functions actually differ.

reviewed_competitors.title: SplineCam: Exact Visualization and Characterization of Deep Network Geometry and Decision Boundaries
reviewed_competitors.difference: SplineCam exactly computes CPWL network geometry over a specified data-space region and supports decision-boundary sampling on or off a manifold. It offers certified cell geometry where the reviewed paper relies on uncertified SLSQP roots along 1D probes, although its exact computation is limited by region size and network complexity.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Local Complexity of Linear Regions in Deep ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Patel and Montufar define local complexity over an input distribution, show that learned low-dimensional features reduce it, and connect it to function total variation, robustness, and optimization. This supplies task- and representation-facing links absent from the reviewed paper's manifold-volume count and avoids assigning the effect to an operator-norm geometry constant.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compelling ReLU Networks to Exhibit Exponentially Many Linear Regions at Initialization and During Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Milkert et al. constrain weights so a depth-d network has exactly 2^d regions at initialization and retains them during training, producing large 1D approximation gains and preliminary multidimensional extensions. It directly acts on the reviewed paper's proposed region-concentration direction, but does not target curved data manifolds or prove distribution-level benefits.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Computational Complexity of Counting Linear Regions in ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current audit of region definitions and exact counting
reviewed_competitors.difference: Stargalla et al. distinguish several non-equivalent meanings of linear region and prove NP- and number-P hardness even for shallow networks, with stronger approximation hardness for deeper ones. Their taxonomy and hardness results sharpen what an 'exact count' must mean, whereas the reviewed paper uses local numerical roots without a completeness certificate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Characterizing the Discrete Geometry of ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current geometric characterization beyond raw counts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Gaines and Bi study the adjacency graph of the entire ReLU polyhedral complex, proving degree and diameter bounds and examining trained networks on synthetic and real data. This moves from the reviewed paper's boundary density on selected paths to how regions connect globally, while not specifically modeling a smooth data manifold.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign Overfitting in Linear Regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational rigorous characterization that the reviewed paper extends from benign versus non-benign to a three-way spectral taxonomy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bartlett et al. give finite-sample upper and lower bounds using effective ranks for minimum-norm linear interpolation under explicit distributional conditions. The reviewed paper obtains a memorable finer label and closed power-law factor, but relies on a nonrigorous Gaussian-universality risk equivalent and asymptotic tails rather than comparable guarantees for actual kernel matrices.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Current arXiv record for the 2020 PNAS article

reviewed_competitors.title: Consistency of Interpolation with Laplace Kernels is a High-Dimensional Phenomenon
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct predecessor proving fixed-dimensional Laplace minimum-norm interpolation is not benign.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Rakhlin and Zhai supply a rigorous inconsistency lower bound for any data-dependent bandwidth but do not distinguish bounded from divergent excess risk. The reviewed paper calls the fixed-dimensional Laplace limit tempered and proposes its 1/d scale, adding a sharper category under its surrogate while sacrificing rigor about real eigenfunctions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Distributional Generalization: A New Kind of Generalization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Empirical antecedent for identity-like DNN label-noise profiles and a more granular account of how corruption transfers to test predictions.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nakkiran and Bansal study the full distribution of train/test outputs and show class-specific corruption can transfer at similar rates across models. The reviewed paper compresses that phenomenon into scalar risk curves and an asymptotic taxonomy, which is simpler but loses conditional structure and does not add a DNN limit theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Shortest Program Interpolation Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Early successor proving tempered overfitting and finite-sample guarantees for a nonlinear interpolation rule.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Manoj and Srebro analyze the minimum-program-length interpolator rigorously under random label noise, including agnostic finite-sample guarantees. It validates the reviewed category beyond kernels but studies an abstract complexity rule rather than trained DNNs or spectral mechanisms.

reviewed_competitors.title: From Tempered to Benign Overfitting in ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct theoretical successor addressing the reviewed paper's largest gap for nonlinear neural networks.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kornowski, Yehudai, and Shamir prove tempered behavior in an extreme one-dimensional two-layer ReLU setting and transitions toward benign behavior in high dimensions. This replaces visual finite-n DNN classification with model-specific theorems and confirms that dimension can change the category rather than merely its severity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Noisy Interpolation Learning with Shallow Univariate ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct rigorous stress test showing that the category depends on risk functional and mode of convergence.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Joshi, Vardi, and Srebro prove a minimum-norm two-layer univariate ReLU interpolator is tempered with high probability under L1 loss but catastrophic under L2 or expected risk. That result exposes dimensions absent from the reviewed three labels: the same learner can change category with loss and expectation, so every taxonomy claim must bind those choices explicitly.

reviewed_competitors.title: An Agnostic View on the Cost of Overfitting in (Kernel) Ridge Regression
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Successor refining the outcome from absolute asymptotic risk to the finite-sample cost of choosing interpolation over optimally tuned ridge.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou et al. compare ridgeless and optimally regularized risk for arbitrary target functions and sample sizes, avoiding the reviewed paper's confounding of task hardness with the cost of overfitting. It still openly relies on the same nonrigorous Gaussian-universality ansatz, so it refines the metric rather than resolving universality.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: arXiv v2, revised 2024-03-22; ICLR 2024 camera ready

reviewed_competitors.title: Characterizing Overfitting in Kernel Ridgeless Regression Through the Eigenspectrum
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest rigorous successor to the kernel spectral trichotomy.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cheng et al. use non-asymptotic condition-number and random-matrix bounds to rigorously establish polynomial-spectrum tempered and exponential-spectrum catastrophic behavior under sub-Gaussian design. Crucially, they find feature independence matters and explicitly raise concern about Gaussian-design approximations in earlier work, sharply qualifying the reviewed theorem's transfer to real kernels.

reviewed_competitors.title: Generalization in Kernel Regression Under Realistic Assumptions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Rigorous successor expanding beyond Gaussian universality to common kernels, arbitrary dimensions, regularization, and finite samples.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barzilai and Shamir derive realistic excess-risk bounds and self-regularization from heavy spectral tails, finding benign high-dimensional and nearly tempered fixed-dimensional behavior plus time-dependent neural-kernel bounds. It offers the rigorous bridge and finite-n rates missing from the reviewed asymptotic surrogate, though not the same exact alpha constant.

reviewed_competitors.title: Overfitting Behaviour of Gaussian Kernel Ridgeless Regression: Varying Bandwidth or Dimensionality
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct extension of the reviewed Gaussian-kernel conclusion to learning procedures whose bandwidth or dimension varies with n.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Medvedev, Vardi, and Srebro show fixed-dimensional Gaussian ridgeless regression remains inconsistent even with tuned bandwidth, characterize increasing-dimension scalings, and produce benign Gaussian interpolation with sub-polynomial dimension growth. This makes explicit that a kernel family has no single category without specifying the whole n-indexed procedure; it retains the nonrigorous universality ansatz.

reviewed_competitors.title: Provable Tempered Overfitting of Minimal Nets and Typical Nets
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later theorem proving tempered overfitting for genuinely deep neural-network hypothesis classes.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Harel et al. analyze deep fully connected binary-weight networks under both minimum-size and random interpolating rules using threshold-circuit bounds, without extreme input dimension. This validates the category for deep nets but not SGD-trained real-valued ResNets, showing the reviewed DNN conclusion was prescient yet empirically underidentified.

reviewed_competitors.title: Benign overfitting in Fixed Dimension via Physics-Informed Learning with Smooth Inductive Bias
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Counterexample to treating fixed dimension as inherently tempered when the learning problem supplies stabilizing operator structure.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wong et al. derive learning curves for physics-informed inverse problems and show PDE operators plus smooth inductive bias can stabilize minimum-norm interpolation to benign behavior even in fixed dimension. It extends the reviewed paper's own open question by showing that task/operator geometry, not eigendecay alone in an ordinary regression abstraction, can change the regime.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond Benign Overfitting in Nadaraya-Watson Interpolators
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Recent extension showing all three regimes can occur non-monotonically within one classical interpolating method.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barzilai, Kornowski, and Shamir vary a single bandwidth-like parameter and rigorously move through catastrophic, benign, and tempered Nadaraya-Watson behavior in a non-monotonic order. This enriches the reviewed table: categories are not a simple monotone spectrum of model complexity and tuning errors can be directionally asymmetric.

reviewed_competitors.difference: DSR supplies the recurrent grammar policy, in-situ constraints, and top-quantile risk-seeking update used here. This workshop paper changes exploration and initialization around that engine rather than introducing a new symbolic-regression learner.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Symbolic Regression that Scales
reviewed_competitors.difference: NeSymReS amortizes equation discovery by pretraining a transformer over synthetic functions and uses its predictions to guide inference. The reviewed paper learns a fresh rollout policy from black-box rewards and targets within-task exploration, avoiding labeled pretraining but paying online search cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: Policy Gradient Search: Online Planning and Expert Iteration without Search Trees
reviewed_competitors.difference: Policy Gradient Search emphasizes the root action during online planning and distills search into a policy. Hierarchical entropy extends positional emphasis across every prefix but is evaluated only in offline symbolic-expression generation rather than interactive planning domains.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Generative Symbolic Regression with Monte-Carlo-Tree-Search
reviewed_competitors.difference: DGSR-MCTS stores and plans over expression mutations using a pretrained context-aware neural proposal refined online, and evaluates on SRBench. The reviewed method remains tree-free and lightweight but offers no comparable real-world or out-of-distribution evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Controllable Neural Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Controllable NSR conditions a pretrained generator on desired symbolic properties and constraints. The reviewed soft length prior injects only a hand-set positional size preference during online policy search and does not learn conditional control from a synthetic corpus.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformer-based Planning for Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: TPSR adds Monte Carlo tree search to transformer decoding so fitting error and expression complexity guide planning. Hierarchical entropy alters a recurrent policy's rollout distribution without an explicit search tree, making it cheaper in memory but unable to reuse visited-state statistics.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Neural-Guided Dynamic Symbolic Network for Exploring Mathematical Expressions from Data
reviewed_competitors.difference: DySymNet uses reinforcement learning to grow and optimize dynamic symbolic networks and reports broader low- and higher-dimensional SRBench experiments. The reviewed method searches prefix expressions directly and isolates two exploration heuristics on the much smaller Nguyen suite.

reviewed_competitors.title: Complexity-Aware Deep Symbolic Regression with Robust Risk-Seeking Policy Gradients
reviewed_competitors.difference: CADSR targets vanishing top-tail policy gradients, uses transformer breadth-first generation, and puts complexity into a BIC reward. The reviewed paper retains the original recurrent risk-seeking update and affects exploration through entropy and initial logits, with complexity only observed as an outcome.

reviewed_competitors.title: Operon C++: An Efficient Genetic Programming Framework for Symbolic Regression
reviewed_competitors.difference: Operon maintains an explicit evolutionary population and emphasizes high-throughput tree search and numerical optimization. The reviewed method learns a compact proposal distribution with no population archive; its paper does not directly compare diversity, compute, or recovery against Operon.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pareto-Optimal Fronts for Benchmarking Symbolic Regression Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Absolute Pareto fronts measure attainable fit at each expression size on 34 SRBench datasets. That protocol would test whether the reviewed method's shorter outputs are genuinely superior rather than relying on three separately averaged metrics over Nguyen tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bayesian Symbolic Regression with Entropic Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: ERRLESS uses maximum-entropy RL to sample a posterior over expression structures, turning diversity into epistemic uncertainty and predictive averaging. The reviewed method instead seeks one best expression and weights entropy by token position, without posterior calibration.

reviewed_competitors.title: VaSST: Variational Inference for Symbolic Regression using Soft Symbolic Trees
reviewed_competitors.difference: VaSST relaxes combinatorial tree selection into gradient-based variational inference and represents uncertainty over symbolic structures. The reviewed method preserves discrete valid expressions and black-box rewards but provides neither posterior uncertainty nor a continuous optimization path.

reviewed_competitors.title: Poly-time universality and limitations of deep learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Foundational universality and noisy-GD lower-bound framework
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abbe and Sandon make sufficiently expressive SGD polynomial-time universal and use cross-predictability to limit noisy/full GD on distributions of targets. The present paper replaces average cross-predictability with target-specific group alignment, but its SGD hardness is necessarily restricted to symmetry-constrained FC training and does not refute unrestricted universality. The arXiv record also carries an admin overlap note with arXiv:1812.06369.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Power of Differentiable Learning versus PAC and SQ Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct precision/batch-size boundary for differentiable learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work proves that SGD/GD can simulate SQ and, with sufficiently fine precision relative to batch or sample size, can simulate PAC learning; in a coarse-enough regime SGD is SQ-equivalent. The symmetry paper fixes a noisy bounded-precision model and adds architecture/target-specific obstructions inside that landscape rather than a general characterization of precision regimes.

reviewed_competitors.title: The staircase property: How hierarchical structure can guide deep learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: It defines Fourier staircase chains and proves polynomial-time layerwise stochastic coordinate descent for staircase functions on regular networks, with supporting ResNet experiments. The present paper supplies lower bounds from absent orbit alignment and an l-MSP necessity result; it is not the first staircase mechanism or a matching positive theorem for standard SGD.

reviewed_competitors.title: The merged-staircase property: a necessary and nearly sufficient condition for SGD learning of sparse functions on two-layer neural networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: The predecessor gives necessity and near sufficiency for sparse Boolean functions under two-layer mean-field SGD with O(d) samples and separates nonlinear training from fixed features. The present paper broadens only the necessity direction to permutation-equivariant noisy population GD and arbitrary leap l. Its current v2 postdates the reviewed paper and should not be cited with only the 2022 submission state.

reviewed_competitors.title: An initial alignment between neural network and target is needed for gradient descent to learn
reviewed_competitors.difference: It introduces INAL and proves that normalized-i.i.d.-initialized fully connected networks without noticeable initial alignment cannot learn Boolean targets in polynomial time under noisy GD. The present work generalizes the organizing quantity to compact-group orbit alignment, real targets, spherical harmonics, and nonzero baselines; it did not introduce alignment lower bounds as a general idea.

reviewed_competitors.title: Distribution-Specific Hardness of Learning Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest earlier distribution-specific gradient/SQ hardness comparator cited by the authors
reviewed_competitors.difference: Shamir extends Fourier/SQ hardness beyond the Boolean cube and shows that nice targets or nice input distributions alone do not ensure learnability. The reviewed paper emphasizes that the closest SGD argument required whitening/preconditioning, whereas its sign-flip reduction avoids that preprocessing; Shamir's result should not be redescribed as the same cryptographic reduction.

reviewed_competitors.title: SGD learning on neural networks: leap complexity and saddle-to-saddle dynamics
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct successor on l-MSP/leap time complexity
reviewed_competitors.difference: It introduces leap complexity, conjectures a tilde-Theta(d^{max(Leap(f),2)}) training-time law, and proves a restricted Gaussian two-layer SGD result with extra assumptions via saddle-to-saddle dynamics. It supplies trajectory-level positive and negative structure beyond leap one, but its headline scaling remains a conjecture rather than an unrestricted exact characterization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Gradient Descent Fails to Learn High-frequency Functions and Modular Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Takhanov et al. analyze negligible gradient variance for large-frequency periodic functions and modular multiplication classes using approximate orthogonality. That is a direct conceptual alternative to the reviewed paper's modular target, but it uses a gradient-variance/SQ-style mechanism rather than the sign-flip LPGN reduction and studies different modular functions.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the hardness of learning under symmetries
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Most direct later computational-hardness successor for explicit equivariant architectures
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kiani et al. prove superpolynomial or exponential CSQ lower bounds for shallow GNNs, CNNs, invariant polynomials, and frame-averaged models under permutation subgroups. It confirms that known architectural symmetry does not erase computational hardness while covering architecture classes and a CSQ framing not supplied by the FC training-algorithm G-alignment paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: Hardness of Learning Neural Networks under the Manifold Hypothesis
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later extension from Boolean/Gaussian inputs to geometric data support
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kiani, Wang, and Weber extend SQ and cryptographic hardness to bounded-curvature input manifolds and identify additional volume/reconstructibility assumptions that permit interpolation. This broadens the input-geometry axis and shows that low intrinsic dimension alone is not the same kind of learnability guarantee as staircase structure or symmetry alignment.

reviewed_competitors.title: Achieving Approximate Symmetry Is Exponentially Easier than Exact Symmetry
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current successor addressing the exact-versus-approximate symmetry gap
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tahmasebi and Weber introduce averaging complexity and separate the cost of enforcing exact symmetry from approximate symmetry, with linear versus logarithmic dependence on group size under their conditions. They do not repair or generalize the reviewed paper's noisy-GD lower bound; instead they formalize an adjacent design tradeoff motivated by exactly the approximate-symmetry limitation left open here.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Minimal Degree Bias in Generalization on the Unseen for non-Boolean Functions

reviewed_competitors.title: Why are Sensitive Functions Hard for Transformers?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Explains Transformer bias against sensitive Boolean functions through loss-landscape isolation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies an architecture-specific geometric mechanism that unifies low-sensitivity and low-degree behavior instead of treating influence agreement as an empirical optimizer bias.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Learn Low Sensitivity Functions: Investigations and Implications
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Directly studies sensitivity as a Transformer inductive bias and connects it to Boolean Fourier order, robustness, loss-landscape flatness, and grokking.

reviewed_competitors.title: Parity, Sensitivity, and Transformers

reviewed_competitors.title: A Sharper Picture of Generalization in Transformers

reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives PAC-Bayes bounds from low-sharpness Transformer constructions and tests their predictions mechanistically, offering a current degree-and-sparsity account of IID generalization rather than the reviewed paper's canonical-holdout influence proxy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding the Parameter Space Geometry of Transformers Encoding Boolean Functions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Provides a current parameter-geometry explanation for why sensitive Boolean functions are hard to learn despite being representable.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It replaces scalar average sensitivity with the full sensitivity profile and shows that sensitive targets occupy vanishing parameter-space regions, offering a more mechanistic and finer-grained account than Boolean influence alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why are Nonlinear Fits to Data so Challenging?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Transtrum, Machta, and Sethna establish the hyper-ribbon geometry of nonlinear prediction manifolds and use geodesic acceleration to improve fitting near boundaries. MBAM reuses that geometry for a different objective: crossing toward a boundary, interpreting its singular limit, and deleting a parameter combination rather than avoiding boundaries during optimization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Manifold boundaries give gray-box approximations of complex models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Transtrum's follow-up broadens the empirical survey to elementary functions, dynamical systems, networks, probability models, and models with symmetries, and makes MBAM's pitfalls more explicit. It supports the method's reach but also reinforces that a boundary hierarchy is an empirical property, not a theorem for arbitrary statistical models.

reviewed_competitors.title: The underlying connections between identifiability, active subspaces, and parameter space dimension reduction
reviewed_competitors.difference: Brouwer and Eisenberg unify local identifiability, sloppiness, and active subspaces through a sensitivity Fisher matrix and emphasize that local-versus-global and linear-versus-nonlinear choices must follow the scientific question. MBAM goes beyond identifying a low-dimensional parameter subspace by altering the model equations through a boundary limit, but it inherits the comparator's warning that a local Fisher spectrum need not describe global behavior.

reviewed_competitors.title: Unwinding the model manifold: choosing similarity measures to remove local minima in sloppy dynamical systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Francis and Transtrum show that oscillatory or chaotic dynamics can generate high effective dimensionality and wound manifolds, then change the fitting metric to recover hyper-ribbon structure. This exposes a concrete preconditioning step and a failure regime absent from the original MBAM presentation: reduction may depend critically on the observation metric.

reviewed_competitors.title: Stability of the manifold boundary approximation method for reductions of nuclear structure models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Imbrisak and Nomura directly test MBAM under Monte Carlo variation of starting parameters in a nuclear energy-density functional and connect geodesic termination to a vanishing Fisher determinant that separates parameter-space regions. It provides a domain-specific stability audit beyond the original paper's qualitative multi-start statement, but does not establish general robustness.

reviewed_competitors.title: Selecting simple, transferable models with the supremum principle
reviewed_competitors.difference: The supremum-principle work constructs multiple MBAM reductions for distinct target behaviors and selects their least upper bound to combine mechanisms for unobserved regimes. It directly addresses the original method's risk of over-specializing to one prediction set, while adding an information-topology selection layer rather than changing the boundary-reduction primitive.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Sloppy Model Universality Class and the Vandermonde Matrix
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct conceptual predecessor from the same research program that introduced log-uniform sensitivity spectra and the Vandermonde explanation of a proposed sloppy-model universality class.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It compares sloppy and non-sloppy examples and establishes one limiting ensemble result, whereas the target expands the claim into global manifold widths, curvature, boundaries, and optimization rules.

reviewed_competitors.title: Universally Sloppy Parameter Sensitivities in Systems Biology
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The empirical systems-biology foundation for the target's claims about widespread sloppy Hessian spectra and prediction-focused inference.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It surveys a collection of biological models and parameter uncertainties but does not develop the target's model-graph, curvature hierarchy, or geodesic algorithm.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why Are Nonlinear Fits So Challenging?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: The same authors' immediate short-paper predecessor already presents generalized interpolation, hierarchical widths, manifold boundaries, low extrinsic curvature, and geodesic acceleration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The target is a substantially expanded treatment adding the model graph, pragmatic priors, detailed curvature taxonomy, evaporation estimates, derivations, and more algorithm discussion; its headline geometric and acceleration concepts were already public.

reviewed_competitors.title: Improvements to the Levenberg-Marquardt Algorithm for Nonlinear Least-Squares Minimization
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct algorithmic follow-up by two target authors that broadens evaluation of geodesic acceleration and adds uphill-step and Broyden-Jacobian variants with open-source code.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It is closer to an implementation and benchmark paper, while the target's contribution is the geometric rationale and preliminary demonstrations.

reviewed_competitors.title: Geodesic Acceleration and the Small-Curvature Approximation for Nonlinear Least Squares
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A theoretical follow-up that derives the correction without differential geometry and adapts convergence proofs.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It supplies a small-curvature justification and cubic-order analysis that the target's empirical geometric narrative and limited tests do not establish.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sloppy Models Can Be Identifiable
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct counterpoint separating Hessian-spectrum sloppiness from structural and practical identifiability and testing how data, noise, and experimental design change both.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It warns that a sloppy spectrum alone can mislead about uniqueness and confidence, whereas the target often uses geometry to motivate broad statements about parameter evaporation and uncertainty.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Geometry of Sloppiness
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A later mathematical foundation that defines model manifolds and sloppiness relative to a noise-induced premetric and a reference metric.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It directly repairs the target's coordinate-dependence ambiguity and extends analysis beyond infinitesimal Euclidean Fisher eigenvalues, but it is diagnostic rather than an optimizer proposal.

reviewed_competitors.title: Delineating Parameter Unidentifiabilities in Complex Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A finite-radius alternative that links multiscale sloppiness to confidence-region geometry and likelihood-ratio tests while recovering functional unidentifiability relations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It targets practical interpretation and model simplification beyond a local Fisher matrix, whereas the target mainly extrapolates local spectra through a hyper-ribbon caricature.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Limitations of Model-Based Experimental Design and Parameter Estimation in Sloppy Systems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A follow-up from the same broader program that studies parameter estimation when optimally informative experiments expose omitted model physics.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It complicates the target's idea that better data simply constrains more widths: experimental design can reduce apparent sloppiness yet increase model discrepancy and reduce predictive reliability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chebyshev Approximation and the Global Geometry of Sloppy Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A formal successor connecting smoothness to global intrinsic bounds on model predictions and manifold widths through Chebyshev approximation.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It gives explicit bounds for specified smooth model classes, narrowing and strengthening the target's heuristic polynomial-interpolation universality argument.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Structural and Practical Identifiability
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A modern identifiability review arguing that Fisher-information diagnostics can be severely misleading for finite-noise nonlinear ODE models and recommending profile likelihood.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It prioritizes statistically thresholded global parameter profiles and prediction identifiability, providing a necessary companion to the target's local metric and evaporation analysis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Maximizing the Information Learned from Finite Data Selects a Simple Model
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A Bayesian information-theoretic successor addressing how finite data should induce priors on hyper-ribbon model manifolds.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It derives a mutual-information-maximizing prior that concentrates on lower-dimensional boundaries, contrasting with the target's pragmatic reciprocal penalties that deliberately repel those boundaries.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sloppiness and Emergent Theories in Physics, Biology, and Beyond
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A broad same-lineage synthesis that turns the target's manifold boundaries into the Manifold Boundary Approximation Method for interpretable model reduction.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It treats boundaries as scientifically meaningful effective theories to be approached, whereas the target primarily treats them as hazards to fitting and uses damping or priors to avoid premature arrival.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Levenberg-Marquardt Method for Nonsmooth Regularized Least Squares
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A modern competing Levenberg-Marquardt framework for smooth nonlinear residuals plus potentially nonconvex nonsmooth regularization, with global first-order convergence and complexity results.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It handles explicit regularizers and trust-region subproblems outside the target's smooth Gaussian geometry, but does not use geodesic acceleration or claim hyper-ribbon structure.

reviewed_competitors.title: Constrained Variable Projection for Structured Problems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A current structured alternative for separable nonlinear least squares that exactly eliminates linear variables, supports convex constraints, and uses differentiation through the reduced problem.
reviewed_competitors.difference: For models like amplitude-plus-rate exponential sums, it can reduce dimension before optimization and avoid some sloppy directions by construction; its applicability is narrower than the target's generic residual-map geometry.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Gittens et al. derive additive compositionality and analogy behavior under a Zipf/uniform corpus model and propose a nonlinear operator when assumptions fail; the reviewed paper replaces those distributional assumptions with explicit paraphrase and dependence errors but still assumes a suitable embedding projection.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Ethayarajh et al. characterize linear analogies in SGNS through co-occurrence-shifted PMI, frequency weighting, and information-theoretic distance; the reviewed paper instead defines analogies via shared paraphrase transformations and decomposes their residuals.

reviewed_competitors.title: On the Emergence of Linear Analogies in Word Embeddings

reviewed_competitors.title: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Translating on Hyperplanes
reviewed_competitors.difference: TransH explicitly identifies TransE's reflexive and one-to-many/many-to-one/many-to-many failures, projects entities onto a relation-specific hyperplane, and adds relation-aware negative sampling at nearly the same asymptotic parameter order. It is the closest early test of whether one extra relation-specific degree of freedom repairs TransE's cardinality bottleneck.

reviewed_competitors.title: Embedding Entities and Relations for Learning and Inference in Knowledge Bases
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. unify several embedding scores and show that the diagonal bilinear DistMult formulation can substantially outperform TransE while retaining linear parameter and scoring complexity. DistMult cannot represent antisymmetry, but it demonstrates that TransE's simplicity was not unique to translation and adds relation-composition rule mining.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Entity and Relation Embeddings for Knowledge Graph Completion
reviewed_competitors.difference: TransR projects entities from a common entity space into a separate space for each relation before translating them. It directly targets the reviewed paper's assumption that one shared coordinate system exposes every semantic aspect, trading substantially more relation parameters and computation for capacity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Observed versus latent features for knowledge base and text inference
reviewed_competitors.difference: Toutanova and Chen show that simple observed path features exploit unrealistic redundancy in FB15k and WN18, then construct the inverse- and near-duplicate-reduced FB15k-237 split. This work materially narrows how TransE's original absolute and relative scores should be interpreted.

reviewed_competitors.title: Complex Embeddings for Simple Link Prediction
reviewed_competitors.difference: ComplEx uses a Hermitian trilinear product in complex space to model symmetric and antisymmetric relations while remaining linear in entities, relations, and dimension. It supplies a direct answer to TransE's symmetric-relation collapse without adopting a heavy neural tensor.

reviewed_competitors.title: TorusE: Knowledge Graph Embedding on a Lie Group
reviewed_competitors.difference: TorusE formalizes the adverse interaction between TransE's unit-sphere projection and Euclidean translations, then places translations on a compact torus so embeddings need no norm constraint. It preserves the core translational idea while directly revisiting a training assumption left unanalyzed in the reviewed paper.

reviewed_competitors.title: SimplE Embedding for Link Prediction in Knowledge Graphs
reviewed_competitors.difference: SimplE couples head and tail entity roles with inverse relations, remains linear in embedding size, proves full expressivity, and supports selected background constraints. It is a strong counterexample to the idea that a severe expressivity restriction is necessary for a simple scalable model.

reviewed_competitors.title: RotatE: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Relational Rotation in Complex Space
reviewed_competitors.difference: RotatE replaces translation with elementwise complex rotation and explicitly models symmetry/antisymmetry, inversion, and composition, while adding self-adversarial negatives. It retains a compact geometric operator but addresses several algebraic patterns that one Euclidean offset cannot.

reviewed_competitors.title: TuckER: Tensor Factorization for Knowledge Graph Completion
reviewed_competitors.difference: TuckER uses a shared Tucker core, proves full expressivity with dimension bounds, and shows several linear KGE models as special cases. It is a more appropriate strong linear baseline for testing whether TransE's parameter savings outweigh its restricted relation algebra.

reviewed_competitors.title: Realistic Re-evaluation of Knowledge Graph Completion Methods: An Experimental Study
reviewed_competitors.difference: Akrami et al. identify reverse, duplicate, and Cartesian-product relations as pervasive easy cases in FB15k and WN18 and report much poorer performance after removing unrealistic triples. Their analysis challenges the benchmark premise behind the reviewed paper rather than proposing merely another score function.

reviewed_competitors.title: PairRE: Knowledge Graph Embeddings via Paired Relation Vectors
reviewed_competitors.difference: PairRE assigns two vectors to each relation, scales head and tail coordinates separately, and targets both complex cardinalities and symmetry, inversion, composition, and subrelations. It is a direct modernized test of how far one can go with only a small constant-factor increase over TransE's vector budget.

reviewed_competitors.title: SpaceE: Knowledge Graph Embedding by Relational Linear Transformation in the Entity Space
reviewed_competitors.difference: SpaceE makes the core limitation explicit: translations and rotations are injective and therefore cannot exactly model many-to-one maps. Singular matrix transformations provide non-injectivity, full expressivity, and non-Abelian composition at a larger parameter cost.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Foundation Models for Knowledge Graph Reasoning
reviewed_competitors.difference: ULTRA constructs relation representations from relational interactions and pretrains across graphs, enabling zero-shot link prediction on unseen graphs with arbitrary entity and relation vocabularies across 57 KGs. This directly escapes TransE's requirement that every entity and relation receive a graph-specific learned lookup vector.

reviewed_competitors.title: KG-FIT: Knowledge Graph Fine-Tuning Upon Open-World Knowledge
reviewed_competitors.difference: KG-FIT combines graph structure with text and LLM-guided hierarchical entity clusters and evaluates on leakage-resistant FB15k-237, YAGO3-10, and PrimeKG. It uses far more external information and compute, but illustrates how current systems address hierarchy and open-world semantics rather than asking one offset vector to recover everything from graph IDs.
