reviewed_competitors.difference: Hille et al. use multiloop fRG with frequency and momentum dependence, truncated-unity momentum treatment, high-frequency asymptotics, self-energy consistency, and comparisons to parquet and determinant quantum Monte Carlo. The reviewed work compresses a cheaper static one-loop teacher and does not externally validate its reconstructed physics, so it addresses representation rather than quantitative solver fidelity.

reviewed_competitors.title: High-performance functional renormalization group calculations for interacting fermions
reviewed_competitors.relationship: prior deterministic compression and scaling alternative
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lichtenstein et al. derive truncated-unity fRG by exchange parametrization and form-factor projections, test convergence on the square-lattice t-t' Hubbard model, and report multicore speedups. NeuralFRG instead learns an unconstrained latent basis from solved trajectories; it avoids a fixed physical truncation basis but supplies neither a convergence control nor a measured speedup.

reviewed_competitors.title: TU$^2$FRG -- a scalable approach for truncated unity functional renormalization group in generic fermionic models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Profe and Kennes unify real- and momentum-space truncated unity to improve scaling for large unit cells and broken translation symmetry. This is a solver-level, reusable factorization derived from the equations; the reviewed model is a supervised surrogate tied to a fixed 48-patch, single-band, translation-invariant training family.

reviewed_competitors.title: Single boson exchange representation of the functional renormalization group for strongly interacting many-electron systems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bonetti et al. split the vertex into physically interpretable single-boson exchange terms and a residual four-fermion vertex, reducing the effort of high-frequency treatment and supporting DMF2RG from weak to strong coupling. NeuralFRG learns opaque latent coordinates and simply omits frequency dependence in its teacher, so the two approaches trade data adaptivity against physical structure and frequency-capable generality.

reviewed_competitors.title: Single-boson exchange functional renormalization group application to the two-dimensional Hubbard model at weak coupling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fraboulet et al. apply SBE-fRG to the square-lattice Hubbard model at half filling and finite doping and show that residual functions remain small at weak coupling, yielding a physics-based reduction of the two-particle vertex. The reviewed work instead tests one van-Hove line and gives no matched accuracy-cost comparison with this structured representation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Physics-informed neural networks for solving functional renormalization group on a lattice
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yokota trains a PINN from the fRG equation residual to represent a high-dimensional effective action, demonstrating a zero-dimensional O(N) lattice model up to N=100 without labeled solution trajectories. It studies a different field-theory object, but directly challenges NeuralFRG's dependence on thousands of precomputed teacher vertices and suggests residual-based validation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Solving Functional Renormalization Group Equations with Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tan et al. embed fRG equations in the loss, require no precomputed labels, use an analytic large-N plus learned correction to control stiffness, and benchmark O(N) scalar flows against finite-difference and discontinuous-Galerkin solvers, including critical regimes and fixed points. It is not a fermionic full-vertex compressor, but it provides the quantitative equation-level validation and no-teacher training absent from the reviewed supervised surrogate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Machine learning accelerated computational fluid dynamics
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kochkov et al. learn corrections inside a differentiable two-dimensional turbulent CFD solver and report equivalence to numerical grids 8-10x finer, 40-80x speedups, long stability, and forcing/Reynolds generalization. The focal paper covers more solver interaction types and a 3D wake but uses less controlled CPU/GPU speed comparisons and does not match a finer solver at equal accuracy.

reviewed_competitors.difference: List et al. extend solver-unrolled learned correction to three two-dimensional turbulence regimes, add turbulence-informed losses and a gradient-subrange scheme, and evaluate long-term a-posteriori statistics. This strengthens the focal horizon finding while addressing its limited physical losses and long-backpropagation scalability, but it remains focused on differentiable fluid simulation.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: subsequent systems method for reducing differentiable-solver training cost

Solver-in-the-Loop establishes the benefit of exact recurrent interaction but pays the full selected horizon and does not adapt solver fidelity or separately control primal and backward work.

reviewed_competitors.difference: MultiPDENet learns stencil-structured spatial derivatives, advances a PDE Physics Block with fine-scale RK4, and applies neural correction at a coarser time scale to control temporal accumulation under small or downsampled data. The focal method uses a fixed source discretization and corrects every step, offering a simpler generic interaction recipe but less explicit numerical structure and multiscale timing.

reviewed_competitors.difference: INC analyzes the focal style of direct state correction as a source of autoregressive error amplification, then inserts learned corrections into the governing equations instead. Its accepted NeurIPS 2025 record reports broader 1D-to-3D benchmarks, formal error reduction, and improved long-rollout stability; Solver-in-the-Loop contributes the earlier exposure-matched training insight but supplies no comparable guarantee for direct correction.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This work inserts learned corrections into a coarse CFD pipeline for high-Rayleigh-number convection; the focal model replaces time integration end to end, which is simpler to port but lacks the numerical solver's built-in structure and guarantees.

reviewed_competitors.title: Turbulence forecasting via Neural ODE
reviewed_competitors.difference: The Neural ODE formulation learns continuous-time reduced turbulence dynamics and examines phenomenology and dissipation; the focal work predicts full coarse grid states at fixed discrete steps and validates on more demanding 3D solver-generated regimes.

reviewed_competitors.title: Accelerating Eulerian Fluid Simulation With Convolutional Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tompson et al. use a CNN to approximate the pressure projection while retaining the classical Eulerian operator-splitting pipeline; the focal paper learns the full coarse transition and therefore removes more engineering at the cost of less explicit physics.

reviewed_competitors.title: Learning Mesh-Based Simulation with Graph Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: MeshGraphNets applies encode-process-decode message passing and denoising-style training on unstructured adaptive meshes; the focal paper transfers those principles to simpler grid CNNs and focuses on turbulent spectral and statistical fidelity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Message Passing Neural PDE Solvers
reviewed_competitors.difference: MP-PDE uses message passing and temporal bundling to handle irregular discretizations and generalize across PDE parameters, topology, and resolution; the focal CNN has stronger specialized turbulence diagnostics and 3D Athena++ data but retrains by domain and step size.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differentiable Turbulence: Closure as a partial differential equation constrained optimization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Differentiable Turbulence optimizes closures through PDE-constrained rollouts and systematically studies inductive biases and OOD behavior; the focal method is easier to deploy without a differentiable solver but cannot inherit its conservation structure or solver-coupled objective.

reviewed_competitors.difference: This approach couples graph neural closures with differentiable finite elements on unstructured 2D and 3D domains and targets generalization across geometry; the focal model is restricted to structured grids and shows that translation-equivariant convolutions alone do not solve box-size extrapolation.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct optimization precursor that extracts low-lying CFT data by minimizing the norm of crossing error after severe OPE truncation.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Established rigorous numerical-bootstrap route using arbitrary-precision semidefinite optimization to derive certified bounds.
reviewed_competitors.difference: SDPB exploits positivity to produce exclusion bounds and high-precision Ising constraints with auditable solver tolerances. SAC directly proposes candidate spectra and can in principle drop unitarity, but sacrifices certification and was not benchmarked for precision or compute against SDPB-based tools.

reviewed_competitors.title: Navigator Function for the Conformal Bootstrap
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest contemporary high-dimensional search alternative, replacing binary feasibility with a differentiable global function and an analytic SDP gradient.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The navigator uses quasi-Newton optimization on a continuous, everywhere-defined function tied to rigorous allowed/excluded regions and demonstrates navigation to the 3D Ising island. The SAC method searches truncated spectra without gradients or certificates; the Letter asserts less start-point sensitivity but provides no direct navigator comparison.

reviewed_competitors.title: Conformal Bootstrap with Reinforcement Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Same-authors companion study providing the detailed SAC implementation, more examples, and the full evidence base underlying this six-page Letter.
reviewed_competitors.difference: The companion extends evaluation to tricritical Ising and up to 36-dimensional searches and discusses errors in much greater detail. It confirms that the Letter is an initial demonstration, while still relying on known 2D theories, fixed spin partitions, and uncontrolled truncations rather than solving the broad arbitrary-CFT claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Finite Temperature Bootstrap
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Later neural bootstrap from two target authors that models the infinite high-spin/operator tail rather than simply deleting it at a finite cutoff.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Niarchos et al. combine KMS conditions, thermal dispersion relations, exposed low data, and neural tail functions, explicitly avoiding uncontrolled truncation and positivity dependence. It addresses the target paper's largest analytic error source, though in a finite-temperature setting and with its own modeling assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.title: Bootstrapping non-unitary CFTs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current direct nonunitary-compatible spectrum search using cross-ratio stability of linearly inferred OPE data and an evolutionary algorithm.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. analytically invert OPE coefficients for each trial spectrum and use their variation across cross-ratios as a truncation-sensitive objective, reducing the nonlinear search dimension. Their genetic search reproduces Virasoro minimal models including nonunitary cases, directly realizing a scope the 2022 SAC Letter only claimed.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Spectral Bias and Conformal Correlators I: Introduction and Applications

reviewed_competitors.difference: Ghosh et al. test feed-forward neural reconstruction across unitary and nonunitary 2D models, 3D Ising, 4D supersymmetric correlators, and thermal data, and analyze implicit smoothness bias. It greatly broadens empirical coverage and explains the NN selection mechanism, but yields approximate correlators rather than a certified full spectrum and relies on anchor/gap priors.

reviewed_competitors.title: Localizing Task Information for Improved Model Merging and Compression
reviewed_competitors.difference: TALL-masks finds sparse, mostly nonoverlapping task supports in existing task vectors and Consensus Merging removes catastrophic weights, recovering over 99% of single-task accuracy in its reported settings without linearized inference. It operationalizes locality at parameter level and scales evaluation to 20 tasks.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fine-Tuning Attention Modules Only: Enhancing Weight Disentanglement in Task Arithmetic
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jin et al. explicitly target this method's doubled costs and reduced individual-model performance by fine-tuning only attention modules, arguing those modules exhibit sufficiently kernel-like behavior. It is a more deployable partial restriction but a narrower architectural prescription.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-Task Model Merging via Adaptive Weight Disentanglement
reviewed_competitors.difference: Adaptive Weight Disentanglement subtracts learned redundant components so task vectors become more orthogonal while preserving task performance. It treats interference as vector geometry rather than NTK function localization and avoids linearized inference, although it introduces its own optimization and norm assumptions.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: Combines a continuous relaxation with a score-function control variate to retain unbiasedness while reducing variance.
reviewed_competitors.difference: REBAR spends extra machinery to target unbiased gradients; ReinMax accepts extension-dependent bias for an ST-like single-backward implementation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Rao-Blackwellizing the Straight-Through Gumbel-Softmax Gradient Estimator
reviewed_competitors.relationship: GR-MCK reduces STGS variance without additional downstream function evaluations by integrating conditional Gumbel randomness and Monte Carlo sampling.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It improves variance/MSE of a relaxation-based estimator; ReinMax changes the bias approximation itself using endpoint derivative quadrature and is cheaper than high-sample GR-MCK.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training Discrete Deep Generative Models via Gapped Straight-Through Estimator
reviewed_competitors.relationship: GST constructs a deterministic gap to reduce STGS variance without repeated samples and is a principal experimental baseline.
reviewed_competitors.difference: GST retains a Gumbel-relaxation-inspired backward rule with task-sensitive variants; ReinMax derives a categorical pairwise finite-difference approximation and claims a more uniform configuration story.

reviewed_competitors.title: Coupled Gradient Estimators for Discrete Latent Variables
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Develops unbiased low-variance binary and categorical estimators via coupling, stick breaking, and Rao-Blackwellization.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It remains score-function based and can handle nondifferentiable f, whereas ReinMax exploits the derivative vector of a smooth extension and remains biased.

reviewed_competitors.title: Double Control Variates for Gradient Estimation in Discrete Latent Variable Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Uses two control-variate levels to reduce the variance of unbiased leave-one-out REINFORCE estimators at standard training cost.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It optimizes variance while preserving unbiasedness for binary latents; ReinMax instead attacks local approximation bias for general categorical variables.

reviewed_competitors.title: Low Bias Low Variance Gradient Estimates for Boolean Stochastic Networks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Analyzes low-bias, low-variance estimators for Boolean stochastic networks and connects straight-through-like rules to linear approximations.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It focuses on Boolean deep networks and specialized estimators; the reviewed paper gives a simple multinomial identity and a trapezoidal upgrade applicable as a categorical drop-in.

reviewed_competitors.title: Beyond ReinMax: Low-Variance Gradient Estimators for Discrete Latent Variables
reviewed_competitors.relationship: A direct later follow-up reports that ReinMax's lower-bias numerical rule can carry high variance and adds Rao-Blackwellized and control-variate variants.
reviewed_competitors.difference: It targets the main unresolved bias-variance weakness rather than changing the Heun-like core approximation, and explores alternative quadrature views.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-Context Learning Creates Task Vectors
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest concurrent hidden-state task-vector account of ICL.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Hendel et al. extract a task vector from a single hidden-state location and frame ICL as compressing demonstrations into that state; Todd et al. use head-level causal restoration to select a cross-task carrier set and sum projected head outputs.

reviewed_competitors.title: In-context Vectors: Making In Context Learning More Effective and Controllable Through Latent Space Steering
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Concurrent top-down latent-vector alternative for demonstration-conditioned steering.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. derive a controllable direction from demonstration latent embeddings and emphasize behavior/style control and prompt compression; Function Vectors select causally influential attention heads and target discrete input-output mappings.

reviewed_competitors.title: Comparing Bottom-Up and Top-Down Steering Approaches on In-Context Learning Tasks
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct empirical comparison of Function Vectors and In-Context Vectors.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Brumley et al. find task-dependent reliability: FVs work better on functional mappings but can fail or steer adversely on sentiment transfer, while ICVs have complementary strengths. This narrows any universal steering interpretation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Label Words as Local Task Vectors in In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct mechanistic qualification of the global task-vector hypothesis.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zheng et al. find separate demonstration-local rule vectors and report that a global vector does not form for categorization rules requiring multiple demonstrations; Todd et al. average simple-task activations into one global FV.

reviewed_competitors.title: Steering off Course: Reliability Challenges in Steering Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Largest accepted cross-model reliability audit directly re-evaluating Function Vectors.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Da Silva et al. test up to 36 models from 14 families and find high variance, no gain, or degradation for many model-task pairs even after tuning; the original paper's five checkpoints show much more consistent selected-task gains.

reviewed_competitors.title: One Task Vector is not Enough: A Large-Scale Study for In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Large-scale task-diversity test of single-vector compression.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tikhonov et al. expand to 3,096 tasks with Llama 3 8B and Qwen 3 8B and conclude that complex tasks often require multiple subtask-specific vectors; Todd et al. mostly evaluate compact lexical and extraction functions represented by one vector.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Task Vectors in In-Context Learning: Emergence, Functionality, and Limitations
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Theoretical and empirical account of when a single task vector should fail.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dong et al. model a task vector as a linear combination behaving like one synthetic demonstration and predict failure on high-rank mappings, motivating multiple-vector injection; Todd et al. provide empirical causal extraction without such a capacity boundary.

reviewed_competitors.title: Causality != Invariance: Function and Concept Vectors in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Accepted direct test of whether causal FVs are abstract across formats.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Opielka et al. find that FVs extracted from different response formats can be nearly orthogonal and introduce RSA-selected Concept Vectors that transfer better across format and language; this directly narrows the original portability claim.

reviewed_competitors.title: Relational Knowledge Distillation Using Fine-tuned Function Vectors
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct learned-FV successor for relations and analogies.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kang et al. optimize FVs from about 20 word pairs and learn weighted composites, improving relation-word decoding and analogy performance beyond causally averaged original vectors; Todd et al. use training-free extraction and fixed arithmetic.

reviewed_competitors.title: Steerable but Not Decodable: Function Vectors Operate Beyond the Logit Lens
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct large cross-template audit of FV steering versus vocabulary decodability.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Nadaf tests 4,032 cross-template pairs across six newer models and finds steering can succeed while linear and even some nonlinear decoders cannot recover the answer, reinforcing the computational-trigger reading while rejecting a coupled steerability-decodability premise.

reviewed_competitors.title: Fast & Faithful Function Vectors
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current method-level replacement for FV head selection and insertion.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pham et al. replace expensive causal head sweeps with gradient-based Layer-wise Relevance Propagation and find distributed steering more accurate than aggregating every head output into one vector, directly revising two central design choices in Todd et al.

reviewed_competitors.title: Exploring Length Generalization in Large Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Anil and collaborators already show that naive fine-tuning fails length extrapolation while scratchpad and in-context formats can substantially improve it. Faith and Fate broadens diagnosis to three computation-graph tasks and trace errors, but its broad negative reading must be reconciled with representation-dependent positive results already available before publication.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Algorithms can Transformers Learn? A Study in Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhou and collaborators connect strong length generalization to tasks with short RASP-L programs and show that scratchpad format can help or hurt depending on the algorithm. This supplies a representation- and task-conditional boundary rather than the target's generic subgraph-matching account.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compositional Capabilities of Autoregressive Transformers: A Study on Synthetic, Interpretable Tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ramesh and collaborators demonstrate generalization to combinatorially many function compositions and isolate benefits from intermediate outputs plus harms from order bias. The result directly counters an unconditional inability to compose while agreeing that sequence representation and training distribution govern success.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Expressive Power of Transformers with Chain of Thought
reviewed_competitors.difference: Merrill and Sabharwal formally show that intermediate autoregressive tokens enlarge transformer expressiveness as chain length grows. Their result makes the amount and encoding of serial computation a central resource; Faith and Fate's empirical scratchpad failures do not imply that CoT cannot supply compositional capacity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Chain of Thought Empowers Transformers to Solve Inherently Serial Problems
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feng and collaborators construct transformers whose T chain-of-thought steps evaluate Boolean circuits of size T and empirically study serial tasks including permutation composition. This does not guarantee learnability from ordinary data, but it refutes an architecture-only reading of inevitable serial-composition failure.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Limitations of the Transformer Architecture
reviewed_competitors.difference: Peng and collaborators derive communication-complexity limitations for function composition under explicit transformer and input-distribution assumptions. It supports genuine limits in particular regimes while illustrating what Faith and Fate's generic stochastic-function theory lacks: a direct bridge from architecture and resources to a lower bound.

reviewed_competitors.title: Can Transformers Reason Logically? A Study in SAT Solving
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pan and collaborators construct a decoder-only transformer using deduction and backtracking CoT to decide 3-SAT non-uniformly and find strong OOD behavior within trained sizes but limited length generalization. The mixed result supports a conditional account based on algorithm, supervision, and scale rather than shallow matching alone.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Transformers Able to Reason by Connecting Separated Knowledge in Training Data?
reviewed_competitors.difference: The FTCT study asks whether models connect separated training facts and reports that few-shot CoT plus sufficient similarity can enable unseen composition, interpreting success as program learning. It identifies positive training conditions absent from Faith and Fate's conclusion while retaining failures when demonstrations or similarity are inadequate.

reviewed_competitors.title: Compositional Reasoning with Transformers, RNNs, and Chain of Thought
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work formalizes compositional reasoning queries and separates resource regimes: standard transformers require logarithmic depth, RNNs can use logarithmic embedding dimension, and transformers with CoT trade tokens for serial computation. It provides a more precise architecture/resource frontier than generic error accumulation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Provably Learn Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: This analysis gives an optimization guarantee for learning state-tracking CoT with length generalization and extends it through recursive self-training to algebraically structured, NC1-complete tasks. Its premises are structured, but it shows that learned systematic extrapolation is provable in regimes excluded by the target's broad rhetoric.

reviewed_competitors.title: Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prystawski, Li, and Goodman prove a bias reduction from chaining local inferences in a chain-structured probabilistic model and test autoregressive models on locally observed Bayes-net variables. The target explicitly follows this locality account and instantiates it as path stitching in DAGs, adding generated-route, temperature, motif, and embedding analyses but offering no comparable theorem or matched causal isolation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Language Models Are Greedy Reasoners: A Systematic Formal Analysis of Chain-of-Thought
reviewed_competitors.difference: Saparov and He use formal first-order worlds to verify every GPT-3/InstructGPT deduction and find that individual steps are often correct while proof planning fails when alternatives must be explored. The target adapts the local-misstep versus planning distinction to a small trained path model, but its fixed DAG and complete edge exposure remove the proof-search and language-model conditions central to PrOntoQA.

reviewed_competitors.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
reviewed_competitors.difference: Dziri et al. decompose multiplication, logic puzzles, and dynamic programming into computation graphs and argue that LLM performance reflects linearized subgraph matching with compounding errors. The target constructs the graph explicitly and offers an embedding-distance readout for one minimal model, but does not causally distinguish pattern matching from a learned search algorithm or test natural-language LLMs.

reviewed_competitors.title: Dissecting Chain-of-Thought: Compositionality through In-Context Filtering and Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Li et al. give experimental and theoretical evidence that CoT decomposes in-context learning of composed MLPs into filtering and single-step learning, with sample-complexity consequences. The target's motif chains are a graph-structured analogue with explicit ghost-edge exemplars, but the evidence is one short empirical curve that already falls to roughly 30% at the maximum training length.

reviewed_competitors.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
reviewed_competitors.difference: Feng et al. use circuit complexity to separate immediate answers from constant-size autoregressive Transformers that generate derivations for arithmetic, equations, and dynamic programming, then add learning experiments. The target supplies a more inspectable navigation benchmark and empirical phenomena, but fixed-size curves cannot determine whether its gap comes from computational expressivity, intermediate supervision, or data locality.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Expressive Power of Transformers with Chain of Thought
reviewed_competitors.relationship: contemporaneous formal account of reasoning-token length
reviewed_competitors.difference: Merrill and Sabharwal characterize how logarithmic, linear, and polynomial numbers of intermediate decoding steps change decoder-only Transformer complexity classes, including graph connectivity motivation. The target measures chains of only one to six intermediate motifs and makes an empirical training-range claim; it does not connect path length to model size, computational class, or a compute-matched direct architecture.

reviewed_competitors.title: The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration
reviewed_competitors.difference: Holtzman et al. compare maximization and stochastic Transformer decoders on likelihood, human quality, diversity, and repetition and introduce nucleus sampling to avoid unreliable tails. It is not a graph-accuracy study, but it directly precedes and materially narrows the target's broad claim that a Transformer output accuracy-diversity tradeoff had never been quantified; the target's distinctive contribution is exact valid-path coverage under temperature.

reviewed_competitors.title: ALPINE: Unveiling The Planning Capability of Autoregressive Learning in Language Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: ALPINE also trains autoregressive Transformers on source-target path sequences, but mathematically constructs adjacency and reachability representations, analyzes gradient dynamics, identifies failure to learn transitive reachability, extracts the matrices from weights, and checks Blocksworld. It substantially overlaps the target's core abstraction while providing stronger formal and real-task support and a different, testable internal mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Transformer Reasoning Capabilities via Graph Algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sanford et al. classify graph tasks by realistic depth, width, and extra-token regimes, prove logarithmic depth necessary and sufficient for connectivity in their efficient regime, and benchmark Transformers against GNNs on GraphQA. The target instead stores one fixed graph in weights and emits paths; it offers detailed behavioral probes but no scaling hierarchy or graph-level OOD evaluation.

reviewed_competitors.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
reviewed_competitors.difference: Cabannes et al. identify specialized iteration heads in controlled tasks, trace their appearance at attention level, and measure transfer of the resulting CoT skill across tasks. The target's goal-current embedding rule is simpler and graph-specific but is a correlational surrogate of a reduced architecture, without the circuit tracking and transfer evidence used to support an actual iterative mechanism.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Far Can Transformers Reason? The Globality Barrier and Inductive Scratchpad
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later theory and intervention for length generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abbe et al. connect learnability to target globality, show that agnostic scratchpads need not help, and design inductive scratchpads that break the barrier and extrapolate up to six times training length on some tasks. The target documents failure immediately beyond its training range with ordinary path traces; it neither characterizes why the trace fails nor tests a scratchpad structured for OOD induction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Struggle to Learn to Search
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later direct graph-search stress test and mechanistic audit
reviewed_competitors.difference: Saparov et al. train small Transformers on effectively unlimited, shortcut-resistant graph-connectivity data, extract a parallel reachability-expansion computation graph, and find learning becomes harder with graph size even as parameters increase; in-context CoT does not remove the problem. This directly challenges extrapolation from the target's one 200-node memorized graph and provides stronger search controls and causal interpretability tooling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-head Transformers Provably Learn Symbolic Multi-step Reasoning via Gradient Descent
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later optimization theory for autoregressive path finding
reviewed_competitors.difference: Yang et al. analyze backward and forward path generation on unseen trees and prove that gradient descent trains one-layer multi-head Transformers whose heads specialize and coordinate across the two stages. The task is narrower than arbitrary DAG navigation, but it supplies optimization and generalization guarantees for the very phenomenon the target infers from attention maps and endpoint-pair accuracy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Provably Learn Chain-of-Thought Reasoning with Length Generalization
reviewed_competitors.difference: Huang et al. prove how algebraic state-tracking structure governs Transformer length generalization, identify attention concentration as a retrieval mechanism, and use recursive self-training to extend solvable lengths beyond the base model. This turns the target's qualitative hypothesis about training-length limits into formal, falsifiable conditions and demonstrates a route around the observed failure.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhang et al. use modular subnetwork introspection to find invariant subnetworks inside biased models and optimize Modular Risk Minimization for OOD performance. It directly connects sparse structure to generalization, whereas the reviewed work offers a more explicit paired causal test for constituent functions but does not test whether its modules improve OOD recombination.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sparse Interventions in Language Models with Differentiable Masking
reviewed_competitors.difference: De Cao et al. optimize sparse neuron interventions tied to changes in language-model output probabilities for subject-verb agreement and gender bias. The reviewed paper instead masks weights and tests paired subroutine selectivity plus complement behavior, broadening to vision but relying on synthetic odd-one-out labels and much heavier hyperparameter search.

reviewed_competitors.title: Circuit Compositions: Exploring Modular Structures in Transformer-Based Language Models

It tackles the reviewed paper's unanswered reuse question more directly, though in a narrow transformer/grammar setting and with circuit-level rather than fixed weight-subset modularity.

reviewed_competitors.title: Discovering Knowledge-Critical Subnetworks in Pretrained Language Models

It strengthens the preservation objective and scale relative to the reviewed study, but localizes knowledge collections rather than testing composition and reuse of constituent computations.

reviewed_competitors.relationship: direct prior on sparse attention patterns
reviewed_competitors.difference: Likhosherstov, Choromanski, and Weller show that a fixed self-attention module can approximate input-dependent sparse matrices with O(log N) hidden dimension using random projections. The reviewed paper specializes the idea to q-subset averaging, improves the q dependence with compressed-sensing certificates, and adds lower bounds against attention, dense, and recurrent models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Inductive Biases and Variable Creation in Self-Attention Mechanisms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Edelman et al. prove that bounded-norm single-head transformers represent sparse Boolean functions with sample complexity logarithmic in context length. The reviewed paper studies an explicit sequence-to-sequence retrieval average and worst-case architecture-size separations, but its own experiment does not supply an analogous sample-complexity theorem.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers Provably Learn Sparse Token Selection While Fully-Connected Nets Cannot
reviewed_competitors.relationship: later direct extension of sparse averaging
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang et al. explicitly build on this paper's sparse token-selection task, strengthen the fully connected lower bound to an average-case setting, and prove gradient-descent learning plus out-of-distribution length generalization. That addresses the reviewed paper's largest gap between a nonuniform representation construction and a learned inductive bias.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers, parallel computation, and logarithmic depth
reviewed_competitors.difference: Sanford, Hsu, and Telgarsky relate constant transformer depth to rounds of Massively Parallel Computation and obtain logarithmic-depth algorithms for broader tasks. It develops the multilayer side that is only heuristic for Match3 here and shows why a one-layer pairwise limitation should not be generalized directly to deep transformers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Separations in the Representational Capabilities of Transformers and Recurrent Architectures
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bhattamishra et al. use nearly orthogonal codes and communication reductions on index lookup, nearest neighbor, bounded Dyck, equality, and disjointness. reviewed_competitors.difference: Webb et al. already interpolate between independent and end-to-end ensemble training, show overparameterized failure, model dominance and deletion brittleness, and find intermediate coupling can be best. reviewed_competitors.title: Generalized Negative Correlation Learning for Deep Ensembling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Buschjäger et al. derive a twice-differentiable-loss bias-variance decomposition and a GNCL objective that smoothly interpolates between independent and joint training while discussing failure conditions. The reviewed paper gives a distinct loss-difference formulation, probability-averaged cross-entropy expression, beta>1 bound, and detailed collusion audit, but its generalized interpolation is not wholly new.

reviewed_competitors.title: DICE: Diversity in Deep Ensembles via Conditional Redundancy Adversarial Estimation
reviewed_competitors.difference: DICE explicitly retains individual classification losses while adversarially reducing conditionally redundant features and evaluates calibration, OOD detection, and co-distillation. It targets useful feature diversity rather than optimizing aggregate loss alone, offering the type of member-quality constraint absent from the reviewed joint objective.

reviewed_competitors.title: Repulsive Deep Ensembles are Bayesian
reviewed_competitors.difference: D'Angelo and Fortuin add kernelized repulsion in weight or function space to independently anchored posterior objectives and analyze the dynamics as a particle flow. This is genuine cross-member interaction with explicit per-member fit, unlike the reviewed aggregate-only loss whose cancellation directions are underconstrained.

reviewed_competitors.title: Diversity and Generalization in Neural Network Ensembles
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ortega et al. connect diversity to generalization for squared, cross-entropy, and 0-1 losses and study PAC-Bayesian ensemble objectives. The reviewed paper focuses instead on why training-set loss-derived disagreement can be pseudo-diversity and suggests worst-case bounds as a route forward.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Ensembles Work, But Are They Necessary?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abe et al. argue that many accuracy, robustness, and uncertainty gains of deep ensembles can be matched by a larger single model and are not explained by diversity alone. This reinforces the reviewed paper's warning against maximizing disagreement, while raising a capacity-normalized baseline that its joint-versus-independent study does not include.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Unified Theory of Diversity in Ensemble Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wood et al. derive exact bias-variance-diversity decompositions across many losses and explicitly argue for managing rather than maximizing diversity. Their theory more carefully ties diversity to sampling and model fit; the reviewed paper contributes a concrete deep-joint-training pathology and diagnostics rather than the broadest unification.

reviewed_competitors.title: Pathologies of Predictive Diversity in Deep Ensembles
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abe et al. study nearly 600-1000 ensembles and find that diversity-promoting interventions often hurt high-capacity members and are dominated by simply scaling component quality. The reviewed paper provides a more specific aggregate-loss cancellation mechanism and beta path, while Abe et al. supply much broader evidence for the member-quality/diversity tradeoff.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multi-Symmetry Ensembles: Improving Diversity and Generalization via Opposing Symmetries
reviewed_competitors.difference: Loh et al. build complementary invariant and equivariant hypotheses through separate supervised/contrastive objectives and report transfer, uncertainty, and generalization gains. It illustrates that semantically structured complementarity can be useful even though unconstrained output-space disagreement near aggregate-only training is pathological.

reviewed_competitors.title: Sharpness-diversity tradeoff: improving flat ensembles with SharpBalance
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lu et al. show that sharpness reduction can collapse diversity and propose SharpBalance to preserve member separation while improving flatness, evaluating both ID and OOD performance. It operationalizes a multi-factor balance rather than treating aggregate training loss or raw diversity as sufficient.

reviewed_competitors.title: Promoting Ensemble Diversity with Interactive Bayesian Distributional Robustness for Fine-tuning Foundation Models
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pham et al. couple ensemble particles through a distributionally robust Bayesian objective for foundation-model fine-tuning and preserve individual posterior/robustness structure. Its VTAB and language results show that cross-member interaction can help when the interaction is constrained, a materially different regime from aggregate-only collusion.

reviewed_competitors.title: On Joint Regularization and Calibration in Deep Ensembles
reviewed_competitors.difference: Fredsgaard and Schmidt jointly tune weight decay, temperature, and early stopping for otherwise independently trained members and generally match or improve individual tuning, with overlapping holdouts as a compromise. This sharpens the reviewed conclusion: joint weight optimization can collude, while joint validation and hyperparameter selection can still be beneficial.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Jordan et al. show that alignment alone can leave activation-variance collapse and explicitly renormalize interpolated activations, including ImageNet-scale ResNets. That magnitude-sensitive failure complements and challenges LLFC's predominantly directional cosine analysis: feature directions can look aligned while scale still creates a loss barrier.

reviewed_competitors.difference: Lubana et al. ask whether connected models implement similar mechanisms under controlled latent interventions and show mechanistically dissimilar models cannot be linearly connected in their settings. reviewed_competitors.title: The Empirical Impact of Neural Parameter Symmetries, or Lack Thereof
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lim et al. construct architectures with reduced parameter symmetries and observe LMC even without alignment, experimentally separating symmetry from other causes. This weakens any reading that permutation-induced commutativity is a general explanation of LMC, while LLFC remains a more direct hidden-feature measurement in aligned and spawned models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Vanishing Feature: Diagnosing Model Merging and Beyond
reviewed_competitors.difference: Qu and Horvath identify layerwise attenuation of input-induced features as a cause of variance collapse and build Preserve-First Merging. Their magnitude-sensitive propagation analysis directly addresses a blind spot in direction-only LLFC diagnostics and turns the feature view into an intervention, albeit still mainly for vision models.

reviewed_competitors.title: Analyzing the Role of Permutation Invariance in Linear Mode Connectivity
reviewed_competitors.difference: Zhan et al. prove a width-dependent double-descent barrier and an O(m^-1/2) wide-regime rate for two-layer teacher-student ReLU networks, with learning-rate-induced sparsity effects. This is a more quantitative explanation of when permutations work than LLFC's low-rank conjecture, but it does not resolve deep-network feature paths.

Their own evidence remains limited to small vision benchmarks and large width multipliers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Second Order PAC-Bayesian Bounds for the Weighted Majority Vote
reviewed_competitors.difference: Masegosa et al. use tandem error and PAC-Bayesian estimation to optimize weighted majority votes, including a binary disagreement bound. Theisen et al. impose competence to halve the cited binary oracle expression and extend a related population inequality to K classes, but do not derive a finite-sample PAC-Bayes certificate or learning algorithm.

reviewed_competitors.title: Diversity and Generalization in Neural Network Ensembles
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ortega et al. give diversity decompositions across squared, cross-entropy, and zero-one losses and both averaging and weighted voting. Theisen et al. narrow to classification error and majority vote but introduce relative normalization, competence, and the interpolation-focused empirical diagnosis.

reviewed_competitors.title: Deep Ensembles Work, But Are They Necessary?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Abe et al. compare deep ensembles with accuracy-matched larger single networks and find that uncertainty and shift benefits can be replicated by one larger model. Theisen et al. instead diagnose relative classification-error gain using DER across broader ensemble families, without matching total parameters, inference cost, or compute.

reviewed_competitors.title: Are Ensembles Getting Better all the Time?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mattei and Garreau characterize when expected ensemble loss decreases monotonically with member count: convex losses always improve for exchangeable members, whereas nonconvex metrics depend on member quality. That directly studies adding classifiers, while Theisen et al. compare an ideal distribution-level majority vote to average member error through competence and disagreement.

reviewed_competitors.title: How Good is a Single Basin?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Lion et al. intervene on loss-landscape connectivity and show same-basin ensembles underperform multi-basin deep ensembles unless distilled from other basins. It probes where functional diversity comes from; Theisen et al. measure when hard-label disagreement is large enough relative to error, without resolving basin structure.

reviewed_competitors.title: How many classifiers do we need?
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct successor and strongest theoretical competitor
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kim et al. add polarization, finite-member corrections, restricted-entropy bounds, and asymptotic disagreement laws that predict larger-ensemble performance from smaller ensembles. It directly addresses Theisen et al.'s unexplained architecture-dependent slopes and practical ensemble-size question while retaining their competence framework.

reviewed_competitors.title: No Free Lunch From Random Feature Ensembles: Scaling Laws and Near-Optimality Conditions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Ruben et al. prove that an optimally regularized single random-feature ridge model minimizes risk when total trainable parameters are fixed, then test analogous CNN and transformer tradeoffs. Theisen et al. diagnose improvement over an average same-capacity constituent and therefore do not answer whether ensembling beats allocating the same total budget to one larger model.

reviewed_competitors.title: Do Deep Ensembles Actually Capture Uncertainty in Graph Neural Networks?
reviewed_competitors.difference: Vieira et al. report little gain and epistemic collapse across seven graph datasets because independently trained GNNs converge to functionally similar predictions. This supplies a 2026 application-level failure case aligned with low disagreement, but evaluates uncertainty as well as accuracy in graph learning rather than proving general majority-vote bounds.

reviewed_competitors.title: Understanding Adaptive, Multiscale Temporal Integration In Deep Speech Recognition Systems
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Direct methodological and conceptual predecessor from the same research lineage.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Keshishian et al. use temporal context invariance and speech stretching/compression to estimate compact windows and directly separate time-yoked from structure-yoked integration in DeepSpeech2, recurrent and convolutional systems. The reviewed paper adapts the question to discrete words and Transformers with simpler swaps, but its adjacent-boundary statistic is a less direct test of structural rescaling.

reviewed_competitors.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Closest prior word-swap and layerwise structure-perturbation method.
reviewed_competitors.difference: Alleman et al. already compare hidden representations under word/n-gram/span swaps and find sensitivity to larger spans and hierarchical phrase structure across Transformer layers. The reviewed paper's novelty is the distance-decay functional form and boundary-change summary, not input swapping or the broad claim that later layers integrate larger linguistic structures.

reviewed_competitors.title: Perturbed Masking: Parameter-free Probing for Analyzing and Interpreting BERT
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wu et al. infer inter-token dependencies by nested masking in BERT and validate induced syntactic structure. It is architecture-specific to masked models and not aimed at temporal decay, while the reviewed swap method works for causal and bidirectional hidden states but lacks a downstream structural validation of comparable strength.

reviewed_competitors.title: What Context Features Can Transformer Language Models Use?
reviewed_competitors.difference: O'Connor and Andreas retrain/evaluate models under controlled context ablations and quantify usable predictive information, finding that long context helps but much detailed structure contributes little. The reviewed paper offers cheap internal localization, but does not show that its long-tailed or structure-yoked hidden changes are usable for prediction.

reviewed_competitors.title: Quantifying Context Mixing in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mohebbi et al.'s Value Zeroing intervenes on value vectors inside each Transformer block and evaluates linguistic rationales, probing and faithfulness, avoiding raw-attention limitations. It is less architecture-agnostic but isolates layer-local context mixing more directly; the reviewed input swaps capture total downstream effects and enable cross-architecture comparisons.

reviewed_competitors.title: Token-wise Decomposition of Autoregressive Language Model Hidden States for Analyzing Model Predictions
reviewed_competitors.difference: Oh and Schuler derive an essentially exact one-forward-pass decomposition of final hidden states into input-token contributions and evaluate changes in next-word probability, directly tying influence to outputs. The reviewed paper requires many counterfactual forwards but applies at every layer and to non-Transformer architectures without deriving their internals.

reviewed_competitors.title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
reviewed_competitors.difference: Liu et al. move relevant evidence through long contexts and show U-shaped positional performance on retrieval and multi-document QA. This demonstrates that an LLM can accept and internally react to distant tokens yet fail to use them robustly, providing the behavioral validation axis absent from the reviewed hidden-window study.

reviewed_competitors.title: RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?
reviewed_competitors.difference: RULER evaluates retrieval, multi-hop tracing and aggregation over configurable lengths in 17 models and finds advertised windows overstate usable context. It measures successful computation rather than hidden sensitivity; combining its length curves with the reviewed layer profiles would test whether heavy tails predict real effective context.

reviewed_competitors.title: Transformers need glasses! Information over-squashing in language tasks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Barbero et al. prove decoder-only Transformers can map distinct inputs to arbitrarily close final-token representations and empirically connect lost sensitivity to counting/copying errors. This supplies task-relevant failure theory for the same broad phenomenon that the reviewed perturbation curves describe empirically.

reviewed_competitors.title: Jacobian Scopes: token-level causal attributions in LLMs
reviewed_competitors.difference: Jacobian Scopes uses local input-output Jacobians to quantify how context tokens affect predictions and exposes signed/directional causal structure around a prompt. It requires gradients and a local linearization, whereas the reviewed finite swap is gradient-free and captures nonlinear total effects but is much more expensive and not directly output-grounded.

reviewed_competitors.title: Multiscale temporal integration organizes hierarchical computation in human auditory cortex
reviewed_competitors.difference: Norman-Haignere et al. estimate sensory integration windows from intracranial recordings and find a roughly 50-400 ms hierarchy linked to acoustic versus category selectivity. The reviewed paper borrows the integration-window framing but measures word perturbations in hidden coordinates and performs no matched model-brain comparison.
reviewed_competitors.source_version: Nature Human Behaviour 2022 version of record

reviewed_competitors.title: Long-range and hierarchical language predictions in brains and algorithms
reviewed_competitors.difference: Caucheteux et al. map model representations to fMRI from 304 listeners and find that adding long-range forecast representations improves brain prediction with cortical forecasting hierarchies. It directly evaluates a model-brain relationship, while the reviewed paper offers a mechanistic model-only prediction about window shape and boundaries.

reviewed_competitors.title: Temporal integration in human auditory cortex is predominantly yoked to absolute time
reviewed_competitors.relationship: Current biological test of structure-yoked integration.
reviewed_competitors.difference: This later intracranial study validates its yoking metric on computational speech models but finds human auditory windows lengthen hierarchically while remaining mostly time-yoked (median structure-yoking about 0.04). It cautions against inferring biological structure yoking from the reviewed LLM boundary effects and supplies a stronger experimental test of that analogy.

reviewed_competitors.title: Path-SGD: Path-Normalized Optimization in Deep Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Neyshabur et al. precondition gradients using rescaling-invariant path geometry; the reviewed work selects a grouped l2 path penalty enabling convexification of wide parallel branches.

reviewed_competitors.title: Neural Networks are Convex Regularizers: Exact Polynomial-time Convex Optimization Formulations for Two-layer Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Pilanci and Ergen introduce activation-pattern convexification and block-l1 regularization for two layers; the reviewed paper adds a second nonlinear layer, sign enumeration, and path regularization.

reviewed_competitors.title: Global Optimality Beyond Two Layers: Training Deep ReLU Networks via Convex Programs
reviewed_competitors.difference: The predecessor convexifies constrained weight-decayed three-layer branches; path regularization removes those norm restrictions and permits richer hidden interactions, while retaining severe enumeration.

reviewed_competitors.title: Parallel Deep Neural Networks Have Zero Duality Gap
reviewed_competitors.difference: Wang, Ergen, and Pilanci prove deep parallel zero duality gap under sufficient width and suitable regularization; the reviewed paper relies on it for a future depth extension but only explicitly constructs three layers.

reviewed_competitors.title: Efficient Global Optimization of Two-layer ReLU Networks: Quadratic-time Algorithms and Adversarial Training
reviewed_competitors.difference: Bai et al. give ADMM and sampled-program guarantees in a shallower setting, closer to the heuristic sampled regime used empirically here.

reviewed_competitors.title: Optimal Sets and Solution Paths of ReLU Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Mishkin and Pilanci characterize optima, stationary points, pruning, and regularization paths for two-layer models; the reviewed work reaches deeper branches but not their full solution set.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convex Relaxations of ReLU Neural Networks Approximate Global Optima in Polynomial Time
reviewed_competitors.difference: Kim and Pilanci prove a logarithmic-factor polynomial approximation for random-data two-layer networks, trading depth and exactness for conventional tractability.

reviewed_competitors.title: Convex Formulations for Training Two-Layer ReLU Neural Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Prakhya et al. separate an exact completely positive convex formulation from its tractable SDP relaxation, highlighting that convex representation alone does not imply practical solution.

reviewed_competitors.title: A Convex Relaxation Approach to Generalization Analysis for Parallel Positively Homogeneous Networks
reviewed_competitors.difference: Tadipatri et al. connect parallel homogeneous ERM to convex prediction-space bounds and study population generalization, which the reviewed optimization-focused paper leaves open.

reviewed_competitors.title: Data Distributional Properties Drive Emergent In-Context Learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chan et al. introduce the same Omniglot sequence family and show that burstiness, many rare classes, and dynamic labels promote ICL, but stop around 500,000 steps and treat the emerged capability as persistent. The reviewed paper's main novelty is the much longer horizon and explicit ICL-versus-IWL trajectory.

reviewed_competitors.title: What needs to go right for an induction head? A mechanistic study of in-context learning circuits and their formation
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh et al. move to an ICL-required synthetic task and use activation interventions during training to causally study induction-head formation and subcircuits. That framework offers stronger circuit evidence than the reviewed paper's width and selective-decay proxies, but it does not itself study ICL-IWL replacement.

reviewed_competitors.title: Differential learning kinetics govern the transition from memorization to generalization during in-context learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: This work models memorizing and generalizing subcircuits as largely independent and derives their different learning rates plus a task-diversity scaling law that explains sharp and transient ICL transitions. It supplies quantitative theory for a competition the reviewed paper infers mainly from controlled curves.

reviewed_competitors.title: Competition Dynamics Shape Algorithmic Phases of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: Panwar and colleagues use a Markov-chain sequence model and decompose behavior into four retrieval or inference algorithms with unigram or bigram statistics, showing phase transitions as context and training scale vary. This makes transience an identifiable competition among algorithms rather than a binary evaluator crossover.

reviewed_competitors.title: Strategy Coopetition Explains the Emergence and Transience of In-Context Learning
reviewed_competitors.difference: The same research line identifies the late solution as context-constrained IWL, uses shared-subcircuit interventions, and argues that ICL and CIWL both compete and cooperate during emergence. It supersedes the reviewed paper's preliminary pure-IWL competition story with a hybrid asymptotic strategy and direct mechanistic evidence.

reviewed_competitors.title: An evolutionary perspective on modes of learning in Transformers
reviewed_competitors.difference: Singh and collaborators vary environmental stability and contextual cue reliability in sinusoid regression and Omniglot to predict whether ICL or IWL is favored, observing transitions in both directions. This generalizes the reviewed paper's class-count and Zipf interventions into a broader two-factor account of strategy selection.

reviewed_competitors.title: Reconciling In-Context and In-Weight Learning via Dual Representation Space Encoding
reviewed_competitors.difference: Chen et al. attribute ICL-IWL conflict partly to a shared encoding space and propose separate dual task and sample representation spaces, with theory and synthetic experiments aimed at retaining both capabilities. Their goal is architectural reconciliation rather than diagnosing a naturally transient phase.

reviewed_competitors.title: Training In-Context and In-Weights Mixtures Via Contrastive Context Sampling
reviewed_competitors.difference: Malu et al. train small LLMs with contexts spanning similarity levels so models retain stable mixtures and switch between ICL and IWL by relevance, avoiding collapse to memorization or label copying. It tackles the practical stable-mixture objective left open by the reviewed paper and validates beyond the synthetic Omniglot setting.
